title: Assessing the Spiritual Well-Being of Filipino Cancer Patients: A Nursing Perspective
abstract:
Cancer is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Philippines. It is a serious disease that can result in not just physical and psychosocial difficulties but also spiritual distress. Knowing Filipinos have a high reverence to God, this can affect their health-related behavior and responses to illness like cancer.

This study aimed to assess the spiritual well-being of Filipino adult cancer patients ages nineteen (19) to sixty (60) years old in a tertiary hospital. The objectives were: to determine the spiritual well-being of the patients (as measured by the Ideal and Personal states of Spiritual well-being and presence of Spiritual Dissonance); to determine the relationship between the spiritual well-being of the patients and the patient factors, and to describe the spiritual well-being experiences of the patients.

A descriptive correlational research was used. The results showed that the patients had the highest spiritual well-being in the Transcendental Domain which describes one’s relationship with God. Seven (7) out of the ninety (90) participants had spiritual dissonance which made them at possible risk for spiritual distress. Age, the type of cancer, and the treatment received had significant relationship with the patient’s spiritual well-being. Triangulation of qualitative data based on the patients’ response of the HOPE Questions was also done. Themes identified were “love of God, family, and friends”, “community affinity”, “fidelity to prayer”, “test of Faith”, and “empathy”.

In conclusion, Filipino adult cancer patients have high spiritual well-being despite the cancer burden. Havin this illness was a test of faith in which time had been an important component. At first, the patients experienced doubts their spiritual beliefs but eventually, with the acceptance of the illness comes a stronger faith in God. God, family, and friends had been their main source of strength, motivation, and hope. The religious community of the patients also helped develop the patient’s spiritual well-being through prayer and other spiritual acts, and by providing support to the patients.

In the presence of cancer where the body and mind go weak, the cancer patients rely on the spirit to pull him or her through. This is where nursing plays an important role. The therapeutic interpersonal process between a nurse and a patient can help the patient develop aspects of life that he or she deems important in his or her spiritual health. Nurses can provide spiritual care to the cancer patients by identifying their spiritual needs, praying with them, allowing them to practice their spiritual beliefs, and by empathizing with them.

title: The ASEAN Single VISA Scheme and Its Implications to Border Security in the Region: A Philippine Perspective
abstract:
The vision of the ASEAN Single Visa Scheme is to boost tourism in Southeast Asia with the hope of bolstering regional tourism business and investment through the influx of international travelers amongst ASEAN member states (AMS). However, security and sovereignty issues have hampered the discussions of a regional common visa. As a contribution to scholarly discussions in the security aspect of such a scheme, this thesis offers to answer how the ASEAN Single Visa will affect security governance in the Region, particularly in the Philippines. In addition, the questions regarding implications of the scheme on visa policy and border security situation of the Philippines, factors affecting the adoption, and measures necessary for the realization of the scheme were answered using quantitative and qualitative analyses in a sequential explanatory design.

By analyzing the Bureau of Immigration (BI) statistical data, key respondents' interviews from the BI, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and several AMS embassies particularly Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand, it was shown that there is a significant difference between visa-required and visa-free nationals on security-related violations in the country in relation to the current visa policy of the Philippines. It also revealed that (1) security and sovereignty; (2) the development of internal sharing mechanism; (3) support border control management; (4) synchronization of visa issuance systems; (5) human resource development; and (6) upgrades of infrastructure and technology of immigration agencies were factors hampering the realization of the ASEAN Single Visa scheme in the country.

In spite of this, key officials from the BI, DFA, and select embassies said that the single visa scheme would be beneficial to the Philippines and the Region. The ASEAN Single Visa scheme is set to bring about positive impact for ASEAN security governance as it intends to bolster closer inter-agency and regional cooperation between the Philippines and AMS. Thus, its implementation will become an impetus among AMS to work together to improve border management capabilities of the Region in the realization of the ASEAN Single Visa Scheme.

However, discussions regarding a common visa are hindered by concerns over security and sovereignty. This research investigates how the scheme affects security governance, specifically focusing on the Philippines. The study examines implications for Philippine visa policy and border security, factors affecting adoption, and necessary measures for realization.

Using a sequential explanatory design, the researcher utilized quantitative and qualitative analyses, including statistical data from the Bureau of Immigration and interviews with officials from the Bureau of Immigration, the Department of Foreign Affairs, and embassies from Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Findings show a significant difference between visa-required and visa-free nationals regarding security-related violations in the Philippines. Factors hampering the scheme include security and sovereignty concerns, the need for an internal sharing mechanism, requirements for border control management support, and the necessity of synchronizing visa issuance systems. Additionally, human resource development and upgrades to immigration infrastructure and technology are required.

Despite implementation complexities, stakeholders from the Bureau of Immigration, the Department of Foreign Affairs, and select embassies view the scheme as beneficial. Implementation is expected to improve ASEAN security governance by fostering inter-agency and regional cooperation. The study concludes the scheme will encourage ASEAN member states to work together, improving regional border management and balancing economic tourism benefits with security and sovereignty protections.

title: An Assessment of the Implementation of the ASEAN Cosmetic Product Notification Scheme: Focus on the Philippines
abstract:
Cosmetics as a consumer good is gaining an importance in the lifestyles of Association of Southeast Asian Nation (ASEAN) consumers. The experience of competition in ASEAN cosmetics has given impetus to contribute to the promotion of regional economic integration.

The aim of the study is to assess the benefits, outcome and impact of the regulatory scheme agreed by the ASEAN Consultative Committee on Standards and Quality-Cosmetic Product Working Group (ACCSQ-CPWG). The ASEAN Economic Ministers signed the Agreement on the ASEAN Harmonized Cosmetic Regulatory Scheme (AHCRS) at the 35th ASEAN Economic Ministers Meeting in Cambodia in September 2003. The objective of the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive (ACD) is to provide the framework for the harmonization and mutual recognition of the Standard, Technical Regulation and Conformity Assessment Procedures (STRACAP), to eliminate unnecessary Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT).

Through a questionnaire survey of key cosmetics industry players in the Philippines, the study generated primary data to analyze the impact of the ACD. The study also collected secondary data and information to support the analysis. The study obtained copies of relevant Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issuances, reports, slide presentations, and visited related websites on cosmetics. Library research was done to collect copies of ASEAN Secretariat Reports and minutes of the ASEAN Cosmetic Committee (ACC) meetings, standard source of industry information such as Euromonitor international. The study was supplemented by emails, non-structured interviews and communications with past and current delegates to ACCSQ-CPWG and/or ACCSQ-ACC.

The respondents in the survey confirmed significant milestones and accomplishments, benefits and impact after 10 years of implementing the cosmetic online Product Notification (PN, the e-Notification, by the Philippine FDA and the rest of the ASEAN Member State (AMS) National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs).

The study has the following conclusions:
a) The ACCSQ-CPWG successfully designed the ACD PN scheme to eliminate TBT.
b) ASEAN member countries through their respective NRAs have established online PN systems, which increased efficiency in processing time. The Philippine FDA instituted the most efficient e-Notification system in ASEAN.
c) The cosmetic industry sector was instrumental in ensuring ASEAN regulatory harmonization.
d) The cosmetic industry significantly benefited in terms of ease of doing business in the region and accessing the international market, advancing globalization.
e) Up to this time, cosmetics is one of the most developed and earliest among the successfully regulated industry in ASEAN, showcasing the benefits and advantages of harmonization of standards, procedures and regulatory mechanisms in ASEAN.
f) Consumers are the ultimate recipient of the benefits and advantages of the ACD PN System.
g) ASEAN harmonization of STRACAP is possible when the public and private sectors cooperate and collaborate to ensure that free trade is sustainable in the region.
h) Trade data and trends point towards sustained growth and development of the cosmetic industry sector and the ASEAN market.

By ensuring participation of the NRAs, the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC)-ACCSQ accomplished not only an increase in ASEAN trade in cosmetics, but also established a greater degree of assurance of consumer safety and welfare.

The study is recommending key points towards a proposed strategic action plan to further promote and achieve a Single Regulatory Regime for ASEAN on cosmetics. The proposed action plan will further sustain the initial gains during the 10 years of implementing the ACD PN.

By ensuring the participation of NRAs, the ASEAN Economic Community-ACCSQ has increased regional trade and established greater assurance regarding consumer safety and welfare. two:
The study addresses the growing importance of cosmetics in the lifestyles of consumers within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the resulting competition in the sector. This competition has acted as a catalyst for promoting regional economic integration. The central problem involves assessing the implementation of the regulatory framework designed to manage this growing market. Specifically, the research evaluates the benefits, outcomes, and impacts of the regulatory scheme agreed upon by the ASEAN Consultative Committee on Standards and Quality-Cosmetic Product Working Group (ACCSQ-CPWG). This scheme stems from the Agreement on the ASEAN Harmonized Cosmetic Regulatory Scheme (AHCRS), signed by ASEAN Economic Ministers in September 2003. The primary objective of the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive (ACD) is to establish a framework for the harmonization and mutual recognition of Standards, Technical Regulation and Conformity Assessment Procedures (STRACAP) to eliminate unnecessary Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT).

The research context is centered on the Philippines and its adherence to the ACD. To evaluate the effectiveness of the scheme, the author employed a mixed-methods approach to gather both primary and secondary data. Primary data was generated through a questionnaire survey distributed to key players within the Philippine cosmetics industry. Secondary data was collected through a variety of sources, including Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issuances, reports, slide presentations, and official websites. The researcher conducted library research to obtain ASEAN Secretariat Reports and minutes from ASEAN Cosmetic Committee (ACC) meetings, as well as industry information from sources like Euromonitor International. Furthermore, the study was supplemented by emails, non-structured interviews, and communications with former and current delegates to the ACCSQ-CPWG and/or ACCSQ-ACC.

The findings of the study reveal significant milestones and accomplishments following ten years of implementing the cosmetic online Product Notification (PN) system, also known as e-Notification, by the Philippine FDA and other ASEAN Member State National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs). The survey respondents confirmed that the ACD PN scheme successfully achieved its goal of eliminating Technical Barriers to Trade. A key finding is that ASEAN member countries have established online PN systems that have increased efficiency in processing times. Notably, the Philippine FDA was found to have instituted the most efficient e-Notification system within the ASEAN region.

The study also found that the cosmetic industry sector played an instrumental role in ensuring regulatory harmonization. As a result of these efforts, the industry has significantly benefited from increased ease of doing business within the region and improved access to international markets, which advances globalization. The research highlights that the cosmetics sector remains one of the most developed and earliest successfully regulated industries in ASEAN. This success showcases the advantages of harmonizing standards, procedures, and regulatory mechanisms. Ultimately, the study finds that consumers are the final recipients of the benefits provided by the ACD PN System.

The conclusions drawn from the research emphasize that ASEAN harmonization of STRACAP is achievable when the public and private sectors cooperate and collaborate to ensure sustainable free trade in the region. The study notes that trade data and trends indicate sustained growth and development for both the cosmetic industry sector and the broader ASEAN market. By ensuring the participation of NRAs, the ASEAN Economic Community-ACCSQ has achieved more than just an increase in regional trade; it has also established a greater degree of assurance regarding consumer safety and welfare.

Based on these findings, the study offers implications in the form of recommendations for a proposed strategic action plan. This plan is intended to further promote and achieve a Single Regulatory Regime for ASEAN cosmetics. The goal of this proposed action plan is to sustain the initial gains achieved during the first ten years of implementing the ACD PN system.

title: Patient Safety Culture Among Healthcare Provide RS in Ambulatory Healthcare Centers in a High-Income Arab Country
abstract:
Safety culture is one of the crucial cornerstones of healthcare quality and patient safety management worldwide. We conducted a patient safety culture survey in June 2016 among the healthcare providers in 38 ambulatory care centers in a high-income Arab country such as the United Arab Emirates particularly in the emirate of Abu Dhabi. Among the patient safety culture dimensions, the Nonpunitive Response to Error received the lowest rating (M=2.78) followed by Staffing (M=3.09) suggesting that these are priority areas for improvement. The organization had a high perception scores on Teamwork within Units (M=4.08), Organizational Learning—Continuous Improvement (M=3.98) and Management Support for Patient Safety (M=3.93) suggesting a strong potential towards improving the baseline of patient safety culture.

The study shows that there were statistically significant differences of patient safety culture according to professional experience, tenure in the center and in the type of profession in the Island Region, Middle Region and Eastern Region. There was statistically significant difference of patient safety culture according to the nature of patient contact in the Middle and Eastern Region ambulatory care centers. Also, patient safety grade and number of incidents reported showed significant difference according to region of ambulatory care centers.

The study suggests that there is punitive culture across all regional locations such that this may have resulted to low number of incident reporting or underreporting. However, there is a potential to improve the patient safety culture in the network of ambulatory care centers due to the high level of positive response in the teamwork within units, organizational learning and management supports as well as optimism shown in the patient safety grade ratings. This could be derived from the experiences of healthcare providers in international accreditation. These areas for improvement can be used to develop the structures and processes toward better patient safety outcomes.

This research examines the role of safety culture in healthcare quality and patient safety management within ambulatory healthcare centers in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The study aimed to identify the current state of patient safety culture among providers and determine which dimensions require improvement to enhance safety outcomes. Using a survey conducted in June 2016 across 38 ambulatory care centers, the research assessed various safety culture dimensions and analyzed differences in perceptions based on professional experience, tenure, profession, geographic region, nature of patient contact, patient safety grades, and the number of reported incidents.

The findings reveal a complex landscape where "Nonpunitive Response to Error" received the lowest mean rating (M=2.78), followed by "Staffing" (M=3.09), marking them as primary priorities for improvement. Conversely, high scores were found in "Teamwork within Units" (M=4.08), "Organizational Learning—Continuous Improvement" (M=3.98), and "Management Support for Patient Safety" (M=3.93). Significant differences in perceptions were observed based on professional experience, tenure, profession, and geographic location.

The study concludes that a pervasive punitive culture exists across all regions, which may lead to underreporting of errors. However, high levels of teamwork and management support provide a strong foundation for progress. To improve outcomes, administrators should focus on addressing staffing levels and fostering nonpunitive responses to error to encourage transparent incident reporting.

title: An Ode to Unheralded Heroism: The Volunteer Nurses’ Experiences in the Aftermath of Typhoon Haiyan
abstract: Disaster events are extraordinary healthcare practice settings. Healthcare provision in these scenarios require extensive competencies and adaptability from healthcare workers. Involvement in these efforts have increased, as supranational initiatives in disaster response has caused the influx of volunteer disaster healthcare workers. The purpose of this study was to explore the experiences of volunteer disaster nurses in the aftermath of typhoon Haiyan using Colaizzi's (1978) Model to gain an understanding on the experience. Nine volunteer nurses who served immediately after the typhoon hit the central Philippines in late 2013. with each representing specific fields of specialty within nursing practice, were selected purposively as participants. The study's findings yielded five themes: Motivation, Realities of the Volunteer Disaster Nurse Experience, Coping while Caring, Leaving a Mark, and A Journey towards Self-discovery. Motivation was the source of the decision to help. It was also the driving force for volunteers to go through the obstacles and cope effectively. Once this has been successfully achieved, the nurses gained learnings and reflections both as human beings and as health professionals which in turn, renewed their altruism. These findings can be used by healthcare workers. educators, and health policy-makers on the practical side to promote the well-being of disaster healthcare workers by being more cognizant to their problems, challenges, and motivations. The study's findings can also be a jumping point for more in-depth inquiries and/or investigations in other disaster settings.

title: Health Service Satisfaction of Animal Bite Victims in Siniloan, Laguna, Philippines: A Retrospective Study
abstract: Patient satisfaction is an important indicator of quality of care, providing useful insights for delivering efficient health care which meets the needs of the patients. What influences a person's health is the encounter between health care customer/patient and provider; therefore it is critical that this encounter be pleasant. This retrospective study of health service satisfaction of animal bite victims in Siniloan, Laguna from January to December 2015 was done to evaluate effectiveness of the health services of the rural health unit, measured using both quantitative (surveys) and qualitative (interviews) data. There were 244 survey respondents among the recorded 450 animal bite victims. The study showed that 15-year-old and below female students were the most common victims, the majority of which were bitten by dogs. Results revealed that the extent of knowledge and practices of animal bite victims ranges from excellent to very good with a mean range of 3.47-3.64, SD = 0.657-0.703. Animal bite victims generally are satisfied in terms of level of client satisfaction ranges from 3.33-3.52, SD= 0.624-0.766. Overall, Animal Bite victims were satisfied in terms of information, dissemination about rabies elimination program and extent of impact of human rabies elimination program with overall mean range of 3.30-3.45, SD= 0.621-0.759. Almost all variables had a very weak association in terms of association of socio-demographic profile (age, sex highest educational attainment and type of who bit the bite victims to the knowledge of rabies, practices on the prevention and control of rabies, client satisfaction, information dissemination about rabies elimination program and extent of impact of human rabies elimination program. It is recommended in this study the improvement of the control through health promotion campaign must be done to further strengthen the rabies control program. The study also recommended that in order to understand further the associate of the variables tested a higher statistical analysis should be done such as a regression modeling.

title: Work Preferences in Rural Health Job Posting Among Medical Interns in the Philippines
abstract: Timely empirical evidence is important in the success of health systems, and in health human resources in the Philippines, such evidence is necessary for informed policy making to address imbalances in the health workforce. This study provides qualitative and quantitative information on the preferences of newly graduated medical doctors regarding rural job postings. Key informant interviews and focus group discussions identified the roles of wages, equipment status, and presence of supervision as important factors in considering a rural job post. Discrete choice experiment results verified the relative value of supervision, location of family from the work area, and availability of career opportunities in the respondents' preferences to work in rural areas: respondents are willing to sacrifice significant salary for better levels of supervision, family location, and career opportunities, and uptake rates for job postings with these incentives also tend to significantly increase recruitment in rural job posts. Combinations of wage and high-impact non-wage incentives tend to produce the highest increases in uptake rates. Age, sex, and economic status do not appear to factor in the respondents' preferences, but those with rural backgrounds tend to value supervision and career opportunities more than their urban counterparts. Young graduates who came from rural backgrounds also tend to consider rural practice soon after graduation, suggesting rural job posting policies may focus on this specific cohort of medical graduates.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
The success of health systems depends on timely empirical evidence regarding health human resources. In the Philippines, data is needed to address medical workforce imbalances. This study investigates the preferences of newly graduated medical doctors regarding rural job postings to assist policymakers in designing recruitment strategies for a more equitable distribution of the workforce.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the research employed qualitative interviews and focus group discussions alongside a quantitative discrete choice experiment. Qualitative findings identified wages, medical equipment status, and supervision as critical factors. The quantitative results refined these findings, showing that supervision, proximity to family, and career opportunities are significant drivers for rural work. title: Occupational Health Safety Culture Among Cadet Seafarers in the Philippines
abstract: The maritime workplace remained to be one of the world's high risk occupations (Nielsen et al, 2013). Maritime standards, competencies. and health and safety policies and practices were proven to be inadequate in preventing work related injuries and accidents on board seafaring vessels. It was in this light that safety culture was adopted ill the shipping industry. The study aimed to compare the tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures among cadet seafarers using cross sectional design. A total of 116 respondents participated in the study (101 PMMA cadet seafarers, 2 maritime educators, 7 maritime officers, 5 seafarers and 1 maritime administrator). The study conducted a survey adopting the Shipboard Safety Culture Questionnaire (American Bureau of Shipping, Inc.), key informant interviews and a focus group discussion. Data gathered from KII and FGD were classified by themes. Computed chi square scores revealed no significant difference between the tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures in all eight safety factors. In conclusion, tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures yielded no significant difference, despite more reported unsafe work conditions/ acts and on board health injuries/ accidents in bulk vessel types. The study recommended coordinating with the International Maritime Organization in identifying and accrediting regional maritime groups to monitor health and safety practices on board; and to actively involve maritime schools, maritime training centers and shipping companies in revitalizing safety culture promotion and heightening safety practices in the work place.

one:
The maritime workplace is recognized as one of the high risk occupations in the world. Despite the existence of maritime standards, competencies, and various health and safety policies and practices, these measures have proven to be inadequate in preventing work related injuries and accidents on board seafaring vessels. Because of these ongoing challenges in preventing accidents, safety culture has been adopted within the shipping industry as a necessary framework. The research addresses the problem of how safety culture manifests in different maritime environments, specifically focusing on the comparison between tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures among cadet seafarers.

The context of this study is centered on the training and experiences of cadet seafarers in the Philippines. To investigate the differences in safety culture, the researcher employed a cross sectional design. The study involved a total of 116 respondents who provided the necessary data for the investigation. This participant group was composed of 101 PMMA cadet seafarers, 2 maritime educators, 7 maritime officers, 5 seafarers, and 1 maritime administrator. By including a diverse range of stakeholders, including students, educators, officers, and administrators, the study sought to capture a comprehensive view of the safety culture experienced by those entering the profession.

The methodology utilized a multi-faceted approach to data collection. The researcher adopted the Shipboard Safety Culture Questionnaire from the American Bureau of Shipping, Inc. to gather quantitative data. In addition to this survey, the study incorporated qualitative methods through key informant interviews and a focus group discussion. The data gathered from the key informant interviews and the focus group discussion were classified by themes to provide a deeper understanding of the qualitative aspects of safety culture. This combination of quantitative and qualitative methods allowed for a robust analysis of the safety culture factors present in both tanker and bulk shipboard environments.

The findings of the study revealed that there was no significant difference between the tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures across all eight safety factors, as indicated by the computed chi square scores. This result is particularly noteworthy because it stands in contrast to the reported realities of maritime operations. Even though there were more reported unsafe work conditions or acts and more reported on board health injuries and accidents in bulk vessel types, the safety culture scores did not show a significant statistical difference between the two vessel types. This suggests that while the physical outcomes and incidents may differ between tankers and bulk carriers, the underlying safety culture perceived by the respondents remained consistent across these environments.

The study concludes that tanker and bulk shipboard safety cultures yield no significant difference. The lack of a significant difference in safety culture scores, despite the higher frequency of accidents and unsafe conditions reported in bulk vessels, highlights a complex relationship between perceived safety culture and actual workplace incidents. The research emphasizes that the current state of safety culture among cadet seafarers does not vary significantly based on the type of vessel they are associated with, regardless of the differing levels of reported injuries and unsafe acts.

The implications of these findings suggest a need for systemic changes in how maritime safety is monitored and promoted. The study recommends coordinating with the International Maritime Organization to identify and accredit regional maritime groups that can monitor health and safety practices on board vessels. Furthermore, there is a recommendation to actively involve maritime schools, maritime training centers, and shipping companies in the process of revitalizing safety culture promotion. By heightening safety practices in the workplace through the collaboration of educational institutions and industry players, the maritime sector can work toward better preventing the injuries and accidents that current policies have failed to eliminate.

title: Evaluation of the Environmental Users' Fee System Among User Firms Within the Laguna de Bay Region
abstract:
The study attempted to evaluate the effect(s) of environmental user's fee system (EUFS) not only in the Laguna de Bay Region itself, but also among all stakeholders, particularly user firms. The user firms referred in this study are those establishments which use the environment as the recipient of their wastes in the form of water.

        The study attempted to establish a pulse monitor for the acceptance of the system by the user firms as a whole, and the individual polluters as well. This research also focused on EUFS' effects on the user firms' capacity to sustain their respective operations.

        The environmental user's fee system (EUFS) is a pilot program of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). Phase I of the program was implemented by LLDA in January 1997. During the launching stage of this EUFS, five (5) industrial sub-sectors were classified as critical lake polluters namely: food processing, piggeries and slaughterhouses, beverages, dyes and textile, and pulp paper. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) was the only parameter that was initially covered. In the succeeding phases of implementation, additional industrial sub-sectors were included such as food chain and restaurants, cluster dwelling and others. Consequently, total suspended solids (TSS) was added as a pollution parameter.

        The EUF system revealed both positive and negative effects on the user firms. Positive effects included: (I) optimization of water consumption through adoption of waste minimization and recycling activities; (ii) application of best practices to improve the firms' operations; and (iii) promotion of environmental protection awareness among the polluter firms. On the other hand, the policy's negative effects were: (I) construction of wastewater treatment facilities as an added investment; (ii) profits of the small medium scale firms were reduced; and (iii) production output or sales especially among the small-scale firms was also reduced.

        Furthermore, the study revealed that the positive effects of implementing EUFS far outweighed the negative effects. The study also recommends that the regulatory agencies concerned should consider amending some of their policies so that the negative effects. The study also recommends that the regulatory agencies concerned should consider amending some of their policies so that the negative effects of the program to the user firms, particularly small companies, could be addressed appropriately.

title: The Value of the Arts and Humanities to Science Outcomes in the Philippines: A report to the British Council on The Creative Turn in the Sciences project
abstract:
This report discusses interim findings from the Creative Turn in the Sciences project, in which we explore and describe the state of art and science activities and collaborations—what has been variously referred to as “sciart” or “artscience”—in the Philippines. We argue that creative, transformative science can be supported along multiple fronts by engagement with the arts and humanities. As such, our view of creative industries need not be limited to currently identified ranges of cultural products and services. Artists can access new sources of not only funding and support, but also knowledge and inspiration, through engaging artscience in their work. If one of the value propositions of the arts is that it can provide a service, we propose that the arts and humanities could productively offer their services to the science R&D community in novel and underexplored ways. Our main contribution is the SHARES framework for enabling arts and humanities contribution to science research and translation (section 4).

Based on our interviews, the arts only minimally influences science and tech R&D in the Philippines, but only because it is usually not usually afforded the opportunity to do it more regularly or more deeply, if at all. However, the arts and humanities can lead to transformative and creative science processes and outcomes, and there is a nascent artscience community of practice in the Philippines that could benefit from support. To this end, funders, professional research organizations, and educational institutions can contribute to enabling shares through a number of ways:

# Keep (or include) the Arts in the ST(R)EAM acronym
# Retrofit existing programs to include discussion on and practice in artscience
# Create opportunities for internships and real-world alternative learning activities
# Ringfence funding for artscience collaborations
# Provide mechanisms for long-term monitoring and evaluation
# Consider new forms of cultural work and new models for patronage
# Take the lead as coordinators and mentors
# Provide opportunities for both formal disciplinal dialogue and serendipitous interactions
# Strike while the iron is hot

In "The Value of the Arts and Humanities to Science Outcomes in the Philippines," Diego S. Maranan investigates how "artscience" collaborations can enhance scientific research, innovation, and economic resilience. The study addresses a lack of systematic engagement between the arts and the scientific research and development sector in the Philippines. While the Philippine Creative Industries Development Act aims to bolster the creative economy, current frameworks often focus on cultural goods rather than the intersection of creativity and scientific inquiry. Additionally, the "Arts" component in STEAM education is frequently sidelined or redefined.

Using qualitative methodology involving grounded theory and narrative inquiry, the researcher conducted an Open Call and performed semi-structured interviews with 30 individuals. The findings reveal a nascent community of artscience practice where practitioners use creative inquiry to bridge the "two cultures" of science and art. Practitioners are motivated by the desire to explore new forms of knowledge and find novel ways to communicate complex scientific ideas. However, artscience remains minimally influential in Philippine science R&D due to a lack of specialized funding, limited interdisciplinary training, and poor coordination between research organizations and the arts.

The report concludes that artscience can provide transformative value to induction-based inquiry, technology transfer, and public engagement. The author proposes the SHARES framework and recommends retrofitting STEAM programs, ringfencing specific funding for collaborations, and having research organizations act as coordinators to facilitate dialogue between scientists and artists.

A case study of the author's work with the UK-based CogNovo program demonstrates how transdisciplinary research, such as wearable technology for body awareness, can lead to practical applications in neurophysiology and rehabilitation.

The report, "The Value of the Arts and Humanities to Science Outcomes in the Philippines," authored by Diego S. Maranan, investigates the potential for "artscience" collaborations to enhance scientific research, innovation, and economic resilience within the Philippine context. Prepared for the British Council, the study seeks to move beyond traditional definitions of the creative economy to explore how the arts and humanities can serve as a strategic tool for future-proofing the creative sector and enriching scientific culture.

The problem addressed is the lack of systematic engagement and recognition of the arts and humanities within the scientific research and development (R&D) sector in the Philippines. While the Philippine Creative Industries Development Act seeks to bolster the creative economy, current frameworks often focus on the production of cultural goods and services rather than the intersection of creativity and scientific inquiry. The author notes that while artscience is well-documented in the Global North, the Philippine landscape remains largely unmapped, with existing literature showing a significant gap in peer-reviewed research specifically addressing art-science convergence in the country.

The context of the study is shaped by the recent disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, which highlighted the vulnerability of the creative sector. The report suggests that fostering a more robust relationship between the arts and sciences can build systemic resilience. Furthermore, the report notes that while "STEAM" education (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics) is discussed in the Philippines, the "Arts" component is frequently sidelined or redefined to mean other sectors, such as agriculture or fisheries, rather than the humanities and creative practices.

The methodology employed is a qualitative study using grounded theory and narrative inquiry. The research team conducted an Open Call to identify artscience initiatives in the Philippines, which resulted in 89 written contributions. From these, 30 individuals were selected through purposive sampling based on criteria of teleological aim, potential impact (scientific, economic, or educational), and notability. The researchers then conducted 1.5-hour semi-structured interviews to explore the motivations, conceptual framings, and enablers/hindrances experienced by these practitioners.

The findings reveal a nascent but existing community of artscience practice in the Philippines. The study identifies several key themes:
- Conceptual Framing: Practitioners view artscience as a way to bridge the "two cultures" of science and art, using creative inquiry to address fundamental and applied scientific questions.
- Motivators: Practitioners are driven by the desire to explore new forms of knowledge, create transformative outcomes, and find novel ways to communicate complex scientific ideas.
- Enablers and Hindrances: The study finds that while there is significant interest, artscience is minimally influential in Philippine science R&D because practitioners are often not afforded the opportunity for regular or deep engagement. Key hindrances include a lack of specialized funding, limited interdisciplinary training, and a lack of coordination between professional research organizations and the arts.

The report includes a case study of the author’s own work enabled by the UK-based CogNovo program, which demonstrates how transdisciplinary research—such as the development of "Haplós" (a wearable technology for body awareness) and "Bisensorial" (multisensory biofeedback)—can lead to practical applications in neurophysiology, psychology, and rehabilitation.

The report concludes that artscience can provide transformative value to science processes, including induction-based inquiry, technology transfer, public engagement, and even scientific revolutions. To facilitate this, the author proposes the SHARES framework (Support from the Humanities and the Arts for Radical Excellence in the Sciences).

The implications and recommendations are directed at several key stakeholders:
- Educators: Should maintain the "Arts" in STEAM, retrofit existing programs to include artscience practice, and create internship opportunities that bridge the two fields.
- Funders: Should ringfence specific funding for artscience collaborations, provide mechanisms for long-term monitoring and evaluation, and explore new models of patronage.
- Professional Research Organizations: Should act as coordinators and mentors, providing platforms for both formal disciplinary dialogue and serendipitous, informal interactions between scientists and artists.

Ultimately, the report argues that the arts and humanities are not merely decorative additions to science but are essential partners capable of driving innovation and providing new perspectives that can benefit the scientific community and the broader public.

The *KM4D Casebook: Sectoral and Thematic Knowledge Management at the National, Regional, and Global Levels* by Alexander G. Flor serves as an empirical companion to theoretical studies on Knowledge Management for Development (KM4D). The work is structured to transition students from abstract conceptualization to the practical application of knowledge management within the international development assistance sector.

**Problem**
The text identifies a significant structural problem in the global landscape: the persistence of deep-seated inequities between "center" and "periphery" nations. Despite the rise of Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs), which some argue have leveled the playing field, dominance relationships remain. In the realm of knowledge, these inequities are manifested through the "digital divide," where access to and control over information, data, and knowledge remains asymmetric. Furthermore, the author notes a gap in the development sector where, despite increased capacities for generating research and new technologies, there is a failure to effectively capture, share, and reuse this knowledge. This lack of effective knowledge management prevents research findings from being fully utilized to address critical global issues.

**Context**
The book is situated within the context of globalization and technological determinism. The author argues that globalization is a natural consequence of ICTs that have "killed distance," undermining national and regional boundaries. Within the Southeast Asian context, the text highlights a stark disparity in human development and ICT indicators. While countries like Singapore and Malaysia show high levels of development and ICT access, others like Lao PDR and Cambodia face significant poverty and low technological penetration. This context is further complicated by the "digital divide" within sectors, where the agricultural and rural development sectors are identified as the most information-poor, lagging far behind the business and industrial sectors.

**Method**
The book is a compilation of case studies derived from the author's personal engagement in various knowledge management initiatives between 2000 and 2018. These initiatives were conducted through various international and regional organizations, including the SEAMEO Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture (SEARCA), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and the Deutsche Gesellschaft fuer Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ). The methodology involves presenting field examples of how KM has been applied to specific development themes and sectors. The author utilizes various analytical frameworks, such as the "Stratframe Matrix," "Problematique Maps," and the "Delivery Systems Framework," to evaluate and design KM systems. The case studies cover a range of scales, from national programs to regional networks and global concepts.

**Findings**
The findings are organized into three parts: networks, sectoral applications, and thematic applications. In terms of networks, the author finds that decentralized networks are more sustainable and reciprocal than centralized ones. The failure of the ATEP-IMD Network is cited as an example of how centralized configurations can be short-lived. Regarding regional cooperation, the text explores "niche making," suggesting that ASEAN nations should focus on specific ICT competencies (such as hardware, software, or content) to remain competitive.

Sectoral findings highlight the application of KM in food security, natural resource management, climate change adaptation, and biodiversity. Thematic findings demonstrate the necessity of KM for indigenous peoples, agricultural research capacity development, and smallholder agriculture. A recurring finding is the correlation between high human development and high ICT indicators, reinforcing the idea that knowledge management is a critical tool for poverty reduction. The text also identifies that the most promising competencies for the future lie in the convergence of information science, computer science, and communication science.

**Conclusions**
The author concludes that knowledge management is the optimum solution for the international development assistance sector, provided it is implemented equitably. To achieve "horizontalization"—the reduction of vertical, asymmetric relationships between centers and peripheries—knowledge must be managed through non-hierarchical networks that promote self-reliance. The text also concludes that academic institutions must adapt to the rapid pace of technological change. The author warns against "parochial minds" and conservative academic traditions that allow curricula to become obsolete before they are even implemented. To remain globally competitive, educational systems must shift toward flexible, learner-centered paradigms, such as distance and open learning.

**Implications**
The implications of this work are both practical and strategic. For development practitioners, the book implies that KM must move beyond mere content management to include the management of the systems that carry content, effectively creating a "digital nervous system" for organizations. For policymakers in the ASEAN region, the text implies a need for regional cooperation and the establishment of de facto standards for knowledge capture and information exchange to make regional networks functional. Finally, for the academic sector, the work implies a radical need to redesign curricula to focus on the specific competencies required in a knowledge-based economy, particularly in the intersection of ICT and development (ICT4D).

abstract:

half:
The research titled "Fixing Information Disorder in Social Media" addresses the critical issue of information disorder facilitated by social media platforms, which can inadvertently amplify rumors and lead to the rapid spread of disinformation and misinformation. This study focuses on the early days of the global COVID-19 pandemic within the Philippine social media setting, specifically analyzing public Facebook posts and tweets from Filipinos during the first wave of the pandemic to understand how information disorder manifests during a global health crisis.

The methodology employs a multi-phase approach. First, researchers conduct a content analysis of posts and tweets containing COVID-19 keywords using a coding method based on the framework established by Wardle and Derakhshan (2017). Second, the researchers plan to fact-check the information to confirm the existence of information disorder and track its first occurrences in cyberspace. This timeline will be mapped against significant events, such as government announcements, mainstream media messages, and communications from organizations like the World Health Organization.

The study is guided by three research questions: identifying the specific types of information disorders committed during the pandemic, characterizing the actors engaging in these disorders, and gaining insights based on the characteristics of the entities publishing such posts. The ultimate goal is to promote smarter digital behavior through enhanced digital literacy, creating a body of knowledge to empower users and encourage responsible social media usage.

The researchers aim to create a framework or body of knowledge to empower users, inform the public, and encourage responsible social media usage. The research project "Re(Constructing Aging): An Online Exhibit on the Filipinos' Meanings of Aging" investigates how Filipinos construct the meaning of growing older to address challenges in designing environments for an aging population. The study moves beyond generalized views by focusing on specific cultural nuances and associations attributed to aging across different age groups within the Filipino population.

The project has three primary objectives: identifying the meanings and associations of aging across various age groups, analyzing these meanings through illustrations and artworks, and designing an online exhibit to host these artistic representations. The methodology employs a multi-stage approach integrating qualitative and participatory elements. Researchers utilize an online survey to gather data, while illustrations and artworks are used to capture visual and symbolic dimensions. The study design includes a participatory component where online exhibit visitors can contribute responses, and social media is used for data gathering and engaging volunteer artists.

Findings are presented through an online exhibit that serves as a platform for artworks representing how Filipinos construct the meaning of aging. This exhibit acts as both a display for artistic interpretations and a tool for ongoing data collection. The research provides essential cultural insights for designing age-friendly environments and social interventions. By using an online exhibit for both data presentation and gathering, the project offers an innovative approach to qualitative research to foster more inclusive and culturally sensitive designs.

The loss of biodiversity represents a significant threat that will undermine 80% of the Sustainable Development Goals targets. To address this crisis, the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services calls for a system-wide reorganization involving technological, economic, and social factors. This requires a fundamental shift in paradigms and values, moving away from a focus on economic growth toward traditional ways of relating to the world, such as fostering respect and protection for nature.

The work involves reframing the human place within a larger community of life. Older cultures often engage nonhuman life in social relationships, which can regulate behaviors to ensure abundance. Recent scientific discoveries have provided evidence of nonhuman sociality and subjective agencies, including the agency and communication of trees, plants, and animals.

To address these issues, the authors propose a workshop design aimed at cultivating more-than-human communities. Using a mixed-methods pretest-posttest survey design that incorporates qualitative approaches, the workshops focus on attuning the senses through poetry, dialogue, contemplative practices, and somatic practices. The goal is to foster environmental empathy and a deeper connection to the nonhuman world. Implementation has taken place at Cotehele, a National Trust site in Cornwall, England, with plans for future sites in the Philippines and Japan to test effectiveness across different geographic and cultural contexts.

The implications of this work suggest that addressing the ecological crisis requires more than just technological or economic adjustments. It requires a fundamental shift in how humans perceive their relationship with other living beings. By recognizing the agency and sociality of plants and animals, and by utilizing practices that attune the senses, it may be possible to develop new ways of living that support biodiversity. The project seeks to bridge the gap between scientific understanding of nonhuman agency and the practical, lived experience of human beings within their ecosystems. Through the cultivation of environmental empathy, the authors suggest that humans can move toward a more inclusive and sustainable way of existing within the larger community of life.

In "Connecting to the Life of Agta Community: Inspirations and Aspirations," Jandy Danzalan and Charlotte De Leon examine the intersection of indigenous knowledge and transformative education. The research addresses the tension between existing educational structures and the unique knowledge systems of indigenous communities, investigating how current policies impact these groups. To ensure the study was grounded in the specific social and cultural context of the Agta people, the researchers utilized an immersive participatory ethnographic method involving deep engagement, collaboration, and locale profiling.

The findings reveal a profound disconnect between how indigenous communities perceive their potential and the limitations imposed by current societal and educational structures. The authors observe that perceived barriers to progress could instead serve as foundational starting points if approached differently. The research posits that the Agta community possesses inherent strengths within their indigenous knowledge systems and practices (IKSPs). If these communities integrate their existing knowledge, they have the potential to transform into citizens with capabilities exceeding their current imaginations.

The authors conclude that there is an opportunity for a "real awakening" regarding governmental programs for Indigenous Peoples. They argue for a model where indigenous wisdom and formal schooling work in tandem rather than viewing indigenous knowledge as something to be replaced. This calls for an integrative, grass-rooted, and contextualized education revolution that moves away from top-down approaches to embrace localized realities.

title: Biodiversity in Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park: An Assessment of the Adequacy of Current Data
abstract:
This study is aimed at assessing the adequacy of available biodiversity data to support conversation efforts in Puerto Princesa Subterranean River national Park, Palawan Island, Philippines. Eleven studies which were undertaken fom 1993 to 2002 were reviewed.

        Systematic species inventories and baseline data generation had been the primary focus of previous works. A preliminary list of plants, mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and some invertebrates can be obtained from these studies. However, there are large gaps of knowledge on the basic biology and ecology of many key species.

Knowledge of the park's biodiversity is limited and is presently outdated.

        There is a critical need for a research agenda that is up-to-date, of high quality and not redundant.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
Jeanne Tabangay-Baldera’s study, "Biodiversity in Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park: An Assessment of the Adequacy of Current Data," examines whether existing information is sufficient for effective conservation management in the park on Palawan Island, Philippines. The research identifies a critical problem: current biodiversity data is both inadequate and outdated, failing to provide the comprehensive biological and ecological information required for modern conservation planning.

Using a review method, the study evaluated eleven specific studies conducted between 1993 and 2002 to determine the scope of gathered information and identify significant voids. The findings indicate that previous research primarily focused on systematic species inventories and baseline data. These studies successfully compiled preliminary lists for several taxonomic groups, including plants, mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles, and certain invertebrates, providing a foundational starting point for understanding species within the park.

However, the review reveals substantial deficiencies. While species lists exist, there are large gaps regarding the basic biology and ecology of many key species, such as how they interact with their environment or respond to changing conditions. Because the reviewed studies were conducted over a decade prior to the assessment, the author concludes the data is insufficient for long-term conservation strategies. The study emphasizes the need for a new research agenda that prioritizes up-to-date, high-quality, and non-redundant research focused on filling these ecological knowledge gaps.

There is a clear disconnect between the need for detailed ecological understanding and the current availability of such information.

This proposed agenda must prioritize research that is up-to-date, high quality, and non-redundant. Rather than simply repeating previous inventories, future efforts should focus on filling the identified gaps in biological and ecological knowledge. Establishing this high-quality data framework is essential for ensuring that conservation efforts in the park are based on accurate, contemporary scientific evidence.

title: Archiving as Artistic and Personal Practice: Tools, Methods, Examples, and Learning Resources
abstract:
This presentation was given at the Philippine Documentary Heritage Webinar Series: Digital Technology and Documentary Heritage. See https://www.facebook.com/PHDHDigitalRepository/videos/2798957150400534 for the full video of the presentation. See also:

faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In "Archiving as Artistic and Personal Practice: Tools, Methods, Examples, and Learning Resources," Diego S. Maranan, PhD, explores archiving as a multifaceted spectrum that extends beyond traditional institutional frameworks. Maranan positions archiving at the intersection of information science and creative practice, distinguishing between archiving for administrative, academic, or expressive and speculative goals.

The methodology categorizes archiving into two main streams: institutional and personal/artistic. Institutional examples, such as the UPOU Institutional Repository and the COVID-19 Tech Database, provide stability and academic rigor. In contrast, artistic archiving serves as a medium for exploring complex themes. Examples include Ēngines of Ēternity, which uses biological metaphors for cultural immortality, and OpenSourceDance.org, which engages with cultural movements and copyright.

Maranan identifies specific digital tools for these distinct needs. For organizational and personal use, tools like Airtable, Notion, and Evernote are highlighted. For formal or institutional purposes, the presentation recommends DSpace, Zenodo, and Mukurtu. DSpace is noted for its compliance with self-archiving and indexing, Zenodo for its community support, and Mukurtu for its cultural significance in serving as a repository for sacred materials.

The work concludes that archiving is not a monolithic activity. The choice of method is tied to the archivist's intent, whether managing data or exploring human themes. This framework suggests that both information professionals and artists can benefit from these diverse methods to contribute to cultural memory.

In the presentation "Archiving as Artistic and Personal Practice: Tools, Methods, Examples, and Learning Resources," Diego S. Maranan, PhD, explores archiving as a multifaceted practice that extends beyond traditional institutional frameworks. Maranan positions archiving as a spectrum of activities that can be simultaneously institutional, immediate, pragmatic, personal, speculative, and artistic. This work sits at the intersection of information science and creative practice, distinguishing between archiving for administrative and academic purposes and archiving for expressive or speculative goals.

The methodology involves categorizing archiving practices into two main streams: institutional and personal/artistic. Institutional examples include the UPOU Institutional Repository, the BAMS Helpdesk System, and the COVID-19 Tech Database. Personal and artistic examples include the Ed Maranan Digital Archive, OpenSourceDance.org, ApologyGrove.org, I’m Sorry Because It’s Useful, and the transdisciplinary project Ēngines of Ēternity.

The findings illustrate how these different streams serve distinct functions. Institutional archiving provides stability and academic rigor, such as the UPOU repository which supports student research and provides stable references. Conversely, artistic archiving serves as a medium for exploring complex themes. For example, Ēngines of Ēternity uses biological phenomena like DNA repair as metaphors for cultural immortality, while OpenSourceDance.org and ApologyGrove.org engage with cultural movements, legalities like copyright, and personal expression.

Maranan identifies specific digital tools tailored to these different needs. For organizational and personal use, tools such as Airtable, Notion, and Evernote (combined with Postach.io) are highlighted. For formal or institutional purposes, the presentation recommends DSpace, Zenodo, and Mukurtu. DSpace is noted for its compliance with self-archiving requirements and Google Scholar indexing, while Zenodo is recognized for its community support and documentation. Mukurtu is specifically highlighted for its cultural significance, having been designed for the Warumungu people of Australia to serve as a "dilly bag" for sacred materials. Sanity.io is also listed as a tool.

The presentation concludes that archiving is not a monolithic activity but a spectrum of practices. The choice of tool and method is deeply tied to the archivist's intent, whether managing institutional data or exploring human themes through art. The presentation "Haplós: Structured Vibrotactile Stimulation for Embodied Learning" by Diego S. Maranan explores the intersection of computing science, contemporary dance, and somaesthetics. The work focuses on developing wearable technology designed to enhance body awareness and transform the felt experience of the body (the soma).

The core problem addressed is the "disconnected self," a state where individuals may not feel whole or comfortable sensing their own bodies. This can manifest in various ways, ranging from general lack of body awareness to clinical conditions such as body dysmorphia, depersonalization, or changes in the perception of body size and shape. The research seeks to address these issues by providing a technological means to "fill in the gaps" in bodily awareness.

The context for this research is rooted in somaesthetics and somatic practices, specifically the Feldenkrais Method. The Feldenkrais Method is a sensorimotor intervention that emphasizes learning through gentle movement, curiosity, and the perception of "just noticeable differences" to refine the self-image and motor behavior. The presentation also draws on Shusterman’s somaesthetics and Sally Dean’s somatic costumes to frame the body not just as an object of external perception, but as a "living, self-sensing, internalized perception of oneself."

The method employed is a design research process focused on creating Haplós, a wearable vibrotactile technology. The development involved iterative prototyping of various interfaces, including custom-built undergarments, modified back support braces, and clothing with integrated components. The technical implementation involved using microcontrollers (such as Arduino), motors, and conductive thread or wires to deliver vibrotactile stimuli. The research also considers the psychophysical aspects of stimulation, referencing the Weber-Fechner Law and Stevens’ power law regarding how humans perceive stimulus intensity. The goal was to create a non-intrusive, structured way to deliver tactile input that mimics the learning principles of the Feldenkrais Method, such as using oscillation and bilateral symmetry to facilitate movement choices and awareness.

Findings from evaluation workshops and preliminary studies indicate that Haplós can measurably increase bodily awareness. Participants in public demonstrations reported feeling "more of myself" and experiencing a "sharper image" of their body, specifically noting increased sensitivity to the location of their back and the contact between their body and the floor. The technology appears to increase the resolution with which a person can feel their own body. Furthermore, the presentation cites research suggesting that vibrotactile and electrical stimulation can induce neuroplastic changes in the primary motor cortex. A specific study mentioned regarding food cravings showed that an experimental group wearing a body vest with motors experienced a significantly lower frequency of chocolate cravings compared to a control group, suggesting potential for neuroadaptive therapies.

In conclusion, the research suggests that Haplós and similar RE/ME (re-me) patterns can serve as aids for enhancing self-monitoring and proprioceptive/motor awareness. The technology functions as a stimulus that is more targeted and potentially less invasive than Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS). The study concludes that subtlety and first-person approaches are critical in somatic technologies.

The implications of this work are broad, spanning medical, aesthetic, and everyday applications. Potential uses include individualized neuroadaptive therapies for managing intrusive thoughts or food cravings, stroke rehabilitation, and improving fine motor skills or addressing hemineglect. It also holds promise for treating chronic pain, phantom limb sensations, and aiding in meditation or mindfulness. Beyond clinical use, the technology has implications for musical and sensory pleasure, communication/alarms, and remote presence, ultimately aiming to bridge the gap between the physical body and the felt experience of the self.

title: Student Co-Creation in an Online University: successes, failures, and how to move forward
abstract:
I embark on a Digital Collective project in 2018 to engage students and other stake holders to co-create knowledge in a learning platform and tap the full potential of open educational practice at the University of the Philippines Open University. The project tried to co-create OERs with students and alumni to explore the idea of building an online learning community as the foundation over which co-creation was to be conducted. I recruited volunteers from UPOU’s Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program to join me in the project, which ran for much of 2018. The purpose of this auto-ethnographic study is to assess and reflect on the strengths and weaknesses of how the project was conducted. These preliminary findings using auto-ethnography can hopefully help the University in drawing up a plan that can effectively build this online community.

Key themes were identified as factors for the project’s success. Through self-reflection, review of project notes, and a group discussion with some participants with respect to these themes, participation, and output can be attributed to setting clear goals for participants, level of incorporation into the curriculum, institutional support, and adopting an appropriate method of organization. The data suggest a more defined approach following a community of practice model rather than that of a learning community, as these may lead to not just improved project management and productivity, but also less dependency on any formal ties with the curriculum.

title: On Benchmarking for Crowdsourcing and Future of Work Platforms
abstract:
Online crowdsourcing platforms have proliferated over the last few years and cover a number of important domains, these platforms include from worker-task platforms such Amazon Mechanical Turk, worker-forhire platforms such as TaskRabbit to specialized platforms with specific tasks such as ridesharing like Uber, Lyft, Ola etc. An increasing proportion of human workforce will be employed by these platforms in the near future. The crowd sourcing community has done yeoman’s work in designing effective algorithms for various key components, such as incentive design, task assignment and quality control. Given the increasing importance of these crowdsourcing platforms, it is now time to design mechanisms so that it is easier to evaluate the effectiveness of these platforms. Specifically, we advocate developing benchmarks for crowdsourcing research.

Benchmarks often identify important issues for the community to focus and improve upon. This has played a key role in the development of research domains as diverse as databases and deep learning. We believe that developing appropriate benchmarks for crowdsourcing will ignite further innovations.
However, crowdsourcing – and future of work, in general – is a very diverse field that makes developing benchmarks much more challenging. Substantial effort is needed that spans across developing benchmarks for datasets, metrics, algorithms, platforms and so on. In this article, we initiate some discussion into this important problem and issue a call-to-arms for the community to work on this important initiative.

The authors identify a lack of standardized benchmarks as a primary problem, which prevents fair comparison of algorithms and obscures research directions. The field is currently fragmented across disciplines, and the inherent diversity of FoW makes creating universal benchmarks difficult. To resolve this, the authors propose a comprehensive taxonomy for benchmarks that includes metrics for accuracy, efficiency, diverse datasets, platform simulations, and organized competitions. They categorize necessary metrics into three stakeholder groups: platforms, workers, and tasks. Platform metrics should include crowd size, diversity, and efficiency, while worker metrics should include expertise and motivation. Task metrics should focus on accuracy, cost-benefit tradeoffs, and fairness.

The authors suggest developing synthetic benchmarking data to provide the statistical clarity that real-world datasets often lack. They conclude by identifying research challenges, such as incorporating qualitative human factors like fairness, the complexity of multi-objective optimization, and the need to evaluate human-AI interactions. Establishing this ecosystem would allow the community to transition toward a cohesive era of innovation.

A successful benchmark should include metrics for accuracy and efficiency, diverse datasets, platform simulations, reference implementations, open-source academic platforms, and organized competitions. They categorize necessary metrics into three stakeholder groups: platforms, workers, and tasks. Platform metrics should include crowd size, diversity, participation rates, worker skill distribution, task complexity, efficiency (latency and throughput), reliability, robustness, and usability. Worker metrics should move beyond task approval rates to include expertise, motivation, and worker-worker affinity. Task and requestor metrics should focus on accuracy, cost-benefit tradeoffs, completion rates, and fairness.

Regarding data, the authors suggest that while real-world datasets are valuable, they often lack the statistical clarity required for rigorous testing. Therefore, they propose developing synthetic benchmarking data. For workers, this data should incorporate distributions for expertise, preferences, and activeness. For tasks, it should reflect varying categories, difficulty, budgets, completion times, and required response counts.

The authors conclude by identifying several research challenges, including the difficulty of incorporating qualitative human factors like fairness and satisfaction into quantitative metrics. They also note the computational complexity of multi-objective optimization, the need for benchmarks that evaluate human-AI interactions, and the difficulty of ensuring reproducibility given the volatility of human behavior. Finally, they highlight the need for mechanisms to detect adversarial behavior and methods to generate synthetic data that accurately reflects real-world distributions. Establishing this benchmarking ecosystem would allow the community to transition from fragmented studies to a cohesive era of innovation, providing industry with reliable tools and ensuring the social dimensions of digital labor receive scientific rigor.

The article "On Benchmarking for Crowdsourcing and Future of Work Platforms" addresses the critical need for standardized evaluation mechanisms within the rapidly expanding field of online crowdsourcing and the "Future of Work" (FoW). As platforms ranging from Amazon Mechanical Turk to Uber become integral to the global workforce, the authors argue that the research community must move beyond developing isolated algorithms for specific components and instead adopt a holistic framework for evaluating platform effectiveness.

The problem identified by the authors is the lack of standardized benchmarks, which hinders the ability to fairly compare competing algorithms and identify the most promising research directions. While the crowdsourcing community has made significant strides in incentive design, task assignment, and quality control, the field remains highly fragmented. Research is conducted across diverse disciplines, including computer science, psychology, and management, which can lead to a duplication of efforts or the development of incompatible outcomes. Furthermore, the inherent diversity of FoW—spanning various domains and involving multiple stakeholders with conflicting objectives—makes the creation of universal benchmarks significantly more difficult than in more established fields like databases or deep learning.

To address this, the authors propose a comprehensive taxonomy for benchmarks, suggesting that a successful benchmark must encompass more than just datasets. They identify several essential dimensions: metrics to measure accuracy and efficiency; diverse datasets covering various task types; platform simulations and synthetic datasets to model worker and task dynamics; reference implementations to allow for standardized comparisons; open-source academic platforms to facilitate prototyping; and organized competitions to drive innovation.

The authors categorize the necessary metrics into three primary stakeholder groups: platforms, workers, and tasks. For platforms, they suggest measuring crowd size, diversity, and participation rates, as well as worker skill distribution and task complexity. They also emphasize the importance of efficiency metrics like latency and throughput, as well as platform reliability, robustness against adversaries, and user interface usability. For workers, the authors advocate for a holistic approach that moves beyond simple task approval rates to include human factors such as skill/expertise levels, motivation (both intrinsic and extrinsic), and group-based factors like worker-worker affinity. For tasks and requestors, they highlight the importance of accuracy, cost-benefit tradeoffs, completion rates, and fairness-related metrics to ensure equitable treatment of workers.

Regarding benchmarking data, the authors note that while real-world datasets are valuable, they often lack the statistical clarity needed for rigorous testing and may not represent worst-case scenarios. Consequently, they propose the development of synthetic benchmarking data. For workers, this data should incorporate distributions for expertise, task preferences, and activeness. For tasks, the data should reflect varying categories, difficulty levels, budgets, completion times, and the required number of worker responses.

The article concludes by outlining several research directions and challenges for the community. Developing benchmarks that are broadly applicable across academia and industry is a primary concern, as is ensuring these benchmarks are widely accepted by all stakeholders. The authors highlight the difficulty of incorporating qualitative human factors—such as fairness, equity, and satisfaction—into quantitative metrics. They also note the computational complexity of handling multi-objective optimization problems where multiple metrics must be satisfied simultaneously. Additionally, the rise of AI agents requires benchmarks that can evaluate human-AI interactions, and the inherent volatility of human behavior necessitates methods to ensure the reproducibility of results. Finally, the authors emphasize the need for robust mechanisms to detect adversarial behavior and the development of sophisticated methods for generating synthetic data that accurately reflects real-world distributions.

The implications of this work are significant for the future of the field. By establishing a standardized benchmarking ecosystem, the research community can transition from fragmented, component-specific studies to a more cohesive and accelerated era of innovation. Such a framework would allow researchers to confidently claim state-of-the-art performance, provide industry with reliable evaluation tools, and ensure that the social and human dimensions of the future of work are given the scientific rigor they require. The authors issue a "call-to-arms," urging the community to prioritize these benchmarking initiatives to shape the future of digital labor.
