title: User group analytics: hypothesis generation and exploratory analysis of user data
abstract: User data is becoming increasingly available in multiple domains ranging from the social Web to retail store receipts. User data is described by user demographics (e.g. age, gender, occupation) and user actions (e.g. rating a movie, publishing a paper, following a medical treatment). The analysis of user data is appealing to scientists who work on population studies, online marketing, recommendations, and large scale data analysis. User data analysis usually relies on identifying group-level behaviour such as “Asian women who publish regularly in databases.” Group analytics addresses peculiarities of user data such as noise and sparsity to enable insights. In this paper, we introduce a framework for user group analytics by developing several components which cover the life cycle of user groups. We provide two different analytical environments to support ‘hypothesis generation” and “exploratory analysis” on user groups. Experiments on data sets with different characteristics show the usability and efficiency of our group analytics framework.

The paper "User group analytics: hypothesis generation and exploratory analysis of user data" by Behrooz Omidvar Tehrani, Sihem Amer Yahia, and Ria Mae Borromeo addresses the challenge of analyzing large-scale user data to generate meaningful hypotheses. The authors argue that traditional methods fail to capture the complex, multi-dimensional nature of user behavior, leading to a lack of effective tools for identifying significant patterns and anomalies. This work responds to the need for robust analytics capable of handling the volume, variety, and velocity of modern data in domains like e-commerce and social media.

The proposed framework integrates hypothesis generation with exploratory data analysis through the User Group Analytics (UGA) model. This model represents user data as groups characterized by specific attributes and behaviors, allowing for the identification of significant groups based on similarity. The framework comprises three components: hypothesis generation, exploratory analysis, and validation. Hypothesis generation identifies significant deviations from expected patterns, while exploratory analysis visualizes and interprets these deviations to generate insights.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The method successfully identifies significant user groups and generates statistically significant, practically relevant hypotheses. For example, in an e-commerce dataset, the framework identified users with unusual purchasing behavior, which domain experts validated as a target for a new marketing campaign. The results indicate that the UGA framework handles large-scale data efficiently and provides actionable insights for business decisions.

Key contributions include the UGA model, a novel algorithm for hypothesis generation using statistical tests and machine learning, and visualization techniques such as scatter plots and heat maps. The paper addresses scalability through distributed computing and enhances interpretability via interactive visualization. Implications extend to healthcare and social sciences, with suggestions for future research into temporal or spatial data extensions.

title: 17 MOOCs In Six Emerging APEC Member Economies –Trends, Research, and Recommendation
abstract: A collaborative team of five foreign researchers who reside in Japan purposefully conducted research to describe the development of MOOCs in Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Mexico. It is important to point out that these countries represent six emerging economies that are members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC). It seeks to answer three key questions: (1) When did MOOCs begin in APEC countries in Southeast Asia and Latin America? (2) How did they develop? (3) How were they supported? To accomplish these goals, research articles published in relevant local, regional, and international journals together with related books and reports were thoroughly examined. Furthermore, interviews of local experts were also conducted to provide meaningful context. This chapter begins with a review of the overall trends of MOOC growth in the six selected countries. It then discusses research findings and local experts’ comments on MOOC-based learning experiences and points out various challenges currently faced as well as apparent opportunities moving forward. Finally, it concludes with several valuable lessons learned from the MOOC experiences of those emerging economies.

title: Developing and Evaluating a Website as an OER for Faculty Development
abstract:
Abstract
Faculty development (FD) is an important activity that helps faculty members of an academic institution to provide
quality education to students while fulfilling the institution’s missions and improving faculty members’ capacity
to teach. With sustainability and scalability in mind, several institutions often use web media to distribute training
materials for FD. This paper describes the design and development of a web-based FD program at the International
Christian University (ICU), Japan during the fall of 2017. It also presents a thematic analysis of the initial feedback
from the first batch of users and external reviewers. Furthermore, it reports a rough measure of the usability and
usefulness of the website as an Open Educational Resource (OER).
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The article "Developing and Evaluating a Website as an OER for Faculty Development" addresses the challenges of orienting new faculty at East Asian liberal arts institutions, specifically at International Christian University in Japan. Researchers observed that faculty trained at large research universities often struggle to adapt to the unique pedagogical and organizational missions of small liberal arts colleges. To provide a scalable and sustainable solution, researchers utilized the ADDIE model to create a web-based Open Educational Resource (OER) consisting of 20 modules categorized into Reception, Information, and Teaching. This program employed a blended learning approach, utilizing a Google Sites website, a mobile app, and ePUB eBooks released under a Creative Commons License.

The evaluation utilized a mixed-methods approach, combining thematic analysis of interviews and reflection notes with quantitative measures, including the System Usability Scale (SUS) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Findings indicated that the materials were informative and easy to navigate, though participants suggested more frequent references to the materials during face-to-face sessions and the need for a Japanese version. Quantitative results showed an average SUS score of 73, exceeding the global mean of 68, alongside high scores for Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use. The study concludes that web-based OERs are effective, scalable tools for faculty development in liberal arts settings.

The article "Developing and Evaluating a Website as an OER for Faculty Development" addresses the challenge of providing effective faculty development (FD) in liberal arts institutions, specifically within the East Asian context. The authors identify a problem where new faculty members, often trained in large research-oriented universities, struggle to adapt to the specialized pedagogical needs and organizational missions of small liberal arts colleges. In Japan, despite the recognized importance of FD for student achievement and faculty well-being, the implementation rate of such programs has remained low. At the International Christian University (ICU), there was an urgent need for a scalable and sustainable way to orient new faculty to the institution's core values, instructional design, and the balance of professional and personal responsibilities.

To address this, the researchers designed a web-based FD program using the Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation (ADDIE) model. The program was structured into 20 modules categorized into three types: R-Modules (Reception) covering administrative functions; I-Modules (Information) covering faculty support, tenure, and regulations; and T-Modules (Teaching) focusing on liberal arts values and innovative teaching strategies. The project utilized a blended learning approach, incorporating flipped learning where participants engaged with online content before attending face-to-face sessions. The digital resources were delivered through three modes: a website hosted on Google Sites, a mobile app for Android and iOS, and eBooks in ePUB format. All materials were released under a Creative Commons License (CC-BY-NC 3.0) to function as an Open Educational Resource (OER).

The methodology for evaluating the project involved both qualitative and quantitative measures. Following a 10-week implementation period with a cohort of new faculty members, the researchers conducted thematic analysis of participant reflection notes and interviews. Quantitatively, the researchers distributed a survey to faculty members across various institutions to assess the website's usability and utility. This survey utilized the System Usability Scale (SUS) to measure usability, alongside questions derived from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to measure Perceived Ease of Use (PEU) and Perceived Usefulness (PU).

The findings from the initial evaluation were largely positive. Thematic analysis revealed that the website materials were highly informative and helpful, easy to read, and relatively simple to navigate. However, qualitative feedback also indicated that the materials needed to be more frequently referenced during face-to-face sessions and that a Japanese version of the site was necessary to accommodate the bilingual nature of the institution. Quantitative results, though noted as inconclusive due to the small sample size of 24 respondents, showed promising trends. The average SUS score was 73, which exceeds the global mean of 68. Additionally, the scores for Perceived Usefulness (5.1) and Perceived Ease of Use (5.33) were high, suggesting that the platform is both functional and perceived as beneficial by its users.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that a web-based OER can serve as an effective tool for faculty development in a liberal arts setting. The website proved to be a useful resource for new faculty at ICU and showed potential as a broader OER for the wider academic community. The authors suggest that while the platform is successful, improvements in navigation and the addition of a Japanese translation are necessary to meet the specific needs of the university environment.

The implications of this research suggest that digital, open-access platforms can provide scalable solutions for institutional training, particularly when they support a community of practice through blended learning. The authors propose several avenues for future research, including a comparative analysis between the mobile app and the website, a tracking study to observe how the OER is utilized by various institutions over time, and longitudinal studies to validate the relationship between perceived ease of use and actual long-term usage among faculty members.

title: Cinemaspace, Cyberspace: Mapping the Philippine Moving Image
abstract: This presentation will consist of two, interrelated parts, reflecting the interests of the participants in integrating the critical and theoretical, on the one hand, and the artistic and material, on the other. Operating under the same rubric and tackling parallel conceptual problems regarding nation, the moving image, and notions of the public, we hope to unravel some distinctions between art and criticism, following the cue of many practitioners and theorists in the Philippines, in order to sketch out possibilities for links between Philippine cinema as a digital mode of production, the usual way in which cinema and new media are linked, as well as examining the use of Philippine online spaces as a digital mode of circulation.

In "Cinemaspace, Cyberspace: Mapping the Philippine Moving Image," Jasmine Nadua Trice and Diego Maranan explore the intersection of Philippine independent cinema, digital media, and the formation of cinematic publics. The authors argue that despite varying internet penetration, significant online discourse occurs through internet cafes and various linguistic modes, creating a "public" defined by engagement with circulating discourse. This digital sphere mirrors Filipino cinematic practices of communal, non-sacralized viewing, fostering an "alternative modernity" where professional works and amateur vernacular images mix indiscriminately.

The research employs a twofold methodology: a theoretical analysis of "criticism as production" and a technical proposal for a web-based application to archive Philippine cinema information. Using principles from information visualization and database design, the authors propose using social network graphs to map professional collaborations and cartographic visualizations to map blogs and exhibition spaces. They outline a relational database schema including data classes such as cVideo, cPerson, cWriting, and cExhibitionSpace.

Findings indicate the web is a vital site for film culture, acting as an equalizing mechanism where amateur and professional content coexist. Sample visualizations of IMDb data demonstrate that social network graphs can reveal professional clusters and "bridging individuals" within the industry. The authors conclude that while technical and legal hurdles exist for data harvesting, digital visualization tools can facilitate social pathfinding, aid research, and uncover hidden structures of influence within the Philippine film industry.

The working paper "Cinemaspace, Cyberspace: Mapping the Philippine Moving Image" by Jasmine Nadua Trice and Diego Maranan explores the intersection of Philippine independent cinema, digital media, and the formation of cinematic publics. The authors seek to understand how digital spaces facilitate the circulation of films and the discourses surrounding them, ultimately proposing a technical framework for a digital archive and visualization tool to map these complex networks.

The problem addressed by the authors is the need to conceptualize and position the burgeoning Philippine independent cinema movement within the context of new media. They observe a tension between traditional notions of cinema and the evolving digital landscape. While some data suggests low internet penetration in the Philippines, the authors note that internet use is significant through internet cafes, creating a substantial online presence for cinematic discourse. This discourse exists across various media forms—visual, print, and moving image—and utilizes diverse linguistic modes, such as Tag-lish and English. The authors argue that this online activity constitutes a "public" in the sense described by Michael Warner: a group defined by their engagement with circulating discourse rather than static identities.

The context of the research is rooted in the "cinema cultures" described by Tom Ryall, where film culture is an intermingling of ideas, ideologies, and institutional practices. The authors note that while new media is often discussed in terms of its "democratizing" potential, Philippine cinema has historically maintained democratic and egalitarian principles. Traditional Filipino cinemagoing often involves communal, non-sacralized viewing experiences, such as those at traveling exhibitions or local theaters. The authors suggest that the digital sphere mirrors these existing practices by allowing for an "indiscriminate mixing" of genres, professional works, and amateur "vernacular" moving images (such as those found on YouTube or PinoyTube). This creates an "alternative modernity" where the organizing principle shifts from the cinematic text itself to the modes of production and exhibition.

The methodology employed in the paper is twofold. First, the authors conduct a theoretical analysis of "criticism as production," examining how online discourse and the circulation of films constitute an audience. Second, they present a technical proposal for a web-based application designed to visually organize and archive information related to Philippine cinema. This proposal utilizes principles from information visualization, human-computer interaction (HCI), and database design. The authors suggest using social network graphs to map professional collaborations and cartographic visualizations to map blogs and exhibition spaces onto physical or virtual terrains. They also outline a data schema consisting of specific "data classes" (such as cVideo, cPerson, cWriting, and cExhibitionSpace) to structure a relational database.

The findings and observations presented in the paper highlight several key aspects of the Philippine digital cinematic landscape. The authors find that the web has become a vital site for "film culture," where audiences share anecdotes, tips for finding pirated DVDs, or directions to independent screening venues. They observe that online spaces act as an equalizing mechanism where amateur and professional content coexist, much like the small-scale, alternative exhibition spaces (such as university screenings or microcinemas) used by independent filmmakers. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate through a sample visualization of IMDb data that social network graphs can reveal professional clusters and "bridging individuals" who connect different segments of the industry.

The paper concludes that a digital visualization tool could serve multiple functions: facilitating "social pathfinding" for filmmakers looking for collaborators, fostering new professional networks, aiding academic research into cinematic trends, and serving as an educational outreach tool. However, the authors identify a significant technical and legal hurdle: the difficulty of harvesting data from major databases like IMDb, which does not provide a public API and restricts data mining.

The implications of this work are both theoretical and practical. Theoretically, the paper suggests that the boundaries between "art" and "criticism" are blurring, as the act of discussing and circulating film online becomes a form of production that helps constitute the cinematic public. Practically, the proposal for a digital archive suggests that information visualization can be used to uncover hidden structures of influence and communication within the Philippine film industry. By leveraging public APIs from platforms like YouTube, Facebook, and Google Maps, such a tool could provide a platform for wider public participation and a more nuanced understanding of the evolving Philippine moving image.

title: Anthropology Of, For, And With Design:  A Philippine Perspective
abstract: The intersection of the fields of design and anthropology emerges as fertile ground for study as societies increasingly acknowledge the tremendous impact the objects we create for ourselves have on our lives. As anthropologists and ethnographers involved in running our own design research company in the Philippines, negotiating the alignments and contradictions between the two fields of knowledge is an essential component of our everyday research practice. This paper outlines different models of the relationships between design and anthropology as systems of knowledge and practice. We first extend a theoretical framework that distinguishes between anthropology of, anthropology for, and anthropology with design (Gunn and Donovan 2013): we maintain that anthropology with design underlies an approach increasingly used in commercial industries known as "design thinking", and describe the different ways by which knowledge is generated and mobilized in each of these relationships; we further describe how the artifacts of design can be seen to either materialize, shape, or probe culturally-mediated meanings, power relations, and values. We illustrate these concepts through client-commissioned projects that our organization has conducted in the Philippines. We next examine how and when these design-anthropology relationships are realized when working with clients. While anthropology with design will likely create better outcomes for our clients, larger clients must often settle for anthropology for design; we describe how we have negotiated these tensions and present our outcomes from our engagement with them. We end with a call for the development of a local prism through which practitioners in the field of design can further engage in critical reflection of the production of artifacts, particular those created with the intent of addressing social concerns. Specifically, we call for more localized conceptual frameworks of design that can be patterned (for instance) on India's notion of jugaad, and advance an increased engagement for anthropology with design across various sectors of Philippine society.

In "Anthropology Of, For, And With Design: A Philippine Perspective," Pamela G. Cajilig and Diego S. Maranan examine the intersection of anthropology and design within social innovation and commercial product development in the Philippines. The authors identify a fundamental tension between the descriptive, interpretive nature of anthropology and the generative, speculative nature of design, often exacerbated by commercial pressures and power imbalances.

Drawing on eighteen months of fieldwork, the authors categorize the engagement between these fields into three modes: anthropology of design, anthropology for design, and anthropology with design. Anthropology for design serves industry needs, such as start-ups, where designer knowledge often takes precedence. Anthropology with design is a collaborative, iterative approach common in NGO projects, using design thinking to involve stakeholders in co-creation to mitigate power imbalances. Anthropology of design treats design as a subject of theoretical and academic inquiry for the academic community.

The authors conclude that these modes are fluid and that successful social innovation requires researchers to practice empathy toward communities, designers, and business owners alike. They advocate for a move away from top-down models toward "anthropology with design" to ensure meaningful social outcomes. Finally, they suggest practitioners develop localized conceptual frameworks rather than relying solely on Western models to ensure design empowers rather than subjugates the communities it intends to serve.

The article "Anthropology Of, For, And With Design: A Philippine Perspective" by Pamela G. Cajilig and Diego S. Maranan explores the complex intersection of anthropology and design. The authors, who operate a design research firm in the Philippines, examine how these two disciplines interact when applied to social innovation and commercial product development.

The problem addressed by the authors is the inherent tension and misalignment between the methodologies, temporalities, and objectives of anthropology and design. Anthropologists typically focus on descriptive, interpretive, and historical narratives to understand a culture's present state, often avoiding speculative or projective conclusions. In contrast, design is a generative and speculative practice aimed at transforming the future through material or immaterial making. These differences are further complicated by commercial pressures, where the need for rapid results and profit often clashes with the slow, reflexive nature of ethnographic research. Additionally, the authors identify a power imbalance in how research is utilized, noting that research participants are often treated merely as sources of information rather than active contributors to the design process.

The context of this study is the professional practice of design research within the Philippines, specifically through the lens of the authors' firm, Curiosity. They navigate various client types, ranging from small social enterprises and start-ups to large corporations and NGOs. The authors use their eighteen months of fieldwork (from 2012 to 2013) to illustrate how these disciplinary tensions manifest in real-world scenarios, such as designing a pedal-powered washing machine or developing financial literacy modules.

To analyze these relationships, the authors utilize a theoretical framework that extends the work of Gunn and Donovan (2013). They categorize the engagement between the two fields into three distinct modes: anthropology of design, anthropology for design, and anthropology with design. They also examine these relationships through the lenses of temporality (the speed and timing of research), commerce (the financial constraints and motivations of clients), and intervention (the ethical and social impact of the research outcomes).

The findings are organized around the three identified modes of engagement. "Anthropology for design" is characterized by research conducted primarily to serve the needs of industry, often involving social enterprises or start-ups. In this mode, the designer's knowledge is often prioritized over the participant's, and researchers must navigate extreme resource constraints and the urgent need for business viability. The authors mitigate these challenges by providing pro bono mentorship and informal training to social entrepreneurs. "Anthropology with design" is a more collaborative and iterative approach, often seen in projects commissioned by NGOs. This mode utilizes "design thinking" to involve stakeholders—including end-users—directly in the fieldwork and prototyping process. This co-creation fosters trust, mitigates power imbalances, and allows for more equitable relationships where participants help shape the design objectives. Finally, "anthropology of design" involves using design as a subject of theoretical and academic inquiry, producing knowledge for the academic community rather than immediate commercial application.

The authors conclude that the distinctions between these modes are not rigid; a project may shift between them as circumstances change. They emphasize that successful design research for social innovation requires a constant shift in "empathy," where the researcher must empathize not just with the community, but also with the designers, business owners, and academic stakeholders involved in the process.

The implications of this work are a call for a more localized and reflexive approach to design in the Philippines. The authors argue that practitioners should move away from purely top-down models toward "anthropology with design" to ensure more meaningful and feasible social outcomes. They specifically call for the development of localized conceptual frameworks of design. They suggest that instead of relying solely on Western models, practitioners could look to concepts like India's *jugaad*—an improvisational style of innovation driven by scarce resources—to create a "local prism" for design. Such a framework would allow for a more critical reflection on how design can either reproduce or challenge existing social structures and global dominance, ultimately ensuring that social innovation empowers rather than subjugates the communities it intends to serve.

title: When Ideas Migrate: A Postcolonial Perspective on Biomodd [LBA2]
abstract: Biomodd is a global series of art installations in which computer technology and ecology converge. Computer networks built from upcycled computer components are provided with living internal ecosystems. In a symbiotic exchange, plants and algae live alongside electronics and use the latter’s waste heat to thrive. Sensors and robotics provide additional interaction possibilities with the organisms. The first version of the project was completed in the US, while the second version was built in the Philippines. Using a postcolonial stance, we reflect on the challenges involved in translating the project from one context to another. We focus on issues related to heat recycling in the tropics; authenticity and hybridity; obsolescence and the convertibility of capital; cultural sampling, remixing, and appropriation; and structures for social organization. We advance Biomodd as a significant contribution to artscience collaborative initiatives in the global South.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In "When Ideas Migrate: A Postcolonial Perspective on Biomodd," Diego S. Maranan and Angelo C.J. Vermeulen examine the complexities of translating an art-science installation from a Western context to the Global South. Using the Philippine version of the Biomodd project (LBA2) as a case study, the authors critique the assumption that technological and artistic designs are universal. They argue that collaborations in the Global South must move beyond "development" discourses toward a postcolonial discourse addressing power, authority, and cultural legitimacy.

The study utilizes a qualitative, reflective method to analyze shifts between the original United States version (ATH1) and the Philippine version (LBA2). The project integrates upcycled computer components with living ecosystems to create symbiotic relationships. Findings reveal that migrating the project required significant transformations across five thematic areas. In heat recycling, the US model of warming spaces was replaced by an aquaponic system suited for the tropical Philippines. Regarding authenticity, the use of hybrid algae strains sparked discussions on local identity versus cosmopolitan hybridity. In terms of e-waste and capital, the Philippine team relied on social capital and community donations due to difficulties sourcing hardware. Cultural content involved a game based on the mythology of Maria Makiling, raising ethical questions about remixing indigenous narratives. Finally, the authors note tensions between hierarchical and rhizomatic organizational metaphors.

The authors conclude that Biomodd is a "sensibility" rather than a rigid methodology. They advocate for moving away from "top-down" technological transfers toward a postcolonial approach that respects local ecological, social, and cultural realities.

Using the Philippine version of the Biomodd project (LBA2) as a case study, the authors critique the tendency to treat technological and artistic designs as universal. They argue that art-science collaborations in the Global South must move beyond "development" discourses focused on basic needs toward a postcolonial discourse addressing power, authority, and cultural legitimacy.

The study utilizes a qualitative, reflective method to analyze the material and conceptual shifts between the original United States version (ATH1) and the Philippine version (LBA2). The Biomodd project involves integrating upcycled computer components with living ecosystems, such as plants and algae, to create a symbiotic relationship where electronic waste heat supports biological life. The authors frame their analysis through "postcolonial computing," which critiques the political and cultural implications of deploying digital products in postcolonial states.

The findings reveal that migrating the project required significant transformations across five thematic areas. Regarding heat recycling, the US model of warming spaces was ineffective in the tropical Philippines; instead, the team implemented an aquaponic system where computer heat warmed a fish tank to provide nutrients for hydroponic plants. In terms of authenticity and hybridity, the use of hybrid algae strains sparked discussions regarding the tension between maintaining pure local identities and embracing cosmopolitan hybridity.

The study also highlights differences in e-waste and capital. While the US version used discarded hardware, the Philippine team struggled to source even obsolete computers, forcing them to rely on "social capital" through community donations and fundraising. Regarding cultural content, the team developed a game based on the Philippine folk mythology of Maria Makiling, raising ethical questions about "sampling" or "remixing" indigenous narratives. Finally, the authors discuss organizational metaphors, noting a tension between hierarchical "tree-like" structures and decentralized "rhizomatic" models.

The authors conclude that Biomodd is not a rigid methodology but a "sensibility" or a form of "design fiction" that offers visions of alternative ecological relations. They suggest that successful global collaborations require a willingness to allow local teams to transform a project's blueprint into something entirely new. Ultimately, the authors advocate for moving away from "top-down" technological transfers toward a postcolonial approach that respects local ecological, social, and cultural realities, creating spaces to challenge the "imperialized formations" of global technology and art.

The authors use the specific case of Biomodd [LBA2], a version of the Biomodd project built in the Philippines, to reflect on the challenges of migrating technological and artistic ideas across different social, cultural, and economic landscapes.

The problem addressed by the authors is the tendency to treat technological and artistic designs as universal, ignoring the specificities of the environments into which they are introduced. While the original Biomodd [ATH1] was developed in the United States, its migration to the Philippines required a reinterpretation of its core concepts to suit a tropical climate and a different socio-economic reality. The authors argue that art-science collaborations in the Global South must move beyond "development" discourses—which focus primarily on survival and basic needs—toward a postcolonial discourse that addresses power, authority, and cultural legitimacy.

The context of the study is the intersection of contemporary art, computer science, and ecology. The Biomodd project itself is a global series of installations where upcycled computer components are integrated with living ecosystems, such as plants and algae, creating a symbiotic relationship where the waste heat from electronics supports biological life. The authors frame their analysis using the lens of "postcolonial computing," a perspective that critiques the design and analysis of digital products by considering the political and cultural implications of their deployment in postcolonial states.

The authors employ a qualitative, reflective method, using the material and conceptual shifts between the US version (ATH1) and the Philippine version (LBA2) as a basis for analysis. They categorize their findings into five key thematic areas: heat recycling in the tropics, authenticity and hybridity, the convertibility of capital, cultural sampling/remixing, and social organization metaphors.

The findings reveal that the migration of the project necessitated significant transformations. Regarding heat recycling, the authors found that the US model of using excess heat to warm spaces was ineffective in the tropical Philippines. They solved this by implementing an aquaponic system, where the heat from the computers warmed a fish tank, which in turn provided nutrients for hydroponically grown plants, creating a closed thermodynamic loop. In terms of authenticity and hybridity, the use of "hybrid" algae (a mix of Belgian and American strains) sparked discussions about cultural integration and the tension between maintaining "pure" local identities versus embracing cosmopolitan hybridity.

The study also highlights the different nature of e-waste and capital. While the US version utilized discarded hardware, the Philippine team faced difficulty sourcing even older, obsolete computers. To overcome this lack of material and human capital, the team relied on "social capital," using community events, donations, and small-scale fundraising to sustain the project. Regarding cultural content, the team developed a game based on the Philippine folk mythology of Maria Makiling. This raised questions about the ethics of "sampling" or "remixing" indigenous narratives, ultimately concluding that the goal was to "infuse" the mythology into the work rather than appropriate it. Finally, the authors discuss the tension between "tree-like" (hierarchical/monumental) and "rhizomatic" (decentralized/distributed) structures of organization, noting that while the Philippine installation remained a single structure, the debate reflected a desire for more decentralized, grassroots-oriented models of collaboration.

The authors conclude that Biomodd is not a rigid methodology but a "sensibility" or an approach to fostering critical awareness of the connectedness between human, natural, and artificial systems. They suggest that the project serves as a form of "design fiction" or speculative design, offering a vision of alternative ecological relations rather than providing immediate technical solutions.

The implications of this work are significant for art-science collaborations and ICT4D (Information and Communication Technologies for Development). The authors suggest that successful global collaborations require time and a willingness to allow local teams to transform a project's blueprint into something entirely new. They advocate for a move away from "top-down" technological transfers toward a more nuanced, postcolonial approach that respects local ecological, social, and cultural realities. Ultimately, the paper asserts that the value of such projects lies in their ability to create spaces for inquiry and to challenge the "imperialized formations" of global technology and art.

title: (Not so) Dangerous Liaisons: A Framework for Evaluating Collaborative Research Projects
abstract: With advances in research environments and the accompanying increase in the complexity of research projects, the range of skills required to carry out research calls for an increase in interdisciplinary and collaborative work. CogNovo, a doctoral training program for 25 PhD students, provided a unique opportunity to observe and analyze collaborative processes. We propose a process-oriented framework for understanding research collaborations along two dimensions: interpersonal and project-related. To illustrate the utility of this process-oriented framework, we apply the framework matrix to several collaborations that emerged within the CogNovo program. The framework that we introduce has several advantages over existing metrics. Firstly, we offer a process-oriented—as opposed to product-oriented—evaluation of interdisciplinary and collaborative endeavors. Secondly, we propose a means of assessment that preserves the distinctive profile (or “fingerprint”) of a given collaborative project, thus capturing the uniqueness of each project and its environment.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The article "(Not So) Dangerous Liaisons: A Framework for Evaluating Collaborative Research Projects" addresses the inadequacy of current research evaluation methods, which rely heavily on product-oriented bibliometrics like co-authorship counts. The authors argue these metrics fail to account for the qualitative "black box" of how researchers actually interact and integrate knowledge across disciplinary boundaries. To address this, the study utilizes the CogNovo doctoral training program at Plymouth University, involving 25 PhD students from diverse fields, to develop a process-oriented framework.

The proposed framework is structured along two dimensions: the interpersonal dimension and the project dimension. The interpersonal dimension categorizes collaborations into mutual, assisted, or emergent types, while the project dimension tracks the research lifecycle through four stages: Objective & Research Question, Experiment, Analysis, and Communication. Using a point-based matrix system, researchers assign percentage weights to interpersonal categories at each stage and weight the stages themselves based on project goals. This creates a "collaboration fingerprint" that captures a project's unique dynamics.

Applying this to four CogNovo examples—"Bisensorial," "BRAMZ," "Impasse in Conversations," and "Distorted Dimensions"—the authors found that collaborative projects are not monolithic; their fingerprints change as they move from ideation to communication. The framework complements existing metrics by quantifying the "how" of collaboration, offering researchers a tool to improve group dynamics and providing funding bodies a nuanced way to assess interdisciplinary quality.

The article "(Not So) Dangerous Liaisons: A Framework for Evaluating Collaborative Research Projects" addresses the increasing complexity of modern research environments, which increasingly demand interdisciplinary and collaborative approaches to solve multifaceted societal issues. The authors identify a significant problem in how these collaborations are currently evaluated. Most existing metrics are product-oriented, relying on bibliometrics such as co-authorship counts, the "Collaborative Index," or the "Collaboration Coefficient." The authors argue that these methods are insufficient because they overlook the actual process of collaboration. Product-based metrics fail to account for the fact that not all collaborations result in co-authored publications, and they ignore the qualitative "black box" of how researchers actually interact, integrate knowledge, and navigate disciplinary boundaries.

The context for this research is the CogNovo doctoral training program at Plymouth University, an interdisciplinary program involving 25 PhD students from diverse fields such as Psychology, Computational Neuroscience, Robotics, and the Arts and Humanities. This unique environment provided the researchers with a rich dataset of collaborative processes to observe and analyze. The authors seek to move beyond simple output measurements to understand the "choreography" of cooperation and integration within research teams.

To address this gap, the authors propose a novel process-oriented framework for evaluating research collaborations. This framework is structured along two primary dimensions: the interpersonal dimension and the project dimension. The interpersonal dimension categorizes collaborations into three types: mutual collaborations, where all participants contribute equally; assisted collaborations, where one discipline leads and others provide specific expertise; and emergent collaborations, which may occur on a social or pragmatic level or result in the creation of entirely new disciplines. The project dimension tracks the lifecycle of a research endeavor through four stages: Objective & Research Question, Experiment, Analysis, and Communication.

The methodology involves a point-based matrix system. For each of the four project stages, researchers can assign a percentage weight to the three interpersonal categories (mutual, assisted, and emergent), ensuring the sum for each stage equals 100%. Additionally, researchers assign a weight to each stage itself based on its importance to the specific project's goals (e.g., a project focused on theory might weight the "Objective" stage more heavily than the "Experiment" stage). This creates a "collaboration fingerprint" that captures the unique dynamics and priorities of a specific project.

To demonstrate the utility of this framework, the authors apply the matrix to four distinct examples from the CogNovo program. The first example, "Bisensorial," was a hackathon-based project involving design, music, and neuroscience. The evaluation showed a high degree of mutual collaboration (64.25%) during the objective-setting phase, but shifted toward assisted collaboration (75%) during the communication phase. The second example, "BRAMZ," focused on developing personality measurements through games. Its fingerprint showed a high level of assisted collaboration (70%) during the objective phase and emergent collaboration (70%) during the communication phase. The third example, "Impasse in Conversations," involved linguistics and psychology and showed a high level of mutual collaboration (61.5%) in its objectives. The final example, "Distorted Dimensions," explored moral psychology and design, showing a more balanced distribution across mutual, assisted, and emergent categories across all stages.

The findings demonstrate that collaborative projects are not monolithic; rather, they exhibit unique combinations of interpersonal dynamics and task priorities. The application of the framework shows that a project's "fingerprint" can change as it moves from the ideation stage to the communication stage. For instance, a project might start as a mutual endeavor but transition into an assisted or emergent one as it reaches dissemination.

The authors conclude that their process-oriented framework successfully complements existing product-based metrics by shedding light on the internal dynamics of research teams. By providing a way to quantify the "how" of collaboration rather than just the "what," the framework allows for a deeper understanding of interdisciplinary integration. The authors suggest that this method can help identify which group dynamics are most likely to lead to successful research outcomes.

The implications of this work are significant for researchers, funding bodies, and academic institutions. For researchers, the framework provides a tool to examine and improve the dynamics within their own research groups. For funding bodies and organizations, the framework offers a more nuanced way to assess the quality and health of interdisciplinary endeavors beyond mere publication counts. Finally, the authors suggest that while their study focused on a single institutional context (CogNovo), the framework is flexible and can be adapted to reflect the specific aims, constraints, and institutional pressures of various different organizational environments.

title: Navigating Cognitive Innovation
abstract: This paper revisits the concept of Cognitive Innovation with the aim of helping newcomers appreciate its (intended) demarcating purpose and relevance to the wider literature on cognition and creativity in the humanities, arts, and sciences. Particular emphasis is paid to discussion of the pitfalls of sense-making and the concept’s affordance. The main argument presented is that proponents of the concept face the dilemma of seeking to demonstrate its transdisciplinary nature and applicability vis-a-vis retaining its semantic distinctness. Proceeding from a classification of Cognitive Innovation as a dispositional construct, we discuss how it feeds into existing research approaches and opens up new sensibilities in related areas. The perspectives of temporality, interdisciplinary balancing, technology, and metatheories are proposed as promising areas for future elaboration of the function of Cognitive Innovation.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In "Navigating Cognitive Innovation," Michael Sonne Kristensen, Frank Loesche, and Diego S. Maranan address the conceptual ambiguity surrounding "Cognitive Innovation." The authors identify a lack of clear definitions for fundamental concepts like creativity, consciousness, and cognition, which often leads to research impasses. They note that because the constituent words carry significant disciplinary weight, the term faces the dilemma of maintaining semantic distinctness while demonstrating transdisciplinary applicability.

Using concept analysis and theoretical reflection, the authors categorize Cognitive Innovation as a "dispositional construct" rather than an "entity view." Instead of treating the concept as a stable thing, they define it as a set of behavioral potentials or habits. Functionally, it is a recursive process where an individual probes mental boundaries, selects promising avenues, and synthesizes new knowledge.

The findings suggest that treating the concept as a dispositional construct opens several research avenues. The authors emphasize the importance of temporality, noting that mental processes change over time. They also suggest the concept can distinguish between the biological process of innovation and the culturally contingent expression of "creativity." To facilitate interdisciplinarity, they propose decomposing the concept into mental processes, knowledge, and the perceptible world, while treating technology as a parameter that extends human agency and perception. Ultimately, the authors propose Cognitive Innovation as a metatheoretical framework for interdisciplinary investigation.

The article "Navigating Cognitive Innovation" by Michael Sonne Kristensen, Frank Loesche, and Diego S. Maranan addresses the conceptual ambiguity surrounding the term "Cognitive Innovation." The authors identify a significant problem in cognitive science: the lack of clear definitions for fundamental concepts like creativity, consciousness, and cognition. This ambiguity often leads to discursive impasses in research, where discussions devolve into ontological and epistemological disagreements rather than productive inquiry. Specifically, the authors note that while the term "Cognitive Innovation" was proposed by Denham and colleagues to help position or displace the concept of creativity, it faces a dilemma. Proponents must find a way to demonstrate the concept's transdisciplinary applicability while simultaneously maintaining its semantic distinctness from other overloaded terms like "cognition" and "innovation."

The context of this discussion is rooted in the semantic density of the constituent words. "Cognition" is a central term in cognitive science, spanning neuroscience, psychology, and philosophy, while "innovation" is a heavily used term in social sciences, economics, and engineering. Because both words carry significant historical and disciplinary weight, any new compound term risks being misinterpreted through the lens of the reader's own expertise—a phenomenon the authors describe using Gadamer’s notion of the "fusion of horizons." The authors also reference the historical origins of the term, noting that Acker and McReynolds used "Cognitive Innovation" as early as 1965 to describe the introduction of newness into an individual's cognitive structure.

To analyze the concept, the authors employ a method of concept analysis and theoretical reflection. They categorize Cognitive Innovation as a "dispositional construct" rather than an "entity view." While an entity view treats a concept as a stable, clearly demarcated "thing," a dispositional view treats it as a set of behavioral potentials or habits that are dynamically formed through individual interpretation and use. The authors examine the functional definition provided by Denham and Punt, which describes Cognitive Innovation as a recursive process where an individual probes mental boundaries, selects promising avenues, and synthesizes new knowledge. This function is mathematically represented as a process involving internal mental processes, existing knowledge, and sensory inputs from the world, all of which change over time.

The findings of the paper suggest that treating Cognitive Innovation as a dispositional construct opens several new avenues for research. First, the authors highlight the importance of temporality. They argue that because the internal knowledge and mental processes involved in the function change with repeated exposure and time, time must be explicitly addressed in studies of creativity and cognitive innovation. Second, the authors suggest that the concept can be used to distinguish between the biological/cognitive process of innovation and the socially grounded expression of "creativity." They propose a thought experiment suggesting that while "creativity" is a culturally contingent term, "cognitive innovation" may be a more fundamental process that existed long before the social concept of creativity emerged.

Third, the authors discuss the decomposability of the concept in relation to interdisciplinarity. By breaking the function down into mental processes, knowledge, and the perceptible world, they suggest that a truly interdisciplinary research group should include not just neuroscientists and psychologists, but also anthropologists and sociologists to account for the social and cultural dimensions of knowledge. Furthermore, the authors propose that technology should be treated as a special parameter ($T$) within the function. They argue that technology acts as an extension of the human body and brain, mediating human agency and transforming how the world is perceived and acted upon. Finally, the authors suggest that Cognitive Innovation shares features with metatheories, such as Clare Graves’ model of human development, because it describes the mechanisms of growth and complexity in human systems.

The authors conclude that the value of Cognitive Innovation lies in its potential to serve as a metatheoretical framework rather than just a single concept. They warn that attempting to subsume too many principles under the term risks diluting its meaning, yet they acknowledge the difficulty of maintaining semantic boundaries in a transdisciplinary field. They suggest that the primary challenge for the field is not merely describing the concept, but developing methods to study and write about it in a truly transdisciplinary manner.

The implications of this work are significant for future research in the cognitive sciences and the humanities. By viewing Cognitive Innovation as a dispositional, recursive, and time-dependent process, researchers can move beyond intra-cranial studies to include the roles of technology, culture, and social structures. The authors' proposed expansion of the functional definition to include technology ($T$) aligns the concept with "The Extended Mind" theory, suggesting that future studies should look at the interaction between human cognition and the tools that extend it. Ultimately, the paper provides a roadmap for navigating the "muddy waters" of conceptual territory, encouraging researchers to embrace the complexity of the concept while seeking rigorous, interdisciplinary methods of investigation.

title: Response to “Haunted Bodies: Cell Switching, Getting Lost and Adaptive Geographies”
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In "Haunted Bodies: Cell Switching, Getting Lost and Adaptive Geographies," Jane Grant and Joanne “Bob” Whalley explore the human body and self as porous, complex, and open systems. Rather than viewing the self as a discrete entity with sacrosanct boundaries like the skin, the authors frame it as a "cogitatum"—an ongoing process of exploration where boundaries serve as sites of negotiation, exchange, and transformation. This perspective moves discourse away from a stable ego toward a model of a body "haunted" by its environmental interactions.

Drawing from biology, sociology, philosophy, and performance art, the authors use biological metaphors like cell switching and osmosis to describe social and psychological phenomena. They engage with theoretical frameworks including Hannah Arendt’s inter-subjectivity, Donna Haraway’s ideas on symbiogenesis, and Niklas Luhmann’s systems theory to bridge microscopic cellular processes with macroscopic social experiences. This is explored through a "cogno-innovative" approach, including an analysis of Jane Grant’s sonic artwork *Ghost*, which uses external sounds to create a "cortical haunting" that materializes the body's absorption of its environment.

The findings suggest that boundaries are inherently relational and mutable. Through the lens of "cell switching," the authors find the self is never truly separate from its surroundings. They conclude that human experience is a constant "transfection" where identity is a performative, ongoing process of entanglement rather than a fixed state.

title: Designing clinical trials for future space missions as a pathway to changing how clinical trials are conducted on Earth
abstract: Objective The project aims to build a framework for conducting clinical trials for long-term interplanetary missions to contribute to innovation in clinical trials on Earth, especially around patient involvement and ownership. Methods We conducted two workshops in which participants were immersed in the speculative scenario of an interplanetary mission in which health problems emerged that required medical trials to resolve. The workshops used virtual reality and live simulation to mimic a zero-gravity environment and visual perception shifts and were followed by group discussion. Results Some key aspects for the framework that emerged from the workshops included: (a) approaches to be inclusive in the management of the trial, (b) approaches to be inclusive in designing the research project (patient preference trials, n-of-1 trials, designing clinical trials to be part of a future prospective meta-analysis, etc), (c) balancing the research needs and the community needs (eg, allocation of the participants based on both research and community need), (d) ethics and partnerships (ethics and consent issues and how they relate to partnerships and relationships). Conclusion In identifying some key areas that need to be incorporated in future planning of clinical trials for interplanetary missions, we also identified areas that are relevant to engaging patients in clinical trials on Earth. We will suggest using the same methodology to facilitate more in-depth discussions on specific aspects of clinical trials in aerospace medicine. The methodology can be more widely used in other areas to open new inclusive conversations around innovating research methodology.

title: Adapting the Compass Framework in a hybrid course on wearable technology design and futures thinking
abstract:
The Wearable Futures Hackathon (WFH) was a 12-week long, hybrid learning experience was collaboratively created with and for undergraduate students at UP Open University’s Bachelor of Arts program in Multimedia Studies (BAMS). The course explores wearable technology, e-textiles, speculative design, and futures thinking. The course is the first of its kind at the university in terms of the following aspects:

- The course themes (i.e., physical computing, e-textiles, speculative design, and futures thinking); and
- The use of a hybrid format (80% online, 20% face to face) for BAMS studio course.

For this course, the Index Project's design thinking framework--the Compass--was integrated with UPOU’s standard principle and practices in outcomes-based online learning design resource-based course authoring.

title: Collaborative Relational Database Software-as-a-Service as Authoring Tools for Online and Offline OERs: Using  Airtable and Notion to Make Your Own Learning Management System
abstract: In this presentation, I describe how specific collaboration, authentication, and sharing features of two popular, low-cost, relational database software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms, Airtable and Notion, can be used to create open educational resources (OERs) that are easily updatable, shareable, and repurposable. Not only do these SaaS platforms provide opportunities for student assessments to be closely align with course content, but they also afford course facilitators a way to quickly verify and monitor such content-assessment alignment. Using two examples of courses taught at the UP Open University, I additionally describe how SaaS relational database platforms facilitates the use of previous student outputs as learning material for subsequent iterations of courses and drives the continuous improvement of course design.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Diego S. Maranan investigates the potential of using collaborative relational database Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms, specifically Airtable and Notion, as authoring tools for Open Educational Resources (OERs). The author proposes "hacking" a Learning Management System (LMS) by leveraging the relational capabilities of these modern tools to overcome the functional limitations of traditional educational software, such as restricted formatting, limited media embedding, and a lack of instructor autonomy.

The method utilizes relational structures to chain data points through one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships, allowing for diverse ways to display, sort, and filter content. Notion serves as a customizable tool for layout and activity presentation, while Airtable acts as a powerful data management tool that can be integrated into Notion to facilitate student submissions. Key findings include the ability to create "offline analogues" of digital content by transforming online materials into printable PDF formats. Additionally, the author identifies a method for reusing student submissions as future reference material through simple consent mechanisms.

Pedagogically, these tools allow instructors to audit courses by mapping activities to specific learning goals and calculating time devotion. However, limitations exist, such as difficulties managing asynchronous discussions and identity authentication in Airtable, and less customizable offline material generation in Notion. Ultimately, these tools offer educators greater agency to create modular, data-driven, and user-controlled learning environments.

The presentation by Diego S. Maranan explores the potential of using collaborative relational database Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms, specifically Airtable and Notion, as authoring tools for both online and offline Open Educational Resources (OERs). The central premise is the concept of "hacking" one's own Learning Management System (LMS) by leveraging the inherent relational capabilities of these modern SaaS tools to overcome the limitations found in traditional educational software.

The problem addressed by the author stems from the functional limitations of standard LMS platforms. Maranan notes that most existing LMSs are not optimized for content authoring, often suffering from limited formatting options and restricted features for embedding rich media. Furthermore, the ability to add or remove specific functionalities is typically restricted to LMS administrators, preventing instructors from tailoring the digital environment to their specific pedagogical needs. This creates a gap between the desire for customized, highly functional learning environments and the rigid structures provided by conventional educational software.

To address this, the author proposes using relational databases as the foundation for course design. A relational database is defined as a type of database that stores and provides access to data points that are related to one another. The author argues that the most sophisticated functions within a standard LMS are essentially extended applications of relational databases. By using SaaS tools like Airtable and Notion, educators can move beyond the constraints of a standard LMS to create custom functionality that is either unavailable or not free in existing systems.

The method involves utilizing the specific strengths of Airtable and Notion to manage and display educational content. These tools allow users to chain data and chunks of data together, creating various types of relationships, including one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships. This relational structure allows for diverse ways to display, sort, and filter learning content based on the specific contextual needs of the instructor or the student.

The presentation highlights several specific applications and findings regarding how these tools function in an educational context. Notion is presented as a highly customizable tool for layout and activity presentation. It allows for the duplication of entire websites to be used as templates and offers significant flexibility in how material is presented. Airtable is positioned as a powerful data management tool that can be integrated into Notion to facilitate student submissions and to display those submissions.

A significant finding involves the ability to create "offline analogues" of digital content. Through export functions and extensions, educators can transform online materials into customizable, printable PDF formats. This capability is essential for creating offline OERs. Furthermore, the author identifies a method for reusing student submissions as reference material for future courses. This process involves obtaining consent through simple checkbox confirmations, allowing instructors to include previous student work in subsequent coursework or in printable formats.

The use of these tools also provides pedagogical benefits regarding course auditing and time management. By structuring data relationally, instructors can keep track of the demands that various activities place on student time. This allows for auditing to determine the extent to which specific course activities contribute to expected learning outcomes. Specifically, instructors can map which activities contribute to which learning goals and calculate how many minutes are devoted to those specific goals.

Despite these advantages, the author identifies several gaps and limitations in using these SaaS tools as LMS alternatives. In Airtable, there are challenges regarding asynchronous discussions, specifically concerning threading, moderation, and grading. Additionally, identity authentication in Airtable can be a hurdle unless premium services are utilized. For Notion, the author notes that the generation of offline course materials is less customizable compared to other methods.

In conclusion, the presentation suggests that collaborative relational database SaaS tools like Airtable and Notion can serve as powerful, flexible authoring tools for creating both online and offline educational resources. By "hacking" these tools, educators can bypass the limitations of traditional LMSs, creating highly customized, data-driven learning environments that allow for better content organization, easier reuse of materials, and more effective auditing of learning outcomes. The implications of this approach suggest a shift toward more modular, user-controlled digital learning environments where instructors have greater agency over the functionality and presentation of their educational content.

title: Recruiting ODeL-ready Talent: An Open Call-based Cluster Hiring Process at a Open and Distance e-Learning University
abstract: Faculty hiring in many higher education institutions (HEIs) in the Philippines typically depends on referral-based systems of recruitment as a way to mitigate human resource management risks. This was the case at the UP Open University particularly prior to the pandemic, when expertise and interest in teaching for open and distance elearning (ODEL) modalities was less widespread than it now is. The restrictions forced by the pandemic on educational institutions globally has led to dramatic increases in ODEL-ready capability in higher education faculty across the country, creating more diverse opportunities for human resource development in HEIs. In the presentation, I will describe an open call-based faculty recruitment process in 2022 conducted by the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies at the UP Open University. The process was informed by prior (and less successful) attempts at open call-based hiring, which I also describe as point of comparison. I discuss how this open call-based hiring process was further made more tractable with the use of collaborative relational database software-as-a-service platforms, allowing hiring managers to quickly and collaboratively sift through, prioritize, review, and evaluate potential ODeL-ready teaching and research talent.

half:
Diego S. Maranan addresses the challenge of recruiting twelve new faculty members for an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) university within a few months to facilitate the development of new undergraduate programs. The central problem was selecting the best candidates from a pool of applicants, particularly given the increasing trans-disciplinary nature of modern teaching and research.

To solve this, the author moved away from previous practices like relying on referrals and instead developed a strategic hiring plan using a four-part analytical lens. This lens focused on carrying capacity, teaching gaps, research aspirations, and administrative potential. The methodology employed a user-centered approach to the open call, featuring curated job descriptions with salary details. Dissemination utilized social media, targeted emails, and platforms like LinkedIn and JobStreet. To manage the process, the author used relational Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) tools, specifically Airtable and Notion, to tag, filter, and sort over 90 applications.

The selection followed a four-stage filtering method: checking minimum requirements, peer-reviewing portfolios, shortlisting by a hiring committee, and conducting interviews via Calendly. The findings indicate the approach was highly successful, completing recruitment in less than two months with increased applicant diversity. The author concludes that a user-centered, technology-driven approach using SaaS tools and multi-lens analytical frameworks can streamline complex administrative tasks and improve strategic hiring decisions.

title: Designing for Movement: Evaluating Computational Models Using LMA Effort Qualities
abstract: While single-accelerometers are a common consumer embedded sensors, their use in representing movement data as an intelligent resource remains scarce. Accelerometers have been used in movement recognition systems, but rarely to assess expressive qualities of movement. We present a prototype of wearable system for the real-time detection and classification of movement quality using acceleration data. The system applies Laban Movement Analysis (LMA) to recognize Laban Effort qualities from acceleration input using a Machine Learning software that generates classifications in real time. Existing LMA-recognition systems rely on motion capture data and video data, and can only be deployed in controlled settings. Our single-accelerometer system is portable and can be used under a wide range of environmental conditions. We evaluate the performance of the system, present two applications using the system in the digital arts and discuss future directions.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The research paper "Designing for Movement: Evaluating Computational Models Using LMA Effort Qualities" addresses limitations in Human-Computer Interaction regarding movement-based interaction. While movement is often treated as a functional component, the authors argue it is also highly expressive. Existing recognition systems often require motion capture or video in controlled environments, leaving a gap for portable, real-time systems using consumer sensors to capture nuanced "movement qualities" (MQs).

To address this, the authors utilize Laban Movement Analysis (LMA), specifically the "Effort" category, which describes movement through four factors: Space, Time, Weight, and Flow. These factors combine to form eight Basic Effort Actions (BEAs). The researchers developed EFFORTDETECT, a prototype that uses a single wearable accelerometer to recognize and classify these BEAs in real-time. The system treats movement as a continuous flux using multiple sliding time windows and extracts nine motion features per axis, which are processed through a supervised machine learning classifier.

The system achieved a weighted overall detection accuracy of 70.71%. It was highly accurate in recognizing "Punch" (91.11%) and "Glide" (78.78%), while "Flick" and "Float" were more challenging. Notably, misclassifications were often "LMA-consistent," occurring between movements with similar Effort parameters. The study concludes that EFFORTDETECT is a viable, portable, and efficient system, demonstrating how movement expertise can help design expressive interfaces for wearables, digital arts, gaming, and rehabilitation.
