The research paper "Designing for Movement: Evaluating Computational Models Using LMA Effort Qualities" addresses limitations in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) regarding movement-based interaction. While movement is often treated as a functional component focused on ergonomics, the authors argue it is also highly expressive. Existing recognition systems typically require motion capture or video data in controlled environments. There is a lack of portable, real-time systems using common consumer sensors, such as single accelerometers, to capture the nuanced "movement qualities" (MQs) that define how a movement is executed.

To address this, the authors utilize Laban Movement Analysis (LMA), specifically the "Effort" category. Effort describes movement through four factors: Space (Direct/Indirect), Time (Sudden/Sustained), Weight (Light/Strong), and Flow (Bound/Free). These factors combine to form eight Basic Effort Actions (BEAs). The researchers designed and evaluated EFFORTDETECT, a prototype capable of real-time recognition and classification of these BEAs using a single wearable accelerometer.

The methodology involved a wearable hardware unit consisting of a wireless transmitter and a 5DOF accelerometer mounted on an elastic band for the wrist. Unlike methods requiring discrete segmentation, EFFORTDETECT treats movement as a continuous flux using a multiple sliding time windows approach across three different time scales. The system extracts nine motion features per axis to create feature vectors, which are processed through a supervised machine learning classifier trained by a Certified Laban Movement Analyst (CMA).

The evaluation involved a professional dancer and a CMA to ensure movements were consistent with LMA standards. The researchers collected 80 profile streams to assess accuracy. The system achieved a weighted overall detection accuracy of 70.71%. It was highly accurate in recognizing "Punch" (91.11%) and "Glide" (78.78%), while "Flick" (61.11%) and "Float" (58.97%) were more challenging. Notably, misclassifications were often "LMA-consistent," occurring between movements that share similar Effort parameters.

The authors demonstrated the system's utility through two artistic applications: triggering real-time changes in light, sound, and projection in a restaging of Trisha Brown’s *Astral Convertible*, and integration into the EMVIZ visualization tool to map movement qualities to abstract visualizations.

The study concludes that EFFORTDETECT is a viable, portable, and computationally efficient system. The authors emphasize that their primary contribution is the methodology of using movement expertise to plan and evaluate such systems. By moving toward higher-level semantic movement qualities, designers can create more expressive interfaces applicable to mobile devices, wearables, digital arts, gaming, and rehabilitation.
two:
The research paper "Designing for Movement: Evaluating Computational Models Using LMA Effort Qualities" addresses the limitations of current movement-based interaction in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). While movement has traditionally been treated as a functional component focused on ergonomics and efficiency, the authors argue that it is also highly expressive and experiential. Existing systems for recognizing movement qualities often rely on motion capture or video data, which require controlled environments, specific camera positioning, and a priori segmentation of movement into discrete parts. There is a lack of portable, real-time systems that can utilize common consumer sensors, such as single-accelerometers, to capture the nuanced "movement qualities" (MQs) that define how a movement is executed.

To address this, the authors utilize Laban Movement Analysis (LMA), a rigorous framework for describing movement expressivity. Specifically, they focus on the "Effort" category, which describes movement through four factors: Space (Direct/Indirect), Time (Sudden/Sustained), Weight (Light/Strong), and Flow (Bound/Free). By combining these factors, Laban defines eight Basic Effort Actions (BEAs), which serve as the qualitative descriptors for the study. The goal was to design and evaluate a system called EFFORTDETECT, a prototype capable of real-time recognition and classification of these BEAs using a single wearable accelerometer.

The methodology involved designing a wearable hardware unit consisting of a wireless transmitter and a 5DOF accelerometer mounted on an elastic band for the wrist. Unlike previous methods that require segmenting movement into discrete parts, the EFFORTDETECT system treats movement as a continuous flux. It employs a multiple sliding time windows approach, analyzing data across three different time scales (large, medium, and small windows) to capture both quick and sustained motions. The system extracts nine motion features per axis—including current difference, average difference, trajectory, number of direction changes, and stillness—to create feature vectors. These vectors are processed through a supervised machine learning classifier (implemented via Weka) that was trained by a Certified Laban Movement Analyst (CMA) performing the BEAs.

The evaluation was conducted with a professional dancer and a CMA to ensure the movements performed were legible and consistent with LMA standards. The researchers collected 80 profile streams to quantitatively assess the system's accuracy and confidence. The results showed that while the system did not outperform high-end motion capture systems, it achieved significant results given its reliance on a single, portable sensor. The weighted overall detection accuracy was 70.71%. The analysis revealed that the system was highly accurate in recognizing "Punch" (91.11%) and "Glide" (78.78%), while "Flick" (61.11%) and "Float" (58.97%) were more challenging. Notably, the researchers found that when the system misclassified a movement, the error was often "LMA-consistent"—meaning the misclassification occurred between movements that share similar Effort parameters, such as mistaking a "Flick" for a "Dab."

The authors demonstrated the practical utility of the system through two artistic applications. First, in a restaging of Trisha Brown’s *Astral Convertible*, EFFORTDETECT was used to trigger real-time changes in light, sound, and projection based on the dancers' movement qualities. Second, the system was integrated into the EMVIZ visualization tool, which maps movement qualities to parameterized abstract visualizations. This application allowed both performers and audiences to engage with the aesthetic and communicative properties of movement through real-time visual feedback.

The study concludes that EFFORTDETECT is a viable, portable, and computationally efficient system for recognizing Laban Effort qualities in real-time. The authors emphasize that their primary contribution is not just the recognition system itself, but the methodology of using movement expertise to plan and carry out the evaluation of such systems. They argue that using LMA provides a stable, replicable language for designing more nuanced and meaningful movement-based interactions.

The implications of this research are significant for the field of HCI. By moving beyond simple functional gestures (like tilting a phone) toward higher-level semantic movement qualities, designers can create more expressive interfaces. The portability of the single-accelerometer approach makes it highly applicable to mobile devices, wearable technology, and public interactive installations. The authors suggest that this technology could expand into various domains, including digital arts, gaming, rehabilitation, and large-scale public entertainment. Future work will focus on refining the recognition model by training it on movements that interpolate between the eight BEAs and exploring multi-modal representations of movement data.

title: Openness across disciplines: Reflecting on a multiple disciplinary summer school
abstract: In this book chapter, we observe an exceptional example of addressing messy and ill-defined problems through several disciplinary lenses during the ColLaboratoire 2016 Summer School (https://collaboratoire.cognovo.eu). We discuss the requirements and conditions under which this approach is an effective and appropriate alternative to mono-disciplinary research.This chapter is structured as follows: first, we critically reflect on the role of openness in multiple disciplinary research. Because ColLaboratoire was modelled heavily on the organisers’ experiences of working across the disci- plinary boundaries within CogNovo, we subsequently review selected features, activities, and outputs of this doctoral training programme. We then discuss the organisation of ColLaboratoire, including how its decisions drew on the experience from CogNovo as a multiple disciplinary work environment. Following this, we reflect on the experiences of the ColLaboratoire participants and evaluate the outcomes of individual projects and the summer school as a whole. Within this chapter, we define openness as ‘an accommodating attitude towards new, unconventional, and useful ideas and experiences,’ and we reflect on the key factors that contributed to the realisation of ColLaboratoire. We conclude that these were enabled by what we identify as three forms of openness: multi-perspective, inter-perspective, and trans-perspective openness.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This chapter examines the tension between academic specialization and the need for multidisciplinary approaches to solve complex, real-world problems. While specialization manages vast knowledge, it creates disciplinary silos that hinder progress on issues like climate change. Researchers face a collective action problem where the pressure to publish in mono-disciplinary journals discourages interdisciplinary collaboration due to high coordination costs and differing epistemological standards.

To address this, the authors present a case study of "ColLaboratoire," a peer-led, project-based summer school at the University of Plymouth. The program aimed to move beyond simple multidisciplinarity toward inter-perspective and trans-perspective openness through international recruitment and a physical environment designed to foster sociality and proximity.

The findings show that the summer school successfully fostered innovation, resulting in four specific projects involving physiological data sonification, networked consciousness, robotic theatre, and social entrainment. These projects produced tangible outputs such as peer-reviewed articles and software, with many collaborations persisting beyond the event. The results indicate that physical and social proximity are essential for building the trust and psychological safety required for high-risk experimentation. Ultimately, success requires three forms of openness: multi-perspective, inter-perspective, and trans-perspective. For multidisciplinary research to be sustainable, individuals must adopt an open attitude, and institutions must provide the time, proximity, and flexibility necessary for integration.

This chapter examines the complexities of modern academic specialization and the necessity of multidisciplinary approaches to address "messy" real-world problems. While fragmentation allows for the management of vast knowledge, it creates "disciplinary silos" that can hinder the resolution of complex issues like climate change or epidemic diseases. The authors argue that because real-world knowledge is applied in an integrated fashion, research practices and learning environments must become more permeable to foster innovation.

A central tension exists between the benefits of mono-disciplinary research—such as established methods and predictable evaluation—and the necessity of collaboration. Researchers often face a "collective action problem," where the pressure to publish in high-impact, mono-disciplinary journals discourages interdisciplinary work due to perceived lower status or higher coordination costs. Additionally, communication gaps arise from differing methodological and epistemological standards between fields, such as the tension between the conceptual openness of the humanities and the rigor of the sciences.

To investigate these issues, the authors present a case study of "ColLaboratoire," a multidisciplinary summer school held at the University of Plymouth in August 2016. Modeled on the CogNovo doctoral training programme, the summer school was designed to be peer-led, project-based, and practice-oriented. Key design features included a project-based structure, international recruitment to ensure mobility, and a physical environment designed to foster sociality and proximity. The goal was to move beyond simple multidisciplinarity toward inter-perspective and trans-perspective openness.

The findings demonstrate that the summer school successfully fostered collaborative research and innovation. Four specific projects emerged: the sonification of physiological data for music, the exploration of networked consciousness, robotic theatre and social perception, and social entrainment through dance and movement. These resulted in tangible outputs like peer-reviewed articles, software, and exhibitions, with many collaborations continuing after the event. The results suggest that physical proximity (shared meals and workspaces) and social proximity (informal time) are essential for building the trust and psychological safety required for high-risk experimentation.

The authors conclude that success depends on three forms of openness: multi-perspective (listening without prejudice), inter-perspective (softening disciplinary borders), and trans-perspective (allowing methods and data to transcend boundaries). Openness acts as both an enabler and an outcome of collaboration. For multidisciplinary research to be sustainable, individuals must develop an "open attitude," while institutions must create "spaces for integration" that provide the time, proximity, and flexibility necessary for exploration. The chapter explores the complexities of modern academic specialization and the necessity of multiple disciplinary approaches to solve "messy" real-world problems. While academic disciplines have become increasingly fragmented and specialized to manage the growing volume of human knowledge, this fragmentation creates "disciplinary silos" that can hinder the resolution of complex issues like climate change or epidemic diseases. The authors argue that because real-world knowledge is applied in an integrated fashion, learning environments and research practices must evolve to be more permeable, encouraging interaction across traditional boundaries to foster creativity and innovation.

The central problem addressed is the tension between the benefits of mono-disciplinary research—such as established methods, prestige, and predictable evaluation—and the necessity of multiple disciplinary collaboration. The authors note that researchers often face a "collective action problem," where the pressure to publish in high-impact, mono-disciplinary journals discourages the pursuit of interdisciplinary work, which may be perceived as having lower status or higher coordination costs. Furthermore, the chapter identifies the need for "openness" to bridge communication gaps caused by differing methodological and epistemological standards between fields, such as the perceived tension between the conceptual openness of the humanities and the rigor of the sciences.

To investigate these issues, the authors present a case study of "ColLaboratoire," a multiple disciplinary summer school held at the University of Plymouth in August 2016. This event was modeled on the experiences of the CogNovo doctoral training programme, which had previously explored working across disciplinary boundaries. The methodology of the summer school was intentionally designed to be peer-led, project-based, and practice-oriented rather than theory-driven. The organizers utilized several key design features: a project-based structure where participants worked on specific research goals; high mobility through international recruitment; and a physical environment designed to foster sociality and proximity. The summer school aimed to move beyond simple multidisciplinarity (gathering disciplines) toward inter-perspective and trans-perspective openness.

The findings from the ColLaboratoire case study demonstrate that the summer school was highly successful in fostering collaborative research and innovation. The authors highlight four specific projects that emerged: one involving the sonification of physiological data for musical production; one exploring the possibility of networked consciousness; one involving robotic theatre and social perception; and one exploring social entrainment through dance and movement. These projects resulted in tangible outputs, including peer-reviewed articles, software, and exhibitions, and many participants continued their collaborations long after the event concluded. The results suggest that the combination of physical proximity (shared meals and workspaces) and social proximity (informal, unstructured time) was essential for building the trust and psychological safety required for high-risk, interdisciplinary experimentation.

The authors conclude that the success of such initiatives depends on three specific forms of openness: multi-perspective openness (listening to different disciplines without prejudice), inter-perspective openness (softening disciplinary borders to allow multiple avenues of inquiry), and trans-perspective openness (allowing methods and data to transcend traditional boundaries). They argue that openness is both an enabler and an outcome of successful collaboration; it is required to start the work, but the collaborative process itself nurtures and expands that openness in the participants.

The implications of this study suggest that for multiple disciplinary research to become sustainable, changes are needed at both the individual and institutional levels. For individuals, the development of an "open attitude" is crucial for navigating the complexities of collaborative research. For institutions and organizations, the study implies that creating "spaces for integration"—environments that provide the time, physical proximity, and flexibility to allow for mistakes and exploration—is vital. The authors suggest that summer school models like ColLaboratoire can serve as effective tools for training young researchers to acquire the disciplinary openness necessary to thrive in an increasingly interconnected scientific landscape.

title: Wearable Futures Hackathon – Co-creating a Hybrid, Interdisciplinary Learning Experience
abstract: This paper is a personal reflection and autoethnographic account of the primary author's experience revolving around the participation in the Wearable Futures Hackathon course as a co-creator for the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program (BAMS). It documents how his perceived participation evolved from being a consultant into co-creator of one of the Multimedia Studies course, the challenges he had to face reconciling the difference between the two, and how co-creation can possibly benefit the academe, the faculty, and the students as participants and as co-creators in developing engaging, innovative, and participatory workshops and classes, not only through online but also offline, first-person perspectives will be employed hereafter.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This autoethnographic study by Lucky Angelo P. Vengua examines his transition from a student collaborator to a co-creator within the "Wearable Futures Hackathon" (WFH) course at the University of the Philippines Open University. The 12-week hybrid course explores wearable technology, e-textiles, speculative design, and futures thinking. The research addresses the discrepancy between the traditional role of students as passive consumers and the industry standard of co-creation found in creative sectors.

Using an autoethnographic method and analyzing roles through models by Bovill et al. (2015) and Fielding (2001), the author documents his progression through various levels of involvement. He moved from providing passive feedback to becoming an active respondent who proposed iterations for course outlines and requirements. Ultimately, he reached a state of full co-creation by participating in designing forms, selecting participants, and developing weekly tasks. This shift increased his personal investment, moving his motivation from grade acquisition to the overall success of the project.

The findings suggest that co-creation fosters engagement and excitement among participants. However, the transition requires a significant shift in mindset for both faculty and students. Success depends on faculty willingness to relinquish authority and students' willingness to accept responsibility. The study concludes that while institutions must address power distribution and set clear expectations, co-creation provides valuable preparation for professional environments where collaborative design is standard.

This paper presents an autoethnographic reflection by Lucky Angelo P. Vengua regarding his transition from a student collaborator to a co-creator for the "Wearable Futures Hackathon" (WFH) course at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The WFH is a 12-week hybrid course exploring wearable technology, e-textiles, speculative design, and futures thinking. The study addresses the traditional role of students in higher education, which is often limited to being passive consumers or providers of feedback through generic forms, whereas co-creation is a standard practice in creative and marketing industries.

The study is situated within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program at UPOU. The WFH course was designed to introduce physical computing through a hybrid model, combining synchronous and asynchronous online sessions with face-to-face activities at the Bukas Lab, a makerspace for collaboration and prototyping. Using an autoethnographic method, the author combines personal reflection with ethnographic observation to document group dynamics and the evolution of their own role. The analysis utilizes Bovill et al.’s (2015) model of student roles and Fielding’s (2001) levels of involvement.

The findings detail the author's progression through different stages of involvement. Initially acting as a collaborator providing passive feedback, the author's role evolved into an "active respondent" by proposing iterations for the course outline, requirements, and mentor selection. This eventually transitioned into full "co-creation," where the author participated in designing forms, selecting participants, and developing weekly tasks. The author found that being granted autonomy and responsibility significantly increased their investment in the project's success, shifting motivation from merely seeking a grade to ensuring the project's overall success. Observations of course participants indicated that knowing a fellow student helped create the course fostered engagement and excitement, despite initial intimidation regarding technical requirements.

The paper concludes that co-creation in academia offers benefits for both faculty and students, potentially leading to more innovative learning experiences. However, the transition from collaborator to co-creator is a primary challenge, requiring a shift in mindset from both parties. Success depends on the faculty's willingness to relinquish authority and the students' willingness to accept responsibility. The study suggests that institutions must address power distribution and responsibility sharing by setting clear expectations and goals. Ultimately, the experience of co-creation serves as valuable preparation for students entering professional industries where collaborative design and user-centric development are standard.

This paper presents an autoethnographic reflection by Lucky Angelo P. Vengua regarding his experience transitioning from a student collaborator to a co-creator for the "Wearable Futures Hackathon" (WFH) course at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The WFH is a 12-week hybrid course exploring wearable technology, e-textiles, speculative design, and futures thinking.

The problem addressed is the traditional role of students in higher education, which is often limited to being passive consumers or mere providers of feedback through generic end-of-course forms. The author notes that while co-creation is a standard practice in the creative and marketing industries—where end-users are involved in the development process to ensure market relevance—it is less common in academia. In educational settings, students are typically viewed as consumers rather than active partners in curriculum development.

The context of the study is the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program at UPOU. The WFH course was designed as a unique offering to introduce physical computing, a topic not previously covered in the program. The course utilized a hybrid model, combining synchronous and asynchronous online sessions with face-to-face activities at the Bukas Lab, a makerspace designed to foster collaboration and hands-on prototyping.

The author employs an autoethnographic method, combining personal reflection with ethnographic observation. This approach allows the researcher to document the nuances of group dynamics and the evolution of their own role. The study utilizes several theoretical frameworks to analyze the levels of involvement, including Bovill et al.’s (2015) model of student roles (consultant, co-researcher, co-designer, and representative) and Fielding’s (2001) levels of involvement, which range from being a mere data source to becoming a researcher.

The findings detail the author's progression through different stages of involvement. Initially, the author acted as a collaborator, assuming a passive role by providing feedback on ideas proposed by faculty. However, the role evolved into that of an "active respondent" when the author began proposing specific iterations for the course outline, requirements, and mentor selection. This transitioned into full "co-creation," where the author participated in designing forms, selecting participants, and developing weekly tasks.

The author found that being granted autonomy and responsibility significantly increased their investment in the project's success. The findings suggest that when students are given genuine decision-making power, their motivation shifts from merely seeking a grade to ensuring the project's overall success. Observations of the course participants also indicated a positive reception; while students initially felt intimidated by the technical requirements, the knowledge that a fellow student helped create the course fostered engagement and excitement.

The paper concludes that co-creation in academia offers significant benefits for both faculty and students, potentially leading to more innovative and engaging learning experiences. However, the author notes that the transition from collaborator to co-creator is a primary challenge, as it requires a shift in mindset from both parties. The success of this process depends on the willingness of faculty to relinquish some authority and the willingness of students to accept the responsibility that comes with autonomy.

The implications of this study suggest that co-creation can be a powerful tool for curriculum innovation and student engagement. To be successful, institutions must address concerns regarding power distribution and responsibility sharing by setting clear expectations, goals, and limitations at the onset of the collaborative process. The author suggests that further research is needed to determine the long-term viability of co-creation across different disciplines and to understand how it can be scaled within larger academic institutions. Ultimately, the experience of co-creation serves as a valuable preparation for students entering professional industries where collaborative design and user-centric development are standard.

title: Ēngines of Ēternity: An Artistic Inquiry Into Space Settlement Ideology Using Rotifer Experiments on Board the ISS
abstract: Ēngines of Ēternity is a transdisciplinary project that takes the biological phenomena of cloning and DNA repair as metaphorical departure points for an art installation about humanity’s enthrallment with cultural immortality. Cultural immortality has long fascinated humankind, with such diverse examples as the Roman Empire, the Han Dynasty, and the Mayan Civilization, all assuming perpetuity through monumental works in art and architecture. This aspiration of cultural immortality is also deeply embedded in the imaginary of space exploration. Space settlements are often presented as the culmination of technological and cultural evolution. However, the quest for cultural immortality is often imbued with conflict because of convictions of superiority and impulses of colonialism, and this will be no different in outer space. Ēngines of Ēternity explores these human tendencies through the lens of the smallest animals on Earth, rotifers. On the surface, rotifers seem an unchanging biological culture, perfected through evolution, cloning itself endlessly, and surviving extreme conditions such as drying or freezing. However, during drying, genetic material gets broken and repaired, and in the process diversity is generated. Moreover, DNA from totally different organisms such as fungi, bacteria and plants were discovered inside the rotifer’s genome. This horizontal gene transfer is another mechanism through which rotifers seek out diversity. In Ēngines of Ēternity it’s precisely this contrast between stasis and flux that is used as a metaphorical device to reflect critically on the aspirations of humankind in space. What concept of culture and identity will we develop in space? Who will have a say in this? And if we end up with a rich diversity of cultures and identities, how will we maintain cohesion? Ēngines of Ēternity is a joint effort between SEADS and the laboratory of Karine Van Doninck (UNamur/ULB). In a series of space biology experiments, rotifers were sent to the ISS in 2019 and 2020. SEADS sent a human fingerprint code along with the rotifers. This code formed the algorithmic seed for an evolving artwork. After each space mission the genetic expression of the rotifers was used to parametrically evolve the art. As such, Ēngines of Ēternity engenders new forms of co-creation between humans, biological organisms, algorithms, and outer space. In this talk, the core concepts of the Ēngines of Ēternity project will be presented, together with reflections on the challenges of transdisciplinary research and the need for a more holistic perspective on our future in outer space.

The resulting outputs included 3D-printed "Data Monument" sculptures, murals, and digital video essays. The findings demonstrate that space acts as an active co-creator, using rotifer resilience to advocate for a more holistic and diverse perspective on human habitation in space.

The project *Ēngines of Ēternity* addresses the complex intersection of human aspirations for cultural immortality and the biological realities of survival in extreme environments. The authors identify a tension in the current discourse regarding space settlement. While space exploration is often framed as the ultimate culmination of human technological and cultural evolution—exemplified by the visions of entrepreneurs like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos—these narratives frequently overlook the potential for conflict, colonialism, and the imposition of monolithic cultural identities. The authors argue that the quest for perpetuity often ignores the necessity of diversity and the inevitability of change, posing critical questions about what kind of culture and identity will be developed in space and how cohesion can be maintained in such environments.

To explore these themes, the researchers use the biological phenomena of cloning and DNA repair as metaphorical starting points. They focus on the bdelloid rotifer (*Adineta vaga*), a microscopic animal capable of surviving extreme conditions such as desiccation, freezing, and high levels of ionizing radiation. While rotifers appear to be a model of biological stasis due to their ability to clone themselves endlessly, they actually exhibit significant genetic flux. During the process of desiccation and rehydration, their DNA undergoes breakage and repair, which generates genetic diversity. Furthermore, rotifers engage in horizontal gene transfer, assimilating genetic material from fungi, bacteria, and plants. This contrast between the appearance of stasis and the reality of constant genetic flux serves as a metaphor for the tension between the human desire for cultural permanence and the necessity of adaptation and diversity.

The methodology of this transdisciplinary project involves a collaboration between the Space Ecologies Art and Design (SEADS) collective and the RISE (Rotifer in Space) scientific project. The research was conducted through a series of space biology experiments on the International Space Station (ISS) in 2019 and 2020. During the RoB1 experiment, hydrated rotifers were sent to the ISS to study the effects of microgravity and space radiation on biological pathways. Simultaneously, SEADS contributed an artistic component by hand-printing unique, abstract glyphs—representing the infinity symbol and the DNA double helix—onto the specimen bags containing the rotifers. This ensured that the artwork was physically present in the space environment alongside the biological samples.

Following the return of the samples to Earth, the researchers utilized the resulting transcriptomic data to drive the artistic evolution of the project. The scientific team performed a comparative analysis of gene expression between the rotifers exposed to the ISS and a control group maintained on Earth. SEADS then used this data to perform algorithmic data visualization. By mapping the differential gene expression onto a Gene Ontology (GO) hierarchy, the team created visual representations of how the space environment altered the organisms' genetic information. These data-driven insights were used to morph the original thumb-printed glyphs through a gravity-inspired algorithm. The final artistic outputs included 3D-printed sculptures known as the "Data Monument," which juxtaposed the original glyphs with their "evolved" versions, as well as large-scale murals, digital video essays, and various multimedia installations.

The findings of the project demonstrate that space is not merely a backdrop for art, but an active co-creator in the creative process. The transcriptomic data provided a direct, material link between the harshness of the space environment and the transformation of the artwork. The resulting "Data Monument" sculptures physically manifested the impact of spaceflight on the biological entities, creating a new form of co-creation between humans, biological organisms, algorithms, and the space environment itself. The project successfully translated complex biological responses into a tangible, aesthetic form that communicates the interconnectedness of science and art.

The authors conclude that *Ēngines of Ēternity* represents a significant shift in how art engages with space exploration. Rather than using space as a passive gallery, the project mobilizes the space environment as an active participant in the work. The project highlights the importance of transdisciplinary research, where artists and scientists with shared backgrounds facilitate a deeper level of engagement than traditional collaborations. Ultimately, the work serves as a critical provocation, using the biological resilience and adaptability of rotifers to encourage a more holistic, ethical, and diverse perspective on the future of human habitation in outer space, warning against the dangers of monolithic thinking and the repetition of terrestrial colonial patterns.

title: ACES: Automated Academic Essay Scoring Using a Natural Language Processing-Based Regression Mechanism
abstract: Academic essays are essential testing instruments that evaluate the students’ ability to organize thoughts and synthesize information. However, grading them is an exhausting and cumbersome process that requires considerable manpower. It may be prone to errors, and there are also serious concerns about fairness, such that an essay graded B+ today may be graded B- tomorrow by the same checker. Therefore, the author proposes ACES, an essay scoring mechanism that employs natural language processing (NLP) to address the issue at hand. NLP is a sub-field of artificial intelligence (AI) concerned with granting computers the ability to understand texts in much the same way humans can. With essay scoring reformulated as a regression problem, ACES takes the essay answer as the input, converts it to a vector representation of numbers in the embedding space, and feeds it to the neural network model (which serves as the approximate regression function) to predict its score as the output. In this paper, the author successfully implements four versions of ACES that employ different embedding sources and neural network models, with the ACES variant that considers context and word frequency information performing the best (i.e., ACES-BERT).
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In the research paper "ACES: Automated Academic Essay Scoring Using a Natural Language Processing-Based Regression Mechanism," Reinald Adrian Pugoy addresses the inefficiencies of manual essay grading, including time consumption, manpower requirements, and human error. The author proposes ACES, an automated scoring mechanism that utilizes natural language processing and machine learning to treat essay scoring as a regression problem. The system converts essays into numerical vector representations within an embedding space and processes them through a neural network to predict scores.

The methodology compared four model variants: ACES-MLP, which uses TF-IDF scores with a Multilayer Perceptron; ACES-CNN, which employs fastText word embeddings through a Convolutional Neural Network; ACES-3CNN, which uses three parallel CNN blocks; and ACES-BERT, which utilizes a fine-tuned BERT model for contextualized representations. The study used the Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, containing 12,976 English essays from Grades 7 through 10.

Findings indicate that ACES-BERT is the most effective model, achieving the lowest error rates with an MAE of 0.4860 and an RMSE of 0.8490, highlighting the importance of capturing contextual information. ACES-MLP performed second best, suggesting word frequency is a crucial feature. The CNN-based models performed the worst, likely due to the loss of word frequency information during max-pooling, though ACES-3CNN outperformed ACES-CNN. The author concludes that NLP-based regression models can effectively automate scoring if they capture context and word frequency.

In the research paper "ACES: Automated Academic Essay Scoring Using a Natural Language Processing-Based Regression Mechanism," Reinald Adrian Pugoy addresses the difficulties associated with manual essay grading, such as the time-consuming nature of the process, the need for significant manpower, and the potential for human error and inconsistency. To mitigate these issues, the author proposes ACES, an automated scoring mechanism that utilizes natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to reformulate essay scoring as a regression problem. The system converts student essays into numerical vector representations within an embedding space and processes them through a neural network to predict a score.

The methodology involved implementing and comparing four distinct variants of the ACES model. ACES-MLP uses Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) scores with a Multilayer Perceptron. ACES-CNN employs fastText word embeddings through a Convolutional Neural Network. ACES-3CNN utilizes three parallel CNN blocks to simulate ensemble or random forest methods. Finally, ACES-BERT utilizes a fine-tuned BERT model to provide contextualized language representations. All models were trained using the AdamW optimizer and the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function.

The study utilized the Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, consisting of 12,976 English essays from students in Grades 7 through 10 across eight topics. Ground-truth scores were determined by averaging scores from two checkers. The dataset was split into 80% for training and 20% for testing, with performance evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE).

The findings indicate that ACES-BERT is the most effective model, achieving the lowest error rates with an MAE of 0.4860 and an RMSE of 0.8490. This performance underscores the importance of capturing contextual information and the dynamic semantic sense of words. The ACES-MLP model performed second best, suggesting that word frequency information is a crucial feature for accurate scoring. Conversely, the CNN-based models, ACES-CNN and ACES-3CNN, performed the worst, which the author attributes to the potential loss of word frequency information during the max-pooling process. However, ACES-3CNN outperformed ACES-CNN, suggesting that parallel CNN structures can offer benefits similar to ensemble methods.

The author concludes that NLP-based regression models can effectively automate essay scoring, provided they capture contextual information and word frequency. Future research directions include incorporating unsupervised learning techniques to allow the system to function without large sets of labeled training samples.

The research paper titled "ACES: Automated Academic Essay Scoring Using a Natural Language Processing-Based Regression Mechanism" by Reinald Adrian Pugoy addresses the challenges inherent in the manual grading of academic essays. The author identifies that while essays are vital tools for evaluating a student's ability to organize thoughts and synthesize information, the manual grading process is exhausting, time-consuming, and requires significant manpower. Furthermore, manual grading is prone to human error and raises concerns regarding fairness and equity, as a single grader may provide inconsistent scores for the same essay at different times.

To address these issues, the author proposes ACES, an automated essay scoring mechanism that utilizes natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The primary objective is to develop a concise architecture that reformulates essay scoring as a regression problem. The proposed system takes a student's essay as input, converts the text into a numerical vector representation within an embedding space, and processes it through a neural network model that acts as an approximate regression function to predict a score.

The methodology involves the implementation and comparison of four distinct variants of the ACES model, each utilizing different embedding sources and neural network architectures. The first variant, ACES-MLP, uses Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) scores as input for a Multilayer Perceptron. The second, ACES-CNN, employs fastText word embeddings processed through a Convolutional Neural Network. The third, ACES-3CNN, utilizes three parallel CNN blocks to simulate ensemble or random forest methods. The fourth and final variant, ACES-BERT, utilizes a fine-tuned BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model, which provides contextualized language representations. All models were trained using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function and the AdamW optimizer.

The study utilized the Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset from Kaggle, which contains nearly 12,976 English essays written by students in Grades 7 through 10 across eight different topics. The ground-truth scores were determined by averaging the scores provided by two different checkers. The dataset was split into 80% for training and 20% for testing. Performance was evaluated using two metrics: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE), where lower values indicate higher accuracy.

The findings demonstrate that ACES-BERT is the most effective model, achieving the lowest error rates with an MAE of 0.4860 and an RMSE of 0.8490. This performance highlights the importance of considering context and the dynamic semantic sense of words, a capability unique to the BERT model among the tested variants. The ACES-MLP model, which utilizes TF-IDF, performed second best, suggesting that maintaining word frequency information is a crucial feature for accurate scoring. In contrast, the CNN-based models (ACES-CNN and ACES-3CNN) performed the worst, which the author attributes to the potential loss of word frequency information during the max-pooling process. However, the results also showed that ACES-3CNN outperformed ACES-CNN, supporting the idea that parallel CNN structures can provide benefits similar to ensemble methods.

In conclusion, the author successfully developed the ACES mechanism, proving that NLP-based regression models can effectively automate essay scoring. The results emphasize that capturing contextual information and word frequency is essential for achieving high accuracy in automated grading. For future work, the author suggests enhancing these regression models by incorporating unsupervised learning techniques, which would allow the system to function without the need for large sets of labeled training samples.

title: Flow: Expressing Movement Quality
abstract: Flow was an improvised dance performance at the User in Flux workshop at the 2011 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems. Movement qualities are extracted in real time from the performer’s body using EffortDetect. EffortDetect is a real-time machine-learning system that applies Laban Movement Analysis, a rigorous framework for analyzing the human movement, to extract movement qualities from a moving body in the form of Laban Basic Efforts. It produces a dynamic stream of Laban Basic Effort qualities in real time. We extended the use of EffortDetect by designing a visualization system that uses movement quality parameters to generate an abstract visualization for use in dance performance.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Subyen, Maranan, Carlson, Schiphorst, and Pasquier examine the intersection of human-computer interaction, new media art, and dance through the concept of the "user in flux." As Web 2.0 technologies have transitioned users from passive consumers to active performers, artists are exploring new production methods, such as online performance art. This research investigates the evolving roles of artists, designers, and scientists in this landscape, specifically addressing the problem of recognizing movement quality through computational means for integration into live artistic performances.

To address this, the researchers developed EffortDetect, a real-time machine-learning system that applies Laban Movement Analysis (LMA) to extract movement qualities. The system identifies Laban Basic Efforts by analyzing three parameters: Space, Time, and Weight. Using a multi-disciplinary team of experts, the researchers developed "Flow," a five-minute improvised dance performance where EffortDetect maps a dancer's real-time movement qualities to abstract visualizations via specific design rules and color palettes. They also tested a prototype installation, “Paint with Your Efforts,” allowing gallery attendees to interact with the system using wearable sensor gloves.

The findings emphasize the benefits of a research team with shifting roles, which allowed members to exchange knowledge across disciplinary boundaries. In the performance, the dancer embodies the "user in flux," acting simultaneously as a user, an author of visualizations, and a performer. The authors conclude that the "user" is a figure in constant negotiation, encompassing the collective group that designs, develops, and performs through system interaction.

title: The Bukas Lab: Exploring Creative Physical Spaces for a Virtual University
abstract: BUKAS is a physical space and collaboration platform for pluridisciplinary and intersectoral initiatives in art, design, technology, and futures literacy centered around the context of the sustainable development and socioeconomic justice in the context of the Philippines in particular and the Global South in general. In this institutional presentation, we describe the constitution of BUKAS and a sampling of its current and past projects and initiatives.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In "The Bukas Lab: Exploring Creative Physical Spaces for a Virtual University," Diego S. Maranan addresses the challenge of fostering creativity and interdisciplinary connection in virtual university settings. The central problem is the lack of physical colocation in virtual environments, which prevents the accidental discoveries and serendipitous encounters that occur when people share a physical space. Maranan suggests that even virtual institutions must explore how creative physical spaces can support their unique needs.

Situated at the intersection of information and communication studies, somatic learning, and the arts, the work draws on research regarding hybrid games and somatic techniques like the Feldenkrais Method. It references vibrotactile somaesthetic technologies, such as the Haplós project and the RE/ME project, which explore body awareness and reshaping self-image through touch and sound. The research is framed within postcolonial perspectives on technology and the value of the arts and humanities to science.

Findings emphasize that colocation is a vital driver for innovation, as interdisciplinary relationships often result from physical encounters rather than purely digital interactions. Integrating sensory modalities like touch and sound can enhance body awareness and well-being. The author concludes that for a virtual university to thrive, it must consider the role of physical, creative spaces like the "Bukas Lab" to facilitate the serendipitous encounters necessary for interdisciplinary breakthroughs.

title: Use of User Tour, Contact Form, and Accessibility Plugins in Enhancing a Moodle-Based Virtual Conference Experience
abstract: Academic conferences have been conducted in an online or hybrid setup ever since the onset of the pandemic. Various virtual platforms have arised to address this need but most of them are costly and offer varying features. The use of Moodle as a virtual conference platform is now being explored worldwide. The University of the Philippines Open University has used Moodle together with user tour function and plugins such as contact support and accessibility for its semi-annual National Conference on Open and Distance eLearning this 2022. The purpose of integrating these features is to enhance a Moodle-based virtual conference experience. A survey was conducted at the end of the conference to measure the effectiveness of using these features. Results showed that using user tour, contact support and accessibility plugins significantly enhanced the Moodle-based virtual conference experience of the participants. The use of these Moodle features can also still be improved in the future as suggested by the participants.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The study "Use of User Tour, Contact Form, and Accessibility Plugins in Enhancing a Moodle-Based Virtual Conference Experience" investigates the effectiveness of using the Moodle Learning Management System as a cost-effective alternative to expensive third-party virtual conference platforms. Conducted during the National Conference on Open and Distance eLearning (NCODeL) 2022 at the University of the Philippines Open University, the research explored whether integrating specific Moodle features—user tours, accessibility plugins, and contact forms—could improve the participant experience.

The technical setup utilized a Linode cloud server with the "almond" theme. To enhance usability, researchers integrated user tours for navigation, an accessibility block for customizing text size and color, and a contact form plugin for support. A badge enrollment system was also implemented to incentivize engagement. Data was collected via an event evaluation and a System Usability Scale (SUS) assessment.

Findings indicate that the integrated features significantly enhanced the experience. The user tour was highly successful, with 93.52% of participants finding it useful and informative. The contact support form received positive feedback, with 65.74% of users finding it useful. While 59.26% found the accessibility block useful, 50% of participants reported being unaware of or not using it. The platform received a SUS score of 70.14, placing it in the "Good" category. The researchers concluded that Moodle is a viable platform for virtual conferences when customized with specific plugins.

The study titled "Use of User Tour, Contact Form, and Accessibility Plugins in Enhancing a Moodle-Based Virtual Conference Experience" investigates the effectiveness of utilizing the Moodle Learning Management System (LMS) as a platform for hosting academic conferences. The research was conducted in the context of the National Conference on Open and Distance eLearning (NCODeL) 2022, hosted by the University of the Philippines Open University.

The problem addressed by the authors stems from the shift toward online and hybrid academic conferences necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic. While various virtual platforms exist to facilitate these gatherings, many are prohibitively expensive or offer inconsistent features. The researchers sought to explore whether Moodle, an open-source platform, could serve as a cost-effective and functional alternative to high-cost third-party virtual reality or specialized conference platforms. Specifically, the study focused on whether integrating specific Moodle features—user tours, accessibility plugins, and contact forms—could enhance the overall participant experience.

To address this, the researchers utilized a methodology centered on the implementation and evaluation of a Moodle-based platform. The technical setup involved using a Linode cloud server running Apache and a MySQL database, with the "almond" theme selected for its clean interface. The researchers implemented several specific features: "user tours" to provide step-by-step navigation guides, an "accessibility block" to allow users to customize text size and color schemes, and a "contact form" plugin to facilitate support requests. To incentivize engagement and track progress, a badge enrollment system was used, where participants earned digital badges for attending sessions, which eventually granted access to a survey and a downloadable certificate. Data was collected through two surveys administered at the end of the conference: an evaluation of the NCODeL 2022 event and an assessment of the conference platform using the System Usability Scale (SUS), a standardized 10-item questionnaire for measuring usability.

The findings indicate that the integrated Moodle features significantly enhanced the virtual conference experience. The user tour was highly successful, with 93.52% of participants finding it useful; qualitative feedback described it as informative, user-friendly, and easy to use. The contact support form also received positive feedback, with 65.74% of those who used it finding it useful. However, the accessibility block saw lower engagement, with 59.26% of users utilizing it and 59.26% of those users finding it useful; a significant portion of the total participants (50%) reported being unaware of or not using the block. Regarding the overall platform usability, the study yielded a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 70.14, which falls into the "Good" category.

The researchers concluded that Moodle, when customized with specific plugins, is an effective and viable platform for hosting virtual conferences. The integration of user tours, accessibility tools, and contact forms contributed positively to the participant experience. However, the study also noted that there is room for improvement, particularly regarding the visibility and awareness of accessibility features and the overall navigation of the user interface.

The implications of this study suggest that institutions and organizations looking to host cost-effective virtual conferences should consider Moodle as a robust option. To optimize the experience, the authors recommend several improvements for future implementations. These include producing video tutorials to guide users through the platform—which may also increase awareness of features like the accessibility block—and conducting pre-conference surveys to better understand participant needs to shape the user interface. Additionally, addressing navigation issues, such as page length and the placement of session links, could further improve the usability score. The study serves as a guide for other organizations aiming to transition to or improve their Moodle-based virtual event experiences.

title: Postpartum Breastfeeding Self-Efficacy and Success of Mothers on Home Maternity Care (Kraamzorg) In The Hague
abstract: Breastfeeding has been shown repeatedly to be the single most effective way to prevent infant death. It plays a major role in children’s health and development, and significantly benefits the health of mothers. The investigator believes that the perceptions mother have in their ability to breastfeed, or their breastfeeding self-efficacy influences their intent, continuation and success to breastfeed. Maternal breastfeeding confidence and self-efficacy is a variable that is modifiable through interventions such as education and support. This study is needed to identify the level of breastfeeding efficacy in postpartum mothers in The Hague because a strong sense of self-efficacy encourages individuals to engage themselves fully in the activity, to endure hardships and setbacks. Postpartum mothers who were on their 8-10 days home-maternity care in The Hague (Kraamzorg) were asked to fill-in a questionnaire to measure their levels of breastfeeding self-efficacy before after home maternity care and their breastfeeding success at the end of this 8-10 days period. Results indicate that postpartum level of breastfeeding self-efficacy of mothers before home maternity care is lower than after home maternity care. Furthermore, there is no significant statistical relationship as to the mother’s demographic characteristics and breastfeeding self-efficacy, except for the type of delivery. The demographic characteristics of mothers showed no significant statistical relationship with breastfeeding success of mothers in The Hague. Lastly, there is a direct correlation between the breastfeeding self-efficacy and success among postpartum mothers.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
Maria Theresa A. Dieters conducted research on the importance of breastfeeding for infant and maternal health, focusing specifically on the role of breastfeeding self-efficacy. This variable, defined as a mother's perception of her ability to breastfeed, is considered a modifiable factor that can be improved through education and support. The study was situated within the context of Kraamzorg, or home maternity care, in The Hague, aiming to assess how this care influences maternal confidence and breastfeeding outcomes.

Using a quantitative approach, the researcher employed a questionnaire to measure breastfeeding self-efficacy and breastfeeding success among postpartum mothers receiving 8 to 10 days of Kraamzorg. The findings indicate that breastfeeding self-efficacy is higher after receiving home maternity care than it was before the care began, suggesting that the Kraamzorg period positively impacts a mother's confidence. While most demographic factors showed no significant statistical relationship with self-efficacy or breastfeeding success, the type of delivery was an exception regarding self-efficacy.

The most significant finding is the direct correlation between breastfeeding self-efficacy and breastfeeding success. This confirms that a mother's perception of her own ability is closely linked to her actual success. Maria Theresa A. Dieters conducted research addressing the critical importance of breastfeeding for infant and maternal health. Breastfeeding is identified as the most effective method for preventing infant death and is vital for the long-term health and development of children, while also providing significant health benefits to mothers. The study focuses on the influence of breastfeeding self-efficacy—a mother's perception of her ability to breastfeed—on her intent, continuation, and ultimate success in breastfeeding. The researcher posits that maternal breastfeeding confidence is a modifiable variable that can be improved through targeted interventions like education and support.

The study was situated within the context of Kraamzorg, or home maternity care, in The Hague. The researcher identified a need to assess breastfeeding efficacy among postpartum mothers in this setting. The theoretical framework suggests that strong self-efficacy is crucial because it encourages individuals to engage fully in an activity and provides the psychological resilience necessary to endure the hardships and setbacks encountered during the breastfeeding process.

Using a quantitative approach, the study employed a questionnaire to measure variables among postpartum mothers in The Hague who were receiving 8 to 10 days of Kraamzorg. The research design focused on measuring two primary components: the mothers' levels of breastfeeding self-efficacy before and after the home maternity care period, and their breastfeeding success at the conclusion of this period.

The findings reveal several key insights. The results indicate that postpartum breastfeeding self-efficacy is higher after receiving home maternity care than it was before the care began, suggesting that the Kraamzorg period has a positive impact on a mother's confidence. Regarding demographic factors, most characteristics showed no significant statistical relationship with breastfeeding self-efficacy, with the exception of the type of delivery. Additionally, demographic characteristics showed no significant statistical relationship with actual breastfeeding success in The Hague.

The most significant finding is the identification of a direct correlation between breastfeeding self-efficacy and breastfeeding success among postpartum mothers. This confirms the hypothesis that a mother's perception of her own ability is closely linked to her actual success in breastfeeding. The implications suggest that interventions aimed at increasing breastfeeding self-efficacy can be effective in improving breastfeeding outcomes. Because self-efficacy is a modifiable variable, providing support and education during the home maternity care period can bolster a mother's confidence, which is directly correlated with her success. This highlights the importance of the Kraamzorg system in supporting maternal confidence during the critical early postpartum period.

title: The Practices Betel Quid Chewing and Oral Health Status Among Selected Sitio Residents of Eastern Samar
abstract:
Betel quid chewing has been reported in literature as part of traditional practices in several countries including the Philippines. The practices, beliefs, and social implications of betel quid chewing has been described in the context of tradition and socialization stating that chewing betel quid initiates binding especially from small cultures. It also helps to foster friendship, close association and enhances interaction. The level of awareness on health implications especially on oral health status need to be studied. Literatures have also reported the implications on the development of disease states, such as cancerous states and cardiovascular disease.

This study aimed to describe the lived experiences of betel quid chewers in the context of interpersonal and family influence, interpersonal and situational influence, and personal and psychosocial and cultural factors. The Health Promotion Model by Nola Pender provided support for the theoretical framework. The phenomenological approach was used to describe the lived experiences of betel quid chewers in a sitio in Borongan, Easter Samar. The descriptive correlational design was used to assess the knowledge on betel quid chewing and health practices, the oral health status of the betel quid chewers and its associated demographic factors. Purposive sampling was used given the inclusion criteria. Ethics approval to conduct the research was granted through the UPOU.

There were 18 participants, mostly males, for the description of the lived experiences of betel quid chewers. Saturation of data was attained at this level. For the assessment of oral status and level of knowledge, there were 83 participants (64 males, 19 females) from the community of Siha, Borongan Eastern Samar. The demographic profile are as follows: mean age is 52 years majority belonging to age range of 51 to 60 years old (28.95), married, average of 17.58 years of chewing betel quid, and mostly able to consume about one to five betel quid in a day. The highest educational attainment is mostly elementary undergraduate (55.4%) with 63.9% working as farmers. For the average monthly income are below the poverty threshold falling into the range of 0 to PhP5,000.00 a month.

Results showed that for the level of knowledge, the respondents have an average of 55.2% correct response in all questions on factors related to health practices. Oral health assessment revealed that most of the betel quid chewers have about three to four teeth broken, worn-out, or even damage and missing teeth. Mouth sores was also common as a result of using too much slaked lime. Betel quid staining is also observed to majority of the betel quiz chewers. For the demographic profiles, only occupation and age have shown significant relationship with oral health status.

Description of the lived experiences: Interpersonal influences in terms of family involvement and motivation for chewing betel quid show the influence of parents and grandparents, highlighting traditional hand-down practices. The presence of peers in the community who are betel quid chewers strengthens the practice of betel quid chewing and is a means of passing the practice to others. For the interpersonal and situational influences of betel quid chewing, the study shows that the practice promotes socialization, strengthens camaraderie, friendship, belongingness, and peer identity. There is oneness that is fostered by sharing ingredients among betel quid chewers. There appears to be enjoyment and solidarity when done in groups. The personal factors that were deemed relevant included descriptions of its benefit when working in rice fields or in fishing that the practice increases their tolerance to cold and make their body feel warm. Awareness of health consequences were verbalized, such as development of mouth sores when there is increase slaked lime in the ingredients. The discoloration of the teeth and subsequent staining appears to be an accepted situation. When ingredients were reportedly more than what is required, there were reports of increased perspiration, sticky sweat, urge to vomit and urge to defecate. These were remedied by intake of a pinch of table salt and a glassful of water. To clean their teeth, in addition to brushing, a slice of areca nut husk is used for cleaning. Betel quid chewers were considerate about splitting quid when in public and expressed ways to avoid unpleasant sight. Of note is the sense of competition that results in producing the reddest spit implying that the person is able to produce the perfect mix of ingredients and the mastery of the betel quid chewing.

Betel quid chewing is identified as a traditional practice in several countries, including the Philippines, where it serves various social functions. Beyond its cultural role, literature suggests that the practice is linked to significant health implications, including the development of cardiovascular disease and various cancerous states. The research seeks to understand the lived experiences of those who chew betel quid, specifically looking at interpersonal, situational, and psychosocial factors, while also assessing the level of knowledge regarding health implications and the actual oral health status of the chewers.

The theoretical framework for this research is supported by Nola Pender’s Health Promotion Model. To address the research objectives, the author employed a dual methodological approach. A phenomenological approach was used to describe the lived experiences of the chewers, while a descriptive correlational design was utilized to assess the participants' knowledge of health practices, their oral health status, and associated demographic factors. The study utilized purposive sampling to select participants based on specific inclusion criteria. Ethics approval for the research was granted through the UPOU.

The study involved two distinct groups of participants. For the phenomenological description of lived experiences, 18 participants were interviewed, most of whom were male, until data saturation was reached. For the assessment of oral status and knowledge levels, 83 participants were surveyed, consisting of 64 males and 19 females. The demographic profile of the survey participants revealed a mean age of 52 years, with the majority falling into the 51 to 60 age range. Most participants were married and had been chewing betel quid for an average of 17.58 years. The typical daily consumption was between one and five betel quids. Regarding socio-economic status, the majority of participants were elementary undergraduates (55.4%), worked as farmers (63.9%), and had an average monthly income below the poverty threshold, specifically in the range of 0 to PhP5,000.00.

The findings regarding knowledge and oral health revealed significant concerns. The respondents demonstrated an average of 55.2% correct responses regarding factors related to health practices, indicating a moderate level of knowledge. The oral health assessment showed that most chewers suffered from dental issues, including having three to four teeth that were broken, worn-out, damaged, or missing. Mouth sores were a common occurrence, attributed to the excessive use of slaked lime, and betel quid staining was observed in the majority of chewers. In terms of statistical relationships, the study found that only occupation and age showed a significant relationship with oral health status.

The phenomenological description of lived experiences provided deep insight into the social and personal drivers of the practice. Interpersonal influences were heavily rooted in family traditions, with parents and grandparents serving as primary motivators through the hand-down of the practice. The presence of peers in the community further reinforces the habit and facilitates the passing of the practice to others. Situationally, chewing betel quid serves as a tool for socialization, fostering camaraderie, friendship, a sense of belongingness, and peer identity. The act of sharing ingredients among chewers creates a sense of "oneness," enjoyment, and solidarity when performed in groups.

Personal factors also played a role in the continuation of the practice. For dental hygiene, participants used brushing in addition to using a slice of areca nut husk to clean their teeth. Socially, chewers were mindful of public etiquette, such as splitting the quid to avoid unpleasant sights, and some even engaged in a form of competition to produce the "reddest spit," which was viewed as a sign of mastery in mixing the ingredients.

title: Biomodd: A Case Study In Combining Online Learning With On-Site New Media Art Practice
abstract: Biomodd is a new media art project that integrates cross-cultural dialogue, ecology and technology while encouraging innovative collaboration. The project started in 2007 in the United States, and has since spawned multiple versions that have been built both by the people that originally came up with the idea, and by other communities throughout the world. During its run in the Philippines, a team was formed to build an installation that went on display was exhibited in two cities in the Philippines. The UP Open University, in return for its sponsorship, employed the project as a springboard in a course for students to explore and practice new media art. Since Biomodd involved a series of on-site workshops and classroom sessions, the challenge was to find a way to engage students despite their ability to physically attend the workshops. This was addressed through the use of various online applications to accomplish tasks outside the construction of the art installation. Communication was coursed through several avenues, including the university's official learning management system, text messaging, mailing lists, online photo albums, personal blogs and mass media. Through an analysis of the exchanges conducted through these various channels of communication, we show how learners and course facilitators were able to build and sustain a sense of community, as well as connect with external stakeholders who enabled learners to extend their exploration in new media art practice as shaped by their experience of working on Biomodd, thus constituting a highly enriching learning experience.

The Biomodd project serves as a case study for integrating online learning with on-site new media art practice through a blended learning approach. Implemented by the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) for its Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program, the project explores the symbiosis between nature and technology. The study addresses the challenge of engaging students in hands-on, on-site artistic practice within an open and distance e-learning environment, which often faces issues such as social isolation and a lack of physical interaction.

The curriculum combined face-to-face workshops covering topics like plant care, game design, and hardware hacking with online communication and collaboration tools. To bridge the gap between remote and on-site learning, instructors utilized a learning management system, mailing lists, Google Docs, and social media platforms. Students were assessed on their physical contributions to an installation, their ability to design new media art proposals, and their participation in discussions.

Findings reveal that the blended learning environment supported a four-stage developmental process: students moved from being "naïvely sophisticated" to "paralyzed," then "explorative," and finally "empowered." The online components were vital during the initial stages, providing forums for articulation and support. Results showed high academic performance and the creation of projects large enough to be exhibited at a major event on the University of the Philippines campus. The combination of online and on-site interaction also helped build a strong sense of community.
