The Biomodd project serves as a case study for integrating online learning with on-site new media art practice through a blended learning approach. The project, which explores the symbiosis between nature and technology, was used by the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as an educational platform for its Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program.

The central problem addressed by the authors is the challenge of engaging students in a hands-on, on-site artistic practice within an open and distance e-learning environment. Traditional online learning often faces issues such as social isolation, varying levels of technical expertise, and a lack of physical interaction. Because the Biomodd installation required physical presence for workshops and construction, the researchers sought to determine if a blended learning model—combining online tools with face-to-face sessions—could effectively facilitate complex, creative, and collaborative artistic learning.

The context of the study is the Biomodd[LBA2] project in the Philippines. Biomodd is a nomadic, collaborative art project that utilizes themes such as hardware hacking, the creative reuse of e-waste, digital gaming culture, and the relationship between biological and electronic systems. The project emphasizes open-source principles and local cultural reinterpretation. In 2008, UPOU partnered with the project to create Multimedia Studies 198 (MMS 198), a course designed to move students from artistic concept to physical execution through the construction of the installation.

The methodology employed a blended learning design involving 24 students across two course offerings. The curriculum combined face-to-face workshops—covering topics like plant care, game design, and hardware hacking—with a variety of online communication and collaboration tools. To bridge the gap between remote and on-site learning, the instructors utilized the university's learning management system, mailing lists, Google Docs for scheduling and feedback, and social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter for public engagement and resource sourcing. Multimedia tools such as YouTube and Picasa were used to document progress and share prototypes. Students were assessed based on their physical contributions to the installation, their ability to design new media art proposals, and their participation in discussions.

The findings reveal that the blended learning environment supported a four-stage developmental process for the learners. Students moved from a state of "naïvely sophisticated" (having creative ideas without understanding technical feasibility) to being "paralyzed" (realizing their visions were non-viable), then "explorative" (using simple activities to understand media properties), and finally "empowered" (successfully manifesting artistic intent through physical artifacts). The online components were particularly vital during the "naïve" and "paralyzed" stages, providing forums for articulation and support.

The results showed high academic performance among the majority of students. Many students exceeded expected engagement levels, with many choosing to work in groups to create projects larger than anticipated, some of which were exhibited at a major event on the University of the Philippines campus. Furthermore, the study found that the combination of online and on-site interaction helped build a strong sense of community. This community existed not only among the students but also between the students and the external Biomodd team, as evidenced by passionate and argumentative discourse in student blogs and digital communications.

In conclusion, the authors state that the teaching method, combined with a strong sense of community, had a significant positive effect on learner academic performance. The study demonstrates that blended learning can successfully facilitate high-level, skills-based creative practice in a distance education setting.

The implications of the study suggest that while blended learning is effective, there are areas for refinement. The authors recommend investigating the reasons why a small percentage of students dropped out to improve accessibility. Additionally, they note that while gaming was a core theme of Biomodd, it was not effectively utilized as a learning tool in the course, suggesting that future iterations could better integrate gaming to enhance learning outcomes.

title: Living with and Caring for a Type I Diabetic Child: Coping and Depression Symptoms in Mothers
abstract: Voices of mothers living with and caring for their children with Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) will be explored in this study through the use of photovoice lens and survey. Studies show that parental coping with the stress of diabetes is likely to play an important role in child and family adjustment to the disease. Their coping skill not only influences their psychosocial health and wellbeing but it also affects their children’s psychosocial adjustment and quality of life (QOL). Thus, the paper aims to create a framework on the effect of the coping styles used by mothers of children with T1D to mothers’ psychosocial adjustment to the disease by using a combination of grounded theory, photovoice, and survey research design as methodology. With a 2-year reference period (2016-2018), around 50 mothers with Type 1 Diabetic children from at least three (3) Diabetic Club Organizations within Laguna will serve as the respondents of the study. Ten to 20 of them will be randomly selected to participate in a series of workshops or focus group discussions (FGDs) and photography sessions. Researcher-administered questionnaires will first be distributed to gather data onsocio-demographic characteristics, coping styles, and depression symptoms. The study will adopt the questions from The Center for Epidemiologic Studies - Depression Scale (CES-D; Radloff, 1977) questionnaire to assess symptoms of depression in mothers; and the Responses to Stress Questionnaire (RSQ) (Connor-Smith, 2000) to determine mothers’ coping styles. A workshop for randomly selected participants will then be conducted to explain to them how photovoice is conducted its specific do’s and dont’s. Photography sessions will be conducted to collect more in-depth data on mothers’ coping styles. Focus group discussions will serve as venue for the mothers to explain the meanings of their respective photographs; emerging patterns from their explanations will be observed. Data from the survey and photovoice sessions will then be analyzed to develop the framework. Key informant interviews (KIIs) with officials from the Provincial Health Office and randomly selected City/Municipal Health Offices will also be done to review existing policies and programs on Type 1 Diabetes in Laguna. These factors contribute significantly to the success of an effort (e.g. future health programs). Furthermore, gaining the support of policy makers is an essential part in strategic program planning (FAO, 2014). Recommendations based on the results of the study could help improve the identified existing policies and programs on Type 1 Diabetes and guide future activities, particularly on coping skills training for mothers to help lessen the impact of T1D on parents and families.

two:
The study addresses the challenges faced by mothers who are living with and caring for children diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes. Research indicates that how parents cope with the stress associated with diabetes is a significant factor in the adjustment of both the child and the family to the disease. A mother's coping skills are important because they influence her own psychosocial health and wellbeing, which in turn affects the psychosocial adjustment and quality of life of her child. The central problem involves understanding these coping styles and their relationship to the psychosocial adjustment of mothers to the disease.

To address this problem, the researchers aim to create a framework that illustrates the effect of various coping styles used by mothers of children with Type 1 Diabetes on their psychosocial adjustment. The study is set within a reference period spanning 2016 to 2018. The research context is located in Laguna, involving mothers of children with Type 1 Diabetes from at least three Diabetic Club Organizations.

The methodology employs a combination of grounded theory, photovoice, and survey research design. The study involves around 50 mothers who will serve as respondents. From this group, ten to 20 participants will be randomly selected to engage in a series of workshops, focus group discussions, and photography sessions. The data collection process begins with the distribution of researcher-administered questionnaires to gather information regarding socio-demographic characteristics, coping styles, and depression symptoms. To assess depression symptoms, the study utilizes questions from The Center for Epidemiologic Studies - Depression Scale. To determine coping styles, the Responses to Stress Questionnaire is employed.

Following the survey, a workshop will be conducted for the randomly selected participants to explain the specific do's and dont's of the photovoice method. Photography sessions will then be held to collect in-depth data regarding the coping styles of the mothers. The photovoice method is supplemented by focus group discussions, which provide a venue for mothers to explain the meanings behind their photographs. During these discussions, researchers will observe emerging patterns from the participants' explanations. The data gathered from both the survey and the photovoice sessions will be analyzed to develop the proposed framework. Additionally, the researchers will conduct key informant interviews with officials from the Provincial Health Office and randomly selected City/Municipal Health Offices to review existing policies and programs regarding Type 1 Diabetes in Laguna.

The findings of the study are intended to be derived from the integrated analysis of the survey data, the photovoice sessions, and the interviews with health officials. By examining the patterns in the photographs and the explanations provided in focus groups alongside the quantitative data from the questionnaires, the researchers seek to understand the complex relationship between coping mechanisms and psychosocial adjustment.

The conclusions and implications of this research are centered on the improvement of support systems for families dealing with Type 1 Diabetes. The study suggests that gaining the support of policy makers is an essential component of strategic program planning. By reviewing existing policies and programs through key informant interviews, the research aims to identify how current efforts can be made more successful. The ultimate goal is to provide recommendations that can help improve identified existing policies and programs. Furthermore, the study intends to guide future activities, with a specific focus on implementing coping skills training for mothers. Such training is intended to help lessen the overall impact of Type 1 Diabetes on both parents and their families.

title: Analysis of Reasons for filing Leave of Absence (LOA) and Application for Dropping of Course/s (DRP) of the Faculty of Management and Development Studies (FMDS) Students
abstract:
Literature about online learning as well as strategies developed for keeping students enrolled concentrated on both men and women in general without disaggregating findings (Mueller, 2008). However, it is essential to examine gender in relation to distance education since this is extensively promoted to women and it is also an institution where gender and power differences are constructed (Kramarae, 2003). Bean and Metzner (1985) considered gender as an important variable in studying attrition rates given the gender-specific roles the students carry outside their classes which would influence their decisions in their studies. 

In the Philippines, UP Open University offers online baccalaureate, post baccalaureate, continuing education programs, and massive open and distance e-learning courses. With the changing issues and challenges faced by women in society, gender differences on student attrition must be examined to better capture the realities and perspectives of women in the Philippines. Examining the various issues and challenges faced by online learners surfaced through their reasons for filing a leave of absence (LOA) or authorized dropping (DRP) of course will help institutions develop policies and programs for more effective student support. The study identified the challenges faced by the students leading to their decision to file for LOA or DRP and surfaced the gender implications at play in the said decisions
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This research addresses student attrition in distance education by focusing on why students file for a leave of absence or an application for dropping of courses. The study identifies a gap in existing literature, which often fails to disaggregate findings by gender. The authors argue that examining how gender influences these decisions is necessary, particularly because distance education is extensively promoted to women and serves as a space where gender and power differences are constructed.

The study is situated within the Philippines, focusing on students at the Faculty of Management and Development Studies at the University of the Philippines Open University. Because women face changing issues and challenges in society, the research examines gender differences in attrition to capture the specific realities and perspectives of women. This is based on the premise that gender is an important variable due to the gender-specific roles students carry outside of their formal classes, which influence their academic decisions.

The method involves analyzing the reasons students file for a leave of absence or authorized dropping of courses to uncover underlying factors that disrupt academic progress. The findings suggest that the reasons for leaving are not gender-neutral and that roles occupied outside of coursework play a significant role in enrollment. The study concludes that understanding these gendered realities is vital for institutional development, helping institutions create effective support systems and policies to address student needs and mitigate attrition.

title: Empowering Women Entrepreneurs through Open and Distance Learning: The Case of the Germany Alumnae
abstract:
This research will look into how Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) empower women entrepreneurs specifically in their ability to use what they have learned from the course in another context; ability to work independently and share experiences with other participants, among others.

Specifically, it will look into how the entrepreneurship online modules were designed and implemented; the perception of participants regarding the online program; the business plans as immediate outputs of the program; the knowledge and competencies gained by the participants; and the progress of at least three projects presented by them.
The research will focus on the case of the Blended Learning Course on Entrepreneurship for Germany Alumnae that was conducted by the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) and Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ). Further, it will also follow up on three business ideas that were developed by three participants of the program.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This research investigates the role of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) in empowering women entrepreneurs, specifically examining their ability to apply online course knowledge to various contexts, work independently, and share experiences with peers. The study focuses on a Blended Learning Course on Entrepreneurship designed for Germany Alumnae, a collaborative effort between the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ).

Utilizing a case study approach, the methodology evaluates the design and implementation of entrepreneurship online modules, participant perceptions, and the business plans generated as immediate curriculum outputs. To assess how theoretical knowledge translates into practical progress, the researcher employs a longitudinal aspect by following three specific business ideas developed by individual participants. This allows for an empirical assessment of the competencies gained and the actual trajectory of women-led business projects.

The findings address the effectiveness of ODeL in fostering empowerment through structured, flexible learning environments that support independent work and peer-to-peer engagement. The study concludes that ODeL serves as a significant tool for female economic participation and professional development. By demonstrating a link between online modules and real-world business progress, the research highlights the potential for collaborative international digital learning frameworks to support women entrepreneurs.

title: Development of a Counselling Framework for Mothers of Children with Perinatally Acquired Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Disease
abstract: HIV cases in the Philippines are increasing every month according to the HIV/AIDS & ART Registry of the Philippines of the Department of Health and so are cases of mothers with perinatally infected children (Department of Health Epidemiology Bureau, 2016). At present, psychosocial and nutrition counseling is only provided after 6 months post delivery. The purpose of this study is to develop a framework for counselling mothers of children with perinatally acquired HIV disease. It will utilize a grounded theory approach, using interviews and focus group discussions of mothers living with HIV, as well as experts in HIV and counselling. Themes and their relationships will be identified to create a framework for counselling the participants.

A significant gap exists in current healthcare delivery, as psychosocial and nutrition counseling is only provided to these mothers six months after delivery. This delay results in a lack of immediate support during the critical early postpartum period. To address this, the study aims to develop a specialized, structured counseling framework to guide practitioners in supporting this specific demographic.

The researcher employs a qualitative methodology using a grounded theory approach. Data collection involves interviews and focus group discussions with both mothers living with HIV and experts in the fields of HIV and counseling. By engaging both primary stakeholders and subject matter experts, the study seeks to capture a comprehensive range of perspectives. The methodology focuses on identifying specific themes and the relationships between them through systematic qualitative data analysis. title: Gender Sensitivity of UPOU-Produced Open Educational Resources
abstract: In support of the Magna Carta of Women and to further promote gender mainstreaming, the Philippine national government issued a circular directing government agencies, including state colleges and universities to adopt Gender Equality Guidelines in the development of media policies and programs. Studies (Benavot, 2016; Blumberg, 2007; Jenkins & Phillips, 1995; Kerkhoven, Russo, Land-Zandstra, Saxena, & Rodenburg, 2016; Mills & Mustapha, 2015;) showed that gender bias and language insensitivity in learning materials negatively affect female students’ general performance. The Multimedia Center (MC), the unit of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) that is tasked to design, develop, produce, and disseminate multimedia course materials has been implementing practices to make UPOU multimedia learning materials more inclusive and gender fair. This study examines the gender fairness of the “Open Educational Resources (OER) for Technology for Teaching and Learning” video series. These series of videos produced by the MC is disseminated to the learners and general public via the UPOU Networks, the university’s virtual repository of learning materials. To study the gender sensitivity of the videos, content analysis will be done using the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) gender-sensitive indicators and the Philippine Commission on Women Towards a Gender Fair Media guidelines.

The research addresses the problem of potential gender bias and language insensitivity within learning materials, as existing studies have demonstrated that such biases can negatively affect the general performance of female students. Because multimedia course materials are a significant component of modern education, ensuring they are inclusive and gender fair is a critical concern. The Multimedia Center at UPOU is responsible for the design, development, production, and dissemination of these materials. This specific study focuses on evaluating the gender fairness of the “Open Educational Resources (OER) for Technology for Teaching and Learning” video series.

To address the research problem, the study employs a content analysis method using established frameworks, specifically the gender-sensitive indicators provided by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Philippine Commission on Women Towards a Gender Fair Media guidelines. The study aims to systematically examine how gender is represented and how sensitive the language and content are within the video series.

title: Gender Portrayal in UP Open University Social Media Sites
abstract: The UP Open University (UPOU) social media sites with about 40,000 followers accross its social media pages is assumed to have a significant role in disseminating information and knowledge for most of its learners both local and offshore. According to The Statistics Portal (statista.com), the number of social media users around the globe is estimated to increase from 2.46 billion in 2017 to 2.77 billion in 2019. Three (3) of four (4) internet users use social media, with women (76%) using social networking sites more than men (72%). title: Knowledge Management in the University of the Philippines Open University: Exploring Gender Differences of Student Support Employees
abstract: When the COVID-19 global pandemic broke out, the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) made adjustments to its operations to address the heightened need for its support services. These support services are mainly provision of information and knowledge of and about the university stored both physically and digitally, with more women providing support services than men. To ensure knowledge is accessible and available amidst any disruption, knowledge management practices must be streamlined and sustained. However, studies analyzing gender differences in knowledge management of educational institutions are lacking. This study aims to fill the current research gap in the context of an educational institution, and study the gender differences in UPOU in terms of knowledge management practices. Data will be collected from targeted respondents who provide support services to UPOU constituents. Descriptive statistics and cross tabulations will be used to analyze the data gathered.

title: Chatbot Gender and User Behavior and Satisfaction
abstract: As a pioneer in open and distance e-Learning in the Philippines, UPOU continues to explore various information and communication technologies in enhancing not just its course development and delivery, but its provision of support and information services as well. One of the tools that is gaining popularity in businesses and even in universities in recent years is artificial intelligence (AI). The integration of AI-based tools such as chatbots in an organization’s systems and processes promise some degree of streamlining given the increasing demand of customers. This proposal will document and share the to compare the number of chatbot inquiries and conversations by gender before and during the global public health crisis. Data will be collected using document analysis through an existing chatbot monitoring tool. Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations will be utilized to analyze the study data. This study puts forward its assumption that male and female users of the UPOU chatbot will have different frequencies of chatbot inquiries and conservations, and different user behaviors based on the UPOU chatbot’s gender.

The study focuses on the increasing use of AI-based tools, such as chatbots, which organizations employ to streamline processes in response to growing demands.

The central problem addressed is how user demographics, particularly gender, influence interactions with AI-driven support tools. The researchers aim to investigate whether significant differences exist between male and female users regarding their engagement with the UPOU chatbot, specifically comparing the frequency of inquiries and the nature of conversations. Additionally, the research explores whether the perceived gender of the chatbot itself influences user behavior and satisfaction levels. The study is framed by the global public health crisis, which forced a shift in service delivery models; thus, the researchers intend to compare chatbot engagement data from the period before the crisis to the period during the crisis.

The proposed methodology utilizes document analysis of data gathered from an existing chatbot monitoring tool. Using descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations, the study tests the hypothesis that male and female users will exhibit different inquiry frequencies and that behaviors will vary depending on the chatbot's assigned gender. The findings aim to provide empirical data on gendered patterns of AI interaction, which could inform how universities design inclusive AI personas and optimize chatbot programming to serve a diverse student population.

title: Social Support as a Protective Factor Against Online Pornography and Sexual Aggressive Behavior among High School Students in Los Baños, Laguna
abstract: With the advent of new technologies such as the internet, adolescent access to pornography has substantially expanded. Research show that the prevalence of online pornography viewing among adolescents has increased significantly, partly attributed to the availability of such online materials. Their exposure to internet pornography has been linked to stronger beliefs in gender stereotypes, particularly in relation to sex and attitudes and behaviors supportive of sexual violence—perpetrated particularly against women and children. While the adolescents’ internet pornography use and its negative effects on healthy sexual development have been extensively investigated, the protective factors that can prevent or mitigate these adverse effects have not been explored much. Based on the conceptualization of a stress-buffering model of social support, this study will determine whether social support would provide a buffer against the negative effects of internet pornography on sexually aggressive behaviours of High School students in Los Baños, Laguna. The respondents will be asked to accomplish an online adopted survey which includes questions on their internet pornography use, sexually aggressive behaviours, and perception of social support from parents, school teachers, and friends. Data will be analyzed using a combination of descriptive and inferential statistics. Results of this study will provide insights for the development of interventions aimed at preventing adolescents’ use of internet pornography and practice of sexual aggressive behaviors to promote healthy sexual development.

Framed within the stress-buffering model of social support, the research investigates whether social support acts as a buffer against the negative effects of internet pornography on the sexually aggressive behaviors of high school students in Los Baños, Laguna. Using a quantitative method, the researchers will employ an online survey to measure three primary variables: the extent of internet pornography use, levels of sexually aggressive behaviors, and perceived social support from parents, school teachers, and friends. Data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to identify relationships between these variables.

The study aims to determine if higher levels of perceived social support from parents, teachers, and friends significantly mitigate the link between pornography consumption and sexual aggression. The findings are expected to provide empirical evidence on whether interpersonal connections function as protective factors. Ultimately, the research seeks to offer insights into adolescent sexual development and the influence of digital media, aiming to inform targeted interventions designed to prevent problematic pornography use and reduce sexually aggressive behaviors.

title: The Relationship of Gender Difference and Self- Regulation Among Online Learners in the Philippines
abstract: The drastic shift to online education has continued to persist among learners as the COVID-19 pandemic continues to affect every nation worldwide. Besides the issue of the digital divide, the current online learning environment of learners has also paved the way for issues based on gender and academic performance. Using the Winne and Hadwin’s Self Regulation Theory, this study will explore the relationship of the gender identity of online learners from the University of the Philippines Open University to their self regulation practices through measuring their academic performance. Utilizing a mixed-method approach, the researchers will aim to give an emphasis on the aspect of gender in online learning which is seldom realized. In addition, this study also aims to contribute to the information-building of gender and online learning in the Philippines.

The core problem addressed by this research is the ongoing shift toward online education caused by the persistent effects of the COVID-19 pandemic across the globe. While much of the discourse surrounding remote learning focuses on the digital divide, this study identifies a need to investigate issues related to gender and academic performance within these digital environments. The researchers suggest that the current online learning landscape has created specific challenges and dynamics based on gender that have not been sufficiently explored.

The context of this research is situated within the specific educational setting of the University of the Philippines Open University. By focusing on this institution, the study seeks to understand how learners within this specific framework navigate the complexities of remote instruction. The researchers note that the aspect of gender in online learning is a factor that is seldom realized, indicating a gap in current academic understanding and institutional awareness regarding how gender identity interacts with digital pedagogy.

To address this problem, the study utilizes Winne and Hadwin’s Self Regulation Theory as its theoretical framework. This framework allows the researchers to explore the relationship between the gender identity of online learners and their self-regulation practices. The methodology employed is a mixed-method approach, which allows for a comprehensive investigation by combining different types of data to provide a more holistic view of the phenomenon. The researchers intend to measure self-regulation practices through the measurement of academic performance, using these metrics to determine if significant relationships exist between a learner's gender and their ability to regulate their own learning processes.

The findings and conclusions of the study are intended to contribute to the broader body of knowledge regarding gender and online learning within the Philippines. By employing a mixed-method approach, the researchers aim to provide a nuanced understanding that goes beyond simple quantitative correlations, potentially uncovering the qualitative experiences of learners as they manage their studies remotely. The study seeks to emphasize the importance of gender as a variable in the success of online education, moving the conversation beyond mere access to technology and toward the social and individual identities of the students themselves.

The implications of this research are significant for educators, policymakers, and institutions operating in the digital space. By highlighting the relationship between gender and self-regulation, the study aims to provide information that can help in building a more inclusive and effective online learning environment. Understanding how gender influences self-regulation practices can lead to more targeted support systems for students, helping to mitigate the academic disparities that may arise from the unique demands of online learning. Ultimately, the work seeks to contribute to the information-building process concerning the intersection of gender and digital education in the Philippine context.

title: Locating the Gender Voice in the Disaster Risk and Reduction Management Discourse of ASEAN
abstract: Hearing the disaster risk and reduction management (DRRM) approach of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states (AMS) from the AMS themselves is an attempt to decenter the non-ASEAN critical discourse that says ASEAN is lacking dedication in forwarding a truly holistic and proactive approach to natural disaster. While understanding the contexts, perceptions, and discourses that could forward the discussions regarding the ASEAN Member States (AMS) and their experience of natural disasters provides a space for the AMS, there are other voices that can be surfaced, not just the institutional voice. This study shall re-examine the AMS speeches performed in intergovernmental fora and conferences to locate the gender voice. How do the AMS represent gender in the natural disaster discourse? What space do the AMS provide for gender voice in natural disaster management discourse? Using discourse analysis, the recorded speeches (with audio, visual, and written speech transcription) from each of the ten (10) ASEAN Member States (Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Viet Nam) through their representative in inter-governmental fora or conferences relating to Natural Disasters will be analyzed to surface the gender voice.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
The research study "Locating the Gender Voice in the Disaster Risk and Reduction Management Discourse of ASEAN" examines the tension between official institutional discourse and critical external perspectives regarding the disaster risk and reduction management (DRRM) approaches of ASEAN member states. While external critics often suggest ASEAN lacks the dedication for a proactive approach to natural disasters, the authors argue that focusing only on institutional voices may overlook vital perspectives. The study aims to move beyond the official narrative to determine how gender is integrated into the broader regional discourse on natural disaster management.

Situated within the intergovernmental discourse of the ten ASEAN member states, the research employs a qualitative discourse analysis. The researchers re-examine multi-modal data, including audio, visual, and written transcriptions of speeches performed by representatives during intergovernmental fora and conferences. The study is guided by two primary questions: how member states represent gender within natural disaster discourse, and what specific space, if any, is provided for the "gender voice" within these management discourses.

The intended outcome is to locate the "gender voice" within the official DRRM discourse of ASEAN. By identifying the presence or absence of gendered perspectives in high-level speeches, the research seeks to challenge or validate existing critical discourses. Ultimately, the findings may highlight gaps in regional policies and provide a basis for more inclusive disaster management strategies that account for gendered vulnerabilities and roles.

title: Finding the Gender Space in Indigenous Peoples Civil Society Organizations Engagement with the ASEAN
abstract:
While Indigenous People Civil Society Organizations (IP CSOs) are able to forward various concerns such as indigenous peoples’ rights, human rights, and environmental issues, one issue
that has not been emphasized is gender. Though it is assumed that the issues forwarded carry with them the concept of intersectionality, there is a need to uncover the extent as to how gender is prioritized in their advocacy. This research shall re-examine existing IP CSOs’ views and engagement practices with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that emerged in three engagement spaces where ASEAN and CSOs engage: ASEAN-established, ASEAN-recognized, and “created” spaces to find the gender space. How does each view represent gender? What gender representation practices are innate in the identified views and engagement practices? Through an interpretative content analysis anchored on ethnomethodology, the gender representation practices shall be extracted from IP CSO’s documents available at the web such as official minutes of engagement, official statements, press releases, website postings, and social media posts dated from 2017 to 2020.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This research investigates a gap in the advocacy efforts of Indigenous Peoples Civil Society Organizations (IP CSOs), specifically regarding the under-emphasis of gender within their discourse. While it is often assumed that the human rights and environmental issues championed by these organizations inherently incorporate intersectionality, the authors argue for a formal investigation into the actual extent to which gender is prioritized within their advocacy frameworks.

The study focuses on the engagement between IP CSOs and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), categorizing these interactions into three spaces: ASEAN-established, ASEAN-recognized, and "created" spaces. Using an interpretative content analysis anchored in ethnomethodology, the researchers examined digital materials from 2017 to 2020, including official minutes, statements, press releases, website postings, and social media posts. The study seeks to understand how gender is conceptualized and manifested within these formal and informal structures of regional cooperation.

The research aims to determine how gender is represented and what specific representation practices are innate to these engagement spaces. The findings seek to reveal whether gender is treated as a standalone issue, a secondary concern, or integrated into broader struggles for sovereignty and environmental justice. Ultimately, the study aims to clarify the state of gender mainstreaming in IP CSO engagements, offering a tool for IP CSOs to ensure intersectionality and providing ASEAN with insight into how civil society represents the diverse needs of indigenous communities.

title: Women’s Participation in the Philippine Technology  Startup Ecosystem: A Baseline Survey
abstract: Over the last decade, the Philippine technology startup ecosystem has been continuously expanding due to the influx of venture capital, incubators, accelerators, and tech entrepreneurs and government support in terms of financial incentives, tax breaks, and access to funding. In the global context, ample literature reports the contributions of women in the survival and growth of technology startups. Despite this, there has been a dearth of local studies on the involvement of Filipino women in the success of many technology startups in the country. In this project, a scoping study will be conducted to generate baseline information on the representation and extent of involvement of women in the technology startup ecosystem. The findings of this project will be used in the formulation of a supportive framework for women's engagement with technology startups and the course development of non-formal education and degree programs related to women and gender studies.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
The research project "Women’s Participation in the Philippine Technology Startup Ecosystem: A Baseline Survey," authored by Lianne Angelico Depante, Leo Mendel Rosario, Pedcris Orencio, and Joane Serrano, addresses a significant gap in understanding gender dynamics within the expanding Philippine technology sector. Despite the growth of the local ecosystem driven by venture capital, incubators, and government support, there is a notable lack of local research regarding the involvement of Filipino women in the success of these startups.

The authors identify the dearth of specific data concerning women's representation and involvement as a primary problem, noting that without such information, it is difficult to understand their role or the challenges they face. To address this, the researchers conducted a scoping study using a survey to generate baseline information regarding the level of representation and extent of involvement of women within the Philippine technology startup ecosystem.

The findings are intended to serve as a critical resource for future development. The researchers plan to use this baseline data to formulate a supportive framework designed to enhance women's engagement with technology startups. Additionally, the results aim to inform the development of educational curricula, specifically regarding degree programs and non-formal education related to women and gender studies, bridging the gap between global knowledge and local reality.

title: Breaking the Glass Ceiling:  A Case Study of Challenges and Successes of Women Leadership Positions in the Philippine Technology Startup Ecosystem (PTSE)
abstract: Despite an increasing number of women entrepreneurs in the Philippines, the technology startup ecosystem is still dominated by men. There is a lack of research focusing on the experiences of women in leadership positions within the Philippine technology startup ecosystem (PTSE), and this study seeks to fill that void. This research can offer insights that can guide the development of policies and programs to support the advancement of women in leadership roles within the PTSE by obtaining an understanding of the difficulties faced by women in leadership positions within the PTSE and the methods they have used to overcome those difficulties. By understanding the challenges experienced by women in leadership roles within the PTSE, initiatives, strategies, and approaches that can enhance the environment for women in leadership positions in Philippine technology startups can be developed. This study can also advance our understanding of how gender dynamics may differ in various social, cultural, and economic contexts when it comes to entrepreneurship and leadership. This can also serve as a valuable case study for future studies in this field by providing a thorough understanding of the experiences of women leaders in technology startups in the Philippines. The study's findings will be used to devise a framework for promoting the development of an environment that would allow women to fully participate in the ecosystem of technology startups. The study will adopt a case study approach in order to understand the challenges encountered by women in leadership roles within the PTSE and the strategies they have employed to overcome them. A purposeful selection of women executives from Philippine-based digital startups will make up the sample.

In the Philippines, traditional gender roles prioritizing caregiving can impede professional pursuits, while a lack of visible female role models prevents younger women from envisioning themselves in leadership.

Using a mixed-methods case study approach involving surveys, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussions, the research aims to identify barriers, success factors, and the influence of cultural factors on leadership. The ultimate goal is to develop a supportive framework to create a more inclusive environment. Findings are intended to inform non-formal continuing education and guide policy development to address specific barriers like mentorship and funding, ultimately fostering gender diversity to drive innovation and economic growth.

title: Gender Fairness of UPOU-Produced Open Educational Resources
abstract: In support of the Magna Carta of Women and to further promote gender mainstreaming, the Philippine national government issued a circular directing government agencies, including state colleges and universities to adopt Gender Equality Guidelines in the development of media policies and programs. Studies (Benavot, 2016; Blumberg, 2007; Jenkins & Phillips, 1995; Kerkhoven, Russo, Land-Zandstra, Saxena, & Rodenburg, 2016; Mills & Mustapha, 2015;) showed that gender bias and language insensitivity in learning materials negatively affect female students’ general performance. The Multimedia Center (MC), the unit of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) that is tasked to design, develop, produce, and disseminate multimedia course materials has been implementing practices to make UPOU multimedia learning materials more inclusive and gender fair. This study examines the gender fairness of the “Open Educational Resources (OER) for Technology for Teaching and Learning” video series. These series of videos produced by the MC is disseminated to the learners and general public via the UPOU Networks, the university’s virtual repository of learning materials. To study the gender sensitivity of the videos, content analysis will be done using the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) gender-sensitive indicators and the Philippine Commission on Women Towards a Gender Fair Media guidelines.

title: Analysis of Gender Portrayal in UP Open University Social Media Sites
abstract: The UP Open University (UPOU) social media sites with about 40,000 followers accross its social media pages is assumed to have a significant role in disseminating information and knowledge for most of its learners both local and offshore. According to The Statistics Portal (statista.com), the number of social media users around the globe is estimated to increase from 2.46 billion in 2017 to 2.77 billion in 2019. Three (3) of four (4) internet users use social media, with women (76%) using social networking sites more than men (72%). This study aims to examine the portrayal and representation of women and men in the graphics and videos posted across UPOU social media sites: Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter. This study will make use of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) as its theoretical and analytic framework. The study will make use of the Gender-Sensitive Indicators for Media (GSIM) by UNESCO (2012) as the analytical tool in analyzing gender portrayal and representation in UPOU social media posts.

Given that UPOU utilizes various platforms to reach a diverse population of local and offshore students, the study examines whether the university's digital content reflects or reinforces specific gender dynamics. This investigation is situated within the context of rising global social media usage, noting that women utilize social networking sites at a higher rate than men.

The primary aim of the research is to examine the portrayal and representation of women and men within the visual content posted on UPOU’s Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter accounts. Specifically, the researchers seek to understand how gender is depicted in the graphics and videos that constitute the university's digital communication strategy.

To achieve this objective, the study employs Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) as both the theoretical and analytic framework to examine how language and imagery function to shape meaning and power dynamics. The researchers utilize the Gender-Sensitive Indicators for Media (GSIM) established by UNESCO in 2012 as the primary analytical instrument to measure and categorize the portrayal and representation of gender within the selected social media posts.

title: Breaking the Glass Ceiling? A Case Study of Challenges and Successes of Women Leadership Positions in the Philippine Technology Startup Ecosystem (PTSE)
abstract: Despite an increasing number of women entrepreneurs in the Philippines, the technology startup ecosystem is still dominated by men. There is a lack of research focusing on the experiences of women in leadership positions within the Philippine technology startup ecosystem (PTSE), and this study seeks to fill that void. This research can offer insights that can guide the development of policies and programs to support the advancement of women in leadership roles within the PTSE by obtaining an understanding of the difficulties faced by women in leadership positions within the PTSE and the methods they have used to overcome those difficulties. By understanding the challenges experienced by women in leadership roles within the PTSE, initiatives, strategies, and approaches that can enhance the environment for women in leadership positions in Philippine technology startups can be developed. This study can also advance our understanding of how gender dynamics may differ in various social, cultural, and economic contexts when it comes to entrepreneurship and leadership. This can also serve as a valuable case study for future studies in this field by providing a thorough understanding of the experiences of women leaders in technology startups in the Philippines. The study's findings will be used to devise a framework for promoting the development of an environment that would allow women to fully participate in the ecosystem of technology startups. The study will adopt a case study approach in order to understand the challenges encountered by women in leadership roles within the PTSE and the strategies they have employed to overcome them. A purposeful selection of women executives from Philippine-based digital startups will make up the sample.

title: Artscience Thinking for the Global South
abstract: Pluridisciplinary practices that span art and science are well-known in Western research and creative communities. Some of the most interesting and significant of these works confront audiences with deep questions about "life, the universe, and everything” (with apologies to Douglas Adams). But in the Global South—where addressing basic human needs, achieving economic and political security, and adapting to the unfolding climate crisis—are widely regarded as priorities, is there even space or time for the same? Using recent artscience research and creative projects I have been involved in, I argue that despite—or indeed because—of the challenges confronting the Global South, research, practice, and education on the intersections of the arts and the sciences is more necessary than ever.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Diego S. Maranan’s "Artscience Thinking for the Global South" explores the intersection of arts, humanities, and sciences through a multidisciplinary lens. Maranan argues that while artists and scientists often seek answers to similar fundamental questions, they frequently operate in isolation. He proposes "Artscience Thinking" as a framework to bridge this gap, moving beyond simple science communication toward a deep, integrated engagement where both fields inform and transform one another. This approach seeks to move away from a dichotomy between the arts and sciences, focusing instead on nurturing curiosity, openness, and risk-taking to address complex global challenges.

The methodology combines multidisciplinary research, hands-on prototyping, and community-based co-creation. Research avenues include "dancerly knowledge" and somatic research, which uses technology to explore the lived, internal perception of the body. Other methods include "Science by Way of Art," involving diverse professionals in artistic processes, and "futures thinking" through speculative design to prototype future scenarios.

Findings illustrate diverse applications: somatic technology projects like *Haplós* demonstrated that vibrotactile stimuli can increase bodily awareness, while ecology projects like *Biomodd* showed how technology and ecology can converge in symbiotic exchanges. Research also found that engaging arts with science often takes on a political or advocacy bent, such as decolonizing knowledge. Ultimately, Maranan suggests this approach helps prepare individuals to navigate future complexities and develop deeper empathy.

Diego S. Maranan’s presentation, "Artscience Thinking for the Global South," explores the intersection of arts, humanities, and sciences through a multidisciplinary lens. Maranan posits that while artists and scientists often seek answers to similar fundamental questions regarding human existence, they frequently operate in isolation. He proposes "Artscience Thinking" as a framework to bridge this gap, moving beyond simple science communication toward a deep, integrated engagement where both fields inform and transform one another. This approach seeks to move away from a dichotomy that forces individuals to choose between the arts or the sciences, focusing instead on nurturing creative traits like curiosity, openness, and risk-taking to address complex global challenges.

The methodology combines multidisciplinary research, hands-on prototyping, and community-based co-creation. Maranan utilizes several research avenues, including "dancerly knowledge" and somatic research, which uses technology to explore the "soma," or the lived, internal perception of the body. Another method is "Science by Way of Art," which involves open calls to diverse professionals—such as philosophers, chemists, and science fiction writers—to engage with scientific research through artistic processes. Finally, the presenter utilizes "futures thinking" and speculative design, such as hackathons and meta-futurism labs, to prototype future scenarios and resist received images of the future.

Findings from these projects illustrate the diverse applications of Artscience Thinking. In somatic technology, the project *Haplós* demonstrated that vibrotactile stimuli can increase bodily awareness and sensation. In ecology and systems thinking, the *Biomodd* and *Biodiversity Tower* projects showed how computer technology and ecology can converge in symbiotic exchanges, such as using waste heat from electronics to support living ecosystems. Furthermore, the research found that when the arts are engaged with science, the engagement often takes on a political or advocacy bent, such as decolonizing knowledge. The presenter also notes that many interesting outcomes arise from serendipitous, accidental inquiry.

The conclusions suggest that Artscience Thinking provides a unique toolkit for both fields: the arts help sciences identify new questions and expand models of human experience, while the sciences offer the arts new tools for public engagement. The implications are significant for education, technology design, and social engagement. In education, it suggests teaching art within an artscience framework to develop systems thinking. In technology design, "designing with/for the soma" could lead to new medical technologies for neuroadaptive therapies. Ultimately, Maranan suggests this interdisciplinary approach helps prepare individuals to navigate future complexities and develop deeper empathy for the self, others, and the world.

title: Understanding Menopausal Experiences of Dumagat Women: A Qualitative Study
abstract: Around the time of transition to menopausal period, women experience mental, and psychological disorders that require adequate attention to these symptoms. Women have different experiences around menopause and after it due to physiological, emotional, and psychological changes. This study is an attempt to make a significant contribution to the MENSESC project at the University of Lincoln which aims to determine how women live and understand the menopause in low SES settings across cultural contexts; ascertain what factors may shape women’s experience of the menopause in these contexts; identify what aspects of women’s lives, if any, are impacted during menopausal time and determine what women themselves need in these contexts to have quality of life during and beyond the menopause.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This research addresses how women experience the transition into menopause, specifically focusing on the mental and psychological disorders that can arise during this period. Because women undergo significant physiological, emotional, and psychological changes, individual experiences vary widely. The study seeks to address a gap in understanding how women in low socio-economic status settings navigate these changes across different cultural contexts. By focusing on a specific indigenous group, the research aims to provide a deeper understanding of the unique challenges faced by women in such environments.

The study is situated within the MENSESC project at the University of Lincoln, which aims to determine how women live and understand the menopause in low socio-economic status settings. The research intends to identify which aspects of women's lives are impacted and what these women need to maintain a high quality of life. Utilizing a qualitative research design, the methodology involves interviews and focus group discussions with a sample of 15 menopausal Dumagat women residing in Rizal. Data collection will continue until data saturation is reached.

The findings aim to document the lived experiences of Dumagat women, highlighting the specific changes they encounter and the cultural and environmental factors that influence how they perceive and manage the transition. The conclusions are expected to serve as an assessment for future research and offer insights that can be coordinated with research efforts in different countries. The work emphasizes the need for adequate attention to mental and psychological symptoms in nursing and healthcare to inform culturally sensitive support systems.

Because women undergo significant physiological, emotional, and psychological changes during and after menopause, individual experiences vary widely. The study seeks to address a gap in understanding how women in low socio-economic status settings navigate these changes across different cultural contexts. By focusing on a specific indigenous group, the research aims to provide a deeper understanding of the unique challenges faced by women in such environments.

The context of this study is situated within the broader MENSESC project at the University of Lincoln. This larger project is designed to determine how women live and understand the menopause in low socio-economic status settings across various cultural contexts. The research aims to ascertain the specific factors that may shape a woman's experience of menopause within these particular contexts. Furthermore, the study intends to identify which aspects of women's lives are impacted during the menopausal period and to determine what these women themselves need to maintain a high quality of life both during and beyond menopause.

To achieve these objectives, the study utilizes a qualitative research design. The methodology involves conducting interviews and focus group discussions with a sample of Dumagat menopausal women. The researchers plan to recruit 15 menopausal Dumagat women residing in Rizal, the area where the Dumagats live. The data collection process will continue until data saturation is reached. A specific set of questions has been prepared to guide the focus group discussions and the individual interviews to ensure the research goals are met.

The findings of the study are intended to contribute to the existing body of knowledge regarding menopausal experiences in marginalized or low socio-economic settings. By documenting the lived experiences of Dumagat women, the research will highlight the specific physiological, emotional, and psychological changes they encounter. The study aims to uncover the cultural and environmental factors that influence how these women perceive and manage the menopausal transition. Through the qualitative data gathered from the interviews and focus group discussions, the researchers hope to identify the specific needs of these women to ensure their well-being and quality of life.

The conclusions drawn from this research are expected to serve as an assessment for future research on menopausal women. By providing a localized perspective from the Dumagat community, the study will offer insights that can be coordinated with research efforts in different countries. The implications of this work extend to the field of nursing and healthcare, as it emphasizes the need for adequate attention to the mental and psychological symptoms women experience during menopause. Ultimately, the study seeks to inform better support systems and interventions that are culturally sensitive and tailored to the needs of women in low socio-economic status settings.

title: The BUKAS Lab: Opening artscience exploration and futures literacy in the Global South
abstract: BUKAS is a physical space and collaboration platform for pluridisciplinary and intersectoral initiatives in art, design, technology, and futures literacy centered around the context of the sustainable development and socioeconomic justice in the context of the Philippines in particular and the Global South in general. In this institutional presentation, we describe the constitution of BUKAS and a sampling of its current and past projects and initiatives.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The BUKAS Lab is a collaborative platform and physical space designed to foster pluridisciplinary initiatives at the intersection of art, design, technology, and futures literacy. Operating within the context of sustainable development and socioeconomic justice in the Philippines and the broader Global South, the lab addresses the need for transdisciplinary approaches to navigate complex realities by bridging the gap between the arts and sciences. The initiative is a partnership between the University of the Philippines – Open University (UPOU), which provides a foundation in open and distance learning, and Space Ecologies Art and Design (SEADS), which contributes a transdisciplinary, cross-cultural perspective.

The lab employs various hybrid and hands-on approaches, including interdisciplinary research, the SHARES framework to enable humanities contributions to science, speculative design, and residency programs focusing on themes like deep time and indigenous perspectives. Findings from these projects demonstrate practical applications of these methods. The "Creative Turn in the Sciences" project identified an under-supported artscience community in the Philippines and developed tools to integrate the humanities into scientific research. The "Wearable Futures Hackathon" resulted in student-led prototypes addressing local needs, such as soil pH detection gloves and anti-sexual-assault underwear. Additionally, the "Emerging Futurist Residency" facilitated radical critiques of cultural symbols. Ultimately, the lab demonstrates that integrating art-based thinking with scientific inquiry can address complex socioeconomic and environmental challenges.

It addresses the need for transdisciplinary approaches to navigate complex and uncertain realities by bridging the gap between the arts and sciences to develop alternative models through critical inquiry and experimentation.

UPOU provides a foundation in open and distance learning, ensuring accessibility for a broad range of Filipinos, including those studying overseas. SEADS contributes a transdisciplinary, cross-cultural perspective, bringing together artists, scientists, engineers, and activists from various countries. SEADS utilizes methodologies centered on community building, co-creation, bottom-up design, and a hacking/open-source ethos.

The BUKAS Lab serves as a physical space and a collaborative platform designed to foster pluridisciplinary and intersectoral initiatives. Centered on the intersection of art, design, technology, and futures literacy, the lab operates within the specific context of sustainable development and socioeconomic justice in the Philippines and the broader Global South. The name "BUKAS" draws on the Filipino language to reference both "openness" (*bukás*) and "the future" (*búkas*), signaling a vision for an inclusive and possible future.

The primary problem addressed by the BUKAS Lab is the need for transdisciplinary approaches to navigate complex, uncertain, and turbulent realities. By bridging the gap between the arts and sciences, the lab seeks to move beyond dominant paradigms of the future and instead develop alternative models through critical inquiry and hands-on experimentation. The initiative aims to support a nascent artscience community of practice in the Philippines, providing the recognition and structural support necessary for these creative and scientific endeavors to thrive.

The context of the lab is rooted in the unique educational landscape of the Philippines. It is an initiative born from a partnership between the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies at the University of the Philippines – Open University (UPOU) and Space Ecologies Art and Design (SEADS). UPOU provides a foundation in open and distance learning, having pioneered online teaching in the country since 1995. This institutional background ensures that the lab's initiatives are accessible to a broad range of Filipinos, including those studying overseas. SEADS contributes a transdisciplinary, cross-cultural perspective, bringing together artists, scientists, engineers, and activists from various countries, including Belgium, the UK, Malaysia, Kosovo, the US, and the Philippines. SEADS utilizes methodologies centered on community building, co-creation, bottom-up design, and a hacking/open-source ethos.

The method employed by the BUKAS Lab involves a variety of collaborative, hybrid, and hands-on educational and research-based approaches. These include:

*   **Interdisciplinary Research and Framework Development:** Using research to map existing artscience activities and creating frameworks, such as the SHARES framework, to enable contributions from the arts and humanities to science research and translation.
*   **Hybrid Learning Experiences:** Implementing long-term, hybrid courses that combine virtual and in-person elements to explore speculative design, wearable technology, and futures thinking.
*   **Residency Programs:** Hosting hybrid virtual/in-person residencies that support multidisciplinary teams in exploring themes such as deep time, indigenous perspectives, and critical digital literacies.
*   **Workshops and Mentorship:** Utilizing hands-on workshops in speculative design and wearable computing to provide ongoing mentorship to students and researchers.

The findings and outputs of the lab's various projects demonstrate the practical application of these methods. Through the "Creative Turn in the Sciences" project, the lab identified a growing but under-supported artscience community in the Philippines and developed tools to integrate humanities into scientific research. The "Wearable Futures Hackathon" has resulted in student-led prototypes designed to address specific local needs, such as gloves for Filipino farmers to detect soil pH, devices to display carbon footprints, wearable tokens for sensitive political information, and anti-sexual-assault underwear. Additionally, the "Emerging Futurist Residency" has facilitated radical critiques of cultural symbols, such as the 2022 focus on reimagining the *terno*, a traditional Filipino dress that has been co-opted by political elites.

In conclusion, the BUKAS Lab functions as a vital bridge between public educational institutions in the Global South and international artscience communities. It demonstrates that by finding common ground through shared concerns, transdisciplinary and speculative practices can contribute significantly to both local and global discussions regarding future possibilities. The lab successfully integrates art-based thinking with scientific inquiry to address socioeconomic and environmental challenges.

The implications of the BUKAS Lab's work suggest that moving toward a more inclusive future requires the active involvement of diverse sectors. By fostering "futures literacy," the lab empowers individuals to imagine and anticipate future issues through creative and speculative lenses. This approach suggests that the integration of the arts into scientific and technological development is not merely an aesthetic addition but a necessary component for addressing the complex social and political realities of the Global South. The lab's model provides a template for how international collaborations can support local creative economies and promote socioeconomic justice through innovative, open-access educational frameworks.

title: The Universe as Home: Exploring the tension between climate change and the space race through somatic experiences, speculative design, and interactive performance
abstract: In this presentation, we describe the process and outcomes of a two-week workshop with participants of the 2022 Winter School at the Royal Institute for Theatre, Cinema and Sound (RITCS) in Brussels, which explored the tension between the climate crisis and the new space race. As workshop facilitators, we proceeded from the assumption that while it might seem that confronting climate change and investing in space exploration are strategies opposite to each other, they are really both concerned with survival and with the search for humanity’s place in this universe. To this end, we invited workshop participants (students from RITCS’ theatre, music, and radio programmes) to act as radical agents and to develop multisensory expressions and imaginations beyond what we can ordinarily see. The initial prompts for the workshop were a series of provocative questions: Could participants create a multisensory performance in which audiences really, deeply experience the complex and invisible forces that are shaping the planet’s climate? Would it be possible to craft an experience that helps the audience feel in their body the vastness, emptiness and incomprehensible age of the universe? Participants were led through a series of discussions, speculative design sessions, and somatic experience explorations to prime their creative process. The final outcome was a prototype of a multisensory, multimedia, site-specific, interactive performance that showcased the unique blend of skills and disciplines of the workshop participants, and offered a experiential, embodied way to reimagine the universe as home.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The presentation "The Universe as Home" details a two-week workshop conducted during the 2022 Winter School at the Royal Institute for Theatre, Cinema and Sound (RITCS) in Brussels. Led by Diego Maranan and the SEADS collective, the project explored the tension between the Earth's climate crisis and the burgeoning space race. The researchers posited that both endeavors are driven by the same human impulse: the search for humanity's place in the universe and the drive for survival.

The workshop involved an interdisciplinary group of students from fields such as dance, theatre, animation, film, and radio. The methodology bridged scientific concepts, including astrophysics and embodied cognition, with artistic practice. Pedagogical strategies included theoretical talks, somatic exploration using the Feldenkrais Method, speculative fiction workshops, and sensory experiments involving the rubber hand illusion, binaural beats, and clothing experiments.

The findings were illustrated through a final performance using two distinct environments. The first stage featured a dark, cold, and foggy sub-basement designed to evoke the vastness of space through acoustic properties, dim projections of Earth, and whispers of terrestrial scents. The second stage transitioned to a warm, lit tent, shifting the sensation to the intimacy of a home where participants acted as colonists. The experience concluded by playing back audience recordings of smells that remind them of home. The researchers conclude that multisensory and embodied design can foster a visceral connection to the universe.

The experience concluded with an interactive element where audience members recorded messages containing a smell that reminds them of home; these whispers were played back in the dark basement, creating a technological and emotional link between the two spaces.

The researchers conclude that the students successfully integrated somatic training, speculative fiction, and sensory experimentation to craft an embodied expression of the universe as a home. The presentation, titled "The Universe as Home: Exploring the tension between climate change and the space race through somatic experiences, speculative design, and interactive performance," details a two-week workshop conducted during the 2022 Winter School at the Royal Institute for Theatre, Cinema and Sound (RITCS) in Brussels. Led by Diego Maranan and a transdisciplinary team from the SEADS collective, the project sought to explore the relationship between Earth's climate crisis and the burgeoning space race through embodied, multisensory artistic creation.

The core problem addressed is the perceived contradiction between investing in space exploration and the urgent need to address environmental degradation on Earth. The researchers posited that both endeavors are fundamentally driven by the same human impulse: the search for humanity's place in the universe and the drive for survival. The challenge presented to the students was to move beyond visual representations and develop multisensory expressions that could help audiences feel a deeper connection to the vastness of the universe and the nature of our home planet.

The context for this work was an interdisciplinary research creation module involving students from diverse fields, including dance, theatre, animation, film, and radio. The workshop was designed to bridge the gap between scientific concepts—such as astrophysics and embodied cognition—and artistic practice.

The methodology employed a variety of pedagogical and creative strategies over a ten-day period. The process began with theoretical foundations through talks on topics like the large-scale structure of galaxies and sensory disorientation. This was followed by somatic exploration using the Feldenkrais Method to increase body awareness. Students engaged in speculative fiction workshops, such as those run by the MetaFuturist Lab, where they imagined future societies and solved hypothetical problems, such as a mysterious plummeting of body temperatures in a distant star system. Other methods included sensory experiments (such as the rubber hand illusion and binaural beats), clothing experiments to alter body perception, and "machine exercises" where participants functioned as interconnected subsystems of a moving, sounding entity.

The findings are presented through the description of the students' final performance, which successfully translated these abstract concepts into a tangible, multisensory experience. The performance utilized two distinct environments to create a narrative of interstellar travel. In the first stage, the audience was led through a dark, cold, and foggy descent into a massive sub-basement. This space used acoustic properties to create a sense of immense, echoing vastness, featuring a dim projection of a spinning Earth that appeared incredibly distant. The audience experienced a sense of sensory deprivation and disorientation, punctuated by disembodied, whispered sounds of terrestrial scents like "freshly cut grass" or "chocolate cookies."

In the second stage, the audience was transitioned into a warm, lit tent, shifting the sensation from the cold void of space to the intimacy of a home. Here, the participants were cast as colonists who had arrived at a new exoplanet. The experience concluded with an interactive element where audience members were asked to record a message containing a smell that reminds them of home. These intimate whispers were then played back in the dark, vast basement, creating a technological and emotional link between the two spaces and the two different sensory states.

The researchers conclude that the students successfully integrated the workshop's various activities—somatic training, speculative fiction, and sensory experimentation—to craft an embodied expression of the universe as a home. By utilizing scale, temperature, light, and sound, the performance allowed participants to physically experience the tension between the vast, empty void of space and the intimate, sensory-rich concept of home.

The implications of this work suggest that multisensory and embodied design can be a powerful tool for addressing complex, large-scale global issues like climate change and space exploration. By moving beyond purely intellectual or visual discourse and engaging the body's proprioceptive, thermal, and auditory senses, artists and designers can foster a deeper, more visceral connection to the universe and our place within it. The researchers intend to continue analyzing the workshop to understand how such transformative experiences might influence the long-term creative processes of the participating artists.
