title: Conference Track Description: “Death, Degrowth, and Finitude in the Age of the Lifelike” (PoM Conference Aachen 2024)
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Presented at the 2024 Politics of the Machines Conference, the track "Death, Degrowth, and Finitude in the Age of the Lifelike" examines the intersection of biological mortality and advancing lifelike technologies. As biological engineering and artificial life blur the boundaries between the organic and inorganic, the inquiry focuses on whether concepts of death should be applied to machines, agents, and systems. Using a transdisciplinary approach involving anthropology, digital humanities, biohacking, speculative design, and new media art, the research seeks to understand the functions of death, renewal, adaptation, and evolution within the lifelike.

Key dimensions include the design of lifelike systems and whether they should incorporate self-limiting mechanisms or transformational phases to provide ecological benefits. The research also questions the ethical imperative of forgetting to prevent the burden of eternal memory in lifelike agents. Furthermore, the work explores the implications of pre-programmed immortality and the ethical questions surrounding artificially sustained biological functioning and the authority to cease life support. Technology-mediated memory is also considered for its potential to create new forms of nostalgia, mourning, or hauntology. Ultimately, as the distinction between organic and inorganic blurs, the authors suggest that future technology design must grapple with senescence, obsolescence, decay, and mortality, potentially requiring new social technologies or behavioral innovations to navigate these shifting perspectives.

Additionally, the track considers how technology-mediated memory might interact with what has ceased to exist, potentially creating new forms of nostalgia, mourning, or hauntology.

The work concludes that as the distinction between the organic and inorganic becomes increasingly unclear, humanity may be forced to reframe the processes and experiences of dying. The design of future technologies must grapple with concepts such as senescence, obsolescence, decay, degrowth, deterioration, disintegration, decomposition, and mortality. Ultimately, the authors suggest that navigating the age of artificial life and programmable biology may require new social technologies or behavioral innovations to support these shifting perspectives.

title: Practice Environment and Patient-Centered Care Behaviors Among Nursing Staff in a Military Hospital in Saudi Arabia
abstract:
Introduction: A high-quality nursing practice environment is vital for nurses to provide patient-centered care, directly impacting patient outcomes and healthcare quality. Nurses’ daily interactions make their supportive environment key to delivering compassionate care.

Method: This cross-sectional, descriptive, correlational study in April-May 2025 surveyed 233 nurses in a Saudi military hospital. Data from a demographic profile, the Practice Environment Scale (PES-NWI), and the Caring Behaviors Assessment (CBAN-SF) were analyzed. IBM-SPSS 28 used frequency, percentages, means, Spearman’s rho, and Chi-square (p<0.05) to examine relationships.

Results: A moderate positive correlation (rs=.513, p<.001) was found between practice environment and patient-centered care. Nationality significantly correlated with environment perception (χ2=41.19, p=0.022). A weak negative correlation (rs=-.143, p=0.029) was noted between a nurse’s educational level and caring behavior, possibly due to burnout.

Conclusion: Improving the nursing practice environment through better staffing and resources directly enhances patient-centered care behaviors. While most demographics don’t influence caring behaviors, further study is needed on the weak negative link with education level. Strategies to improve the nursing practice environment must consider nationality to address the complexities of a diverse workforce.

This study investigates the relationship between the nursing practice environment and patient-centered care behaviors among nursing staff at a military hospital in Saudi Arabia. The research was motivated by the need to improve patient satisfaction and address challenges within the Saudi healthcare system, such as high attrition rates, nurse shortages, and communication barriers resulting from a reliance on foreign staff. The study specifically examines how organizational factors, including staffing, leadership support, and nurse participation in hospital affairs, influence patient-centered behaviors.

Using a cross-sectional, descriptive, correlational research design, data were collected between April and May 2025 from 233 nurses. The researcher utilized the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI) and the Caring Behaviors Assessment (CBAN-SF) to collect data, which were analyzed using IBM-SPSS 28.

The findings revealed a moderate positive correlation between the practice environment and patient-centered care behaviors, indicating that improved work environments lead to better care delivery. Nationality was found to significantly correlate with perceptions of the practice environment. Notably, a weak negative correlation was observed between a nurse’s educational level and their caring behaviors, potentially due to burnout. The study concludes that improving the nursing practice environment through better staffing and resources directly enhances patient-centered care, emphasizing that a supportive environment is essential for providing compassionate, personalized care.

title: A Comparative Study of Laws and Policies on Plastic Waste Management Between Indonesia and the Philippines
abstract:
This study presents a comparative analysis of plastic waste management laws, policies, and practices in Indonesia and the Philippines, two of Southeast Asia’s most plastic-intensive economies. Grounded in five central pillars—policy and regulation, community capacity and management, technological innovation, partnerships and collaboration, and behavioral and cultural transformation—the research examines both institutional frameworks and community-level interventions to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of current approaches. Through thematic qualitative analysis, the study identifies recurring implementation gaps linked to enforcement challenges, infrastructure limitations, and inconsistent public participation, despite the presence of comprehensive legal instruments such as Indonesia’s National Plan of Action on Marine Debris and the Philippines’ Ecological Solid Waste Management Act.

The findings culminate in a 10-point strategic framework designed to guide local and national decision-makers toward scalable, inclusive, and systems-oriented solutions. Key themes include the rise of hybrid waste management models blending technology with grassroots engagement, the evolving role of informal sectors, and the critical need for cross-sector alignment in achieving circular economy goals. The study underscores the importance of maintaining momentum in regulatory development while strengthening mechanisms for community integration, inter-agency coordination, and private sector engagement.

Beyond the national lens, this research contributes to the broader ASEAN agenda on environmental cooperation by offering context-specific insights and replicable practices that can support regional harmonization of plastic waste strategies. Ultimately, it offers a timely reminder that meaningful progress in addressing plastic pollution requires not only policy commitment but sustained, multi-level alignment across institutional, societal, and market-driven actors.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This comparative study examines plastic waste laws, policies, and management practices in Indonesia and the Philippines. Both archipelagic nations are major contributors to marine plastic pollution due to rapid urbanization, growing middle-class populations, and a heavy reliance on a "sachet economy" involving small, non-recyclable packaging. Additional drivers include the surge in e-commerce packaging and increased consumption of single-use personal protective equipment during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Using a comparative design with qualitative and quantitative methods, the research analyzed national laws, international reports, and case studies through five thematic pillars: policy and regulation, community management, technological innovation, partnerships, and behavioral outcomes. Findings indicate that while both countries have established comprehensive legal instruments, such as Indonesia’s National Plan of Action on Marine Debris and the Philippines’ Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, significant implementation gaps persist. Indonesia faces high waste generation compounded by outdated infrastructure, while the Philippines struggles with inconsistent enforcement and insufficient government investment in recycling.

Both nations are moving toward single-use plastic bans and Extended Producer Responsibility laws, yet enforcement remains a hurdle. A gap exists between public awareness and actual waste segregation, and technological innovations like waste-to-energy systems remain underutilized. The study concludes that addressing pollution requires a systemic approach to root causes like overproduction rather than simple clean-up campaigns. It proposes a 10-point strategic framework emphasizing localized laws, strengthened infrastructure, and a shift toward adaptive, participatory governance.

**Methodology**

The study employs a comparative research design using both qualitative and quantitative methods. The findings reveal that while both countries have established comprehensive legal instruments, significant implementation gaps persist. In Indonesia, plastic waste generation is high, with a significant portion of waste being mismanaged due to limited and outdated infrastructure. In the Philippines, the country is ranked as a top global contributor to plastic waste entering marine environments, with challenges stemming from inconsistent enforcement and a lack of government investment in recycling.

The study identifies several recurring themes. In terms of policy, both nations have moved toward implementing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) laws and single-use plastic bans, though enforcement remains a major hurdle. Regarding community engagement, there is a notable gap between public awareness and actual waste segregation practices. Technological innovation is present but remains underutilized, with limited adoption of waste-to-energy systems or advanced recycling technologies. Partnerships between governments, NGOs, and the private sector show promise but require better alignment to achieve circular economy goals. Finally, the study notes that while behavioral shifts occur when mandates are visible, long-term cultural change is hindered by the economic necessity of using cheap, single-use plastics.

**Conclusions**

The study concludes that addressing plastic pollution in these regions requires moving beyond "false solutions" like simple clean-up campaigns or focusing solely on specific items like straws. Instead, a systemic approach is required to address the root causes, such as overproduction and weak regulatory enforcement. The research highlights that current efforts are often fragmented, with a lack of coordination between national mandates and local implementation. While the transition toward a circular economy is underway, it is currently hampered by inadequate infrastructure and the economic realities of the sachet economy. The study emphasizes that meaningful progress depends on multi-level alignment involving institutional, societal, and market-driven actors.

**Implications**

The research culminates in the proposal of a 10-point strategic framework designed to guide decision-makers toward scalable and inclusive solutions. This framework includes recommendations for proper cascading and localization of laws, strengthening infrastructural foundations, fostering technological innovation, and promoting behavioral enculturation. The study implies that for policies to be effective, they must be accompanied by significant investment in waste management infrastructure and a concerted effort to provide resources and funding. Furthermore, the research suggests that regional cooperation within ASEAN is vital to manage transboundary pollution. Ultimately, the study advocates for a shift from a "command-and-control" governance model to a more adaptive, participatory approach that integrates community engagement and private sector accountability to ensure long-term environmental sustainability.

title: Automating Repository Management and Knowledge Sharing: Practices in BPO Support Services for Research and Development
abstract:
This qualitative case study analyzes the use of automation in knowledge-sharing and repository management within the IT Support Services (ITSS) department of a business process outsourcing (BPO) company for research and development. It focuses on the effects of three automation tools: Chatbot Automation, Technology Resource and Support Automation, and Remote Work Access Automation, examining how they affect job performance and information-sharing practices. The study rests on ethnomethodology, which focuses on how social practices are organized, and applies thematic analysis to derive patterns across the automation processes. The findings indicate that automation transcends a purely technical solution, functioning instead as a process shaped by users' social interactions and contextual modifications.

Chatbot Automation enhances self-service and provides responsive support, allowing users to choose assistance options based on their specific needs and familiarity with the system. Technology Resource and Support Automation promotes peer-led, collaborative knowledge building, where employees contribute insights, workarounds, and feedback that shape the evolving repository. Remote Work Access Automation enables users to engage with repositories across devices and locations, supporting knowledge sharing in flexible and distributed work environments. Together, these automation practices reflect the organization’s underlying values of autonomy, responsiveness, and co-development. They promote continuity, adaptability, and user-centered knowledge sharing. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on practice-based automation by highlighting the essential role of support services in sustaining R&D-related knowledge infrastructures in S&T-driven settings.

The problem addressed is the potential disconnect between the design of automated systems and the lived experiences of the users who rely on them to sustain R&D-related knowledge infrastructures. The study is situated within the context of digital, distributed workplaces where BPO support teams act as essential catalysts for R&D activities. Although the research site is an IT support department rather than a formal R&D unit, its functions are deeply embedded in the R&D ecosystem through the management of digital infrastructure and information systems. To explore these dynamics, the researcher employed a qualitative case study method guided by the framework of ethnomethodology. This approach focuses on how social order is created and maintained through everyday practices and interactions with technology. Rather than relying on interviews, the study utilized documentary analysis of system-generated data, including user activity logs, screenshots of automated interfaces, manuals, and personal observations of system interactions. Thematic analysis was applied to identify patterns across three specific automation tools: Chatbot Automation, Technology Resource and Support Automation, and Remote Work Access Automation.

The findings reveal that automation functions as a "situated infrastructure" that is constantly reshaped by user agency. This tool allows users to determine their own interaction paths, choosing between automated troubleshooting or escalating to a live agent, which provides a sense of control and empowerment. Technology Resource and Support Automation promotes peer-led, collaborative knowledge building. Remote Work Access Automation supports flexibility and continuity by providing secure, mobile access to essential work tools and managed applications, ensuring that knowledge sharing is not restricted by physical office boundaries.

The findings demonstrate that automation becomes a reliable part of the organizational routine when it is co-developed through user interaction and adapts to the specific needs of the workforce. Finally, the study calls for continued research using practice-based and ethnographic approaches to better understand how automation is lived and reconfigured in various specialized professional environments.

title: Impact Assessment of a Marikina Bioreactor Composting Technology Developed by the Department of Science and Technology-Industrial Technology Development Institute
abstract:
This study assesses the impact of a bioreactor composting technology developed by the Department of Science and Technology-Industrial Technology Development Institute (DOST-ITDI) and used in Marikina City, Philippines. Using the Multi-dimensional Sustainability Framework (MSF) and the Context, Input, Process, Product (CIPP) Model, it evaluated the environmental, economic, social, technological, and institutional effects of the bioreactor in managing organic waste in compliance with Republic Act No. 9003. Data were gathered through interviews and
focus group discussion with Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) staff and secondary sources within the project area. Findings indicate that the bioreactor helps reduce landfill waste and greenhouse gas emissions, produces nutrient-rich compost that improves soil, and creates community jobs and involvement. While the technology expedites composting and reduces manual work, it faces challenges like machine wear and need for better support. The study suggests improving design, training, and monitoring. Overall, the bioreactor is a sustainable and effective solution for organic waste that benefits the environment, society, and economy while supporting national and global sustainability goals.

title: Space and Exchanges: Information Grounds of Selected Filipino Migrants in Bangkok, Thailand
abstract: This study explored the information grounds (IG) of Filipino migrants in Bangkok (FMTs) by examining the characteristics of significant places for information exchange, the types of information sought and shared, and the social dynamics involved in these interactions. Guided by the Information Ground Theory and utilizing Fisher et al.'s (2007) people-place-information trichotomy as an analytical framework, the research employed a quantitative survey with 101 Filipino migrant respondents recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. Data collected via an online survey revealed that FMTs communicated in both physical spaces and increasingly in digital environments as they mentioned social media, workplaces, and churches as their primary IGs. These IGs are frequently visited for information exchange and social interaction, with preferences influenced by convenience and accessibility. The information shared often centers on work-related issues, personal matters, and news from the Philippines. Most FMTs interact in small groups of five or fewer, playing the role of information seekers while fostering moderate familiarity among members. Social interaction remains a primary motivator for engagement in these IGs. In conclusion, IGs are vital lifelines for FMTs in Bangkok, providing not only access to information but also fostering resilience, community ties, and adaptability in a foreign context. Strengthening these IGs through targeted strategies can address the unique challenges faced by Filipino migrants. This highlights the need for policies that enhance communication and support networks, and ensuring that FMTs thrive while preserving their cultural identity and connections.

title: Public-Private Partnerships in R&D: An Autoethnomethodological Study of its Role on Organizational Leadership
abstract:
Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) have long been associated with infrastructure development, however, their application in research and development (R&D) remains limited, especially in the Philippines. This study investigated the role of PPPs within R&D through ethnomethodology as research framework and autoethnography as methodological approach. Given the nature of autoethnography, this study was written from a first-person perspective. By drawing from the author’s lived experiences in PPPs and naturally occurring data, the research highlighted the dynamics of leadership that influence R&D project progress.

The results highlighted how leadership visibility, proactive facilitation, strategic task delegation, network building and collaborative leadership significantly influenced these partnerships.

The study provides actionable insights, emphasizing that PPP in R&D can be encouraged by integrating diverse leadership practices, perspectives, and promoting a culture of continuous collaboration.

half:
Anna Patricia R. Condemilicor’s thesis, "Public-Private Partnership In R&D: An Autoethnomethodological Study of Its Role on Organizational Leadership," investigates leadership dynamics within Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) in the Research and Development (R&D) sector. Addressing a research gap in the Philippines, the study explores the leadership competencies required to navigate bureaucratic hurdles, cultural differences, and conflicting organizational objectives. Using ethnomethodology and autoethnography, the researcher utilizes her lived experiences as an R&D manager in both public and private sectors to examine social facts created through communicative acts and decision-making. Data was gathered through participation in two PPP projects involving product development for farmers and MSME export readiness.

The findings identify five core leadership practices essential for sustaining R&D PPPs: leading with visible commitment to foster trust, agile and proactive facilitation to manage bureaucracy, strategic delegation based on expertise, collaborative leadership through shared decision-making, and network building to ensure continuity. These practices act as social constructs that facilitate coordinated behavior across distinct organizations. The study concludes that leadership in PPPs is a continuous process of relationship-building rather than mere formal authority. Successful partnerships require leaders to bridge cultural gaps through respect and clear role delineation. The researcher suggests that future research should examine leadership in different R&D settings and recommends that university curricula incorporate PPP-related subjects to prepare future leaders for cross-sector collaboration.

While PPPs are frequently studied regarding physical infrastructure, their application in R&D remains limited, particularly in the Philippines. The study addresses the lack of research regarding the specific leadership competencies required to navigate the complexities of these partnerships, such as bureaucratic hurdles, cultural differences, and the difficulty of harmonizing diverse organizational objectives.

The researcher utilizes ethnomethodology as a theoretical framework and autoethnography as the methodological approach. This allows for the examination of "social facts" created through everyday communicative acts and decision-making patterns. Data was collected through observations and participation in two distinct PPP projects: one focused on product development for farmers and another aimed at making MSME products export-ready.

The findings identify five core leadership practices that encourage and sustain PPPs in R&D: leading with visible commitment, agile and proactive facilitation, strategic delegation of tasks, collaborative leadership, and network building. Leading with visible commitment involves active participation from top-level managers to foster trust and accountability. Agile and proactive facilitation involves navigating bureaucratic processes by initiating groundwork in parallel with formal documentation. Strategic delegation involves assigning responsibilities based on expertise to increase efficiency. Collaborative leadership is demonstrated through shared decision-making and open communication, while network building through professional relationships ensures long-term continuity. These practices are driven by underlying perspectives that act as social constructs to facilitate coordinated behavior across culturally distinct organizations.

The study concludes that leadership in PPPs is a continuous practice of relationship-building rather than just a matter of formal authority. Successful R&D partnerships require leaders to bridge the gap between different organizational cultures through respect, open communication, and clear role delineation. When leaders are proactive, bureaucratic processes can be managed effectively without sacrificing compliance, creating an environment conducive to innovation.

This thesis, titled "Public-Private Partnership In R&D: An Autoethnomethodological Study of Its Role on Organizational Leadership" by Anna Patricia R. Condemilicor, investigates the leadership dynamics within Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) specifically applied to the Research and Development (R&D) sector. While PPPs are widely studied in the context of physical infrastructure, the author notes that their application in R&D remains limited, particularly in the Philippines. The study seeks to understand how leadership practices and underlying perspectives influence the success and innovativeness of these collaborative research initiatives.

The problem addressed is the lack of extensive research regarding the applicability of PPPs in R&D and the specific leadership competencies required to navigate the complexities of such partnerships. The author observes that while PPPs offer significant advantages—such as shared funding, risk distribution, and increased innovation—organizations often hesitate to engage in them due to bureaucratic hurdles, cultural differences, and the difficulty of harmonizing diverse organizational objectives. The research aims to bridge this gap by examining how leadership can facilitate these collaborations to expedite technological innovation and knowledge production.

To explore this problem, the researcher utilizes ethnomethodology as a theoretical framework and autoethnography as the methodological approach. Ethnomethodology allows the study to examine the "social facts" created through everyday communicative acts, decision-making patterns, and informal interactions between stakeholders. Autoethnography enables the researcher to use her own lived experiences as an R&D manager—having worked in both the public and private sectors—as primary data. This approach captures the nuances of complex decision-making, stakeholder interactions, and the emotional and professional realities of managing cross-sector collaborations. The data was collected through the researcher's observations and participation in two distinct PPP projects: one focused on meeting the needs of farmers through product development and another aimed at making MSME products export-ready.

The findings of the study identify five core leadership practices that encourage and sustain PPPs in R&D: leading with visible commitment, agile and proactive facilitation, strategic delegation of tasks, collaborative leadership, and network building. Leading with visible commitment involves the active participation of top-level managers, which fosters trust, accountability, and a shared sense of ownership. Agile and proactive facilitation is characterized by the ability to navigate bureaucratic processes by initiating groundwork in parallel with formal documentation, thereby accelerating project progress. Strategic delegation of tasks involves assigning responsibilities based on individual expertise, which increases efficiency and empowers team members. Collaborative leadership is demonstrated through shared decision-making and open communication, which optimizes resources and fosters innovation. Finally, network building through the maintenance of strong professional relationships ensures long-term continuity and future collaboration.

The study also identifies the underlying perspectives that drive these practices. These include the belief that visible leadership builds trust, that agile strategies accelerate progress, that maximizing individual strengths increases efficiency, that strategic collaboration optimizes outcomes, and that strong relationships ensure future collaboration. These perspectives act as social constructs that facilitate coordinated behavior across culturally distinct organizations.

The researcher concludes that leadership in PPPs is not merely a matter of formal authority but is a continuous practice of relationship-building. Successful PPPs in R&D require leaders to bridge the gap between different organizational cultures through open communication, respect, and the clear delineation of roles. The study demonstrates that when leaders are actively engaged and proactive, bureaucratic processes can be managed effectively without sacrificing compliance, and the resulting environment is highly conducive to innovation.

The implications of this research are both practical and academic. For practitioners, the study provides a framework for navigating R&D partnerships, emphasizing that leadership visibility and collaborative decision-making are essential for project success. For the academic community, the study suggests that future research should explore leadership practices in different R&D settings, such as theoretical or clinical research, and investigate the direct relationship between these leadership practices and the specific level of innovation achieved. Additionally, the author recommends that R&D management curricula in universities incorporate subjects related to PPPs to prepare future leaders for the complexities of cross-sector collaboration.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Self-Efficacy in Dementia Care Among Nurses in Two Health Institutions in Metro Manila
abstract:
The number of people with dementia in the Philippines is rising rapidly. This means that the healthcare workforce, most specifically nurses, must be prepared to take care of this patient group in hospital settings. Increasing the self-efficacy of nurses might improve patient outcomes and quality of care for PwD and their families. The purpose of this study is to determine the knowledge and attitudes of Filipino nurses towards dementia care and their influence on self-efficacy. A total of 182 registered nurses from a private and a public hospital in the Philippines were recruited for the study. Their levels of knowledge, attitudes, and self-efficacy on dementia care were measured.

Filipino nurses have inadequate knowledge, positive attitudes, and a high level of self-efficacy in dementia care. Correlation statistics revealed that attitudes were significantly correlated with self-efficacy (Spearman ρ = 0.243, p = 0.001) while general knowledge was not (Spearman p = 0.143; p-value = 0.054). A ‘higher level of knowledge’ based on experience and observations of people with dementia which forms the cognitive aspect of nurses’ attitudes had the highest correlation with self-efficacy (Spearman p = 0.275, p-value = <0.01). Age and length of experience were significantly associated with dementia knowledge. There is a need to sustain Filipino nurses’ positive attitudes on dementia care as it can influence their self-efficacy and therefore, their ability to provide person-centered care, the gold standard in dementia care.

two:
The thesis titled "Knowledge, Attitudes, and Self-efficacy in Dementia Care among Nurses in Two Health Institutions in Metro Manila" by Melissa Margret Fiel investigates the preparedness of the Filipino nursing workforce to manage the rising number of dementia cases in hospital settings.

**Problem**
The study addresses the growing challenge of an aging population in the Philippines, with dementia cases projected to reach 1.5 million by 2030. Despite this, there is a lack of a national dementia plan and limited specialized resources in the country. In acute hospital settings, nurses often prioritize treating acute medical conditions over the holistic needs of people with dementia (PwD), sometimes viewing dementia-related behaviors as disruptive. The researcher identifies a gap in the literature regarding the specific knowledge, attitudes, and self-efficacy of Filipino nurses, noting that most existing research is centered on Western or developed nations.

**Context**
The research is situated within the healthcare landscape of the Philippines, specifically focusing on the role of nurses as the mainstay of management for PwD in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The study highlights the tension between the rapid demographic shift toward an aging society and the current lack of dementia-specific training and services in general hospitals. It also considers the cultural context, where family-based care is common, and the potential for stigma or "hiya" (shame) to influence how dementia is managed and discussed.

**Method**
The study employed a cross-sectional descriptive-correlational quantitative research design. The sample consisted of 182 registered nurses recruited from one public hospital (Jose R. Reyes Memorial Medical Center) and one private hospital (Cardinal Santos Medical Center) in Metro Manila. Inclusion criteria required nurses to have at least two years of experience and to have cared for patients over the age of 60 within the last six months. Data were collected using three validated instruments: the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale (DKAS), the Dementia Attitudes Scale (DAS), and the Sense of Competence in Dementia Care Staff (SCIDS) scale. Data analysis involved descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank correlation to examine the relationships between the variables.

**Findings**
The results indicated that Filipino nurses possess inadequate knowledge regarding dementia care, but they maintain positive attitudes and a high level of self-efficacy. Specifically, the study found that:
*   **Knowledge:** Nurses showed inadequate levels of dementia knowledge. However, age and length of professional experience were significantly associated with higher knowledge scores.
*   **Attitudes:** Nurses demonstrated positive attitudes toward dementia care. A specific subscale regarding "higher level of knowledge" based on experience and observations (the cognitive aspect of attitudes) showed the strongest correlation with self-efficacy.
*   **Self-Efficacy:** Nurses reported a high level of self-efficacy in providing dementia care.
*   **Correlations:** Statistical analysis revealed that attitudes were significantly correlated with self-efficacy (Spearman ρ = 0.243, p = 0.001). Conversely, general knowledge was not significantly correlated with self-efficacy (Spearman p = 0.143; p-value = 0.054).

**Conclusions**
The study concludes that while Filipino nurses are confident in their ability to provide care (high self-efficacy) and hold positive views toward patients with dementia, they lack the necessary foundational knowledge to be fully prepared for the dementia epidemic. The significant correlation between attitudes and self-efficacy suggests that the way nurses perceive and feel about dementia is a critical driver of their confidence in providing care. The findings suggest that the current nursing workforce in the Philippines may be relying on experience and positive intent rather than formal, specialized knowledge to manage the complexities of dementia in acute care settings.

**Implications**
The findings have several implications for various stakeholders. For nursing educators and hospital administrators, there is a clear need to develop and implement targeted dementia education and in-service training programs to address specific knowledge gaps. For policy makers, the study supports the push for a national dementia strategy that includes specific provisions for nursing training and geriatric care in general hospitals. For nursing practice, the study emphasizes the importance of sustaining positive attitudes among staff, as these attitudes directly influence self-efficacy and the ability to provide person-centered care—the gold standard for dementia management. Finally, the study highlights the need for more context-specific research in LMICs to develop practical, cost-effective interventions for an aging population.

title: Knowledge Management System Enhancement for a Private R&D Unit in the Philippines
abstract: This case study aims to enhance the Knowledge Management System (KMS) of a private Research and Development (R&D) unit in the Philippines. The insights of all four R&D staff were gathered using semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis of the qualitative data yielded five key themes: KMS Effectiveness and Challenges, Knowledge Quality and Documentation Practices, Knowledge Sharing and Collaboration, Knowledge Acquisition and Learning, and Organizational Support and Training. The commonalities, contradictions, and complementarities of the participant responses within each theme were explored to illustrate the KMS landscape. Then, the facilitating and hindering factors of the current KMS were distilled. Participant proposals for improvement were combined with literature recommendations to resolve the observed hindrances. The findings led to the following recommendations to enhance the KMS: Centralize and Standardize Documentation, Leverage AI to Enhance Efficiency, Nurture a Culture of Openness and Inquiry, Align and Increase Training Opportunities, and Formalize and Communicate Incentives.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
Danzen F. Dang-awan’s study, "Knowledge Management System Enhancement for a Private R&D Unit in the Philippines," investigates how a private Research and Development (R&D) unit can improve its Knowledge Management System (KMS) to better support organizational goals. The research addresses the unit's struggle to convert R&D efforts into sales and its difficulties in retaining both institutional knowledge and talent. Using a qualitative case study design, the researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with four R&D engineers. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis method.

The findings revealed five key themes. Regarding KMS effectiveness, knowledge storage is highly fragmented across Microsoft Teams, Excel, and Outlook, making retrieval difficult and time-consuming. Documentation practices are hindered by a lack of standardized guidelines and heavy workloads. In terms of collaboration, a psychological barrier exists in formal settings where some participants reported a "fear of voicing out." Knowledge acquisition is currently driven by self-reliance and informal learning due to a lack of formal KMS tool training and a perceived misalignment between existing training and strategic goals. Finally, there is a lack of formal incentives for documenting and sharing knowledge.

The author proposes several actionable enhancements: centralizing and standardizing documentation by utilizing MS Teams as an integrated repository with strict naming and formatting guidelines; leveraging AI tools to assist in drafting technical reports; nurturing a culture of openness through structured meeting formats and communication training; aligning training opportunities through needs analyses; and formalizing incentives by redesigning performance appraisal systems.

The study titled "Knowledge Management System Enhancement for a Private R&D Unit in the Philippines" by Danzen F. Dang-awan investigates how a private Research and Development (R&D) unit can improve its Knowledge Management System (KMS) to better support organizational goals.

The problem addressed is that despite the strategic importance of KMS for innovation, this specific private R&D unit in the Philippines struggles with converting R&D efforts into sales and faces difficulties in retaining both institutional knowledge and talent. These issues suggest that the current KMS is insufficient for the unit's specific needs. The study specifically seeks to evaluate the perceived effectiveness of the current system, determine how it facilitates or hinders the storage and retrieval of historical experimental data, and develop an actionable proposal for enhancement.

The research was conducted within a private R&D unit of a long-standing business-to-business company in an urban setting in the Philippines. The author employed a qualitative case study design to gain an in-depth understanding of the complex issues within a real-world context. The participants consisted of four R&D engineers selected through purposive sampling. These participants were all project owners with at least one year of experience in the unit. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews lasting between 15 and 30 minutes. The researcher used thematic analysis following the six-phase method of Braun and Clarke to identify patterns, commonalities, contradictions, and complementarities within the qualitative data.

The findings revealed five key themes: KMS Effectiveness and Challenges, Knowledge Quality and Documentation Practices, Knowledge Sharing and Collaboration, Knowledge Acquisition and Learning, and Organizational Support and Incentives. Regarding effectiveness, participants reported using Microsoft Teams, Excel, and Outlook, but noted that knowledge storage is highly fragmented across these different platforms, making retrieval difficult and time-consuming. Documentation practices are hindered by a lack of standardized guidelines for naming and formatting, as well as heavy workloads that leave little time for thorough recording.

In terms of collaboration, while daily team meetings and informal conversations are viewed as productive and supportive, a psychological barrier was identified in formal settings, where some participants reported a "fear of voicing out." Knowledge acquisition is currently driven by self-reliance and informal learning, as there is a lack of formal KMS tool training and a perceived misalignment between existing training and strategic goals. Finally, while leadership is viewed as supportive, there is a notable lack of formal incentives for documenting and sharing knowledge, with most motivation being intrinsic or tied to general performance evaluations.

The study concludes that while the R&D unit possesses a strong foundation of collaborative culture and useful existing documentation, the current KMS is limited by fragmentation, lack of standardization, and insufficient formal training and incentives. The absence of a centralized repository and clear documentation protocols creates significant barriers to efficient knowledge absorption and retrieval.

Based on these findings, the author proposes a combined actionable proposal for KMS enhancement. The recommendations include:
*   **Centralizing and Standardizing Documentation:** Utilizing MS Teams as an integrated repository and establishing strict guidelines for file naming, keywords, and formatting to ensure easy retrieval.
*   **Leveraging AI for Efficiency:** Using AI tools like Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini to assist in drafting technical reports to mitigate the impact of heavy workloads, supplemented by a peer-review system.
*   **Nurturing a Culture of Openness:** Implementing structured meeting formats, such as pre-meeting reports, and providing communication training to reduce psychological barriers in formal settings.
*   **Aligning Training Opportunities:** Conducting training needs analyses to ensure that both KMS tool training and external knowledge acquisition (like supplier visits) align with strategic organizational goals.
*   **Formalizing Incentives:** Redesigning performance appraisal systems to be more transparent regarding knowledge-sharing contributions and increasing the frequency of appraisals to make rewards more visible.

title: Factors Influencing the Attrition and Retention of Employees in the Research and Development Department of a Food Manufacturing Company in the Philippines
abstract: This study examines the key factors affecting retention and attrition among R&D staff at a food manufacturing company in the Philippines, using Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory and Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs for analysis. Findings show that hygiene factors, such as salary, job security, and the work environment, make up 68% of the reasons employees leave. In contrast, motivator factors, especially opportunities for career growth, are vital for long-term retention. Attrition is highest within the first 1-2 years due to unmet career advancement needs, and it rises again after five years when psychological needs remain unmet. Conversely, employees with 3-6 years of service and high motivator satisfaction tend to stay longer. The study highlights the importance of dual retention strategies: meeting hygiene factors while fostering growth, recognition, and meaningful work. Practical, tenure-sensitive strategies, such as job enrichment, structured career planning, recognition programs, and lateral movements, are recommended to boost engagement and reduce talent loss in the R&D team.

half:
This thesis investigates the drivers of employee attrition and retention within the Research and Development (R&D) department of a food manufacturing company in the Philippines. Recognizing that high turnover among technical personnel threatens innovation and organizational knowledge, the study identifies specific attrition drivers, high-risk employee segments, and temporal turnover patterns to develop effective retention mechanisms. Using a case study approach with qualitative and quantitative methods, data were collected from former and current employees through archived exit interviews and semi-structured surveys based on Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory and Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.

Findings indicate a distinction between factors causing departure and those encouraging retention. Applying Herzberg’s theory, 68% of attrition reasons among former employees related to hygiene factors, such as salary, work conditions, and supervision. The primary reasons for leaving were career growth opportunities, personal reasons, and pay. Conversely, current employees cited salary, growth opportunities, and work conditions as primary reasons for staying, suggesting that while hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, motivator factors like career growth drive long-term retention.

Attrition risk is highest during the first two years of service and after five years. Employees aged 26–30 and those in supervisory roles are particularly susceptible, as are members of the Technical Services Group. The study recommends a dual-strategy approach: maintaining hygiene factors through salary benchmarking and manager training, while addressing motivators through transparent career development, job enrichment, and recognition programs.
one:
This thesis investigates the factors driving employee attrition and retention within the Research and Development (R&D) department of a food manufacturing company in the Philippines. Given the strategic importance of R&D for innovation and business continuity in the food and beverage sector, high turnover among technical personnel poses a risk to organizational knowledge and market competitiveness. The study sought to identify specific drivers of attrition, determine which employee segments are most at risk, identify temporal patterns of turnover, and develop effective retention mechanisms.

Using a case study approach with qualitative and quantitative methods, data were collected over three months from former R&D employees (who left between 2019 and 2023) and current employees with at least one year of service. The researcher utilized total enumeration sampling, reviewing archived exit interview data and administering semi-structured surveys based on Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory and Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.

The findings reveal a distinction between factors causing departure and those encouraging retention. Applying Herzberg’s theory, 68% of attrition reasons among former employees were related to hygiene factors, such as salary, work conditions, and supervision. The top reasons for leaving were better career growth opportunities (30%), personal reasons (27%), and pay (13%). Conversely, current employees cited salary (33%), growth opportunities (16%), and work conditions (15%) as primary reasons for staying. This suggests that while hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, motivator factors—particularly career growth—are the primary drivers of long-term retention.

Attrition patterns vary by tenure and demographics. Risk is highest during the first one to two years of service due to unmet expectations regarding career advancement, and again after five years when psychological needs remain unfulfilled. Employees aged 26–30 and those in supervisory roles are particularly susceptible to leaving due to motivator-related issues. Additionally, the Technical Services Group reported lower motivator satisfaction than the Product Management Group, indicating higher attrition risk in that unit. Regarding Maslow’s Hierarchy, former employees frequently cited unmet self-actualization and safety needs as primary drivers for departure.

The study concludes that a dual-strategy approach is necessary: maintaining hygiene factors as a baseline while focusing on motivator factors like professional growth, recognition, and meaningful work. Recommendations include regular salary benchmarking and manager training to address hygiene factors, alongside transparent career development plans, job enrichment, and formal recognition programs to address motivators. To prevent stagnation in long-tenured employees, the researcher suggests lateral job rotations and mentorship programs, as well as performance metrics that reward innovation and creativity to boost intrinsic motivation.

This thesis investigates the factors driving employee attrition and retention within the Research and Development (R&D) department of a food manufacturing company in the Philippines. The study addresses the critical need for workforce stability in R&D to ensure innovation productivity and business continuity, particularly as the food and beverage sector is a major driver of the Philippine economy. The researcher notes that while R&D is vital for food security and innovation, high turnover rates among technical personnel pose a risk to organizational knowledge and market competitiveness.

The research problem centers on the significant turnover rates observed within the R&D department despite the strategic importance of its staff. Initial observations suggested that uncompetitive pay, limited career growth, and personal reasons were contributing factors. The study sought to identify the specific drivers of attrition and retention, determine which employee segments are most at risk, identify temporal patterns of turnover, and develop effective retention mechanisms.

The study utilized a case study approach, employing both qualitative and quantitative methods. Data were collected over a three-month period from two primary groups: former R&D employees (who left between 2019 and 2023) and current R&D employees with at least one year of service. The researcher used a total enumeration sampling method for the participants. Data collection involved reviewing archived exit interview data from Human Resources and administering a semi-structured survey via Google Forms. The survey was designed around Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory and Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, utilizing Likert-scale and open-ended questions. Data analysis included descriptive statistics (mean and frequency) and manual thematic coding for qualitative responses.

The findings reveal a clear distinction between the factors that cause employees to leave and those that encourage them to stay. According to Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, 68% of the reasons for attrition among former employees were related to hygiene factors, such as salary, work conditions, and supervision. Specifically, the top reasons for leaving were better career growth opportunities (30%), personal reasons (27%), and pay (13%). Conversely, current employees cited salary (33%), growth opportunities (16%), and work conditions (15%) as the primary reasons for staying. This suggests that while hygiene factors like salary are essential to prevent dissatisfaction, they are not sufficient for long-term engagement; motivator factors, particularly career growth, are the primary drivers of retention.

The study also identified specific patterns based on employee demographics and tenure. Attrition is most prevalent among employees in their first one to two years of service, primarily due to unmet expectations regarding career advancement and self-actualization. A second peak in attrition risk occurs after five years of service, often when psychological needs remain unfulfilled. Demographic segmentation showed that employees aged 26–30 and those in supervisory roles are particularly susceptible to leaving due to motivator-related issues. Furthermore, the study found that employees in the Technical Services Group reported lower motivator satisfaction compared to those in the Product Management Group, indicating a higher risk of attrition in that specific unit.

In terms of Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, current employees reported that belongingness, esteem, and self-actualization needs were generally well-met, while physiological and safety needs were only partially fulfilled. However, former employees frequently cited unmet self-actualization and safety needs as primary drivers for their departure.

Based on these findings, the study concludes that a dual-strategy approach is necessary for R&D workforce management. Hygiene factors must be maintained as a baseline to prevent dissatisfaction, but they do not guarantee long-term commitment. True retention is driven by motivator factors, specifically opportunities for professional growth, recognition, and meaningful work. The research highlights that attrition is a lifecycle-dependent issue, requiring different management approaches for early-career, mid-career, and long-tenured employees.

The implications of this study suggest that the company must move beyond simple compensation adjustments to foster a culture of growth and recognition. The researcher provides several recommendations to enhance retention. To address hygiene factors, the company should conduct regular salary benchmarking, provide training for managers to foster a supportive and psychologically safe work environment, and implement wellness programs. To address motivator factors, the study recommends establishing transparent career development plans, implementing job enrichment and vertical job loading to provide autonomy, and creating formal recognition programs tied to research milestones. Additionally, the researcher suggests lateral job rotations and mentorship programs to prevent stagnation among long-tenured employees. Finally, the study suggests that the company should implement performance metrics that specifically reward innovation and creativity to boost intrinsic motivation.

title: Government - Industry Linkage Supporting R&D Based Product Development and Technology Commercialization of a Start - Up Food Manufacturing Company in Metro Manila, Philippines
abstract: Food manufacturing companies hold a crucial role in addressing the food insecurity problems in the country, addressing the SDG 2: zero hunger. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) as start-up companies engaged in Research and Development, can help a lot with the support of the government. With government support for MSMEs in product development and technology commercialization, these businesses can contribute to the economy and help tackle food insecurity in the country; both the economy and MSMEs will benefit from this collaboration. This study explores how MSMEs can maximize the help of the government in their food manufacturing business, which government agencies have the program to help the food industry and the implementation of their programs. The study shows that government linkage is essential and played a vital role with their support in product development, access to technology, training and regulatory guidance resulting in improved quality of products and wider market access.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
This research examines the role of food manufacturing Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in addressing food insecurity in the Philippines, specifically regarding Sustainable Development Goal 2: Zero Hunger. Focusing on start-up MSMEs in Metro Manila, the study investigates how these businesses can maximize government assistance to facilitate Research and Development (R&D) based product development and technology commercialization. A central theme is the necessity of establishing effective linkages between the government and the industry to help small businesses navigate product innovation and market entry.

The investigation explores the mechanisms through which MSMEs leverage government support and examines how collaborations facilitate the transition from R&D to commercialized products. Findings indicate that government linkage is essential for success in the food manufacturing sector. This collaboration provides critical support in areas such as product development, access to technology, training, and regulatory guidance. The study demonstrates that active linkages result in tangible improvements, specifically regarding improved product quality and wider market access.

The study concludes that collaboration is mutually beneficial; the government achieves economic growth and food security goals, while MSMEs gain the resources necessary to scale operations. Strengthening ties between government agencies and the food industry is identified as a strategic necessity for addressing national challenges like food insecurity. Optimizing support programs can empower MSMEs to become more innovative and resilient, contributing to a stable food supply chain.

title: Biological Pump Potential: A Plankton Spatio-Temporal Modeling in the Philippine Sea with Emphasis on the Effects of Typhoons
abstract:
Current carbon sequestration technologies are not meeting targets to deliver the 2050 global net zero goal. Hence, there is an increase in campaigns for nature-based solutions (NBS) rather than depending on engineered sequestration technologies, which is by far harder to scale up. Though amplifying the NBS that are already inherent in the environment is a matter of increased activities, the current changing climatic conditions complicates this, such as site-targeted mangrove rehabilitation, regenerative forestry, and restorative agriculture. These land-based solutions comprise approximately half of the global total carbon sequestered, while the other 50% are the materials that naturally sink in the depths of the ocean.

Harnessing the potential of ocean productivity is a huge leap in the world’s carbon sequestration thrust. Not only does this process happen in the natural world, but quantification, monitoring, and forecasting activities can aid future policymaking to amplify productivity in our ocean–which is also expected to serve as a driver to the placement of programs geared toward water quality preservation, conservation, and treatment in inland waters. This study focuses on the quantification and forecasting of the Biological Pump potential in the Philippine Sea, specifically inside the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Variabilities and disturbances such as increased sea surface temperature, and considering the geographic location of the Philippines, receiving high frequency of annual typhoons, were investigated to affect ocean productivity. Spatio-temporal maps were generated to provide visualization for the trends and phenomena before, during, and after typhoon occurrence for the years 2019 until 2021. The normal scenario for typhoons was reflected in 2019 while both 2020 and 2021 recorded rare high-intensity super typhoons Rolly (Goni) and Odette (Rai), respectively. NASA Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG) Ocean Color data were used to produce spatiotemporal maps for both chlorophyll (CHL) and Sea surface temperature (SST). Correlating these maps with typhoon occurrence, and SST, the Biological Pump potential annual estimate was generated.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
The global effort to reach net-zero emissions by 2050 has increased interest in the ocean biological carbon pump, a process driven by phytoplankton that transports biogenic carbon to the deep ocean. Because ocean warming may accelerate microbial decomposition and release carbon, monitoring ocean productivity is essential. This study quantifies and forecasts the biological pump potential within the Philippine Exclusive Economic Zone by investigating how sea surface temperature and the high frequency of annual typhoons affect ocean productivity. Using NASA Ocean Biology Processing Group data, the research produced spatio-temporal maps for chlorophyll and sea surface temperature across the Philippine Sea, Sulu Sea, and West Philippine Sea.

Findings indicate that high productivity occurs primarily in the West Philippine Sea near Palawan and in land waters between Mindanao. Productivity was lower in deeper, high-salinity areas of the Philippine Sea compared to shallower regions. Seasonal trends showed peak chlorophyll levels during the cool dry season from December to February, while the lowest levels occurred during the rainy season from June to November. The annual net primary production estimate for 2019-2021 was approximately 0.34 PgC y-1, with a peak anomaly in July 2021. While the overall linear relationship between chlorophyll and sea surface temperature was weak, a high R2 value of 0.81 was observed for 2020, coinciding with super typhoon Rolly.

The impact of typhoons on chlorophyll levels is not uniform. Near transect 1, typhoons such as Goring, Betty, Marce, Carina, Kiko, Jolina, Maring, and Nando caused chlorophyll values to drop. Conversely, near transect 2, typhoons Amang and Auring caused chlorophyll values to increase due to wind-driven upwelling. The study suggests that typhoon frequency affects productivity more significantly than sea surface temperature. The Philippine EEZ serves as a carbon sink through its net primary production. While typhoons can boost productivity through upwelling, stratification caused by warming oceans may hinder nutrient transfer. The study recommends prioritizing monitoring in Transect 3 and Transect 4 due to high productivity and commercial fishing disputes.

two:
The global effort to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 has highlighted the limitations of current carbon sequestration technologies, leading to an increased interest in nature-based solutions. While land-based solutions account for approximately half of global carbon sequestration, the remaining 50% is managed by the ocean through materials that naturally sink into the depths. This process is driven by the ocean biological carbon pump, which involves the downward transport of biogenic carbon to the deep ocean. Phytoplankton play a critical role in this framework by providing primary services to the global carbon and nutrient cycles. Because ocean warming can accelerate the growth and decomposition of microorganisms, which may lead to the direct export of carbon into the atmosphere, it is essential to develop advanced methods for monitoring and forecasting ocean productivity.

This study focuses on the quantification and forecasting of the biological pump potential within the Philippine Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). The research investigates how variabilities and disturbances, specifically increased sea surface temperature (SST) and the high frequency of annual typhoons in the Philippines, affect ocean productivity. The study aims to establish spatio-temporal maps of phytoplankton, compare phytoplankton responses to seasonal variability and typhoon occurrences, and generate potential productivity forecasts for the Philippine biological pump.

The methodology utilized NASA Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG) Ocean Color data to produce spatio-temporal maps for both chlorophyll (CHL) and SST. The study area encompassed the marine surface waters within the Philippine EEZ, including parts of the Philippine Sea, Sulu Sea, and West Philippine Sea. Image processing was conducted using Python and Matlab, employing a k-nearest neighbor (KNN) machine learning algorithm to classify map data and extract CHL and SST values based on NASA color scales. To analyze the relationship between productivity and weather events, the researcher correlated these maps with typhoon occurrence and SST. Net primary production (NPP) was estimated using the Vertically Generalized Production Model (VGPM), which incorporates CHL, SST, and photosynthetically active radiation.

The findings revealed that high productivity occurs primarily in the West Philippine Sea, near Palawan, and in land waters between Mindanao. In deeper oceans with high salinity, such as parts of the Philippine Sea, productivity was found to be lower than in shallower oceans like the West Philippine Sea. Regarding seasonal trends, peak CHL levels were generally observed during the cool dry season from December to February, with the lowest levels occurring during the rainy season from June to November. However, some variability was noted in specific transects during the rainy season. The annual NPP estimate for the period 2019-2021 was approximately 0.34 PgC y-1, with a notable peak anomaly recorded in July 2021. Regression analysis showed a weak linear relationship between CHL and SST when using all data from 2019-2021, though a high R2 value of 0.81 was observed for the year 2020, which coincided with the passage of super typhoon Rolly.

The analysis of the relationship between CHL and typhoons showed that the impact is not uniform. In some instances, such as when typhoons Goring, Betty, Marce, Carina, Kiko, Jolina, Maring, and Nando traversed near transect 1, CHL values dropped. Conversely, in other cases, such as when typhoons Amang and Auring traversed near transect 2, CHL values increased. These increases can be attributed to ocean mixing caused by wind-driven upwelling, which brings nutrient-rich deep waters to the surface. The study suggests that the high frequency of typhoons appears to affect productivity more significantly than the negating effects of SST.

The study concludes that the Philippine EEZ provides a carbon sink through its net primary production. The results demonstrate that typhoon frequency does not necessarily hinder productivity; in fact, typhoons can boost productivity through upwelling effects. However, the researcher notes that the counter-effect of stratification caused by warming oceans cannot be ignored, as it may affect nutrient transfer. The study also highlights that the NASA CHL product showed high confidence when validated against in-situ data, with only a small percentage of points presenting an overestimate.

Several implications and recommendations are presented. The study provides a low-cost methodology for identifying hotspots of ocean productivity, which can aid in future intensive management and regenerative studies. It is recommended that monitoring efforts be prioritized in Transect 3 (West Philippine Sea) and Transect 4 (Sulu Sea) due to their relatively high productivity and ongoing commercial fishing disputes. To improve accuracy, future research should explore the use of Sentinel-2 data for higher spatial resolution and incorporate more ground truth data. Additionally, further research is needed to understand the coupling effect of typhoons, such as how typhoon-induced urban runoff might impact the ocean's role as a carbon source, and to better understand upwelling dynamics for long-term management of nature-based carbon sequestration.

title: Exploring Philippine Futures Through Intergenerational Lenses: Four Alternative Scenarios of the AmBisyon Natin 2040 Vision
abstract:
This study probes the alternative futures of the Philippines through the lens of AmBisyon Natin 2040, the nation's long-term vision for a matatag (strongly rooted), maginhawa (comfortable), at panatag (secure) na buhay. Utilizing Jim Dator's Four Scenario Archetypes-Growth, Collapse, Discipline, and Transformation - the research constructs four plausible, divergent futures to support more adaptive, inclusive, and forward-looking development planning. Drawing on intergenerational Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with participants from Generation Z, Millennials, and Generation X, the study applies participatory foresight tools including the Futures Triangle, scenario matrix plotting, and narrative co-creation to capture how each cohort’s distinct experiences, values and priorities shaped the drivers, barriers and trade-offs embedded in each scenario. Incorporating intergenerational perspectives strengthened both the credibility and relevance of the scenarios. Generation Z often pushed for forward-looking and innovation-oriented pathways, Millennials grounded the discussion with pragmatic system-level insights, while Generation X contributed historical awareness and stability-focused considerations. Together, these dynamics shaped the development and character of each archetype.

The Growth scenario affirms the current trajectory envisioned in AmBisyon Natin 2040, reflecting incremental improvements in governance, education, health, and digital infrastructure. It presents a future that is stable and moderately inclusive, yet still constrained by persistent structural inequalities.

The Collapse scenario envisions a breakdown of institutions, widespread disillusionment, and systemic dysfunction brought about by unaddressed political, economic, and environmental crises. It serves as a cautionary tale of neglecting present vulnerabilities and failing to build societal resilience.

The Discipline scenario imagines a tightly controlled society in which peace and stability are achieved through centralized governance, strict policies, and enforced conformity. It highlights the trade-offs between security and civic freedom, and the consequences of prioritizing order over participation.

The Transformation scenario presents a radically reimagined Philippines where inclusive innovation, decentralized governance, and cultural revitalization redefine national progress. It explores a break from the status quo, illustrating how deep systemic shifts-fueled by emerging technologies and social movements-can produce a more equitable, empowered, and regenerative society.

These narratives were translated into short-form animated videos to maximize accessibility, emotional resonance, and engagement across generations and sectors. In doing so, the study advances development communication by blending foresight and visual storytelling to foster public imagination, policy reflection, and futures literacy. It underscores the importance of integrating participatory, creative, and generationally diverse approaches into national planning processes, especially as the Philippines navigates uncertainty on the path to 2040.

title: Construction of Entertainment News as a Collaborative and Negotiated Communication and Discourse: An Autoethnographic Study
abstract:
The qualitative study investigated how Entertainment news as a discourse and its meaning come into being. It also interrogated the roles of editorial and Public Relations and Corporate Communications personalities who take part in it, the communication systems and the power relations that enact and shape the construction of Entertainment news. Utilizing analytic autoethnography and thematic analysis, the 10 themes that emerged were “Source” of the “source” of Entertainment news; What and who lands on the Entertainment page; The avenues and sites for Entertainment news; What questions to ask and get to ask; Questions and answers as basis for Entertainment news; The culture of giving; The writer’s making sense of Entertainment event; Entertainment narratives: Events to personalities; Stories people are talking about and whose voice; and New way of gathering and writing Entertainment news. They also revealed different points of communication, collaboration, negotiation and tension in relation to the construction of Entertainment news.

Themes were based on the recollections and experiences of the researcher and the five other informants. In the interplay of their voices, the researcher’s perspective took the lead in understanding how Entertainment news emerges. Using Fairclough and Foucault’s conceptions of discourse and Berger and Luckmann’s The Social Construction of Reality as lenses, the study analyzed and discussed Entertainment news, from the text and discursive levels to the social practice level and encompassing surfaces of emergence and authorities of deliminations, and the habitualization, institutionalization and legitimation of practices and policies. The qualitative study legitimizes the value of Entertainment news and that it is never a neutral site of communication and discourse.

half:
This study investigates the construction of entertainment news as a negotiated communicative act rather than a neutral transmission of facts. The research examines how the interplay between editorial personnel and Public Relations and Corporate Communications professionals shapes the content and delivery of this genre. Using a qualitative methodology involving analytic autoethnography and thematic analysis, the researcher utilized personal recollections and professional experiences from themselves and five informants to interpret how news emerges from intersecting professional interests and social practices.

The findings are organized into ten themes mapping the lifecycle of entertainment news, including identifying news sources, determining what content is selected for publication, and identifying dissemination sites. The research highlights procedural aspects, such as the nature of questioning and interactions, alongside social dimensions like the "culture of giving" and the transformation of events into personality-driven stories. The results suggest an evolution toward a new method of gathering and writing news characterized by constant communication, collaboration, and tension between stakeholders.

Theoretically, the study applies Fairclough and Foucault’s conceptions of discourse to examine news at the text, discursive, and social practice levels, alongside Berger and Luckmann’s theory of the social construction of reality. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that entertainment news is a highly constructed phenomenon manufactured through negotiated communicative acts and institutionalized practices that reflect broader social power dynamics.

Rather than viewing entertainment news as a neutral transmission of facts, the research interrogates it as a negotiated communicative act shaped by the interplay between editorial personnel and Public Relations and Corporate Communications professionals. The research seeks to understand the specific mechanisms, communication systems, and underlying power relations that shape the content and delivery of this genre.

The researcher employed a qualitative methodology utilizing analytic autoethnography and thematic analysis. Data was derived from the personal recollections and professional experiences of the researcher and five other informants. This approach allowed the researcher to use lived experiences as a primary lens to interpret how entertainment news emerges from the intersection of various professional interests and social practices.

The findings are organized into ten distinct themes that map the lifecycle and construction of entertainment news. These themes include identifying the "source" of the "source" of news, determining what and who ultimately lands on an entertainment page, and identifying the sites where news is disseminated. The research highlights procedural aspects of news gathering, such as what questions are asked, who is permitted to ask them, and how the resulting interactions serve as the fundamental basis for content. Furthermore, the findings address social and cultural dimensions, such as "the culture of giving," the transformation of events into personality-driven stories, and the social nature of news regarding whose voices are represented. The results suggest an evolution toward a "new way of gathering and writing entertainment news," characterized by constant communication, collaboration, and tension between stakeholders.

The study applies several theoretical frameworks to analyze these findings.
