title: Sining Para sa Pagbabago: Examining How Sharing Protest Art Online Shapes the Attitudes and Actions of Young Filipinos Towards Socio-Political Advocacy Groups
abstract:
With the internet’s unrelenting presence in people’s lives today, the distribution, reach, and accessibility of protest art has been changed irrevocably. In the evolving landscape of protest art and its audiences, this study endeavored to identify and discuss the societal implications of sharing digital protest artworks in online spaces, examining how they shape the attitudes and actions of young Filipino audiences towards socio-political advocacy groups. 

Through semi-structured, open-ended interviews and surveys with organization representatives, local artists, and audiences, the data used in this research were analyzed using the Grounded Theory approach by Glaser and Strauss. This research study culminated in a paradigm entitled “Effect Beyond The Screen” that explains the starting grounded theory, “The ‘Societal Implications of Sharing Digital Protest Art’ is dependent on the consideration of ‘Audience-Influencing Factors’ in the production of the artworks that serve as the ‘Means of Introduction’ which consequently restarts the process.”

Even with the overarching positive sentiment on the efficacy of sharing digital protest art in shaping Filipino audiences’ attitudes and actions towards socio-political advocacy groups, this study found that while digital protest art is a valuable tool, it is most effective when integrated into a broader framework that emphasizes subsequent calls to action and offline engagement beyond digital activism. Awareness, engagement, and participation in digital protest artworks do not necessarily equate to actual, productive community engagement and collective action, as the outcome still relies heavily on the individual’s decisions.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Dasha Elisa T. Lariosa’s study, "Sining Para sa Pagbabago: Examining How Sharing Protest Art Online Shapes the Attitudes and Actions of Young Filipinos Towards Socio-Political Advocacy Groups," investigates how the transition from physical to digital protest art affects the ability of advocacy groups to mobilize support and influence public perception. The research explores whether increased accessibility to digital art fosters genuine interest in advocacies, identifies resonant elements of digital art for Filipino audiences, and determines if online engagement translates into tangible actions or remains limited to digital awareness.

Using a qualitative research design and the Grounded Theory method, the researcher gathered insights from twenty-three respondents, including local artists, audience members, and representatives of socio-political advocacy groups. The study resulted in the formulation of the "Effect Beyond The Screen" model. This paradigm posits that the societal implications of sharing digital protest art depend on "Audience-Influencing Factors" in the production of artworks that serve as a "Means of Introduction," which subsequently restarts the cycle of engagement.

The findings indicate an overarching positive sentiment regarding the efficacy of digital protest art in shaping attitudes and actions, noting it is a valuable tool for raising awareness and fostering discussion. However, a critical gap exists: digital engagement does not necessarily equate to productive community engagement or collective action. The outcome of digital activism remains heavily dependent on an individual's personal decision to move from the digital sphere to the physical one. The study concludes that digital protest art is most effective when integrated into a broader framework that emphasizes calls to action and offline engagement, serving as a complement to traditional activism rather than a replacement.

The study titled "Sining Para sa Pagbabago: Examining How Sharing Protest Art Online Shapes the Attitudes and Actions of Young Filipinos Towards Socio-Political Advocacy Groups" by Dasha Elisa T. Lariosa investigates the impact of digital protest art on the political engagement of young Filipinos. The research addresses the problem of how the shift from traditional, physical protest art to digital, social media-based art affects the ability of advocacy groups to mobilize support and influence public perception. Specifically, the study seeks to understand if increased accessibility to digital art leads to genuine interest in advocacies, what specific elements of digital art resonate with Filipino audiences, and whether online engagement translates into tangible actions like volunteering or donating, or if it remains limited to digital awareness.

The context of the research is rooted in the evolving landscape of Philippine activism, shaped significantly by the COVID-19 pandemic and the high social media usage among Filipino youth. The author notes that while protest art has a long history in the Philippines—from the colonial era to the Martial Law period—the digital age has introduced new complexities. While social media offers unprecedented reach and anonymity, it also presents challenges such as censorship, the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020, algorithmic echo chambers, and the risk of "clicktivism," where online engagement fails to result in meaningful offline action.

To investigate these dynamics, the researcher employed a qualitative research design using the Grounded Theory method. This approach allowed for an iterative process of data collection and analysis to develop a substantive theory. The study utilized stratified random sampling and theoretical sampling to gather insights from twenty-three respondents, including representatives of local socio-political advocacy groups, local artists, and audience members. Data were collected through semi-structured, open-ended interviews conducted via videoconferencing and online open-ended surveys. The researcher used MAXQDA software to perform open, axial, and selective coding to extract themes from the transcripts and survey responses.

The findings of the study led to the formulation of a new paradigm entitled the "Effect Beyond The Screen" model. This model posits that the societal implications of sharing digital protest art are dependent on "Audience-Influencing Factors" in the production of artworks that serve as the "Means of Introduction," which subsequently restarts the cycle of engagement. The research found an overarching positive sentiment regarding the efficacy of digital protest art in shaping attitudes and actions. Digital art is a valuable tool for raising awareness and fostering discussion. However, the study highlights a critical gap: awareness, engagement, and participation in digital protest art do not necessarily equate to productive community engagement or collective action. The outcome of digital activism remains heavily dependent on the individual's personal decisions to move from the digital sphere to the physical one.

The study concludes that while digital protest art is a powerful medium for education and information dissemination, it is most effective when it is integrated into a broader framework that emphasizes subsequent calls to action and offline engagement. Digital activism should be viewed as a complementary platform to traditional activism rather than a replacement for it. The research emphasizes that for digital art to achieve "ultimate material impact," it must be designed to bridge the gap between online visibility and real-world mobilization.

The implications of this research are significant for local artists and socio-political advocacy groups. For creators, the study suggests that understanding the specific elements that resonate with the Filipino audience is crucial for effective dissemination. For advocacy groups, the findings imply that digital art should not be the end goal of a campaign but rather a "means of introduction" to deeper forms of involvement. The study recommends that future research include older demographics to compare generational shifts in digital engagement and should focus on regional areas outside of Metro Manila to capture a more diverse range of socio-political perspectives. Finally, the researcher suggests that future studies be conducted by larger teams to enhance the credibility and pacing of the data analysis process.

title: Convergences and Divergences in Perspectives on Flexible Learning at a Private Higher Education Institution: An Exploration Using the Iron Triangle Framework
abstract:
This study investigated the convergences and divergences in stakeholder perspectives—specifically faculty, students, and administrators—on the implementation of flexible learning (FL) in a private higher education institution and explored what accounted for such convergences and divergences.

Framed in the Iron Triangle framework, which highlights the interconnected dimensions of access, cost, and quality, the research adopts an abductive case study approach to explore how these stakeholder perspectives, when triangulated with institutional responses to challenges encountered during FL implementation, reflect the tensions arising among issues of access, cost, and quality.

Findings showed that the extent to which these dilemmas are resolved or left unresolved is shaped by their perspective of FL. Specifically, the persistence of the dilemmas can be attributed to the perspective that FL is just a solution to the disruptions caused by the pandemic. While the convergent theme that portrays FL as a combination of traditional and digital modalities provides a plausible basis for institutional engagement in FL, this limited understanding of the relationship between technology and learning also explains the institution’s inability to sustain FL beyond the immediate crisis.

These findings provide implications on the critical role of social perspectives and their interactions in the emergence of the tensions but also the extent to which they are addressed. Recommendations for educational administrators implementing FL are presented along with further areas for research.

half:
This study investigates the convergences and divergences in stakeholder perspectives regarding the implementation of flexible learning at a private higher education institution. By examining the viewpoints of faculty, students, and administrators, the research seeks to understand how these perspectives align or differ and explores the underlying factors that account for these similarities and differences. The research is framed using the Iron Triangle framework, which emphasizes the interconnected dimensions of access, cost, and quality, serving as a lens to examine the tensions that arise when attempting to balance these three competing elements. Using an abductive case study approach, the researcher triangulates stakeholder perspectives with institutional responses to challenges encountered during implementation.

The findings indicate that the extent to which dilemmas associated with the Iron Triangle are resolved or left unresolved is shaped by the specific perspective held toward flexible learning. A significant finding is that the persistence of these dilemmas can be attributed to a perspective that views flexible learning merely as a solution to the disruptions caused by the pandemic. A convergent theme emerged among stakeholders, portraying flexible learning as a combination of traditional and digital modalities. However, the study suggests this limited understanding of the relationship between technology and learning contributes to the institution’s inability to sustain flexible learning beyond the immediate crisis.

The study concludes that social perspectives and their interactions play a critical role in the emergence of tensions regarding access, cost, and quality. The conceptualization of flexible learning as a temporary response to a crisis rather than a long-term pedagogical evolution impacts the institutional capacity to manage the trade-offs between access, cost, and quality.

title: Deceptive by Design: An Interactive Website Exploring, Simulating, and Discussing Dark Patterns
abstract:
Dark patterns are deceptive user interface and user experience techniques that affect consumers into making choices that they usually wouldn't make, and those choices benefit the corporation or developers of the service at the cost of the consumer. This concern has been on the rise in digital platforms, and studies have shown that these practices are effective in influencing consumers. As such, this has led the European Union and the Federal Trade Commission to create legislation to prevent dark patterns from affecting their citizens. At the moment, there is a lack of legislation that protects Filipinos from these deceptive tactics, aside from legislation, there is also a lack of awareness regarding dark patterns in the Philippines. 

This study seeks to bring awareness to dark patterns through an interactive website that simulates, explains, and provides examples to showcase this problem, and provides an opportunity for individuals to become aware of the presence of dark patterns without being in harm's way. Furthermore, a survey was conducted in order to determine the effectiveness of the website and to see if individuals become aware of dark patterns, and whether they agree that there should be legislation in the country to protect citizens from dark patterns? 

In the survey where twenty respondents participated, it was found that prior to interacting with the website, there was a significant lack of awareness of the concept of dark patterns, and yet all believed that at one point they faced a situation wherein they felt pressured by a website or program to make a choice they didn't intend to make. After interacting with the website, the majority of the respondents became aware of dark patterns and believe that there is a need for legislation and for corporations to also be fined for the presence of dark patterns on their platforms. Lastly, all participants of the survey said that they are now more confident in future encounters with dark patterns.

While these practices have become increasingly sophisticated in digital spaces, a significant legislative gap exists in the Philippines. Although the National Privacy Commission has issued guidelines, these are not legislated into law and cannot enforce sanctions, leaving Filipino consumers vulnerable to financial and psychological harm.

This study addressed this problem by creating an interactive website titled Deceptive by Design. The project aimed to educate users by simulating dark patterns in a safe environment to increase awareness and provide context. Using a design-based research approach, the website was built using Framer with a minimalist design. Effectiveness was evaluated through a quantitative survey of twenty respondents who interacted with the website to learn about at least eight dark patterns.

Findings revealed that prior to interacting with the website, there was a significant lack of awareness regarding dark patterns, despite nearly all participants having experienced feeling tricked or pressured by online interfaces. After interaction, the majority of respondents became familiar with the basics, and all participants reported feeling more confident in their ability to recognize and avoid such patterns. Data showed a correlation between education levels and the ability to recognize dark patterns. Furthermore, respondents supported the idea of legislation and fines for companies using these tactics.

While rooted in historical tactics like bait-and-switch marketing, these practices have become increasingly sophisticated in digital spaces. The research objectives include demonstrating the power of UI/UX design to be used both positively and negatively, showcasing interactive media as an educational tool, and contributing to the research gap in the Philippines to potentially aid future legislative efforts.

To evaluate effectiveness, a quantitative survey was conducted via Google Forms. The survey targeted internet users and required them to interact with the website and learn about at least eight dark patterns before answering questions regarding their awareness, confidence, and views on potential legislation and corporate fines.

title: Drag as Creative Expression: Exploring the Lived Experiences of Filipino Drag Queens in Reality Shows
abstract:
This study examines the lived experiences of Filipino drag queens in local drag reality shows, Drag Race Philippines and Drag Den with Manila Luzon, and how these shape their creative expression. Using a transcendental phenomenological approach, in-depth interviews with four participants reveal drag as a powerful and evolving art form that challenges heteronormative norms and promotes LGBTQ+ visibility in a society
where queer identities are often marginalized. The research highlights how drag is not only a mode of artistic expression but also a form of resistance that reshapes cultural narratives and identity.

While reality shows provide a valuable platform for visibility and social transformation, they also introduce challenges such as media commodification and the reinforcement of stereotypes. Participants shared how their creative autonomy was affected by the narratives constructed by television, limiting the authenticity of their drag personas. Despite these constraints, Filipino drag performers continue to use their art to inspire change, confront stigma, and redefine gender and sexual norms. This study contributes to the broader discourse on media representation and LGBTQ+ visibility in the Philippines, offering insights for media practitioners, policymakers, and advocates seeking more inclusive and respectful portrayals of the drag community.

The study examines the transition of Philippine drag from traditional comedic impersonation to a mainstreamed television art form, focusing on the tension between increased LGBTQ+ visibility and authenticity. Using a transcendental phenomenological approach, the researcher conducted in-depth interviews with four participants: Pura Luka Vega, Nicole Pardaux, Elvira, and Margaux.

The findings reveal that drag serves as a multifaceted tool for identity formation, creative expression, and social resistance, allowing performers to communicate queer narratives and social issues like SOGIE rights. Furthermore, media construction can set narrow standards for drag, potentially marginalizing those without Manila-based resources and creating economic disparities through commercialization. The study concludes that while these shows empower performers, they also introduce constraints by viewing drag through the lens of commercial viability. Ultimately, drag has evolved into a significant medium for social advocacy and reclaiming space in a heteronormative society.

This thesis, titled "Drag as Creative Expression: Exploring the Lived Experiences of Filipino Drag Queens in Reality Shows," investigates how participation in local drag reality shows—specifically *Drag Race Philippines* and *Drag Den with Manila Luzon*—influences the creative expression and identities of Filipino drag performers.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the evolving landscape of Philippine drag culture, which has transitioned from traditional comedic female impersonation in local fiestas and bars to a mainstreamed art form showcased on television. While the rise of reality shows has significantly increased LGBTQ+ visibility in the Philippines, the author notes a tension between visibility and authenticity. The research addresses a gap in existing literature regarding the specific lived experiences of Filipino queens navigating the intersection of artistic expression and mass media. The problem centers on how media portrayals, often driven by commercial interests and competition formats, shape the way drag queens perceive their own art and how they construct their creative personas.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a transcendental phenomenological approach to capture the essence of the participants' lived experiences. Data were gathered through in-depth interviews with four participants: Pura Luka Vega, Nicole Pardaux, Elvira, and Margaux. The study utilized Giorgi’s steps for phenomenological data analysis and applied Hall’s constructionist lens to analyze how media constructs the identity of drag queens. Ethical considerations were maintained through informed consent and bracketing to ensure the researcher's personal biases did not overshadow the participants' voices.

**Findings**
The findings reveal that drag serves as a multifaceted tool for creative expression, identity formation, and social resistance. Participants described drag as a way to explore diverse identities, ranging from high-glamour to "alternative" styles, and as a platform to communicate queer narratives and social issues such as SOGIE rights and discrimination.

Regarding media portrayals, the study found that reality shows act as a "double-edged sword." On one hand, they provide a massive platform for visibility, skill development, and professional growth, acting as a "bootcamp" that refines technical skills like makeup and styling. On the other hand, the competition format imposes significant pressures, often forcing queens to prioritize competition over authentic storytelling. Participants noted that television narratives can be "glossy" and may not capture their true reality, sometimes casting them in specific roles (such as the "villain") to suit a scripted storyline. Furthermore, the study identified a trend of "media construction" where reality shows set narrow standards for what "good" drag looks like, potentially marginalizing queens from provinces who lack the same resources or designers as those in Manila. There is also a noted risk of commercialization, where the mainstreaming of drag creates economic disparities between televised queens and those performing in local venues.

**Conclusions**
The study concludes that while reality shows are powerful engines for LGBTQ+ visibility and personal empowerment, they also introduce new forms of constraint. The media does not merely reflect drag; it actively constructs it, often through a lens of commercial viability and competitive tension. For many queens, the "real" competition begins after the show, as they navigate the professional and social consequences of their televised personas. Ultimately, drag in the Philippines has evolved into a significant medium for communication and social advocacy, allowing performers to reclaim space in a society that remains largely heteronormative.

**Implications**
The research offers several implications for various stakeholders. For media practitioners and television producers, the findings suggest a need for more nuanced and authentic representations of the LGBTQ+ community that move beyond repetitive templates or scripted archetypes. For LGBTQ+ advocacy groups, the study highlights the importance of using drag as a tool for social change and the need to support queens who may be marginalized by the mainstreaming of the art form. For policymakers, the study underscores the ongoing need for comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation (such as the SOGIE Equality Bill) to protect the rights of the community. Finally, for the academic field of Development Communication, the study validates the use of drag and queer narratives as significant resources for understanding social transformation and media's role in promoting equality.

title: Examining the Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge (TPACK) of Pre-Service Social Studies Teachers
abstract:
The study examined the preparedness of pre-service Social Studies teachers to assume the role of a beginning teacher at the secondary level using the Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. The study also sought to determine the factors that influenced the development of TPACK among these teachers as they teach the Social Studies subject. This case study employed mixed methods research, specifically the convergent parallel design among 43 fourthyear pre-service teachers engaged in the practice teaching course of Alonso Teachers College in Laguna. The mixed-method design was used to address the limitation of self-report measures in terms of accurately measuring the respondents’ knowledge of the seven domains of TPACK. The quantitative data was collected using a modified TPACK survey instrument while the qualitative data was gathered using open-ended questions and focus group discussions. 

The result of the study showed that the perceived level of knowledge of the seven domains of TPACK is adequate. Among the seven domains, PK had the highest mean score followed by TPK, PCK, TCK, TK, and CK are the three domains that have the lowest overall mean. The development of TPACK among the respondents was influenced by the mode of instruction, ICT infrastructure, teacher factor, field study and teaching internship, and personal characteristics.

title: A Digital Platform for the Documentation and Exploration of Drag Culture and Artistry in the Philippines
abstract:
Makulay: A Digital Platform Prototype for the Documentation and Exploration of Drag Culture and Artistry in the Philippines is a project addressing the need for structured, inclusive, and accessible digital spaces for Filipino drag. Filipino drag remains underdocumented even though drag has gained visibility through popular culture and media. To address this gap, Makulay is designed as a digital platform that functions as a cultural archive, educational resource, and community hub dedicated to preserving and amplifying drag artistry in the Philippines. 

As informed by Queer Theory, Performance Theory, and the Queer Speculative Design for Cultural Empowerment (QSDCE) framework, this study employs a User-Centered Design (UCD) methodology. These perspectives guide both the conceptual grounding and design process, hence it ensures that the platform is inclusive, responsive, and culturally empowering. With that, the prototype integrates features such as drag artist profiles, an interactive historical timeline, a drag culture dictionary, a multimedia repository, and virtual interactive community hub.

The data collection involved in this study were interviews, surveys, and user evaluations, which were analyzed thematically to identify user needs and challenges. Findings highlight four recurring themes: the urgency of archiving drag culture, the demand for representation and visibility, structural challenges faced by drag communities, and the potential of digital platforms to provide spaces of preservation, education, and empowerment.

By situating Filipino drag within a digital framework, Makulay contributes to cultural preservation, queer representation, and multimedia design practices. The project demonstrates the role of digital platforms in legitimizing drag artistry and sustaining community engagement.

title: A Narrative Inquiry into the Meaning of Smoking among Farmworkers in Southern Philippines
abstract: Cigarette smoking is recognized as a global health threat. By the same token, it remains highly prevalent in low and middle-income families like farmworkers, despite efforts by the government and private health agencies to prevent smoking. Thus, this study explored the meaning of smoking among farmworkers and how the meanings reproduced their tenets while living in a farming community. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study that qualitatively investigated the smoking phenomenon among farmworkers in a rural area in Southern Philippines— a topic that has not been treated in much detail in the literature. The research framework used in this work is the socio-cultural tradition (SCT) of communication theory, which theorizes communication as the (re)production of the social order. Using narrative inquiry, the study delved into the seven narratives of farmworker participants about the meaning of smoking. Individual open interviews were conducted among the participants to elicit stories relative to their experience with smoking. The data were analyzed through re-storying and narrative thematic analysis, yielding five themes constituting their meaning of smoking that reproduced a new social order. Results showed that smoking is (1) a parent and peer influence, (2) a means to manage negative feelings and emotions, (3) a thought-provoker and organizer, (4) a culture among friends, and (5) an integral part of life. All these meanings consequently formed and reinforced a new social order, seemingly an indestructible barrier to smoking cessation. Anchored on SCT, it can be surmised that farmworkers’ tenets, while living in their community, were reproduced by these meanings of smoking that governed their lives.

The study "A Narrative Inquiry into the Meaning of Smoking among Farmworkers in Southern Philippines" by Reymark P. Malinda and Benjamina Paula G. Flor investigates why cigarette smoking remains prevalent among low- and middle-income farmworkers despite medical risks and national health laws. Using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, the researchers conducted open interviews with seven male farmworkers in a rural area of the Southern Philippines. Data were analyzed using problem-solution re-storying and narrative thematic analysis to explore the participants' lived experiences and identity-related connections to tobacco use.

The findings identified five primary themes. First, parental and peer influence is significant, with smoking serving as a marker of masculinity or a tool for social inclusion. Second, smoking acts as a psychological coping mechanism for managing emotions like anxiety, anger, fatigue, and loneliness. Third, participants perceive smoking as a cognitive aid for organizing thoughts or solving problems. Fourth, smoking serves as a social vehicle to maintain "pakikisama" (social harmony) and "damayan" (mutual support). Finally, smoking is viewed as an integral, deeply ingrained part of daily routine.

The study concludes that these meanings create a self-reinforcing social order that acts as an "indestructible barrier" to cessation. Because smoking is tied to social identity and cultural norms, traditional anti-smoking campaigns may be insufficient. The authors recommend community-specific interventions, such as targeted counseling and engaging educational tools like comics, alongside better enforcement of tobacco control laws through local officials.

Using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, the researchers conducted open interviews with seven male farmworkers in a rural area of the Southern Philippines. The participants were selected through purposeful sampling based on age, smoking status, residency, and at least five years of farming experience. Data were analyzed using problem-solution re-storying and narrative thematic analysis to unpack the participants' lived experiences and identity-related connections to tobacco use.

The findings identified five primary themes regarding the meaning of smoking. First, parental and peer influence plays a significant role; many participants began smoking in their teenage years after observing parents who smoked without reprimand. Peers also use smoking as a tool for social inclusion or as a marker of masculinity. Second, smoking serves as a psychological coping mechanism to manage negative emotions such as anxiety, anger, fatigue, and loneliness. Third, participants perceived smoking as a cognitive aid that helps them organize thoughts or solve practical problems. Fourth, smoking is a social vehicle used to maintain "pakikisama" (social harmony) and "damayan" (mutual support) among friends. Finally, smoking is viewed as an integral part of daily life, often becoming a deeply ingrained routine that feels inseparable from existence.

The study concludes that these meanings create a self-reinforcing social order that acts as an "indestructible barrier" to smoking cessation. Because smoking is tied to social identity, emotional regulation, and daily rituals, it functions as a cultural norm rather than just a physical addiction. Consequently, traditional anti-smoking campaigns may be insufficient if they fail to account for these socio-cultural meanings.

The authors suggest that public health professionals and local government units should move beyond simple information dissemination toward community-specific interventions. Recommendations include providing targeted counseling, conducting community-based health seminars, and using engaging educational tools like comics or audiovisual materials designed for low-education populations. Additionally, the study emphasizes the need for better enforcement of tobacco control laws in rural areas through coordination with local barangay and purok officials to ensure health initiatives address the unique cultural realities of farming communities.

The study titled "A Narrative Inquiry into the Meaning of Smoking among Farmworkers in Southern Philippines" by Reymark P. Malinda and Benjamina Paula G. Flor investigates the complex relationship between cigarette smoking and the lives of farmworkers in rural areas. Despite global health warnings and national legislative efforts in the Philippines—such as the Sin Tax Law and the Graphic Health Warnings Law—smoking remains highly prevalent among low- and middle-income groups, particularly in rural farming communities. The authors note that while tobacco use is linked to severe health risks, including cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, and was exacerbated during the COVID-19 pandemic, the effectiveness of current anti-smoking measures in rural areas remains questionable. This research seeks to understand the nuanced, qualitative meanings that farmworkers assign to smoking, which may explain why they continue the habit despite economic and health-related deterrents.

The research is grounded in the socio-cultural tradition (SCT) of communication theory, which views communication as a symbolic process that produces and maintains social order. The authors hypothesize that the meanings farmworkers attribute to smoking help reproduce a specific social order or set of tenets within their community. Using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, the researchers conducted individual open interviews with seven male farmworkers in a rural area of the Southern Philippines. These participants were selected through purposeful sampling based on criteria including age, smoking status, residency in the study area, and a minimum of five years of farming experience. Data were analyzed using a two-phased approach: problem-solution re-storying and narrative thematic analysis. This method allowed the researchers to unpack the participants' lived experiences, including their cultural, historical, and identity-related connections to smoking.

The findings revealed five primary themes that constitute the meaning of smoking for these farmworkers: (1) a parent and peer influence, (2) a means to manage negative feelings and emotions, (3) a thought provoker and organizer, (4) a culture among friends, and (5) an integral part of life. Regarding parental and peer influence, participants reported that smoking often began in their teenage years, modeled after parents who were smokers. The lack of reprimand from parents regarding their smoking habits provided a sense of implicit permission. Peers also played a significant role, often using smoking as a tool for social inclusion or as a marker of masculinity.

Psychologically, smoking served as a coping mechanism for managing negative emotions such as anxiety, anger, fatigue, and loneliness. Participants described using cigarettes to calm themselves during stressful work incidents or to manage frustrations caused by family issues, such as a relative's gambling. Furthermore, smoking was perceived as a cognitive aid; some participants reported that it helped them organize their thoughts or provided "eureka moments" when solving practical problems, such as repairing machinery. Socially, smoking was deeply embedded in their friendships, acting as a vehicle for socialization and a way to maintain "pakikisama" (social harmony) and "damayan" (mutual support) through the sharing of cigarettes. Finally, smoking was described as an integral part of their daily routine, often being the first thing they sought upon waking, making it a deeply ingrained habit that felt inseparable from their daily existence.

The study concludes that the meanings assigned to smoking by farmworkers create a self-reinforcing social order that acts as an "indestructible barrier" to smoking cessation. Because smoking is tied to their social identity, emotional regulation, and daily rituals, the habit is not merely a physical addiction but a cultural norm. The researchers suggest that because smoking is so deeply woven into the social fabric of the farming community, traditional anti-smoking campaigns may be insufficient if they do not account for these socio-cultural meanings.

The implications of this research are significant for public health professionals, local government units, and development communication specialists in the Philippines. The authors recommend that anti-smoking campaigns move beyond simple information dissemination and instead focus on community-specific interventions. This includes providing targeted counseling for farmworkers, conducting community-based health seminars, and utilizing more engaging educational tools like comics or audiovisual materials designed for low-education populations. Furthermore, the study highlights a need for better enforcement of tobacco control laws in rural areas, suggesting that coordination with local barangay and purok officials is essential to ensure that health initiatives reach beyond urban centers and effectively address the unique cultural realities of rural farming communities.

title: Laboratory Resilience: Enabler for Organizational Resilience and Public Service Continuity
abstract:
This qualitative study investigated how laboratory personnel define and enact resilience within a regional public sector environmental laboratory in the Philippines, and how these practices contribute to institutional resilience and the continuity of public service. Using an ethnomethodological approach, this research examines how resilience emerges from everyday routines, interactions, and work systems – as a dynamic, context-dependent practice. Data from semi-structured interviews and written responses revealed that laboratory resilience is expressed across four temporal domains: (1) risk management (before), (2) response (during), (3) recovery (after), and (4) refinement (post-disruption), each anchored in leadership’s resolve to deliver mission-critical services despite disruptions caused by both internal vulnerabilities and external threats.

The analysis of resilience practices revealed three central themes: (1) Leadership – commitment, values, and systems; (2) People – availability, behavior, and competence; and (3) Process Reliability. These themes illustrate how personnel manage uncertainty, uphold accountability, and sustain operational continuity. Resilience was found to be not only technical in nature, but also deeply rooted in cognitive, behavioral, and transformative capacities, as well as in visionary leadership, and strong institutional values.

This study underscored the critical role of laboratory resilience in fostering organizational resilience and maintaining public service continuity. It allows laboratory operations to remain functional, adaptive, and credible amid disruption. The findings of this study contribute to resilience theory and public sector research by demonstrating that resilience is dynamic, ethically grounded, and shaped by the unique demands of frontline regulatory environments.

This qualitative study investigates laboratory resilience as a dynamic, socially constructed practice enacted through the everyday routines and interactions of personnel, rather than a static structural outcome. Using an ethnomethodological approach, the research focuses on the Environmental Research and Services Laboratory (ERSL) in Central Luzon, Philippines, a region highly vulnerable to natural and man-made hazards. The study addresses the lack of empirical research regarding how frontline laboratory operations contribute to national and institutional resilience during disruptions.

Data were collected between July and December 2023 through semi-structured interviews, written questionnaires, field notes, observations, and secondary data. Analysis followed a three-phase interpretive coding approach. Findings reveal that personnel define resilience through four temporal domains: risk management, response, resumption/restoration, and refinement. These practices are categorized into three central themes: leadership, people, and process reliability. Leadership resilience involves commitment and ethical governance; people-centered resilience involves staff competence, emotional strength, and teamwork; and process reliability is maintained through standardized protocols and quality assurance.

The study concludes that laboratory resilience is a situated, socially enacted practice that promotes organizational resilience by ensuring uninterrupted operations and building adaptive capacity. Theoretically, it introduces a temporal-process model of laboratory resilience. The researcher recommends that policy makers integrate micro-level insights into Public Service Continuity Plans and suggests that practitioners formalize resilience-oriented leadership training and embed risk management tools into daily routines.

This qualitative study investigates the concept of laboratory resilience and its role in fostering organizational resilience and ensuring the continuity of public services. Using an ethnomethodological approach, the researcher examines how resilience is not merely a static structural outcome but a dynamic, socially constructed practice enacted through the everyday routines, interactions, and work systems of laboratory personnel.

The research is situated within the context of the Philippines, a country identified by the UN University – Institute for Environment and Human Security as being highly vulnerable to natural, man-made, and technological hazards. The study specifically focuses on the Environmental Research and Services Laboratory (ERSL) in Central Luzon, a region prone to volcanic eruptions, typhoons, and floods. The problem addressed is the lack of empirical research regarding laboratory resilience within the public sector, particularly how frontline laboratory operations contribute to the broader mission of national and institutional resilience during disruptions.

The methodology employed is ethnomethodology, which focuses on the "methods" individuals use to make sense of their social environment and maintain order. Data were collected between July and December 2023 through semi-structured interviews with ten laboratory and administrative personnel, supplemented by structured written questionnaires from six participants. The researcher also utilized field notes, observations, and secondary data such as the laboratory’s website and news articles. Data analysis followed a three-phase interpretive coding approach: first-order coding (tagging responses by temporal markers of before, during, and after disruption), second-order coding (grouping patterns by functional similarity), and third-order coding (thematic synthesis).

The findings reveal that laboratory personnel define resilience through four temporal domains: risk management (anticipatory/before), response (during), resumption/restoration (after), and refinement (post-disruption). These practices are categorized into three central themes: leadership, people, and process reliability. Leadership resilience is characterized by commitment, values, and systems, where leaders model ethical governance and provide the necessary infrastructure. People-centered resilience involves the competence, emotional strength, and adaptability of staff, including their ability to maintain psychological safety and teamwork during crises. Process reliability is maintained through standardized protocols, such as quality assurance, equipment calibration, and safety manuals, which ensure operational consistency.

The study concludes that laboratory resilience is a situated, socially enacted, and ethically grounded practice. It is not a fixed organizational trait but is produced through daily activities and interpersonal coordination. When these laboratory-level practices are successful, they promote organizational resilience by ensuring uninterrupted operations, fostering personnel engagement, building adaptive capacity, and maintaining the credibility and reputation of the institution through reliable public service.

The implications of this research are multifaceted. Theoretically, the study introduces a contextual theory of laboratory resilience, proposing a temporal-process model that moves beyond top-down perspectives to highlight how resilience is enacted at the micro-sociological level. Institutionally, it identifies laboratory personnel as vital agents of organizational resilience and highlights leadership as a moral enabler of governance. For policy, the findings suggest that Public Service Continuity Plans (PSCPs) should be refined to integrate these micro-level laboratory insights, aligning with national mandates like the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act. Finally, for practice, the study recommends formalizing resilience-oriented leadership training, institutionalizing regular safety drills, and embedding risk management tools, such as Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (FMEA), into daily laboratory routines.

title: How Online Collaboration Makes Telework Possible: An Ethnomethodological Study
abstract: This ethnomethodological research employed conversation analysis (CA) to examine how the communicative practice of online collaboration makes the phenomenon of telework possible. This study was framed within the perspective of the sociocultural tradition that theorizes communication as “a symbolic process that produces and reproduces shared cultural patterns (Craig, 1999, p.144).” Through conversation analysis, this study revealed teleworkers’ tacit, unacknowledged, and taken-for-granted collaborative practices, as well as their common sense, which enables them to create order and achieve work. This study utilized a pre-recorded Zoom recording of a remote session conducted by teleworkers. The pre-recorded remote session recording aligned with CA’s preference for recorded conversations, which are more natural and non-experimental, rather than provoked by the researcher (ten Have, 2011e, p. 4). The online written interaction found in the remote session recording was also added to the dataset used in this research. This study was guided by the research questions: “What practices do teleworkers employ to accomplish the organization? What organizational arrangement is created in telework?” Its findings include discovering six key practices that enable telework, which are: connecting, synchronizing/coordinating, sharing information, using digital technologies, initiating repair, and complying with data privacy and information security policies. It also proposed an organizational arrangement of telework, which provided a representation of how social order is formed during telework and a symbolic representation of how online collaboration is constituted for the purpose of accomplishing telework.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This ethnomethodological study, titled "How Online Collaboration Makes Telework Possible," investigates the communicative practices that enable telework. Framed within the sociocultural tradition of communication theory, the research examines how microlevel interaction processes in online collaboration facilitate the macrolevel phenomenon of telework. The study addresses the specific practices teleworkers use to accomplish organizational order and the organizational arrangements created through telework.

Using an ethnomethodological approach and Conversation Analysis, the researcher studied talk-in-interaction and practical reasoning through a pre-recorded Zoom video of a remote technical support session involving participants in Mali and India. Data collection included the video recording and written interactions via TeamViewer chat. Analysis focused on turn-taking, sequence organization, repair organization, turn-design, and Membership Categorization Analysis to examine role management.

The findings identify six key practices that enable telework: connecting, synchronizing/coordinating, sharing information, using digital technologies, initiating repair, and complying with data privacy and information security policies. The study concludes that telework is not simply a change in location, but a social order that must be actively and continuously "accomplished" through communicative practices. The researcher proposes a "Proposed Organizational Arrangement of Telework" representing how social order is formed through stages of connecting, synchronizing, sharing, using digital tools, and initiating repairs. This research contributes to Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and communication studies by providing a qualitative perspective on how digital tools and human interaction create a functional work environment.

This ethnomethodological study, titled "How Online Collaboration Makes Telework Possible," investigates the communicative practices that enable the phenomenon of telework. The research is framed within the sociocultural tradition of communication theory, which views communication as a symbolic process that produces and reproduces shared cultural patterns and social order. The study seeks to understand how microlevel interaction processes in online collaboration facilitate the macrolevel phenomenon of telework by answering two primary research questions: what practices do teleworkers employ to accomplish organizational order, and what organizational arrangement is created through telework?

The context of the study is rooted in the proliferation of digital technologies and the shift toward remote work arrangements, a trend significantly accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. While telework offers benefits such as business continuity and flexibility, it introduces unique challenges, including physical distance, temporal distance, and the loss of non-verbal cues inherent in face-to-face communication. The researcher notes that while existing literature explores various aspects of telework and collaboration, there is a gap in understanding the specific communicative processes through which online collaboration constitutes the social order necessary to make telework functional.

To address this gap, the researcher employed an ethnomethodological approach, specifically utilizing Conversation Analysis (CA). This method focuses on the study of talk-in-interaction and the practical reasoning used by participants to manage social action. The data collection involved a pre-recorded Zoom video of a remote technical support session conducted on July 27, 2021. This session involved the researcher (acting as the host) collaborating with customers and vendors located in Mali and India. The dataset included the video recording and the corresponding online written interactions via TeamViewer chat. The researcher adhered to strict ethical guidelines, obtaining permission from the organization's Data Privacy Officer and supervisor, and used letter codes to protect participant identities in the transcripts.

The methodology involved a rigorous four-phase process: data collection, transcription, data analysis, and generating conclusions. Transcription followed a simplified version of the Jeffersonian Transcription System, capturing not only spoken words but also sounds, silences, overlaps, and pace to ensure the data was suitable for sequential analysis. The analysis focused on four types of interactional organization: turn-taking, sequence organization, repair organization, and the organization of turn-design. The researcher also utilized Membership Categorization Analysis to examine how participants' roles were managed during the interaction.

The findings of the study identify six key practices that enable telework through online collaboration: connecting, synchronizing/coordinating, sharing information, using digital technologies, initiating repair, and complying with data privacy and information security policies. The study details how teleworkers navigate the complexities of remote interaction, such as using screen sharing to provide visual cues, requesting verbal acknowledgments to confirm visibility or audibility, and managing technical contingencies through coordinated use of technology. The analysis of the specific sequences in the Zoom recording demonstrates how participants use these practices to maintain a shared understanding and resolve technical issues in real-time.

Based on these findings, the study concludes that telework is not merely a matter of being in a different location, but is a social order that must be actively and continuously "accomplished" through communicative practices. The research demonstrates that online collaboration constitutes the very social order that makes telework possible. The study proposes a "Proposed Organizational Arrangement of Telework," which serves as a symbolic representation of how social order is formed during remote work through stages of connecting, synchronizing, sharing, using digital tools, and initiating repairs.

The implications of this research are both theoretical and practical. Theoretically, the study contributes to the field of Computer-Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) and communication studies by providing a qualitative, bottom-up perspective on how digital tools and human interaction combine to create a functional work environment. It moves beyond quantitative measures of telework effectiveness to explain the "how" of remote collaboration. Practically, the findings offer insights for organizations looking to optimize telework arrangements. By understanding the specific communicative practices required to maintain coordination and resolve repairs, organizations can better design digital workflows, training, and communication protocols to support a more resilient and effective remote workforce.

title: Clickstream Mosaic: A Mixed-Methods Study of Photo Dumping's Impact on Laguna College Students' Communication, Lifestyle, and Self-Discovery
abstract:
The popularity of photo/video dumps has captured the attention of many social media users, particularly during the peak of the pandemic wherein in-person interactions were limited or strictly prohibited in order to safeguard everyone's health and well-being. This mode of virtual engagement allowed individuals in the digital sphere to share their moments, memories, and experiences through a curated collection of photos and videos or a combination of both digital mediums. However, there’s an existing debate whether this form of online interaction prioritizes an idealized perception of oneself to follow a trend or gain some public attention. Others argue that its essence lies in authentic and genuine sharing of personal experiences transparently and in an enjoyable manner. Notably, this trend has resonated notably with the Gen Z demographic, particularly among college students, including those in the Filipino college community. As these students navigate post-pandemic challenges with the return to face-to-face learning nvironments, they face a unique set of hurdles and adjustments.

The researcher's objective was to explore the influence of photo/video dumps on the lifestyle and self-discovery of college Instagram users, with a focus on students in Laguna, Philippines. Employing a Convergent Parallel design, combining both quantitative and qualitative research methods, the study aimed to comprehend user engagement, communication, and behavior related to photo/video dumps. A total of 100 eligible respondents were surveyed, and from these, 10 respondents were selected for Online Interview and Observation to delve deeper into the research. The data collected were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency distribution and percentages. Transcriptions were also made to further understand the data obtained from the Online Interview and Observation phase.

For self-discovery, the practice serves as a reflective tool to track personal growth and express moods. Aguilar investigates the phenomenon of "photo/video dumps" on Instagram. This trend involves sharing curated collections of unfiltered or spontaneous photos and videos to convey a narrative or mood. The study specifically focuses on how this digital behavior influences the lifestyle and self-discovery processes of college students in Laguna, Philippines, particularly within the Gen Z demographic.

The problem addressed by the researcher stems from an ongoing debate regarding the authenticity of social media trends. While some argue that photo dumps are a tool for genuine, transparent self-expression and memory preservation, others suggest they may be a form of "clout chasing" used to maintain an idealized self-image or simply to follow a trend. Given the unique academic and social pressures faced by Filipino college students navigating post-pandemic environments, the researcher sought to understand whether these digital practices serve as meaningful tools for personal reflection or merely as superficial social engagement.

To address these questions, the study employed a Convergent Parallel mixed-methods research design. This approach combined quantitative and qualitative data collection to provide a comprehensive view of the phenomenon. The quantitative phase involved an open-ended survey distributed via Google Forms to 100 eligible respondents residing in Laguna. The participants were primarily college students, with a significant majority being in their fourth year and belonging to the 21-25 age bracket. The qualitative phase consisted of online interviews and observations with 10 participants selected through purposive sampling. During these sessions, participants were asked to discuss their motivations and, in some cases, demonstrate their curation process via screen sharing to provide insight into their creative and organizational behaviors.

The findings from the survey revealed that Instagram usage among the respondents is significant, with 44% of participants spending one to two hours on the platform daily. Most respondents engage in photo/video dumps "occasionally," and the most common content shared includes random events, special events, and self-expression. Interestingly, video dumps are favored over photo dumps, and a high percentage of users (77%) utilize third-party applications, most notably CapCut, to edit their content.

The qualitative data provided deeper insight into the motivations behind this behavior. The primary reasons for engaging in photo dumps include archiving old collections to free up device storage, sharing life events with social circles, and seeking social connection or "clout." The study also identified self-expression, creativity, and simple self-enjoyment as significant drivers. Regarding lifestyle, 62% of respondents reported that participating in photo dumps has influenced their lifestyle. This influence manifests through the establishment of routines, such as posting "monthly dumps," and the practice of "memory making," where students use the platform to document and appreciate small, significant moments amidst stressful academic schedules. In terms of self-discovery, the activity serves as a tool for reflection, allowing users to track their personal growth and express their moods and feelings.

The study concludes that while photo/video dumps may have originated as a social media trend, they have evolved into a functional tool for personal reflection, memory preservation, and self-expression. For many college students, these "clickstream mosaics" act as a digital journal that helps them navigate the complexities of student life. The practice allows for a balance between maintaining an online presence and engaging in authentic self-presentation, often serving as a way to "romanticize" daily life and find joy in mundane moments.

The implications of this research are multifaceted. For social media users, the study highlights the importance of exercising discretion and prioritizing transparency to ensure that digital engagement remains a positive force for well-being. For application developers, particularly in the Philippines, the findings underscore a demand for tools that balance creative flexibility with time efficiency. For creatives, the study illustrates how visual curation can be a powerful medium for communication. Finally, for future researchers, this work provides a foundational understanding of how evolving social media trends impact the psychological and social development of young adults in a specific regional context.

title: All Kinds of Blue: Exploring the Emotional Effect of Lucy's Blue Album on Selected Filipino Fans' Mental Well-Being
abstract:
The pandemic has led to increased reports of depression and anxiety worldwide. While research on the emotional and well-being benefits of pop music is gradually increasing and evolving, there remains a gap in understanding the effects
of foreign music on an individual's well-being and multimedia experiences. This study specifically analyses the effects of BLUE, an album by the Korean band LUCY, on the mental well-being of their Filipino fanbase. Using a qualitative approach, interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with eleven (11) adult Filipino fans. The data collected were analysed through the frameworks of the Social Cognitive and Behavioral Theory as well as the Reception Theory. The study's findings indicate that the album has a positive effect on the fanbase, providing comfort through its ability to uplift, release, reflect, relax, distract, and excite individuals. This suggests that foreign music, including the dynamics of K-Pop or K-Band fandom culture, can serve as a healthy coping mechanism for mood regulation and enhance positive experiences through multimedia art. The study concludes that BLUE is seen as a valuable tool for mental support within the fandom. It is recommended that future research explore the dependent variables and examine similarities and differences among various audience types.

The study concludes that the album serves as a resource for mood regulation and demonstrates that multimedia art can transcend linguistic barriers.

The study was guided by the Social Cognitive and Behavioural Theory and Reception Theory to understand how the audience interprets media based on their personal experiences and how social environments influence cognitive and emotional responses.

Participants reported that the music provides comfort through its ability to uplift, release, reflect, relax, distract, and excite. The tracks within the album were found to be healing; for instance, the title track Rolling Rolling was noted for providing a sense of escape from repetitive daily life, while other tracks like Dream and Hug offered specific emotional resonance. title: Seeds of Change: An Instructional Design for an Urban Gardening Education Program for Less Privileged Residents of Barangay Batong Malake, Los Baños, Laguna
abstract:
This study presented the instructional design for Seeds of Change, an urban gardening education program aimed at empowering underprivileged residents of Brgy. Batong Malake, Los Baños, Laguna Malake to cultivate their own food, addressing the issue of food insecurity. Guided by pedagogical approaches such as the ADDIE Model, Seeds of Change program sought to foster a sustainable, inclusive approach to urban food production, with a focus on practical, cost-effective techniques, particularly container gardening, vertical gardening, and hydroponics.

Eight topics were selected from a pre-survey conducted from April to May 2024, gauging the respondents’ familiarity and interest with certain areas of urban gardening, as well as their experience in gardening.

An “evaluation day” for 15 residents of “Riverside”, an impoverished residential area which best represented the target demographics of the program, was held on August 25, 2024. The pilot test, however, was met with several limitations, particularly the use of English language when most of the participants could not understand it, leading to a decline in post-test performance. Nevertheless, these learners were able to acquire and apply new urban gardening knowledge as they honed their gardening skills and experience, reinforcing the constructivist learning theory.

Despite the challenges faced by the target learning audience, the Seeds of Change program could be used as a blueprint for urban gardening education programs tailored for marginalized individuals and households using resources available to their communities.

Alfonso addresses food insecurity among marginalized residents facing rising food costs and limited agricultural knowledge. Despite interest in gardening, residents are constrained by limited land, financial limitations, and a lack of technical expertise in urban-specific methods.

Using a quantitative descriptive research design, the study employed the ADDIE model and the "Understanding by Design" framework to create a 28-page instructional booklet. The material covers topics including plant biology, crop selection, vertical and container gardening, pest management, watering, organic fertilizers, hydroponics via the SNAP system, and harvesting and marketing.

Findings revealed that while 73.33% of residents have gardening experience, they possess low familiarity with technical topics like hydroponics. An expert review suggested the booklet needs more step-by-step instructions and image captions. During pilot testing, some participants had lower post-test scores than pre-test scores, which the author attributed to the use of English. However, learner perception was overwhelmingly positive, with 93.33% agreeing the booklet increased their knowledge. To improve inclusivity, the author recommends translating materials into the local language, incorporating hands-on activities, and using diverse audiovisual materials. The program demonstrates that tailored instructional designs can effectively promote agricultural literacy and urban food security.

The technical report titled "Seeds of Change: An Instructional Design for an Urban Gardening Education Program for Less Privileged Residents of Barangay Batong Malake, Los Baños, Laguna" by Jason Gabriel C. Alfonso addresses the critical issue of food insecurity among marginalized communities. Despite the proximity of Barangay Batong Malake to the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB), a premier center for agricultural excellence, many low-income residents lack access to agricultural education and face rising food costs exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, many residents possess an interest in gardening but are constrained by limited land area, financial limitations, and a lack of technical knowledge regarding urban-specific methods.

The study's context is rooted in the need for sustainable, cost-effective food production solutions for urban dwellers. The author identifies that traditional farming is often unfeasible for residents in densely populated areas due to space constraints. Consequently, there is a significant opportunity to utilize urban gardening techniques—such as container gardening, vertical gardening, and hydroponics—to promote food security, environmental stewardship, and community socialization. The project aligns with several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including Zero Hunger, Quality Education, Sustainable Cities and Communities, and Life on Land.

The methodology employed a quantitative descriptive research design. The process began with a needs assessment pre-survey conducted between April and May 2024 to gauge the familiarity and interest of residents in various gardening topics. Using quota sampling, the researcher gathered data from various "puroks" (zones) within the barangay. The instructional design was developed using the ADDIE model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) and was informed by the "Understanding by Design" (UbD) framework, which utilizes "backwards design" to ensure learning activities align with desired outcomes. The final output was a 28-page instructional booklet covering eight key topics: basic plant biology, crop selection, vertical and container gardening, pest and disease management, proper watering, organic concoctions and fertilizers, hydroponics (specifically the SNAP system), and harvesting and marketing.

The implementation phase involved a pilot test on August 24, 2024, with 15 residents from the "Riverside" area, a low-income neighborhood. The evaluation phase included an expert review by a faculty member from UPLB-CAFS and a learner perception assessment.

The findings revealed several important insights. The pre-survey indicated that while many residents had some gardening experience (73.33%), they had low familiarity with technical topics like hydroponics and crop rotation, but high interest in learning them. The expert review noted that while the content was valuable, the booklet had some deficiencies, such as a lack of detailed step-by-step instructions for some activities and the need for more captions for images. A significant finding during the pilot test was that post-test scores were lower than pre-test scores for some participants; the author attributes this to the use of English as the medium of instruction, which was a barrier for many residents. However, learner perception was overwhelmingly positive. Despite the language barrier, 86.67% of learners found the language clear and understandable, and 93.33% agreed that the booklet contributed to their knowledge and skills. All 15 participants stated they were likely to recommend the booklet to others, and the most well-liked topic was basic plant biology.

In conclusion, the "Seeds of Change" program was successful in achieving its primary objectives of helping learners recall basic gardening knowledge and identifying various urban gardening methods. The study demonstrates that even with limited resources and time, an instructional design tailored to the specific needs of a community can effectively promote agricultural literacy. The project reinforces constructivist learning theory, as participants were able to build upon their existing gardening experiences to acquire new, practical skills.

The implications of this study suggest that for urban gardening education to be truly inclusive and effective for marginalized populations, instructional materials must be accessible. The author provides several recommendations: first, instructional materials and evaluation tools should be translated into the local language (Filipino or Tagalog) to overcome linguistic barriers; second, the inclusion of collaborative, hands-on activities—such as gardening diaries or community projects—would better support the constructivist learning process; and third, a combination of projected and non-projected audiovisual materials should be used to cater to diverse learning styles (visual, auditory, and kinesthetic). Ultimately, the "Seeds of Change" booklet serves as a viable blueprint for developing community-based agricultural education programs aimed at enhancing food security in urban environments.

title: Modular Learning Experiences of Senior High School Tanglaw Pag-asa Residents
abstract: The Juvenile Justice Law mandates providing psychosocial and education-focused interventions to Children in conflict with the law (CICLs). The Department of Education (DepEd)’s Alternative Learning System (ALS) program, provides education opportunities to CICLs in youth rehabilitation centers for their reintegration into society. The program adopts a modular learning approach, where learners use self-learning modules (SLMs) anchored on DepEd’s Most Essential Learning Competencies, or skills learners must develop to succeed academically and be job-ready. This study aimed to describe Tanglaw Pag-asa Residents’ modular learning experiences. The participants are three ALS-SHS students at St. Martin de Porres Catholic School. The data was collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Challenges participants face include feeling overwhelmed by their workload, maintaining motivation, and lacking background knowledge of some topics. Participants are intrinsically and extrinsically motivated. They mentioned guidance from more knowledgeable others when asked how to enhance their learning experiences.

Castro investigates the educational experiences of children in conflict with the law (CICL) within a rehabilitation setting. The study focuses on how these individuals navigate the Alternative Learning System (ALS) through a modular learning modality while residing at the Tanglaw Pag-asa Youth Rehabilitation Center in Bulacan.

The problem addressed in this study stems from the challenges inherent in providing effective education to CICLs. While the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Law mandates psychosocial and educational interventions to aid reintegration, the lack of direct and constant supervision in modular learning poses significant hurdles. There is a specific concern regarding whether residents can effectively apply acquired knowledge without the immediate presence of instructors, and how their unique circumstances affect their ability to engage with self-learning modules (SLMs). The researcher identifies a need to understand the specific learning needs, challenges, and motivational factors of these students to improve the design and delivery of educational interventions.

The context of the study is situated within the Philippine juvenile justice system and the Department of Education’s (DepEd) ALS program. Tanglaw Pag-asa is a youth rehabilitation center managing 37 residents, 14 of whom are Senior High School (SHS) students. These students utilize SLMs anchored on DepEd’s Most Essential Learning Competencies (MELCs) to continue their education during rehabilitation. The study is framed by several theoretical perspectives: Vroom’s Expectancy Theory of Motivation, Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory (specifically the concept of the Zone of Proximal Development and scaffolding), and Fleming’s VARK model of learning styles.

To investigate these experiences, the researcher employed a qualitative descriptive research design. The study utilized purposive sampling to select three ALS-SHS students at St. Martin de Porres Catholic School for participation. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews, which allowed for in-depth investigation and follow-up questions. The researcher used interview guides and recording devices to capture the participants' narratives. The collected data was then analyzed using deductive thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes within the transcripts.

The findings of the study revealed five primary themes: increased autonomy, academic challenges, extrinsic and intrinsic sources of motivation, the need for diverse activities, and the necessity of scaffolding. Regarding autonomy, participants noted that modular learning allows them to learn at their own pace and manage their own schedules. However, this is countered by significant academic challenges, including managing heavy workloads, maintaining motivation, and struggling to understand complex content due to a lack of prior knowledge.

Motivation was found to be driven by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Extrinsically, participants were motivated by parental support, recognition of their hard work, and praise from others. Intrinsically, they expressed a strong desire to learn to build a better future for themselves and their families. The findings also highlighted a critical need for "More Knowledgeable Others" (MKOs) to provide scaffolding, particularly in difficult subjects like Mathematics. Participants expressed a desire for more diverse, interactive activities—such as oral presentations—which are often absent in a purely modular setup.

The study concludes that while modular learning offers beneficial autonomy and supports the rehabilitation process, it is insufficient on its own for this specific population. The lack of direct instruction and the difficulty of self-studying complex topics without guidance can negatively impact motivation and learning outcomes. The research affirms that for education-focused interventions to be successful for CICLs, they must be paired with psychosocial support and tailored to the learners' specific needs and motivations.

The implications of this research suggest several pathways for improvement in educational delivery for residents in rehabilitation centers. The researcher recommends the integration of television-based instruction to provide multimedia support, which may better cater to visual and auditory learners. Additionally, incorporating hands-on activities is suggested to support kinesthetic learners, provided there is adequate supervision by center staff. For policymakers and educators, the study emphasizes the importance of designing modules that are flexible and inclusive of diverse learning styles. Finally, the researcher suggests that future studies should explore other variables, such as the level of parental involvement and the readiness of learners for self-paced instruction, to further refine educational support for children in conflict with the law.

title: Designing Self-Learning Modules on Project Management for the Sangguniang Kabataan Council of Barangay Sapangbato
abstract: Project management is a vital part of the public sector whose fundamental function is to develop projects that create effective services and enhance the existing ones (Selepe, 2023)—making project management skills a core competency for public officials like the Sangguniang Kabataan Council. In an initial assessment with the SK Council of Barangay Sapangbato, Angeles City, Pampanga, weak project management skills were revealed to be the council’s most pressing issue, specifically in time management and task division areas. This paper seeks to address this problem through instructional design by developing three (3) digital Self-Learning Modules on project management developed using instructional and multimedia design principles, theories of learning, learning objectives development, methods of assessment, Open Education concepts, and Online Learning models. A synchronous online class was conducted to pilot-test the first SLM. The summative assessment revealed the learners’ understanding of basic project management concepts such as project characteristics, life cycles, constraints, and relevant intrapersonal and interpersonal skills. The skills and knowledge that the learners can gain from the SLMs will enable them to design and conduct projects that aid in the holistic development of their members. Moreover, the SLMs can be a significant addition to the limited number of project management materials specially designed for the SK Council.
