Aiko Marie J. Fujino’s technical report addresses the need for specialized project management training for the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) Council of Barangay Sapangbato. The study identified that while council members possess some knowledge of budgeting and proposals, they struggle with time management and task division. Existing online resources were found to lack the specific context required for their unique roles.

Using the ADDIE model, the author developed three digital Self-Learning Modules (SLMs) grounded in Mayer’s Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, Constructivist principles, and Bloom’s Taxonomy. Learner analysis revealed that the ten council members prefer visual learning and are proficient with digital tools. The resulting modules cover project characteristics and life cycles, methodologies like Waterfall and Agile, and practical tools such as Gantt charts and Work Breakdown Structures.

Pilot testing of the first module via a synchronous online class yielded highly positive results. Summative assessments confirmed that learners understood core concepts, and post-pilot surveys indicated high satisfaction, with participants finding the materials informative and relevant. Despite some technical issues regarding internet connectivity and QR code scanning, the study concludes that instructional design effectively bridges the gap between theory and practical public service duties. The author recommends that future developers contextualize materials using local language and community activities to further enhance effectiveness for SK Councils nationwide.

The technical report titled "Designing Self-Learning Modules on Project Management for the Sangguniang Kabataan Council of Barangay Sapangbato" by Aiko Marie J. Fujino addresses the critical need for specialized project management skills among youth leaders in the public sector. The study focuses on the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) Council of Barangay Sapangbato in Angeles City, Pampanga.

The problem identified is that the SK Council struggles with effective project management, specifically regarding time management and task division. While various project management resources exist online, there is a significant lack of materials specifically tailored to the unique roles, duties, and contexts of the SK Council. This deficiency can hinder the council's ability to develop effective community services and initiatives.

To address this, the author utilized an instructional design approach to develop three digital Self-Learning Modules (SLMs). The methodology followed the ADDIE model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation). The process began with a needs assessment conducted through an in-person interview with the SK Council chairperson, which confirmed that weak time and task management were the most pressing issues. This was followed by a learner analysis using an online survey to identify the characteristics, technological access, and prior knowledge of the ten SK Council members.

The instructional design was grounded in several theoretical and conceptual frameworks. Mayer’s Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning served as the primary theoretical framework to ensure the modules effectively used text and visuals to promote deeper learning. The design also incorporated Constructivist principles, emphasizing learner-centeredness and active knowledge construction. The modules were developed using Open Educational Resources (OERs) to ensure accessibility and were structured using Bloom’s Taxonomy to create aligned learning objectives and assessments.

The findings from the learner analysis revealed that the target learners have diverse learning styles, with a prominent preference for visual learning. The learners demonstrated existing knowledge in areas such as project proposals, budgeting, and evaluation, but showed a need for improvement in time management. Regarding technology, the learners were found to be proficient in using digital tools, such as word processing, search engines, and collaboration tools, and were comfortable with online learning environments.

The developed SLMs were designed to be self-paced and self-directed. Module 1 covers project characteristics, life cycles, constraints, and necessary interpersonal skills. Module 2 focuses on project management methodologies, such as Waterfall and Agile. Module 3 addresses practical tools like Gantt charts and Work Breakdown Structures (WBS). The modules were evaluated by a content expert—a former SK Council chairperson and teacher—to ensure quality in content, multimedia use, and ease of use.

The first module was pilot-tested through a two-hour synchronous online class. The results of the pilot testing were highly positive. Summative assessments indicated that learners understood basic project management concepts, such as project constraints and life cycles. A post-pilot testing survey showed high learner satisfaction, with participants describing the class and modules as informative, engaging, and beneficial. Learners specifically highlighted the relevance of the real-life scenarios and the practical application of theories to their specific roles in the SK Council. However, some technical issues were noted, such as difficulties with QR code scanning and inconsistent internet connectivity.

The study concludes that instructional design is an effective method for addressing the specific educational needs of public officials. The development of tailored SLMs successfully bridged the gap between abstract project management theories and the practical requirements of the SK Council's duties. The project demonstrated that when learning materials are designed with the specific characteristics and needs of the learners in mind, they can significantly enhance knowledge acquisition and skill development.

The implications of this work suggest that public sector institutions should consider utilizing instructional design to help officials acquire specialized skills. The author recommends that future developers contextualize and localize instructional materials by using the local language and specific community activities to increase relevance. Additionally, the report suggests that future implementations should account for technical risks, such as connectivity issues, and consider various learning modalities beyond purely synchronous online sessions. Finally, the author notes that while these modules were designed for Barangay Sapangbato, they could serve as a valuable resource for other SK Councils across the country.

title: Designing Multisensory Activities for Teaching Prepositions to the Young Learners of the Integrated Jubilation Montessori Center of Biñan (IJMC-B)
abstract: The special project that was developed is an instructional design for students in the Kindergarten level of the Integrated Jubilation Montessori Center of Biñan (IJMC-B) to learn about the topic of prepositions under the subject of Language. The ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation and Evaluation) instructional design model was the methodological approach utilized in the instructional design project. Based on the assessment through a sit-in observation in the Kindergarten classroom and a discussion with the key personnel, the instructional needs identified is the integration of different sensory modalities in the learning activities through media, visuals and colorful instructional materials for motivation as the students were recognized as visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners. On the other hand, the learning needs identified are the linguistic gap on the common mistakes with the use of prepositions in sentences and phrases. Although the IJMC-B follows the K to 12 Basic Education Curriculum by the Department of Education (DepEd) across all grade levels, the topic of prepositions was not found in the curriculum for the Kindergarten level. The instructional design project aimed to design an instructional plan that involves multisensory activities and instructional materials, including slide presentations, flashcards, printed objects and printed worksheets for teaching prepositions. The four-step method of instruction serves as the inspiration for the methodology used for the flow of the instructional plan. The design of the learning activities utilized several learning theories including the multisensory approach, Social Learning Theory, positive reinforcement in operant conditioning and Activity-Based Learning.

Furthermore, a curriculum gap exists as prepositions are not explicitly included in the DepEd Kindergarten Curriculum Guide, the MATATAG Curriculum, or the Alternative Learning System curriculum.

The study focused on 15 Kindergarten students, aged 5 to 6, who were identified as visual, auditory, and kinaesthetic learners. Using the ADDIE instructional design model, the author implemented a multisensory approach incorporating Social Learning Theory, operant conditioning, and Activity-Based Learning. The instructional plan consisted of two sessions covering various prepositions using materials such as slide presentations, flashcards, videos, and real objects.

Implementation showed that the design was successful; students demonstrated high engagement and achieved learning objectives, with the first session resulting in an average score of 91.7%. While technical issues, pacing difficulties, and schedule delays occurred, the project successfully enhanced students' vocabulary and language development. The author recommends that educators test technological devices and prepare alternative formats like printed flipbooks. Additionally, the author suggests that prepositions should be formally included in the Philippine Kindergarten curriculum to support early language acquisition.

The technical report titled “Designing Multisensory Activities for Teaching Prepositions to the Young Learners of the Integrated Jubilation Montessori Center of Biñan (IJMC-B)” by Reine Gerbie R. Labarrete addresses the linguistic development of Kindergarten students through specialized instructional design.

The problem identified is a linguistic gap regarding the correct use of prepositions in sentences and phrases among young learners. The author notes that while prepositions are essential for following instructions and locating objects, they are often a significant challenge for English as a Second Language (ESL) learners. Furthermore, a curriculum gap was identified: the topic of prepositions was not explicitly found in the DepEd Kindergarten Curriculum Guide, the MATATAG Curriculum, or the Alternative Learning System (ALS) curriculum. Additionally, the author observed that existing classroom instruction was primarily textbook-based, offering limited opportunities for interactive learning.

The context of the study is the Integrated Jubilation Montessori Center of Biñan (IJMC-B), a school serving Pre-Kindergarten to Grade 10 students. The target learners for this project were 15 Kindergarten students (ten boys and five girls) aged 5 to 6 years old. Through a sit-in observation and discussions with school personnel, the author identified that these students are visual, auditory, and kinaesthetic learners. The learning environment was described as having colorful, child-friendly walls, though physical conditions like air circulation were noted as inadequate during the summer season. Available resources were minimal, consisting of a blackboard, a small television, and limited visual aids, with more advanced technology like laptops and projectors located in the administration office.

To address these needs, the author utilized the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) instructional design model. The methodology was informed by several learning theories: the multisensory approach (VAKT: visual-auditory-kinesthetic-tactile), Social Learning Theory, positive reinforcement within operant conditioning, and Activity-Based Learning. The design phase involved creating an instructional plan consisting of two specific learning sessions: "Prepositions: In, On, Under, Over" and "Prepositions: Behind, In Front Of, Beside, Between." The development phase included the creation of various instructional materials such as slide presentations, flashcards, printed objects, printed worksheets, videos, and real objects like toys and boxes.

The implementation phase involved pilot-testing these sessions. The first session focused on basic spatial prepositions through video presentations, hands-on object categorization, and worksheet matching. The second session expanded on these concepts using a four-step method of instruction: preparation, presentation, application, and evaluation. During the application phase, students engaged in hands-on activities, such as placing objects in specific positions and creating their own sentences.

The findings from the evaluation phase indicated that the instructional design was successful. Students demonstrated high engagement, characterized by attentiveness and eager participation. The students achieved their learning objectives, with the first learning session resulting in an average score of 91.7% on the evaluation worksheets. The implementers were able to follow the structured methodology, and the multisensory materials effectively catered to the students' diverse learning styles.

However, several challenges were encountered during implementation. Technical issues arose when attempting to project slide presentations on a small television, requiring a quick shift to a laptop. The implementers also faced difficulties with pacing; the first session exceeded the allotted time due to the students' pace, and the second session had certain activities omitted due to time constraints. Additionally, the schedule for the second session was delayed by external factors such as class suspensions and school events.

The report concludes that the instructional design project successfully met its objectives of enhancing the students' vocabulary and language development through multisensory engagement. The use of visual aids and interactive activities proved effective in helping Kindergarten students recognize and apply prepositions.

The implications of this work suggest several paths for future practice. For educators, the author recommends ensuring all technological devices are tested prior to lessons and preparing alternative formats, such as printed flipbooks, in case of technical failure. It is also recommended that implementers carefully align their teaching pace with the students' response rate to maintain engagement. On a broader scale, the author suggests that the topic of prepositions should be formally included in the Kindergarten curriculum in the Philippines to support early language acquisition. Finally, the project serves as a model for instructional designers to create community-based, multisensory interventions that bridge linguistic gaps in early childhood education.

title: Applying Literature-Based and Play-Based Approach Accompanied by Non-Projected Instructional Materials in a Child Development Center
abstract: This project explores an innovative, cost-effective approach to improving early childhood development in a resource-limited daycare center in Polillo Islands, Quezon, Philippines. A needs assessment revealed key development delays in cognitive, socio-emotional, and motor skills of children enrolled in the center, largely due to inadequate funding and infrastructure. In response, this initiative introduced a flexible, Play-based and Literature-based instructional plan accompanied by handcrafted, recycled teaching aids. Pilot testing showed promising results, with increased child engagement and participation, making learning fun, focused, and accessible. Even though challenges in complex topics delivery emerged, this project demonstrates how resourceful, locally tailored solutions can overcome educational barriers and support essential childhood development and growth.

This technical report by Shella May M. Mendoza investigates strategies to improve early childhood development in resource-limited settings, specifically at the Paubay Child Development Center in Polillo Islands, Philippines. A needs assessment revealed significant developmental gaps in children's cognitive, socio-emotional, and gross motor skills. These delays were attributed to systemic issues, including a reliance on traditional, teacher-centered instructional methods, a lack of play-based activities, and severe resource constraints such as insufficient funding and unreliable electricity.

To address these issues, the author implemented a special project using the ADDIE instructional design model. The methodology involved a two-week pilot implementation using two nature-themed modules that integrated literature-based and play-based pedagogies. To circumvent the lack of funding and electricity, the author designed cost-effective, reusable materials—such as big books, rolling storyboards, and 3D mock-ups—utilizing recycled materials like cardboard. The implementation was guided by developmental theories from Mildred Parten, Kenneth Rubin, and Lev Vygotsky, alongside Robert Gagne’s principles of instructional design.

Findings indicated that this integrated approach effectively increased child engagement and participation. The literature-based approach piqued interest, while the play-based approach allowed for active exploration. Non-projected materials successfully provided visual and tactile stimulation despite the lack of digital technology. However, challenges included difficulties in encouraging participation from all children, maintaining teacher consistency, and time constraints. The study concludes that resourceful, locally tailored, and low-cost solutions can mitigate the impact of inadequate infrastructure.

This technical report by Shella May M. Mendoza investigates strategies to improve early childhood development in resource-limited settings. The study focuses on the Paubay Child Development Center in Polillo Islands, Quezon, Philippines, a rural community where economic challenges impact educational resources.

A needs assessment and learner analysis revealed that children showed significant delays in cognitive, socio-emotional, and gross motor skills. To address these issues, the author implemented a special project using the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) instructional design model. The methodology involved a two-week pilot implementation consisting of two modules themed around nature ("God created a beautiful world around us"). The approach integrated literature-based and play-based pedagogies, supported by non-projected instructional materials. These materials—such as big books, rolling storyboards, flashcards, pulling charts, and 3D mock-ups—were designed to be cost-effective, flexible, and reusable, specifically utilizing recycled materials like cardboard to circumvent the lack of funding and electricity.

The implementation was guided by various developmental theories, including Mildred Parten’s stages of social play, Kenneth Rubin’s theories of play, and Lev Vygotsky’s social constructivism. The author also applied Robert Gagne’s principles of instructional design to ensure the lessons captured attention and facilitated learning through formative assessments. The pilot sessions included diverse activities such as storytelling, role-playing, sensory play, music and movement, and hands-on activities like planting.

The findings from the pilot implementation indicated that the integrated approach was effective in increasing child engagement and participation. The literature-based approach served to pique interest and provide thematic focus, preventing cognitive overload, while the play-based approach allowed children to explore concepts actively. The non-projected materials successfully provided visual and tactile stimulation in an environment where digital technology was unavailable. However, the study noted some challenges, including difficulties in encouraging participation from all children, maintaining teacher consistency in following the instructional plan, and time constraints. Additionally, the author noted that while non-projected materials are highly effective for resource-limited settings, they may pose challenges when attempting to explain highly complex topics compared to multimedia resources.

In conclusion, the project demonstrates that resourceful, locally tailored, and low-cost instructional solutions can effectively mitigate the impact of inadequate funding and infrastructure in early childhood education. By shifting from teacher-centered to learner-centered approaches, the project successfully fostered a more engaging and interactive learning environment that supports essential developmental domains.

Based on these results, the author offers several recommendations for improving child development center outcomes. First, there is a need to enhance the capacity of child development workers through specialized training. Second, while non-projected materials are vital, they should ideally be used in conjunction with multimedia and technological resources when available. Third, educators should maintain a variety of differentiated play-based and literature-based activities to sustain child interest. Finally, the author emphasizes the importance of continuous evaluation, recommending a cycle of ongoing feedback and assessment regarding both children's progress and teaching performance.

title: The MQP Joint-Project: Youth Ministry E-ntegration 1st Section
abstract:
This capsule project is part of a two-phase joint-intervention program targeted towards the chosen locale of Mary the Queen Parish (MQP), a religious institution under the Roman Catholic Christian denomination which also serves as an institution facilitating learning to parish members and church-goers through seminars and team-building activities. The uniqueness of the institution’s context as a place wherein worship and learning occurs simultaneously underpins a delicate learning process that balances the Catholic doctrine with the conventional methods and strategies for learning. A field inspection and context analysis of the Institution
revealed particular gaps and issues being faced by the parish which pertain to the need for instructional materials, manuals, and an exploration of technology-integration within the parish particularly on the part of the BA Core Youth Ministry which was identified to be inactive and scattered. In order to address these gaps, instructional design was utilized to design and create digital instructional materials and manuals that are print compatible which serves the purpose of helping resolve the aforementioned gaps within the institution. This phase of the joint-project focused on developing instructional materials to be used by the target learners during the BBS 1 youth seminar, with the developed materials garnering positive feedback from the target audience. With that said, feedback showed split preference between the digital and print version of the material. Length also became a deciding factor as the final combined output of the joined-project was deemed to be too lengthy which warranted changes in the sectioning and presentation of its content.

The study focuses on revitalizing an inactive youth ministry by integrating technology and open education principles to improve the Basic Bible Seminar 1 (BBS 1). Previously, the parish relied on unappealing, low-quality, text-based materials that failed to engage late teenagers and young adults.

Using the Training Cycle Model, the proponent redesigned the BBS 1 modules by applying Skinner’s Behaviorism, Sweller’s Cognitive Load Theory, Mayer’s Multimedia Learning Theory, and Nash’s Visual Principles. The new materials were developed to be both digital and print-compatible, utilizing multimedia principles like spatial contiguity and signaling to create an effective visual schema.

Evaluation results showed positive feedback regarding content validity and presentation. However, a split preference emerged: 50% of participants preferred digital versions, while 50% preferred printed versions. This divide was influenced by the costs of mass production versus the digital literacy required for electronic modules. Implementation challenges included scheduling, resource contextualization, and resistance from older members regarding the use of gamification. Ultimately, the project demonstrates that modern instructional design can improve non-formal religious education, providing flexible tools for ministry. The study recommends prioritizing digital literacy training and early stakeholder engagement when implementing interactive strategies.

two:
The MQP Joint-Project: Youth Ministry E-ntegration 1st Section is a capstone project by Anthony Jonathan T. Rosantina that addresses educational gaps within a non-formal educational setting. The project focuses on Mary the Queen Parish (MQP), a Roman Catholic institution in Taytay, Rizal. The study explores how technology integration and open education principles can revitalize a youth ministry that was identified as being inactive and scattered.

The problem identified through field inspections and discussions with parish leadership was a significant lack of updated, appropriate, and engaging instructional materials for the parish's Basic Bible Seminar 1 (BBS 1). The existing materials were described as being primarily text-based, monochrome, and of low visual quality, making them unappealing to the target audience of late teenagers and young adults. Furthermore, the parish faced challenges in utilizing its available technological resources, such as projectors and computers, to enhance the learning experience. There was also a noted need for trained facilitators to lead these seminars, as the current leadership lacked the necessary instructional tools to engage the youth effectively.

To address these issues, the proponent utilized an instructional design approach based on the Training Cycle Model (derived from the ADDIE model), which includes analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. The project was designed as a joint-intervention, with the first phase focusing on the development of digital and print-compatible instructional materials for the BBS 1 seminar. The design was underpinned by several theoretical frameworks: Skinner’s Behaviorism, Sweller’s Cognitive Load Theory, Mayer’s Multimedia Learning Theory, and Nash’s Visual Principles of Instructional Media and Technologies for Learning. The project also embraced the principles of Open Education, intending to license the final materials under Creative Commons to allow for future adaptation and remixing by the parish.

The methodology involved a multi-stage process beginning with a needs assessment through ocular observations, informal interviews, and discussions with the Parish Priest. The target audience was narrowed down to the BA Core Group, a subset of the youth ministry consisting of individuals aged 18 and up who are being trained as future facilitators. During the design phase, the proponent overhauled the original, low-resolution text-based module into a redesigned version that included prayers, songs, Bible verses, and conference topics. These were presented using multimedia principles, such as spatial contiguity and signaling, to ensure the content was visually engaging and easy to process. The implementation phase consisted of a controlled distribution of the module followed by an online pilot testing seminar to gauge the effectiveness of the new materials.

Findings from the evaluation phase were overwhelmingly positive regarding the content's validity, arrangement, and presentation. The incorporation of multimedia principles helped create a more effective visual schema for the learners. However, the results also revealed a split preference regarding the medium of delivery; 50% of participants preferred digital versions, while the other 50% preferred printed versions. This split was driven by different priorities: some participants were concerned about the cost of mass-producing printed modules, while others were concerned that digital modules might be difficult to navigate for those with limited digital literacy. Additionally, the length of the module was a point of contention, as some participants found the 200-page printed version too cumbersome, whereas the digital version allowed for easier sectioning.

The project also encountered several challenges during implementation. Coordinating with the Parish Priest was difficult due to his busy schedule, and finding existing contextualized resource materials was a hurdle until the proponent attended a seminar to gain firsthand knowledge. Furthermore, the proponent faced difficulties in scheduling implementation due to the costs of in-person printing and the limited participation during the online pilot sessions. A significant institutional challenge arose when the proposed use of gamification—intended to increase engagement—was met with conflicting opinions from older parish members who feared it might make the religious content seem less serious.

In conclusion, the project successfully demonstrated that technology integration and the application of instructional design theories can significantly improve the quality of non-formal religious education. The redesigned materials provided a more engaging and accessible way for the youth to engage with Catholic doctrine. The project achieved its goal of creating a flexible, high-quality instructional tool that can be used both digitally and in print, thereby addressing the immediate needs of the BBS 1 seminar.

The implications of this study suggest that non-formal educational institutions, such as churches, can benefit greatly from adopting modern instructional design practices. The findings highlight the importance of creating materials that are compatible with multiple formats to accommodate varying levels of technology access and user preferences. The study also recommends that institutions should prioritize digital literacy training to support the transition to digital learning. Finally, the project suggests that when implementing interactive strategies like gamification in religious contexts, it is crucial to engage with community stakeholders early in the process to align educational strategies with the institution's traditions and values.

title: Play-Based Multi-Sensory Instructional Materials for Cognitive & Language Development of Preschool Learners
abstract:
Move.Org Foundation Inc. (MovEd) is a non-stock, non-profit organization that provides early childhood care and development programs to children and their families in underserved communities in the Philippines. It has nineteen (19) learning labs in total and one of which is located in La Huerta, Parañaque City, which is the chosen project locale of the researcher. The purpose of the study is to identify the instructional gap that exists in MovEd La Huerta learning lab and address this gap through an instructional solution.

Results of the needs, context, and learner analysis reveal that the participants, MovEd preschool learners, have deficiency in their cognitive domain and language skills, and there is a lack of variety in the instructional materials available that will help develop these deficiencies. As such, the goal of the study is for the participants to improve on their cognitive and language skills as compared to their pre-assessment results through play-based multi-sensory instructional materials.

The researcher is an eight-week instructional plan consisting of eight (8) modules that contain mainly play-based learning activities and multi-sensory instructional materials. The Module 5 Day 2 lesson was pilot-tested by the preschool teachers (implementers) for the researcher and her external adviser (project gatekeeper) to evaluate the effectiveness of the instructional design. Evaluation results reveal that the participants showed improvements in the post-assessment as compared to their pre-assessment results. It is recommended that the other MovEd learning labs adopt the instructional design.

half:
Shaina Marie P. Sia’s technical report, "Play-Based Multi-Sensory Instructional Materials for Cognitive & Language Development of Preschool Learners," addresses instructional gaps at the MovEd La Huerta learning lab in Parañaque City. Analysis revealed deficiencies in the cognitive and language domains, noting that a reliance on print storybooks and worksheets contributed to short attention spans and insufficient preparation for primary education.

Utilizing the ADDIE instructional design model, the researcher developed an eight-week instructional plan consisting of eight modules aligned with the Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Council’s curriculum. The design integrated play-based and multi-sensory learning theories, including Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory, Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory, and the Theory of Multiple Intelligences. The materials included multimedia resources, a teachers' manual, and hands-on activities such as tactile letter drawing and alphabet puzzles to enhance memory, problem-solving, vocabulary, and listening comprehension.

Findings indicated that learners' primary needs were in the cognitive (61.3%) and language (51.6%) domains. Pilot testing demonstrated effectiveness, with most learners successfully distinguishing between healthy and unhealthy foods. The study concludes that guided play and multi-sensory materials are essential for holistic development in resource-constrained environments. Recommendations include adopting this design in other learning labs, providing continuous teacher training, translating the manual into Filipino, and securing donor support and local government partnerships to ensure sustainability.

two:
The technical report titled "Play-Based Multi-Sensory Instructional Materials for Cognitive & Language Development of Preschool Learners" by Shaina Marie P. Sia addresses the instructional needs of preschool learners in underserved communities. The study focuses on the MovEd La Huerta learning lab in Parañaque City, a facility operated by Move.Org Foundation Inc. that provides free early childhood care and development programs.

The problem identified through a thorough needs, context, and learner analysis is a significant instructional gap at the MovEd La Huerta learning lab. Specifically, the researcher found a deficiency in the participants' cognitive domain and a lack of variety in available instructional materials. The analysis revealed that the current materials, which primarily consist of print storybooks, worksheets, and chalkboards, were insufficient to address the learners' needs. This limitation often resulted in short attention spans among the students. Furthermore, there was a noted need to improve the learners' reading and writing skills to better prepare them for primary education.

To address these issues, the researcher employed the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) instructional design model. The methodology began with a needs assessment involving semi-structured interviews with teachers, surveys with parents, and on-site classroom observations. Using purposive sampling, the researcher gathered data to identify the specific developmental deficiencies of the 31 preschool learners (comprising PS1 and PS2 groups) enrolled for the 2024-2025 school year.

The design phase involved creating an eight-week instructional plan consisting of eight modules. These modules were aligned with the Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Council’s curriculum, specifically focusing on the theme of "My Family." The instructional approach integrated play-based and multi-sensory learning theories, drawing on Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory, Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory, and the Theory of Multiple Intelligences. The goal was to enhance memory retention, problem-solving, vocabulary, and listening comprehension through hands-on, sensory-rich activities such as tactile letter drawing, alphabet puzzles, and audiovisual storytelling.

The development phase included the creation of multimedia materials, a teachers' manual, and various learning activities. The researcher adhered to visual principles to ensure that print and non-projected materials were legible and engaging. For the implementation phase, a specific lesson (Module 5, Day 2, titled "Prutas Pampalusok at Pampalakas") was pilot-tested by the teachers. The evaluation phase utilized Kirkpatrick’s model of evaluation, assessing the project through four levels: reaction, learning, behavior, and results.

The findings from the analysis and pilot testing indicated that the learners' primary developmental needs were in the cognitive (61.3%) and language (51.6%) domains. The pilot test results demonstrated the effectiveness of the design, as five out of seven learners were able to successfully distinguish between healthy and unhealthy foods in a post-assessment. This confirmed that the multi-sensory, play-based approach helped bridge the gap between the learners' current subpar skills and the desired learning outcomes.

In conclusion, the researcher determined that the instructional design was effective in improving the cognitive and language skills of the participants. Despite facing implementation challenges—such as deviations from the intended plan by the implementers—the post-assessment results validated the design's utility. The study concludes that guided play and multi-sensory materials are essential tools for fostering holistic development in preschool learners, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

The implications of this study suggest several recommendations for educators and organizations. It is recommended that other MovEd learning labs adopt this instructional design to ensure consistency and quality across their facilities. For teachers, the researcher suggests continuous training in play-based and multi-sensory methodologies to better manage the short attention spans of preschool learners. Additionally, the researcher recommends that the teachers' manual be translated into Filipino to facilitate easier implementation. To ensure sustainability, the report emphasizes the need for continued support from donors and partnerships with Local Government Units (LGUs) to provide necessary supplies and funding. Finally, the researcher suggests that future iterations of the design include visual aids like music videos and sample output guides to further assist teachers and learners in the implementation process.

title: Transnational Mothering: An ASEAN Perspective on Filipino Migrant Mothers in Toronto, Canada
abstract:
The feminization of migration has given rise to the phenomenon of transnational mothering, where mothers leave their native countries to work abroad, maintaining parental roles across borders. This research explores the lived experiences of Filipino migrant mothers in Toronto, Canada, through the lens of matricentric feminism and intersectionality. Employing a qualitative, phenomenological approach, in-depth semistructured interviews were conducted with ten Filipino mothers with various immigration statuses. The research reveals that while their core identity as mothers remains constant, their self-perception is reshaped by economic pressures, with downward occupational mobility impacting their self-worth. Despite their resilience,
feelings of guilt and inadequacy persist. Family relations are influenced by their own upbringing, and they have a strong desire to create a better emotional experience for their children. The uncertainty of family reunification also complicates this. The preservation of cultural ties, on the other hand, focuses on transmitting values rather than consuming material culture, while  addressing concerns about perceived cultural differences. Furthermore, their parental responsibilities are impacted by a complex interplay of economic, sociocultural, and political factors. This is evident in how lowwage
and demanding jobs strain finances and limit social integration, and how
temporary immigration status increases vulnerability to exploitation and discrimination. Transnational mothering changes household dynamics as financial contributions alter power relations. Mothers earn greater decision-making authority, but this shift creates tension with partners who may feel a loss of their provider status. These insights provide a lens for understanding similar patterns across other ASEAN countries that share similar cultural values. The research also highlights broader ASEAN themes, such as the primacy of the family and gendered migration. By connecting the mothers' lived realities to the region's core pillars, the study contributes to ASEAN Studies through advocating for more inclusive and people-centered policies.

The study investigates how transnational mothering, driven by the feminization of migration, reshapes identities, family dynamics, and parental roles across geographical borders.

Furthermore, intersectional factors like immigration status and economic standing dictate vulnerability to exploitation and access to support. Ultimately, the research concludes that transnational mothering is a transformative process contingent upon economic, sociocultural, and political forces. It advocates for inclusive, people-centered policies that facilitate family reunification and protect the rights of migrant workers.

The researcher employed a qualitative, phenomenological approach combined with a critical tradition. This methodology aimed to capture the essence of the participants' lived experiences while challenging dominant societal narratives regarding family and power. Data was collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with ten Filipino mothers in Toronto. These participants represented a variety of immigration statuses, including permanent residents, temporary residents (students and work permit holders), and naturalized citizens, all of whom had left-behind children in the Philippines.

title: Digital Ageism and the Communicative Marginalization of Older Persons: A Socio-Cultural Approach to Ageist Discourse on a Civil Society Organization's Facebook Page
abstract:
As societies age and technology rapidly advances, ageism has evolved into a digital construct, with its discourse migrating from offline to online platforms. This phenomenon, termed digital ageism, refers to a variety of personal and societal biases that include negative representations of older persons in online communication environments. Adopting the sociocultural tradition in communication as a framework for critical discourse analysis (CDA), this dissertation explores how communicative practices shape digital ageism. It identifies four Discourses of active dependency, digital deficiency, age-based exceptionalism, and automated empathy from the public Facebook page of COSE (Coalition of Services of the Elderly) – a non-government organization advocating for the welfare of older persons. These Discourses were shaped by COSE’s communicative practices that include capacitating older persons through multi-sectoral and international support, highlighting the importance of training older persons to be digitally literate, celebrating the accomplishments of older persons as age-defying expectations, and facilitating technology mediation of care. The study concludes that COSE, while it advocates for the welfare and rights of older persons, inadvertently reproduces ageism as an interplay of communicative practices in the digital realm. The study recommends future research that integrates critical gerontology with discourse analysis to provide deeper insights into the intersection of aging, language, and power. The study further recommends the incorporation of multimodal discourse analysis, encompassing text, video, and images to capture the complex and layered ways in which age-related meanings are constructed and communicated across diverse media forms.

A practical recommendation for COSE is to revisit its content creation practices by emphasizing narratives of empowerment, agency, and collaboration rather than those that imply dependency or deficiency. By adopting more enabling and inclusive discourse, COSE’s communication can both enhance the visibility of older persons as capable digital citizens and resist the reproduction of ageist assumptions in online environment

title: Understanding the Child Marriage Practice: A Rhetorical Study of Child Marriage Facebook Posts
abstract:
Various efforts advocating to end child marriage practice have been focused on finding evidence for its harmful effects and ways for development actors to fight against it. While the strategies include key messaging, there is a lack of focus on engaging communication as a social science (Calhoun, 2011). This dissertation utilized the Rhetorical Tradition in Communication Theory to answer this question: What are the rhetorical acts of the defenders and opposers of child marriage? By combined coding of themes and speech acts, and analysis of rhetorical appeals, devices and strategies performed in comments in Facebook posts on child marriage, it finds that the defenders of child marriage assert a collaborative and unified adherence to a belief in the superior form of religion. In contrast, opposers of child marriage vary in their acts, some with anti-religious rhetoric. Overall, combining the speech acts brought the study to the conclusion that the overarching rhetorical act of defenders is religious superiority in matters such as child protection and religious living. In contrast, the speech acts of opposers are scattered.

Advocates to end the child marriage practice have the rhetorical space of situatedness of child welfare as a common ground with defenders. As a precaution, advocates should consider politeness by being selective when calling child marriage a “practice.” For the defenders, the girl’s marriage is mainly a sacred act towards religious perfection under divine law, which is above any material, social, and other worldly concerns.

half:
This research addresses the persistence of child marriage despite global human rights frameworks. While many studies focus on socio-economic drivers, this study examines the rhetorical acts used by those who defend the practice. The researcher utilizes Facebook as a site of knowledge production and rhetorical exchange, employing rhetorical analysis, thematic analysis, and speech act theory to analyze 200 Facebook comments.

Findings reveal that defenders of child marriage assert a collaborative adherence to a belief in a superior form of religion. Their speech acts center on religious superiority, portraying marriage as a sacred act for religious perfection under divine law. They utilize themes such as child protection, the prevention of sin, and parental responsibility to justify the practice. Defenders also argue that marriage serves as a practical solution to issues like teenage pregnancy and social shame, emphasizing religious laws over human laws.

In contrast, the speech acts of opposers are scattered, focusing on human rights or the protection of children. The two sides often fail to find common ground, as defenders perceive opposers as being judgmental or lacking knowledge of religious and cultural nuances. The study concludes that child marriage is sustained by how defenders frame the practice through a relational mindset focused on community and faith. Advocates are encouraged to move away from accusation-focused strategies and instead adopt persuasive, relational, and culturally sensitive communication.

title: Digital Social Marketing in Philippine Mission-Centric Social Enterprises: Exploring Founders' Influence and Strategic Approaches
abstract:
This dissertation examines how founders' cultural-cognitive orientations and communication practices shape digital social marketing strategies in Philippine mission-centric social enterprises. The research introduces the Founder-Driven Authentic Digital Storytelling Framework through digital ethnography and case studies as a novel theoretical contribution integrating cultural sensitivity with strategic communication in digital spaces.

The study reveals that effective digital social marketing emerges from founders' ability to authentically adapt communication while aligning with their cultural values and social missions. The research demonstrates that successful digital engagement requires founders to balance cultural understanding with strategic storytelling across digital platforms.

The findings establish authentic digital storytelling as the primary mechanism for building trust and fostering meaningful connections with target communities. The introduced framework provides a structured approach to understanding how founders' personal narratives and cultural backgrounds influence their digital marketing strategies.

This work makes significant theoretical contributions by synthesizing authentic digital storytelling with cultural-cognitive and communication accommodation perspectives in social enterprise marketing. The practical implications offer actionable insights for social enterprise founders seeking to enhance their digital marketing impact while maintaining mission alignment.

The study addresses the gap in literature regarding how leaders navigate the tension between financial sustainability and social missions through digital platforms. Using Communication Accommodation Theory and Cultural-Cognitive Theory, the research employs a qualitative design involving digital ethnography, case studies, semi-structured interviews, digital artifact analysis, and non-participant observation.

The findings reveal that effective digital social marketing is rooted in authentic digital storytelling, which serves as the primary mechanism for building trust and fostering connections. Key themes include founders acting as cultural mediators by using personal narratives to bridge the gap between enterprise missions and audience values, and utilizing adaptive digital engagement by adjusting communication styles across platforms to resonate with diverse stakeholders. The research emphasizes the necessity of mission-market alignment to ensure commercial activities support rather than overshadow core social missions.

The study concludes that successful digital engagement requires a balance between cultural understanding and strategic communication. It introduces the "Founder-Driven Authentic Digital Storytelling Framework" to explain how personal narratives and cultural backgrounds influence marketing. Practically, the research suggests that nuanced communication can enhance impact and encourages rethinking success indicators to include qualitative assessments of community building and social impact alongside commercial metrics.

title: Multimodal Inquiry of Special Religious Development (SPRED) Program: Towards a Friendship Model of Inclusive Catechetical Communication
abstract:
This multimodal inquiry investigates inclusive catechetical communication within the Special Religious Development (SPRED) program in the Archdiocese of Chicago, focusing on persons with developmental and intellectual disabilities (PDID). The central research question examines how catechists implement and refine inclusive catechetical communication to engage and support PDID effectively. Existing research highlights significant gaps in catechetical programs tailored for PDID, often due to the limitations of traditional methods and materials.

This research addresses these gaps by employing a triangulation approach, integrating content analysis, artifact analysis, and socio-spatial analysis. The study utilized SPRED newsletters, educational materials, religious artifacts, and
observations of the catechetical environment to gather comprehensive insights. This multifaceted methodology ensures a robust understanding of the dynamics involved in inclusive catechetical praxis.

Findings reveal the critical importance of adapted communication methods, accessible educational materials, and supportive physical environments. Key themes include the necessity for continuous adaptation of materials to meet PDID needs, the positive impact of sensory-friendly features, and the role of community support in fostering inclusivity. The socio-spatial analysis highlights the importance of wellorganized, accessible environments that enhance engagement and interaction. 

This research highlights the significant benefits of inclusive catechetical communication, such as enhanced spiritual and personal growth, deeper emotional connections, and a profound sense of belonging for PDID. The study underscores the necessity of strategies like non-verbal communication, emotional support, sensory-friendly materials, and community integration. Catechists’ reflections and artifact analyses reveal that inclusive practices foster mutual enrichment, reduce social exclusion, and celebrate unique contributions, thereby promoting a more inclusive and
supportive faith community.

Central to this study is the Friendship Model of Inclusive Catechetical Communication, which encompasses three key dimensions: intimacy, inter-animating collaboration, and interculturality.

Intimacy involves creating supportive relationships through personal engagement and emotional support. Catechists use gestures, facial expressions, and symbols to communicate effectively with individuals who may have difficulty with
verbal communication. This dimension fosters trust and meaningful engagement, ensuring participants feel valued and supported.

Inter-animating transformation focuses on mutual growth and learning through reflective practice and empowerment. Catechists and participants engage in activities that promote mutual learning and spiritual connections. This collaborative environment allows both catechists and participants to gain insights from each other, leading to deeper spiritual enrichment.

Interculturality ensures that catechetical practices respect and incorporate diverse cultural backgrounds. Catechists demonstrate cultural sensitivity and adapt practices to be culturally appropriate, creating a welcoming environment for all participants. This dimension promotes social inclusion and mutual respect, enhancing the quality of friendships and community bonds.

In conclusion, this study contributes to the field of religious education by providing practical recommendations for enhancing inclusivity in catechetical communication. It advocates for the adoption of adaptive communication methods, continuous refinement of educational materials, and strategic modifications to the physical environment. These findings offer valuable insights for improving catechetical practices and fostering a more inclusive community within SPRED and similar settings.

The dissertation titled "Multimodal Inquiry of Special Religious Development (SPRED) Program: Towards a Friendship Model of Inclusive Catechetical Communication" by Marlon Bobier Vargas investigates how inclusive communication strategies are implemented within the SPRED program in the Archdiocese of Chicago. The study focuses on the communicative needs of persons with developmental and intellectual disabilities (PDID) to ensure their full integration into the life of the Church.

The problem addressed is the significant gap in catechetical programs tailored for PDID. Traditional religious education often relies on verbal instruction and abstract concepts that fail to meet the cognitive, sensory, and communicative needs of individuals with disabilities. This mismatch can lead to the social isolation and spiritual neglect of PDID, despite Church teachings affirming their inherent dignity. The researcher notes that while research exists regarding social work and community inclusion, there is a deficiency in studies focusing specifically on the unique perspectives and challenges of catechists who act as frontline communicators in these religious settings.

The context of the study is the SPRED ministry, a pastoral program that utilizes a "Method Vivre" approach. This method emphasizes everyday interactions and universal emotions to foster spiritual growth. In this setting, participants are referred to as "friends" rather than using clinical labels, a terminology rooted in the biblical concept of discipleship. This relational approach aims to move beyond mere doctrinal instruction toward a holistic faith formation that emphasizes belonging and personal connection.

To investigate this, the author employs a multimodal inquiry using a triangulation approach. The methodology integrates three primary data collection methods: content analysis of SPRED newsletters, artifact analysis of educational materials and religious objects, and socio-spatial analysis of the physical catechetical environment. This multifaceted method allows for a comprehensive understanding of the technological, social, and discursive realms of the SPRED communicative ecology.

The findings are organized into three distinct realms of communicative ecology. In the technological realm, the study finds that adapted communication methods, accessible materials, and sensory-friendly features are critical. The socio-spatial analysis highlights that well-organized and accessible physical environments enhance engagement and interaction for PDID. In the discursive realm, the research shows that inclusive practices foster mutual enrichment, reduce social exclusion, and celebrate the unique contributions of PDID, thereby promoting a sense of belonging. The analysis of newsletters further reveals themes of community support, relational communication, and the importance of creating a "mindful" and calm environment to facilitate engagement.

Based on these findings, the researcher proposes the "Friendship Model of Inclusive Catechetical Communication." This model consists of three key dimensions:
1. Intimacy: This involves creating supportive relationships through personal engagement and emotional support. Catechists use non-verbal cues, such as gestures and facial expressions, to connect with individuals who may struggle with verbal communication.
2. Inter-animating Collaboration: This dimension focuses on mutual growth and learning. It emphasizes a collaborative environment where both catechists and participants engage in reflective practice and spiritual connection, leading to mutual enrichment.
3. Interculturality: This ensures that catechetical practices respect and incorporate diverse cultural backgrounds, creating a welcoming environment that promotes social inclusion and mutual respect.

The study concludes that inclusive catechetical communication is essential for the spiritual and personal growth of PDID. By moving from traditional, purely intellectual instruction to a holistic, relational, and experiential model of faith formation, the Church can better fulfill its mandate of universal inclusion. The research demonstrates that when communication is adapted to meet diverse sensory and cognitive needs, it fosters a deeper sense of belonging and agency for individuals with disabilities.

The implications of this research are both practical and theoretical. Practically, the study advocates for the adoption of adaptive communication methods, the continuous refinement of educational materials, and strategic modifications to physical learning environments. It suggests that training programs for catechists should focus on developing expertise in inclusive communication to increase their effectiveness. Theoretically, the study contributes to the fields of religious education and disability studies by providing a framework—the Friendship Model—that can be applied to other inclusive religious settings. Ultimately, the work serves as a call to move inclusivity from a theoretical concept to a practical reality within faith communities.

title: Multiple Streams Analysis on the Tax Treatment of Digital Assets in Malaysia and Singapore: Understanding the Policy Through Agenda-Setting
abstract:
The evolving technology of digitalization is paving the way for emerging financial channels through which the economy interacts with society, one of which is channels is the formation of digital assets (DAs). Within the ASEAN bloc, Malaysia and Singapore are the frontrunners in digital transformation among their regional peers, and they provide a fertile foundation for assessing the existing tax treatment of DAs and their implications for regional integration.

This study applies Kingdon’s Multiple Streams Framework (MSF) to analyze how the problem, policy, and politics streams converged to shape the tax treatment of DA across the regional bloc. To assess it, the study utilizes Stake’s multiple case study approach, drawing from official documents, policy papers, and institutional guidelines issued by the central bank (e.g., Bank Negara Malaysia, Monetary Authority of Singapore), tax authorities and regulators (e.g., Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia, Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore), as well as securities commissions (e.g., Securities Commission Malaysia). This study also considered secondary academic, policy, and industry perspectives to understand their respective insights on DA regulation.

Based on the gathered data, the findings indicate that while both Malaysia and Singapore share a common British law heritage and an income-based tax system, their approaches to DA tax treatment differ. Malaysia employs a broad, interpretive “badges of trade” approach under the Malaysian Income Tax Act 1967, which affords flexibility but introduces case-by-case uncertainty. In contrast with Singapore, it adopts a functional classification system that distinguishes between payment, utility, and security tokens, providing greater clarity and predictability. In indirect taxation, Malaysia imposes Sales and Services Tax (SST) on DA-related activities and transactions, whereas Singapore exempts qualifying digital payment tokens from Goods and Services Tax (GST).

The study can be drawn about the situation of Malaysia and Singapore regarding the DA regulation. The study identified that DA classification ambiguity, compliance risks, and global pressures shaped the problem stream; stakeholder proposals and institutional guidance shaped the policy stream; and political determination, agency leadership, and ASEAN commitments shaped the politics stream. The coupling of these streams opened policy windows for DA reform in both AMS, with regulatory agencies serving as policy entrepreneurs. This comparative analysis provides insights into how Malaysia and Singapore’s DA tax frameworks can inform ASEAN’s ongoing efforts toward tax harmonization and collaboration.

This thesis investigates the regulatory and tax frameworks governing digital assets (DAs) in Malaysia and Singapore, utilizing Kingdon’s Multiple Streams Framework (MSF) to understand how policy is shaped through the convergence of problem, policy, and politics streams. As the digital economy expands within the ASEAN bloc, the study highlights the necessity of harmonized regulatory mechanisms to support regional integration and economic competitiveness.

**Problem and Context**
The rapid proliferation of digital assets, including cryptocurrencies, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), and decentralized finance (DeFi), has outpaced traditional financial and legal frameworks. This technological shift presents significant challenges for regulators, including asset classification ambiguity, increased risks of money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF), and the difficulty of taxing decentralized, cross-border transactions. Within the ASEAN context, the lack of standardized definitions and regulatory fragmentation poses a threat to the objectives of the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC), which seeks a highly integrated and cohesive economy. The study focuses on Malaysia and Singapore because they are regional frontrunners in digital competitiveness, making their regulatory approaches critical benchmarks for the rest of the ASEAN member states (AMS).

**Methodology**
The researcher employed Stake’s multiple case study approach, conducting a comparative analysis of Malaysia and Singapore. Data was gathered from official documents, policy papers, and institutional guidelines issued by central banks (Bank Negara Malaysia and Monetary Authority of Singapore), tax authorities (Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia and Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore), and securities commissions. The study also incorporated secondary academic, policy, and industry perspectives to provide a comprehensive view of the regulatory landscape.

**Findings**
The comparative analysis reveals that while both nations share a British legal heritage and an income-based tax system, their specific approaches to DA regulation differ significantly.

In terms of income tax, both countries follow a similar principle: capital gains are generally not taxed, but income derived from active trading, mining, or receiving DAs as remuneration is subject to tax. However, Singapore provides greater clarity through a functional classification system that distinguishes between payment, utility, and security tokens. Malaysia utilizes a broader, interpretive "badges of trade" approach under the Malaysian Income Tax Act 1967, which offers flexibility but introduces case-by-case uncertainty for taxpayers. Regarding indirect taxation, Malaysia imposes Sales and Services Tax (SST) on certain DA-related activities, whereas Singapore exempts qualifying digital payment tokens from Goods and Services Tax (GST).

Applying the Multiple Streams Framework, the study identifies how policy windows opened in both nations:
*   **Problem Stream:** Both countries faced fragmented frameworks, associated DA risks (such as volatility and custody issues), cross-border jurisdictional gaps, and global/ASEAN pressures to align with international standards.
*   **Policy Stream:** Responses included the development of unified licensing frameworks, expanded regulatory perimeters to cover custodial services, and efforts to harmonize tax treatments with OECD substance-based norms.
*   **Politics Stream:** Policy adoption was driven by national digital transformation agendas (such as Malaysia’s MyDIGITAL), agency leadership, and the need to meet international compliance standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

The study notes that Singapore’s approach is characterized by proactive, centralized, and preemptive regulation, often led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). In contrast, Malaysia’s approach is more incremental and reactive, often relying on inter-agency collaboration and enforcement-driven measures, such as "Ops Token," to address emerging issues.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that the coupling of problem, policy, and politics streams allowed regulatory agencies in both countries to act as "policy entrepreneurs," successfully institutionalizing DA regulations. Singapore’s early and centralized legislative overhaul provided a more organized governance structure, whereas Malaysia’s step-by-step reforms demonstrated an adaptive, though sometimes delayed, capacity to manage digital transformation.

The implications for "ASEANology" and regional policy are significant. The findings suggest that for ASEAN to achieve its goal of a single digital market, there is an urgent need for tax harmonization and the alignment of technical standards. The study highlights that regulatory divergence can lead to inefficiencies and tax evasion. Therefore, the experiences of Malaysia and Singapore serve as a foundational reference for other AMS. The research suggests that moving toward a coordinated regional framework—potentially through the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (ADEFA)—will be essential to mitigate risks, ensure investor protection, and harness the economic potential of the digital economy across the region.

title: Surfacing Communication in Extension: A Phenomenological Study of Communication Experiences of University Extension Project Beneficiaries in Cagayan Valley
abstract: This study explores the dynamics of communication within the context of a university's extension project in the Cagayan Valley Region, with the aim of gaining insight into the nature of extension communication. Transcendental phenomenology was employed to investigate the lived experiences of beneficiaries participating in an extension project focusing on communication phenomena that have been termed as "Communication peripheralization with instances of centricity." Through in-depth thematic analysis, six emergent themes illuminate the communication experiences of beneficiaries, ranging from communication dynamics to temporal and spatial factors, errors of omission and commission, domestication aspects, critical reflectivity, and views on extension communication. These themes collectively depict the interplay between peripheralization and centricity in communication. The study also clarifies extension communication positioning it as a specialized form that emphasizes empowerment and participation, contextual sensitivity, critical introspection, genuineness, and sustainability & coherence. The study also challenges traditional extension paradigms, emphasizing nurturing communication principles' transformative potential.

This study investigates communication dynamics within university extension projects in the Cagayan Valley Region, focusing on the phenomenon of "communication peripheralization with instances of centricity." This concept describes the tension where communication is often marginalized in extension activities yet occasionally serves as a vital, central component of engagement. Using a transcendental phenomenological research design and thematic analysis, the researcher explored the lived experiences of beneficiaries to capture the essence of their encounters with communication processes.

Six themes emerged from the analysis: information flow dynamics, the influence of temporal and spatial factors, errors of omission and commission, domestication aspects of information internalization, critical reflectivity regarding processes, and the beneficiaries' overall views. The findings clarify that extension communication is a specialized interaction distinct from general communication, defined by empowerment, participation, contextual sensitivity, critical introspection, genuineness, and sustainability.

The study concludes that extension communication is a multifaceted process that can either marginalize or empower participants. While treating communication as a peripheral activity limits its potential, integrating it as a central, specialized practice makes it a transformative force. Theoretically, the research challenges paradigms that view communication as a secondary functional component, suggesting it should be at the heart of extension strategies. Practically, it implies that practitioners must adopt participatory, context-sensitive models that prioritize empowerment and authenticity to ensure project success and sustainability.

title: A Grounded Theory of Developer Communication in Extreme Programming Practices
abstract:
There is evidence that Extreme Programming (XP) software development practices are still actively used by Information Technology (IT) projects under the Agile methodology, one of the famous software development life cycle (SDLC) models. However, more information about the communication between programmers or developers for these XP practices is needed. Thus, this study, employing a constructivist grounded theory (CGT) design which emphasizes the construction of knowledge through the interpretation of data, was conducted to explore developer communication for significant XP practices.

For the initial data, the researcher was fortunate to have the participation of eleven out of fifteen IT professionals, each with at least a decade of work experience. Their expertise was invaluable in shaping the direction of the research. Three out of four identified developers also participated in a follow-up questionnaire. Subsequently, semi-structured key informant interviews were conducted, focusing on their top three practices: Planning Game, Test-Driven Development (TDD), and Small Releases, which were selected based on their perceived importance in IT projects.

During the interviews, it became evident that the developers play multiple roles, each significantly influencing communication. These fourteen identified roles highlight their work’s diverse and complex nature: Assessor, Collaborator, Coordinator, Designer, Developer, Documenter, Interpreter, Learner, Mentor, Negotiator, Presenter, Researcher, Tester, and Translator. The developers interacted with seven teams categorized into four groups based on their modes of communication: Direct Managers and Change management under Linear-Interactional, Business Team under Interactional, External Developers, Functional Resources, and Technical Team under Interactional-Transactional, and Transactional-Interactional for Internal Developers.

With all the combined practices, roles, and interactions, this study has proposed an XP Developer Communication (XPDC) model. This framework can serve as a guide for understanding and improving developer communication in XP projects. For instance, it can help identify the key roles and their communication needs or guide the selection of appropriate communication modes for different teams. Although not all XP practices are covered, the components are enough to cover all the essential developer communication practices in XP.

Viray’s dissertation, "A Grounded Theory of Developer Communication in Extreme Programming Practices," investigates communication dynamics among developers using Extreme Programming (XP) within Agile methodologies. Addressing a gap in theoretical frameworks regarding developer-specific communication, the study utilizes a Constructivist Grounded Theory design. Data was gathered through semi-structured questionnaires and interviews with IT professionals and developers, managed via ATLAS.ti Web using inductive and deductive coding.

The findings identify three primary XP practices significant to developers: the Planning Game, Test-Driven Development (TDD), and Small Releases. The research identified 14 distinct roles played by developers, such as Assessor, Collaborator, Designer, and Mentor. Developers interact with seven different teams categorized into three communication modes: Linear-Interactional, Interactional, and Interactional-Transactional. While the "Documenter" role is essential across all three practices, TDD involves the highest number of developer roles.

The researcher proposes the "XP Developer Communication (XPDC) Triangle" model. This model places Internal Developers at the center, surrounded by the three interaction modes enhanced by Media Richness Theory. The model integrates the three core practices and the 14 identified roles, illustrating that developer communication is a complex web of interactions essential to XP success. The study suggests that organizations can use the XPDC model to select appropriate communication modes to increase productivity, while recommending further research into Pair Programming and whether computer code functions as a medium for transactional communication.
