The thesis titled "The Effects of Literature-based Instruction on Reading Motivation and Willingness to Communicate of Thai Collegiate Students" by Kathylene P. Remegio investigates how a literature-based pedagogical approach influences two critical affective variables in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners: reading motivation and willingness to communicate (WTC).

The problem addressed by the researcher is the persistent lack of reading motivation and the reluctance to communicate in English among Thai collegiate students. The author notes that many EFL learners experience frustration due to insufficient linguistic competence or a lack of interest in reading materials. This issue is compounded by traditional teaching methods, such as the Grammar Translation Method (GTM), which focuses on rote grammatical rules and translation rather than meaningful communication. Furthermore, the emphasis on national examinations in Thailand often leads to teaching language skills in isolation, which fails to foster communicative competence or a genuine interest in literacy.

The context of the study is a Thai university, specifically involving 21 English-major freshmen aged 19 to 21 enrolled in an "English Learning through Drama" course. The researcher implemented a 16-week intervention using a "Thematic Language and Literacy Learning Package" (TLLLP). This package utilized diverse literary works, including short stories (such as "The Necklace"), plays (such as "Macbeth"), and mythological excerpts (such as "The Judgement of Paris), to create a communicative and engaging learning environment.

The study employed a mixed-methods research design. Quantitative data were gathered through a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design using the Adolescent Motivation Reading Profile (AMRP) to measure reading motivation (specifically self-concept as a reader and the value of reading) and a Willingness to Communicate questionnaire to assess readiness to participate in L2 communication across listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and student personal journal entries to capture the participants' personal views and experiences.

The findings indicate that literature-based instruction significantly improved both reading motivation and willingness to communicate. Quantitative analysis via t-tests showed significant differences between pretest and posttest scores for both variables. Specifically, the intervention led to higher scores in reading motivation and increased classroom WTC. Additionally, the study found a moderate positive linear relationship between reading motivation and WTC, suggesting that improvements in one variable are linked to improvements in the other. Qualitative data supported these results, revealing that the instructional strategies provided students with opportunities to interact with peers, enhanced their confidence in using English, and allowed them to take ownership of their learning. The shift from a focus on grammatical competence to a communicative approach through literature helped improve students' vocabulary, literary skills, and enthusiasm for literacy tasks.

The researcher concludes that literature-based instruction is an effective method for enhancing the reading motivation and willingness to communicate of Thai EFL collegiate learners. The study demonstrates that when instruction moves away from isolated grammar drills and toward meaningful, authentic engagement with literary texts, students become more engaged and confident. The results suggest that the social and expressive nature of literature-based activities—such as drama and group discussions—directly addresses the affective barriers to language learning.

The implications of this study are significant for language and literacy educators. The author suggests that teachers should integrate activities that cater to learners' specific needs, interests, and paces to provide more opportunities for language use. By using literature-based approaches, instructors can foster a more supportive environment that encourages students to use English communicatively without feeling pressured or anxious. The study also serves as a reference for future research into how literature-based instruction can support targeted instruction in language arts and reading for various EFL and second language learners.

title: Contextualization of Grade 3 Instructional Materials;Basis for a Design of Bulacan Tagalog-Based Science Materials
abstract: This qualitative research aims to develop a Grade 3 instructional material in science using Bulacan-Tagalog as the medium of instruction. To develop the material, the researcher proposed a framework that will serve as a guide in developing contextualized science instructional materials in the mother tongue. The researcher observed three science classes from three special science public schools in Baliwag and Bustos using the Classroom Observation Rubric (COR) by CREDE, 2011; interviewed the science teachers using a self-made Interview Protocol and conducted document analysis on the instructional materials used in the Grade3 science lessons using the Level of Contextualization Rubric by Heaslip’s (2013). This qualitative research study, conducted by Ma. Nina I. Adriano, investigates the contextualization of Grade 3 science instructional materials using Bulacan-Tagalog as the medium of instruction. The study was prompted by the implementation of Republic Act 10533, which mandates Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) from Kindergarten to Grade 3. The researcher highlights that while the policy aims to support linguistic, cultural, and cognitive development, there is a significant dearth of instructional materials that are specifically contextualized to the local dialects and cultural contexts of learners.

The problem addressed in this study is the lack of appropriate, localized, and culturally sensitive science instructional materials for Grade 3 learners in Bulacan. The researcher notes that many existing materials are either written in English or use a "deep" variety of Tagalog that is unfamiliar to children, creating a gap between the learners' home language and the language used in school. Furthermore, the study identifies challenges such as insufficient teacher training in teaching science through the mother tongue, the discrepancy between instructional languages in different school sections, and the difficulty teachers face when they must improvise or translate high-level materials for younger learners.

The research context is centered on the province of Bulacan, a region with a rich cultural heritage and specific linguistic nuances, particularly the Bulacan-Tagalog dialect. The study focuses on Grade 3 learners, as this grade level serves as a critical transition period before students move to English-based instruction in higher grades. The researcher emphasizes that preserving linguistic diversity is closely linked to preserving cultural and biological diversity, suggesting that using the mother tongue in schools is a vital tool for cultural preservation.

The methodology employed a qualitative research design. The researcher conducted observations of three science classes in three special science public schools in Baliwag and Bustos, Bulacan, using the CREDE (2011) Classroom Observation Rubric. Additionally, the researcher conducted interviews with science teachers using a self-made interview protocol and performed a document analysis of existing Grade 3 science instructional materials using Heaslip’s (2013) Level of Contextualization Rubric.

The findings of the study reveal several key insights regarding the current state of science instruction in the locale. The analysis of instructional materials showed varying levels of contextualization, often highlighting the need for more materials that reflect the learners' actual linguistic variety. In the classroom observations, the researcher examined how teachers implement the mother tongue as a medium of instruction and how learners respond to it. The teacher interviews generated themes regarding the extent of MTB-MLE implementation, the medium of instruction used in science classrooms, the availability of training, and the specific challenges faced by educators, such as the lack of prepared materials and the tendency to use English in certain school sections.

In response to these findings, the researcher developed a new framework for designing contextualized science instructional materials called the "5Is" model. This framework is designed to ensure that materials are learner-centered and deeply rooted in the students' local context. The 5Is model consists of five components:
*   **Iugnay (Relating):** Presenting new concepts through real-life situations and familiar cultural experiences.
*   **Isagawa (Experiencing):** Engaging learners in hands-on, experiential, or discovery-based activities.
*   **Ilapat (Applying):** Providing opportunities for learners to apply concepts to believable, real-world problem-solving situations.
*   **Ibahagi (Cooperating):** Encouraging collaborative learning and interaction among peers.
*   **Itawid (Transferring):** Enabling learners to use their acquired knowledge in new, novel, or practical contexts outside the classroom.

The researcher successfully applied this framework to develop a sample Grade 3 science instructional material focused on the states of matter (solids, liquids, and gases). This material utilized Bulacan-Tagalog and incorporated local references, such as the use of "suob" (steam inhalation) and local news reports, to make the science concepts more relatable and accessible to the learners.

The study concludes that there is a pressing need for instructional materials that are specifically designed using a contextualization framework to support the MTB-MLE program. The developed 5Is model provides a structured approach for educators and material developers to create lessons that are not only linguistically appropriate but also culturally relevant. The researcher concludes that effective contextualization helps bridge the gap between a child's home environment and the formal school setting, thereby facilitating better understanding and retention of scientific concepts.

The implications of this research are significant for several stakeholders. For the Department of Education, the study provides a model for producing high-quality, localized materials that align with the K-12 curriculum. For teachers, the 5Is model offers a practical template for designing lessons that reduce the burden of improvisation and translation. For instructional material developers, the study highlights the importance of using the specific dialect spoken by the target learners rather than a standardized or "deep" version of the language. Finally, for learners, the study implies that contextualized instruction can lead to increased engagement, better academic performance, and a stronger sense of cultural identity. The researcher recommends that future studies extend this work to test the effectiveness of the 5Is-based materials in improving the actual level of contextualization and learning outcomes in science classrooms.

title: Enhancing Selected Literacy Programs of a University Volunteer Service Program Through Outcomes-Based Education
abstract: The research focused on integrating the Outcomes-Based Education (QBE) approach to enhance the two selected literacy programs namely, the Reading Enhancement and Appreciation Development Program (READ) and the Environmental Awareness Program (EAP) that are being implemented by a university volunteer service program. Utilizing a multi-case research design, the study identified and described the components of the two selected literacy programs in terms of the programs' plan, design, implementation, and assessment and evaluation. The abovementioned components of the selected literacy programs were evaluated to be either consistent or inconsistent with the OBE approach. From the findings, a literacy program model that integrates the nature and principles of the QBE approach was provided. The recommended literacy program highlighted the need for the program outcomes to be aligned with the Institutional Vision, Mission, and Goals (VMGs) and with the global and national education standards. Clear specific program outcomes for all the main beneficiaries which include the volunteer facilitators and the learners should be identified. For the plan, reviewing current literacy program objectives, identifying modified literacy program objectives, identifying target learners, conducting needs assessment, accomplishing learner profile with the aid of reliable instruments, including various stakeholders in the program plan, identifying the strategies to ensure program sustainability, and constructing a clear process map for the key people involved were recommended. For the design, identifying the program outcome, integrating specific literacy models and theories in the development of the program and learning outcomes and modules, integrating the QBE framework in the development of the program and learning outcomes and modules, including various stakeholders in the program design, and retooling of key people on module development were recommended. For implementation, integrating experiential learning and participatory approaches and of QBE in teaching-learning systems were recommended. For assessment and evaluation, identifying performance indicators and targets and tools for assessment and integrating program, effectiveness, impact, and policy evaluations were recommended.

Despite government initiatives, there is a need for effective, tailor-fitted literacy programs for underserved populations. The researcher identifies a gap in the evaluation of existing volunteer-led programs, noting that these initiatives have utilized the same framework since 1994 and lack intensive quality and impact assessments. Data collection methods included content and thematic analysis of learning modules and secondary sources such as annual and terminal reports. Primary data were gathered through face-to-face interviews with twenty respondents, including the program director, coordinators, module designers, volunteer facilitators, and partner teachers. Additionally, class observations were conducted during READ and EAP sessions. The analysis was guided by the seven-step OBE instructional design, the CHED OBE framework, and various literacy development theories.

For the EAP program, the study involved identifying intended objectives, developing learning guides, constructing a process map, and designing interactive learning tools. The implementation and assessment phases were also analyzed to determine how well the programs met their intended goals.

The results suggest that program outcomes must be explicitly aligned with the Institutional Vision, Mission, and Goals (VMGs) as well as global and national education standards. The researcher emphasizes the necessity of identifying clear, specific program outcomes for all beneficiaries, including both the learners and the volunteer facilitators.

title: Lesson Study for Language Teachers’ Professional Development
abstract:
Teachers strongly need to experience quality professional development in order to improve student learning and teacher instruction. However, teacher professional development efforts are often criticized by educators for their lack of continuity and ability to produce effective changes in teacher practice and student learning. So far, teacher professional development is seen as static, top-down 2nd policy-oriented (Marialac, 2010). Teachers who undergo this cascading model of training try to implement innovations but are constrained by time, materials required, and the lack of instructional or administrative support. Thus, they often go back to their former teaching approaches and habits.

This study presented a teacher professional development initiative based on the Japanese lesson study model described by Catherine Lewis (1998) in "A Lesson is Like a Swiftly Flowing River". Lesson study is an inquiry model of teacher professional development used extensively throughout Japan. Advocates, usually from the Maths and Sciences fields, say it is a powerful professional development process that can lead to stronger lesson plans and teaching practices. In describing the lesson study process undergone by English teachers from a public junior high school in Quezon City, this present study sought to investigate such process as an alternative app~oach to English teachers' professional development while improving their skills in applying Communicative Language Teaching methods in their classes.

title: Impact of English Language Teaching and National Identity on Filipinos in the Call Center Industry
abstract:
The Call Center Industry (CCI) in the Philippines has been attracting employees from different national and linguistic backgrounds The industry requires employees to have a strong command of the English language~ more specifically, American English. which serves as the model for the English language requirements. However., these requirements may have a negative impact on the linguistic and national identity of Filipino employees.

This study explored the Filipino English language trainers' and Customer Service Representatives' integration with the American culture and language and whether this has any influence on the way they teach or use the language. It also investigated whether training in the business process outsourcing (BPO) and training schools has any impact on the language and national identity of Filipino employees through strategies used to teach, transact amongst themselves, and with the American customers, and through the wavs these employees perceive themselves as call center employees, as employees in the BPO training schools, and as Filipinos.

title: Relationship Among Reading Teachers’ Content Knowledge, Professional Development, Use of Instructional Materials and Strategies and Student Engagement
abstract: This study investigated the profiles of Grade Four teachers in terms of professional development, use of instructional materials, level of content knowledge, and instructional strategies used in reading. It also looked at the relationship between teachers' level of content knowledge and their teaching strategies used in reading, relationship between teachers' level of professional development and level of content knowledge, and how instructional materials enhance students' engagement. The study utilized the descriptive survey method with the application of both quantitative and qualitative analyses of data. Descriptive research was used to elicit data on teachers' profile and teachers' content knowledge in reading. Qualitative measures were used to detetmine the instructional strategies of Grade Four teachers and the effectiveness of these instructional materials to enhance students' engagement. Participants of the study were the Grade Four teachers in a district of Quezon (3 8). Six teachers were observed through purposive sampling to assess their instructional strategies. Each of the six classes was also observed to determine how the instructional materials enhanced students' engagement. Data were obtained through the following instruments: Instrument 1 -Teachers Profile in terms of the following contextual factors: professional development and instructional materials; Instrument 2- Teachers Level of Content Knowledge in Reading - TLCKR; Instrument 3 - Teaching Reading Observation Checklist; and Instrument 4 -Students' Engagement Rubric.

title: Effects of Sustained Silent Reading on Filipino Adolescents’ Reading Motivation and Reading Comprehension
abstract:
Teenagers do not read enough, if they read at all.

This statement is a common source of fmstration of parents and teachers of adolescents. For teachers, teaching children how to read is not the end goal. There is that never ending task of motivating them to read more, and to read deeply and widely so that they get better at it, gain confidence, knowledge, and e~perience to _take their reading lives wherever their imagination and curiosity lead them. The question is how to do this: to raise motivation so that readers pick up the reading habit and continue it for the rest of their lives. There has been little research on this topic in the PhiIippines. 

This study aimed to investigate the effects of a sustained silent reading program (SSRP) on the reading motivation and comprehension of adolescents. The SSRP was based on the principles of pleasure reading and reading choice, using reading habits, interests, and preferences identified through a descriptive inventory. The sample was a heterogeneous Grade 8 class of 37 students in a public laboratory high school, who was exposed to a thirty-minute SSRP for fitly (50) sessions, over three (3) grading periods. The subjects' reading motivation and comprehension levels were measured before and after the intervention. In addition, after the intervention, a comparison group's (an honors class) reading motivation and comprehension were measured and compared to those of the sample. After the 50-session SSRP, it was found out that not only did the sample"'s reading motivation and comprehension significantly improve, they were also higher than those of the compruison group. These improvements in the srunple were confinned through a qualitative ruialysis of data gathered from different tools administered at various points in the study. Based on the results, recommendations in connection to sustained silent reading, pleasure reading, a11d reading choice have been drawn.

title: Readability of Philippine Literature in English in Commercially Published English Textbooks
abstract:
Readability studies in the United States have a long history spanning over 70 years, but here in the Philippines, these studies are rare. Readability studies are important in the evaluation of texts to match the readers and their textbooks so that communicative competencies will be developed.

This study explored the readability of nine (9) Philippine short stories written in English that are featured in commercially published Grade 7 English textbooks. Three (3) readability indices were used to describe the level of text difficulty: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Cloze Test, and Readability Checklist. The texts were tested for the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level through online readability calculators. The same texts were converted into cloze tests and were given to 75 Grade Six students of one (I) private and one (I) public school in a first class urban municipality outside of the National Capital Region. Three (3) Grade 7 English teachers and 20 Grade 8 students evaluated the difficulty level using the readability checklist.

title: Pre-service Teachers' Teaching Reading Efficacy Beliefs, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TCPK) Levels, and Their Teacher Educators' Modeling
abstract:
Preparing efficacious literacy teachers for technology-enhanced instruction is beginning to become a main concern for many teacher education institutions. With the emerging technologies coming into the landscape, pre-service teachers and teacher preparation programs are challenged to embrace the opportunities in improving the teaching-learning process along the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK) Framework. This study investigated the relationships among the pre-service teachers' perceived teaching reading efficacy beliefs, TPCK levels, and teacher educators' TPCK modeling.

A descriptive survey method with focus on quantitative data collection and analysis was adapted. Forty-seven respondents were lottery drawn from 157 graduating pre-service teachers of Bachelor of Elementary Education at the Philippine Nonnal University Lopez, Quezon campus. Three self-report Likert type instruments were employed for self-􀃱ssment of the respondents' teaching reading efficacy beliefs, TPCK levels and their teacher educators' TPCK modeling.

half:
This study addresses concerns in teacher education regarding the preparation of efficacious literacy teachers for technology-enhanced instruction. Using the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Framework, the research investigates the relationship between the perceived teaching reading efficacy beliefs of pre-service teachers, their own TPCK levels, and the TPCK modeling performed by their teacher educators. The research was situated within the Bachelor of Elementary Education program at the Philippine Normal University Lopez, Quezon campus, focusing on graduating pre-service teachers. Using a descriptive survey method, the researcher sampled forty-seven respondents selected through a lottery draw from a total population of 157 graduating pre-service teachers.

The findings reveal that pre-service teachers maintain a high sense of efficacy regarding their ability to teach reading and reported having very good TPCK levels. Regarding instructor modeling, pre-service teachers reported that university-based teacher educators possess high competence and oftentimes model TPCK, while cooperating teachers during the student teaching program showed some competence and sometimes demonstrate TPCK. Statistical analysis established a moderate but statistically significant relationship between teaching reading efficacy beliefs and the pre-service teachers' TPK and PCK levels. A significantly strong positive relationship was found between the TPCK levels of the pre-service teachers and the TPCK modeling of their university-based teacher educators.

The research concludes that the university environment is vital in shaping the technological pedagogical content knowledge of future teachers. The findings imply that teacher preparation programs must ensure teacher educators actively and effectively model integrated skills. Additionally, the discrepancy between the high competence of university educators and the reported competence of cooperating teachers suggests a need for better alignment and professional development for field mentors.

two:
The study addresses the growing concern within teacher education institutions regarding the preparation of efficacious literacy teachers for technology-enhanced instruction. As emerging technologies continue to reshape the educational landscape, both pre-service teachers and teacher preparation programs face the challenge of embracing opportunities to improve the teaching-learning process. This research specifically focuses on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK) Framework as a means to navigate these changes. The core problem investigated is the relationship between three specific variables: the perceived teaching reading efficacy beliefs of pre-service teachers, their own TPCK levels, and the TPCK modeling performed by their teacher educators.

The context of this research is situated within the Bachelor of Elementary Education program at the Philippine Normal University Lopez, Quezon campus. The study focuses on graduating pre-service teachers who are preparing to enter the profession. By examining these specific groups, the research seeks to understand how the training received in a university setting and the subsequent experiences during student teaching programs influence the readiness of future educators to integrate technology into literacy instruction.

To investigate these relationships, the researcher adopted a descriptive survey method that prioritized quantitative data collection and analysis. The sample consisted of forty-seven respondents who were selected through a lottery draw from a total population of 157 graduating pre-service teachers. The study utilized three distinct self-report Likert type instruments designed for the self-assessment of the respondents. These instruments measured the three primary variables: the pre-service teachers' teaching reading efficacy beliefs, their TPCK levels, and the TPCK modeling they observed in their teacher educators.

The findings of the study provide a detailed look at the current state of pre-service teacher readiness and the quality of instruction they receive. The results reveal that pre-service teachers maintain a high sense of efficacy regarding their ability to teach reading. Furthermore, the respondents reported having very good TPCK levels. Regarding the modeling of these skills by instructors, the pre-service teachers reported that their university-based teacher educators possess high competence and oftentimes model TPCK within the classroom setting. In contrast, the findings regarding cooperating teachers during the student teaching program showed that these mentors have shown some competence and sometimes demonstrate TPCK.

Statistical analysis using the Pearson r was applied to determine the relationships between the variables at the .05 level of significance. The data established that a moderate but statistically significant relationship exists between teaching reading efficacy beliefs and the pre-service teachers' TPK and PCK levels. However, the study found no significant relationship between the pre-service teachers' efficacy beliefs and the TPCK modeling provided by their teacher educators. Additionally, the research found no significant relationship between the TPCK levels of the pre-service teachers and the TPCK modeling of the Grade 1 to 6 cooperating teachers. Despite these lack of significant relationships in certain areas, a significantly strong positive relationship was found, when viewed as a whole, between the TPCK levels of the pre-service teachers and the TPCK modeling of their university-based teacher educators.

The conclusions drawn from this research highlight the importance of the university environment in shaping the technological pedagogical content knowledge of future teachers. The strong positive relationship between the modeling of university educators and the TPCK levels of the students suggests that the instructional methods used in higher education play a critical role in developing these essential competencies. While pre-service teachers feel confident in their reading instruction efficacy, the connection between that confidence and the modeling they observe is not statistically significant, suggesting that efficacy may be driven by other factors or that the modeling, while high in competence, may not directly translate to a sense of personal efficacy in the same way it translates to knowledge acquisition.

The implications of these findings are directed toward the transnational leadership of school administrators and teacher educators operating within the 21st century educational paradigm. The results suggest that for teacher preparation programs to be successful in the digital age, there must be a concerted effort to ensure that teacher educators are not only competent in TPCK but are also actively and effectively modeling these integrated skills in the classroom. Because the university-based modeling showed a strong positive relationship with student TPCK levels, strengthening these instructional practices is a vital strategy for improving teacher readiness. Furthermore, the discrepancy between the high competence of university educators and the "some competence" reported for cooperating teachers suggests a need for better alignment and professional development for mentors in the field to ensure that the transition from university to the classroom maintains a high standard of technological pedagogical content knowledge.

title: Language Anxiety and Selected Learner Variables, and Anxiety-Reducing Strategies of Speech Communication Students
abstract: The study attempted to look into the relationship of language anxiety and specific learner factors and identified the coping strategies used by university students enrolled in speech communication classes. Chi square test results showed that the level of anxiety of the learners had no significant relationship with gender but had significant relationships with their (a) self-re ported competence in us ing Engli sh as a whole and for oral communication, (b) instances of English use outside class, and ( c) use of Engli sh at home. Lastly, coping strategies which fall under the cognitive and self-encouragement categories are always effective for learners with low level of anxiety and mostly effective for the highly anxious ones, while physical relaxation techniques are mostly effective, regardless of the learners' anxiety level. Faith-based strategies such as praying, asking for divine guidance, or being inspired by one's religion are considered to be always effective strategies to cope with anxiety in the classroom. Based on the analysis of data results, recommendations for the learners, teachers, and curriculum developers were also given.

title: Cultural Heritage Maintenance and Equitable Participation in Multicultural Education: An Autoethnographic Study on the Development of a Filipino Heritage Curriculum in Canada
abstract:
Canada's official policy of multiculturalism envisions a society where cultural diversity is valued by all. Immigrants are encouraged to maintain their cultural heritage and participate in all aspects of society, including education. This study aimed to determine the curriculum content and pedagogy of a Filipino heritage curriculum in Canada aligned with Berry's acculturation theory, in which cultural heritage maintenance and equitable participation are necessary for personal cultural integration and societal multiculturalism.

The autoethnographic research method was used to narrate and examine the acculturation (acculturative stress, behavioral shifts, acculturation strategies) and adaptation (psychological and sociocultural) of a Filipino immigrant parent who has raised second-generation Filipino Canadian children from Preschool to Grade seven. This study found that collaboration, representation, sustainability, and empowerment were essential themes in developing a Filipino heritage curriculum in Canada. Indigenous Filipino culture found in Filipino folk tales, folk dances, martial arts and culinary arts taught by Filipino Canadians in collaboration with education, culture and arts institutions in Canada were found to align with cultural heritage maintenance and equitable participation and supported multicultural and multigenerational Filipino heritage learning in Canada.

Focusing on second-generation Filipino Canadians, the research identifies a gap in mainstream curricula, which often present Eurocentric narratives that omit Filipino contributions. This omission, alongside the stigmatization of Filipino identity due to over-representation in caregiving roles, contributes to identity struggles and lower educational attainment among youth.

Using a phenomenological perspective, the researcher employed autoethnography to examine the lived experiences of a Filipino immigrant parent. The study is grounded in Dr. John W. Berry’s acculturation theory, which suggests that an "integration" strategy—balancing heritage maintenance with equitable participation—is most effective for achieving personal and societal multiculturalism.

Findings reveal limited resources for heritage maintenance and significant cultural gaps between first-generation immigrants and their children. The study suggests that Filipino culture is most effectively maintained through creative collaboration and positive representation. Vital elements for curriculum development include folk tales, folk dances like *Tinikling*, martial arts such as *Arnis*, and culinary arts. The researcher concludes that a successful curriculum must be built on indigenous Filipino culture and guided by social solidarity. This framework encourages an integrationist pedagogy that helps youth bridge ancestral roots with Canadian identities to achieve psychological well-being and sociocultural competence.

This autoethnographic study, conducted by Ramona Anna Maria P. Lavina, explores the intersection of cultural heritage maintenance and equitable participation within the context of multicultural education in Canada. The research focuses on the development of a Filipino heritage curriculum designed to support second-generation Filipino Canadians.

**Problem and Context**

The study is situated within Canada's official policy of multiculturalism, which encourages immigrants to maintain their cultural heritage while participating equitably in society. Despite this policy, the researcher identifies a significant gap in the mainstream Canadian curriculum: the lack of adequate Filipino heritage content. Historical research cited in the study indicates that Canadian history textbooks often present a Eurocentric narrative that omits the contributions and presence of Filipinos.

Furthermore, the researcher highlights social challenges facing the Filipino Canadian community. Due to immigration patterns, many Filipinos are over-represented in caregiving roles, which has led to a stigmatization of Filipino cultural identity in Canadian society. This has contributed to issues among second-generation Filipino Canadians, including struggles with cultural identity, belonging, and lower levels of educational attainment compared to their parents. The study notes that while community organizations have worked to address these issues, there is a need for a research-based curriculum that aligns with provincial educational standards to foster positive identity formation.

**Methodology**

The researcher employed an autoethnographic research method, utilizing a phenomenological perspective to examine the lived experiences of a Filipino immigrant parent raising second-generation children from preschool to Grade seven. This method allowed the researcher to serve as both the subject and the researcher, using personal narratives and artifacts to understand broader cultural experiences.

The study is theoretically grounded in Dr. John W. Berry’s acculturation theory. This framework posits that the most effective strategy for achieving personal cultural integration and societal multiculturalism is the "integration" strategy, which requires both cultural heritage maintenance and equitable participation. The research used this framework to analyze acculturation phenomena—including acculturative stress, behavioral shifts, and acculturation strategies—and their resulting psychological and sociocultural adaptations.

**Findings**

The autoethnographic analysis revealed several key themes regarding the immigrant experience and the requirements for an effective heritage curriculum. The researcher identified limited resources for cultural heritage maintenance and noted significant cultural gaps between first-generation immigrants and their second-generation children. Additionally, the study highlighted the inequitable participation of non-Eurocentric cultures within the broader Canadian social fabric.

The findings suggest that Filipino culture is most effectively maintained and shared through creative collaboration and positive representation. The researcher identified specific areas of indigenous Filipino culture that are vital for curriculum development, including Filipino folk tales, folk dances (such as *Tinikling*), martial arts (*Arnis*), and culinary arts. The study found that when these elements are taught in collaboration with local Canadian education and arts institutions, they support both multiculturalism and multigenerational learning.

**Conclusions and Implications**

The study concludes that a successful Filipino heritage curriculum must be built upon the pillars of indigenous Filipino culture and guided by the principle of social solidarity. The proposed curriculum framework emphasizes that Filipino heritage is "strong and beautiful" and should be integrated into the learning process through pedagogy that encourages interaction rather than isolation.

The implications of this research are twofold. For educators and curriculum developers, the study provides a methodological template for using acculturation theory to create inclusive, research-based multicultural curricula. By moving away from polarized models of assimilation or segregation and toward an integrationist approach, educators can help students navigate complex identities. For the Filipino Canadian community, the study reinforces the importance of using cultural heritage as a tool for empowerment, helping youth bridge their ancestral roots with their Canadian identities to achieve psychological well-being and sociocultural competence.

abstract:
This study looks into the perspectives on multicultural education of teacher educators in the Bachelor in Secondary Education (BSEd) major in Social Studies program of the Western Mindanao State University (WMSU). The research questions are: 1) What are the teacher educators perspectives (i.e. knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes) on multicultural education? and 2) What factors account for the teacher educators' perspectives on multicultural education?

Using a qualitative methodology consisting of a survey of 13 teacher educators handling the professional education courses in the BSEd Social Studies program, interviews of nine of these teacher educators, and an analysis of the program prospectus and course syllabi, the study finds that the teacher educators as a whole have positive conceptions of and attitudes towards multicultural education. There is also a consensus among the teacher educators regarding the relevance of multicultural education in the Philippine context and the need to integrate it in pre-service teacher education. However, the teacher educators' practice of multicultural education appears to be limited due to lack of formal training in multicultural education at the pre-service and in-service level, and lack of other forms of support for faculty, such as relevant teaching resources and adequate time to plan course delivery. At present the teacher educators' practice of multicultural education in their teaching is anchored only on a positive attitude and prior knowledge obtained through personal experiences. But as a group they are confronted with constraints to implementing multicultural education that require a more holistic and systematic response at the program and institutional level.

title: Lived Experiences of Pre-service Teachers in Online Practice Teaching: An Exploration of the Connectivist Pedagogies
abstract:
The connectivist pedagogy, based on connectivist learning theory, is a widely used approach in open and distance e-learning that enables learners to gather information and exchange knowledge through various online tools and platforms. One of the benefits of technological advancement is the use of online practice teaching programs in higher education institutions. While these programs offer new opportunities, they also present unique challenges. Despite the extensive research in online teaching practices, uncertainty surrounding the application of connective principles and networked learning characteristics has persisted. This area of study remained largely unexplored, necessitating further investigation. To address this research gap, it was deemed essential to comprehend how pre-service teachers (PTs) acquire knowledge in the context of emerging technologies.

A phenomenological-hermeneutic approach was utilized to investigate the lived experiences of twelve (12) PTs who had completed online practice teaching within connectivist pedagogies. The study was conducted at a state university in the Philippines, where the integrated networked learning approach was implemented. Focus group discussions with a reflective framework, interviews conducted using a phenomenological interview framework, and journal reflections served as the primary data collection methods. The collected data were analyzed through thematic analysis.

half:
This study explores the lived experiences of twelve pre-service teachers participating in online practice teaching within a state university in the Philippines. Using a qualitative phenomenological-hermeneutic approach, the research investigated how these teachers navigate learning through emerging technologies and networked learning via an Internationalization Program on Practice Teaching. Data were gathered through focus group discussions, one-on-one interviews, and journal documents, then processed using thematic analysis.

The findings reveal that pre-service teachers engaged in a mesh-type network characterized by a cyclical process. This cycle involved seeking information, understanding student needs, finding essential tools and resources, collaborating within the network, enhancing teaching approaches, and reflecting. These activities strengthened their Professional Learning Networks by leveraging various tools for information exchange, knowledge exchange, and social engagement.

However, challenges such as communication barriers, difficulties maintaining student engagement, technical issues, and unspoken conflicts with mentors and peers emerged. Pre-service teachers addressed these through coping mechanisms like improving communication methods, adapting instructional strategies, and engaging in reflective practice. They also used prior knowledge to adapt traditional methods to the online environment.

The study concludes that online practice teaching grounded in connectivist pedagogies allows pre-service teachers to build professional networks and adapt to the digital era. The research proposes an Online Practice Teaching Program Model and suggests that Higher Education Institutions use these findings to develop policies and best practices.

title: Perspectives and Practices of Inclusivity in an Online Learning Environment: An Ethnomethodological Study of an International School in Indonesia
abstract:
To make an online learning environment inclusive, it is important that schools must value diversity so that teaching practices may be responsive to the academic needs of not just some but all students. Inclusion is not about the shortfall of an individual because of one’s disability, disorder, or being gifted but it is how the school environment adjust to the individual. If so, then inclusion is of a social construct which entails an ethnomethodological approach in understanding inclusion. Instead of studying institutions that are committed and dedicated towards inclusive practices, this study zeroed in on an international school and inquired on practices that emerged from teachers’ personal practical or sense making knowledge which has been developed overtime through their experiences. This study answered the following:
1.What teaching practices do western teachers in an international school aim tofoster inclusivity in an online learning environment?
2.What is the perspective of the school on inclusivity that defines those practices?

To explore how teachers’ actual ordinary and mundane discussion produce an answer as to how they (the teachers) make inclusion happen, this study analyzed the conversation of western international teachers on how they are making sense of policies brought forward by the school. The findings included ten (10) points that may guide schools on how to implement inclusion in an online learning environment. The contribution of this study to distance education includes the value of reflexive (sense-making) accountability of teachers. Such accountability contributed to the orderliness and shared performance to carry out inclusive education in an online learning environment.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
This ethnomethodological study by Erdolfo L. Lardizabal investigates how Western expatriate teachers at an international school in Indonesia navigate and implement inclusive education within a synchronous online learning environment. Conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic at an International Baccalaureate school in Jakarta, the research focused on the English Department of the Diploma Programme. Using conversation analysis on a Microsoft Teams meeting involving three teachers from Canada and the United Kingdom, the study examined how educators use common-sense reasoning and collaborative discussion to adapt school policies to the realities of virtual teaching.

The findings reveal that teachers foster inclusivity through practical sense-making rather than strict adherence to formal policy. When addressing hyperactivity, teachers shifted focus from clinical diagnoses to observable behaviors, noting that traditional methods like "time-out" corners can be isolatory online, leading them to explore engagement-based strategies like fidget tools. Regarding inattentiveness, teachers discussed the utility of student planners and meaningful feedback, though time constraints sometimes led to "compliance" behaviors, such as stamping planners without thorough checks.

The study concludes that inclusivity in an online environment is a social construct achieved through the reflexive accountability and sense-making of teachers. Rather than merely following policies, teachers actively negotiate and adapt them to create an inclusive social reality. The research suggests that schools should move beyond static policies to support practical sense-making and adopt a "whole school approach" to inclusive routines.

Rather than focusing on formal institutional policies, the research examines how teachers use daily, mundane interactions and sense-making processes to "make inclusion happen" amidst the unique barriers presented by distance education.

The study was conducted at a prestigious International Baccalaureate (IB) school in Jakarta during the COVID-19 pandemic. The researcher focused on the English Department of the Diploma Programme, consisting of teachers from Canada and the United Kingdom. Using an ethnomethodological design and conversation analysis, the researcher analyzed an audio-visual recording of a Microsoft Teams meeting involving three teachers. The analysis focused on how these educators used common-sense reasoning and collaborative discussion to interpret and adapt school policies to the realities of virtual teaching.

The findings revealed that teachers often prioritize "real-world" applicability over "ideal-world" policy, sometimes engaging in "compliance" behaviors, such as stamping planners without thorough checks, due to time constraints and the difficulties of remote monitoring.

two:
This ethnomethodological study, conducted by Erdolfo L. Lardizabal, investigates the perspectives and practices of inclusivity within an online learning environment at an international school in Indonesia. The research focuses on how Western expatriate teachers navigate and implement inclusive education through their daily, mundane interactions and sense-making processes, rather than focusing on formal institutional policies.

The problem addressed by the study is the difficulty of implementing inclusive education in a distance education modality. While inclusive education is intended to cater to the learning needs of all students, including those with disabilities or neurodivergent traits, the transition to synchronous online learning creates unique barriers. The author notes that traditional inclusion research often focuses on physical classroom spaces or specific diagnostic labels, frequently overlooking how teachers actually "make inclusion happen" through their practical, everyday reasoning when faced with the constraints of a virtual environment.

The context of the study is a prestigious International Baccalaureate (IB) school in Jakarta, Indonesia, specifically during a period of synchronous online learning necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The study focuses on the English Department of the Diploma Programme (DP), consisting of Western teachers from Canada and the United Kingdom. These teachers were engaged in a departmental meeting to review the school's inclusion policies in preparation for an IB authorization visit.

The researcher employed an ethnomethodological research design, specifically utilizing conversation analysis (CA). This qualitative approach allowed the researcher to examine the "how" of social interaction—specifically how teachers use common-sense reasoning and collaborative discussion to interpret and adapt school policies to the realities of online teaching. Data collection involved an audio-visual recording of a Microsoft Teams meeting among three DP teachers (identified as JM, SG, and NY). These recordings were transcribed using the Jefferson Transcription System to capture nuances of interaction. The analysis focused on how teachers negotiated meaning regarding student behaviors, such as hyperactivity and inattentiveness, and how they challenged or adapted formal protocols to fit the virtual classroom.

The findings are categorized into teaching practices and school perspectives. Regarding teaching practices, the study identified several ways teachers foster inclusivity through sense-making. In discussions regarding hyperactivity, teachers moved away from clinical diagnoses to focus on observable behaviors. They discussed the limitations of "time-out" corners, noting that such practices can feel isolatory or punitive in a virtual setting, and instead explored more supportive, engagement-based strategies like using "spinners" or fidget tools to help students focus. In discussions regarding inattentiveness, teachers explored the use of student planners and the importance of providing meaningful, non-superficial feedback. The findings revealed that teachers often prioritize "real-world" applicability over "ideal-world" policy solutions, sometimes engaging in "compliance" (such as stamping planners without checking them) due to time constraints and the practical difficulties of remote monitoring.

The school's perspective on inclusivity, as reflected in the teachers' discussions of policy, emphasizes the removal of barriers to learning and the avoidance of diagnostic labeling. The teachers' interactions suggest a perspective that values student empowerment and the recognition of individual needs, though they noted that formal policies sometimes lack the specificity required for effective online implementation.

The study concludes that inclusivity in an online environment is a social construct achieved through the reflexive accountability and sense-making of teachers. The research highlights that teachers do not merely follow policies; they actively negotiate, challenge, and adapt them through collaborative discussion to create an orderly and inclusive social reality. The study suggests that inclusive education is not just about the presence of a policy, but about the skillful accomplishment of teaching practices that respond to student needs in real-time.

The implications of this research suggest that for inclusive distance education to be successful, schools must move beyond providing static policies and instead support the "sense-making" work of teachers. The study recommends a "whole school approach" to inclusive routines to prevent "slippage" in implementation. Furthermore, it implies that professional development should focus on practical, classroom-based strategies—such as managing neurodivergent behaviors in a virtual space—rather than just theoretical or diagnostic frameworks. Finally, the study contributes to the field of distance education by emphasizing the importance of teacher collaboration and the need for institutional tools (like ManageBac or Microsoft Teams) to be effectively integrated into inclusive pedagogical practices.

title: Distance Education Perspectives and Practices of Educators in an Allied Medical Program: A Grounded Theory Approach within the Phenomenological Tradition
abstract:
Framing the study within the Phenomenological Tradition, it asked the questions why do educators engage in distance education. To discover the meaning and purpose of distance education to educators in the allied medical field the study looked into the perspectives of the educators and their practices in Distance Education.

The phenomenological tradition with the methodology of the grounded theory approach was applied in this study to gather data, analyze and understand the accounts of six teachers in an allied medical program at a private university. The phenomenological tradition in research can obtain authentic data by providing open ended questions and flexibility that may allow the participants to narrate salient events and experiences significant to distance education. By applying the strength of the traditional qualitative research approach to a methodical approach in data analysis, theory is built thru the analysis of relationships thru the components revealed within a phenomenon (Brower 1995, in Jeong, 2009).
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
This thesis investigates the experiences of educators in a Bachelor of Science in Speech and Language Pathology (BSSLP) program in the Philippines during the transition from face-to-face to distance education (DE) caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Because allied medical programs are traditionally delivered in person, the sudden shift presented challenges, including a lack of formal training in distance pedagogy and concerns regarding whether DE could achieve the same competency levels as traditional modes, particularly for clinical skills.

Using a qualitative grounded theory approach within the phenomenological tradition, the researcher conducted semi-structured online interviews with six educators and administrators. The study resulted in the development of the "TIE Theory," which consists of three interconnected components. First, transitioning to DE requires meticulous departmental planning and accessible resources to ensure the quality of life for both educators and learners. Second, instructional design and technology are intertwined; educators shifted from teacher-centered to student-oriented frameworks, using digital tools and complex case analyses to address transactional distance and maintain academic integrity. Third, DE can be equivalent to face-to-face education if varying communication modes are used to meet learner needs. One participant noted that the online cohort showed improved holistic thinking and theory-to-practice connections. The study concludes that DE is an effective modality for complex curricula when supported by strategic planning, formal training in instructional design, and a shift toward student-directed learning.
one:
This thesis, titled "Distance Education Perspectives and Practices of Educators in an Allied Medical Program: A Grounded Theory Approach within the Phenomenological Tradition," investigates the experiences of educators in a Bachelor of Science in Speech and Language Pathology (BSSLP) program during the transition from face-to-face to distance education (DE) caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. In the Philippines, allied medical programs are traditionally delivered through face-to-face instruction. The sudden shift to distance learning presented challenges, as many educators lacked formal training in instructional design and distance pedagogy. Furthermore, there was ambiguity regarding whether DE could achieve the same competency and learning outcomes as traditional modes, particularly in a field requiring clinical and practical skills.

The researcher employed a qualitative research design using a grounded theory approach within the phenomenological tradition to explore the essence of the phenomenon through lived experiences. Using purposive sampling, the study selected six educators and administrators from a BSSLP program at a private university who had experience teaching in both traditional and distance modes. Data were collected through individual semi-structured online interviews and analyzed using a three-stage coding process: initial, intermediate, and advanced coding using the storyline technique.

The study resulted in the development of the "TIE Theory," which explains the phenomenon through three interconnected components. First, transitioning to DE requires meticulous planning and accessible learning resources. Successful transition involves departmental planning rather than individual efforts, ensuring specialists are included in the strategy to promote the quality of life for both educators and learners. Second, instructional design and technology are inextricably intertwined. Educators shifted from teacher-centered to student-oriented frameworks, using digital tools to address "transactional distance." This included transforming assessments from simple recall-based exams to complex case analyses to maintain academic integrity and ensure students could apply theoretical knowledge to clinical scenarios. Third, DE can be equivalent to face-to-face education if it utilizes varying modes of communication to address learner needs. One participant noted that the online cohort exhibited more holistic thinking and a better ability to connect theory to clinical practice than previous face-to-face cohorts, potentially due to the intensive use of case studies and formative feedback.

The study concludes that distance education in allied medical programs is a dynamic modality that can effectively deliver complex curricula when implemented with strategic planning and robust technological support. For administrators, the findings highlight the necessity of providing formal training in instructional design and distance pedagogy, as well as the importance of departmentalized planning. For educators, successful DE requires a paradigm shift toward student-directed learning and the creative use of technology to facilitate critical thinking.
two:
This thesis, titled "Distance Education Perspectives and Practices of Educators in an Allied Medical Program: A Grounded Theory Approach within the Phenomenological Tradition," investigates the experiences of educators in a Bachelor of Science in Speech and Language Pathology (BSSLP) program during the transition from face-to-face to distance education (DE) necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated in the context of the sudden shift in educational modalities caused by the global pandemic. In the Philippines, allied medical programs, such as BSSLP, were traditionally delivered through face-to-face instruction. The sudden migration to distance learning presented significant challenges, as many educators lacked formal training in instructional design and distance pedagogy. There was an underlying ambiguity regarding whether DE could achieve the same competency and learning outcomes as traditional modes, particularly in a field requiring clinical and practical skills. The researcher noted a lack of existing formal studies regarding the appropriation of DE within BSSLP programs in the local context, creating a need to understand how educators perceive and practice this modality to ensure educational quality.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a qualitative research design using a grounded theory approach within the phenomenological tradition. This approach allowed for the exploration of the "essence" of the phenomenon through the lived experiences of the participants. The study utilized purposive sampling to select six educators and administrators from a BSSLP program at a private university. These participants were chosen because they had experience teaching the program in both traditional and distance modes. Data were collected through individual semi-structured online interviews conducted via Google Meet and Viber. The analysis followed a rigorous three-stage coding process: initial coding to identify emerging concepts, intermediate coding to categorize these concepts, and advanced coding (using the storyline technique) to integrate findings into a cohesive theory.

**Findings**
The study resulted in the development of the "TIE Theory" on distance education in the allied medical field, which explains the essence of the phenomenon through three interconnected components:

First, the study found that transitioning to DE requires meticulous planning and the provision of accessible learning resources. This transition is not merely a change in medium but a process that aims to promote the quality of life for both educators and learners. The findings suggest that successful transition involves departmental planning rather than individual efforts, ensuring that specialists are included in the transition strategy.

Second, the research revealed that instructional design and technology are inextricably intertwined in teaching practices. Educators had to "think out of the box," shifting from teacher-centered to student-oriented frameworks. This involved using various digital tools (such as LMS, Zoom, and Google Meet) to address "transactional distance"—the gap in communication and interaction. Educators also had to transform assessments, moving from simple recall-based exams to complex case analyses and application-based individual outputs to maintain academic integrity and ensure students could apply theoretical knowledge to clinical scenarios.

Third, the study found that DE can be equivalent to face-to-face education if it utilizes varying modes of communication to address learner needs and achieve program outcomes. Interestingly, one participant noted that the cohort undergoing online learning exhibited more holistic thinking and a better ability to connect theory to clinical practice compared to previous face-to-face cohorts, suggesting that the intensive use of case studies and formative feedback in the DE environment may have enhanced certain cognitive skills.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that distance education in allied medical programs is a dynamic, evolving modality that, when implemented with strategic planning and robust technological support, can effectively deliver complex curricula. The TIE Theory provides a framework for understanding how transitioning, teaching practices, and educational equivalence interact.

The implications of this research are significant for higher education institutions. For administrators, the study highlights the necessity of providing formal training in instructional design and distance pedagogy, as many educators were forced to adapt without prior expertise. It also emphasizes the importance of departmentalized planning and the integration of technical support and subject-matter specialists during transitions. For educators, the findings suggest that successful DE requires a paradigm shift toward student-directed learning and the creative use of technology to facilitate critical thinking. Ultimately, the study serves as a guide for institutions to conduct needs assessments and program evaluations to maintain educational quality in an increasingly digital academic landscape.

title: Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning-Based Laboratory At-Home in Biochemistry: Effects on Student Attitude, Motivation, Confidence and Achievement
abstract:
This study involved developing and assessing a laboratory-at-home manual using the Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning (POGIL) approach as an alternative laboratory component in the general biochemistry course of the secondyear students of the Bachelor in Medical Laboratory Science. The first phase of the study covered designing, developing, pre-testing, and evaluating (validity and reliability) instruments: Instructional Material Evaluation Tool for Experts and Instructors, Biomolecules Achievement Test, and Instructional Material Evaluation Tool for Students, Attitude, Motivation, and Confidence in Laboratory Skills Questionnaire, and Perception Interview Guide Questions for Instructors and Students. The second phase involved designing, developing, and evaluating the POGIL-based Laboratory-at-Home (PLAH) and non-POGIL Laboratory-at-Home (nPLAH) Manuals on Biomolecules. The overall evaluation of experts, instructors, and students on PLAH and nPLAH manuals is high. 

The effect of the PLAH on student achievement attitude, motivation, and confidence in laboratory skills was determined using a quasi-experimental pretestposttest research design. The results were compared to other treatments using nPLAH and the Video (Traditional Manual with Video demonstrations) Manuals. Results showed that the students significantly increased their achievement scores after implementing the three different treatments. In addition, the students in the PLAH group gained more than those in the nPLAH and Video groups regarding achievement, attitude, motivation, and confidence in laboratory skills. Results showed that the gain before and after the treatments was significantly different except for the motivation level of the Video group. However, no significant difference was seen among the interventions except for confidence in laboratory skills, where Video is substantially different.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Jinky Marie T. Chua’s study addresses the challenges of teaching experimental sciences in the Philippines, specifically regarding large class sizes, limited funding, and inadequate laboratory space. These issues were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced a shift to distance learning. Because biochemistry is particularly difficult due to its abstract concepts, the researcher developed a "Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning-based Laboratory-at-home" (PLAH) manual. This manual uses safe, everyday household items and the POGIL approach to encourage critical thinking and self-managed teamwork.

The study utilized a three-phase quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design involving second-year Bachelor in Medical Laboratory Science students at Cagayan State University. Participants were divided into three groups: the PLAH group, a non-POGIL Laboratory-at-home (nPLAH) group, and a Video group.

Findings showed that both the PLAH and nPLAH manuals received high ratings for content, clarity, and usefulness. While all groups showed significant increases in achievement scores, the PLAH group demonstrated higher gains in achievement, attitude, motivation, and confidence in laboratory skills compared to the other groups. Qualitative data indicated that students found the PLAH manual fun and fulfilling, improving their teamwork and critical thinking. The study concludes that the PLAH manual is an effective tool for remote or resource-limited settings, proving that inquiry-based learning can be successfully transitioned to a home environment.

title: Rural-Upland Rehabilitation Ecoturism Strategies (RURES) Framework: A Rationalized Authentic Ecotourism Activity Planning Framework for Degraded Upland Areas in the Philippines A Case Study of Brgy. Salde, Culasi, Antique
abstract:
Tourism is economically important in the Philippines. Some of the natural destinations are in Protected Areas (PA) under established laws and managed by national government institutions. Some equally beautiful and unique natural areas are not part of PAs. Poor utilization, planning, and management of these areas cause their degradation. This is further exacerbated by climate change and disaster risks. Degradation affects the biophysical, economic, and socio-cultural aspects of the environment, which is detrimental to the survival of communities, especially those living in the rural-upland areas. Ecotourism unites conservation, community needs, and sustainable travel. It is seldom incorporated properly because its principles are sadly overlooked. Current planning methods of sustainable development and environmental rehabilitation typically follow either Top-Down or Bottom-Up Approach. There are disjuncts between involved parties and minimal integration of various theoretically related concepts leading to a more “patchwork” solution than an integrated one. This study formulates a new framework that will lay the groundwork for inventory and analysis of the potential of existing elements and requirements of the site and stakeholders while integrating key concepts such as Ecotourism and Landscape Architectural Approaches to planning. The process of gathering and synthesizing the data will be through a Middle-Out Approach that will incorporate inputs from all actors in all levels – Middle, Top, and Bottom – into a more cohesive ecotourism activity development strategy. A case study of the newly formulated of environmental degradation, livelihood issues, disaster risk, and their desire to delve into tourism development. However, COVID-19 pandemic constraints caused the case study to halt. The environmental site scanning and focused group discussions stage
was not completed. Even with the abrupt end of the data gathering, lack of data synthesis, and solution recommendations, the framework has created a guide for the data needed to be gathered, syntheses needed to be made, and plans that are needed to be formulated. When the researcher can continue the study, there will be no disjunct between the previously gathered data and the continued process of the Ecotourism Activity Planning.

This framework moves away from uncoordinated top-down or bottom-up models, aiming instead to balance economic viability, social equity, and environmental integrity while respecting Indigenous Knowledge Systems.

title: Knowledge, Attitude, and Practices on Human Milk Banking among Healthcare Professionals in a Maternal and Neonatal Area of a Tertiary Hospital in National Capital Region
abstract:
Premature or sick babies fed with formula milk are at high risk of developing complications such as intestinal infections which can be prevented if they receive human breast milk (Mothers’ Milk Bank, 2020). Since human breastmilk provides the optimal nutrition for babies and reduces risk of intestinal infections, the human milk bank is an important medium in providing a reliable and consistent supply of human breastmilk to this vulnerable population.

Healthcare professionals (HCPs) play a crucial role in the process of the milk bank such as human milk donation, human milk banking, and the use of donor milk. Mothers are more likely to participate if their HCPs are knowledgeable and encouraging. 

Since there are few studies in the perception of HCPs in human milk banking, the study was done to explore the knowledge and attitude of HCPs towards human milk banking. The findings provide a groundwork study in managing HCPs for planning and establishing a human milk bank. It was done in a Level III hospital that specializes in Maternal and Child Health with a human milk bank. The results show that HCPs are knowledgeable and have a positive attitude towards human milk banking. It also shows that there is no relationship between the knowledge and attitude, therefore, training should be done in improving both the areas. The significantly higher knowledge of physicians is a strength in their hospital. In practice, HCPs have more knowledge on the aspect of human milk banking in which they are more focused in practicing. Education and training of the HCPs with an encouraging attitude, and the awareness and education of the mothers and the community are important to establish the human milk bank and continue its operations. Insufficient resources and support are challenges identified as barriers in human milk banking.

half:
This research addresses the critical need for human milk banks to protect premature or sick infants from complications like intestinal infections, which occur more frequently with formula use. Because healthcare professionals (HCPs) are central to the donation, banking, and clinical use processes, their involvement is vital, as mothers are more likely to donate if providers are knowledgeable and encouraging. The study was conducted at a Level III Maternal and Child Health hospital in the National Capital Region to explore the specific knowledge and attitudes of professionals working directly with vulnerable populations.

The findings indicate that HCPs possess a high level of knowledge and maintain a positive attitude toward human milk banking. However, the results reveal no relationship between the level of knowledge and the attitude held by the professionals. Physicians demonstrated significantly higher knowledge levels, and HCPs possessed more knowledge in the specific aspects of human milk banking that they are actively practicing.

The study concludes that because knowledge does not automatically dictate attitude, training should be implemented to improve both areas simultaneously. To ensure successful operation, the study emphasizes the importance of education and training for HCPs to foster encouraging attitudes, alongside the need for awareness for mothers and the broader community. Additionally, addressing systemic barriers, such as insufficient resources and support, is necessary to ensure the sustainability of human milk banking.

title: Pearl of Peace: Unmuting Women’s Voices in Peacebuilding
abstract:
The meaningful participation and leadership of women was key in the success of the Bangsamoro peace process in the Philippines. This study focuses on the communicative aspect of the sensemaking experiences of seven key women peacebuilders and explores the unmuting of women’s voices in peacebuilding from the lenses of gender, language, and tradition using hermeneutic phenomenology as research methodology. By integrating the different frames of narratives and conversations with these women peacebuilders, five major themes were derived in the synthesis of meanings, “making sense” of the sensemaking of the women peacebuilders. Integrating and refining the five interwoven themes using the hermeneutic circle has led to an illuminating “epiphany”: The overarching dimension of the sensemaking and communication experiences of women in peacebuilding is power.

Power, both internal and external, has the capacity to impact change in consciousness, culture, and political processes. This study contributes the Kite Flying Model in Place Communication for a deeper appreciation of how power interplays with peace in the meaningful engagement and leadership of women in peace processes. It also presents the Quadrant Matrix of Peace Communication that is useful for elvating peace communication approaches from simply engendered to “engendered.” Like the grain of sand that shifts the inner composite matter of the oyster to painstakingly give birth to an iridescent pearl, this study is paradigm-shifting as it navigated an unexplored terrain in the male-dominated seascape of peace and security to re-discover the pearl of peace.
