Aseneta’s dissertation, "Pearl of Peace: Unmuting Women’s Voices in Peacebuilding," investigates the communicative sensemaking experiences of women peacebuilders within the Bangsamoro peace process in the Philippines. Addressing the historical marginalization of women in male-dominated negotiations, the study uses a qualitative hermeneutic phenomenological design to explore the "life-world" of seven women, including government officials, civil society leaders, and negotiators.

The research identifies power as the central epiphany, manifesting both internally and externally with the capacity to transform consciousness, culture, and political processes. Findings reveal that women use communication to navigate gender relations, language nuances, and traditional constraints to influence decision-making and advocate for social justice. This engagement serves as a transformative force that addresses discrimination and power relations, moving beyond the mere absence of war. The study emphasizes that women's voices are essential for a truly "en-gendered" peacebuilding process, noting that sensemaking acts as a vital leadership capability for bridging current realities with future visions.

Theoretically, the researcher proposes a "Quadrant Matrix of Peace Communication," categorizing approaches as Engendered, En-gendered, Emaciated, or Endangered. Practically, the "Kite Flying Model in Peace Communication" illustrates the dynamic interplay between peace and power. Ultimately, the work advocates for moving from tokenistic participation toward substantive, en-gendered practices that empower women as catalysts for lasting peace.

For the discipline, the researcher proposes a "Quadrant Matrix of Peace Communication," which categorizes approaches into four types: Engendered, En-gendered, Emaciated, and Endangered Peace Communication. This framework provides a theoretical tool for scholars to evaluate how gender is integrated into peace discourse. For practice, the study introduces the "Kite Flying Model in Peace Communication," which illustrates the dynamic interplay between peace and power. This model suggests that effective peace communication requires a balance of power and peace to ensure meaningful engagement. Ultimately, the work advocates for elevating peace communication from tokenistic participation to a substantive, en-gendered practice that empowers women to act as "trust champions" and catalysts for lasting peace.

title: Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist Teaching Approach: Effects on Students' Conception, Attitude, Learning Experiences, and Achievement in Mathematics
abstract:
The study aimed to contribute a contextualized perspective of mathematics and, consequently, its classroom implications for a better understanding of its nature, the genesis and developmental stages of mathematical concepts, and their applications.

The study made a comparative analysis of the effects of Strict Absolutist, Strict Constructivist and Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist teaching approaches on students’ mathematics conception, attitude, learning experiences and achievement. The study used the quasi-experimental three-group pretest-posttest research design. However, the mathematics achievement posttest was not administered due to the sudden class suspension and community lockdowns caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The quizzes were used, instead, where each item in the mathematics achievement test was matched to an item in the quiz that measured similar concept or skill.

The results of the study revealed that the Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist approach to mathematics teaching significantly improved students’ mathematics conception, attitude, learning experiences and achievement.

Based on the results, it is recommended to provide students with learning opportunities that impart understanding of the nature of mathematics, its history and application, and to allow students to be creative and curious in mathematics.

The dissertation by Rainilyn L. Duque investigates the effectiveness of a "Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist" (AC) teaching approach in mathematics. This approach is proposed as a way to resolve the long-standing pedagogical divide between strict absolutism—which views mathematics as a collection of immutable, objective truths discovered by humans—and strict constructivism, which views mathematics as a subjective, human-constructed mental activity. The researcher argues that mathematics is "partly found and partly made," suggesting that while mathematical truths are stable and universal, the domain of these truths can expand and evolve through human discovery and application.

The problem addressed by the study is the polarization in mathematics education. Traditional absolutist methods often rely on rote memorization and lecture-based instruction, while radical constructivist methods may fail to account for the stability and universality of mathematical knowledge. The study seeks to determine if a contextualized approach—one that links theoretical constructs to real-world applications and acknowledges both the stability and the developmental nature of mathematics—can improve students' mathematical conception, attitudes, learning experiences, and achievement.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a quasi-experimental, three-group pretest-posttest research design. The sample consisted of three intact classes of freshmen Bachelor of Science in Mathematics students at Bulacan State University during the first semester of the 2019-2020 academic year. The study compared the Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist approach against a Strict Absolutist (conventional) group and a Strict Constructivist group. The curriculum covered topics including propositions, tautologies, logical equivalence, arguments and proofs, sets, operations, and divisibility. Due to COVID-19 lockdowns, the final mathematics achievement posttest was replaced by matched quiz items to measure student performance.

The findings of the study indicate that the Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist approach significantly improved all measured variables. Specifically, students in the AC group showed significantly higher posttest mean scores in mathematics conception, attitude, learning experiences, and achievement compared to the other two groups. Regarding mathematics conception, the AC approach led to a better understanding of the nature of mathematics and stronger beliefs about the learning and use of mathematics. In terms of attitude, the approach positively impacted the affect, behavior, and cognitive dimensions of the students' attitudes toward the subject. Furthermore, the study found positive relationships between students' mathematics conception and attitude, between their understanding of the nature of mathematics and their appreciation for learning, and between their beliefs about mathematics and their learning strategies. Finally, multiple linear regression analysis revealed that students' mathematics conception, attitude, and learning experiences are positive predictors of mathematics achievement.

The researcher concludes that the Contextualized Absolutist-Constructivist approach is a superior pedagogical framework for mathematics education. By melding the stability of absolutism with the developmental nature of constructivism, the approach allows students to master mathematical skills through drill and rigor while simultaneously engaging in creative, real-world problem-solving. This method helps students view mathematics not as a static set of rules, but as a dynamic discipline that grows through human agency and application.

The implications of this research are significant for various stakeholders in education. For teachers, the study suggests a need to move away from purely rote or purely discovery-based methods toward a balanced approach that emphasizes the history, genesis, and practical application of mathematical concepts. For school administrators, the findings highlight the importance of creating a school climate that encourages curiosity and creativity rather than just mechanical skill acquisition. For curriculum developers, the study advocates for policies that tailor mathematics education to the needs and real-world contexts of learners. Ultimately, the research encourages a paradigm shift in how mathematics is perceived and taught, moving toward a model that recognizes mathematics as a universal truth that is simultaneously capable of expansion and evolution.

title: Mereology-based Instruction: Effects on Chemical Identity Thinking, Critical Thinking, and Chemistry-based Health Literacy
abstract: This study is an attempt to utilize mereology-based instruction, an innovative approach in teaching biochemistry to health science students by linking biochemistry principles to health concepts. Specifically, it investigated the effects of mereology-based instruction (MBI) and conventional instruction (Cl) to the chemical identity thinking (CIT), critical thinking in chemistry (CTC), and chemistry-based health literacy (CbHL) of medical laboratory science students. A total of 13 intact classes of second year Medical Laboratory Science were randomly assigned into two groups, mereology-based instruction and conventional instruction. Seven intact classes (N = 290) were assigned to the mereology-based instruction group and six intact classes (N = 287) were assigned to the conventional instruction group. The students participated in the study for 12 weeks in a tertiary private academic institution in Baguio City. Data were obtained using Rasch analysis, an approach of mathematical modelling anchored on a latent trait to measure person ability and item difficulty related to the latent trait in a single logit scale. Mereology-based instruction was found to bo more effective than conventional instruction in increasing chemical identity thinking, critical thinking in chemistry, and chemistry-based health literacy of health science students, but these students exposed to MBI experienced higher cognitive load. The effects of MBI in chemical identity thinking {CIT), critical thinking in chemistry {CTC) and chemistry-based health literacy (CbHL) is topjc-specific, and has an "enhancement" effect in CIT, "corrective" effect in CTC, and either "corrective" or "enhancing" effect in CbHL. Conventional instruction has a "cor:-ective• effect in chemical identity thinking, critical thinking in chemistry, and chemistry-based health literacy. Based on multiple linear regression analysis, an increase in posttest ability of students in chemical identity thinking is predicted by prior knowledge of chemistry concepts, pretest ability in chemical identity thinking, and male gender in the MBI group. In the Cl group, student posttest ability in chemical identity thinking is redicted by prior knowledge of chemistry concepts and pretest ability in chemical identity thinking. An increase in posttest student ability in critical thinking in chemistry in the MBI group is predicted by prior knowledge of chemistry concepts, prior knowledge of visual representations and pretest ability in critical thinking in chemistry. In the C~ group, an increased posttest student ability in critical thinking in chemistry is predicted by prior knowledge of chemistry concepts, prior knowledge of visual representations, pretest ability in critical thinking in chemistry and male gender. An increase in posttest student ability in chemistry--based health literacy is predicted by prior knowledge of visual representations, pretest ability in chemistry-based health Uteracy, male gender, and cognitive load in the MBI group. In tha Cl group, student posttest ability in chemistrybased health literacy is predicted by prior knowledge of chemistry concepts and pretest ability in chemistry-based health literacy. Results indicate that mereology- based instruction in biochemistry has a potential to address the expected learning outcomes in health science programs in the Philippines as it promotes a thinking process which targets misconceptions and enhances prior level of conceptual understanding related ~o chemical identity thinking, critical thinking in chemistry and chemistry-based health hteracy. Achieving these learning outcomes is deemed to be effective in building the capacity of future health science graduates in making appropriate and rot ust healthrelated decisions.

title: Biology Teachers’ Pedagogical Content Knowledge and Decision Making in Implementing the Inquiry Approach: a Multi-Case Study
abstract:
This study was conducted to determine the general pattern of the PCK of four ( 4) Grade 8 science teachers who used the inquiry approach in teaching cell division and Mendelian Genetics, find out how they developed their PCK, enumerate the active components of their PCK when using the inquiry approach, determine their mental construct of the inquiry approach, describe how they practice the inquiry approach, and find out the general pattern of their decision-making process. Through interviews, classroom observations, and analysis of artifacts, the data were collected and analyzed using constant comparative analysis.

The analysis of multiple sources of data identified the general PCK pattern in which the four PCK components (i.e., knowledge of content, knowledge of instructional strategies, knowledge of students' understanding of science, and knowledge of assessment) were integrated and used in teaching cell division and Mendelian genetics. The highest frequency of integration done by all the teachers was between knowledge of instructional strategies and knowledge of students' understanding of science. The PCK pattern observed was that before the lesson, teachers do any activity as an instructional strategy (knowledge of instructional strategy). During the lesson, teachers teach the content (knowledge of content) through the use of cooperative learning, models and multimedia materials, and a variety of activities (knowledge of instructional strategies). This teaching of content facilitates student learning (knowledge of students' understanding of science) and develops critical thinking and conceptual understanding. After the lesson, in the context of slow learners, assessment follows, which is through giving extra work or remedial class (knowledge of assessment). While the three teachers (Ace, Ces, and Des) start with a motivational activity, Teacher Bes starts the lesson with another approach. Results also identified emergent themes of the PCK components. For knowledge of content, the identified theme was clear discussion of the basic concepts of cell division and Mendelian genetics. The identified emergent themes for knowledge of instructional strategies were use of cooperative learning, starting a lesson with motivational activities, use of models and multimedia materials, and use of a variety of activities. The identified emergent themes for knowledge of students' understanding of science were developing or stimulating students' critical thinking by asking questions, use of multi-assessment tools, teaching to develop conceptual understanding, critical or analytical thinking skills, and problem-solving skills, and correction/prevention of misconceptions. Finally, for knowledge of assessment, the identified theme was giving extra work or remedial class to slow learners.

title: Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education
abstract: This study aimed to develop technology-mediated learning modules in practical mathematics for the technical vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum using the design research model of Mckenney and Reeves (2003). It also sought to: a) characterize the these learning modules in terms of the selected design principles; b) determine their effectiveness; c) determine how beneficial the design research approach is in developing these modules compared to a traditional curriculum development approach; d) compare the practical mathematics test scores of the design research group and comparison group; and e) make improvements on the leaming modules. The theoretical and practical outputs of the study are of significant use to curriculum developers, mathematics teachers, technical vocational schools, and practitioners of design research. Two iterations were done in developing the modules, where data were gathered from randomly selected samples from a private sectarian college using researcher-made instruments. Test result indicated a non significant difference in the gain scores of the design research group and the comparison group. However, research participants' assessment of the modules show that the modules developed using the design research were effective in teaming practical mathematics concepts. The focus group discussion with research participants and the review of a subject expert both show preference in the modules developed using design research. The study thus recommends the use of design research in developing technology-mediated learning modules in mathematics for the technical vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum, and the use of its practical output in the online learning and teaching of practical mathematics concepts.

Aves investigated the development of technology-mediated learning modules for practical mathematics, specifically designed for the technical vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines. The study addressed a lack of online learning technology in core mathematics courses for vocational students, aiming to create engaging, authentic, and relevant instructional materials. The researcher employed a design research approach based on the model by McKenney and Reeves (2003), utilizing two iterations of a systematic design cycle involving analysis, design, implementation, and evaluation. Data were gathered from students at a private sectarian college through evaluation rubrics, observation guides, interviews, and focus group discussions. A comparison group using modules developed through traditional curriculum development was used to evaluate effectiveness.

The findings showed that the second iteration of the technology-mediated modules received "excellent" ratings regarding the online learning approach, teaching roles, technology tools, and module presentation. The Mann-Whitney U test revealed no significant difference in pretest scores or gain scores between the design research group and the comparison group, though the design research group had a higher mean rank. Qualitative findings indicated a strong student preference for the design research modules, with students in the comparison group expressing a desire for the small-group discussions and problem-solving activities included in the design research modules. The researcher concluded that the design research approach is a highly effective method for developing technology-mediated learning modules.

Aves investigates the development of technology-mediated learning modules for practical mathematics, specifically designed for the technical vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines. The study addresses a research gap regarding the lack of online learning technology application in core mathematics courses for vocational students. The researcher sought to determine if a design research approach is more beneficial for developing these modules than traditional curriculum development methods, aiming to create instructional materials that are engaging, authentic, and relevant to students preparing for immediate employment.

The researcher employed a design research approach based on the model by McKenney and Reeves (2003), which is characterized as interventionist, iterative, process-oriented, utility-oriented, and theory-oriented. The study utilized two iterations of a systematic design cycle involving analysis, design, implementation, and evaluation. Data were gathered from randomly selected students at a private sectarian college using researcher-made evaluation rubrics, observation guides, interview protocols, and focus group discussions. To compare the effectiveness of the design research approach against traditional methods, the researcher introduced a comparison group that used modules developed through a traditional curriculum development approach characterized by direct instruction and teacher-led lectures. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to analyze differences in pretest and gain scores between the two groups.

The findings showed that the second iteration of the technology-mediated modules received "excellent" ratings from students regarding the online learning approach, teaching roles, technology tools, and module presentation. The Mann-Whitney U test revealed no significant difference in pretest scores between the design research group and the comparison group, indicating equal baseline knowledge. There was also no significant difference in the gain scores between the two groups, although the mean rank of the design research group was higher. This dissertation by Benedicto Norberto V. Aves investigates the development of technology-mediated learning modules for practical mathematics specifically designed for the technical vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the context of the increasing importance of online learning and the implementation of the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines. While online learning has become a vital component of vocational education globally to reach time-bound or place-bound students, the author notes a research gap: there is a lack of application of online learning technology in the core mathematics courses of the technical vocational track in the Philippines. Specifically, the study addresses the need for instructional materials that are engaging, authentic, and relevant to students who are preparing for immediate employment in technical vocations. The researcher seeks to determine if a design research approach is more beneficial for developing these modules than traditional curriculum development methods.

**Method**
The researcher employed a design research approach based on the model by McKenney and Reeves (2003), which is characterized as interventionist, iterative, process-oriented, utility-oriented, and theory-oriented. The study utilized two iterations of a systematic design cycle, involving analysis, design, implementation, and evaluation. Data were gathered from randomly selected samples of students from a private sectarian college. The researcher used several instruments, including researcher-made evaluation rubrics, observation guides, interview protocols, and focus group discussions. To compare the effectiveness of the design research approach against traditional methods, the researcher introduced a comparison group that used modules developed through a traditional curriculum development approach (characterized by direct instruction and teacher-led lectures). The study also utilized the Mann-Whitney U test to analyze differences in pretest and gain scores between the design research group and the comparison group.

**Findings**
The study's findings are multifaceted. Regarding the characterization of the modules, the second iteration of the technology-mediated modules received "excellent" ratings from students in terms of the online learning approach, the roles of teaching, the technology tools used, and the presentation of the modules. In terms of academic performance, the Mann-Whitney U test revealed no significant difference in the pretest scores between the design research group and the comparison group, indicating equal baseline knowledge. Furthermore, there was no significant difference in the gain scores between the two groups, although the mean rank of the design research group was higher.

Qualitative findings from focus group discussions and subject expert reviews indicated a strong preference for the modules developed through design research. Students in the comparison group expressed a desire for the small-group discussions and problem-solving activities that were inherent in the design research modules but absent in the traditional modules. The design research group benefited from collaborative learning through synchronous and asynchronous discussions via Facebook group chats, whereas the comparison group relied on direct instruction and a discussion board.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The researcher concludes that the design research approach is a highly effective method for developing technology-mediated learning modules. The iterative nature of the process allowed for continuous improvements, moving student evaluations from "good" in the first iteration to "excellent" in the second. The study validates that a student-centered, constructivist, and technology-enhanced environment—facilitated by collaborative problem-solving and social presence—is preferable for teaching practical mathematics in an online vocational context.

The implications of this study are significant for several stakeholders. For curriculum developers, the study provides a re-conceptualized framework and validated design principles that can guide the creation of technology-mediated mathematics curricula for other technical vocational courses. For mathematics teachers, the study offers practical online modules and validated design strategies to manage effective online classes, particularly for students with time or location constraints. For technical vocational schools, the modules serve as models for offering online courses that connect mathematics to real-world workplace applications. Finally, for practitioners of design research, the study contributes to the body of knowledge by demonstrating the utility of introducing a comparison group to evaluate the benefits of the design research approach against traditional curriculum development.

title: Pre-Service Biology Teachers’ Exposure, Understanding, Attitude, Self-efficacy. Predisposition, Progressivist views, and Application of Inquiry-based Instruction
abstract:
This piece of work described pre-service biology teachers (PSBTs) in terms of their exposure to inquiry-based science instruction (IBSI), and how they were able to apply IBSI practices during teaching practicum. Moreover, the study profiled the PSBTs according to their I8SI understanding, attitudes, self-efficacy, and predispositions, including their learner-centered views. Finally, the study determined the inter-relationships among the PSBTs' IBSI variables.

Sixty-six (66) PSBTs from three teacher-education institutions in Baguio City and Benguet participated in the study. Eight instruments were used to gather data -Science Teachers' Inquiry Practices Scale (STIPS), Pedagogy of Science Testing Test - Biology Items (POSTT-8), Attitude Scale for IBSI Use (ASIU), Inquiry-Based Science Instruction Self-efficacy Scale (IBSISES), Test for Inquiry Pedagogy in Science - Biology (TIPS-B), Modified Reformed Teaching Observation Protocol (mRTOP), Modified Inquiry Teaching Self-Assessment Instrument (mlTSAI), and the Educational Philosophies Self-Assessment Instrument (EPSAI). The PSBTs lesson plans were also analyzed to support the result on the level of I8S1 application during teaching internship. Follow-up interviews on both PSBTs and their cooperating teachers were also conducted to supplement the quantitative results gathered from the research instruments. 

Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to summarize data, while inferential statistics {Analysis of Variance and Tukey HSD) were used to test for significance among means. Pearson correlation and step-wise multiple regression procedures were employed to describe the relationship among the PSBTs' 18SI variables.

title: Phenomenography of Teachers’ and Students’ Understanding, Beliefs and Experiences of Physics Learning Assessment
abstract:
The purpose of this phenomenographic study was to explore the understandings, beliefs, and experiences of Physics Learning Assessment (PLA) of senior high school Physics teachers and students in General Physics 1, a subject in the curriculum for the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) strand. Specifically, this study answered the following research questions: (1) What are the SHS teachers' and students' ways of understanding Physics Learning Assessment in the fol!o~ving dimensions of understanding: knowledge, purpose, and process? (2) \f\/hat are the SHS teachers' and students' beliefs about the effectiveness and efficiency of Physics Learning Assessment? (3) What do the SHS teachers' and students' find significant in their lived experiences of PLA as inferred from their most significant stories, emotions evoked by and insights gained from these experiences? (4) What are the teachers' and students' categories of description of PLA? And (5) What are the relationships among the teachers' and students' conceptions of PLA?

The study employed the exploratory-descriptive research design; hence, the sources of data included semi-structured interviews of the teacher-informants and focus group discussions (FGDs) with the student-participants. Classroom observation during a given PLA session and analysis of shared PLA tools for each FGD group of the four teachers were additional sources of data.

title: Inquiry-based Laboratory Activities: Effect on Students’ Inquiry Skills, Conceptual Understanding and Attitude Toward Genetics
abstract: The study developed and determined the effects of the inquiry-based laboratory activities on the inquiry skills, conceptual understanding and attitude toward Genetics of undergraduate Biology and Biology major Education students. The quasi-experimental design for quantitative methodology and qualitative data analysis were used to assess the (1) difference in the inquiry skills and conceptual understanding among and between students exposed to inquiry-based laboratory activities and those who are not; (2) change in the attitudes of the students toward Genetics in inquiry-based laboratory activities; (3) correlation among students' inquiry skills, conceptual understanding, and attitude toward Genetics; and ( 4) impact of inquiry-based laboratory activities in Genetics to students who use it. The students enrolled in Genetics class in a state university in the Visayas for the 2nd Semester Academic Year 2014-2015 served as subjects of this study. The students were randomly assigned to two groups - the control and the experimental groups. The control group consisted of one section of Bachelor of Science in Biology (Premed and Biotechnology Track) students taught using the traditional cookbook method in Genetics while the experimental groups consisted of two separate sections of Bachelor of Science in Biology (Microbiology Track) and Bachelor in Secondary Education (major in Biology) students utilized the researcher-made inquiry-based laboratory activities in Genetics. Qualitative analysis was done using focus group interview to obtain an in-depth analysis of the perceptions on the strategy and implementation of inquiry-based laboratory activities. This was further triangulated through students' laboratory reports, inquiry skills, conceptual understanding results, attitude questionnaire responses and observation checklists. The quantitative data on conceptual understanding, inquiry skills and attitude toward Genetics were assessed in a pretest-posttest implementation of the strategy used. In the laboratory period, the control group used the conventional laboratory method, the "cook book" method while the inquiry-based laboratory method was employed in the experimental group. Statistical analyses of the study employed both descriptive and inferential statistics.

title: Perspectives of the Nano-Influencers in Utilizing Chibi Live2D Models: A Qualitative Analysis of The Impact of VTubing as a Branding Tool for Social Entertainment
abstract:
Virtual YouTubers (VTubers) are social media influencers who use 2D or 3D models as their visual identification while creating content online. As feedback, the audience members of a VTuber can create nijisousakus based on the brand identity of the avatar. An example of a nijisousaku is a chibi, a caricature method by super deforming anatomy to highlight emotions, maximize cuteness, and reimagine an avatar into a mini version.

This qualitative study applied Herbert Simon’s (1969) Design Thinking Process to explain the creation of chibi Live2D models. Hand tracking or body physics highlighted the VTubers’ ability to convey figurative expressions through voice and movement, deepening their connection with the audience. The study utilized purposive sampling to select a focus group of three nano-influencers (defined as having 100 to 5,000 followers) from the Philippines and Indonesia. The design process followed Herbert Simon’s (1969) Design Thinking Process, moving through the stages of Empathize, Define, Ideate, Deliver, and Test. To analyze the interpersonal and sociological connections between the creators and their models, the study applied Erving Goffman’s (1959) Theory of Self-presentation, examining the "front-stage" performance of the VTuber and the "backstage" technical and creative activities.

title: Development of "Kalasag": A Modern Security Jacket for Persons with Disability
abstract: The increasing need for enhanced safety and security for persons with disabilities (PWDs) has prompted the development of specialized assistive technologies, also categorized as wearable technologies. This thesis presents the design, development, and evaluation of "Kalasag", which is a modern security jacket for PWDs, specifically for the Deaf, who currently face language barriers amidst verbal and non-verbal communication. The jacket integrates a range of features, including a help caller, security alarm system, and digital health record, embedded in a multifunctional jacket to address various safety challenges faced by individuals with sensory impairments. Employing a user-centered design approach, the project involved consultation with PWDs and experts in clothing and assistive technology to ensure that the jacket meets practical needs while maintaining comfort and ease of use. The development process of the prototype utilized materials and technologies that enhance durability, functionality, and user comfort, including non-static fabrics and the use of basic electronics. Evaluation results from the creative project involving a target group of three Deaf participants demonstrate that Kalasag has shown potential to improve users' confidence in their personal safety and facilitate efficient emergency response. This thesis concludes with recommendations toward the incorporation of more advanced technology and in-depth research towards the creation of the jacket for other PWD classifications for further refinement of the jacket’s features and potential pathways for commercial production and broader dissemination. The findings contribute to the ongoing efforts to enhance the quality of life for PWDs through innovative assistive solutions.

To address these vulnerabilities, the study focuses on the development of "Kalasag," a multifunctional wearable security jacket designed to be both practical and comfortable for daily use.

The study utilized a user-centered design approach, incorporating direct consultations with persons with disabilities and experts in clothing and assistive technology to balance technical requirements with ergonomic and aesthetic needs. The prototype was constructed using non-static fabrics and basic electronics to integrate several key technological components: a help caller, a security alarm system, and a digital health record. These embedded tools allow users to discreetly signal for assistance or provide vital medical information during critical situations.

Evaluation of the prototype through a creative project involving three Deaf participants indicated that the jacket has the potential to significantly improve user confidence regarding personal safety and facilitate more efficient emergency responses. The research concludes that "Kalasag" is a viable assistive technology that enhances the autonomy and security of PWDs. Future work may include incorporating advanced technologies, adapting the design for other disabilities, and pursuing commercial production.

title: Analyzing the Acceptance of Collaborative Learning Tools among Online Students Using the Technology Acceptance Model
abstract: Information and Communication Technologies, such as collaborative learning tools, were used in educational institutions to alleviate geographical restrictions and facilitate easier collaboration in education. This study used the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) to investigate the relationship between online students and their use of collaborative learning tools using a semi-structured survey questionnaire using Google Forms. A convenience sampling technique was used to identify the target participants, and the data from the 67 respondents were analyzed using a combination of data analysis methods. Results showed that online students’ Perceived Usefulness (PU), Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), Attitude Toward Using (AT), and Behavioral Intention to Use (BI) positively influence each component that predicts and confirms the Actual Usage (AU) of collaborative learning tools. Among the six types of collaborative learning tools, the most used is communication, and the least used is consensus building. For advantages, three themes were established from the online students’ responses: workflow, usability, and social. For disadvantages, there are four themes established from the responses of online students: workflow, technical, usability, and none. There are concerns regarding the accessibility and usability of the general collaborative learning tools. This study recommended investigating the workflow and usability concerns about using collaborative learning tools as it further understands the user experience (UX) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), as not all students can keep up before developing learning technologies that guarantee their future usage.

Billones's thesis, "Analyzing the Acceptance of Collaborative Learning Tools among Online Students Using the Technology Acceptance Model," investigates how online students at the University of the Philippines Open University perceive and utilize digital tools for group work. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study also incorporates Vygotsky’s Social Development Theory and Walther’s Social Information Processing Theory. Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher collected data from 67 undergraduate students through semi-structured surveys.

The findings indicate that online students have a positive relationship with collaborative learning tools (CLTs), perceiving them as relatively easy to use and useful for their education. Correlation analysis confirmed that Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) and Perceived Usefulness (PU) have significant positive relationships with Attitude Towards Usage (AT), which in turn positively influences Behavioral Intention (BI) and Actual Usage (AU). Communication is the most frequent application, with Zoom, Google Meet, Discord, and Facebook being the most popular platforms, while Google products dominate resource, project, and presentation management.

Qualitative analysis revealed that workflow, usability, and social engagement serve as both advantages and disadvantages. Benefits include improved efficiency and accessibility, while drawbacks include distractions, coordination challenges, internet dependency, and cost. The study concludes that TAM is a valid framework for predicting CLT adoption. The researcher suggests that institutions provide support or free access to tools to ensure equity, while developers should focus on User Experience to reduce barriers.

The thesis titled "Analyzing the Acceptance of Collaborative Learning Tools among Online Students Using the Technology Acceptance Model" by Jia P. Billones investigates how online students perceive and utilize digital tools designed to facilitate group work and academic collaboration.

The problem addressed by this study is the need to understand the acceptance and effectiveness of collaborative learning tools (CLTs) in a distance education setting. While technology is intended to alleviate geographical barriers and foster essential 21st-century collaboration skills, the experience of using these tools varies among students. The researcher notes that existing studies often focus on the perspectives of instructors rather than students, and many only examine a single aspect of technology acceptance. This study seeks to provide a more comprehensive view by examining multiple determinants of acceptance among students in a fully online environment.

The context of the research is the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), a fully online campus. This setting is particularly relevant because its students have high exposure to online learning. The study is grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) developed by Davis (1989), which posits that Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) and Perceived Usefulness (PU) are primary drivers of a user's attitude and intention to use a technology. The research also draws on Vygotsky’s Social Development Theory and Walther’s Social Information Processing Theory to contextualize the importance of social interaction and interpersonal skills in digital learning environments.

The methodology employed a mixed-methods approach using a semi-structured survey questionnaire distributed via Google Forms. The study utilized convenience sampling to gather data from 67 undergraduate students at UPOU. The research instrument consisted of 27 questions covering socio-demographic profiles, TAM variables (PEOU, PU, Attitude Towards Usage, Behavioral Intention, and Actual Usage), tool usage rankings, and open-ended questions regarding perceived advantages and disadvantages. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis via IBM SPSS Statistics, and qualitative content analysis using QDA Miner.

The findings reveal that online students generally have a positive relationship with collaborative learning tools. Descriptive analysis showed that students perceive these tools as relatively easy to use and useful for their education. Correlation analysis confirmed that Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) and Perceived Usefulness (PU) have significant positive relationships with Attitude Towards Usage (AT), which in turn positively influences Behavioral Intention (BI) and Actual Usage (AU). Specifically, students who find tools easier to use and more useful are more likely to develop a favorable attitude and intend to use them in the future.

Regarding the actual usage of tools, the study found that communication is the most frequently used type of CLT, with Zoom, Google Meet, Discord, and Facebook being the most popular platforms. Resource management, ideation and co-creation, project management, and presentation/archiving followed in usage frequency, while consensus building was the least used. Google products emerged as a dominant force across several categories, including resource management, project management, and presentation.

Qualitative analysis of the advantages and disadvantages revealed overlapping themes. The perceived advantages were categorized into workflow (efficiency and productivity), usability (accessibility and convenience), and social (engagement and community). Conversely, the perceived disadvantages were categorized into workflow (distractions and coordination challenges), technical (internet dependency and privacy), and usability (skill requirements and cost). Notably, workflow and usability appeared as both advantages and disadvantages, suggesting that the impact of these tools depends heavily on how they are implemented and used.

The study concludes that the Technology Acceptance Model is a valid framework for predicting the adoption of collaborative learning tools among online students. The results confirm that ease of use and perceived usefulness are critical drivers of student acceptance. While students find these tools highly beneficial for communication and resource management, there are significant challenges regarding the complexity of group coordination and technical dependencies.

The implications of this research are significant for several sectors. For the education sector, the study suggests that institutions should provide support or free access to these tools to ensure equitable learning. For the multimedia and software industry, the findings highlight the importance of User Experience (UX) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). Specifically, developers should focus on reducing the technical and usability barriers that currently act as disadvantages for students. The researcher recommends that future studies expand the sample size to include different academic programs and graduate students, and further investigate the specific workflow and usability concerns to improve the design of future learning technologies.

title: A Study of Filipino Gen Zs Residing in the Greater Manila Area’s Perception of P-Pop’s Potential as a Global Phenomenon
abstract: Utilizing a quantitative-descriptive research design, this study determines the significant relationship between the level of activeness on social media platforms and the level of awareness and familiarity with P-Pop, determines the significant difference between the perceived P-Pop's ability to achieve global recognition and its factors, and determines the significant difference between the perceived P-Pop's ability to achieve global recognition and its cultural showcase, innovation and representation elements. It surveyed 385 Filipino Gen Zs residing in the Greater Manila Area about their perceptions of P-Pop and its potential to become a global phenomenon. The findings of this study revealed that Gen Zs view P-Pop’s potential to become a global phenomenon positively. In addition, they find that social media presence is the most important factor for P-Pop to achieve such status. Furthermore, cultural representation and innovative elements were also viewed positively and important factors as well. With these findings, the researcher gave recommendations of potential strategies and insights for P-Pop industry stakeholders and future interested researchers.

This study investigates the perceptions of Filipino Generation Z in the Greater Manila Area regarding the potential of Philippine Pop (P-Pop) to become a global phenomenon. Using a quantitative-descriptive design, the researcher collected data from 385 respondents aged 18 to 26 through an online survey. The research specifically examined the awareness, attitudes, and influencing factors regarding P-Pop's international prospects.

The findings reveal that Gen Z holds a positive view of P-Pop’s potential for global recognition. While respondents reported higher familiarity with K-Pop than P-Pop, a significant relationship exists between social media activeness and genre familiarity. Increased social media use correlates with higher awareness, with Facebook and TikTok identified as the primary platforms for content consumption.

Regarding factors influencing global success, social media presence was ranked as the most important, followed by talented performers and catchy music. While respondents agreed that P-Pop can showcase Filipino culture, cultural representation and innovation were ranked lower in immediate importance compared to musical and social media factors. However, the perceived ability to achieve global recognition is significantly dependent on all identified factors, including cultural showcase, innovation, and representation. The study concludes that P-Pop has a strong foundation for success driven by social media engagement. Stakeholders are encouraged to prioritize social media presence and continue incorporating Filipino cultural aspects into their content.

The study specifically examines the level of awareness and familiarity Gen Z has with P-Pop, their attitudes toward its global potential, and the factors influencing these perceptions.

The research utilized a quantitative-descriptive design, collecting data from 385 Filipino Gen Z respondents aged 18 to 26 within the Greater Manila Area, including Metro Manila and the provinces of Bulacan, Cavite, Laguna, and Rizal. Data were gathered through an online survey via Google Forms, which included multiple-choice and Likert-scale questions. To ensure respondents were informed, the survey included viewing popular P-Pop music videos from groups such as SB19, BINI, and ALAMAT. Statistical analysis was performed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and standard deviation.

The findings reveal that Gen Zs in the Greater Manila Area hold a positive view of P-Pop’s potential to achieve global recognition. While many respondents considered themselves only "somewhat familiar" with P-Pop compared to their higher familiarity with K-Pop, a significant relationship was found between social media activeness and familiarity with the genre. Increased social media use correlates with higher awareness of P-Pop, with Facebook identified as the most frequently used platform for consuming content, followed by TikTok.

Regarding factors influencing global potential, social media presence was ranked as the most important factor, followed by talented performers and catchy music. While respondents agreed that P-Pop can effectively showcase and represent Filipino culture, cultural representation and innovation ranked lower in terms of immediate importance for achieving global recognition compared to musical and social media factors. However, the study confirmed that the perceived ability of P-Pop to achieve global recognition is significantly dependent on all identified factors, including cultural showcase, innovation, and representation.

The study concludes that P-Pop has a strong foundation for global success among Gen Z, largely driven by social media engagement. The researcher recommends that P-Pop stakeholders, including artists, management, and record labels, prioritize strengthening their social media presence. Additionally, while maintaining high standards for musicality and performance, stakeholders should continue to incorporate Filipino cultural aspects into their content. The researcher utilized a quantitative-descriptive research design, collecting data from 385 Filipino Gen Z respondents aged 18 to 26. To ensure representativeness and minimize bias, a random sampling procedure was employed with a 5% margin of error and a 95% confidence interval. Data were gathered through an online survey via Google Forms, which included multiple-choice and Likert-scale questions. To ensure respondents were properly informed before answering perception-based questions, the survey included the viewing of popular P-Pop music videos from groups such as SB19, BINI, and ALAMAT. Statistical analysis was performed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and standard deviation to test the study's hypotheses.

The findings reveal that Gen Zs in the Greater Manila Area hold a positive view of P-Pop’s potential to achieve global recognition and become a global phenomenon. While many respondents considered themselves only "somewhat familiar" with P-Pop compared to their higher familiarity with K-Pop, a significant relationship was found between social media activeness and familiarity with the genre. Specifically, increased social media use correlates with higher awareness of P-Pop. Facebook was identified as the most frequently used platform for consuming P-Pop content, followed by TikTok.

Regarding the factors influencing global potential, social media presence was ranked as the most important factor by respondents, followed by talented performers and catchy music. While cultural representation and innovation were viewed positively—with respondents agreeing that P-Pop can effectively showcase and represent Filipino culture—these elements ranked lower in terms of immediate importance for achieving global recognition compared to musical and social media factors. The study also confirmed that the perceived ability of P-Pop to achieve global recognition is significantly dependent on all identified factors, including cultural showcase, innovation, and representation.

The study concludes that P-Pop has a strong foundation for global success among the Gen Z demographic, largely driven by social media engagement. The research confirms that social media is the primary vehicle for familiarity and that the genre's ability to integrate cultural elements is viewed favorably, even if musicality and digital presence are prioritized by the youth.

Based on these results, the researcher recommends that P-Pop stakeholders, including artists, management, and record labels, prioritize strengthening their social media presence, as this is the most critical factor for Gen Z engagement. Additionally, while maintaining high standards for musicality and performance, stakeholders should continue to incorporate Filipino cultural aspects into their content, as these elements are viewed positively and contribute to the genre's unique identity. For future research, the author suggests utilizing shorter data collection timeframes to account for the rapid shifts in the fast-moving P-Pop industry.

title: Exploration of 3D Reconstruction Techniques for the UPOU FMDS’ Perma G.A.R.D.E.N.: Contributing to Its Digital Twin Development
abstract: This project aims to explore emerging 3D reconstruction techniques applied to the UPOU FMDS’ Perma G.A.R.D.E.N., in contribution to its digital twin development. The objectives include providing a simplified overview of how the explored 3D reconstruction methods work, testing these techniques to the garden, and assessing their output models in terms of visual accuracy and usability. The project also addresses and acknowledges various issues, explores an optimal methodology, and includes prototyping and recommendations to provide insights for future developers and researchers working on the garden’s digital twin. Among the three explored techniques—Photogrammetry, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and Gaussian Splatting—Gaussian Splatting was found to be the most suitable for the garden, based on visual accuracy and usability. The optimal methodology utilized the Nerfstudio framework with its “splatfacto” method, which is its Gaussian Splatting procedure. For prototyping, PlayCanvas was used with its support for editing and integrating Gaussian Splatting 3D models. Various issues were addressed and acknowledged during these phases. The insights from this project could benefit future developers and researchers involved in the garden’s digital twin project by demonstrating the differences between the 3D reconstruction methods and their application to the garden. The prototypes provided, which are available as open educational resources, could inspire the enhancement of the current digital twin of the garden, which is its 360-degree photobased Virtual Reality (VR) tour, by integrating walkability through a 3D model, thus increasing its immersive experience. The prototypes can be accessed through the following links: “perma-center” Prototype, “perma-right” Prototype, and “permabridge” Prototype.

half:
Joseph Isaiah M. Chan’s capstone project investigates 3D reconstruction technologies to create a digital twin of the UPOU FMDS Perma G.A.R.D.E.N. The study addresses the complexities of reconstructing environments with dense vegetation, aiming to advance beyond existing 360-degree photo-based VR tours. This research serves as a foundational exploration for the Immersive Spatial Technology and Reality (ISTAR) Labs, focusing on visual accuracy and usability in virtual modeling.

The researcher compared three non-contact techniques: Photogrammetry, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and Gaussian Splatting. After initial testing with an iPhone 11, an optimal methodology was developed using an Insta360 camera and the Nerfstudio framework. Due to hardware limitations, the researcher implemented data sectioning, splitting the 360-degree video into three segments: "perma-center," "perma-right," and "perma-bridge." Prototypes were developed using the PlayCanvas web-based gaming engine to test interactivity.

Findings showed that Photogrammetry produced distorted, "coral-like" meshes that failed to capture fine details. While NeRF and Gaussian Splatting both captured vegetation intricacies with high accuracy, NeRF required mesh conversion that compromised visual quality. Gaussian Splatting was identified as the most suitable technique because it maintained high accuracy and offered flexibility through the .ply format. The study concludes that Gaussian Splatting is the most effective method for this environment, providing functional prototypes that allow for immersive, first-person navigation.

The researcher employed a comparative methodology, testing three non-contact 3D reconstruction techniques: Photogrammetry, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and Gaussian Splatting. Initial testing utilized an iPhone 11 with Polycam and Luma AI. To address limitations in coverage and processing, an optimal methodology was developed using an Insta360 360-degree camera and the Nerfstudio framework (specifically the "splatfacto" method). Due to hardware limitations involving a 6GB GPU, the researcher implemented data sectioning, splitting the 360-degree video into three segments: "perma-center," "perma-right," and "perma-bridge." The models were prototyped using the PlayCanvas web-based gaming engine to test interactivity.

The findings indicate that Photogrammetry struggled with visual accuracy in the garden setting, producing distorted, "coral-like" meshes that failed to capture fine details of leaves and branches. While NeRF and Gaussian Splatting both demonstrated high visual accuracy and successfully captured vegetation intricacies, NeRF required conversion to a mesh for editability, which compromised visual quality. Gaussian Splatting was identified as the most suitable technique because it maintained high visual accuracy while offering flexibility through the .ply format, which is integrable into various web-based viewers. The optimal methodology improved scene coverage, though computational constraints required downscaling and sectioning, which slightly impacted the quality of distant vegetation.

The study concludes that Gaussian Splatting is the most effective technique for reconstructing the complex, vegetated environment of the Perma G.A.R.D.E.N. The research successfully demonstrated a workflow involving 360-degree data collection, the Nerfstudio framework, and PlayCanvas to produce functional prototypes allowing for first-person navigation. These prototypes serve as open educational resources that demonstrate how Gaussian Splatting can enhance current VR tours by adding walkability and immersion. Future research should utilize higher-performance hardware to avoid downscaling, explore drone-based data collection, and investigate the integration of metric/geographical accuracy (GIS) and real-time simulations.
two:
The capstone project titled "Exploration of 3D Reconstruction Techniques for the UPOU FMDS’ Perma G.A.R.D.E.N.: Contributing to Its Digital Twin Development" by Joseph Isaiah M. Chan investigates the application of emerging 3D reconstruction technologies to create a virtual representation of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) Faculty of Management and Development Studies (FMDS) Perma G.A.R.D.E.N.

The problem addressed in this study stems from the complexity of reconstructing environments with dense vegetation, such as the Perma G.A.R.D.E.N., which presents more significant challenges than simpler mechanical objects. While a 360-degree photo-based Virtual Reality (VR) tour of the garden already exists, the faculty aims to develop a more advanced digital twin. The researcher identifies a need to explore which 3D reconstruction methods can effectively capture the intricate details of the garden's flora to support this broader digital twin development plan.

The context of the research is situated within the UPOU FMDS’ initiative to foster sustainability and nutrition through the Perma G.A.R.D.E.N. project. As part of the establishment of the Immersive Spatial Technology and Reality (ISTAR) Labs, this project serves as a foundational exploration into spatial computation and immersive technologies. The study focuses specifically on the virtual modeling aspect of digital twins, excluding physical or data-flow modeling, and limits its assessment to visual accuracy and usability.

The methodology employed a comparative approach by testing three specific non-contact 3D reconstruction techniques: Photogrammetry, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and Gaussian Splatting. Initial testing was conducted using an iPhone 11 and mobile applications, specifically Polycam for photogrammetry and Luma AI for NeRF and Gaussian Splatting. The models were assessed based on perceptual visual accuracy and a usability framework focusing on editability and flexibility. Following the initial tests, an optimal methodology was developed to address limitations in coverage and processing. This involved using an Insta360 360-degree camera for better data collection and the Nerfstudio framework (specifically the "splatfacto" method) for processing. Due to hardware limitations (a 6GB GPU), the researcher implemented data sectioning, where the 360-degree video was split into three segments: "perma-center," "perma-right," and "perma-bridge." Finally, the models were prototyped using the PlayCanvas web-based gaming engine to test integration and interactivity.

The findings reveal that Photogrammetry, while highly editable, struggled with visual accuracy in the garden setting. It produced distorted meshes that failed to capture the fine details of leaves and branches, often resulting in a "coral-like" appearance. NeRF and Gaussian Splatting both demonstrated high visual accuracy and successfully captured the intricacies of the vegetation. However, NeRF required conversion to a mesh to be editable, which compromised its visual quality. Gaussian Splatting was identified as the most suitable technique because it maintained high visual accuracy while offering a degree of flexibility through the .ply format, which is integrable into various web-based viewers. The optimal methodology—using a 360-degree camera and the Nerfstudio framework—successfully improved scene coverage, though the final models required downscaling and sectioning due to computational constraints, which slightly impacted the quality of distant vegetation.

In conclusion, the study concludes that Gaussian Splatting is the most effective technique for reconstructing the complex, vegetated environment of the Perma G.A.R.D.E.N. for digital twin purposes. The research successfully demonstrated an optimal workflow involving 360-degree data collection, the Nerfstudio framework, and PlayCanvas for prototyping. While technical constraints like hardware limitations and the need for data downscaling were present, the project successfully produced functional prototypes that allow for first-person navigation.

The implications of this research are significant for the future development of the garden's digital twin. The prototypes serve as open educational resources that demonstrate how 3D Gaussian Splatting can enhance the current 360-degree VR tour by adding walkability and increased immersion. For future developers, the study provides a roadmap for handling complex organic scenes. The researcher recommends that future work utilize higher-performance hardware to avoid the need for downscaling and data sectioning, and suggests exploring drone-based data collection to improve coverage. Additionally, the study points toward the need for further research into integrating metric/geographical accuracy (GIS) and exploring advanced digital twin features like real-time replication and simulations.

title: Transforming Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Experiences: Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML) in Action
abstract: In the era of remote, modular, and self-paced digital learning, this study applies Mayer's 12 multimedia principles from Cognitive Theory on Multimedia Learning (CTML) into Open Educational Resources (OERs) for a specific Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) at the University of the Philippines Open University – Media and Information Literacy in Today’s World, which ran for 7 weeks (July 3 - August 22, 2023). The Multimedia OERs observed in the study include infographics, motion graphic videos, summary slides, and a Google Sites course package. Aligning pedagogical strategies with multimedia design principles, this research investigates integration's impact on learning experiences and cognitive load management. Methodologically, it involves qualitative and quantitative analyses of data from 766 survey respondents out of 2986 enrollees. Findings reveal 100% achievement of learning outcomes, full and partial support for multimedia principles, reduced cognitive load in comprehending complex lessons, and a rich and interactive media learning experience for participants. It also explored a multitude of benefits and a few challenges in implementing Multimedia OERs in MOOCs from the learners’ perspectives. The study contributes to the growing literature on multimedia learning, MOOCs, and OERs, and offers practical insights for digital education stakeholders (e.g., instructional designers, multimedia practitioners, course coordinators, course enrollees, and distance learning institutions).

half:
Mickey Angel T. Cortez’s study, "Transforming Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Experiences: Mayer’s CTML in Action," investigates the application of Richard Mayer’s Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML) within Open Educational Resources (OERs) for a specific MOOC at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The research addresses challenges in modular distance learning in the Philippines, where text-based modules often cause reading comprehension struggles and cognitive overload. The author seeks to determine how applying multimedia design principles can optimize learning outcomes and manage cognitive load in a MOOC context.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher developed multimedia OERs—including infographics, motion graphic videos, summary slides, and a Google Sites course package—all designed using CTML principles. Data were collected from 766 survey respondents out of 2,986 total enrollees through pre-tests, post-tests, self-reported cognitive load scales, and survey instruments.

The findings indicate a 100% achievement rate of the course's learning outcomes. The results showed full and partial support for the application of multimedia principles across the materials, revealing that integrating these principles helped reduce the cognitive load required to comprehend complex lessons. The multimedia OERs provided a rich and interactive media learning experience, with benefits including increased motivation and visual appeal. The study concludes that anchoring the design of multimedia OERs in Mayer’s CTML is an effective strategy for enhancing MOOC quality and facilitating better comprehension.

title: SEA: A Game-Based Approach in Promoting Southeast Asian Cultural Awareness Through Southeast Asian Folktales
abstract: As stated in the Socio-Cultural pillar of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the regional organization aims to promote and foster a regional identity that acknowledges the cultural heritage of the Southeast Asian people and the importance of the region. A regional Southeast Asian identity is essential for the member states and their people because it offers a non-nation-centric perspective on Southeast Asian decolonization. It fosters a stronger form of regional solidarity, benefiting member states’ developing economies through reduced conflicts, increased social acceptance for people's mobility, and enhanced information sharing and exchange (Fabrian, 2016; Noor, 2020; Prana, 2017). As mentioned by ASEAN (2020), Farid (2020), and Fabrian (2016), one avenue that can help foster this identity is through cultural awareness facilitated by the creative and digital media. In this special project, the researcher developed SEA, a digital media designed to promote cultural awareness by creating mini-games based on Southeast Asian folktales. The methodological framework Agile-Extreme Programming was used in developing the video game because it allows for continuous testing and iteration. Based on the user feedback survey, it was found that SEA is an effective platform enabling users to enhance their awareness and knowledge of the diverse cultures across Southeast Asia.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Joshua Albert C. Dema-ala’s project, "SEA: A Game-Based Approach in Promoting Southeast Asian Cultural Awareness Through Southeast Asian Folktales," investigates how digital media can foster regional identity and mitigate the nation-centric perspectives caused by colonial-era borders. Such fractured identities can lead to cultural disputes and hinder regional economic prosperity. The study aims to use video games as a creative medium to promote cultural awareness and regional solidarity, aligning with the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Blueprint's goal of building a common identity.

Using the Agile-Extreme Programming framework, the researcher developed the project through planning, designing, coding, and testing stages. The project features four folktales: "The Legend of Krai Thong" (Thailand), "The Legend of the Rice Cake: Bánh Chưng and Bánh Giầy" (Vietnam), "The Golden Cucumber - Timun Mas" (Indonesia), and "How the Tinguian Learned to Plant" (Philippines). The resulting pixel-art game, titled "SEA," utilizes various mechanics including foraging adventures, a boss battle, and a 2D platformer-style chasing mechanic.

User feedback surveys indicated that the SEA platform is an effective tool for enhancing users' awareness and knowledge of diverse Southeast Asian cultures. The study concludes that video games are effective educational tools that transform traditional folktales into interactive experiences. This approach demonstrates that digital media can serve as a bridge for regional solidarity and provides a model for representing indigenous cultures in digital products.

two:
The special project titled "SEA: A Game-Based Approach in Promoting Southeast Asian Cultural Awareness Through Southeast Asian Folktales" by Joshua Albert C. Dema-ala explores the intersection of digital media and regional identity. The work addresses the need for a cohesive Southeast Asian identity as part of the ASEAN Socio-Cultural pillar, which aims to foster regional solidarity and social development.

The problem addressed by the researcher is the prevalence of nation-centric perspectives in the decolonization movements of Southeast Asian states. Because modern borders were often drawn by colonial powers, focusing solely on national history can lead to a narrow view of the region's shared heritage. This narrowness can exacerbate cultural ownership disputes and territorial conflicts between member states. Furthermore, the researcher notes that such fractured identities can hinder regional economic prosperity by limiting social acceptance and information exchange. The study seeks to answer how a creative medium, specifically a video game, can be utilized to promote cultural awareness among Southeast Asians.

The context of the study is rooted in the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Blueprint, which emphasizes building a "caring and sharing society" through a common identity. The researcher posits that cultural awareness—understanding the shared traditions, beliefs, and histories of neighboring states—is a key driver for regional unity. By utilizing digital and creative industries, such as video games, the researcher aims to provide a platform where players can discover the cultural relatedness of the region.

The methodology employed for this project was the Agile-Extreme Programming framework. This software development approach was chosen because it allows for continuous testing and iteration, which is essential for refining gameplay mechanics and narrative flow. The development process was divided into four stages: planning, designing, coding, and testing. During planning, the researcher selected four folktales: two from Mainland Southeast Asia ("The Legend of Krai Thong" from Thailand and "The Legend of the Rice Cake: Bánh Chưng and Bánh Giầy" from Vietnam) and two from Maritime Southeast Asia ("The Golden Cucumber - Timun Mas" from Indonesia and "How the Tinguian Learned to Plant" from the Philippines). The design stage involved creating storyboards, collecting cultural references, and designing pixel art using Aseprite. The coding stage utilized the Godot engine and the GDScript language, incorporating Black-box testing to ensure functionality. Finally, the testing stage involved collecting user feedback through statement-based assessments and rating scale surveys.

The findings of the project are presented through the description of the developed game, "SEA." The game is a pixel-art digital product featuring four distinct mini-games, each utilizing different gameplay genres to match their respective stories. For example, "The Legend of the Rice Cake" and "How the Tinguian Learned to Plant" utilize foraging adventure mechanics with open-world maps, while "The Legend of Krai Thong" features a boss battle mechanic, and "The Golden Cucumber" utilizes a 2D platformer-style chasing mechanic. The game includes narrative-dialogue pages that combine storytelling with visual art to immerse the player. The researcher also applied ten Heuristic Principles to the user interface to ensure usability, such as visibility of system status, user control, and aesthetic and minimalist design. The results of the user feedback surveys indicated that the SEA platform is an effective tool for enhancing users' awareness and knowledge of the diverse cultures across Southeast Asia.

The study concludes that video games are effective educational tools capable of promoting cultural awareness. By transforming traditional folktales into interactive experiences, the game "SEA" successfully provides a space for players to engage with the diverse yet interconnected cultures of the region. The project demonstrates that digital media can serve as a bridge for regional solidarity, moving beyond narrow nationalistic views to embrace a broader Southeast Asian identity.

The implications of this research are significant for both the creative industry and regional social policy. For game developers and creatives, the project serves as a model for how indigenous and local cultures can be represented accurately and engagingly in digital products. For the ASEAN community, the project suggests that creative industries can be a powerful instrument for achieving the goals of the Socio-Cultural pillar. By fostering a sense of shared heritage through popular culture, digital media can help mitigate regional conflicts and promote the social and economic integration of Southeast Asian nations.

title: #MOOTOO: An Exploratory Study on Mamamoo as Purveyor of Feminism Ideals
abstract: Feminism has been a polarizing topic for many years and decades, challenging the norms of how women should follow in accord breaking the barrier for people who are marginalized due to their gender and sexuality. At the same time, music artists have been creating subtle messages for listeners and audiences to catch onto their hidden advocacies that can help either empower said listeners and audiences or be taken aback by their music or performances. This is no different with K-pop idols, where some write their songs and insert themes that either divide audiences or unite them due to messages inserted, like environmental issues, feminism, and mental health. One of the well-known K-pop girl groups that have been outspoken in advocacy for feminism has been MAMAMOO. Based on the findings, MAMAMOO does have an influence on how feminism has been perceived by fans, creating a platform that can help avid and other casual listeners to identify female empowerment and be influenced by the girl group. However, it should be noted that not all feminist issues were tackled by MAMAMOO, leaving room for more before fully calling them a feminist girl group.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:

title: Project TALA: A Virtual Exhibit Prototype Celebrating P-Pop, Philippine History and Culture, and Historical and Cultural Advocacy in Web Virtual Reality (VR)
abstract:
There is an urgent need to address the decline in interest and deterioration of Philippine arts and culture, especially indigenous and traditional arts and culture. When encouraged and motivated to engage with Philippine arts, culture, and history, the youth can become potential contributors to the promotion, appreciation, and preservation of culture.

Edutainment is the main theoretical basis of the study, wherein: 1) ALAMAT, a Philippine pop boy group with the concept of “combining both traditional and modern Philippine cultural elements with Western/global influences in the various facets of their music, including dance, fashion, and iconography”, can be considered as using edutainment as they foster cultural awareness and education through their concept and revelations of which elements/references they’ve used as well as a certain amount of educational content; 2) virtual exhibits use edutainment for visitors or users comprehend info better with interactive features; and 3) a combination of the two, wherein a virtual exhibit can be created to present ALAMAT’s concept of promoting Philippine culture, the Philippine elements/references they’ve used, and the significance of their concept in relation to education on Philippine arts, culture, and history.

This practice-based Special Project aims to explore the possibility of creating a virtual exhibit using A-frame, Glitch, and Blender, which will present ALAMAT’s concept, discuss their concept by presenting Philippine historical and cultural elements/references they’ve used for select music videos (namely, “kbye”, “Maharani”, and “Dagundong”), and demonstrate the significance of such a concept especially in relation to cultural awareness and education, with the position that ALAMAT and their concept may contribute to the education on Philippine arts, culture, and history with the youth as the target audience.

The study concludes that creating a virtual exhibit is feasible, though improvements are necessary, such as enhancing accessibility, refining 3D models, and incorporating more interactive features to boost educational and immersive qualities. This project serves as a foundation for future research on the potential of edutainment in virtual exhibits to promote the education of Philippine arts, culture, and history.
