title: Cop or Drop: An Analysis of the Influence of Social Media Marketing on Sneakerheads’ Attitudes and Perceptions among Resellers and Consumers of Rhand Rhelle
abstract: The rise of e-commerce became a promising phenomenon that gave opportunity among numerous sneaker business owners, especially in social media. However, regardless of the rapid growth of the shoe market, there are limited studies illustrating consumer behavior, especially among sneakerheads. Therefore, the researcher was driven to analyze how social media marketing influences the attitudes and perceptions of sneakerheads. In addition, the study attempted to modify the research objectives of Gibson's (2018) study to be more suitable in the context of the sneaker market. Thus, the researcher utilized a quantitative-descriptive research design to suffice the mentioned objectives. In addition, the researcher surveyed 120 consumers of Rhand Rhelle, a sneaker store in Metro Manila. Then, the gathered data were further analyzed through descriptive statistics and presented with tables and figures. Finally, the findings revealed that sneakerheads have a positive attitude towards social media, considering their patronage and engagement on it. In addition, sneakerheads perceive social media marketing as an important tool to acquire customer loyalty, increased profits, and widen audience reach. However, sneaker stores shall consider the type of content they post as it was the most important factor perceived by the respondents that are significant for businesses like them. Further, the researcher concluded that social media marketing can influence the attitudes and perceptions of sneakerheads. With this being the case, the researcher gave recommendations that can be utilized by sneaker business owners as a compass for potential strategies and programs.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This research addresses the limited literature regarding consumer behavior within the sneaker market, specifically concerning the attitudes and perceptions of sneakerheads. The study seeks to bridge the gap in understanding how social media marketing influences purchase decisions, brand loyalty, and interaction with businesses. The investigation is situated within the sneaker community in the Philippines, focusing on Rhand Rhelle, a sneaker and hype streetwear store in Quezon City, Metro Manila. The research is grounded in Marshall McLuhan’s Media Theory to investigate how communication via social media impacts the relationship between the business and its consumers.

Using a quantitative-descriptive research design, the researcher employed a random sampling technique to select 120 respondents, consisting of resellers and consumers of Rhand Rhelle. Participants were required to be adults aged 18 to 64, possess a social media account, be aware of the store's social media presence, and have previously purchased products or services from the store. Data were collected through an online survey and analyzed using descriptive statistics.

The findings reveal that sneakerheads maintain a positive attitude toward social media and engage with it frequently. Most respondents engage as sneaker enthusiasts at least three times a week, and more than half spend between 30 minutes to an hour daily browsing sneaker-related posts. Facebook and Instagram were identified as the most utilized platforms for buying and selling sneakers. Regarding marketing effectiveness, 81.7% of respondents believe that the social media marketing of an online sneaker store affects their purchase behavior. Sneakerheads perceive social media marketing as a vital tool for achieving increased profits, building customer loyalty, and widening audience reach. Respondents highlighted the type of content posted and consistency of posts as the most important factors for a business using social media.

The researcher concluded that social media marketing significantly influences the attitudes and perceptions of sneakerheads, demonstrating that social media is an effective medium for reaching the target audience and fostering engagement. The study implies that businesses should prioritize the quality and type of content they post to maintain engagement and that integrating social media is essential for improving customer interaction, loyalty, and profit. The results can be used by marketers to modify strategies to better suit the demographic profile of sneakerheads.

title: Feminism in Photography
abstract:
Feminism has challenged beliefs where there are prevailing inequalities between men and women. In Saudi Arabia, where women are considered secondclass citizens, photography is an explorable field when it comes to representation of both sexes. This study sought to determine the profile of the Filipino photographers professionally practicing photography in Riyadh along gender, age, highest educational attainment, and schools/institution where trainings are acquired; examine the gap between the percentage of female and male photographer-respondents based on gender; analyze the significance of gender in the enthusiasm of the respondents; identify the factors that affect the level of engagement in photography of the female and male photographers in Riyadh; and propose recommendations to enhance the integration of principles of feminism in photography. Findings show that 70. 83% of the respondents were female photographers. It was also found that 58.33 % of the respondents were 18-34 years old, 87.5% attained tertiary education and 33.3% acquired trainings in photography in COMSOFIL.

Findings show that there is a huge gap of 41.67% between the female and male photographers. Respondents also agree on the perceived significance of gender in the practice of photography with a grand mean of 3.27. It only implies that the respondents recognize the roles and relevance of gender in their engagement in photography. A grand mean of 3.55 shows that the respondents agreed on the factors that affect the level of engagement in photography. With the foregoing findings, it was concluded that the profile of the respondents is varied, more females are involved in photography, gender is significant in the practice of photography. The level of engagement in photography is affected by several factors and gender representation, fresh perspective in their approach to a specific theme, collaboration with peers and clients, familiarity of context, marketing and networking themselves to increase income, and learning new techniques are ways to enhance their level of engagement in photography.

The study is motivated by the researcher's observations of gender disparities in multimedia fields and the unique socio-cultural landscape of Saudi Arabia, where traditional gender roles and legal guardianship systems have historically impacted women's professional freedoms and social visibility.

Specifically, the study aims to determine the demographic profile of Filipino photographers, examine the gap between male and female participation, analyze the perceived significance of gender in photographic practice, and identify the factors that drive engagement in the profession.

The quantitative component utilized a descriptive method to analyze the professional profiles and participation gaps through survey questionnaires administered via Google Forms. The qualitative component involved unstructured interviews to explore the respondents' perceptions regarding the significance of gender in their enthusiasm for photography. The study utilized purposive sampling to select twenty-four event photographers in Riyadh who were graduates of various photography training institutions between 2018 and 2019. Data analysis involved the use of percentage methods for demographic data, weighted means for measuring agreement levels, and qualitative synthesis for interview responses and recommendations.

The findings reveal that the respondent group is predominantly female, accounting for 70.83% of the participants, while males make up 29.16%. This results in a significant gap of 41.67% between the two genders, suggesting that female photographers in this specific locale have a higher participation rate in photographic events. The demographic profile shows that the majority of respondents are young adults (58.33% aged 18-34), have attained tertiary education (87.5%), and received a significant portion of their training (33.3%) from COMSOFIL.

The highest level of agreement was found in the observation that gender influences the interest levels of participants (mean of 4.00), whereas the lowest agreement was found in the idea that gender affects productivity levels (mean of 3.05). It concludes that gender is indeed significant in the practice of photography, particularly in shaping the specific interests and genres that photographers pursue. Additionally, the research concludes that engagement in the field is heavily driven by intrinsic motivations (passion and aesthetics) and extrinsic necessities (financial purposes).

title: An Empirical Study Evaluating the Effects of Gamification in an E-learning Environment
abstract: The University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) is a fully online university that uses open and e-distance learning (ODeL) methods of teaching through the use of a learning management system (LMS) called Moodle, which is considered their virtual classroom. In an ODeL system, students are expected to study independently without meeting with their fellow students and instructors face-to-face. It is said that motivation is the main factor in a student’s learning, especially in a distance learning environment. However, distance learners tend to feel easily demotivated, distracted, and isolated as compared to students in a traditional learning environment (Manlapaz, 2020). This can often lead to lower performance and higher dropout rates. To make distance learners feel more motivated, many institutions have proposed the use of gamification as a way to motivate the students to be more engaged in class and improve their grade performance. In this study, the researcher aims to assess the effects of gamification on undergraduate UPOU students and to see if gamification is a factor that helps improve student performance. The results show that gamification has several positive effects on students in UPOU. There is also a significant difference between the performance and engagement of students in a gamified course compared to a non-gamified course.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
April Felicia C. Fojas conducted an empirical study at the University of the Philippines Open University to evaluate how gamification impacts undergraduate students in e-learning environments. Addressing high dropout rates and isolation in distance learning, the research assessed whether integrating game elements into the Moodle platform improves engagement, psychological well-being, and academic performance. The study utilized a quasi-experimental design, comparing a gamified batch of Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies students against two preceding non-gamified batches. The gamified environment featured twelve badges, a leaderboard, and automatic feedback systems, which served as motivational tools without affecting final grades.

Findings indicated predominantly positive effects. Survey results from 41 students revealed that 66% felt game elements fueled their interest to work harder, while 76% agreed gamification motivated better study habits and increased forum participation. Psychologically, 62% reported increased feelings of belonging that reduced loneliness and stress, and 61% felt their sense of competence and retention improved. Academic data corroborated these self-reports; the gamified batch achieved a General Weighted Average of 86.97, significantly higher than the 65.91 and 75.27 recorded by previous non-gamified batches. Furthermore, 100% of gamified students participated in all discussion forums, compared to low participation in non-gamified groups.

However, negative effects were noted. Twenty-three percent of respondents reported increased anxiety due to competitiveness, with some focusing on collecting rewards rather than learning. Working students occasionally felt pressured by competitive elements. The study concludes that gamification effectively enhances motivation and grades by addressing psychological needs. However, it recommends user-centered design to tailor elements to diverse student needs, warning against a one-size-fits-all approach that may cause anxiety in certain groups.

The research addresses the high dropout rates and low motivation prevalent in distance learning, where students often experience isolation and lack face-to-face interaction. The primary objective was to assess how integrating game elements into the Moodle learning management system influences student engagement, psychological well-being, cognitive performance, and academic grades. The study posits that gamification can serve as an effective tool for improving student performance compared to non-gamified courses by addressing the psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness as defined by Self-Determination Theory.

The methodology focused on a single core course within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program. Due to platform constraints, all students in the batch participated in the gamified version, preventing a traditional control group. Instead, the study employed a quasi-experimental design by comparing the gamified batch’s performance against the mean grades of the two preceding non-gamified batches, which shared the same faculty and course content. The gamification mechanics included twelve distinct badges for completing units, quizzes, and forums, a leaderboard for top scorers, and an automatic feedback system providing encouraging prompts based on exam grades. These elements did not contribute to final grades but served purely as motivational tools. Data collection involved online surveys from 41 consenting students and an analysis of academic records and forum activity.

Findings indicated predominantly positive effects. Survey results showed that 66% of respondents agreed game elements fueled their interest to complete tasks and work harder. Psychologically, 62% reported increased feelings of belonging and connection, which reduced loneliness, stress, anxiety, and boredom. Cognitively, 61% felt the elements enhanced their sense of competence and aided long-term retention of lessons. Additionally, 76% agreed that gamification motivated better study habits, such as studying harder for exams and participating more in discussion forums to earn stars.

Academic performance data corroborated these self-reported findings. The gamified batch achieved a General Weighted Average of 86.97, significantly higher than the 65.91 and 75.27 recorded by the previous non-gamified batches. Engagement in discussion forums was also markedly higher; while participation was low in non-gamified batches, 100% of students in the gamified batch participated in all forums, attributed to the stars awarded for posts and the competitive leaderboard.

However, the study identified negative effects. While most disagreed that gamification caused negative emotions, 23% of respondents agreed it did, primarily due to competitiveness. Some students reported increased anxiety and a focus on collecting rewards rather than learning the material. Qualitative comments revealed that working students sometimes felt pressured by competitive elements or found the gamification minimal compared to their other responsibilities.

The study concludes that gamification is an effective strategy for enhancing motivation, engagement, and academic performance in e-learning. It successfully addressed psychological needs, leading to improved study habits and higher grades. The implications suggest that educational institutions should integrate gamification to combat dropout rates and isolation. However, the researcher recommends using user-centered design to tailor game elements to diverse student needs, as a one-size-fits-all approach may not suit all learners. Future implementations could incorporate narrative-based fantasy or storytelling to further enhance engagement, while educators must remain mindful of the potential for excessive competitiveness to cause anxiety among certain student groups.

title: Creation of Augmented Reality Version of Neat Space’s Products
abstract: This project is a collaboration with Neat Space, an online furniture shop established in mid-2020. Their store is well-known for selling storage solutions such as floating shelves, racks, and rolling carts. Their chosen products, which include the "Heiho shelf set," the "Ozukai floating shelf," and the "Nordic Cube Rack," will be converted into 3-D models that can be viewed using Adobe Aero application. This project aims to develop an Augmented Reality prototype for an existing online store and test it with the store's potential market. The researcher hopes to learn about the impact on potential customers if they will be able to visualize products from online stores like Neat Space not only through images but also through augmented reality.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Trisha Joie D. Lucero’s research, "Creation of Augmented Reality Version of Neat Space’s Products," addresses the limitations of traditional 2D online furniture shopping, where static images make it difficult for consumers to visualize how products like shelves and racks fit in their personal spaces. This lack of visualization can lead to uncertainty regarding size, color, and suitability, impacting purchasing decisions.

The researcher utilized a two-phase methodology. First, prototype development involved converting draft sketches of Neat Space products into 3D images using Adobe Dimension. These models were integrated into the Adobe Aero application using an "image anchor" feature, allowing users to view 3D models in their real-time surroundings by scanning specific QR codes. In the second phase, eight participants tested the AR versions of the "Nordic Cube Rack," "Heiho Shelf Set," and "Oxlai Floating Shelf Set" via the Adobe Aero app.

Findings revealed that all participants were interested in the technology and found the AR versions helpful for visualizing products in their own spaces. While some users encountered minor difficulties, such as needing stable surfaces or locating QR codes, the technology was viewed as an effective way to understand product dimensions and appearance. All participants agreed that AR is beneficial for online shopping and would assist in future purchases. The study concludes that AR prototypes are a viable way to enhance the online shopping experience, increasing consumer confidence and bridging the gap between digital browsing and physical interaction.

The research project titled "Creation of Augmented Reality Version of Neat Space’s Products" by Trisha Joie D. Lucero addresses the challenges faced by online furniture retailers in providing immersive shopping experiences. Specifically, the study focuses on Neat Space, a brand selling storage solutions such as shelves and racks. The problem identified is that traditional online shopping relies on 2D images, which may not adequately help consumers visualize how products will look and fit within their personal spaces. This lack of visualization can lead to uncertainty regarding product size, color, and suitability, potentially impacting consumer confidence and purchasing decisions.

The context of the study is shaped by the rapid advancement of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and the shift in consumer behavior caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic forced a transition toward online shopping, increasing the demand for digital tools that can bridge the gap between physical and digital retail. The researcher notes that Augmented Reality (AR) has become a significant technology in various fields, including education and medicine, and is increasingly being used in e-commerce to allow users to interact with products in their own environments via mobile devices.

The methodology employed a two-phase approach. Phase 1 involved prototype development, where the researcher used draft sketches of Neat Space products and converted them into 3D images using Adobe Dimension. These 3D models were then integrated into the Adobe Aero application using the "image anchor" feature. This allowed the products to be anchored to specific QR codes, enabling users to view the 3D models in their real-time surroundings. Phase 2 consisted of an initial evaluation phase. Eight participants, selected from various e-commerce platforms and social media, were recruited to test the AR prototypes. The participants first completed an online survey guide and were then instructed to use the Adobe Aero app to scan QR codes on product listings (such as those on Shopee) to view the AR versions of the "Nordic Cube Rack," "Heiho Shelf Set," and "Oxlai Floating Shelf Set."

The findings from the study revealed several key insights. General observations showed that all eight participants were interested in the technology, with five out of eight being between the ages of 19 and 25. All participants had experience with online shopping, and five out of eight noted that this was their first time using AR technology. Regarding the experience, participants found the AR versions helpful for visualizing products in their own spaces. While some participants faced difficulties—such as needing a stable surface to anchor the AR model or struggling to find the correct QR code—the technology was generally viewed as a way to better understand product dimensions and appearance.

In terms of consumer behavior, all participants agreed that AR technology is beneficial for online shopping and believed it would help them in future purchases. The results indicated that the AR experience was considered excellent by the participants. Furthermore, the study found that users were highly likely to shop at an online store that offers AR versions of its products.

The study concludes that developing AR prototypes for Neat Space products is a viable and effective way to enhance the online shopping experience. The technology allows consumers to visualize furniture in terms of color, size, and arrangement within their own homes, which can increase consumer confidence and interest. The researcher suggests that if e-commerce companies invest in AR technology, they can provide significant benefits to their customers and potentially increase sales.

The implications of this research suggest that integrating AR into e-commerce platforms can bridge the gap between digital browsing and physical product interaction. For businesses, adopting AR can serve as a competitive advantage and a tool to reduce consumer uncertainty. For consumers, it provides a more interactive and informative shopping journey. However, the study notes several limitations, such as the reliance on the Adobe Aero app and the use of the "image anchor" feature. The researcher suggests that further research could explore more advanced AR technologies that do not require QR codes, as well as developing more stable and high-quality 3D models to improve the overall user experience.

title: Ivatan Memories: A Collection of Historical Photos of Batanes
abstract: This report lays out in detail the making and analysis of Ivatan Memories. Ivatan Memories is a project that aims to collect and showcase old photographs of Batanes in an accessible and user-friendly website. Its intention is to serve as a digital manifestation of the bigger goal of preserving history. As important visual evidence of history, the exhibition of the collection provides old photographs a dedicated space in the virtual world that exceeds its physical counterpart in terms of accessibility and preservation. Major points of interest in this project is the process of collection of old photographs from varied sources, collaboration and crowdsourcing through social media, research involving indigenous groups, and the creation of a website aimed for public viewing at low to zero cost.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Kristelle Joyce G. Adami’s project, "Ivatan Memories: A Collection of Historical Photos of Batanes," aims to preserve the cultural and historical heritage of the Ivatan people. The author identifies a gap where modern travel photography overshadows historical visual evidence, and notes that analog photographs are at risk of deterioration. Furthermore, much historical documentation remains inaccessible to the local community because it is held in institutional archives or by outside researchers.

To address this, the author employed digital curation and crowdsourcing, collecting photographs from social media, local institutions like the Batanes Provincial Library, and online archives such as the US National Archives. Using graphic design, photo editing, and web development skills, the author created a WordPress website featuring a "gallery wall" aesthetic. The project successfully gathered 156 photographs, with 99 selected for display, spanning the years 1907 to 1998. These images are organized into 11 collections categorized by location or landmark.

A survey of 21 Ivatan respondents showed highly positive results; participants rated the importance of preserving these photographs as "very important" and the website's effectiveness as "excellent" or "fairly well." Despite challenges like low bandwidth and COVID-19 restrictions, the project met its objectives by creating an accessible, no-cost online gallery. The work demonstrates how web media can protect the cultural identity of small indigenous populations and serves as a model for creating digital archives for communities lacking extensive physical archives.

title: Exploring Indigenous Igorot Culture in Virtual Reality
abstract:
This practice-based research project explores the possibility and benefits of using virtual reality as a multimedia tool in cultural heritage education particularly that of indigenous Igorot culture. It aims to encourage appreciation of indigenous Igorot culture through immersive and interactive means in light of growing innovations in technology and the digitally evolving mindset of the 21st century person. 

The challenge lies on how to effectively interpret tangible and intangible aspects of Igorot culture in the virtual world and entice its users to interact and learn through virtual exploration. 3D modeling, sounds, video and imagery, application of simple gamification techniques, and interactivity were used such that the ensuing product serves as an immersive snapshot of a period in time in the mountains of the Cordilleras.

The project reveals that in terms of showcasing cultural practices, context is very important such that the viewer needs to be placed in a position wherein he or she will be able to understand why these practices are done and why they are important. Further, in using virtual reality, it is important to note that different intricacies of culture can be explored simultaneously and that implementing a linear approach towards cultural heritage education within the medium means not utilizing the medium to its fullest potential. It also tackles the importance of making virtual reality products that are easy to use with little to no learning curve in order to maximize their effectivity.

Ultimately, this project aims to contribute its learnings and become a use case for virtual reality in the context of indigenous Igorot culture. It hopes to inspire and motivate the creation of more similar products to help the Igorot identity thrive in modern generations.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Maria Nenita Victoria E. Chaluyan’s research, "Exploring Indigenous Igorot Culture in Virtual Reality," addresses the disappearance of Igorot cultural knowledge in the Cordillera region caused by the passing of elders and increasing diaspora. To combat this loss and bridge the digital divide among younger generations, the study explores using a virtual reality (VR) prototype to recreate Igorot practices for both Igorot and non-Igorot audiences.

Using a practice-based research methodology, the author developed a VR prototype via Amazon Sumerian, a browser-based platform chosen for its accessibility. The prototype incorporates 1900s Cordillera imagery, 3D models of artifacts like the *Bale* and *payew*, and ambient sounds to enhance immersion. Testing with friends and family showed that the prototype successfully increased curiosity and engagement, with users describing the experience as "amazing" and "beautiful." However, feedback was mixed regarding cultural depth; some users felt fear during ritualistic elements, others faced mobile playability issues, and many desired more interactivity and interior exploration.

The study concludes that VR is a viable medium for cultural heritage education, provided it offers sufficient narrative context to prevent superficial curiosity. Technical usability and navigation are critical for maintaining engagement. Future development should focus on non-linear exploration and structured storylines. Finally, the research highlights ethical considerations in digital ethnography, specifically regarding factual truthfulness and the appropriate use of gamification when presenting sacred traditions.

Maria Nenita Victoria E. Chaluyan’s research, "Exploring Indigenous Igorot Culture in Virtual Reality," addresses the rapid disappearance of Igorot cultural knowledge in the Cordillera region. As elders pass away and the diaspora increases, traditional rituals and material culture are being lost. This issue is compounded by a digital divide, where younger generations are often more engaged with digital entertainment than their own heritage. The study explores how a virtual reality (VR) prototype can recreate Igorot practices to encourage cultural appreciation among both Igorot and non-Igorot audiences.

The author utilized a practice-based research methodology to design and develop a VR prototype using Amazon Sumerian, a browser-based platform chosen for its accessibility on laptops, mobile phones, and headsets. The development process involved researching 1900s Cordillera imagery, prototyping a layout based on the author's memories of Barlig, Mountain Province, and implementing 3D models of artifacts such as the *Bale* (traditional house), *payew* (rice paddies), and ritual objects like the *Bangkilay*. Ambient sounds were also included to increase immersion. The prototype was tested with a group of friends and family to measure curiosity, engagement, and cultural interest.

The findings demonstrate that the VR prototype successfully increased curiosity and engagement among participants, including a child in the U.S. and an adult in Australia. While users described the experience as "amazing" and "beautiful," feedback was mixed regarding the depth of cultural curiosity. Some users experienced fear during ritualistic elements, and others encountered playability issues on mobile devices. Participants also expressed a desire for more depth, such as the ability to explore building interiors and interact with more objects.

The study concludes that VR is a viable medium for cultural heritage education, especially through accessible browser-based applications. However, the author notes that to teach intangible culture effectively, VR must provide sufficient context or a narrative "jump-off point" to prevent curiosity from remaining superficial. Technical usability, such as navigation and load times, is also critical to maintaining user engagement.

The research suggests that future developers should move toward non-linear, simultaneous exploration and incorporate structured storylines to allow users to become active participants. Finally, the project raises ethical considerations for digital ethnography, specifically regarding the standards for replicating indigenous culture, the necessity of factual truthfulness, and the appropriate use of gamification when presenting sacred or sensitive traditions. The work serves as a case study for using immersive digital archives to help indigenous identities thrive in a technological age.

The research project titled "Exploring Indigenous Igorot Culture in Virtual Reality" by Maria Nenita Victoria E. Chaluyan addresses the rapid loss of indigenous Igorot cultural knowledge within the Cordillera region. The author identifies a significant problem: as elders pass away and the diaspora of Igorot people increases, traditional practices, rituals, and material culture are vanishing. This loss is exacerbated by a digital divide where younger generations, often raised in urban or international environments, are more familiar with digital entertainment than their own heritage. While academic and community efforts exist to preserve this culture, there is a notable lack of interactive, immersive multimedia content that utilizes modern technology to engage the "digital native" generation.

The central research question asks how a virtual reality (VR) prototype can be used to recreate Igorot practices to encourage appreciation of Cordilleran cultural heritage among friends and family. The author seeks to demonstrate that VR can serve as a powerful tool for sharing knowledge and fostering identity among both Igorots and non-Igorots.

The methodology employed is a practice-based research approach involving the design and development of a VR prototype. The author utilized Amazon Sumerian, a browser-based VR platform, to ensure accessibility across various devices like laptops, mobile phones, and VR headsets. The design process followed several stages: pre-production, which included researching 1900s Cordillera imagery and traditional practices; prototyping, which involved creating a layout based on the author's memory of Barlig, Mountain Province; and implementation, which utilized 3D modeling tools like Thimble Sketchup to create artifacts such as the *Bale* (traditional house), *payew* (rice paddies), and various ritual objects like the *Bangkilay*. The author also incorporated ambient sounds of flowing water and birds to enhance immersion. To test the effectiveness of the tool, the prototype was shared with a group of "test subjects" (family and friends) who provided feedback based on questions regarding curiosity, engagement, and cultural interest.

The findings indicate that the VR prototype successfully piqued the curiosity and engagement of the test subjects. Participants described the experience using terms like "amazing" and "beautiful," with some comparing the visual style to the game *Minecraft*. The tool proved effective in engaging users across different demographics, including a 7-year-old living in the U.S. and an adult living in Australia. However, the results were mixed regarding the depth of cultural curiosity; some users experienced fear during ritualistic elements, and others faced playability issues on mobile devices. The feedback also revealed a desire for more depth, with users expressing interest in exploring the interiors of buildings and encountering more interactive objects.

The project concludes that virtual reality is a viable and effective medium for cultural heritage education, particularly through browser-based applications that do not require expensive hardware. The author emphasizes that for VR to be truly effective in teaching intangible culture (such as rituals), it must provide sufficient context. Without a narrative or "jump-off point" to explain the "why" behind a practice, users may experience only a fleeting curiosity rather than a deep cognitive understanding. The study also highlights that usability is paramount; technical issues like long load times or difficult navigation can discourage users and undermine the educational goals.

The implications of this research suggest that future developers of cultural heritage technology should move away from linear approaches and instead embrace the non-linear, simultaneous exploration capabilities of VR. The author suggests that incorporating a structured storyline or "journey" would allow users to become active participants in the culture rather than distant observers. Furthermore, the project raises important ethical questions for the future of digital ethnography, specifically regarding the standards for replicating indigenous culture, the necessity of factual truthfulness in virtual environments, and the boundaries of using gamification when presenting sacred or sensitive indigenous traditions. Ultimately, the work serves as a use case to inspire the creation of more immersive digital archives to help indigenous identities thrive in a modern, technological age.

title: Development of an Online Multimedia Database for Processing Training Requests at the Prince Sultan Cardiac Centre
abstract:
This research project focuses on developing an online interactive multimedia database, which was conceived to be used in processing training request applications at the Prince Sultan Cardiac Center, Riyadh (PSCC).

The database was tested by doctors, interns, and students from various educational institutions, as well as by the administrative staff of PSCC, and it proved that it could be used to replace the current system wherein staff uses a separate Excel sheet to log trainees requests and their information and write 3-4 memos to complete a single request.

This report includes the processes involved to design and create the database and how the trainees and the admin staff at PSCC reacted to the use of the system. 

A review of the literature about multimedia databases provides insights about its importance from both a technological and business standpoint. Through this project, we will find out how this online multimedia database affects the admin staff’s workload and how it can be used as an effective tool for processing training requests and data record-keeping.

At the Prince Sultan Cardiac Centre (PSCC), the Academic and Training Affairs department manages a high volume of trainees, including doctors, interns, and students. In 2018 and 2019 alone, the center received 1,313 trainees. Furthermore, the project faced institutional challenges, such as strict IT Department regulations regarding internet accessibility and the need for a system that ensures continuity of work as the Saudi government implements "Saudization" policies, which involve delegating tasks from expatriates to Saudi nationals.

The system also includes an auto-generated template feature for status notifications. To assist users, an interactive guide was created using Google Web Designer, featuring screen recordings edited in Final Cut Pro to provide step-by-step instructions.

The methodology employed a four-stage research design: preliminary investigation (data collection), design, construction, and validation/testing/revision. Data collection involved reviewing the Academic Affairs’ annual reports and Excel trackers to identify necessary data fields, such as department lists and university information. The design phase utilized Microsoft PowerPoint for process documentation to track changes and guide the programmer. The construction phase involved web technologies including ASP.NET, C#, Javascript, and HTML, with Microsoft SQL Server serving as the database management system. The system was hosted via Internet Information Services (IIS) and proxied by NGINX. For the validation and testing phase, the system was released to a sample of users, including students, interns, and PSCC administrative staff, between October and November 2020. User attitudes were measured using a 5-point Likert Scale, and data was analyzed using descriptive percentage analysis.

Testing revealed that 93.3% of respondents possessed moderate to very skilled computer knowledge, and none of the respondents found the system difficult or complicated to use. This ease of use was further evidenced by the fact that trainees were able to navigate the platform and submit requests without requiring external assistance. Qualitative feedback from users was overwhelmingly positive; a training coordinator from King Saud Bin Abdulaziz University noted that the system would increase trainee responsibility, while a PSCC administrator highlighted the reduction in paper and toner waste. While the system was successful, users identified areas for improvement, such as adding a "return" function to allow applicants to correct errors and implementing stronger identity authentication for security.

In conclusion, the research demonstrates that the online multimedia database is a timely and effective innovation for the PSCC Academic Affairs department. The system achieved 92.9% support from respondents regarding its implementation. The implications of this study are significant for organizational management and digital transformation within healthcare institutions. By automating the administrative workflow, the PSCC can achieve greater operational efficiency and data integrity. The project serves as a model for how specialized departments can transition from fragmented, paper-based systems to integrated multimedia databases to manage high volumes of information. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of user-centric design—such as the inclusion of interactive guides—in ensuring the successful adoption of new technologies by staff with varying levels of technical expertise. Finally, the project underscores the necessity of continuous system evolution, as user feedback regarding security and error-correction functionality provides a clear roadmap for future technological enhancements.

title: Behind the Seams: Tell the Stories Behind Thrifted Clothes Through Multimedia
abstract:
“Behind every fabric, every thread, every button, every pocket – is a story.”

Have you ever thought of the different stories behind thrifted clothes? Behind the Seams takes that question on and attempts to bring these stories to life with multimedia storytelling. It aims to find the best ways to become an immersive online store that is capable to narrate the fictional stories created for the thrifted garments with the various types of multimedia. In addition, I hope that through this project I am able to tackle a different side of resale or thrifted fashion.

Behind the Seams ultimately is a collection of all my interests in one whole assignment. It became a way to further my knowledge and practice in the fields such as web design, photography, and videography. By recording the process, I was able to find mistakes and learn from them. With that, I believe it can also be a way to see through my design process that readers can learn from as well. Where they can get inspiration from and use the various techniques, they may find useful for their own.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Ethan Gabriel G. Ocampo’s special project, "Behind the Seams: Tell the Stories Behind Thrifted Clothes Through Multimedia," investigates how various media modes can breathe life into the history of secondhand garments. By using fictional narratives to create immersive experiences, the project aims to move beyond viewing clothing as mere commodities, potentially attracting new consumers and encouraging environmentally friendly thrifting practices.

The research follows a three-phase practice-based methodology: "Jump Starter" for planning and sourcing; "Story Creation" for developing realistic fictional narratives inspired by the "Significant Objects Project"; and "Project Creation" for the technical production of photography, video, and a WordPress website. The project's findings are demonstrated through three items—high-rise denim jeans, a white dress shirt, and a red track jacket—each paired with a unique narrative, such as a story about a grandfather or a sentimental letter. Technical elements included an "infinity background" for photography and vintage-style video effects.

The author concludes that multimedia storytelling is a powerful tool for reimagining the resale fashion market. While the project successfully demonstrates the technical and creative possibilities of this concept, it also raises questions regarding commercial viability and whether storytelling significantly shifts consumer interest compared to traditional methods. Ultimately, the work serves as a guide for transforming simple objects into meaningful experiences through strategic media use.

The special project titled "Behind the Seams: Tell the Stories Behind Thrifted Clothes Through Multimedia" by Ethan Gabriel G. Ocampo explores the intersection of secondhand fashion and immersive multimedia storytelling. The project seeks to address the question of how to utilize various media modes to breathe life into the history of thrifted garments. By creating fictional narratives for specific clothing items, the author aims to present a different perspective on resale fashion, potentially attracting new consumers to the market and encouraging thrifting as an environmentally friendly practice. Additionally, the project serves as a practical exercise in web design, photography, and videography, documenting the author's design process for the benefit of other practitioners.

The research problem centers on the potential of multimedia to elevate the value of thrifted items beyond their material state. While clothing is often viewed simply as a commodity, the author posits that every fabric and button holds a potential story. The core research question asks how these stories can be effectively communicated through multimedia to create an immersive experience. The author identifies a need to move beyond traditional retail methods by using text, graphics, audio, and video to create multidimensional narratives that transport the audience to different times and places.

To address this problem, the author employed a practice-based research methodology organized into three distinct phases. Phase 1, the "Jump Starter," involved foundational planning, including budgeting, sourcing specific clothing items, and gathering artistic inspiration via platforms like Pinterest. Phase 2, "Story Creation," focused on developing relatable, realistic, and short fictional narratives for the selected garments. The author used the "Significant Objects Project" as a guide, ensuring that the stories were concise and aligned with the visual characteristics of the clothes. Phase 3, "Project Creation," involved the technical production of three main components: photography, video, and a website. The photography included standard product shots against white backgrounds and stylized "polaroid" thumbnails to evoke nostalgia. The video was designed as a vintage-style teaser using lo-fi music and VHS effects to suggest a sense of history. Finally, a single-page website was developed using WordPress and WPJelly to serve as a digital storefront and a hub for the multimedia elements.

The findings of the project are presented through the successful realization of the three project components. In the results phase, the author detailed the selection of three specific items: high-rise washed denim jeans, a basic white dress shirt, and a red track jacket. Each item was paired with a unique narrative; for example, the jeans were linked to a story about a grandfather and grandson, while the red jacket was tied to a sentimental letter regarding a lost pet. The photographic results utilized an "infinity background" technique to mimic professional online boutiques, while the video successfully utilized color grading and vintage presets to achieve a retro aesthetic. The website was constructed with a focus on user experience determinants such as page loading, business content, and navigation efficiency, resulting in a functional, aesthetically pleasing single-page interface that integrated the stories, videos, and product listings.

In the discussion, the author reflects on the achievement of the project goals, noting that the multimedia approach successfully demonstrated how to weave narratives into the thrifting experience. A significant takeaway from the process was the importance of "trusting the process," specifically the necessity of thorough planning and research rather than rushing into production. The author acknowledges areas for future improvement, such as producing individual videos for each garment to deepen the storytelling and utilizing a more diverse range of models to represent different body types, which would enhance the inclusivity and visual appeal of the brand.

The project concludes by affirming that multimedia storytelling is a viable and powerful tool for reimagining the resale fashion market. While the project successfully demonstrated the technical and creative possibilities of the concept, it also raised new questions regarding the commercial viability of such a model. The author wonders if attaching stories to thrifted items would result in a significant shift in consumer interest compared to traditional selling methods. Ultimately, the work serves as a guide for using the advantages of various media types to transform simple objects into meaningful experiences, leaving open the possibility of expanding this concept into a full-scale business in the future.

title: Evaluating Accessibility of the Massive Open Distance e-Learning (MODeL) Platform
abstract:
As one of the constituents of the country’s national university and premier institution of higher learning, the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) provides and delivers Massive Open Online Courses as learning opportunities for more people anywhere in the country or the world. The official platform of UPOU MOOCs is the Massive Open Distance e-Learning website, also called the MODeL platform. The main purpose of this research is to evaluate the accessibility of the platform, the selected course site, and the course materials of that course site, which are available to the students. The selected MOOC was Oral Communication and Conversational Fluency (CFE 101). 
 
The platform, course site, and course materials were evaluated using Initial Checks, the WCAG-EM report tool, along with several web accessibility evaluation tools. In the evaluation and audit reports, there are failures in several WCAG 2.0 guidelines in three levels of conformance, Levels A, AA, and AAA. The students from two batches (March and June) of the selected MOOC were invited to participate in offline and online surveys. The evaluation and the survey revealed that there are accessibility issues that need to be addressed as these are crucial to the overall learning experience of the users and students, especially to persons with disabilities. 

This research concludes that the accessibility issues of the MODeL website be addressed and fixed to provide a better and more effective delivery of MOOCs. This research also allows for more research and more opportunities for the improvement of the university.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Hyacinth C. Celzo’s research, "Evaluating Accessibility of the Massive Open Distance e-Learning (MODeL) Platform," investigates the digital inclusivity of the University of the Philippines Open University’s (UPOU) primary platform for Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). The study focuses on the accessibility and usability of the MODeL platform and the specific "Oral Communication and Conversational Fluency" (CFE 101) course site and materials. The research aims to identify barriers that could hinder learning for users with visual, auditory, cognitive, or physical impairments.

The methodology combined technical audits with user surveys. The researcher performed initial checks regarding page titles, image text alternatives, contrast ratios, and keyboard access, alongside a formal audit using the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) 1.0 to assess conformance against WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 standards. Additionally, an online survey was conducted with 25 students from the CFE 101 course to gather data on usability perceptions.

Findings revealed significant accessibility failures. Technical audits identified missing alternative text for images, low contrast ratios, and text overlapping when browser text was resized. The WCAG-EM report noted non-descriptive page titles, inconsistent navigation, and a lack of error identification in forms. The CFE 101 course site lacked captions, audio descriptions, or sign language interpretations for video content, while PDF materials lacked document titles and bookmarks. Student surveys corroborated these findings, reporting difficulties accessing forums and a lack of text alternatives for visual information. The study concludes that the platform and materials do not fully conform to WCAG standards, necessitating urgent technical fixes and integrated accessibility design to ensure equitable educational opportunities.

The research titled "Evaluating Accessibility of the Massive Open Distance e-Learning (MODeL) Platform" by Hyacinth C. Celzo investigates the digital inclusivity of the University of the Philippines Open University’s (UPOU) primary platform for Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). The study focuses on the accessibility and usability of the MODeL platform, a specific selected course site, and the associated course materials.

The problem addressed is the potential for accessibility barriers within the MODeL platform that could hinder the learning experience of all users, but particularly those with disabilities. While MOOCs are designed for mass participation and openness, the researcher sought to determine if the technical implementation of the UPOU platform meets international standards, thereby ensuring that students with visual, auditory, cognitive, or physical impairments can navigate and interact with the content effectively.

The context of the study is rooted in the growing importance of distance education and the legal and social mandates for web accessibility. The author references Philippine disability laws, such as Republic Act 7277, and the efforts of the Philippine Web Accessibility Group (PWAG) to promote inclusive ICT design. The study specifically examines the "Oral Communication and Conversational Fluency" (CFE 101) course to provide a concrete case study for the evaluation.

The methodology employed a multi-faceted approach combining technical audits and user surveys. The researcher conducted "Initial Checks" (Easy Checks) to perform a quick review of web accessibility, including page titles, image text alternatives, contrast ratios, and keyboard access. This was supplemented by a formal audit using the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) 1.0 to assess conformance against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0 and 2.1 at various levels (A, AA, and AAA). The technical evaluation covered the MODeL platform, the CFE 101 course site, and downloadable PDF course materials. Additionally, the researcher conducted an online survey with 25 students from two batches of the CFE 101 course to gather qualitative and quantitative data regarding their perceptions of the platform's usability and the difficulties they encountered.

The findings revealed significant accessibility failures across all evaluated components. Technical audits of the MODeL platform identified issues such as images lacking alternative text, low contrast ratios on the 2019 MOOCs calendar, and text overlapping or being cut off when the browser text was resized to 200%. The WCAG-EM report for the platform showed failures in several areas, including non-descriptive page titles, inconsistent navigation, and a lack of error identification or suggestions in forms. The CFE 101 course site exhibited poor color contrast in the navigation bar and course title, and lacked captions, audio descriptions, or sign language interpretations for video content. The course materials (PDFs) failed to meet several accessibility standards, including missing document titles, a lack of bookmarks, and insufficient keyboard focus visibility.

The student survey corroborated these technical findings. While many students rated the platform's attractiveness and readability as "good," a significant portion of respondents reported difficulties. Issues cited by students included difficulty accessing forums, problems with the mobile app interface (such as unclickable buttons), and the lack of text alternatives for visual information. Notably, the survey results indicated that accessibility issues could impact the effectiveness of the learning experience, potentially leading to a loss of interest or the inability to complete courses.

The study concludes that the MODeL platform, the CFE 101 course site, and the associated course materials currently possess various accessibility issues that prevent full conformance with WCAG standards. These barriers pose significant challenges to inclusive learning, particularly for students with disabilities. The researcher emphasizes that addressing these issues is crucial for the effective delivery of MOOCs and the university's mission of providing accessible education.

The implications of this research are significant for the University of the Philippines Open University and web developers. The findings suggest an urgent need for the university to implement technical fixes, such as improving color contrast, ensuring text resizes without overlapping, providing alt-text for all meaningful images, and adding captions and transcripts to multimedia content. Furthermore, the study implies that accessibility should be integrated into the design and development phase of all future digital learning tools. By resolving these issues, the university can foster a more inclusive environment, enhance the learning experience for all students, and fulfill its commitment to providing equitable educational opportunities through its MOOC offerings.

title: Exploring Information and Communication Technology Access and Awareness Among People with Disabilities
abstract:
The study aims to raise awareness about the PWD hindered in accessing ICT and other multimedia products, specifically, it seeks to discuss and identify the following objectives:
• Discuss the importance of ICT access to PWD.
• Identify the possible advantages or how ICT access can help PWD.

The virtual reality documentary produced by this study will raise awareness about the present condition of PWD in the information age and how opportunities for them are hindered through certain factors. In addition, the documentary may have an indirect benefit for all PWD by inspiring ICT initiatives to further help PWD in accessing multimedia products. For instance, an improvement to Assistive Technologies (AT) will greatly help in narrowing the disability divide and providing more ICT-related opportunities for PWD.

While the study focuses on PWD, it can also help people without disabilities by realizing how important ICT access is. Therefore, maximizing their potentials in the information age knowing that they are able enough to do certain works.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
James Harvey Maceda’s thesis, "Exploring Information and Communication Technology Access and Awareness Among People with Disabilities," investigates the "disability divide," where the exclusion of people with disabilities (PWD) from ICT design limits opportunities in education, employment, and social integration. The study identifies unique barriers including the high cost of specialized assistive technologies (AT), lack of digital literacy, and socioeconomic challenges like lower income and higher unemployment.

Using a qualitative methodology, the researcher produced a virtual reality (VR) documentary based on semi-structured interviews with five participants from the Grain Foundation for People with Disabilities Inc. representing various impairments. Findings reveal that ICT is a vital tool for empowerment, enabling participants to join support groups, conduct research, and enhance independence through mobile applications and video calls. There is also significant potential for economic independence through online freelance work if training is provided.

However, significant struggles persist, including workplace discrimination, the high cost of devices, and a lack of specialized training or technical support. Furthermore, technological innovations often originate in developed countries, leaving those in developing nations to rely on obsolete equipment. The researcher concludes that bridging this divide requires inclusive design where technologists co-design with PWDs, employers end discriminatory hiring, and governments enforce accessibility laws. Immersive media, such as the VR documentary produced, can help raise public awareness to foster inclusion.

James Harvey Maceda’s thesis, "Exploring Information and Communication Technology Access and Awareness Among People with Disabilities," investigates the intersection of the digital divide and disability. The research addresses how the exclusion of people with disabilities (PWD) from ICT design limits their opportunities in education, employment, and social integration. The study frames this issue as a "disability divide," noting that PWDs face unique barriers including the high cost of specialized assistive technologies (AT), a lack of digital literacy, and socioeconomic challenges such as lower income levels and higher unemployment rates.

The researcher utilized a qualitative methodology centered on the production of a virtual reality (VR) documentary. Data was gathered through semi-structured interviews with five participants from the Grain Foundation for People with Disabilities Inc., representing various impairments including hearing and visual impairments, cerebral palsy, ADHD, and Fanconi Syndrome. The study employed 360-degree camera technology to create an immersive experience, with data analyzed through a coding process to identify key themes.

The findings reveal that ICT is a vital tool for empowerment, providing social, cultural, educational, and economic opportunities. Participants reported that the internet allows them to join support groups, stay informed, and conduct educational research, helping them avoid being "left behind." ICT enhances independence through mobile applications for navigation and video calls for communication. Furthermore, the study identified potential for economic independence through online freelance work, provided individuals receive necessary training.

Despite these benefits, significant struggles persist. Participants reported workplace discrimination, such as being denied jobs despite having technical backgrounds. Other barriers include the high cost of assistive devices, a lack of specialized training, and a lack of ongoing technical support. Additionally, the study noted that many technological innovations originate in developed countries, leaving those in developing nations like the Philippines to rely on obsolete or donated equipment that may not meet specific needs.

The researcher concludes that while ICT can promote inclusion and dignity, its potential is hindered by systemic barriers. Access is deeply tied to socioeconomic status and the availability of affordable assistive technology. Achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals requires bridging this divide through inclusive design. The study suggests that technologists should co-design hardware and software with PWDs, employers must move beyond discriminatory hiring, and governments must enforce accessibility laws. Finally, the researcher suggests that immersive media, like the VR documentary produced, can raise public awareness and foster a more inclusive environment.

The thesis titled "Exploring Information and Communication Technology Access and Awareness Among People with Disabilities" by James Harvey Maceda investigates the intersection of the digital divide and disability. The research addresses the growing gap in technology access, noting that while ICT is essential for modern societal participation, many technologies are designed for general consumers without considering accessibility for people with disabilities (PWD). This exclusion limits opportunities for PWDs in education, employment, and social integration. The study specifically focuses on the importance of ICT access and the potential benefits it offers to this demographic.

The research problem is framed around the "disability divide," a subset of the digital divide. The author notes that while ICT can improve education and business management, PWDs face significant barriers, including the high cost of specialized assistive technologies (AT) and a lack of digital literacy. Furthermore, the study highlights that the digital divide is often a socioeconomic issue, as PWDs frequently face lower income levels and higher unemployment rates, making expensive adaptive tools inaccessible. The researcher also points out a lack of public awareness regarding the specific challenges PWDs face in the information age.

To address these issues, the researcher employed a qualitative methodology centered on the production of a virtual reality (VR) documentary. The study utilized semi-structured interviews with five participants from the Grain Foundation for People with Disabilities Inc. These participants included individuals with various impairments, such as hearing and visual impairments, cerebral palsy, ADHD, and Fanconi Syndrome. The research process involved rigorous pre-production, including the development of an interview protocol and ethical considerations such as informed consent. The production utilized 360-degree camera technology to create an immersive VR experience, and the data was analyzed through a coding process to categorize relevant statements into themes.

The findings of the study reveal that ICT serves as a vital tool for empowerment, providing PWDs with social, cultural, educational, and economic opportunities. Participants reported that the internet allows them to join support groups, stay informed about current events, and conduct research for education, which helps them avoid being "left behind." ICT also enhances daily convenience and independence; for example, visually impaired individuals use mobile applications for navigation, and hearing-impaired individuals use video calls and social media to facilitate communication. Additionally, the study identified opportunities for economic independence through online freelance work, provided the individuals have the necessary training.

However, the findings also highlight significant struggles. Participants reported experiencing discrimination in the workplace, such as being denied jobs despite having relevant technical backgrounds. Other barriers include a lack of interest in ICT due to perceived difficulty, a lack of specialized training, the high cost of assistive devices, and a lack of ongoing technical support. The study also noted that many technological innovations are produced in developed countries, leaving those in developing nations like the Philippines to rely on obsolete or donated equipment that may not meet their specific needs.

The researcher concludes that while ICT is a powerful tool for inclusion and dignity, its potential is currently hindered by systemic barriers. Access to ICT is not merely a matter of availability but is deeply tied to socioeconomic status, education, and the availability of affordable assistive technology. The study emphasizes that achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) requires the full participation of PWDs, which is only possible if the digital divide is bridged through inclusive design and equitable access.

The implications of this study are directed toward several stakeholders. For technologists and innovators, the research suggests a need to engage directly with PWDs to co-design hardware and software that addresses their specific needs from the outset. For employers, the study highlights the need to move beyond discriminatory hiring practices and recognize the competence of PWDs. For governments and policymakers, the findings suggest that implementing and enforcing laws regarding accessibility and equal employment is crucial. Finally, the study suggests that raising awareness through immersive media, such as the VR documentary produced, can foster a more inclusive environment by educating both the public and industry leaders on the realities of living with a disability in a digital world.

title: Dama: Designing a Multisensory Glove
abstract:
The special project intends to design a glove that incorporates vibrotactile technology for sensorimotor rehabilitation. The project is based on several previous works on the use of vibrating motors on the human body.

The project aims to answer the question if it is possible to design a tool that will help a person rehabilitate a part of themselves, and in the case for this project, it will be used on their hands since it is the most common sensorimotor organ. 

The glove’s design is based on several universal principles of design; perceptibility, operability, and prevention. This also includes the principle of Aesthetic-Usability Effect. The motors will be fastened on the joints and are controlled over a Wi-Fi connection through a software programmed in processing that uses patterns. The program or the software is a collaboration with a previous work called “Haplos” that also uses vibrotactile motors. The project combined the use of motors and the LED lights that will create a multisensory stimulation (auditory, tactile and visual).

The focus on this project will be on the process of designing the glove itself, the testing process for the work will be considered for further the research.

half:
The special project "Dama: Designing a Multisensory Glove" by Mariel Francesca I. Reyes addresses the need for affordable sensorimotor rehabilitation tools for stroke survivors in the Philippines. Because limb rehabilitation is often expensive, the author designed an economical and engaging tool to help users regain hand function, which is vital for movement, sensory perception, and communication.

Grounded in haptics and the concept of the Cortical Homunculus, the project evolved from a previous low-cost technology called "Haplos." Through iterative design, the final Dama glove features motors attached to the PIP, MCP, and CMC joints to facilitate bending, extending, gripping, pinching, and stabilization. To ensure usability, the glove utilizes high-contrast colors, Velcro, and metal fasteners. It employs a color-coded system—gray for the left hand and blue for the right—and integrates LED lights with vibrotactile motors to improve stimulus recognition through simultaneous visual and tactile stimulation. The software uses a Particle Photon Wi-Fi module to deliver music-modeled vibration patterns.

Findings indicate that an aesthetically pleasing, low-cost glove can be constructed using accessible materials like cotton ribbons and button-snaps. The researcher established an ideal testing protocol involving two-minute vibration sessions followed by thirty-second rest periods to prevent skin irritation. While the project successfully integrates multimedia technology with medical needs, the author notes that empirical testing is the necessary next step to determine the glove's effectiveness in regaining sensorimotor skills.

two:
The special project "Dama: Designing a Multisensory Glove" by Mariel Francesca I. Reyes addresses the critical need for accessible sensorimotor rehabilitation tools. The problem identified is the high prevalence of stroke, which is a leading cause of death in the Philippines and results in significant financial burdens due to the high cost of limb rehabilitation. Because the hands are essential for sensory perception, movement, and communication, losing motor or sensory skills in the hands can severely impact a person's ability to interact with their environment. The author seeks to design a tool that is economical, relevant to society, and engaging for users.

The context of this project is rooted in the study of the somatosensory system and the "active touch" or haptics, which involves the continuous flow of sensory input and motor output. The research draws on the concept of the "Cortical Homunculus" to understand how the brain prioritizes sensory and motor functions, noting that the hands occupy significant brain space. The project builds upon previous technological developments, specifically "Haplos," a low-cost wearable technology designed to enhance body awareness through vibrotactile stimulation on the back.

The methodology involved an iterative design process, moving from an initial prototype to a more refined, multisensory version. The first prototype focused on placing motors on specific muscles (interossei, hypothenar, and thenar) to stimulate them. However, based on literature regarding the tonic vibration reflex, the researcher shifted the design focus from muscles to joints. The final prototype, the "Dama" glove, features motors fastened to the joints: the Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joints for bending and extending, the Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints for gripping and pinching, and the Carpometacarpal (CMC) joints for stabilization.

The design of the glove incorporates several universal principles of design to ensure usability. Accessibility is addressed through perceptibility (using high-contrast colors), operability (using Velcro and metal fasteners), simplicity (minimizing complicated features), and adaptability (making the glove reversible and adjustable for different hand sizes). To enhance the user experience, the researcher applied the Aesthetic-Usability Effect, ensuring the device is visually appealing to encourage use. Furthermore, the glove is designed to be reversible, using a color-coded system (gray for left, blue for right) to help users distinguish sides easily.

To create a multisensory experience, the researcher integrated LED lights alongside the vibrotactile motors. This approach is based on the principle that the brain can more effectively detect and recognize stimuli when multiple senses—in this case, visual and tactile—are stimulated simultaneously. The software, developed in collaboration with the creator of Haplos, is programmed in "Processing" and uses a Wi-Fi module (Particle Photon) to deliver vibration patterns. These patterns are modeled after music to provide a "visuospatial" component that can relax the user, motivate them, and help them envision the patterns in their head.

The findings of the design phase demonstrate that a low-cost, reversible, and aesthetically pleasing glove can be constructed using accessible materials like cotton ribbons, Velcro, and button-snap fasteners. The researcher established an "ideal protocol" for testing, which involves two-minute vibration sessions followed by a thirty-second rest period to prevent skin irritation, such as itchiness. The protocol includes observing the subject's ability to perform simple gestures, such as opening the hand and gradually gripping an object, while recording feedback on comfort and difficulty.

The project concludes that the design of the Dama glove successfully integrates multimedia technology with medical rehabilitation needs. The researcher successfully created a device that is adaptable to different hand sizes and easy to use, which may reduce user hesitation. While the current scope of the project focused on the design and construction process, the author acknowledges that the next critical step is empirical testing to determine if the glove can effectively help individuals regain sensorimotor skills.

The implications of this work suggest that vibrotactile technology has significant potential across various fields, ranging from video games to medical rehabilitation. By creating a low-cost, multisensory tool, the project opens doors for more accessible rehabilitation options in societies where high-tech medical equipment may be economically out of reach. The researcher notes that future iterations of the design may change as more data is collected regarding the effectiveness of the device in clinical settings.

title: If It Exists: A New Media Artwork
abstract: If It Exists is a new media artwork that incorporates local wireless cloud saving, custom coding, microcontrollers, LED strips, basic projection mapping and crafting in an attempt at making a communal experience that tackles a realized technological version of an afterlife. From the conception of this artwork, it has always been centralized with animal companions in an effort to make it a more universal and accessible experience. It is also a decision that consciously tries to contrasts itself from the artworks of others that tackle the topics of death, loss and the afterlife in a more morbid manner. It is also purposely kitsch, in an effort to make it more relatable, shareable and accessible.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Dan Dominic A. Villena’s new media artwork, *If It Exists*, is a participatory installation exploring death, loss, and the afterlife through the lens of animal companionship. The project aims to legitimize the grief associated with pet loss by providing a collective platform for expression, addressing the social stigmatization of these emotions. The work explores memory as a subjective, decaying process, drawing parallels between human recollection and machine data processing.

The installation utilizes a physical structure resembling a cloud, constructed from a Chinese paper lantern covered in cotton batting. An Arduino microcontroller manages a Neopixel LED strip, while a small LED pocket projector casts user-uploaded images onto the exterior. To simulate the degradation of human memory, custom code written in Processing applies digital artifacts, pixel displacement, and color distortions to the images, mimicking a neural network's data bottleneck to make images increasingly unrecognizable over time.

The project concludes that technology can serve as a tool for catharsis, facilitating shared rituals of remembrance. The media deterioration feature represents the fading nature of memory and manages storage by ensuring only frequently re-uploaded content remains clear. Future objectives include implementing actual neural networks for image processing and creating a "Dead Pets’ Society" website. This website would allow users to link digital tributes to the physical installation via hexadecimal codes, bridging the gap between social media and physical art.
