The new media artwork *If It Exists* by Dan Dominic A. Villena is a participatory installation designed to explore themes of death, loss, and the afterlife through the lens of animal companionship. The project seeks to create a communal space for mourning, utilizing technology to provide a tangible, albeit digital, version of remembrance.

The problem addressed by the artist is the social stigmatization and dismissal of grief related to the loss of pets. Villena notes that relationships with animals are often viewed as frivolous, and the artwork aims to legitimize these intense emotions by providing a collective platform for expression. Furthermore, the work explores the concept of memory as a subjective, decaying process, drawing parallels between human recollection and the way machines process data.

The context of the work is rooted in contemporary new media art and the intersection of technology and human emotion. Villena draws inspiration from several sources: Damien Hirst’s *The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living*, which uses a preserved shark to comment on the limitations of physical preservation; Candy Chang’s *Before I Die*, which emphasizes audience participation; and the work of artists like Terence Broad and Ben Bogart, who use neural networks to explore how AI "remembers" or reconstructs media. The project also references the concept of a "cloud" as both a physical metaphor for heaven and a technical term for remote data storage.

The method involves a complex integration of hardware and custom software. The physical structure consists of a cloud-like object made from a Chinese paper lantern covered in cotton batting, suspended by industrial-grade fishing line. Inside this structure, an LED strip (Neopixel) is controlled by an Arduino microcontroller, and a small LED pocket projector is installed to cast images onto the exterior. The system is connected to a wireless hard drive containing user-uploaded media. To simulate the degradation of human memory, Villena uses custom code written in Processing to apply digital artifacts, pixel displacement, and color distortions to the images. This code simulates the effect of a neural network's data bottleneck, causing images to become increasingly unrecognizable over time.

The findings and results of the creation process highlight the technical challenges of combining digital and physical mediums. The artist encountered significant difficulties with soldering JST connectors to the LED strip, troubleshooting Bluetooth connectivity (eventually opting for a more reliable wired connection), and managing the "throw range" of the projector. Through iterative testing of different lantern sizes and rigging methods—moving from wooden boards to metal struts and plastic containers—the artist successfully achieved a setup where the projector and hard drive are hidden within the cloud, creating a more immersive and cohesive viewer experience.

The conclusions of the project are both artistic and personal. Artistically, the work demonstrates that technology can serve as a tool for catharsis, allowing individuals to participate in a shared ritual of remembrance. The "media deterioration" feature serves a dual purpose: it thematically represents the fading nature of memory and practically manages storage by ensuring that only frequently re-uploaded content remains clear. Personally, the project served as a transformative experience for the author, helping him navigate his own struggles with mental health and his evolving identity as a multimedia artist. He concludes that the legitimacy of art lies in the intent to create and the ability to articulate complex human emotions.

The implications of *If It Exists* suggest a future where new media art can move beyond the gallery and into more accessible, digital spaces. Villena proposes future objectives such as implementing actual neural networks for image processing, developing anti-spamming measures for the data drive, and creating a dedicated website called "Dead Pets’ Society." This website would allow users to upload media and receive unique hexadecimal codes to link their digital tributes to the physical installation, thereby bridging the gap between online social media presence and physical art installations.

title: Camaligan, Camarines Sur Tourism Web Information System
abstract: Camaligan, Camarines Sur River Park (hereinafter referred to as “Camaligan River Park”) is one of the booming tourist spots in the Bicol Region, with several tourist attractions including Camaligan River Cruise, a hanging bridge, private boat rentals, and an open function hall. The absence of an information website and booking system makes it difficult for tourists to know about the place and to reserve a scheduled visit. Similarly, the Camaligan Local Government Unit (“LGU”) makes extra effort to promote the Camaligan River Park and manually assist the visitors. The Camaligan Tourism Web Information System aims to boost the online presence of the Camaligan River Park and other tourist spots within the town. This new system will help facilitate online booking and reservation of the attractions and other facilities, provide up-to-date information and relevant details about the town’s tourism, answer online messages and queries, and support the Camaligan LGU to market places of interest in the municipality. In addition, the system will include a virtual tour of the entire stretch of the Camaligan River Park to give the tourists a holistic view and appreciation of what the place has to offer. An online map of the Camaligan tourist spots is incorporated for users' convenience and ease of navigation. With the Camaligan Tourism Web Information System in place, residents and tourists will have a digitally attractive resource about the Camaligan River Park, including a user-friendly online booking and reservation system. It will likewise help the Camaligan LGU to organize the tours and generate a full report of the bookings and revenues.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Francis Lineoso S. Abilay’s capstone project addresses the lack of a digital presence for tourist attractions in Camaligan, Camarines Sur. Currently, the municipality relies on manual processes like physical visits and Facebook monitoring to manage tourism and reservations for the Camaligan River Park. This manual approach hinders discovery for tourists outside the Bicol Region, results in suboptimal revenue, and creates a tedious experience for visitors attempting to secure slots.

The project aimed to raise awareness of the town's history, aid the Local Government Unit in organizing tours and generating revenue reports, and support the local economy. Developed using the waterfall model, the system features attraction information, an online booking and reservation system, a virtual tour, a tourism map, and a contact page. The technical implementation utilized AWS EC2, XAMMP, HTML, Bootstrap, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, and MySQL, alongside third-party tools like Stornaway.io, Mapme.com, and Google Maps API.

The resulting system allows users to register, select packages, and checkout via a G-Cash link, while providing administrators with tools to manage bookings and generate demographic and revenue reports. Assessments showed high performance: security testing via Immunuweb earned an A- grade, and usability testing with 40 respondents yielded a "Strongly Agree" rating (4.31/5). The study concludes the system effectively showcases attractions and facilitates secure reservations, recommending a one-year trial to evaluate its impact on revenue and tourist influx.

two:
The Camaligan, Camarines Sur Tourism Web Information System capstone project by Francis Lineoso S. Abilay addresses the lack of a digital presence for the tourist attractions in Camaligan, Camarines Sur. The primary problem identified is that the municipality lacks a dedicated website and an automated booking system. Currently, tourism information and reservations for the Camaligan River Park—which includes attractions such as the Camaligan River Cruise, a hanging bridge, and an open function hall—are managed through manual processes. These include physical visits to the tourism office, phone calls, or monitoring a Facebook page. This manual approach makes it difficult for tourists outside the Bicol Region to discover the area, results in suboptimal revenue, and creates a tedious experience for visitors attempting to secure slots for limited attractions.

The project's objectives were to raise awareness of the town's history and tourism, aid the Local Government Unit (LGU) in organizing tours and generating revenue reports, and indirectly support the local economy by providing additional income sources for residents and small businesses. The scope of the project included the development of a website featuring information on attractions and packages, an online booking and reservation system, a virtual tour of the River Park, a tourism map, and a contact/messaging page.

The author employed the waterfall model for the software development life cycle, allowing for a structured, phase-based approach. The system architecture consists of three main components: a database management component for municipality employees, a booking system for customers, and a booking retrieval component for administrative reporting and data analytics. The technical implementation utilized Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2 as the cloud-based server, with XAMMP for the web server stack. The front end was developed using HTML, Bootstrap, CSS, and JavaScript, while the backend and database management relied on PHP and MySQL. Third-party tools were integrated to enhance functionality, including Stornaway.io for interactive virtual tours, Mapme.com for the tourism map, and Google Maps API for location services.

The resulting system provides a comprehensive digital interface for tourists. The home page serves as a portal to the virtual tour, the tourism map, and the booking section. The booking process requires user registration and allows for package selection, quantity adjustment, and secure checkout. To facilitate seamless transactions, the system includes a link with G-Cash for online payments. For administrators, the system provides tools to manage bookings, update information, and generate reports on customer demographics and revenue.

The project underwent several layers of assessment. Security testing via Immunuweb resulted in an A- grade, confirming compliance with web security standards through the implementation of HTTPS, privacy policies, and updated JavaScript/Bootstrap libraries. Performance testing via GTmetrix yielded a grade of B, with specific metrics such as a First Contentful Paint of 691ms and a Speed Index of 1.3 seconds. Finally, usability testing was conducted with 40 respondents, including residents and potential tourists. The survey results, measured via a 5-point Likert scale, showed an overall average of 4.31, which translates to a "Strongly Agree" rating. The system received "Strongly Agree" ratings across usability, interface, performance, functionality, and portability, while the security test received a slightly lower but still positive "Agreed" rating of 4.057.

The study concludes that implementing the Web Information and Booking System effectively addresses the identified problems by providing a dedicated platform to showcase Camaligan's attractions and facilitating secure, online reservations. The testing and evaluation processes confirmed that the system meets industry standards and is user-friendly. The author notes that while the system is ready for implementation, ongoing maintenance and administrative support will be necessary to manage the platform effectively.

The implications of this project suggest that digital transformation can significantly boost tourism exposure for fourth-class municipalities. By automating the booking and reporting processes, the LGU can improve operational efficiency and gain better insights into tourism trends through data analytics. The author recommends a one-year trial period for the website to evaluate its impact on tourist influx and revenue. A key consideration for long-term sustainability is the impact of local weather and climate, specifically the threat of typhoons which have historically damaged local attractions like the hanging bridge and river cruise. If the system demonstrates increased revenue and tourism growth without significant environmental disruption, continued operation is advised.

title: OPENBANKPH
abstract: Despite the growing number of mobile users in the Philippines and the country consistently leading in “time spent on social media” charts, the same cannot be said for the country’s digital banking ecosystem. The lack of mobile financial apps and online banking platforms for the thousands of financial institutions recognized by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas leaves many Filipinos unbanked and prevents many from shifting from face-to-face transactions to digital banking. To help promote financial inclusion through modern technology, a no-cost platform was selected that enabled open banking to simulate a bank with Open API. A mobile-friendly web application was then built using an emerging technology. The result was a usable, functional, and well-performing online app that serves basic banking needs and follows government guidelines. As the system is open-source, it allows hundreds of financial institutions to freely adopt this system to make fast, progressive changes towards digital finance in the Philippines.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Dinia Grace D. Gepte’s capstone project, "OPENBANKPH: Equipping Philippine Banks in a Modern Digital World," addresses the gap between high mobile phone penetration and low digital banking adoption in the Philippines. Many Filipinos remain unbanked, and local financial institutions often lack the digital infrastructure and Open Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) required for interoperability with fintech developers.

The project aimed to develop a low-cost, mobile-friendly web application as a functional demonstration of an Open API-ready system. Using a methodology of open-source technologies and low-code development, the author utilized the Open Bank Project (OBP) to simulate a banking backend, FlutterFlow for client-side development, and Google Firebase for data management. The system was evaluated through functional testing, usability surveys, and security assessments using Zed Attack Proxy (ZAP).

Findings indicate the application is a usable, high-performing platform that adheres to government guidelines. Usability testing showed the interface is intuitive, earning an "excellent" rating for speed and responsiveness. Security testing revealed no critical vulnerabilities, though some medium and low-level alerts were identified. The project successfully demonstrated that the Open Bank Project can support the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Open Finance Framework. The study concludes that adopting Open APIs via open-source and low-code tools allows smaller institutions to modernize and increase financial inclusion without massive capital investment.

The project successfully demonstrated that the Open Bank Project can support the various tiers of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Open Finance Framework, including product, account, and transaction information.

The capstone project "OPENBANKPH: Equipping Philippine Banks in a Modern Digital World" by Dinia Grace D. Gepte addresses the significant gap between mobile phone penetration and digital banking adoption in the Philippines. Despite high mobile usage, a large portion of the Filipino population remains unbanked, and many existing financial institutions, particularly rural banks and cooperatives, lack the digital infrastructure to offer online services. This digital divide prevents many citizens from transitioning from face-to-face transactions to more efficient digital banking, hindering financial inclusion.

The problem is compounded by the fact that while the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has established roadmaps for digital transformation and open finance frameworks, most of the over 400 recognized banks in the country have not yet implemented Open Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). This lack of interoperability makes it difficult for third-party fintech developers to integrate with traditional banks, limiting the variety of digital financial services available to the public.

To address this, the project aims to provide a low-cost, easily deployable solution for banks to prepare for an open banking ecosystem. The primary objective was to develop a mobile-friendly web application that serves as a functional demonstration of how an Open API-ready system can facilitate digital banking. The project sought to showcase a rapid prototyping method that smaller institutions with limited resources could adopt to compete in the digital market.

The methodology employed a combination of existing open-source technologies and low-code development. The author utilized the Open Bank Project (OBP) as the API management tool to simulate a banking backend. The OBP Sandbox API environment was used to provide dummy data for banks, branches, ATMs, and transactions. For the client-side development, the author used FlutterFlow, a low-code platform, which allowed for rapid prototyping and deployment. Google Firebase and Firestore were utilized for application-side data management, including user authentication and storing support tickets. The development process involved configuring over 20 API endpoints to enable core banking functions such as account registration, fund transfers, and profile management. The system was evaluated through functional testing, end-to-end manual testing, and a usability survey involving respondents from various professional backgrounds. Security was also assessed using Zed Attack Proxy (ZAP) to identify potential vulnerabilities.

The findings indicate that the developed application is a usable, functional, and high-performing online banking platform that adheres to government guidelines. Usability testing showed that users found the application intuitive and easy to navigate, with an "excellent" rating for performance, specifically noting its speed and responsiveness. While some minor technical issues were noted on specific mobile browsers, the system remained stable without crashing. Security testing revealed no critical vulnerabilities, though some medium and low-level alerts were identified, such as missing security headers, which the author noted are common in such developments and can be addressed by future developers. Furthermore, the project successfully demonstrated that the Open Bank Project can support the various tiers of the Open Finance Framework established by the BSP, including product information, account information, and transaction capabilities.

In conclusion, the project demonstrates that adopting open banking through Open APIs is a viable and efficient way to modernize the Philippine financial landscape. By leveraging open-source platforms like OBP and low-code tools like FlutterFlow, even smaller financial institutions can rapidly implement digital banking services. This approach reduces the reliance on physical branches, saves costs for both banks and customers, and provides a scalable model for increasing financial inclusion in the Philippines.

The implications of this work are significant for the Philippine fintech ecosystem. For smaller banks, this project provides a blueprint for digital transformation that does not require massive capital investment or the development of proprietary systems from scratch. For the government, it provides a practical example of how the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap can be implemented at the institutional level. For third-party developers, the success of this model suggests a future where a more interconnected banking ecosystem allows for a proliferation of diverse financial applications. The author suggests that future work should include integrating real-world bank connectors, ensuring full ADA compliance for accessibility, and expanding the application to include more complex features like loan management and third-party payment capabilities.

title: The ENHS Student Attendance Monitoring System
abstract: Chronic absenteeism poses a widespread challenge in schools, prompting the need for an advanced attendance monitoring solution beyond the basic features provided by the Department of Education (DepEd) Commons. The Estancia National High School (ENHS), located in Estancia, Iloilo, which has more than 3,900 students and employs approximately 400 teachers, also encounters this problem. To address this issue, the ENHS Student Attendance Monitoring System (SAMS) was designed as a mobile application to streamline and automate attendance tracking processes. It was developed using the Flutter framework, Dart programming language, and NodeJS. It uses MySQL as the database and is currently hosted on an Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2 Instance running Ubuntu Linux 22. The resulting system allows teachers to input student absences per day and generate monthly reports on student absences. An alert is created when a student reaches a certain number of absences. The alert prompts the teacher to take action according to the number of absences. This proactive monitoring and alerting on student absences benefits students, teachers, and parents. Student absenteeism problems can be easily caught, tracked, and remediated before worsening.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The ENHS Student Attendance Monitoring System, developed by Bernard Kenneth T. Lim, addresses chronic absenteeism at Estancia National High School in Iloilo. The school faces challenges with manual attendance processes that are time-consuming, prone to error, and lack a centralized repository. Existing Department of Education tools, such as the Learner Information System, do not provide the granular, proactive monitoring necessary to intervene when students reach specific absence thresholds.

To resolve these issues, Lim developed the SAMS mobile application using the Agile Kanban methodology and the Systems Development Life Cycle framework. The technical architecture utilizes the Flutter framework, Dart, NodeJS, and a MySQL database hosted on an Amazon Web Services EC2 instance. The system features user management for teachers, administrators, students, and parents, alongside an attendance management module. A critical feature is the automated alerting mechanism, which triggers red alerts when a student reaches 3, 5, or 10 absences, prompting teachers to contact parents or conduct home visits. The system also generates monthly attendance reports to assist in analyzing absenteeism patterns.

User testing with five teachers resulted in an average System Usability Scale score of 88.5%, placing the application in the "Excellent" category. The author concludes that SAMS facilitates attendance management by providing a central repository for historical data and reducing administrative burdens. Proposed future enhancements include bulk CSV uploads, a web-based version, and automated generation of the DepEd School Form 2.

Teachers can manage classes, subjects, and school years, and use the attendance management module to input absences. A critical feature is the automated alerting mechanism, which triggers a red alert when a student reaches 3, 5, or 10 absences. This prompts teachers to take specific actions, such as contacting parents or conducting home visits, and record the outcome to update the alert status. The automated alerts are intended to help teachers act promptly to address absenteeism before it escalates. Automating this process reduces administrative burdens and improves record accuracy, helping schools better implement DepEd directives regarding parental notification.

Future enhancements proposed by the author include adding bulk CSV uploads for student data, developing a web-based version, and automating the generation of the DepEd School Form 2 (SF2) Monthly Attendance Report. Other suggested improvements include implementing app notifications for teachers, adding student addresses to facilitate home visits, and enhancing system security and administration.
two:
The ENHS Student Attendance Monitoring System, developed by Bernard Kenneth T. Lim, addresses the persistent challenge of chronic absenteeism at Estancia National High School (ENHS) in Iloilo. The school, which serves over 3,900 students and employs approximately 400 teachers, faces difficulties in managing attendance due to manual processes.

The problem identified by the author is multifaceted. First, the current manual methods for monitoring attendance and maintaining records are time-consuming for teachers. Second, these manual processes are highly prone to human error. Third, there is a lack of a central repository for attendance data; teachers currently maintain individual records that are often lost or become useless after the school year ends. Finally, there is no built-in mechanism to prompt teachers to take specific actions when a student reaches a threshold of absences. While the Department of Education (DepEd) provides systems like the Learner Information System (LIS) and the Electronic Class Record (ECR), these are not specifically designed to facilitate the granular, proactive monitoring of student absences.

To address these issues, the author developed the ENHS Student Attendance Monitoring System (SAMS), a mobile application designed to automate attendance tracking. The project was developed using the Agile Kanban methodology and the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) framework. The technical stack includes the Flutter framework and Dart programming language for the mobile application, NodeJS for the API, and a MySQL database. The system is hosted on an Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2 instance running Ubuntu Linux 22. The design process involved creating Data Flow Diagrams, Entity-Relationship Diagrams, and Use Case Models using tools like LucidChart and Draw.io.

The system provides several core functionalities. It allows for user registration and management for teachers and administrators, as well as student and parent/guardian registration. Teachers can manage classes, subjects, and school years. The primary feature is the attendance management module, which allows teachers to input student absences for specific dates. A critical component is the alerting feature, which triggers a red alert when a student reaches a specific number of absences (3, 5, or 10). When an alert is triggered, the teacher is prompted to take action, such as contacting parents or conducting home visits. Once action is taken, the teacher records the reason and the specific steps taken, which updates the alert status to "Action taken." Additionally, the system can generate monthly attendance reports that can be viewed by date or by individual student to help analyze absenteeism patterns.

The project was assessed through user testing involving five teachers using an Android device. The assessment utilized the System Usability Scale (SUS) to measure user experience. The results yielded an average SUS score of 88.5%, which falls into the "Excellent" rating category. This indicates that the application is highly usable and meets the needs of the intended users.

The author concludes that the ENHS SAMS successfully provides a tool to facilitate student attendance management, from data input to report generation. By creating a central repository, the system allows for the easy retrieval of historical data, which is vital for analyzing absenteeism patterns. The automated alerts are expected to help teachers act consistently and promptly to correct absenteeism problems before they escalate.

The implications of this project suggest that automating attendance can significantly offload administrative burdens from teachers and improve the accuracy of school records. By moving from fragmented, manual records to a centralized digital system, schools can better implement DepEd's directives regarding student attendance and parental notification.

For future work, the author proposes several enhancements to expand the system's utility. These include adding a bulk upload mechanism for student data via CSV files and developing a web-based version of the application to make extensive typing tasks easier. Functional improvements suggested include the automatic generation of the DepEd School Form 2 (SF2) Monthly Attendance Report, the ability to view long-term absenteeism history from previous years, and the implementation of app notifications to remind teachers to check attendance before classes end. The author also intends to add student addresses to facilitate home visits and focus on system administration, security hardening, and the creation of comprehensive user and troubleshooting guides.

title: Overtime Management System for Unix Manila Team of Telus International Digital Solutions
abstract:
The Unix Manila team is a part of Telus International Philippines, Inc.'s Digital Solutions group and consists of 33 systems administrators who provide 24/7 technical support for maintaining the UNIX servers of Telus Communications Canada. To ensure high-quality service to customers, the team occasionally works overtime, which includes covering for absent team members, a practice known as "fill-in." The team previously used a makeshift tool built in Microsoft Sharepoint to manage fill-in requests and track leave projections, however, due to Telus's recent partnership with Google, most applications were migrated to the Google platform and in September 2022, Microsoft Sharepoint was decommissioned. To replace this, the team developed the Overtime Management System (OMS), a web-based system
built in PHP, CSS, HTML, JavaScript, Bootstrap, and MariaDB. In addition to the fill-in application and leave tracking, OMS also includes new features such as offset tracking, additional resource management, and report generation. The system is designed to be scalable, reusable, and flexible, allowing for easy migration in the event of future changes to the organization's infrastructure.

Findings indicate that the OMS exceeds the capabilities of the previous tool. In addition to fill-in applications and leave tracking, the system introduces offset tracking, resource management, and report generation. This purpose-built system provides a robust, centralized platform that manages the complexities of technical support requirements, ensuring the team can maintain service quality without the administrative disruptions caused by organizational infrastructure changes.

title: Implementing a Medication Tracking System Using Blockchain Technologies
abstract: This project aims to address the issue of self-medicating with antibiotics in the healthcare sector. A web application was developed to improve medication therapy compliance and reduce the incidence of antibiotic resistance by enabling the dispatching, reporting, and monitoring of medications using blockchain technologies. The system architecture comprises three layers: a blockchain network powered by Hyperledger Fabric, an API gateway built using Golang and the go-zero code generator, and a user interface developed using React with Progressive Web App (PWA) features for enhanced user experience. Integration testing, unit testing and coverage testing were performed, and Google Lighthouse audits yielded positive results. The use of blockchain technologies in the project provides added benefits of security, reliability, availability, and transparency but also increases the complexity and resource requirements of the system.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Mark Johndy C. Coprada’s capstone project, "Implementing a Medication Tracking System Using Blockchain Technologies," addresses antibiotic resistance in the Philippines caused by self-medication and misuse. While existing systems like the electronic Drug Safety System digitize prescriptions, they do not track patient compliance. This project aims to bridge that gap by monitoring whether patients complete their prescribed therapies, providing real-time data to stakeholders such as pharmaceutical companies and the Department of Health’s Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Program.

The author developed a web application using a three-layer architecture. The backend utilizes Hyperledger Fabric blockchain for security and transparency, an API gateway built with Golang for communication via smart contracts, and a React-based Progressive Web App frontend that supports offline functionality. The system includes three routes: the Collector for patients to report intake, the Dispatcher for pharmacists to manage dispatches and QR codes, and the Inspector for public viewing of compliance data.

Testing through unit, integration, and Google Lighthouse audits showed that the system successfully creates a secure, transparent record of transactions without exposing sensitive personal identities. However, the findings indicate that blockchain introduces significant complexity, requiring intensive administration and high resource overhead. The project serves as a successful proof-of-concept for encouraging therapy completion. Future work should focus on using private data, moving to a production-ready environment, and conducting formal usability testing.

two:
The capstone project titled "Implementing a Medication Tracking System Using Blockchain Technologies" by Mark Johndy C. Coprada addresses the critical public health issue of antibiotic resistance in the Philippines. The author identifies a significant trend where Filipinos frequently self-medicate with antibiotics, often due to financial constraints or the availability of these drugs without a prescription. This behavior, coupled with a preference for "silver bullet" drugs over vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, accelerates the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. While previous government initiatives like the electronic Drug Safety System (eDSS) aimed to digitize prescriptions, they did not focus on tracking patient compliance. The author seeks to bridge this gap by creating a system that monitors whether patients actually complete their prescribed medication therapy.

The primary objective of the project is to improve medication therapy compliance and provide real-time data to stakeholders, such as pharmaceutical companies and the Department of Health’s Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Program (ARSP). By creating a transparent record of medication intake, the system aims to provide evidence of antibiotic misuse, which could serve as a tool to alarm the public about the risks of improper medication use.

To achieve this, the author developed a web application with a three-layer architecture. The backend is powered by a blockchain network using Hyperledger Fabric to ensure security, reliability, availability, and transparency. An API gateway was built using Golang and the go-zero code generator to facilitate communication between the user interface and the blockchain via smart contracts. The frontend was developed using React with TypeScript and implemented as a Progressive Web App (PWA). The PWA features allow the application to be installed on mobile devices and function offline, which is essential for maintaining reliable data collection in areas with unstable internet connectivity.

The system architecture is divided into three user-facing routes: the Collector, the Dispatcher, and the Inspector. The Collector route is designed for patients to report their medication intake; it uses local storage to save data when offline and syncs with the blockchain once a connection is re-established. The Dispatcher route is a dashboard for pharmacists to manage medication dispatches, which generate unique QR codes for patients to scan. The Inspector route is a publicly accessible interface that allows anyone to query and view medication compliance rates through visualized data, such as bar charts.

The project underwent several stages of assessment. Unit testing was performed on the chain code using the Golang testing library, and all test cases passed. The frontend underwent unit and coverage testing, with results deemed acceptable. Integration testing was conducted alongside implementation, and while end-to-end testing was bypassed due to time constraints, the author utilized "dogfooding" to ensure functionality. Google Lighthouse audits were also conducted, yielding positive results for all routes, though the Collector route required further optimization due to its heavy frontend logic.

The findings of the project demonstrate that blockchain technology can successfully create a secure, reliable, and transparent system for tracking medication compliance without exposing sensitive personal information. By focusing on the transactions (dispatches) rather than personal identities, the system maintains privacy while providing high-level data transparency. The author notes that while the implementation was successful as a proof-of-concept, the use of Hyperledger Fabric introduced significant complexity. The system required intensive administration and network operations, particularly when setting up nodes on specific hardware like the Apple M2 chipset.

In conclusion, the project successfully developed a digitized system that encourages patients to complete their medication therapy through their own devices. The author concludes that while blockchain provides the necessary non-functional requirements of security and availability that traditional relational databases might struggle to meet without significant compromise, the technology has a steep learning curve and high resource overhead. The implementation phase was extended due to the complexities of managing the Hyperledger Fabric framework.

The implications of this work suggest that blockchain could be a transformative tool for achieving a "high-trust society" and a digitized government. The author suggests that the principles used here could be applied to other sectors, such as blockchain-enabled digital elections. For future work, the author recommends investigating the use of private data and multiple chains within Hyperledger Fabric to further secure patient information and pharmacy credentials. Additionally, the author suggests moving from a local Kubernetes-based setup to a production-ready environment and conducting formal usability testing to improve the user experience and ensure long-term engagement.

title: Home Theater Room Acoustics Design Management System
abstract:
The company beneficiary of this project is in the sound engineering business and builds home theaters with the aim of creating the best listening experience for the audience. Part of this building process is to create a suitable acoustic design for the room being built. 

This process of creating an acoustically efficient enclosed area is not a new concept and there are systems that already provide the functionalities to design an acoustic room in one way or another. For the stakeholder’s case, existing tools are either difficult to maintain and too granular to use in one place. Even extensive software solutions that offer some of the same functionalities are not suitable for the business because of cost limitations and the absence of some necessary functionalities. Due to this, the company’s current process involves calculations using MS Excel and manual drafting of room drawings to visualize a room’s acoustical properties such as placement of speakers, acoustic panels, and view-optimized listening positions. 

The goal of this project is to build a web information system to manage Home Theater Room Acoustics Design projects and allow the functionalities to quickly design the acoustical properties of a room in one place. An important feature of this project is the simulation of a room’s acoustic impulse response to generate an audio representation of the room. This provides an approximate estimation of how the room will sound based on the specifications of the room. Furthermore, the system shows a visualization of the sound reflections that help locate acoustic panel placement and the visual mapping of room mode lines that are necessary to locate the low frequency resonance pressure locations to treat room modes that degrade a room’s listening experience. 

This project incorporates the latest cloud technologies in AWS, a reliable software stack of Django, Django REST Framework, MariaDB and Vue.js.

title: The Use of NFTs as Membership IDs for Professional Organizations
abstract:
Rationale: Traditional membership registration and renewals are prone to inefficiency and delay caused by the approval process and issuance of physical ID cards. The aim of this project is to digitize membership IDs of members of a professional organization into non-fungible tokens or NFTs to be stored on the blockchain. Certificates can also be issued as NFTs and, together with digital IDs, can be verified as authentic.

Problem: Both registration and renewals usually require members to fill up the same form and wait for the card to be distributed. This process is time-consuming, expensive, unsustainable, and is susceptible to replication or tampering.
Methodology: The project used the Hyperledger Fabric, an open source private and permissioned blockchain system. The strategy was to use the same programming language (JavaScript) for the client app, the backend api and the smart contract. It also explored the use of InterPlanetary File System or IPFS for the storage of NFT images while only their corresponding content identifiers or CIDs will be stored on the blockchain. 

Results: Membership IDs and certificates stored as NFTs makes them tamper-proof, enhances their provenance, and are always available for verification. These NFTs are unique and do not have to contain personal identifiable information as compared to those displayed in their physical counterparts.

Application/Implication: This project opens up the possibility of having these NFT IDs issued as verifiable credentials in a self-sovereign identity system. Other related professional organizations can join as members of the existing blockchain channel consequently contributing as peer nodes.

half:
Traditional membership registration and renewal processes in professional organizations are often inefficient, characterized by repetitive forms and lengthy approval delays. The use of physical membership cards introduces logistical burdens, such as production and postage costs, and presents sustainability issues due to unrecyclable plastic. Furthermore, physical cards pose security risks, as they can be lost, stolen, or tampered with, potentially exposing personal identifiable information.

This project proposes a digital solution using non-fungible tokens (NFTs) to represent membership IDs and certificates. By storing these credentials on a blockchain, the system aims to streamline renewals through automation and eliminate the burdens of physical cards. The methodology involved developing a web application using a multi-layered architecture. The system utilizes Hyperledger Fabric, a private and permissioned blockchain, to store NFTs and metadata, while the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) hosts the NFT images. Personal identifiable information is stored in a MongoDB Atlas document database. The application layer was built using Node.js and Express, with a client-side interface developed using React and Material UI.

Findings indicate that storing credentials as NFTs makes them tamper-proof and enhances provenance. Because NFTs are unique and stored on a decentralized ledger, they are available for verification without exposing personal identifiable information to third parties. The auto-renewal feature, tied to points earned from certificates, serves as a mechanism to increase active participation and timely renewals.
one:
Traditional membership registration and renewal processes in professional organizations are often inefficient and subject to significant delays. Members frequently face repetitive forms and lengthy approval processes. The issuance of physical membership cards involves production, labor, and postage costs, often taking weeks or even months to reach members, particularly those in foreign chapters. Physical cards also present sustainability issues due to unrecyclable plastic and pose security risks, as they can be lost, stolen, or tampered with, potentially exposing personal identifiable information.

To address these challenges, this project proposes a digital solution utilizing non-fungible tokens (NFTs) to represent membership IDs and certificates. By digitizing these credentials and storing them on a blockchain, the system aims to streamline the renewal process through automation and eliminate the logistical and environmental burdens of physical cards. The objective is to provide a platform where an organization can issue unique, tamper-proof, and instantly verifiable digital IDs and certificates that enhance provenance and security without exposing sensitive personal information.

The methodology involved developing a web application using a multi-layered architecture. The system utilizes Hyperledger Fabric, an open-source private and permissioned blockchain, to store the NFTs and their associated metadata. To optimize storage, the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) was used to host the actual NFT images, while only the corresponding content identifiers (CIDs) were recorded on the blockchain. Personal identifiable information (PII) and other application data were stored in a MongoDB Atlas document database. The application layer was built using Node.js and Express, while the client-side interface was developed as a responsive single-page application using React and Material UI. The system also integrates Mailjet for email notifications and JWT for secure communication.

Implementation included functional, usability, interface, and compatibility testing. Security testing using OWASP ZAP identified some vulnerabilities related to NGINX configuration and CSP implementation. User testing was conducted with seven respondents from the IECEP Singapore Chapter using the System Usability Scale (SUS), yielding an average SUS score of 59.6, which is categorized as a good rating. The project successfully demonstrated the ability to issue NFTs, automate membership renewals based on earned points, and provide a verification mechanism via QR codes.

Findings indicate that storing membership IDs and certificates as NFTs makes them tamper-proof and enhances their provenance. Because the NFTs are unique and stored on a decentralized ledger, they are always available for verification and do not require the exposure of personal identifiable information to third parties. The use of IPFS effectively minimizes storage costs, and the integration of a document database allows for efficient management of member profiles while respecting the right to be forgotten. The auto-renewal feature, tied to points earned from certificates, serves as a mechanism to increase active participation and timely renewals.

Traditional membership registration and renewal processes within professional organizations are often characterized by inefficiency and significant delays. Members are frequently required to complete repetitive forms for both initial registration and subsequent renewals, followed by a lengthy approval process. The subsequent issuance of physical membership cards involves production, labor, and postage costs, often taking weeks or even months to reach members, particularly those in foreign chapters. Furthermore, physical cards present sustainability issues due to the use of unrecyclable plastic and pose security risks, as they can be lost, stolen, or tampered with, potentially exposing personal identifiable information.

To address these challenges, this project proposes a digital solution that utilizes non-fungible tokens (NFTs) to represent membership IDs and certificates. By digitizing these credentials and storing them on a blockchain, the system aims to streamline the renewal process through automation and eliminate the logistical and environmental burdens of physical cards. The objective is to provide a platform where an organization can issue unique, tamper-proof, and instantly verifiable digital IDs and certificates that enhance provenance and security without exposing sensitive personal information.

The methodology employed for this project involved the development of a web application using a multi-layered architecture. The system utilizes Hyperledger Fabric, an open-source private and permissioned blockchain, to store the NFTs and their associated metadata. To optimize storage, the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) was used to host the actual NFT images, while only the corresponding content identifiers (CIDs) were recorded on the blockchain. Personal identifiable information (PII) and other application data were stored in a MongoDB Atlas document database to ensure high performance and a flexible schema. The application layer was built using Node.js and Express, while the client-side interface was developed as a responsive single-page application using React and Material UI. The system also integrates Mailjet for email notifications and JWT for secure communication.

The implementation included a comprehensive testing phase consisting of functional, usability, interface, and compatibility testing. The system was also subjected to security testing using OWASP ZAP, which identified some vulnerabilities related to NGINX configuration and CSP implementation. User testing was conducted with seven respondents from the IECEP Singapore Chapter using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The results yielded an average SUS score of 59.6, which is categorized as a good rating. The project successfully demonstrated the ability to issue NFTs, automate membership renewals based on earned points, and provide a verification mechanism via QR codes.

The findings indicate that storing membership IDs and certificates as NFTs makes them tamper-proof and enhances their provenance. Because the NFTs are unique and stored on a decentralized ledger, they are always available for verification and do not require the exposure of personal identifiable information to third parties. The use of IPFS effectively minimizes storage costs by using content addressing, and the integration of a document database allows for the efficient management of member profiles while respecting the right to be forgotten. The auto-renewal feature, tied to points earned from certificates, serves as a mechanism to increase active participation and timely renewals.

In conclusion, the project demonstrates that transitioning from physical to NFT-based digital IDs solves many issues associated with traditional membership management, including high manufacturing costs, logistical delays, and security vulnerabilities. The use of a private blockchain like Hyperledger Fabric ensures privacy and confidentiality while making credentials resistant to replication. This approach provides a secure, sustainable, and efficient alternative to traditional methods, offering instant gratification to members and a streamlined workflow for administrators.

The implications of this work suggest that this technology can be expanded into a self-sovereign identity system where NFT IDs serve as verifiable credentials. Additionally, the project opens the possibility for multiple professional organizations to join an existing blockchain channel, acting as peer nodes to create a collaborative ecosystem. Future work may involve transitioning to managed blockchain services, implementing an IPFS cluster for better data replication, and exploring the issuance of NFTs as part of a broader verifiable credential framework.

title: Conversing with Non-Human: A Narrative Inquiry on the Use of Meta AI and Canva among Public School Teachers
abstract: Anchored in narrative inquiry as a meaning-making process, this study restoryed and examined the narratives of 10 elementary school teachers in Laguna, exploring how they communicate with digital tools like Meta AI and Canva and how these tools shape their instructional practices. Although AI's role in the education landscape is increasing, only a few studies have explored teachers’ engagement with these applications and the motivation behind it. The effects that take place after interacting with these applications contribute to the personal changes in the teachers’ new reality, prompting the need for this study. Teachers’ utilization of the application was based on the perceived role and identity AI has in their lives, from being a mentor, doctor, personal assistant, etc., executing human-capable roles; nevertheless, using the information generated by AI is at the teachers’ discretion and trust of AI's capability, understanding AI has its limitations. Findings revealed that teachers primarily use AI for lesson planning, generating visual aids, and simplifying content preparation. They described prompting AI as an interactive, trial-and-error communication process that requires critical judgment. Teachers noted that AI helped them shift from traditional to digital methods, but also expressed skepticism about the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated outputs. The study also showed that AI reshapes teachers’ professional identity by expanding their role as content curators and decision-makers, rather than solely as authors. Human autonomy strengthens the regulation of AI application usage. These experiences shape the design of teaching materials and teachers’ openness to integrating emerging technologies into instruction.

Using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, the researcher explored the experiences of ten elementary school teachers through semi-structured, one-on-one interviews, observations, and reviews of AI prompts and instructional materials.

The findings reveal that teachers view communication with AI as an interactive, trial-and-error process requiring directness and specific themes. Educators must adjust AI-generated content to ensure it is age-appropriate for their students. Meta AI and Canva facilitate a transition from traditional to digital methods by providing instant results, which significantly expedites tasks like lesson planning and creating visual aids, thereby reducing work-related stress. However, skepticism remains regarding the accuracy and authenticity of AI outputs, leading teachers to cross-reference information with traditional resources to prevent plagiarism and student over-reliance.

Teachers perceive AI as a personal assistant, mentor, or even a "friend," which reshapes their professional identity from sole authors to content curators and decision-makers. The study concludes that AI creates a partnership where human autonomy and critical judgment are essential to validate technological output. Consequently, there is a vital need for teachers to develop digital fitness and critical literacy.

two:
The thesis titled "Conversing with Non-Human: A Narrative Inquiry on the Use of Meta AI and Canva among Public School Teachers" by Lou Marie Karen Q. Macabasco investigates the evolving relationship between educators and generative artificial intelligence. As digital tools become increasingly integrated into daily life, this study explores how public school teachers in Laguna, Philippines, utilize Meta AI and Canva to support their instructional practices and how these interactions influence their professional roles.

The research problem centers on the rapid advancement of AI and the need to understand how teachers engage with these tools. While AI offers significant potential for efficiency, there is a critical need to examine the motivations behind its use, the nature of the communication between humans and machines, and the subsequent effects on teaching practices and professional identity. The study specifically addresses how teachers communicate with these digital tools and how such interactions shape their instructional methods.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative narrative inquiry design. This approach focused on the individual experiences and stories of ten elementary school teachers in Laguna. The participants were selected based on their experience in traditional teaching methods and their active use of Meta AI, Canva, or both. Data were gathered through semi-structured, one-on-one interviews, which allowed for in-depth exploration of the participants' reflections and insights. The researcher also observed non-verbal cues during interviews and reviewed screenshots of AI prompts and the resulting instructional materials to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the teachers' experiences. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, involving open and axial coding to identify patterns in the narratives.

The findings are organized into several key themes. Regarding the communication process, teachers described prompting AI as an interactive, trial-and-error process. They emphasized the importance of being "straight to the point" and providing specific themes to avoid irrelevant results. Teachers also noted the necessity of adjusting AI-generated content to ensure it is appropriate for their specific learners, such as simplifying complex terminology for kindergarten or grade one students.

In terms of workflow shifts, the study found that AI tools facilitate a significant transition from traditional to digital methods. Teachers reported that Meta AI and Canva provide "instant generated results," which significantly expedites tasks like lesson planning, researching information, and creating visual aids. This shift has reduced the time required for certain tasks from hours to mere minutes, thereby reducing work-related stress.

However, the study also revealed significant skepticism regarding AI communication. Teachers expressed concerns regarding the accuracy, authenticity, and legitimacy of AI-generated information. Many participants reported a need to cross-reference AI outputs with traditional resources, such as textbooks, to verify correctness. Furthermore, there was a strong emphasis on regulating AI usage to prevent issues like plagiarism and to ensure that students do not become overly reliant on technology, which could undermine their study habits and cognitive development.

The perceived identity of AI varied among participants, with many viewing the technology as a personal assistant, a mentor, or even a "friend" for quick advice on non-academic matters, such as parenting or health. This interaction has profound ontological implications, as it reshapes the professional identity of teachers. Rather than being the sole authors of content, teachers are increasingly becoming content curators and decision-makers who must critically evaluate and refine machine-generated suggestions.

The study concludes that while AI tools like Meta AI and Canva offer transformative benefits for instructional efficiency and creativity, they do not replace human intelligence. Instead, they create a partnership where human autonomy and critical judgment are essential to regulate and validate the technology's output. The integration of AI is changing the reality of the teaching profession, shifting the focus toward managing and curating digital information.

The implications of this research suggest that as AI becomes a permanent fixture in education, there is a vital need for teachers to develop "digital fitness" and critical literacy. The study highlights the importance of a collaborative approach between teachers and parents to guide students in the ethical and effective use of AI. Furthermore, the findings suggest that for AI to be effectively integrated into the teaching-learning process, the focus must remain on the human elements of education—ensuring that technology serves to enhance, rather than diminish, the quality of instruction and the development of the learner.

title: Investigating Knowledge Management Through a Socio-Technical Systems Lens: The Case of an Academic Unit of a National University in the Philippines
abstract:
Through a socio-technical systems lens, this study investigated how an academic unit of a national university in the Philippines manages its knowledge. Guided by Trist’s (1981) Socio-technical Systems Theory and Toracco’s KM Model (2000), and employing a case study design, the research examined the social, technical, and environmental subsystems of KM in an academic unit of a national university in the Philippines. Data were collected through a survey with staff (n=84), in-depth interviews, and a focus group discussion, and were analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis.

In the social subsystem, KM is defined as embedded in the quadfunction, combining data, information, and KM systems, a systematic process, and contributing to organizational effectiveness. Perceived benefits include improved performance, empowerment, recognition, efficiency, competitiveness, and cohesiveness. Organizational culture assessment revealed current and preferred orientations toward clan and hierarchy culture types, although with a marginal difference from adhocracy and market cultures, suggesting an almost balanced organizational culture.

The technical subsystem was contextualized through Alavi and Leidner’s (2001) KM processes (generation, storage/retrieval, sharing, and application) while four additional processes emerged: linkaging/networking, systems evaluation, safeguarding/stewardship, and co-creation. Smartphones were the main tool for generation (82.14%), record books for storage (73.1%), and email for sharing and application (78.57% and 69.05%).

The environmental subsystem was shaped by university policies, global and national agendas, and the academic unit as a subsystem. SWOT analysis revealed strengths in competitiveness and resource accessibility, weaknesses in integration and security, opportunities in collaboration and funding, and threats such as brain drain, shifting policies, and global agricultural challenges.

Overall, findings suggest that organizational culture affects the implementation of KM processes, including the emerging KM processes. The academic unit can strategically cultivate clan culture to foster collaboration with the hierarchy culture type, to put structures in place enabling KM. Stronger integration across subsystems, especially through an institutionalized DIK system and enhanced organizational adaptability, could further enhance organizational competitiveness and contribute to institutional and larger development goals.

title: Religious Communication Needs and Academic Persistence of Vocational Students in Banilad Center for Professional Development
abstract:
Recent trends on rising dropout rates in the Philippines indicate the critical need to offer vulnerable youth with opportunities to access education and employable skills. Such opportunities are provided by Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) centers which are more accessible to marginalized students with limited financial resources to pursue higher studies.

This study analyzed the role of religious communication needs in improving the academic persistence of vocational students in Banilad Center for Professional Development (BCPD), an all-girls TVET center located in Cebu City, Philippines. Quantitative results showed that there was a moderately high level of academic persistence and significantly high level of satisfaction with the current religious communication in BCPD. Based on the Spearman’s Rank Correlation Coefficient, there was a moderately positive association between the two variables of this study. Furthermore, qualitative results revealed that the majority of the students, including those who did not identify as “religious”, agreed that the current religious communication offered in BCPD played a beneficial role in their academic
persistence.

Ultimately, this study explored religious communication as an alternative intervention strategy to address increasing dropout rates and out-of-school youth rates in the Philippines by providing vulnerable youth with access to higher quality TVET programs that meet their needs, including religious communication needs.

The research utilized a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, incorporating a cross-sectional survey of 54 female Hotel and Restaurant Services students and seven focus group discussions with 16 students. The study is grounded in Ansie Slabbert’s Religious Communication Model.

Quantitative findings revealed a moderately high level of academic persistence and a significantly high level of satisfaction with current religious communication. A Spearman’s Rank Correlation Coefficient analysis showed a moderately positive association between the two variables, supporting the hypothesis that meeting religious communication needs leads to higher levels of academic persistence. The thesis titled "Religious Communication Needs and Academic Persistence of Vocational Students in Banilad Center for Professional Development" by Nicholette Jeanne P. Legaspi investigates the relationship between religious communication and the academic persistence of female vocational students in Cebu City, Philippines. The study is situated within the context of rising dropout rates among vulnerable youth in the Philippines, particularly females. While poverty is a primary driver for leaving school, the researcher notes that lack of interest and existential ambiguity during adolescence also contribute to these trends. Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) centers like the Banilad Center for Professional Development (BCPD) serve as critical pathways for marginalized students to gain employable skills, and the study explores whether addressing religious communication needs can serve as an intervention to improve student retention and persistence.

The research problem focuses on two primary questions: the degree of association between students' level of academic persistence and their satisfaction with current religious communication at BCPD, and how religious communication specifically improves academic persistence. To address these, the researcher utilized a convergent parallel mixed-methods design. The quantitative component involved a cross-sectional survey of 54 female Hotel and Restaurant Services (HRS) students using scales adapted from Thalib et al. (2018) for academic persistence and Ansie Slabbert’s (2022) Religious Communication Model. The qualitative component consisted of seven focus group discussions (FGDs) with 16 randomly selected students to explore the lived experiences and perceptions of the participants.

The theoretical framework is grounded in Ansie Slabbert’s (2022) Religious Communication Model, which posits that religious communication is a symbolic interaction process between an individual and God that meets ontological needs. This model emphasizes three broad realities: external (interpersonal), internal (intrapersonal), and religious (transcendental). The researcher hypothesized that as religious communication needs are met, the effectiveness of communication increases, which in turn leads to higher levels of academic persistence.

Quantitative findings revealed a moderately high level of academic persistence (72.39/100) and a significantly high level of satisfaction with current religious communication (84.83/100). A Spearman’s Rank Correlation Coefficient analysis showed a moderately positive association (rs = +.58, p = 0.001) between the two variables, supporting the research hypothesis. Qualitative analysis through thematic analysis identified three major themes regarding the role of religious communication: it inspires, it empowers, and it edifies. Students reported that religious communication helped them find meaning in life, provided support during life stressors, and encouraged strong work ethics.

The qualitative results further categorized the impact of religious communication into three relational dimensions: Love for God, Love for others, and Love for self. Students described how God is at the center of their lives, often attributing personal successes, such as receiving scholarships or finding time to study, to divine intervention. Religious communication was found to help students manage problems and failures, providing them with the resilience needed to continue their studies despite socioeconomic challenges.

The study concludes that there is a significant positive relationship between meeting religious communication needs and academic persistence. By fulfilling these needs, BCPD helps students derive meaning from their existence, which serves as a powerful motivator to complete their vocational training. The findings suggest that religious communication acts as an edifying force, promoting values like honesty and hard work that are essential for both academic success and future employment.

Based on these findings, the researcher offers several implications and recommendations. The study suggests that religious communication can be an effective alternative intervention strategy for schools facing high dropout rates. The researcher recommends that future studies investigate whether gender acts as a moderating variable by comparing results in all-boys, all-girls, and co-educational vocational environments. Additionally, the researcher suggests that further research should explore the causal effects of religious communication through long-term studies and the implementation of social mobilization programs that focus on providing spiritual and moral formation to at-risk youth.

title: Building Community Resilience: A Case Study on the Localization of the Early Warning System
abstract:
The Philippines has been the world’s most at-risk country since 2022. While disasters cannot be controlled, its negative impacts can be mitigated. One of these is through the institutionalization and operationalization of the Early Warning System (EWS). The elements of EWS namely 1.) Risk Knowledge, 2.) Monitoring and Forecasting, 3.) Dissemination and Communication, and 4.) Preparedness to respond, are of equal significance because each contributes for the safety and resilience of the community.

In the Philippines, the creation and institutionalization of the EWS in every Local Government Unit (LGU) is clearly defined in the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010. The LGUs from the provincial down to the barangay level are obligated to operate a multi-hazard EWS to provide accurate and timely advice for immediate response, and for the information of the general public. The LGUs play a vital role in Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, this includes the creation, institutionalization, and communication of the EWS.

The Philippines having a diverse ethno-linguistic culture makes the communication of EWS also challenging. A lot of studies have explored the preparedness of the LGUs for disasters but research focusing on the communication aspect of DRRM and of EWS, is quite limited.

This research qualitatively explores the communication of EWS of the subject Local Government Unit through Key Informant Interviews to individuals who have a vital role in their communication process. The subject of this study, as the regional hub in Western Visayas and an awardee in disaster resilience, employs various strategies like the localization of its EWS to build a resilient community. The localization of the EWS is not only limited to the language used in communicating its early warning messages, it also pertains to the established mechanisms to ensure that it is responsive, inclusive, and sustainable.

It is crucial to explore and analyze the communication of the EWS to ensure that it is functional and responsive to the needs of the public. With the right and timely information, everybody will be guided as well to do the right actions.

The results of this qualitative research are vital in strengthening the operationalization and the communication of the EWS in the locality. The localization of the EWS, as an innovation, strengthens community resilience as it empowers the community. It ultimately contributes to the development and implementation of an inclusive, sustainable, and innovative DRRM and EWS.

This research is aligned with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, specifically No. 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), No. 13 (Climate Action), and No. 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions).

The thesis titled "Building Community Resilience: A Case Study on the Localization of the Early Warning System" by Aljohn T. Torreta investigates how local government units (LGUs) communicate early warning systems (EWS) to foster community resilience. Using Iloilo City as a case study, the research explores the communication processes, strategies, and challenges involved in disseminating critical disaster information to a diverse population.

**Problem and Context**
The Philippines is identified as one of the most disaster-prone countries globally due to its high exposure to various hazards. While the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 mandates that LGUs operate multi-hazard EWS, research indicates significant gaps in the "Dissemination and Communication" aspect of these systems. A primary problem is that technical, scientific information often fails to reach or be understood by the public, as seen in historical instances where terms like "storm surge" were misunderstood by residents. Furthermore, the diverse ethno-linguistic landscape of the Philippines makes standardized communication difficult. While the national government utilizes platforms like PhilAWARE, there is a critical need to understand how these high-level warnings are localized and communicated at the grassroots level to ensure they are inclusive, understandable, and capable of prompting immediate action.

**Methodology**
The study employed a qualitative case study design to provide an in-depth exploration of the communication phenomenon within Iloilo City. The researcher utilized purposive sampling to conduct Key Informant Interviews (KII) with six key participants: the Head of the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO), the Head of the Public Information Office (PIO), the President of the Liga ng mga Barangay, a DILG officer, the President of the City Hall Press Corps, and a representative from the academe. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic analysis, employing an inductive approach where themes emerged directly from the interview data. The study was grounded in the theoretical frameworks of participatory communication and social mobilization, emphasizing the role of stakeholders as active participants rather than passive recipients of information.

**Findings**
The research identified several key components regarding the communication of the EWS in Iloilo City:

The communication process follows a cascading mechanism. Information originates from the City Government (CDRRMO and PIO) and is disseminated through various channels, including social media, press releases, and media advisories. From the city level, information is passed to the barangay level through the Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Section (BDRRMS). At the grassroots level, barangay officials use interpersonal communication, such as house-to-house visits by Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) and tanods, as well as technological tools like group chats (Messenger) and Public Address (PA) systems.

The most common hazards communicated include flooding, droughts (specifically heat index), and fire prevention. While the city provides general information, the barangay level focuses on immediate local threats.

The study found that localization is a primary strategy. This includes translating messages into Hiligaynon to ensure they are easily understood and using color-coded alert levels (yellow for caution, orange for preparation, and red for evacuation) to simplify technical warnings. Interpersonal communication remains a vital strategy, as it provides a sense of safety and direct engagement with the residents.

Several challenges were identified, including the technical complexity of certain warnings (such as volcanic eruptions) which are difficult to translate into local dialects. There is also a noted lack of "catchy" or impactful messaging that can grab attention. Furthermore, participants highlighted the difficulty of maintaining sustainability in communication efforts due to political transitions; when new barangay officials are elected, previous training and priorities may not be carried over.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that the localization of the EWS—through language translation and the use of simplified, community-based mechanisms—is essential for building community resilience. When communication is localized and involves the community, residents transition from being mere beneficiaries to active participants who can assist in monitoring hazards and making decisions. However, the research also concludes that the effectiveness of these systems is often hindered by the technical nature of the information and the lack of standardized, simplified training for local officials.

The implications of this research are significant for DRRM practitioners and policymakers. There is a clear need to standardize and simplify the training provided to barangay officials so they can effectively translate technical data into actionable local messages. The study suggests that EWS should be more "people-centered," utilizing more engaging and "catchy" communication methods to ensure information is not ignored. Additionally, the findings highlight the importance of institutionalizing these communication protocols into formal plans to ensure sustainability despite changes in local political leadership. Ultimately, strengthening the localization of EWS is a vital step toward creating an inclusive and responsive disaster management framework that empowers even the most vulnerable sectors of society.
