title: Participatory Design and Testing of Food Handling and Entrepreneurship Guidebook for Bukidnon Women
abstract: Designing a material with no regard to user’s needs become useless in the long run. State universities are mandated to do extension work as one of its functions. Usually, extension materials are developed by extension workers without the participation of its intended users. These materials then do not serve its purpose. Thus, this study on participatory design and testing of a guidebook with the Bukidnon women discovered how a learning material can be carried out from an extension project facilitated by a state university. Following the telling-making-enacting framework, it allowed the participants to empathize with the problems encountered in understanding the message content and design produced by a state university, and defined the problem in a user-centered way. It proceeded to ideating and creating a prototype of its own desired material with the significant role of the designer and non -designers’ ideas combined. Exploring participatory design and testing for an improved extension material designed by an intended community yielded positive results when tested by the prospect end-users. Results also showed a unified acceptability, strong agreement on comprehensibility with clear messages in the use of images and texts, provided clear instruction due to the local dialect used, Binukid. Suffice to say that the jointly designed guidebook posed high interest for the next endusers being viewed as an economic and empowering tool in their lives. Hence, participatory design and testing as a method allowed the participants to arrive at agreements on their desired parameters in developing the material. Results as well led to the development of a communication framework for extension workers whose outputs include content and design review report, extension material design plan, extension material, pretesting results, and copyrighted material.

This study addresses the failure of extension materials developed by state universities when they are created without the active participation of target users. To bridge the gap between information producers and recipients, the research focuses on the participatory design and testing of a guidebook for women in Bukidnon, centered on food handling and entrepreneurship. By shifting from a top-down approach to a user-centered approach, the study explores how collaborative processes can improve the effectiveness of extension materials.

The methodology utilized the telling-making-enacting framework, allowing participants to empathize with existing communication problems, define issues from a user perspective, and engage in ideation and prototype creation. This process combined the ideas of professional designers and non-designers to ensure the final material reflected the community's specific needs.

Findings indicate that participatory design and testing yield positive results. The developed guidebook achieved unified acceptability among participants, who noted that the messages were clear due to the effective combination of images and text. Additionally, the use of the local dialect, Binukid, ensured instructions were accessible. Participants viewed the guidebook as an economic and empowering tool, fostering a sense of community ownership. Consequently, the study led to the development of a communication framework for extension workers, suggesting that participatory design can transform extension work into a collaborative process that produces effective, culturally appropriate, and empowering educational tools.

The participatory design and testing method proved successful because it allowed the participants to reach agreements on the specific parameters required for developing the material. By involving the users in the design process, the resulting material was not just a piece of information, but a tool that the community felt ownership over.

The implications of this research are significant for extension workers and academic institutions. The results led to the development of a specific communication framework for extension workers. This framework includes a structured process for producing outputs such as content and design review reports, extension material design plans, the extension materials themselves, pretesting results, and copyrighted materials. Ultimately, the study suggests that moving toward participatory design can transform extension work from a one-way delivery of information into a collaborative process that produces highly effective, culturally appropriate, and empowering educational tools.

title: Digital Health Communication: Narratives of Health Patients using Telemedicine for Primary Healthcare in Lucena City, Philippines
abstract: This study analyzed narratives of health patients who have used telemedicine during the Covid-19 pandemic starting 2020. Focusing on the relation between society and technology, it is underpinned by the social determinism and the social construction theory and is qualitative in nature. Results showed that the participants used telemedicine during the pandemic because they needed to continuously connect with their doctors. They became familiar with telemedicine in different ways - it was advised by the doctor, it was seen on Facebook, or it has become prevalent even at work and in their Church. From the conventional personal visits to the doctor in their clinics or in the hospital, participants needed to learn and adapt to online medical treatment. Some of them who never had Viber (an online messaging app) created one while some extended the use of their Messenger accounts to constantly talk to their doctors. Because telemedicine is digital in nature, it lacks physical examination of patient by the doctor. Hence, the participants were compelled to become technology savvy and more diligent in monitoring their health by carefully taking note of their symptoms, such as their oxygen and heart rates. The participants also had to adjust to the other demands of technology for health consultation. Nonetheless, the participants have apparently embraced telemedicine as they claim that they are satisfied with its use. Even after pandemic, they continue to use telemedicine and now view it as a good alternative for basic healthcare because it is more convenient, faster, safer, and in many cases, cheaper. So, while telemedicine encouraged them to use technology, they also chose what technology to use or a combination thereof that suited their needs. Further, they improvised the technology to overcome any limitations that would help them transact with their doctors or nurses in the most efficient and effective ways.

The study titled "Digital Health Communication: Narratives of Health Patients using Telemedicine for Primary Healthcare in Lucena City, Philippines" by Korina Marie N. Alibuyog investigates the experiences of patients utilizing telemedicine during the Covid-19 pandemic. The research focuses on the intersection of society and technology, specifically examining how individuals navigate digital health communication tools when traditional in-person medical consultations become restricted or altered due to global health crises.

The context of this research is rooted in the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, a period that necessitated shifts in how healthcare services were delivered and accessed. In Lucena City, Philippines, the sudden shift from conventional personal visits to clinics and hospitals toward digital platforms forced patients to adapt to new modes of medical interaction. The study is framed by the theories of social determinism and social construction, exploring how technology influences social behavior and how social needs, in turn, shape the way technology is adopted and utilized within a community.

Methodologically, the study is qualitative in nature, focusing on the narratives of health patients. By analyzing these personal accounts, the researcher sought to understand the transition from traditional healthcare models to digital ones. The study examines the motivations for adopting telemedicine, the specific technologies employed, the challenges faced during the transition, and the long-term attitudes of patients toward these digital tools.

The findings reveal that the primary driver for using telemedicine was the necessity to maintain continuous connection with doctors during the pandemic. The transition to digital health was not uniform but occurred through various social channels; participants became familiar with telemedicine through direct advice from doctors, exposure to information on Facebook, or through its increasing prevalence in workplaces and religious organizations. This indicates that social networks played a significant role in the dissemination and normalization of digital health tools.

The research highlights a significant learning curve for patients who had to adapt from conventional face-to-face medical visits to online treatments. This adaptation involved mastering new digital communication tools. For instance, some participants had to create new accounts on messaging applications like Viber, while others expanded their use of existing platforms, such as Facebook Messenger, to facilitate constant communication with their medical providers.

A critical finding concerns the limitations of the digital medium. Because telemedicine is inherently digital, it lacks the physical examination component of a traditional doctor-patient encounter. To compensate for this absence of physical contact, participants were compelled to become more technology-savvy and diligent in self-monitoring. Patients took on a more active role in their own care by carefully tracking and noting their own symptoms, specifically monitoring vital signs such as oxygen levels and heart rates to provide accurate data to their doctors. Furthermore, patients had to adjust to various other technical demands required to facilitate successful health consultations.

Despite these challenges and the necessity of self-monitoring, the findings show that participants have embraced telemedicine. The narratives indicate a high level of satisfaction with the technology. Rather than viewing it as a temporary emergency measure, participants have continued to use telemedicine even after the peak of the pandemic. It has transitioned from a necessity to a preferred alternative for basic healthcare. The participants cited several benefits that contribute to this sustained use, including increased convenience, faster service, improved safety, and, in many instances, lower costs compared to traditional methods.

The study also highlights the agency of the patients in the digital health landscape. While telemedicine encouraged the use of technology, patients were not passive recipients; they actively chose which technologies or combinations of technologies best suited their specific needs. Additionally, patients demonstrated a capacity for improvisation, finding ways to overcome technological limitations to ensure they could transact with doctors or nurses in the most efficient and effective ways possible.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that the pandemic acted as a catalyst for the adoption of telemedicine in Lucena City, forcing a shift in patient behavior and health monitoring practices. The transition required patients to develop new digital literacies and take on more responsibility for monitoring their own physiological symptoms. However, the perceived benefits of convenience, speed, safety, and cost-effectiveness have led to the long-term integration of telemedicine into the local healthcare landscape.

The implications of this research suggest that telemedicine is no longer just a crisis-response tool but a viable, permanent alternative for primary healthcare. The findings imply that as digital health becomes more integrated, there is a growing need to support patient digital literacy and to recognize the proactive role patients play in managing their health through technology. The ability of patients to improvise and select tools that meet their specific needs suggests that future healthcare delivery models should remain flexible and user-centric to accommodate the diverse ways in which technology is utilized in social and medical contexts.

title: A CSR Practitioner's Communication Practices in Engaging the Local Community in Watershed Conservation: An Autoethnography
abstract:
This study aimed to answer the following questions: What are the CSR practitioner’s communication practices in engaging the local community in watershed conservation and what are the underlying views and assumptions of the communication practices? By positioning himself as the primary subject, the researcher employed autoethnography to deeply explore his interactions and communication practices used to engage a local community. Autoethnography as a research framework and methodology not only allows for an in-depth and reflective examination of his personal experiences but also provides a rich, nuanced understanding of the complexities involved in community engagement.

The research methodology included gathering and review of the CSR practitioner’s personal journals during the implementation of the project from 2022- 2023, as well as a thorough review of related literature.

Thematic analysis was employed to identify and explore recurring themes and provide insights into the patterns of his engagement with the local community. His journals were classified into two vignettes which included his communication practices when in project implementation and when the community is in conflict.

Four communication practices during project implementation emerged in the analysis of data: engaging and empowering community leaders, integrating the local community’s wisdom and traditions; engaging the community in a long-term partnership; and recognizing literacy constraints. Each of these practices is made up of sub-practices, including:

● Sharing roles and responsibilities with the community
● Letting the community lead the completion of the project
● Including local voices in decision-making
● Inviting community leaders to educate employees and stakeholders
● Being mindful of local customs and traditions
● Respecting hierarchical structures
● Using the local language
● Involving community members in the storytelling process
● Bridging the language barrier
● Visiting the community to personally connect
● Immersing in the local community

The findings from this study can inform more effective CSR communication practices and contribute to the growing body of research on the role of communication in fostering successful community engagement and partnerships in
sustainability initiatives.

Using autoethnography as the primary methodology, the researcher conducted a reflective examination of personal experiences through a review of literature and an analysis of personal journals written between 2022 and 2023. The data was organized into two vignettes focusing on communication during active project implementation and during periods of conflict, with thematic analysis used to identify recurring patterns.

The findings reveal four primary communication practices used during project implementation. First, practitioners engage and empower community leaders by sharing roles and responsibilities. Second, they integrate local wisdom and traditions by respecting local customs and hierarchical structures. Third, they engage the community in long-term partnerships by including local voices in decision-making and inviting leaders to educate stakeholders. Fourth, they recognize literacy constraints by using local languages, employing storytelling, and immersing themselves in the community to connect personally.

The study concludes that effective CSR communication requires a shift from top-down instruction to a collaborative model. By moving beyond mere information dissemination toward active participation and cultural respect, practitioners can foster robust connections and successful long-term partnerships in environmental stewardship.

title: No Teacher Left Offline: A Hermeneutic Study of Online Communication and Relationship Building for Near-Retirement Educators at Universities in Manila, Philippines
abstract:
The pandemic forced a shift in the mode of delivery in education. Forcing everyone to migrate to the online platform just to make learning and communication possible. The platform is one thing, but paying attention to the sender of the message in the educational context is also a must to ensure effectiveness despite the trials. With near-retirement educators or those who belong to the baby boomer generation regarded as the tenured and respected individuals in the field, we must ensure support and assistance to help them navigate their way through an unmastered territory. This study seeks to understand the experiences of near-retirement educators and how they adapt to the obligatory online communication setup for relationship-building with their students.

Through purposeful sampling, four near-retirement educators were invited to a one-on-one interview where they shared narratives during the shift to fully online communication. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and following the Hermeneutic approach, analyzed and interpreted.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The global pandemic necessitated a sudden migration to online platforms for all educational participants to maintain learning and communication. While platform availability is a fundamental requirement, the effectiveness of this transition depends heavily on the sender of the message. This is particularly critical for near-retirement educators, often belonging to the baby boomer generation. Although these individuals are typically regarded as tenured and respected members of the academic field, they face significant challenges when navigating unmastered digital territories.

The research addresses the difficulty faced by these veteran educators as they adapt to the obligatory online communication setup. The study seeks to understand the lived experiences of near-retirement educators and how they manage relationship-building with their students through digital mediums. To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative research design using a hermeneutic approach. Through purposeful sampling, four near-retirement educators participated in one-on-one interviews regarding the shift to fully online communication.

The findings highlight the complexities of maintaining professional relationships in a virtual environment. The study emphasizes that the shift to online platforms is not merely a technical change but a social and relational one that impacts how tenured educators connect with their students. Conclusions underscore the importance of providing targeted support for educators nearing retirement to ensure they are not left offline, maintaining the continuity of mentorship and academic stability.

title: Generation Z's Awareness and Willingness to Engage in Climate Change Adaptation: A Case Study in Koronadal City, South Cotabato
abstract:
Climate change has continued to pose significant risks to communities, making the engagement of younger generations essential in advancing adaptation efforts. This study examined the awareness, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and willingness of Generation Z college students in Koronadal City to participate in climate change adaptation, guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). This study assessed students’ climate change knowledge, their behavioral predictors, and their willingness to engage in climate-friendly practices. 
A quantitative survey design was used to gather data. The respondents were college students born between 1999 and 2005 enrolled in private universities in Koronadal City. Findings revealed varying levels of climate literacy and concern among students. Attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted willingness to engage in climate-friendly behaviors, while knowledge along was not always a strong predictor. This was consistent with trends presented in related literature. Year level differences also showed variations in awareness and behavioral intention.
In conclusion, the Generation Z college students’ psychological, social, and contextual factors influenced their willingness to participate in climate change adaptation more strongly than knowledge along. Based on the results, implementation of targeted climate education programs, community outreach activities, and improvements to curriculum content that would strengthen students’ climate awareness, adaptive behavior, and long-term environmental engagement are included in the recommendations.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
Climate change threatens global sustainability, impacting ecosystems and human societies. In the Philippines, a country frequently affected by typhoons and floods, understanding how youth respond to these challenges is vital. This study investigated the awareness, attitudes, social norms, and perceived behavioral control of Generation Z college students in Koronadal City, South Cotabato, and how these factors influence their willingness to participate in climate change adaptation. Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, the research used a quantitative survey design to assess students born between 1999 and 2005 enrolled in private universities.

The findings revealed that respondents possess a high level of awareness regarding climate change, with a weighted mean of 4.34. Attitudes toward climate change adaptation were strongly positive, with a weighted mean of 4.64. Subjective norms showed a positive social influence with a mean of 4.24, while perceived behavioral control was moderate, with a mean of 4.05. The overall willingness of students to engage in climate change adaptation was very high, with a mean of 4.45.

Statistical testing confirmed that higher levels of awareness are significantly associated with a higher willingness to engage in climate-friendly actions. Multiple linear regression showed that attitudes and subjective norms are significant predictors of willingness, while perceived behavioral control was not a significant predictor. No significant differences in awareness, attitudes, or willingness were found across different student year levels. The results highlight an attitude-behavior gap where high awareness and positive attitudes do not always translate into immediate action due to systemic and personal constraints.

Climate change poses a significant threat to global sustainability, impacting ecosystems, economies, and human societies. Generation Z, born between 1995 and 2012, is at the forefront of this crisis due to their technological literacy and access to information. In the Philippines, a country frequently impacted by climate-related disasters like typhoons and floods, understanding how youth perceive and respond to these challenges is vital. This study addresses the gap in local-level research regarding the awareness, attitudes, social norms, and perceived behavioral control of Generation Z college students in Koronadal City, South Cotabato, and how these factors influence their willingness to participate in climate change adaptation.

Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, the research aimed to measure awareness of climate change and adaptation strategies, assess psychological and social predictors of behavior, determine the level of willingness to engage in climate-friendly practices, and identify significant differences across year levels. Using a quantitative survey design and convenience sampling, the study surveyed college students born between 1999 and 2005 enrolled in private universities in Koronadal City. Data were collected through structured questionnaires via Google Forms and physical copies, utilizing a 5-point Likert scale.

The findings revealed that respondents possess a high level of awareness regarding climate change, with a weighted mean of 4.34. Students strongly recognize the severity of the issue and understand its causes and effects, though they reported lower familiarity with national or local programs. Attitudes toward climate change adaptation were strongly positive, with a weighted mean of 4.64, indicating a strong belief in the importance of individual action. Subjective norms showed a positive social influence with a mean of 4.24, with professors and teachers noted as significant motivators. Perceived behavioral control was moderate, with a mean of 4.05, as some students felt limited by external factors or personal constraints.

The overall willingness of Generation Z students to engage in climate change adaptation was very high, with a mean of 4.45. Students expressed strong intention to participate in activities such as recycling, following government environmental policies, and voting for leaders who prioritize climate action. Statistical testing confirmed that higher levels of awareness are significantly associated with a higher willingness to engage in climate-friendly actions. Multiple linear regression showed that attitudes and subjective norms are significant predictors of willingness, while perceived behavioral control was not a significant predictor in this specific model. No significant differences in awareness, attitudes, or willingness were found across different student year levels.

The results highlight an attitude-behavior gap, where high awareness and positive attitudes do not always translate into immediate action due to systemic and personal constraints like cost, access, and convenience. While students are willing to take individual actions like recycling, they are less ready for behaviors requiring significant personal sacrifice. The study recommends that educational institutions integrate practical climate change education into the curriculum to build self-efficacy. Additionally, community-based programs, campus sustainability initiatives, and institutional policies, such as banning single-use plastics, could help remove barriers preventing students from translating environmental concern into consistent, long-term adaptive behaviors.

Climate change represents a significant threat to global sustainability, affecting ecosystems, economies, and human societies. Generation Z, a demographic cohort born between 1995 and 2012, is positioned at the forefront of this crisis due to their technological literacy and access to information. In the Philippines, a country frequently impacted by climate-related disasters like typhoons and floods, understanding how the youth perceive and respond to these challenges is vital. This study specifically addresses the gap in local-level research regarding the awareness, attitudes, social norms, and perceived behavioral control of Generation Z college students in Koronadal City, South Cotabato, and how these factors influence their willingness to participate in climate change adaptation.

The research was guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, which posits that an individual's intention to perform a behavior is driven by three constructs: attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. The study aimed to measure the level of awareness regarding climate change and adaptation strategies, assess the psychological and social predictors of behavior, determine the level of willingness to engage in climate-friendly practices, and identify any significant differences in these variables across different year levels.

To achieve these objectives, a quantitative survey design was employed using convenience sampling. The participants were college students born between 1999 and 2005 enrolled in private universities in Koronadal City. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms and physical copies. The instrument utilized a 5-point Likert scale to measure awareness, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and willingness. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, multiple linear regression, and One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to test the research hypotheses.

The findings revealed that the respondents possess a high level of awareness regarding climate change, with a weighted mean of 4.34. Students strongly recognize the severity of the issue and have a clear conceptual understanding of its causes and effects. However, they reported lower familiarity with national or local programs addressing climate change. Attitudes toward climate change adaptation were strongly positive, with a weighted mean of 4.64, indicating a strong belief in the importance of individual action. Subjective norms showed a positive social influence with a mean of 4.24, where professors and teachers were noted as significant motivators for sustainable practices. Perceived behavioral control was moderate, with a mean of 4.05, as some students felt limited by external factors or personal constraints.

The overall willingness of Generation Z students to engage in climate change adaptation was very high, with a mean of 4.45. Students expressed a strong intention to participate in activities such as recycling, following government environmental policies, and voting for leaders who prioritize climate action. Statistical testing confirmed that higher levels of awareness are significantly associated with a higher willingness to engage in climate-friendly actions. Furthermore, multiple linear regression analysis showed that attitudes and subjective norms are significant predictors of willingness, while perceived behavioral control was not a significant predictor in this specific model. The study found no significant differences in awareness, attitudes, or willingness across different student year levels.

The results highlight an attitude-behavior gap, where high awareness and positive attitudes do not always translate into immediate action due to systemic and personal constraints, such as cost, access, and convenience. While students are aware of what actions are necessary, they often face practical barriers that hinder their ability to live a sustainable lifestyle. The study also noted that while students are willing to take individual actions like recycling, they are less ready for behaviors that require significant personal sacrifice or lifestyle changes.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that Generation Z in Koronadal City is highly aware of climate change and possesses a strong willingness to participate in adaptation efforts. Their intentions are heavily influenced by their attitudes and social influences rather than knowledge alone. To sustain and enhance this engagement, it is recommended that educational institutions integrate practical climate change education into the curriculum, moving beyond theoretical knowledge to focus on building self-efficacy and providing hands-on engagement opportunities. Furthermore, the study suggests that community-based programs, campus sustainability initiatives, and institutional policies, such as banning single-use plastics, could help remove the practical barriers that prevent students from translating their environmental concern into consistent, long-term adaptive behaviors.

title: From Arms to Farms: Communication Triggers Towards Transformation of Former Moro Islamic Liberation Front Combatants
abstract: After years of getting involved in armed conflict, former combatants often face challenges in changing their roles and identities as they transition to civilian life. Various programs had been implemented to support their transformation. In Lanao del Norte, Philippines, the former Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) transitioned to becoming organic farmers through the “From Arms to Farms” program implemented by the local government of Kauswagan. However, the program’s economic opportunities were not just the motivations that pushed them to join the program. Different communication strategies and triggers influenced their decision to transform their lives. Despite existing studies on the transition of former combatants to civilian life, little is known about how communication shapes their decisions toward starting anew. This study filled this gap by exploring how communication facilitated the transformation of former MILF combatants into organic farmers. This study used narrative inquiry and Bruner’s “subjunctivization” concept to examine the narratives of five former MILF combatants and the views of the Municipal Agriculture Officer of Kauswagan town. The results of this study showed the communication triggers that influenced the former combatants to transform their lives such as (a) personal motivations, such as their desire to have financial security and a better future for their families; (b) sincere engagement of the local authorities; (c) peer support and influence; (d) key messaging of the program’s benefits, and (e) consistent communication and regular visits. The local government of Kauswagan also established an online group chat to sustain communication with the former combatants which provided practical and real-time communication to keep them updated and engaged about the program and other activities in the town. The use of this communication channel hastened their transformation process. Moreover, this study highlighted the importance of building trust and providing resources, community-based training, and support in marketing their harvests. Constant dialogue and institutional support were also vital in their transformation.

The thesis "From Arms to Farms: Communication Triggers Towards Transformation of Former Moro Islamic Liberation Front Combatants" by Lou Ellen L. Antonio explores the role of communication in the socio-economic transition of former Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) combatants in Lanao del Norte, Philippines. The study specifically focuses on the "From Arms to Farms" program in Kauswagan, which facilitates the transformation of former combatants into organic farmers.

The problem addressed by the research is the lack of understanding regarding the communication processes and triggers that influence former combatants to abandon armed struggle and embrace civilian life. While existing literature focuses on the economic and political aspects of reintegration and disarmament, there is a significant research gap concerning how communication dynamics shape the decisions and identity reconstruction of individuals transitioning from conflict to productive citizenship. The study seeks to understand the narratives of these individuals and the specific communication triggers that facilitated their transformation.

The context of the study is rooted in the long-standing armed conflict in Mindanao, particularly involving the MILF, a breakaway group of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). Following the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) in 2014, a normalization track was established to facilitate the decommissioning of combatants and their transition to peaceful lives. In Kauswagan, a municipality that suffered extreme poverty and devastation due to historical conflicts, the "From Arms to Farms" program was launched to address the root causes of violence—poverty and food insecurity—by promoting organic agriculture. Unlike traditional disarmament models, this program utilized a "no disarming" approach, focusing on community empowerment and self-reliance.

The researcher employed a qualitative research design using narrative inquiry, which allows for an in-depth exploration of lived experiences through personal stories. The study utilized Bruner’s concept of "subjunctivization" as a theoretical lens to analyze how former combatants imagined and reconstructed their identities from combatants to farmers. The participants included five former MILF combatants from Kauswagan, Munai, Tangcal, and Bacolod who had successfully transitioned into organic farming, as well as the Municipal Agriculture Officer of Kauswagan to provide institutional perspective. Data was gathered through semi-structured interviews, and the analysis focused on identifying themes within the participants' narratives.

The findings reveal several key communication triggers that influenced the transformation of the former combatants. First, personal motivations played a significant role, specifically the desire for financial security and a better future for their families. Second, the sincere engagement of local authorities helped build the necessary trust for the program to succeed. Third, peer support and influence among former combatants provided a social framework for the transition. Fourth, the key messaging of the program, which highlighted the benefits of organic farming, was effective in communicating the program's value. Finally, consistent communication and regular visits from stakeholders ensured that the participants remained engaged. Notably, the local government utilized an online group chat to provide real-time, practical communication, which hastened the transformation process.

The study concludes that communication is a vital component of successful transformation programs. The transition from combatant to organic farmer was not merely an economic shift but a communicative process of identity reconstruction. The research highlights that building trust, providing consistent institutional support, and maintaining open dialogue are essential for the successful reintegration of former combatants. The "From Arms to Farms" program demonstrates that when communication is aligned with local perspectives and provides practical, real-time engagement, it can effectively facilitate sustainable peace and economic stability.

The implications of this research are significant for development communication practitioners, policymakers, and local government units. For practitioners, the study suggests that communication strategies for reintegration should move beyond simple information dissemination to include participatory and sustained engagement. For policymakers, the findings support the "Localized Normalization Implementation" approach, emphasizing that programs must be tailored to the specific needs and aspirations of the local community to be effective. Furthermore, the study underscores the importance of providing holistic support—including technical training, resources, and marketing assistance—to ensure that the transition to new livelihoods, such as organic farming, is sustainable and contributes to long-term peace and the achievement of various Sustainable Development Goals, including poverty reduction and food security.

title: Autoethnography of Human-Animal Interaction and Mental Wellness
abstract:
While there have been existing studies that suggest Human-Animal Interaction helps improvement of people􀂶s physical and mental health (Wauthier, et al. 2022; Poresky & Hendirix, 1990; Barlow, et al., 2012; Thayer & Stevens, 2022; Hoy-Gerlach, et al., 2022; Winsor, et al., 2022; Robino, et al., 2022; Wagner & Pina E Cunha, 2021), most of them were done clinically. This study discusses the lived experience of a Filipino individual who underwent anxiety and depression to understand how nonverbal communication, through Human-Animal Interaction became a means to alleviate his mental health issues. This research uses autoethnography as a study, while the researcher draws on personal experience, all recorded and written as Vignettes, and analyzed using the Immersion-Reflection-Modeling (IRM) model to
expound points.

Of note, this study includes hypersensitive or psychologically triggering and disturbing information as part of its narrative to understand the connection between Human-Animal Interaction (HAI) and its benefits on the mental wellness of humans.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In the thesis "Autoethnography of Human-Animal Interaction and Mental Wellness," Renz D. Balderama explores the therapeutic potential of nonverbal communication between humans and animals. Using an autoethnographic methodology and the Immersion-Reflection-Modeling framework, the researcher utilizes personal vignettes involving his dogs, Chip and Cola, to examine how pet interactions helped manage mental health challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic in the Philippines. The study addresses the need for accessible mental health tools during periods of social isolation and high stress when clinical interventions may be unavailable.

The findings demonstrate that pets are capable of reading human moods through nonverbal cues. Through specific vignettes, the author shows how pets exhibit affect displays to signal worry during the owner's stress and act as regulators to de-escalate domestic tension. These interactions facilitate mental wellness through sensemaking, emotional contagion, and the building of social relationships. Pets provide a nonjudgmental presence and nonverbal cues that encourage self-reflection and the normalization of routines.

The study concludes that human-animal interaction is a continuous process of communication that serves as a significant, low-cost tool for managing psychological distress. The author suggests that recognizing the value of animal-assisted support could inform policies regarding animal welfare and interventions for persons with disabilities. Future research is recommended to explore the effects of these interactions on individuals with developmental disorders or severe mental illnesses.

This thesis, titled "Autoethnography of Human-Animal Interaction and Mental Wellness" by Renz D. Balderama, explores the therapeutic potential of nonverbal communication between humans and animals. Using a personal narrative, the researcher examines how interactions with pets served as a vital tool for managing mental health challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The problem addressed is the significant rise in mental health issues, specifically anxiety and depression, exacerbated by the global pandemic and the subsequent strict community quarantines in the Philippines. The author notes that while clinical interventions like psychotherapy exist, they are often inaccessible due to high costs and a shortage of mental health professionals. The study seeks to understand how nonverbal human-animal interaction (HAI) can act as an accessible, unconventional form of therapeutic communication to alleviate psychological distress.

The research is situated within the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced many Filipinos into work-from-home setups, leading to increased stress, social isolation, and disrupted daily routines. The author draws on several theoretical lenses, including Kincaid and Schramm’s concept of communication beyond human-to-human verbal exchange and Birdwhistell’s Theory of Kinesics, which focuses on body movements and gestures. The study also utilizes the concept of "Communication as Therapy" and Ekman and Friesen’s categories of nonverbal behavior (emblems, illustrators, affect displays, regulators, and adaptors) to analyze the interactions.

The methodology employed is autoethnography, a qualitative approach where the researcher uses personal experience as primary data. The author utilizes the Immersion-Reflection-Modeling (IRM) framework. This involves "immersion" in lived experiences, "reflection" on those experiences, and "modeling" to understand the underlying meanings and relate them to broader communicative theories. Data was collected through the creation of vignettes—short, narrative accounts of specific triggering events and interactions with the author's pets, specifically dogs named Chip and Cola.

The findings are presented through six vignettes that detail the author's descent into depression and his subsequent navigation of mental instability. The results demonstrate that pets are capable of reading human moods through nonverbal cues. For example, the author’s dog, Chip, exhibited "affect displays" such as wide eyes and aggressive pawing to signal worry when the author was under professional stress. In another instance, the pet's behavior acted as a "regulator" during a domestic conflict, helping to de-escalate tension and prompting the author to reflect on his own behavior and seek reconciliation with family members.

The study concludes that human-animal interaction facilitates mental wellness through several key processes: sensemaking, emotional contagion, and the building of social relationships. The author posits that pets provide a unique form of support by offering nonjudgmental presence and nonverbal cues that encourage self-reflection and normalization of routines. The interaction is not a one-time cure but a continuous process of communication that helps the individual navigate emotional distress.

The implications of this research suggest that HAI can be a significant, low-cost tool for managing mental health. The author recommends that the findings contribute to broader conversations regarding accessible mental health support. Furthermore, the study suggests that recognizing the value of animal-assisted support could inform policies related to animal welfare and the integration of animal-assisted interventions for persons with disabilities. For future research, the author recommends exploring the effects of HAI on individuals with severe mental illnesses or developmental disorders such as autism.

title: Sports Information Seeking Behavior and Participation of PWDs in NCR
abstract:
This study explores the relationship between the sports information-seeking behavior of persons with disabilities (PWDs) and their participation in sports, as well as identified the barriers which usually hinder them, with a focus on individuals in the National Capital Region (NCR) of the Philippines. The research involved two distinct clusters: sports-inclined and non-sports-inclined PWDs.

A mixed-method approach, following a concurrent triangulation design, was employed.

The findings reveal a weak yet statistically significant positive correlation between active sports information seeking and sports participation among PWDs. Family and friends come out as strong influencers in PWDs' decisions to engage in sports.

The study recommends developing more effective legislation and policies, enhancing information accessibility and availability, and strengthening social support systems to promote inclusivity and increased sports participation among PWDs. Further research is suggested to explore these relationships and contrasts in greater depth and to develop adapted strategies to overcome the identified barriers and
improve sports engagement among PWDs.

half:
This study investigates the relationship between the sports information-seeking behavior of persons with disabilities (PWDs) and their sports participation in the National Capital Region of the Philippines. The research addresses how information access impacts physical activity and engagement for this marginalized group, noting that participation rates are lower than those of the general population due to socio-structural barriers like inadequate facilities and limited media coverage.

Using a mixed-methods research design and Dervin’s Sense-Making Theory, the researcher employed a concurrent triangulation approach. A multi-stage stratified sampling design selected 174 respondents, including sports-inclined PWDs and non-sports-inclined PWDs. Quantitative data were collected via a seven-part survey, while qualitative data came from focus group discussions and interviews with representatives from the Philippine Sports Commission, the National Council on Disability Affairs, and Philspada.

Findings reveal a weak yet statistically significant positive correlation between active sports information seeking and sports participation. Information is critical to the decision to engage in sports, with family and friends serving as the most influential factors. While interest in sports is high, relevant information is often insufficient. Qualitative themes suggest sports promote social inclusion and personal empowerment, yet barriers like unstable leadership structures and insufficient information campaigns persist. The study concludes that increasing para-sports visibility and ensuring accessible information can drive higher participation through coordinated efforts among government agencies.

title: Communication in Implementing Safety Culture Onboard Seabourn Cruises and the Level of Satisfaction of Crew on Board: An Autoethnographic Study
abstract: This study delves into the critical role of communication in cultivating a robust safety culture aboard Seabourn Cruises, and its subsequent impact on crew satisfaction. Employing an autoethnographic approach, the investigation analyzed thematic data from four participant narratives to derive meaningful insights. The research highlights the indispensable nature of direct and clear communication channels in maintaining safety standards and facilitating the swift dissemination of essential safety information. The study identifies benchmarking against industry standards as a crucial method for improving safety practices, with the approach to safety communication significantly influencing crew satisfaction levels. The establishment of trust in leadership and the active engagement of crew members in safety initiatives were pinpointed as key factors for the successful adoption of safety protocols. The necessity for ongoing enhancements in safety practices, supported by an effective feedback system, was emphasized to accommodate the dynamic nature of the maritime environment. The research also addresses communication challenges, such as the overload of non-essential emails, which can undermine safety efforts, and calls for the adoption of more streamlined communication strategies. title: Tausug Orality: An Analysis of Transmission Practices in a Sitio in Indanan, Sulu
abstract:
This thesis analyzed the transmission practices of Tausug oral traditions in a sitio located in the municipality of Indanan, Sulu. Using sociocultural constructivism as a research lens and reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how these traditions are passed down across four generations in the digital age. The goal is to determine whether the informants continue to use traditional methods of oral communication or have adapted to modern communication technologies. In a rapidly changing society, studying the transmission practices of Tausug oral traditions is essential, as these traditions serve as portals to the rich history and repositories of Tausug religion and customs, playing a critical role in cultural preservation.

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight residents representing the Silent Generation, Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials. The analysis categorized the types of oral traditions mentioned or narrated, further examined in terms of generational differences, community roles, and gender dynamics in their transmission and preservation. Notably, pandu’ (advice and guidance) and maasalla (proverbs and sayings) remain central to Tausug oral traditions, with religious leaders, fathers, and mothers playing key roles in their transmission. These traditions are typically shared during Islamic gatherings and within households, integrating Islamic teachings and parental guidance. However, there is a noticeable decline in the transmission of more complex forms, such as tarasul (poems) and kissa (narratives).

The study also emphasized the growing use of technology, particularly mobile phones and Facebook, in transmitting Tausug oral traditions, with younger generations increasingly embracing these platforms. While older generations are gradually accepting technology, Millennials have fully embraced digital tools to preserve and share these traditions. However, the use of technology in this context raises concerns about authenticity and preservation, as the reliance on digital platforms challenges traditional oral transmission, which historically relies on face-to-face, spoken interaction.

This thesis, titled "Tausug Orality: An Analysis of Transmission Practices in a Sitio in Indanan, Sulu," investigates how the oral traditions of the Tausug people are passed down through generations in the context of rapid technological advancement. The researcher addresses the scarcity of scholarly literature regarding Tausug communication and seeks to understand how the digital age influences the preservation of cultural and religious heritage. Specifically, the study explores how transmission methods differ across four generations and examines the role of modern communication technology in both facilitating and challenging these traditional practices.

The research is situated within the unique socio-historical context of the Sulu Archipelago, a region characterized by its deep Islamic roots and a long history of resistance against colonial powers, including the Spanish and Americans. The Tausug people, meaning "people of the place called Sug," possess a culture where identity is inextricably linked to Islam. Orality serves as a vital repository for their history, religious teachings, and social values. The study focuses on a specific sitio in the municipality of Indanan, Sulu, to provide a localized understanding of these broader cultural dynamics.

To investigate these issues, the researcher employed a qualitative research design using reflexive thematic analysis. The study utilized sociocultural constructivism as a theoretical lens to examine how knowledge is constructed and shared within the community. Data were gathered through semi-structured key informant interviews with eight residents representing four distinct generations: the Silent Generation, Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials. This generational approach allowed for a comparative analysis of how oral traditions are communicated and preserved across different age groups.

The findings reveal that Tausug oral traditions are diverse, encompassing narrative, poetic, homiletic, and musical forms. Among these, *pandu’* (advice and guidance) and *maasalla* (proverbs and sayings) remain central to daily life. These traditions are primarily transmitted through social interactions, such as Islamic gatherings and within the household, with religious leaders, fathers, and mothers serving as primary transmitters. However, the study notes a decline in the transmission of more complex forms, such as *tarasul* (poems) and *kissa* (narratives).

A significant finding of the study is the evolving role of communication technology. While older generations continue to rely on traditional face-to-face spoken interaction, younger generations, particularly Millennials, have increasingly embraced digital tools like mobile phones and Facebook to share and preserve traditions. While technology offers new avenues for cultural visibility and documentation, the researcher notes that this shift raises concerns regarding authenticity. The reliance on digital platforms may challenge the traditional oral transmission process, which historically relies on direct, spoken interaction within specific cultural contexts.

In conclusion, the study highlights a generational shift in how Tausug culture is maintained. While the essence of Tausug orality remains deeply rooted in Islamic teachings and communal values, the methods of transmission are undergoing a significant transformation due to modernization. The transition from purely oral, face-to-face communication to digital engagement represents both an opportunity for preservation and a risk to the traditional nuances of oral performance and social hierarchy.

The implications of this research are multifaceted. For scholars, the study contributes to the limited body of knowledge regarding Philippine Muslim communication and orality. For policymakers and local government units, particularly within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), the findings suggest a need to support digital platforms that are culturally sensitive and designed to safeguard intangible heritage. The researcher recommends the establishment of a Sulu Press to provide local scholars with the resources to document and publish oral traditions. Furthermore, the study suggests that community leaders and religious figures should encourage the integration of traditional oral forms into modern communication channels to ensure that the rich history and values of the Tausug people are preserved for future generations.

title: Family Communication Patterns and Practice of Child Rights among Intermediate Elementary Students in a School in Silang, Cavite
abstract:
The Sustainable Development Goals were created with the dream to uphold, and empower each member of society. These goals are linked to specific human rights that aim to achieve a transformative society by placing everyone at the center of development - leaving no one behind. The children who are the most vulnerable members of the community and future leaders of the society deserve to be protected and respected with their rights as the future lies in their hands.

This study identified the different Family Communication Patterns on the families of Intermediate Elementary Students in a School in Silang Cavite and analyzed the relationship between the different Family Communication Patterns with child rights practice. Through the research instruments used, quantitative results have revealed the prevailing Family Communication Patterns based on Conversation and Conformity orientation. Each type were ranked as Consensual being the most frequent type of Family Communication Pattern followed by Pluralistic, Protective, and Laissez-Faire. The Spearman-Rho Correlation test has shown a positive relationship between Conversation and child rights practice. Though Conformity has presented a weaker positive relationship, it still yields an increase in child rights practice as conformity level increases. This study has exposed the value of open communication in the practice of children's rights.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study investigates the relationship between family communication patterns and the practice of child rights among intermediate elementary students in Silang, Cavite. Grounded in the Family Communication Patterns Theory, the research examines how conversation orientation and conformity orientation influence a child's ability to understand and exercise their entitlements. The study focuses on the fulfillment of essential needs and the ability of children to express their views, aligning with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals regarding Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-Being, and Quality Education.

Using a quantitative approach and a cross-sectional survey design, the researcher surveyed 131 Grade Six students aged 11 to 14 at Silang West Elementary School. The findings reveal that most respondents experience high levels of both conversation and conformity. The consensual communication type was the most frequent, accounting for 57.25% of respondents, followed by the laissez-faire type at 12.21%, the protective type at 19.08%, and the pluralistic type at 11.45%.

Correlation analysis showed a positive relationship between conversation and child rights practice (r = 0.44, p < 0.001). While the relationship between conformity and child rights practice was weaker, it still yielded an increase in child rights practice as conformity levels increased. The study concludes that high conversation orientation is a key indicator in fostering environments where children's rights are upheld, suggesting that open dialogue empowers children to express needs and participate in decisions.

This study investigates the relationship between family communication patterns and the practice of child rights among intermediate elementary students in a school in Silang, Cavite. The research is situated within the context of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, specifically focusing on Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-Being, and Quality Education. While the Philippines is committed to upholding children's rights, challenges such as violence and exploitation remain. The home environment is identified as a foundational setting for protecting these rights, as family communication significantly influences a child's development and their ability to understand and exercise their entitlements.

The theoretical framework is based on the Family Communication Patterns Theory, which posits that families create a shared social reality through two dimensions: conversation orientation and conformity orientation. Conversation orientation refers to the frequency and openness of communication, while conformity orientation measures the extent to which family members share similar attitudes and values. These dimensions combine to form four distinct family communication types: consensual, pluralistic, protective, and laissez-faire. The study aims to determine how these patterns correlate with the practice of child rights, specifically regarding the fulfillment of essential needs and the ability of children to express their views within the family.

Using a quantitative approach and a cross-sectional survey design, the researcher conducted the study at Silang West Elementary School, targeting Grade Six students aged 11 to 14. A total of 131 respondents participated. The research instruments included an adapted version of the Family Communication Patterns Questionnaire and a researcher-designed section to evaluate the practice of child rights in alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, such as weighted means, and the Spearman-Rho Correlation test.

The findings reveal that the majority of respondents experience high levels of both conversation and conformity. Among the four identified family communication patterns, the consensual type was the most frequent, accounting for 57.25% of the respondents. This was followed by the protective type at 19.08%, the pluralistic type at 11.45%, and the laissez-faire type at 12.21%. The results indicate that most families in the study area prioritize both open discussion and adherence to family norms.

The correlation analysis showed a positive relationship between conversation and child rights practice (r = 0.44, p < 0.001). While the relationship between conformity and child rights practice was noted as weaker, it still yielded an increase in child rights practice as conformity levels increased. The data suggests that high levels of conversation are associated with higher levels of child rights practice, supporting the idea that open dialogue empowers children to express their needs and participate in decisions.

The study concludes that family communication patterns, particularly the consensual type, play a significant role in how child rights are practiced. The presence of high conversation orientation is a key indicator in fostering an environment where children's rights are upheld. The findings confirm that the way families interact and establish norms directly impacts the realization of children's rights within the household.

The implications suggest that fostering open communication within the family is vital for the protection and empowerment of children. By encouraging dialogue, families can better support the physical, mental, and educational development of their children. The research highlights the importance of the family as the primary support system in achieving the objectives of the Sustainable Development Goals. The study suggests that interventions and policies aimed at promoting healthier family communication environments could contribute to the overall well-being and rights realization of children in the community.

title: Communicative Practices of Women Information Technology Leaders: An Ethnomethodological Study of Podcast Narratives
abstract:
The study explored the communicative practices of women information technology (IT) leaders, how their views of the industry shape these practices, and what these practices achieve in their leadership roles. The study was grounded in the Sociocultural Tradition of Communication, as proposed by Craig (1999), where communication is viewed as the (re)production of “shared sociocultural patterns.” Using ethnomethodology as a qualitative research method, the study explored the communicative practices of women leaders through narratives present in podcast conversations from four (4) podcast episodes featuring different women IT leaders. These podcasts were transcribed and then subjected to an ethnomethodological analysis.

The findings identified five key views of these women IT leaders: (1) the industry is continuously changing, evolving, and disruptive; (2) the industry requires flexibility, adaptability, and agility; (3) success is defined by resilience and problem-solving; (4) the industry is diverse and highly collaborative; and (5) customer-centricity and satisfaction are important in the industry.

Similarly, the study described five communicative practices among these women IT leaders, particularly: (1) women leaders practice continuous learning and selfimprovement; (2) women leaders practice adaptability and situational leadership; (3) women leaders practice open and transparent communication; (4) women leaders practice empathy and understanding; and (5) women leaders practice data-driven, techenhanced, and customer-focused communication.

Finally, the study also identified four accomplishments and leadership outcomes of the women IT leaders’ communicative practices, which includes: (1) keeping the company stable and sustainable; (2) keeping the company competitive and relevant; (3) improving team collaboration and engagement; and (4) enabling and promoting adaptability and innovation.

Calimlim’s study, "Communicative Practices of Women Information Technology Leaders: An Ethnomethodological Study of Podcast Narratives," investigates how women in IT leadership navigate their professional lives and the "glass ceiling." Using an ethnomethodological approach within the Sociocultural Tradition of Communication, the research analyzed four podcast episodes featuring high-level female executives from the advertising tech, telecom, digital grocery, and digital banking sectors.

The findings identify five key views regarding the IT industry: it is continuously changing and disruptive; it requires flexibility, adaptability, and agility; success is defined by resilience and problem-solving; it is diverse and collaborative; and customer-centricity is paramount. To navigate these industry dynamics, the leaders employ five distinct communicative practices: continuous learning and self-improvement; adaptability and situational leadership; open and transparent communication; empathy and understanding; and data-driven, tech-enhanced, and customer-focused communication.

These practices result in significant leadership accomplishments, such as maintaining company stability, sustainability, competitiveness, and relevance. Furthermore, these communicative approaches improve team collaboration and engagement while enabling innovation. Specifically, empathetic and transparent communication fosters inclusive environments that increase motivation. The study concludes that women IT leaders use communication to make their roles accountable to their teams and organizations. The researcher suggests future studies could use phenomenological lenses or quantitative methods to further explore these findings.

The problem addressed is the persistent underrepresentation of women in IT leadership and the "glass ceiling" that prevents advancement in this male-dominated field. While existing literature has explored the challenges women face, such as gender bias, discrimination, and the digital divide, there is a gap in understanding the specific communicative practices these women use to navigate their professional lives and succeed. The study seeks to provide insights into how language, gender, and leadership intersect in the dynamic IT landscape.

The research is situated within the Sociocultural Tradition of Communication, which views communication as a symbolic process that produces and reproduces shared sociocultural patterns. To explore this, the researcher employed ethnomethodology as both a theoretical framework and a qualitative research method. Ethnomethodology focuses on the "taken-for-granted" aspects of everyday interactions and how individuals make sense of their social reality. The study utilized podcast narratives as the primary data source, specifically analyzing four transcribed episodes from a business podcast featuring women in high-level IT positions: a CEO of an advertising tech firm, a VP for Employee Experience at a telecom provider, a CEO of a digital grocery app, and an Executive Vice President of a digital banking company.

The findings of the study are categorized into three main areas: the views of the leaders, their communicative practices, and the accomplishments of those practices. Regarding their views of the industry, the leaders identified five key themes: the industry is continuously changing, evolving, and disruptive; it requires flexibility, adaptability, and agility; success is defined by resilience and problem-solving; the industry is diverse and highly collaborative; and customer-centricity and satisfaction are paramount.

In response to these industry views, the study identified five distinct communicative practices employed by these women leaders. They practice continuous learning and self-improvement, adaptability and situational leadership, open and transparent communication, empathy and understanding, and data-driven, tech-enhanced, and customer-focused communication. These practices are not static but are adapted based on the specific needs of the team and the evolving nature of the technology sector.

The study further determined that these communicative practices lead to significant leadership accomplishments. Specifically, these practices help in keeping the company stable and sustainable, keeping the company competitive and relevant, improving team collaboration and engagement, and enabling and promoting adaptability and innovation. For instance, the use of empathetic and transparent communication was found to create inclusive environments that foster higher levels of engagement and motivation among team members.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that the communicative practices of women IT leaders are both shaped by and contribute to their views of the industry. Their ability to navigate the complexities of a disruptive and rapidly changing sector is deeply tied to their communicative approach, which emphasizes flexibility, empathy, and continuous learning. The research highlights that women leaders use communication to make their leadership roles "accountable" to their teams and organizations, effectively managing the intersection of technology, people, and business goals.

The researcher offers several recommendations based on these findings. Theoretically, the study suggests that future research could utilize a phenomenological lens to more deeply explore the lived experiences and perceptions of women IT leaders. Methodologically, the researcher recommends incorporating quantitative or mixed-method approaches, such as structured surveys, to validate whether the identified communicative practices apply to the broader population of women in IT leadership.

title: Knowledge, Understanding, and Social Acceptability of Green Coal (Bana Grass) as Energy Source among Residents of Bataan, Philippines
abstract: Climate change is inevitably happening and with its effects comes the action of local and international government offices to combat this phenomenon that has become one of the major threats to the daily lives of people, animals, plants, and the surroundings. On January 2023, the Provincial Government of Bataan in partnership with Mackay Negros Bana Charcoal Corporation signed a Memorandum of Understanding on the plan of establishing a green coal (bana grass) power plant in response with a greener source of energy and the worsening case of climate change. This study aims to know how the level of knowledge and understanding be related to the possible social acceptability of green coal as alternative energy source. Stratified random sampling is used in choosing the respondents wherein Bataan is subdivided into its municipalities and lone cit􀁜. After the 􀂳la􀁜ering􀂴 is done, random sampling is executed to choose as to which barangay will the researcher do the surveying. In this study, 298 random residents in Bataan serve as the sample size as based in a research paper published by Monroe, et al in June 2010 about the use of a Woody Biomass as a Renewable Energy Source abroad. After the validation of the research instrument, survey process and tabulation, the data were then subjected to proper management based on Data Privacy Act of 2012. Spearman rho is the statistical tool used in analyzing the gathered data where it gave a result of 6.78042E-49 for the pvalue denoting a very strong, positive correlation among the involved variables, implying that as the levels of knowledge and understanding of the residents of Bataan increase, their social acceptability with the green coal (bana grass) project also increase.

This research is prompted by the need to combat climate change and the provincial government's initiative to establish a green coal power plant through a partnership with the Mackay Negros Bana Charcoal Corporation. The study seeks to determine how the level of knowledge and understanding among residents relates to the social acceptability of this technology and to identify if a knowledge gap exists between different socioeconomic segments of the population.

The research is framed by the Knowledge Gap Theory, which suggests that as mass media information increases, higher socioeconomic status segments may acquire information faster than lower socioeconomic segments, potentially widening the knowledge gap. The study aims to explore how the dissemination of information regarding the green coal project influences whether residents will welcome or reject this new energy source.

To address these objectives, the researcher employed a quantitative research approach using a descriptive research design. A one-shot survey was conducted among 298 residents of Bataan, selected through stratified random sampling. The sampling process involved subdividing the province into its various municipalities and lone cities, followed by selecting barangays, and finally using simple random sampling to choose individual respondents. The inclusion criteria for participants required them to be at least 18 years old, at least a high school graduate, and residents of Bataan for at least less than three years to ensure they were familiar with the local power supply conditions. Data were collected using a self-made survey questionnaire that was validated and translated into Filipino. The gathered data were analyzed using descriptive statistics for the socio-demographic profile and the Spearman rho statistical tool to test the relationships between the variables.

The findings regarding the socio-demographic profile revealed that the largest age group among respondents was 26 to 44 years old, comprising 50.7% of the sample. Most respondents had lived in Bataan for more than five years, with 93.3% of the sample falling into this category. In terms of education, 53.1% of the respondents were high school graduates. Regarding monthly income, a significant majority, 71.5%, earned below Php 10,957.

The results concerning knowledge and understanding indicated that residents possessed a good to strong level of knowledge regarding the green coal project. Most respondents answered positively to questions regarding climate change, the provincial government's sustainability goals, and the partnership between the government and the Mackay Negros Bana Charcoal Corporation. The data showed that residents were aware of the potential benefits of green coal, such as its impact on electric bills and its role in mitigating global warming.

The statistical analysis using Spearman rho yielded a p-value of 6.78042E-49, which denotes a very strong, positive correlation among the involved variables. This result implies that as the levels of knowledge and understanding of the residents of Bataan increase, their social acceptability of the green coal project also increases.

The study concludes that there is a significant relationship between the knowledge and understanding of the residents and their social acceptability of the green coal project. The findings suggest that higher levels of information and comprehension lead to a greater tendency for the community to accept the implementation of the project.

Based on these conclusions, the researcher offers several recommendations. For future researchers, it is suggested to increase the sample size to reduce sampling error and to explore other renewable energy topics, such as solar panels, or the impacts of coal-fired power plants on public health. Methodologically, the study suggests that a mixed-method approach combining quantitative and qualitative data could be beneficial. Regarding the implementation of the project, the study recommends that the provincial government maximize its use of various media platforms—including radio, television, and printed materials like brochures—to ensure the effective dissemination of information. This is intended to bridge any potential knowledge gaps and ensure that all social classes have free and easy access to information, thereby fostering higher social acceptability for the green coal initiative.
