title: The Community Press Remains Alive Under COVID-19: Lived Experience of Community Journalists
abstract: This interpretative phenomenological study answers how the lived experience of members of the community press under the Covid-19 pandemic shaped their practice of doing community journalism under the new normal. In-depth interviews with seven community journalists, who live and work in the Cordillera Administrative Region, were conducted and analyzed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis. Results showed that the Covid-19 pandemic has amplified the many crises that threaten community journalists ranging from threats to their physical safety, legal safety, psychological or mental health, digital safety, and financial or economic status. The biggest challenge is disinformation. To cope with the difficulties of living under the threat of Covid-19, community journalists had to adjust their data gathering, news writing, and publication methods. They had to learn new journalistic skills in order to adapt to digital publication and find alternative sources of income apart from advertising such as applying for story grants. Camaraderie and a tight community of media practitioners fostered by the Baguio Correspondents and Broadcasters Club (BCBC) also helped a lot in their survival, particularly their physical and mental well-being. These experiences paved the way for their personal and professional transformation. It also shaped a new form of community journalism: one that knows its audience􀂲the community it serves, understands their circumstances, and tries to reach them through hard copy or digital platforms. The new form of community journalism combines traditional methods of data gathering with technology-assisted data gathering tools. It upholds traditional news values packaged in a form and language appropriate for modern multimedia platforms. It is a kind of journalism that continues to wage a war against disinformation by adhering to the age-old journalistic principles of truth, service, and ethics. In essence, it is a kind of journalism which carries with it the same heart and passion for, and commitment to community journalism albeit with different tools.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This thesis investigates how the COVID-19 pandemic shaped the professional practices and personal lives of community journalists in the Cordillera Administrative Region of the Philippines. Using an interpretative phenomenological research design, the study conducted in-depth interviews with seven journalists to understand their transition into a "new normal" and their evolving roles as development communicators.

The findings reveal that the pandemic amplified existing crises. Journalists faced physical infection risks and logistical hurdles from lockdowns, alongside psychological challenges including heightened anxiety, stress, and trauma. Legally, they contended with vague laws like the Anti-Terrorism Act, which posed risks when reporting on government actions. Economically, declining advertising revenues and print sales forced many to choose between ceasing publication or shifting to digital platforms. Additionally, journalists faced increased digital safety concerns due to surveillance and antagonistic online audiences.

Despite these challenges, the study identifies significant adaptations. Many journalists embraced digital transformation, utilizing social media and mobile apps, which fostered professional growth in data journalism and multimedia storytelling. Professional organizations also provided essential social and emotional support. The study concludes that community journalism is undergoing a profound transformation rather than disappearing, moving toward a hybrid approach that combines traditional values with digital distribution. The researcher suggests that journalism curricula should focus more on science and data journalism, and that policymakers must address legal vulnerabilities like libel and "red-tagging."

This thesis, titled "The Community Press Remains Alive Under COVID-19: Lived Experience of Community Journalists," investigates how the COVID-19 pandemic shaped the professional practices and personal lives of community journalists in the Cordillera Administrative Region of the Philippines. The study explores the transition of these practitioners into a "new normal" and examines how their roles as development communicators evolved amidst unprecedented global and local crises.

The research problem centers on the multifaceted threats posed by the pandemic to the community press. Beyond the immediate health risks, the study addresses the economic instability caused by declining advertising revenues, the logistical hurdles of social distancing and quarantine protocols, and the rise of a "disinfodemic" characterized by misinformation, malinformation, and disinformation. The researcher seeks to understand how these journalists maintained their vital function of providing accurate, hyperlocal information while facing physical, legal, psychological, and financial vulnerabilities.

The context of the study is rooted in the unique position of the Philippine community press, which serves as a "newspaper of record" for areas outside Metro Manila. These outlets often operate on thin margins and rely on a delicate balance between financial viability and editorial quality. The pandemic exacerbated existing vulnerabilities, such as the threat of social media competition and the economic pressure of dwindling print sales. The study is framed within the tradition of Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA), focusing on the subjective, lived experiences of the individuals within this media ecosystem.

The methodology employed an interpretative phenomenological research design. The researcher conducted in-depth interviews with seven community journalists living and working in the Cordillera Administrative Region. Data were analyzed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to capture the essence of their experiences. Ethical considerations were prioritized, including the use of participant consent forms and ensuring that the participants' honesty regarding their fears and vulnerabilities was respected.

The findings reveal that the pandemic amplified existing crises for community journalists. Physically, they faced the risk of infection and the logistical strain of navigating lockdowns. Legally, they contended with vague laws, such as the Bayanihan to Heal as One Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act, which posed risks to those reporting on government actions. Psychologically, journalists experienced heightened anxiety, stress, and trauma from reporting on illness and death. Economically, the loss of advertisers and the inability to sell print copies forced many to choose between stopping publication or shifting to digital platforms. Digital safety also emerged as a concern due to increased surveillance and the rise of antagonistic online audiences.

However, the study also identifies significant opportunities and adaptations. Many journalists embraced digital transformation, utilizing social media, websites, and mobile apps to reach their audiences. This shift allowed for new forms of engagement and the ability to access story grants as alternative revenue streams. The pandemic also fostered professional growth, as journalists had to master new skills in digital publication, data journalism, and multimedia storytelling. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of professional camaraderie; organizations like the Baguio Correspondents and Broadcasters Club (BCBC) provided essential social and emotional support, fostering a sense of community that aided their survival.

The conclusions drawn from the study suggest that community journalism is undergoing a profound transformation rather than a disappearance. The "new normal" for community journalism is characterized by a hybrid approach that combines traditional journalistic values—truth, service, and ethics—with modern technology-assisted data gathering and digital distribution. The role of the community journalist has expanded to include navigating complex digital landscapes and combating disinformation. While the medium may shift from print to digital, the core mission of serving the hyperlocal community remains a constant.

The implications of this research are significant for several stakeholders. For the academe, the study suggests that journalism curricula should be updated to include training in science communication, health journalism, data journalism, and digital marketing to prepare students for a technology-driven landscape. For policy makers, the study highlights the urgent need to address the legal vulnerabilities of journalists, specifically regarding the decriminalization of libel and the prevention of "red-tagging" or the weaponization of anti-disinformation laws. Finally, for the community press itself, the findings emphasize the necessity of developing resiliency plans and embracing digital adaptation to ensure long-term sustainability in an increasingly digital and fragmented media environment.

title: Digital Transformation in Government: Chatbot for Communicating Tax Exemption Among Selected Users in the Philippines
abstract:
This is an exploratory descriptive study on the use of the Department of Finances (DOF) TESA Chatbot to communicate tax exemption to selected diplomatic community members and international organisations using the DOF's Enhanced Tax Exemption System-Lite (TESlite). The TESA Chatbot aims to streamline the tax exemption process and contribute to DOF's digital transformation plan.

Guided by the principles of Cybernetics theory, data were collected through key informant interviews with two industry experts and focus group discussions with seven TESA chatbot users. Before the deployment of the chatbot, communication difficulties included long waiting times, strict office hours, and health concerns during the pandemic. Through the chatbot, the users enjoyed the convenience of 24/7 availability, instant responses, and getting answers to their basic inquiries. However, challenges persist, such as the chatbot􀂶s limitations in handling complex queries and providing outdated information. Hence, the participants cited these opportunities for improvement: continuous updating of the system, incorporation of various languages, and expanding the chatbot􀂶s scope. Overall, the pilot TESA Chabot can be a supplement but not a replacement for human interaction and communication in applying for tax exemption online. The chatbot can be the first step for basic inquiries, but human intervention is still deemed highly important and preferred by applicants for special cases or complex queries. Suggestions to improve the pilot implementation are given.

The findings reveal that the TESA chatbot, launched in August 2022, serves as a valuable tool for streamlining communication by providing 24/7 availability, instant responses to basic inquiries, and convenient access to manuals. However, human intervention remains indispensable for specialized cases requiring empathy and precision. Recommendations include continuous accuracy updates, multi-language support, advanced algorithms for complex queries, and interface enhancements.

two:
This exploratory descriptive study investigates the implementation of the Tax Exemption System Assistant (TESA) chatbot by the Philippine Department of Finance (DOF). The research focuses on how this digital tool facilitates communication regarding tax exemptions among members of the diplomatic community and international organizations.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the broader context of digital transformation in government, specifically addressing the need for more efficient public service delivery in the Philippines. Historically, the tax exemption process at the DOF Revenue Office (RO) relied heavily on face-to-face interactions and telephone consultations. This traditional method presented several significant communication difficulties, including long waiting times, limited consulting hours (restricted to standard office hours), and the physical burden of traveling to the DOF office in Manila. These challenges were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which necessitated social distancing and a shift toward "no-contact" policies. Furthermore, the increasing volume of applications—driven by rising numbers of international organizations and specific legislative needs like the Vaccination Program Act—placed a heavy burden on human revenue officers, making manual processing and telephone inquiries increasingly difficult to manage.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed an exploratory descriptive research design to explore the phenomenon from the perspective of the users. The study was conducted at the Department of Finance in Manila. Data collection involved two primary methods: focus group discussions (FGD) with seven registered users of the TESA chatbot and key informant interviews (KII) with two industry experts (one from the DOF and one from the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation). The data were analyzed using thematic analysis following Saldaña’s framework, which involved open, axial, and thematic coding to identify recurring patterns and meanings. The study was guided by the Cybernetics theory of communication, which emphasizes feedback loops and the ability of a system to adapt to its environment through interaction.

**Findings**
The findings reveal that the TESA chatbot, launched in August 2022, serves as a valuable tool for streamlining communication, though it is not a complete replacement for human interaction.

Before the chatbot, users faced significant hurdles such as long travel distances and the inability to seek information outside of standard business hours. With the introduction of the TESA chatbot, users reported several advantages, most notably 24/7 availability, instant responses to basic inquiries, and the convenience of accessing manuals and policy information at their fingertips. The user-friendly interface and the ability to use single-word keywords were also noted as benefits.

However, the study identified several persistent challenges. The chatbot is currently limited to handling basic, frequently asked questions (FAQs) and struggles with complex or highly specific queries. Users expressed frustration when the chatbot provided entire manuals in response to specific questions rather than direct answers. Additionally, technical and design issues were noted, such as a small and unattractive icon that makes the tool difficult to discover. There were also concerns regarding the accuracy of information, as some provided data was outdated. Ultimately, users indicated that while the chatbot is helpful for initial inquiries, they still prefer human intervention for specialized cases due to the need for empathy, precision, and understanding.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that the TESA chatbot functions effectively as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human revenue officers. It acts as a vital first step in the communication process, filtering basic inquiries and reducing the volume of routine questions that reach human staff. However, the "human element" remains indispensable for managing intricate legal cases and providing nuanced guidance.

The implications of this research suggest that for digital transformation to be successful in a government setting, chatbots must evolve beyond simple FAQ repositories. To improve the system, the researcher suggests continuous updates to ensure information accuracy, the incorporation of multiple languages to cater to a diverse international community, and the implementation of more advanced algorithms or machine learning to handle complex queries. Furthermore, enhancing the user interface and making the chatbot's tone more conversational and "human-like" could improve user engagement and rapport. For future research, the study suggests exploring the integration of chatbot services with application tracking features and conducting comparative studies with other government digital tools.

title: Communicating Risk and Disaster Preparedness among Coastal Communities in Gitagum, Misamis Oriental, Philippines
abstract: Risk communication in disasters aims to prepare people to prevent and mitigate disaster impact. The present study explores the influence of risk communications strategies by the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (LDRRMO) on the level of disaster preparedness of the coastal communities of the Local Government Unit in Gitagum, Misamis Oriental. The study employed a quantitative design and a descriptive method of research using survey questionnaires. The respondents were the three hundred eighty-six (386) randomly selected individuals living in the coastal areas and residents living along flood prone roads. Based on the findings, the risk communication strategies used by the LDRRMO of the Municipality of Gitagum, particularly on the timing and frequency of communications and the level of trust in institutions, have a significant impact on the participants’ disaster preparedness. However, the community's trust in the local government's provision of risk information needs to be enhanced. The individual’s attitude and awareness on preparedness are rated as satisfactory, suggesting further for an improved level of knowledge on weather conditions. Therefore, the risk communication strategies, specifically on timing and frequency and trust in institutions, by the LDRRMO can influence the disaster preparedness of a community. The study points to the need of assisting local government units in disaster preparedness on effective dissemination of PAGASA weather advisories.

The thesis titled "Communicating Risk and Disaster Preparedness among Coastal Communities in Gitagum, Misamis Oriental, Philippines" by Rochelle D. Dagang investigates how risk communication strategies employed by the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (LDRRMO) influence the disaster preparedness levels of residents in coastal and flood-prone areas.

**Problem and Context**
The Philippines is highly vulnerable to natural disasters, particularly typhoons and storm surges. In the municipality of Gitagum, Misamis Oriental, coastal communities face significant risks from these weather disturbances. While disaster preparedness is essential for mitigating the impact of such events, effective communication is a critical yet complex component of this process. The study addresses a gap in existing research regarding the specific perspectives of residents on the communication strategies used by local authorities. The central research question asks whether the risk communication strategies of the LDRRMO influence the level of disaster preparedness among these coastal communities.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a quantitative research design using a descriptive-causal method. The study was conducted in the five coastal barangays of Gitagum: Burnay, Matangad, Pangayawan, Poblacion, and Quezon. The respondents consisted of 386 randomly selected individuals who are long-time residents (at least two years) and have been exposed to risk communication from the LDRRMO. Data were collected using a survey questionnaire written in the Cebunao Visayan language, which was validated by experts and tested for reliability using Cronbach’s Alpha. The instrument measured two main groups of variables: Risk Communication Factors (message content and framing, channel of communication, timing and frequency, and trust in institutions) and Disaster Preparedness dimensions (knowledge, awareness, and attitude). Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, and mean) and inferential statistics (Pearson-R correlation and Multiple Linear Regression).

**Findings**
The findings indicate that the risk communication strategies used by the LDRRMO are perceived as generally effective, with an overall mean of 4.16. Specifically, respondents agreed that the message content and framing are clear and comprehensive, and that the channels of communication, such as radio and social media, are effective. The timing and frequency of advisories were also rated positively, suggesting that the LDRRMO provides sufficient lead time for preparation. Regarding trust, while the LDRRMO and PAGASA are viewed as credible sources, the study noted a nuanced perspective where trust in local dissemination systems could be further strengthened.

In terms of disaster preparedness, the respondents' levels of knowledge, awareness, and attitude were rated as satisfactory. The correlation analysis revealed a significant relationship between risk communication strategies and the quality of communication to the respondents' level of preparedness. Furthermore, the multiple linear regression analysis demonstrated that risk communication factors—specifically the timing and frequency of communications and the level of trust in institutions—have a significant influence on the disaster preparedness of the community.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that the risk communication strategies of the LDRRMO in Gitagum significantly impact the disaster preparedness of coastal residents. Effective communication, characterized by timely, frequent, and credible information, is a key driver in enhancing the knowledge and attitudes necessary for community resilience. However, the research also highlights that while general preparedness is satisfactory, there is still room for improvement in terms of community awareness regarding specific weather conditions and the depth of trust in local dissemination processes.

The implications of this research suggest that local government units (LGUs) should prioritize the optimization of communication timing and the strengthening of institutional trust to maximize preparedness. There is a specific need to assist LGUs in the effective dissemination of PAGASA weather advisories to ensure they are not only received but also understood and acted upon. The study serves as a resource for academic institutions and a guide for national government agencies to craft policies that enhance the quality of risk messaging and communication processes in disaster-prone areas.

title: Geospatial Direct-Address Videos As Alternative Participatory Governance Device For Community Problem Identification And Decision-Making At A Subdivision In A City Located In Laguna, Philippines
abstract: This study, by way of a thematic analysis, strived to determine the perspectives of barangay decision-makers and of residents of a subdivision in a city located in Laguna on a series of geospatial direct-address videos as an alternative participatory governance device for community problem identification and decisionmaking using VeneKlasen and Miller’s (2002) distinctions about power and Tufte and Mefalopulos’ (2009) participatory outcomes. The community problems/issues identified by the residents in the direct-address videos were embedded in a digital map of the subdivision so that they can be located geospatially. From the results, Power Over, Power With, and Power Within were observed in some of the residents’ insights, plus Increased Feelings of Ownership and notions that run counter to Actual Influence on Institutions. Put together, they evoke the residents’ proactive efforts, and pride, in resolving their own problems. But also, Power Over, because of instances when their powerlessness as residents was implied in community-level decision-making. As for the barangay decision-makers’ insights on the videos, the most observed was Power Over, which expresses their adherence to the hierarchical ways with which they respond to community problems/issues. As for the participatory outcomes, the most observed, next to N/A, was Improvement of Competencies and Capacities, implying that the barangay decision-makers understand the benefits of using the geospatial direct-address videos as alternative participatory governance device.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Ivan Khalil L. Descartin’s thesis investigates whether geospatial direct-address videos—short clips of residents discussing local grievances embedded into a digital map—can serve as an alternative participatory governance device. Conducted in a subdivision in Laguna, Philippines, the qualitative study used transect walks to collect resident interviews, which were then integrated into an interactive map. This map and the accompanying videos were used during a Focus Group Discussion with barangay decision-makers to facilitate video elicitation.

The findings revealed a disconnect between the perspectives of residents and decision-makers. For residents, the videos evoked elements of Power With and Power Within, fostering a sense of pride, agency, and ownership over their community. However, residents also expressed Power Over, noting a sense of powerlessness regarding actual decision-making processes. Conversely, decision-makers predominantly demonstrated Power Over, adhering to hierarchical methods. While decision-makers recognized the tool's potential for the improvement of competencies and capacities, there was no evidence of actual influence on institutions.

The study concludes that while geospatial direct-address videos effectively make community grievances visible and locatable, they are not a panacea for systemic power issues. For residents, the tool fosters ownership, while decision-makers view it as a beneficial technological advancement for issue management. Ultimately, the research suggests that for such ICT-based tools to drive institutional change, there must be a fundamental shift in how power is distributed within the barangay governance structure.

The thesis titled "Geospatial Direct-Address Videos As Alternative Participatory Governance Device For Community Problem Identification And Decision-Making At A Subdivision In A City Located In Laguna, Philippines" by Ivan Khalil L. Descartin investigates the potential of multimedia tools to enhance community engagement in local governance. The study explores how geospatial direct-address videos—short clips of residents speaking directly to the camera about local grievances, embedded into a digital map for geospatial localization—can serve as an alternative mechanism for residents to identify community problems and for decision-makers to engage in participatory decision-making.

The research addresses the limitations of traditional governance mechanisms in capturing the immediate, lived realities of residents at the barangay level. Conducted in a subdivision in Laguna, Philippines, the study employed a qualitative methodology. The researcher used a transect walk to conduct direct-address interviews with residents, which were then integrated into an interactive digital map. Subsequently, a Focus Group Discussion (FGD) was held with barangay decision-makers, using the digital map and videos as video elicitation. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, applying frameworks regarding power and participatory outcomes.

The findings revealed distinct perspectives between residents and decision-makers. Among residents, the thematic analysis identified elements of Power Over, Power With, and Power Within. The videos evoked proactive efforts and a sense of pride, contributing to increased feelings of ownership. However, "Power Over" was also observed, as residents expressed a sense of powerlessness regarding actual community-level decision-making processes.

In contrast, the insights from barangay decision-makers predominantly reflected "Power Over," characterized by an adherence to hierarchical methods when responding to community issues. Regarding participatory outcomes, decision-makers most frequently demonstrated an "Improvement of Competencies and Capacities," suggesting they recognize the potential benefits of using such digital tools. However, the study found no evidence of "Actual Influence on Institutions" within the decision-makers' responses, indicating that the technology has not yet translated into a shift in institutional power dynamics.

The study concludes that geospatial direct-address videos are powerful tools for making community grievances visible and locatable. For residents, the process fosters agency and ownership, while for decision-makers, the tool is viewed as a beneficial technological advancement for managing community issues, despite remaining rooted in top-down administrative structures. The research implies that while ICT-based tools can bridge information gaps, they are not a panacea for systemic power issues. For these tools to move toward actual institutional change, there must be a shift in how power is distributed within the barangay governance structure.

The thesis titled "Geospatial Direct-Address Videos As Alternative Participatory Governance Device For Community Problem Identification And Decision-Making At A Subdivision In A City Located In Laguna, Philippines" by Ivan Khalil L. Descartin explores the potential of using multimedia tools to enhance community engagement in local governance. The study specifically investigates how geospatial direct-address videos can serve as an alternative mechanism for residents to identify community problems and for decision-makers to engage in participatory decision-making.

The problem addressed by the researcher is the need for alternative platforms for community problem identification at the barangay level. Traditional governance mechanisms often struggle to capture the immediate, lived realities of residents. The study seeks to determine the perspectives of both subdivision residents and barangay decision-makers regarding the use of geospatial direct-address videos—short video clips of residents speaking directly to the camera about local grievances, which are then embedded into a digital map of the subdivision to allow for geospatial localization.

The research was conducted in a subdivision within a barangay in a city in Laguna, Philippines. The methodology employed a qualitative approach, utilizing a transect walk to navigate the subdivision and conduct on-going, direct-address interviews with residents. These video footages were then integrated into an interactive digital map. Following the data collection, the researcher conducted a Focus Group Discussion (FGD) with barangay decision-makers, using the digital map and videos as a form of video elicitation to gather their reactions. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis, specifically applying VeneKlasen and Miller’s (2002) distinctions regarding power and Tufte and Mefalopulos’ (2009) framework for participatory outcomes.

The findings revealed distinct perspectives between the two groups. Among the residents, the thematic analysis identified elements of Power Over, Power With, and Power Within. The results suggested that the videos evoked proactive efforts and a sense of pride in residents' ability to address their own problems, contributing to increased feelings of ownership. However, "Power Over" was also observed, as residents expressed a sense of powerlessness regarding actual community-level decision-making processes.

In contrast, the insights from barangay decision-makers predominantly reflected "Power Over." This was characterized by an adherence to hierarchical methods when responding to community issues. Regarding participatory outcomes, the decision-makers most frequently demonstrated an "Improvement of Competencies and Capacities," suggesting they recognize the potential benefits of using such digital tools for governance. However, the study found no evidence of "Actual Influence on Institutions" within the decision-makers' responses, indicating that while they see the value in the technology, it has not yet translated into a shift in institutional power dynamics.

The study concludes that geospatial direct-address videos serve as a powerful tool for making community grievances visible and locatable. For residents, the process fosters a sense of agency and ownership, even if it simultaneously highlights existing power imbalances. For decision-makers, the tool is viewed as a beneficial technological advancement that could improve their capacity to manage community issues, though they remain largely rooted in hierarchical, top-down administrative structures.

The implications of this research suggest that while ICT-based participatory tools can bridge the gap in information access and provide a platform for "naming the world," they are not a panacea for systemic power issues. For these tools to move beyond mere "capacity building" and toward actual institutional change, there must be a shift in how power is distributed within the barangay governance structure. The study highlights the potential for digital storytelling and geospatial mapping to transform community conversations from passive feedback into active, collaborative governance.

title: Communication and Redefining Home and Identity: Autoethnography of a Filipino Third Culture Kid Belonging to a Returnee OFW Family from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
abstract:
This study explores how communication has been interwoven in my third culture experiences as a member of an OFW family living in Saudi Arabia, and how these communication experiences allowed me to (re)shape my concept of home and identity as a third culture kid now residing in the Philippines. I used socio-cultural tradition as a theoretical lens and autoethnography as a methodology to create a chronology of my experiences based on personal memory data and artifacts.

As a Filipino TCK, redefining home and identity through communication experiences is a continuous arduous process of preserving one's own culture, adapting to new cultural shifts and situations, and maintaining meaningful relationships. This requires having a good support system, consistent practice of the home culture, and embracing the host culture.

Communication, whether verbal, nonverbal, in person, or online, plays an important role in shaping my concept of home and identity as a TCK. While there are many communication difficulties and challenges, communication must be consistent in whatever shape it takes to maintain one's pursuit of home and identity.

half:
Aleia E. Garcia’s thesis, "Communication and Redefining Home and Identity: Autoethnography of a Filipino Third Culture Kid Belonging to a Returnee OFW Family from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," explores the relationship between communication, cultural identity, and the concept of home for a Filipino Third Culture Kid (TCK). The study addresses the displacement and disorientation experienced by children who relocate with parents to countries like Saudi Arabia for economic reasons and subsequently return to the Philippines. Using autoethnography, the researcher utilizes her own lived experiences, supported by artifacts such as diaries, photographs, and social media records, to examine how identities are shaped through communicative interactions.

The findings reveal that for a TCK, home is not a fixed physical location but a relational and emotional construct. While living in Saudi Arabia, home was a blend of Filipino traditions and the host culture, but returning to the Philippines resulted in a "rude awakening" where the author felt like a stranger in her own birthplace. Communication serves as a central tool for navigating these shifts; maintaining the Filipino language and participating in cultural rituals helped preserve identity, while digital communication provided stability during movement. The study concludes that redefining identity is a continuous, arduous process shaped by the interaction between the individual and their changing environment. The research advocates for meaningful communication to help TCKs navigate sociocultural transitions and integrate into new environments.

This thesis, titled "Communication and Redefining Home and Identity: Autoethnography of a Filipino Third Culture Kid Belonging to a Returnee OFW Family from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," explores the complex relationship between communication, cultural identity, and the concept of home for a Filipino Third Culture Kid (TCK). The researcher, Aleia E. Garcia, examines her personal journey of growing up in Saudi Arabia as part of an Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) family and her subsequent transition back to the Philippines.

The problem addressed in this study is the sense of displacement, alienation, and disorientation experienced by TCKs, particularly those from OFW families. While much literature focuses on the individual expatriate or the "left-behind" children in the Philippines, there is a gap in understanding the experiences of children who relocate with their parents and then return to their native country. These individuals often face a "transient" existence, feeling as though they belong everywhere and nowhere at once. The study seeks to understand how communication experiences—verbal, nonverbal, and digital—help these individuals navigate shifting cultural landscapes and redefine their sense of self and belonging.

The context of the study is rooted in the phenomenon of Filipino migration. The author notes that migration is often driven by economic necessity, and for many families, this involves relocating to countries like Saudi Arabia to secure a better future. This relocation creates a "third culture" experience, where children must balance their native Filipino culture with the host culture of their residence. The study is specifically situated within the framework of the socio-cultural tradition of communication, which posits that social order, norms, and identities are produced and reproduced through communicative interactions.

The researcher employs autoethnography as the primary methodology. This approach allows the author to use her own lived experiences as data to understand broader cultural phenomena. The data collection involved a chronology of personal experiences supported by various artifacts, including personal diaries, family photographs, home videos, emails, and social media records. This multimodal approach provides a deep, reflexive look at the researcher's personal history as a means to illuminate the wider TCK experience.

The findings are presented through a chronology of the author's life, divided into several stages: moving to and living in Saudi Arabia, the period of alternating between Saudi Arabia and the Philippines, leaving Saudi Arabia, and finally settling in the Philippines. The research highlights that the concept of "home" for a TCK is not a fixed physical location but is something that is constantly being reproduced and redefined. In Saudi Arabia, home was a blend of Filipino traditions practiced within the household and the surrounding Saudi culture. Upon returning to the Philippines, the author experienced a "rude awakening," feeling like a stranger in her own birthplace.

Communication played a central role in this journey. The findings suggest that communication serves as a tool for maintaining cultural continuity and building a support system. For the author, maintaining the Filipino language and participating in cultural rituals (such as eating Filipino food or attending community gatherings) were vital communicative acts that preserved her identity. Furthermore, digital communication, specifically social media and email, acted as an "emerging sphere" that helped maintain family connections and provided a sense of stability amidst constant movement. The study also notes that intercultural communication skills—such as adaptability and empathy—are developed through these constant cultural shifts.

The conclusions of the thesis emphasize that redefining home and identity is a continuous and often arduous process for TCKs. The research concludes that identity is dynamic and shaped by the interaction between the individual and their changing environment. Home is ultimately revealed to be a relational and emotional construct rather than a purely geographical one. The study also highlights that for returnee OFW families, the transition back to the Philippines requires significant emotional and communicative adjustment to rebuild a sense of belonging in a familiar yet unfamiliar setting.

The implications of this study are both personal and academic. For TCKs and children of OFWs, the research serves to normalize their feelings of displacement and provides a sense of shared experience, suggesting they are not alone in their search for belonging. Academically, the study contributes to the field of Development Communication by providing a unique perspective on the TCK experience through the lens of communication. It advocates for the importance of consistent and meaningful communication—both within the family and with the broader community—to help TCKs navigate their unique sociocultural transitions and successfully integrate into new environments.

title: Communication for Safe(r) Spaces in Coming Out Among Filipino Queer Youth
abstract:
This study explored the Filipino queer youth's communicational perspective of safe spaces for coming out in the Philippine context. Guided by Blumerian Symbolic Interactionism, it uses Charmaz's constructivist grounded theory (Charmaz, 2006) as methodology. A theoretical sample of six Filipino queer youth from official queer student organizations in two universities in Metro Manila were interviewed in-depth online via Zoom from October 2022 to March 2023. Comparative analysis of data, concepts, and categories through reiterative coding steps was done.

The Filipino queer youth identified kanlungan, tahanan, tambayan/takbuhan as the safe spaces because these are where they feel most honest to themselves, accepted, comforted, protected, empowered, and excited. Safe spaces are characterized as chosen (gender identity disclosure is solely their decision), established (initiating disclosure before they expect disclosure from others), all encompassing (safety must be existent in all social institutions), and indefinite (a safe space can be a person/location or both). Safe spaces also have internal and external layers of safeness. Internally, a space is safe if there is no experience of gender dysphoria or self-harm ideations and if their disclosure were decided based on the elements of choice, readiness, timing, and relationship. Moreover, a space is externally safe if religious, socio-cultural, political, educational, and financial factors are all gender-affirmative.

Communication plays a crucial role in creating safe spaces for the Filipino queer youth because it is through verbal and non-verbal communication that they get signs and symbols of whether they are accepted or not. Safe spaces are introduced, disseminated, and negotiated through interactions. The symbols of safe spaces and their meanings are continuously transformed and can produce a universally understood meaning of safe spaces for the queer community through Symbolic Interactionism.

half:
This thesis, titled "Communication for Safe(r) Spaces in Coming Out Among Filipino Queer Youth," investigates how Filipino LGBTQIA+ youth conceptualize and experience safe spaces during the coming-out process. Addressing a gap in Western-centric literature, the study situates the research within the Philippine social climate, where familiarity with homosexuality coexists with persistent discrimination and heteronormative pressures. The research focuses on how communication is used to negotiate safe spaces to mitigate risks such as minority stress, rejection, and violence.

Using a qualitative approach grounded in Charmaz’s Constructivist Grounded Theory, the researcher conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with six Filipino queer youth from two universities in Metro Manila. The findings reveal that these youth identify safe spaces using the terms *kanlungan* (sanctuary), *tahanan* (home), and *tambayan/takbuhan* (hangout/refuge). These spaces are characterized by honesty, acceptance, comfort, protection, empowerment, and excitement. Safe spaces are identified as being chosen, established, all-encompassing, and indefinite. Safeness is categorized into internal layers, involving readiness and freedom from dysphoria, and external layers, involving gender-affirmative religious, socio-cultural, political, educational, and financial factors.

The study concludes that communication is the primary mechanism for introducing and negotiating these spaces. Communicative affirmation is essential for mitigating minority stress. The findings suggest that creating safer environments requires the active cultivation of gender-affirmative communication across all sectors of society.

This thesis, titled "Communication for Safe(r) Spaces in Coming Out Among Filipino Queer Youth," explores how Filipino LGBTQIA+ youth conceptualize and experience safe spaces during the process of coming out. The research seeks to provide a non-Western perspective on a phenomenon that has historically been studied through Western theoretical frameworks.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the complex social climate of the Philippines, where high levels of familiarity and acceptance of homosexuality coexist with persistent discrimination, violence, and heteronormative pressures. The author notes that while there is increasing visibility for LGBTQIA+ individuals in Philippine politics and entertainment, significant barriers remain in religious, educational, and corporate sectors. The research identifies a gap in literature regarding how the communicative aspects of "safe spaces" are negotiated within the specific socio-cultural context of the Philippines. The core problem addressed is the need to understand how Filipino queer youth construe communication for safe spaces and how communication can be used to develop these spaces to mitigate the risks associated with coming out, such as minority stress, rejection, and violence.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a qualitative approach using Charmaz’s Constructivist Grounded Theory. This methodology was chosen to allow the theory to emerge from the participants' lived experiences. The study utilized a theoretical sample of six Filipino queer youth, all of whom were members of official queer student organizations at two universities in Metro Manila. Data collection was conducted through in-depth, semi-structured interviews held online via Zoom between October 2022 and March 2023. The researcher used comparative analysis and reiterative coding steps to process the data, concepts, and categories. The study was guided by Blumerian Symbolic Interactionism, focusing on how meaning is created through social interaction and symbols.

**Findings**
The findings reveal that Filipino queer youth identify specific spaces as "safe," which they refer to using the terms *kanlungan* (sanctuary), *tahanan* (home), and *tambayan/takbuhan* (hangout/refuge). These spaces are defined by the feeling of being honest, accepted, comforted, protected, empowered, and excited. The study identifies four key characteristics of a safe space: they are chosen (disclosure is a personal decision), established (the individual initiates disclosure), all-encompassing (safety should exist across all social institutions), and indefinite (a safe space can be a person, a location, or both).

The research further categorizes safeness into internal and external layers. Internally, a space is safe if it is free from gender dysphoria or self-harm ideation and if disclosure is based on readiness, timing, and choice. Externally, a space is safe if religious, socio-cultural, political, educational, and financial factors are gender-affirmative. Communication is identified as the fundamental tool for negotiating these spaces; through verbal and non-verbal cues, individuals interpret whether they are being accepted or rejected. The study concludes that safe spaces are not static but are continuously negotiated and transformed through social interactions.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that communication is the primary mechanism through which safe spaces are introduced, disseminated, and negotiated. For Filipino queer youth, the ability to communicate effectively—and to be met with communicative affirmation—is central to the coming-out process. The research highlights that safe spaces are essential for mitigating the "minority stress" experienced by LGBTQIA+ individuals, providing a necessary buffer against the external stressors of discrimination and the internal stressors of perceived stigma.

The implications of this research are both academic and social. Academically, it contributes to queer studies by providing a localized, non-Western understanding of identity disclosure. Socially, the findings suggest that creating safer environments requires more than just the absence of violence; it requires the active cultivation of gender-affirmative communication across all sectors of society. The study offers "Filipino Queer Youth Advice for Coming Out," emphasizing the importance of finding spaces that offer both emotional and physical security. Ultimately, the work advocates for more supportive social interactions and dialogues to facilitate the creation of safer environments for the Filipino queer community.

title: Knowledge Practices Within the Health Knowledge Systems in Virac, Catanduanes, Philippines
abstract:
To investigate the knowledge practices within the health knowledge systems in Virac, Catanduanes which includes the provincial and municipal health offices, the rural health unit (RHU), and barangay health workers (BHWs), key-informant interviews, focus-group discussion, and survey were conducted. The study, guided by the Knowledge Utilization Theory of Verkasalo and Lappalainen (1998), examined the following practices on health emergency management: knowledge acquisition, knowledge capture and retrieval, and knowledge transfer among health authorities, as well as the knowledge receival, knowledge perception and knowledge utilization among BHWs.

The study found that health authorities adopt various approaches to acquire knowledge on health emergency management. Explicit knowledge is acquired through formal and systematic structures, while tacit knowledge is acquired through open, spontaneous knowledge sharing. To ensure knowledge transfer to barangay health workers (BHWs), health authorities also conduct various activities such as, but not limited to, training, seminars, meetings, and mentoring. The most popular method of knowledge transfer was found to be the use of the group chat system on Facebook Messenger that enables health authorities to directly connect with BHWs without meeting them face-to-face.

Knowledge sharing practices were also investigated to check whether the tacit knowledge that BHWs have acquired through experience are being communicated to the provincial and municipal level. The findings showed that BHWs are more inclined to share their knowledge with their barangay nurse/midwife supervisors rather than directly with health authorities at the provincial and municipal levels.

Other challenges are organizational, as well as technological barriers that hinder seamless communication among health workers, thereby impeding the sharing of critical knowledge on health emergency management.

Despite these gaps, BHWs still possess and highly utilize the critical knowledge on health emergency management they have received.

The respondents included health authorities from the Provincial Health Office (PHO) and Municipal Health Office (MHO), nurse and midwife supervisors from the RHU, and BHWs.

However, a gap exists in the direction of knowledge sharing; BHWs are more inclined to share their acquired tacit knowledge with their immediate barangay nurse or midwife supervisors rather than communicating directly with provincial or municipal health authorities. title: The Changing Nature of Community Media: A Case Study of Digital Shift Among Selected Publications in the Province of Cavite, Philippines
abstract:
Using a case study approach, this master thesis conducted in-depth interviews with the heads or editors-in-chief of five (5) publications in the province of Cavite. With ethical considerations in mind, the interview yielded meaningful narratives that shed light on how community media continues to adapt in a digital environment. The researcher used an interview guide, a coding sheet, and thematic analysis to explore the "then" and "now" of the selected papers, which underwent a digitization process. Essentially, themes surfaced and were employed to elucidate how community media is adjusting in terms of ownership, manpower, financial resources, production process, and distribution.

In accordance with the analysis, the research revealed that the ownership has not changed since then as most of the publications are still reliant on government support while the other one thrives as a private-owned newspaper. In terms of adaptability, a lot of them were forced to decrease their manpower since in their case, they needed to decrease their size. Others, however, found it to be a struggle since some of them had to shoulder the responsibility of content creation all by themselves.

Additionally, the study clarified how these publications' production altered as a result of reduced delays brought on by time flexibility and the introduction of technology, which made it easier for them to obtain their sources and presented a chance for innovation. Furthermore, their packaging is still ethically upright despite modifications, particularly when it comes to using human sources. They are making an extra effort to be social media responsible because they are now navigating online. Maintaining the paper digitally requires a certain level of familiarity to maintain not only the effective dissemination of information but also the development of integrity and harmony with their community.

As a result, community media continues to stand firm and, despite maintaining its distinctive nature in the digital age, the stories drawn from each case demonstrated that these local newspapers continue to adhere to the ideals and standards of civic journalism. Therefore, these local newspapers and newsletters are co-existing to raise awareness on issues concerned and highlight realities in the hopes of seeing people fulfill their potential to advance as individuals and eventually create an informed society.

title: Environmental Interpretation and Beach Goers' Pro-Environmental Behavior: Perspectives from Members of Generation Z
abstract:
This qualitative research examines the interpretive experience of six female beach goers, who are all members of Generation Z, at Playa La Caleta, a nature resort in Morong, Bataan, Philippines. Using the phenomenological tradition of communication theory and Tilden's philosophy of interpretation as a framework, the research sought to understand the communication process between nature (the beach) and human (the Generation Z beach goers) through an interpretive experience, and how such dialogue or experience of otherness impacted Gen Zers’ understanding, appreciation, and protection of beach environment.

The research revealed a negotiation-like dialogue between the research participants and the beach environment: Keep me clean and I’ll give you peace of mind. This interpretation of their communication process shaped the participants’ proenvironmental behaviors towards the beach environment and their expressed plan of action moving forward. The research highlights the importance of emphasizing tangible and intangible rewards in environmental interpretation initiatives, and highlights the distinct Filipino characteristics of hiya and strong family ties as influencers of pro-environment behaviors among Filipino members of Generation Z. Finally, the research presents recommendations for future related research and for the enhancement of environmental interpretation initiatives in beaches.

This qualitative study investigates the relationship between environmental interpretation and the pro-environmental behavior of Generation Z beachgoers in the Philippines. Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, the researcher explored how dialogue between humans and coastal ecosystems influences the protection of these environments. The study focused on six female Filipino participants aged 22 to 23 during an overnight interpretive experience at Playa La Caleta in Morong, Bataan, which included activities such as beach clean-ups, tree planting, and observing environmental signage.

The findings reveal a complex dialogue between participants and the environment, characterized by the theme "Keep me clean and I’ll give you peace of mind." Participants identified the beach as a vital source of mental rejuvenation, particularly post-pandemic, creating an emotional connection that drives environmental protection. Three interpretive mechanisms were identified: an "exchange deal" using tangible rewards to provide informational nudges; direct engagement through activities like clean-ups that transition participants from extrinsic to intrinsic motivation; and creative, visual communication, such as gamified signage, that makes environmental responsibility "Instagrammable" and fun.

The study concludes that effective environmental interpretation must move beyond transmitting facts to facilitate emotional and personal connections. For Generation Z, protection is most likely when framed as a way to preserve mental well-being or integrated into social, rewarding activities. The research suggests the tourism industry should adopt experiential communication, immediate incentives, and social media integration to foster a sense of reciprocity.

This qualitative research investigates the relationship between environmental interpretation and the pro-environmental behavior (PEB) of Generation Z beachgoers. Using the phenomenological tradition of communication theory and Freeman Tilden’s philosophy of interpretation, the study explores how the dialogue between humans and the natural environment influences understanding, appreciation, and protection of coastal ecosystems.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the context of increasing environmental degradation in Philippine beach destinations, characterized by plastic waste, water pollution, and the "sachet economy." While many tourists express concern for the environment, research indicates a significant gap between environmental awareness and actual pro-environmental behavior. The researcher identifies Generation Z as a critical demographic for intervention, as these "digital natives" are increasingly prioritizing sustainable travel and are estimated to hold significant global spending power. The study specifically addresses the need to move beyond mere factual information toward communication strategies that foster deep, personal connections with nature to encourage sustainable practices.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a qualitative approach using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). The study involved six female Filipino members of Generation Z, aged 22 to 23, who participated in an overnight interpretive experience at Playa La Caleta, a nature resort in Morong, Bataan. The interpretive experience included participating in a beach clean-up, tree planting, observing environmental signages, and attending an informational talk regarding the resort's natural and historical significance. Data were gathered through a recorded semi-structured focus group discussion held immediately after the trip, followed by individual open-ended questions sent via email to validate and deepen the participants' lived experiences.

**Findings**
The findings reveal a complex, negotiation-like dialogue between the participants and the beach environment, summarized by the theme: "Keep me clean and I’ll give you peace of mind."

Participants identified the beach as a vital source of "peace of mind" and mental rejuvenation, particularly following the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic. This emotional connection to the environment was a primary driver for their desire to protect it. The study identified three specific interpretive mechanisms that influenced behavior:

First, the research highlighted an "exchange deal" with nature through tangible rewards. A signage offering free coffee to guests who filled a bucket with beach trash acted as an effective "informational nudge." For Gen Zers, who value instant gratification, this incentive created a win-win scenario where they felt motivated to clean the beach in exchange for a reward.

Second, the study found that intrinsic motivation was triggered through direct engagement. Participating in a beach clean-up provided a sense of fulfillment and "happiness of the heart." This experience transitioned participants from extrinsic motivation (seeking rewards) to intrinsic motivation, where the act of helping the environment became a self-rewarding activity.

Third, creative and visual communication, such as the "Score for the Sea" signage (a basketball-style game for disposing plastic bottles), enhanced the experience by making environmental responsibility "fun" and "Instagrammable." This aligns with Gen Z's tendency to connect nature with digital expression.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that environmental interpretation is most effective when it moves beyond the transmission of facts and instead facilitates an emotional and personal connection to the "otherness" of nature. For Generation Z, the experience of the beach is not just a vacation but a restorative process for mental well-being. When environmental protection is framed as a way to preserve that peace of mind, or when it is integrated into enjoyable, social, and rewarding activities, PEB is more likely to occur.

The research also highlights unique Filipino cultural influences, such as the importance of family travel traditions and the concept of *hiya* (shame/propriety), which can influence how individuals behave in shared public spaces.

The implications for the tourism industry are significant. The study suggests that beach resorts and environmental communicators should move away from purely instructional messaging and toward "experiential" communication. This includes using creative, gamified, and visually appealing signages, offering immediate and sustainable incentives, and providing opportunities for hands-on participation in conservation activities. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the importance of social media as a platform for spreading environmental narratives, as Gen Zers are highly influenced by digital content and social trends. Ultimately, the research suggests that by fostering a sense of "reciprocity" between the tourist and the destination, sustainable tourism can be made both engaging and impactful.

title: Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) on Social Media and Financial Behaviors: A Phenomenological Study of Millennial Overseas Filipino Workers in Singapore
abstract:
This research explored the lived experiences of millennial Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Singapore, focusing on how they experience and make sense of the Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) phenomenon on social media and how it shapes their financial behaviors. Employing a phenomenological approach, the study delved into the actual experiences of OFWs, illustrating how FoMO shaped their financial decision-making and practices.

The study underscored the need for tailored financial literacy interventions that address FoMO, integrating financial education with strategies to mitigate its impact. Policymakers are urged to incorporate comprehensive financial education programs during pre-departure orientations for OFWs to better prepare them for financial challenges abroad.

title: The Social Construction of Inclusivity on a Digital Platform: An Analysis of a Facebook Page of People with Dwarfism
abstract: This research is set within the context of communication studies and social constructionism. It analyzed the social construction of inclusivity based on posts from a Facebook page dedicated to people with dwarfism. The study assumed that the posts made by the Page Administrator represent a shared meaning within the community in the digital space. It sought to answer the questions: what does it mean to be inclusive from the perspective of people with dwarfism, and what are the means for the social construction of inclusivity in the digital space? The posts between January 2023 and May 2024 on the Facebook Page that is publicly accessible were thematically analyzed. The concept of inclusion for those people with dwarfism encompasses visibility, celebration of achievements and contributions (in terms of Focus and Attention), ensuring equal access to resources (Equal Access and Support), societal recognition and engagement (Society Acceptance and Participation), fostering a culture that values diversity and promotes equity (Advocacy and Public Awareness), and equal views of the capacity and ability (Equally Able and Capable). These themes are communicated through continuous engagement on digital platforms in the form of Social Media Campaigns, Documentaries and News Segments, Blogs, Articles, Podcasts, Webinars, and Public Awareness and Systemic Change, shaping a more inclusive and supportive society for people with dwarfism. The digitality of the posts enabled people with dwarfism the opportunity to express their identities and construct networks of support that can influence public opinions and policy. The digital platform facilitates a deeper understanding of the shared meaning and social construction of inclusivity among people with dwarfism, which may be difficult to achieve in non-digital spaces.

In the thesis "The Social Construction of Inclusivity on a Digital Platform: An Analysis of a Facebook Page of People with Dwarfism," Jory Alfonso Pineda explores how digital spaces allow marginalized communities to define and construct their own meanings of inclusivity. Situated within communication studies and social constructionism, the research examines how digital platforms serve as tools for advocacy, identity expression, and community building. The study addresses the systemic exclusion of unique perspectives from people with disabilities in mainstream discourses, noting that digital spaces are often dominated by able-bodied narratives that can trivialize the specific experiences of people with dwarfism.

Focusing on the Facebook page of "Big Dreams for Little People, Inc." (BDLPP), the researcher used a thematic analysis of posts and videos from January 2023 to May 2024. The findings categorize inclusivity through five key themes: focus and attention regarding visibility and achievements; equal access and support for resources; societal acceptance and participation in community life; advocacy and public awareness to promote equity; and the concept of being equally able and capable to challenge notions that physical impairment equates to incapacity. To construct this inclusivity, the community utilizes social media campaigns, documentaries, news segments, blogs, articles, podcasts, and webinars. The thesis concludes that Facebook acts as a powerful advocacy platform, enabling people with dwarfism to move toward a self-defined identity and challenge ableist preconceptions.

This thesis, titled "The Social Construction of Inclusivity on a Digital Platform: An Analysis of a Facebook Page of People with Dwarfism" by Jory Alfonso Pineda, explores how digital spaces allow marginalized communities to define and construct their own meanings of inclusivity. The research is situated within the fields of communication studies and social constructionism, focusing on how digital platforms can serve as tools for advocacy, identity expression, and community building for people with dwarfism.

The problem addressed by the study is the systemic exclusion of the unique perspectives of people with disabilities in mainstream discourses. The author notes that digital spaces are often dominated by able-bodied narratives, which can lead to the trivialization or overlooking of the specific needs and experiences of people with dwarfism. This lack of representation creates a gap in understanding what true inclusivity looks like from the perspective of those living with the condition. The study seeks to understand how a specific digital community—the Facebook page of "Big Dreams for Little People, Inc." (BDLPP)—constructs the meaning of inclusivity and what digital tools are used to facilitate this process.

The research context is centered on the intersection of digital inclusion and disability rights. The author highlights that while people with dwarfism face multifaceted barriers—including physical, social, economic, and legal obstacles—digital platforms offer a unique "safe space" to challenge stereotypes and combat ableism. The study focuses on the period between January 2023 and May 2024, analyzing the publicly accessible posts on the BDLPP Facebook page to understand the shared meanings and social constructions emerging within that digital community.

The methodology employed is a thematic analysis of the Facebook posts and shared videos from the BDLPP page. The study assumes that the content produced by the Page Administrator represents the shared meanings and collective identity of the community in the digital space. By analyzing the themes present in the posts, the researcher identifies how the community communicates its needs, celebrates its members, and advocates for systemic change.

The findings of the research are categorized into two main areas: the perspective of people with dwarfism regarding inclusivity and the means used to construct that inclusivity online. From the perspective of the community, inclusivity is defined through five key themes:
1. Focus and Attention: This involves visibility and the celebration of the achievements and contributions of people with dwarfism.
2. Equal Access and Support: This emphasizes the need for equal access to resources and support systems.
3. Society Acceptance and Participation: This focuses on gaining societal recognition and active engagement in community life.
4. Advocacy and Public Awareness: This involves fostering a culture that values diversity and promotes equity.
5. Equally Able and Capable: This theme challenges the notion that physical impairment equates to incapacity, emphasizing the true potential of individuals.

To construct this inclusivity in the digital space, the community utilizes various means, including social media campaigns, documentaries, news segments, blogs, articles, podcasts, webinars, and efforts toward public awareness and systemic change. The digitality of these posts allows members to express their identities and build support networks that can influence public opinion and policy, a feat that may be more difficult to achieve in non-digital spaces.

The conclusions of the thesis suggest that Facebook serves as a powerful tool for more than just social interaction; it acts as an advocacy and community-supporting platform. The digital environment enables people with dwarfism to create their own understanding of inclusion, moving away from narratives imposed by the able-bodied population toward a legitimate, representative, and self-defined identity. The study concludes that digital platforms facilitate a deeper understanding of shared meanings and provide a vital stage for digital activism that can challenge long-standing ableist preconceptions.

The implications of this research are significant for both development communication and disability advocacy. For practitioners, the study demonstrates how digital tools can be leveraged to amplify the voices of marginalized groups and foster social change. It highlights the importance of self-representation in achieving digital inclusion. For researchers, the study suggests that future inquiries should continue to explore how digital spaces can be optimized to support the empowerment of people with disabilities. Ultimately, the work underscores that digital inclusion is a critical component of broader social justice, providing a platform where diverse experiences can be recognized, valued, and integrated into the social fabric.

title: Lolo and Lola vs. Fraud: The Case of Senior Citizens of Pagsanjan, Laguna Fighting Back Against the ‘Scamdemic’
abstract:
Digital technology continues to evolve, making day-to-day tasks faster and easier. Yet with such rapid evolution has come many risks, as criminals continue to find innovative ways to defraud unwitting victims. This leaves end users at risk, especially senior citizens— a sector especially vulnerable due to scant digital skills.

This narrative inquiry looked at how senior citizens in Pagsanjan, Laguna guard against scams, the extent of their knowledge about the risks, and what they believe could help them better discern scam content. This fills a research gap on how Filipino seniors deal with scams and what support they need for better protection. 

This study examined the experience of six senior citizens, each of whom have had their own brush with fraud, from near misses to actual victimization. It found that the subject seniors have gained self-taught tactics to protect themselves through exposure to news and social media, personal experience, and warnings from reputable organizations and their peers.

But while they expressed confidence that they could protect themselves against fraudsters, they believe the elderly need proper support. This could be delivered in two ways: learning sessions mounted by the government with the help of relevant organizations; and peer guidance.

half:
The rapid evolution of digital technology has introduced significant risks for senior citizens with limited digital skills, a vulnerability exacerbated by the surge in deceptive practices during the pandemic. In the Philippines, fraud targeting the elderly is a growing concern, involving tactics such as romance scams, impersonation of government agencies, or fake prizes. This study employed a qualitative narrative inquiry to explore the experiences of six senior citizens in Pagsanjan, Laguna, aged between 63 and 72. Through in-depth, semi-structured face-to-face interviews, the researcher documented their personal stories to understand how they make sense of online fraud, their sources of knowledge, and necessary support systems.

The findings reveal that all participants were aware of scams, learning about them through television news, social media, and warnings from banks or telecommunications providers. A significant source of information is peer review on social media, where netizens flag fraudulent posts. Identified scam types include promo winners using celebrity names to lure victims into mobile wallet transactions and love scams targeting lonely individuals. Participants developed self-taught discernment skills, adopting a stance of distrust toward unsolicited offers and recognizing red flags like requests for personal details. While personal caution and community feedback on Facebook are effective, some seniors remain vulnerable due to digital ageism or lack of technical proficiency. The study recommends that agencies develop fraud warnings tailored to the elderly using simple language and familiar platforms.

The study identified several types of scam encounters, including "promo winners" where scammers use celebrity names to lure victims into sending money via mobile wallets, and "love scams" that target lonely individuals. One participant recounted a significant loss after being pressured by a scammer into a cash-in transaction under the guise of winning a contest. Other participants described being "reluctant winners" who successfully identified and dismissed unsolicited messages promising large sums of money or legal assistance.

Participants developed self-taught discernment skills, often adopting a stance of distrust toward unsolicited offers. They learned to recognize red flags, such as requests for personal details or demands for small upfront payments to claim larger prizes. Seniors found text advisories from legitimate brands and community feedback on Facebook to be highly effective. Personal caution and lessons learned from past experiences or peers served as primary defense mechanisms. However, some seniors remain vulnerable due to "digital ageism" or a lack of technical proficiency.

Their ability to discern fraud is often tied to media exposure and the support of immediate social circles. title: The Use of New Media for Overcoming Challenges During the COVID-19 Pandemic Among Overseas Filipino Workers in Singapore
abstract:
This study explored how Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Singapore engaged with new media during the COVID-19 pandemic to meet their diverse needs. By employing the Uses and Gratifications Theory, this study examined their media consumption patterns and the interaction between social factors, needs, and media use. The descriptive research found that OFWs primarily accessed new media for communication. Other motivations were information, opportunities, and seeking escape. 

The most utilized new media types were websites, social media, shopping platforms, conferencing tools, and messaging applications. Statistically significant increases were observed in access to online news, learning platforms, and streaming services, with notable surges in telemedicine, video conferencing, and online shopping during the pandemic. Elevated stress among OFWs was linked to job uncertainty, homesickness, worry about family, boredom, and work overload, with the situation of their families in the Philippines being the most pressing concern. 

A higher frequency of new media access was positively associated with the overall effects of new media. It provided OFWs with significant gratifications such as information, education, opportunities, relationships, and relaxation, contributing to high satisfaction with new media and better coping during the pandemic.
