title: Communicating Public Policy: the Case of Ordinance in the City of Metro Manila
abstract:
This study aims to alleviate the widespread case of Internet addiction caused by the proliferation of Internet cafés or computer gaming shops, which is a common dilemma of parents residing in one of the cities in Metro Manila (hereinafter referred to as the “City” for this study). It is noteworthy that the officials of the City have passed a resolution (hereinafter referred to as the “City Ordinance” in this study) to regulate Internet café operations in the City. However, there is a need to address whether the City Ordinance has indeed served its purpose as deemed by this study.

Responses obtained from Internet café users in this study confirmed that excessive visits to computer shops are common among young children in the City. These responses were corroborated with the results of the survey conducted among parents. Both results confirmed that there is an Internet café–related problem among the youth in the City that threatens their good education and bright future. Furthermore, these results suggested that the implementation of and information dissemination done for the City Ordinance, if any, were ineffective.

Given the importance of communication in the success of any public policy, and the changing information environment, the above premise suggests that the very essence of this study—that is, the method used in the dissemination and campaign of the City Ordinance—was examined.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Melinda M. Docallos’s thesis, "Communicating Public Policy: the Case of Ordinance in the City of Metro Manila," investigates the effectiveness of communication strategies used by local authorities to implement regulations for Internet cafés. The study focuses on a specific City Ordinance intended to mitigate the social and academic risks of excessive internet and gaming use among youth, such as academic decline and social isolation. While the ordinance prohibits minors from entering shops during school hours, wearing uniforms inside, or visiting during curfew, a gap exists between the law's existence and its actual impact on behavior.

The research utilizes the Integrated Model of Communication for Social Change, suggesting that successful policy requires a shift from one-way information dissemination to participatory communication. Using a descriptive research design, the researcher gathered data through surveys and interviews from Internet café owners, students, and parents.

The findings confirm that excessive visits to computer shops pose a threat to student education. A critical finding is a disconnect in the communication chain; the implementation and information dissemination of the ordinance have been ineffective. Internet café operators lack sufficient knowledge of the ordinance's provisions, hindering their ability to enforce regulations. Additionally, students frequently violate the ordinance, suggesting that government information has not translated into compliance. The study concludes the ordinance is a "paper policy" failing to achieve intended outcomes due to poor communication and weak enforcement.

Melinda M. Docallos’s thesis, "Communicating Public Policy: the Case of Ordinance in the City of Metro Manila," investigates the effectiveness of communication strategies used by local authorities to implement regulations for Internet cafés. The study focuses on a specific City Ordinance intended to mitigate the social and academic risks of excessive internet and gaming use among youth, such as academic decline and social isolation. While the ordinance prohibits minors from entering shops during school hours, wearing uniforms inside, or visiting during curfew, a gap exists between the law's existence and its actual impact on behavior.

The research is situated in the context of the "infobesity age," where technological advancement has outpaced traditional government communication. The study utilizes the Integrated Model of Communication for Social Change, suggesting that successful policy requires a shift from one-way information dissemination to participatory communication that fosters community engagement. Using a descriptive research design, the researcher gathered data through surveys and interviews from three primary groups in District 2: Internet café owners, students, and parents.

The findings confirm that Internet-related problems are a significant reality for local families, with excessive visits to computer shops posing a threat to student education. A critical finding is a disconnect in the communication chain; the study indicates that the implementation and information dissemination of the ordinance have been ineffective. Internet café operators lack sufficient knowledge of the ordinance's provisions, which hinders their ability to enforce regulations like checking IDs. Additionally, students frequently violate the ordinance by entering shops during school hours or wearing uniforms, suggesting that government information has not translated into compliance.

The study concludes that the ordinance is currently failing to achieve its intended outcomes due to poor communication and weak enforcement. Because the government has not provided sufficient information dissemination to ensure operators understand their responsibilities, the ordinance exists as a "paper policy" lacking the social and administrative support necessary to change behavior. The research emphasizes that policy success is contingent upon the effectiveness of communication and implementation processes rather than just the quality of the law's design.

The implications suggest that policymakers must shift from traditional, one-way communication to participatory and visual methods. Successful public policy requires coordinated efforts between the government, business owners, and the community to create mutual accountability. Without dedicated financial support, training for implementers, and robust information campaigns, the study suggests that similar ordinances are likely to face similar implementation failures.

The thesis titled "Communicating Public Policy: the Case of Ordinance in the City of Metro Manila" by Melinda M. Docallos examines the effectiveness of communication strategies used by local government authorities to implement regulations regarding Internet cafés. The study focuses on a specific City Ordinance designed to mitigate the negative social and academic impacts of excessive internet and gaming use among the youth.

**Problem**
The central problem addressed in this research is the proliferation of Internet addiction and its associated risks among young people, including academic decline, social isolation, and exposure to inappropriate content. While the City Council passed an ordinance to regulate Internet café operations—specifically prohibiting minors from entering during school hours, wearing school uniforms inside shops, or visiting during curfew—there is a perceived gap between the existence of the law and its actual impact on behavior. The researcher identifies a potential failure in the implementation stage, specifically questioning whether the ordinance was effectively communicated to the primary stakeholders: Internet café operators and the citizens (parents and students).

**Context**
The study is situated within the broader context of the "infobesity age," where rapid technological advancement has outpaced traditional government communication methods. The researcher notes that while the internet provides vast knowledge, it also facilitates "Internet Gaming Disorder," a condition recognized by the American Psychiatric Association. In the local context of Metro Manila, the rise of computer gaming shops has become a significant social concern for parents, who report issues such as student absenteeism and school dropouts. The study operates under the theoretical framework of the Integrated Model of Communication for Social Change, emphasizing that for a policy to succeed, it must move beyond one-way "monologic" information dissemination toward "dialogic" or participatory communication that fosters community engagement and behavioral change.

**Method**
The researcher employed a descriptive research design to investigate the level of awareness and compliance regarding the ordinance. The study utilized a multi-perspective approach, gathering data from three primary groups: Internet café owners/administrators, students who frequent these establishments, and parents. Data collection was conducted through surveys and interviews. The sampling was focused on District 2 of the City, with data collection occurring during peak hours (2:00 PM to 7:00 PM) to capture the most active period of internet café usage. The research instruments included structured questionnaires designed to measure knowledge of the ordinance, frequency of visits, duration of gaming, and the specific problems encountered by parents.

**Findings**
The findings confirm that Internet-related problems are a significant reality for families in the City. Survey responses from parents and students corroborate that excessive visits to computer shops are common among the youth, which poses a threat to their education and future. A critical finding is the disconnect in the communication chain: the results suggest that the implementation and information dissemination of the City Ordinance have been ineffective. Specifically, the study indicates that Internet café operators lack sufficient knowledge of the ordinance's provisions, which directly hinders their ability to enforce regulations such as checking IDs or monitoring content. Furthermore, the data reveals that students frequently violate the ordinance by entering shops during school hours, wearing uniforms, or staying past curfew, suggesting that the "sermon" (information) provided by the government has not translated into compliance.

**Conclusions**
The study concludes that the City Ordinance, while well-intentioned and necessary for protecting student welfare, is currently failing to achieve its intended outcomes due to poor communication and weak enforcement. The researcher concludes that the government has not provided sufficient information dissemination to ensure that operators understand their responsibilities. Because the communication has been largely ineffective, the ordinance exists as a "paper policy" that lacks the necessary social and administrative support to change the behavior of the target audience. The study reinforces the idea that policy success is not merely about the quality of the law's design but is heavily contingent upon the effectiveness of the communication and implementation processes.

**Implications**
The implications of this study are significant for policymakers and local government units. First, it highlights the need for a shift from traditional, one-way communication to more participatory and visual communication methods that resonate with the modern information environment. Second, it suggests that for public policy to be successful, there must be a coordinated effort between the government, the business owners (operators), and the community (parents) to create a system of mutual accountability. Finally, the study implies that without dedicated financial support, training for frontline implementers, and a more robust information campaign, similar ordinances in other cities are likely to face the same implementation failures. The research serves as a call to action for city officials to reevaluate their dissemination strategies to ensure that public policy effectively serves the betterment of the community.

title: The Intercultural Communicative Practices of Filipino Women Married to Korean Men In Resolving Marital Conflict
abstract:
The purpose of this study is to understand the views of Filipino women on marital conflict. In addition, it sought to comprehend the intercultural communicative practices of Filipino women in resolving marital conflict with their Korean husbands.

The researcher situated the study within the Ethnomethodological tradition of qualitative research. Participants of the study were chosen purposely, and in-depth interviews were conducted. Interviews were recorded, transcribed and translated to English. Data gathered were analyzed through thematic analysis.

Two main views on marital conflict were present. The Theocentric view explained how the participants sees marital conflict under the orchestration of God. On the other hand, a humancentric view looked at how the participant understood conflict as a clash between two people and their emotions. Theocentric view defined the following communicative practices; the use of silence as non-verbal communication, mindfulness and meditation, adopting another language or mixed language, and “no feedbacking.” On the other hand, humancentric view explained practices which are; identifying “noise” and clarifying message, adjustment and employing genial paralanguage.

Leslie P. Fusin’s study investigates the perspectives and communicative strategies used by Filipino women married to Korean men when navigating marital conflict. Using an ethnomethodological qualitative approach and thematic analysis of in-depth interviews, the research examines how these women view the nature of conflict and the specific practices they utilize to resolve tensions within their intercultural marriages.

The findings reveal two distinct views regarding the nature of marital conflict. The first is the theocentric view, which interprets conflict through a spiritual lens, framing struggles as occurring under the orchestration of God. The second is the humancentric view, which approaches conflict as a secular, interpersonal phenomenon defined by a clash between two individuals and their emotions.

Specific communicative practices are associated with each perspective. Women operating under the theocentric view utilize silence, mindfulness and meditation, the adoption of another language or mixed language, and the practice of "no feedbacking." Conversely, the humancentric view is associated with direct interpersonal management, such as identifying "noise" to clarify messages, making adjustments, and employing genial paralanguage.

The study concludes that a woman's spiritual worldview significantly influences how she perceives and responds to marital discord. Conflict resolution is not a monolithic process but is shaped by the individual's conceptualization of the conflict. Consequently, practitioners like counselors must be sensitive to whether participants view conflict as a spiritual trial or a human interpersonal struggle.

The study conducted by Leslie P. Fusin investigates the perspectives and communicative strategies employed by Filipino women married to Korean men when navigating marital conflict. The research aims to understand how these women view the nature of conflict within their intercultural marriages and to identify the specific communicative practices they utilize to resolve these tensions. By focusing on this specific demographic, the study seeks to illuminate the complexities of intercultural communication within the domestic sphere, particularly when navigating different cultural frameworks and communication styles.

The research is situated within the ethnomethodological tradition of qualitative research. This framework allows the researcher to examine the social practices and methods that individuals use to make sense of their social world and maintain order in their interactions. The study utilized a qualitative approach, employing purposive sampling to select participants who met the specific criteria of being Filipino women married to Korean men. Data collection was carried out through in-depth interviews, which were recorded, transcribed, and translated into English to facilitate analysis. The researcher then applied thematic analysis to the gathered data to identify recurring patterns and core themes regarding the participants' views and practices.

The findings reveal that the participants hold two distinct views regarding the nature of marital conflict. The first is the theocentric view, which interprets marital conflict through a spiritual lens. Under this perspective, participants view conflict as something occurring under the orchestration of God. This suggests that for these women, marital struggles are often framed within a larger religious or divine context, potentially influencing how they perceive the purpose or inevitability of such disagreements. The second perspective identified is the humancentric view. This view approaches conflict as a secular, interpersonal phenomenon, defining it as a clash between two individuals and their respective emotions. This perspective focuses on the psychological and relational dynamics between the spouses rather than a divine influence.

The study further identifies specific intercultural communicative practices associated with each of these two views. For women operating under the theocentric view, the communicative practices identified include the use of silence as a form of non-verbal communication, the practice of mindfulness and meditation, the adoption of another language or the use of mixed language, and the practice of "no feedbacking." These methods suggest a range of responses that include internal reflection, linguistic adaptation, and strategic non-engagement or silence as a means of managing the tension.

In contrast, the humancentric view is associated with different communicative practices aimed at direct interpersonal management. These practices include identifying "noise" and working to clarify messages, as well as making adjustments and employing genial paralanguage. These strategies appear more focused on the mechanics of communication—reducing misunderstandings and using tone or non-verbal cues to soften the impact of the interaction—to resolve the clash between the two parties.

The conclusions drawn from the study highlight the diversity of ways in which intercultural couples manage conflict based on their underlying belief systems. The distinction between theocentric and humancentric views suggests that a woman's spiritual worldview plays a significant role in how she perceives and responds to marital discord. The specific communicative practices identified—ranging from silence and meditation to message clarification and paralanguage—demonstrate the complex toolkit these women use to navigate the linguistic and cultural nuances of their marriages.

The implications of this research suggest that understanding the intersection of culture, religion, and communication is vital for supporting intercultural families. The findings indicate that conflict resolution in these marriages is not a monolithic process but is deeply influenced by the individual's conceptualization of the conflict itself. For practitioners working with intercultural couples, such as counselors or mediators, these results imply that interventions must be sensitive to the participants' underlying views—whether they view conflict as a spiritual trial or a human interpersonal struggle—to be truly effective. Furthermore, the study underscores the importance of recognizing non-verbal and linguistic strategies, such as silence or mixed language, as intentional communicative acts used to maintain relational harmony in a cross-cultural context.

title: "Overseas Filipino Workers' Behavioral Intent for Healthy Lifestyles as Influenced by Corporate  Communication Materials in Dubai, United Arab Emirates"
abstract: One hundred selected OFWs employed in a private company in Dubai, U.A.E. were surveyed on how corporate communication materials influence their behavioral intention to adopt healthy lifestyles. Premised on the Theory of Reasoned Action by Fishbein and Azjen (1980), the study described how independent variables ( printed and electronic corporate communication materials) with the mediating variables (attitude, subjective norms, and perception) influence the dependent variable (OFWs' behavioral intention) to adopt healthy lifestyles. Descriptive statistics such as frequency distribution and percentages were used to describe results. Data analysis shows that OFWs' perception towards corporate communication materials was positively accepted; OFWs' attitude when exposed to communication materials was found to be favourable; subjective norms that influence OFWs' behavioral intention was the social group or organization they belong to. These positive and favorable results led to moderate behavioral intention to adopt healthy lifestyles as influenced by corporate communication materials.

title: Positibo: Looking Into Filipinos Living With HIV/AIDS’ Self-Concept and Interpersonal Communication
abstract:
This study sought to understand how Filipinos living with HIV/AIDS perceive themselves and build relationships through interpersonal communication. Specifically, the study (1) identified the central themes on the self-concept of Filipinos living with HIV/AIDS; (2) described their experiences of interaction and communication with other people; and (3) identified the different types of relationships that they have with other people. The study was guided by Grounded Theory and Theoretical Sampling was used in the selection of research participants.

The selected participants were four Filipinos living with HIV/AIDS who were classified under the category, Men Who Have Sex with Men (MSM). Narrative interviews and observation were the main data gathering methods used. The self-concept themes that were gathered were classified into two core categories: 1) The Negative “I”, and 2) The Positive “I”. In the attempt to describe the experiences of interaction and interpersonal communication, it was realized that interpersonal communication and relationship are in fact interrelated. The common forms and experiences of interaction and communication that they have with others include: 1) Verbal communication and face-to-face interaction (Dyadic or Small Group Communication); 2) non-verbal cues such as hugging, smiling, and touching 3) online communication or Computer-mediated Communication (CMC), such as social media, the internet, and group chats and even 4) Public Communication. The four types of relationships that were derived are: 1) The First Line, 2) The Small Circle, 3) The Online Friends and 4) The Others. These types of relationships were further classified into two categories: 1) Close-Open and 2) The Consensus Reality. Close-Open explains that PLHIV would always feel the need to open up to the people they have a close relationship with, while the Consensus Reality explains that PLHIV would usually be comfortable in talking about HIV/AIDS with people who are not close to them but are also experiencing the same case. The levels and forms of communication in these types of relationships were further explained.

The study realized that Filipinos living with HIV/AIDS value interpersonal communication and relationships and these also affect their self-concept. It also delved into open communication and interpersonal communication in the case of PLHIV. Face-to-face communication and Computer-mediated communication are both important in the communication of PLHIV with other people. The types and forms of communication also vary depending on the level or intimacy of relationships. Future research may be done on the other classification of PLHIV besides MSM. Other researchers can also consider study focusing on the other end of the spectrum to understand how they treat or deal with PLHIV, or a health communication study on activities and tools that can help in raising awareness and stopping stigma in the Philippines.

title: What Do Gender Equality Law and Policies Mean to Me? Japanese Women Making Sense of Lived Experience As They Watch Television Dramas About Women
abstract:
The lack of women in core positions and political ranks, and the unequal treatment of men and women due to gender imparity continuously push Japan's rank down on the Global Gender Gap Report list. Despite the enacted laws and action plans by the government, the country still faces difficulties in achieving its goals to enable women economically, socially, and politically and to establish a gender-equal society for both genders. To support this development, the media has produced television dramas that focus on female characters and new plots. Past studies have focused almost exclusively on the representation of women and/or gender in television dramas. Thus, borrowing the phenomenological lens, this paper sought to advance our understanding of the meaning of the gender equality laws to Japanese women as they watch television dramas about women. Five working Japanese women agreed to participate in this study. The data collected through narrative in-depth interviews was analyzed using the Modified Van Kaam Method. 

Two central themes that describe the essence of the meaning-making system of the participants became clear: Women are Outside the Circle of Gender Equality and What Women Want: Commitment and Change. Upon further review, two sub­themes emerged under theme 1: Not Me: "/ have never and will never experience that"; and To Be in a Leadership Position, a Woman Must Be a Man: "Now, I have so much work like my husband". Theme 2 has one sub-theme: No gender equality at home, no gender equality at work: "My father decided that set-up, but my husband sees me as his equal and treats his staff equally''. 

This study concludes that Japanese women view themselves outside the scope of gender equality laws. However, current economic, social, and political challenges have started to initiate necessary changes in the Japanese mindset.

title: A Communication Analysis of Climate Change Knowledge Gaps Between Uplands and Lowlands Farmers in Nueva Ecija, Philippines: A Validation of the Knowledge Gap Theory
abstract:
This study primarily aims to determine the knowledge level of 120 upland rice farmers and lowland rice farmers in Nueva Ecija, Philippines on climate change, with the hope of validating the Knowledge Gap Theory by Tichenor, Donohue, and Olien. In validating the said theory, the study looked into the relationship of the respondents' socio-economic status with their knowledge level on climate change as hypothesized in the theory. It also aims to recommend policies on disseminating climate change knowledge and information particularly at the local level.

The study used the snowball sampling technique and the data were gathered using quantitative and qualitative methods. The T-test analysis and Pearson Correlation Analysis was used to determine the knowledge level of the respondents and to test the relationship of the variables.

The results show that the respondents from the upland and the lowland were knowledgeable about climate change, its causes, effects, and impacts as well as to the climate change programs of the government. The respondents, however, were Only slightly knowledgeable on the technical aspects of climate change. Most of them were also not familiar with some of the recommended adaptation technologies as those technologies were not introduced to them.

Additionally, the results of the key informant interviews revealed that the local government unit of Carranglan„ Palayan City, and San Isidro, Nueva Ecija were active in disseminating climate change knowledge and information and adaptation technologies. They did this through the conduct of different activities such as seminars, Farmers Field School, and Lakbay-Aral. Of the four local government units (LGUs), Guimba had the least number of activities on agricultural extension concerning climate change adaptation.

The communication activities of various research and development and academic institutions such as the Araullo University, Central Luzon State University, and Central Luzon Agriculture and Aquatic Resources Research and Development Consortium also helped in educating the respondents on climate change.

Drawing on from the results of this study, it is recommended that researchers should explore the effect of other factors—particularly the social and communication factors—in studying the knowledge gaps among groups of interest especially if the form of knowledge that will be tested is global in nature and one that includes technological interventions. It is also recommended among LGUs to strengthen their extension services on climate change. The study also recommends, in particular, the continuous implementation of the Farmers Field School and partnerships with.

However, a significant gap exists regarding technical knowledge, as respondents were only slightly knowledgeable concerning the technical aspects of climate change. Furthermore, many farmers were unfamiliar with recommended adaptation technologies, a deficiency attributed to these specific technologies not being introduced to them.

Qualitative data from key informant interviews provided insight into the role of local government units (LGUs) in knowledge dissemination. The LGUs of Carranglan, Palayan City, and San Isidro were found to be active in communicating climate change knowledge and adaptation technologies through methods such as seminars, Farmers Field School, and Lakbay-Aral. Among the four LGUs studied, Guimba had the least number of agricultural extension activities related to climate change adaptation. Beyond local government efforts, communication activities from research and development and academic institutions—specifically Araullo University, Central Luzon State University, and the Central Luzon Agriculture and Aquatic Resources Research and Development Consortium—contributed to the education of the respondents.

In conclusion, while farmers in Nueva Ecija are aware of general concepts and government programs, there is a lack of technical understanding and familiarity with specific adaptation technologies. The study highlights the importance of local government and academic institutions in bridging these gaps through extension services and educational activities. For researchers, it is suggested that future studies explore the effects of other factors, particularly social and communication factors, when studying knowledge gaps. For local government units, the study recommends strengthening extension services, specifically through the continuous implementation of the Farmers Field School and the fostering of partnerships to improve the dissemination of information and technologies.

title: Communication for Community Mobilization: A Case Study of the Department of Education's Adopt-a-School Program in Malabon City Secondary Schools
abstract:
This study explored the communication strategies-key themes/messages communicated through various media channels-employed by the public secondary schools of Malabon City in the process of mobilizing the community in the implementation of the Department of Education's (DepEd) Adopt-a-School Program (ASP) and Brigada Eskwela (BE). 

Three schools with the highest amount of resources generated under ASP in 2017, and with awards and accolades received in BE, served as caseworks of the study. Two groups of key informants consisted of the implementers (the school principal and the ASP and/or BE Coordinator) and the stakeholders (parent, alumnus, student government, and officer/s of the schools' partner institutions). Through key informant interviews and review of physical artifacts relevant to the study, it was found that in order to engage the participation of partners, donors, and stakeholders in education, the schools communicate five key themes/messages that revolve around philanthropy, shared responsibility, trust and transparency, specificity, and economic and moral gains. 

. 
Guided by the Media Synchronicity Theory (MST) by Dennis, et al. (2008), results further showed that in order to communicate these key themes and messages, the schools utilize an aggregate of media channels that they deem capable to: 1. support lower levels of synchronicity and allow for conveyance of information including print, multimedia, and mass media; 2. support higher levels of synchronicity and allow for convergence or a shared understanding towards the adoption of the school including face-to-face and personal communication; and 3. merge higher and lower levels of synchronicity and allow for both conveyance and convergence including social media and traditional channels. A model/framework on communication for community mobilization is also proposed by this study to serve as guide of public schools in the implementation of partnership programs.

title: A Descriptive Analysis of C4D Model in CSR Communication – The Amway Philippines “One by One Campaign for Children” Case Study
abstract:
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) communication happens extensively during project implementation, across various levels, and between various stakeholders. The importance of communicating the message and intention of the company is vital to the achievement of sustainable goals for individuals and communities that benefit from such initiatives. Amway Philippines' “One by One Campaign for Children” is a global campaign supporting various children’s causes worldwide. In the Philippines, the program is aimed at SDG 4, or supporting quality education through a values-laden literacy through storytelling campaign under the Department of Education’s Adopt-A-School Program (ASP). It was proven that in all locations where the Amway business operates, public school partners and students benefited from library renovations and other related support activities, which resulted in a sustainable relationship through effective communication and technology, such as email communication, social media channels, that mobilized
volunteers across the organization.

Morsing and Schultz (2006), noted that engagement in present times requires a more sophisticated and ongoing stakeholder awareness and more focused CSR communication strategies than previously. This solidifies the need to make a CSR communication platform as that is “sustainable” and more attuned to the needs of various stakeholders. The element of “sustainability”, makes the Amway Philippines One by One Campaign a movement to uplift the lives of its beneficiaries. The communication for development (C4D) model, allows the campaign to tap into various forms of communication, and utilize the technology that allows the implementation on a global and affiliate level. The barriers of distance and time is no longer a challenge since the messaging tools are freely utilized using email, social media channels, and the Amway web-based resources such as blogs, microsites, and websites. Feedback is gathered, and dialogues are made to open up the communication lines either personally or through technology-aided communication.

Set against the context of resource shortages in the Philippine educational landscape, the study investigates how communication can transform Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) from a marketing tool into an instrument for social mobilization. The research employed a descriptive case study design using a mixed-methods approach, including surveys and focus group discussions with CSR leaders, volunteers, and school stakeholders.

The findings indicate that Amway Philippines successfully uses the C4D model to overcome geographical and temporal barriers, resulting in tangible benefits such as renovated libraries and educational materials. Survey data showed 100% effectiveness in several areas: employees reported that CSR objectives aligned with company values, believed the program improved beneficiaries' lives, and felt the CSR Project Officer communicated proactively. Communication acted as "fuel" for social mobilization, exemplified by the "Amway 1K Run," which provided sustainable funding for literacy programs.

The study concludes that CSR implemented through a C4D framework transcends mere marketing to become "marketing with a soul." By managing stakeholder expectations and aligning messaging with corporate values, C4D enables CSR to achieve social transformation. The researcher suggests a potential "intermarriage" between CSR and development communication to achieve sustainable development goals.

The thesis titled "A Descriptive Analysis of C4D Model in CSR Communication – The Amway Philippines ‘One by One Campaign for Children’ Case Study" by Michelle P. Ochoa examines the intersection of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Communication for Development (C4D). The study focuses on how Amway Philippines utilizes communication strategies to drive social change and community development through its "One by One Campaign for Children."

**Problem and Context**

The research is situated within the context of the Philippine educational landscape, where the Department of Education (DepEd) faces significant challenges in providing adequate resources for a growing student population. Despite high literacy rates, there is a notable decline in the survival rate of students finishing primary education, and government expenditure on education remains low relative to the GDP. This creates a gap that necessitates Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs).

The researcher addresses the tension within CSR, noting that it is often viewed with skepticism as a mere marketing tool or a way for corporations to mask self-serving motives. The central problem explored is how communication can transform CSR from a simple act of philanthropy into a meaningful tool for social mobilization and development. Specifically, the study investigates how Amway Philippines manages its "One by One Campaign," which supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) through literacy initiatives under the DepEd’s Adopt-A-School Program (ASP).

**Methodology**

The study employs a descriptive case study design. To gather data, the researcher utilized a qualitative and quantitative approach involving Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) and surveys. The participants included ten respondents from Amway Philippines, consisting of CSR team leaders and volunteers, as well as various partner stakeholders, such as school coordinators, principals, and management. The research analyzed various communication tools used by the company, ranging from traditional methods like Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) and invitation letters to modern digital tools including email, social media, websites, and microsites.

**Findings**

The findings indicate that Amway Philippines successfully utilizes the C4D model to bridge geographical and temporal barriers, allowing for effective implementation across various locations in the Philippines. The "One by One Campaign" has resulted in tangible benefits, such as the renovation of libraries and the provision of educational materials for several schools.

Data from the surveys revealed high levels of effectiveness in the campaign's communication. 100% of the surveyed employees reported that the CSR project objectives were aligned with the company’s values, and 100% believed the program helped beneficiaries improve their lives. Furthermore, 100% of the respondents felt that the CSR Project Officer communicated proactively. Among the stakeholders, the storytelling caravan and "Brigada Eskwela" were highlighted as particularly impactful activities.

The study also found that communication serves as the "fuel" for CSR, enabling social mobilization. For instance, the "Amway 1K Run" acted as a hybrid marketing and CSR event that mobilized thousands of participants and provided sustainable funding for the literacy programs. Additionally, the company’s communication and mobilization capabilities were evident during disaster response efforts, such as the relief operations following Typhoon Yolanda, where the company coordinated with the Philippine Red Cross and utilized various communication channels to gather information and distribute aid.

**Conclusions**

The researcher concludes that CSR, when implemented through a C4D framework, transcends mere marketing and becomes "marketing with a soul." The study validates the hypothesis that communication for development is the discipline that enables CSR programs to achieve their end goals of uplifting individuals and society.

The results suggest that effective communication manages the expectations of all stakeholders—including the government, employees, distributors, and beneficiaries—and ensures that the needs of both the corporation and the community are met. The study also concludes that private corporations are powerful, often underestimated participants in the national development process. By utilizing C4D tools, Amway Philippines was able to create a sustainable relationship with its partners, turning a corporate initiative into a community movement.

**Implications**

The implications of this study are significant for both development communicators and CSR practitioners. For practitioners, the research demonstrates that the use of diverse communication channels—both traditional and digital—is essential for the success of large-scale social mobilization. It highlights the importance of aligning CSR messaging with core corporate values to foster employee pride and volunteerism.

For the field of development communication, the study suggests a potential "intermarriage" between CSR and DevCom. It posits that CSR can be a valid ground for applying development communication principles to achieve social transformation. The research implies that if the intentions of a CSR program are transparent and the communication processes are open to scrutiny, these programs can serve as legitimate and effective tools for addressing societal concerns and achieving sustainable development goals.

title: Family Communication and Reproductive Health Conversations Among Seventh-Day Adventist Families
abstract: Eighty-two parent-residents living within the premises of the Adventist University of the Philippines, Putting Kahoy, Silang, Cavite were surveyed to find out how they talk about reproductive health within the family, premised on the Family Communication Pattern Theory (McLeod & Chafee, 1972), the study determined the nature of family communication of Seventh Day Adventist families in terms of cohesion and conversation levels. It also determined the socio-demographic profile of respondents, analyzed how reproductive health was discussed in the family; assessed what topics were discussed under reproductive health; and determined reasons why they discuss reproductive health. Results showed that family-respondents have children between 15-20 years old, the life stage where adolescents experience various physical and emotional changes; belonged to Generation X; and follow and 8-5 job. Both parents carry out decision-making in the home with regard to reproductive health issues. An open communication environment to talk about reproductive health issues. An open communication environment to talk about reproductive health issues using a casual objective approach was found effective for teenagers to open up to their parents. Proper timing and current issues are anchors to start a reproductive health conversation leading to a more transparent and communicative learning families. Having an open mind of both parents and children can lead to healthier discussions and implied getting children away from dangers of teenage pregnancy or unwarranted sexual behaviors. This implies that SDA parent-respondents know how to deal with teenagers as far as reproductive health conversation are concerned. Indeed, parents who reaffirm the value of their children could help in the development of positive and health attitudes.

title: Communicating Corporate Social Responsibility Initiatives: A Comparative Analysis of Three Philippine-Based Companies
abstract:
This study aimed to understand and describe how Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives addressing youth employability in the country are communicated by Philippine-based companies with the aim of ensuring beneficiary mobilization. This specifically (1) described the CSR initiatives' communication strategies addressing youth employability by three Philippine-based companies, (2) drew insights on the three cases based on beneficiary mobilization resulting from the communication process implemented, (3) identified the best communication strategies for CSR initiatives based on the three case studies of the Philippine-based companies, and (4) recommended a communication model for implementing CSR initiatives for the purpose of beneficiary mobilization.

This study addresses the lack of researches in the field of CSR initiatives implementation by Philippine-based companies, that targets youth employability in the country. 

Three Philippine-based companies conducting CSR initiatives addressing youth employability were the participants of the study. Key Informant interviews and Document Analysis were the data gathering tools used.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study investigates how Philippine-based companies communicate Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives aimed at improving youth employability. Using a comparative case analysis, the researcher examined three companies through key informant interviews and document analysis of press releases, websites, social media, and blogs. The research focused on communication strategies used for beneficiary mobilization, specifically for programs like training-to-employment initiatives and college scholarships.

Findings indicate that CSR initiatives are deeply embedded in corporate identity, specifically within company vision, mission, and core values. While companies use both internal and external communication, external strategies are more effective for mobilization, particularly personal and digital communication. External communication is often a mediated process where companies communicate frameworks and calls for applications through partner organizations, such as schools or foundations, which facilitates both beneficiary and partner mobilization. Additionally, the number of internship and scholarship slots may be proportional to a company's net income.

Applying the Uses and Gratifications theory, the study found that mobilization depends on how communication satisfies the needs of both the audience and the implementers. The researcher recommends a mediated communication model utilizing personal and digital tools. In this model, companies send information to partner organizations that act as filters by endorsing candidates. This targeted approach ensures information reaches appropriate participants, saving time and resources that can be redirected toward supporting programs for unemployed Filipino youth.

This study investigates how Philippine-based companies communicate Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives designed to address youth employability. The research addresses a gap in existing literature regarding how corporations implement programs targeting the employment needs of the country's youth. The primary objective was to describe the communication strategies used by three specific companies to ensure beneficiary mobilization, which involves the successful recruitment and engagement of participants for programs such as training-to-employment initiatives and college scholarship grants.

Using a Comparative Case Analysis methodology, the researcher gathered data through Key Informant Interviews with Corporate Affairs or Communication Managers, Human Resources Managers, and Program Officers. This was supplemented by a document analysis of press releases, company websites, social media content, and blog entries.

The findings reveal that CSR initiatives are deeply embedded in the corporate identity, specifically within the companies' vision, mission, and core values. These programs are implemented internally by the companies' own employees. While both internal and external communication strategies are utilized, external strategies are more effective for beneficiary mobilization. Specifically, personal and digital communication were identified as the most effective tools. The study also found that external communication is often a mediated process where companies communicate frameworks and calls for applications through partner organizations, such as schools or foundations. This mediation facilitates both beneficiary and partner mobilization. Furthermore, the number of internship and scholarship slots may be proportional to a company's net income. Companies pursue these CSR goals with a dual objective: ensuring corporate sustainability while meeting the philanthropic needs of society.

Applying the Uses and Gratifications theory, the study found that mobilization is influenced by how well communication satisfies the needs and motives of both the target audience and the implementers. Grounded in Mersham and Skinner's Theory of Communication, the research concludes that communication is successful when implementers receive positive feedback via beneficiary mobilization. Through the lens of Uses and Gratifications, targeted external communication allows companies to gratify their corporate image and social integrative needs, such as gaining societal acceptance.

The researcher recommends a mediated communication model for beneficiary mobilization. This model categorizes the most effective strategies into personal communication (face-to-face meetings) and digital communication (emails, texts, mobile messaging, and social media). In this framework, the implementer sends calls for applications to partner foundations or schools, which then communicate the information to target participants like college students or unemployed youth. These partners act as filters by endorsing candidates. This targeted approach ensures information reaches appropriate candidates, reducing rework and saving time, energy, and resources. Ultimately, conserving these operational expenses allows companies to redirect more funds toward supporting programs that help unemployed Filipino youth.

The research was conducted using a Comparative Case Analysis methodology. The unit of analysis consisted of three Philippine-based companies and their respective communication strategies. Data were gathered through two primary methods: Key Informant Interviews and Document Analysis. The interview participants included Corporate Affairs or Corporate Communication Managers, Human Resources Managers, and Program Officers who are directly involved in the implementation of the CSR programs. To supplement these interviews, the researcher conducted a document analysis of public materials, including press releases, company websites, social media content (photos, texts, and videos), and blog entries.

The findings revealed several key themes regarding how these companies manage their CSR communication. First, the study found that CSR initiatives are deeply embedded in the corporate identity of the participating companies, as evidenced by their vision, mission, and core values. Second, the implementation of these programs is handled internally by the companies' own employees. Third, while companies utilize both internal and external communication strategies, external strategies are more effective in achieving beneficiary mobilization. These external strategies consist of a combination of personal, print, and digital communication, though the study specifically identified personal and digital communication as the most effective for mobilizing beneficiaries.

The study further discovered that external communication is often a mediated process. Companies communicate their CSR frameworks and calls for applications through partner organizations, such as schools or foundations. This mediation allows for both beneficiary mobilization and partner mobilization. Additionally, the research noted that the number of available slots for internships and scholarships may be proportional to the net income of the implementing company. The findings also indicated that these companies pursue CSR with a dual objective: to ensure the sustainability of the company while simultaneously adhering to the philanthropic needs of society. Finally, applying the Uses and Gratifications theory, the study found that beneficiary mobilization is highly influenced by the ability of the communication to satisfy the needs and motives of both the target audience and the implementers.

The study's conclusions are grounded in Mersham and Skinner's Theory of Communication and the Uses and Gratifications Theory. Based on Mersham and Skinner’s view of communication as a two-way, interactive process, the study concluded that the communication process is successful when the original source (the implementers) receives positive feedback in the form of beneficiary mobilization. Through the lens of Uses and Gratifications, the research concluded that targeted external communication strategies allow companies to gratify their corporate image and their social integrative needs, such as gaining societal acceptance through philanthropic investment.

The researcher recommends a specific external communication model for beneficiary mobilization. This model categorizes the most effective strategies into two types: personal communication (such as face-to-face meetings) and digital communication (such as emails, texts, mobile messaging, and social media chats). These messages are typically disseminated through the company's Corporate Communications or Human Resources departments, or through their corporate foundations. The recommended model is a mediated communication model where the program implementer acts as both a sender and receiver of messages. In this framework, the call for applications is sent to partner foundations or schools, which then communicate the information to the target participants, such as college students or unemployed youth. The partner organizations act as filters, endorsing candidates to the companies.

The implications of adopting this mediated, targeted communication model are significant for corporate implementers. By using partner organizations to filter candidates, companies can ensure that recruitment information reaches the most appropriate candidates, which reduces rework by limiting information to those who meet program requirements. This targeted approach saves the implementers time, energy, and resources. Ultimately, the conservation of these operational expenses allows companies to redirect more funds toward supporting their programs, thereby helping more unemployed Filipino youth equip themselves and their families for better lives.

title: Khadamat: Communicating Struggles of Run-Away Domestic Workers in the Middle East
abstract:
The prevalence of domestic violence suffered by our OFW domestic workers is a serious challenge faced by our government and OFWs. Working as domestic workers abroad can be empowering or oppressive. Empowering as it provides economic gain which enable them to support their families. However, other women see the domestic work as oppressive because of poor working conditions, vulnerability to abuse, limited freedom and mobility.

This thesis investigates the lived experience of four run-away domestic workers under the custody of the Philippine Embassy in Middle East. The goal of the study is to examine how these women construct their experiences as OFW domestic workers through the stories they tell with the intentions of both giving voice to and exploring their “real life stories” involving communication and social problems, and primarily OFW domestic workers, this study attempts
to mainly focus on investigating the communication struggles they encounter while working for their employers.

The methodology involves semi-structured interviews in which participants reflect on their motivation to work abroad, domestic struggles and the difficulties they face in communicating with their employers and also with their families back home. The interviews were audio-recorder, transcribed and then analyzed.

Focused on narrative analyses not only to investigate how stories were being told but also to see the different layers of meaning in order to understand more of the social phenomenon of domestic workers and explore their struggles. All names of the participants have been changed in this thesis to avoid repercussions with regard to domestic issue and illegal work. The findings of this study demonstrate that the small scale of subjects was very much in line with the bigger picture of run-away domestic workers, although findings did not represent the general population.

Communication is crucial to human life, much more to domestic workers who have to deal with foreign employers with limited communication skills. Participants identified four communication barriers they experienced, namely: language barriers, semantic barriers, psychological attitude and perceptions of reality. Participants also revealed their unfortunate situation from the moment they were hired through the recruitment agencies/ and human trafficked until they abandoned their job and ran-away to the Philippine embassy to seek legal assistance.

title: Exposure to Gender-Sensitive Educational Communication Materials and Gender Equality Practices of Polytechnic University of the Philippines’ Students
abstract:
Three hundred ninety-nine students from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Mabini Campus were surveyed to determine their perception of the gender sensitivity of teachers’ educational communication materials and the students’ practices towards gender equality. Banking on the Exposure-Practice Framework, hybrid of Elaboration Likelihood Model and Mere Exposure Theory, the study determined the relationship between the independent variable (exposure of students to gender-sensitive educational communication materials) and the dependent variable (practices of students towards gender equality), and between students’ practices towards gender equality using the Pearson’s correlation test. 

Relationships were tested at 0.05 level of significance. The exposure of the students towards gender-biased educational communication materials was negatively correlated with the students’ practice towards gender equality. This means that as exposure to gender-biased educational communication materials increases, practices of students towards gender equality decreases.

Valila investigates how exposure to gender-sensitive educational communication materials relates to the gender equality practices of students at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Mabini Campus. Grounded in the Exposure-Practice Framework, which combines the Elaboration Likelihood Model and Mere Exposure Theory, the research examines the relationship between the independent variable of exposure to gender-sensitive materials and the dependent variable of students' practices toward gender equality.

Using a quantitative method, the researcher surveyed three hundred ninety-nine students to determine their perceptions of the gender sensitivity of materials provided by teachers. Data were analyzed using the Pearson’s correlation test, with all statistical relationships tested at a 0.05 level of significance.

The findings reveal a significant relationship between the variables. Specifically, the results indicate that exposure to gender-biased educational communication materials was negatively correlated with students’ practice toward gender equality. This implies that as exposure to gender-biased materials increases, the practices of students toward gender equality decrease. The study concludes that gender-biased materials may hinder the development or implementation of gender equality practices. This underscores the importance of the content used by educators in higher education institutions, suggesting a need to ensure that educational communication materials are gender-sensitive to support student practices.

The study conducted by Krupskaya T. Valila investigates the relationship between student exposure to gender-sensitive educational communication materials and the gender equality practices of students at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Mabini Campus. The research seeks to determine how the materials used by teachers in an educational setting influence the ways in which students practice gender equality. By examining these variables, the study addresses broader themes of gender and development, feminism, and the roles of higher education institutions in promoting gender sensitivity.

The theoretical foundation of this research is built upon the Exposure-Practice Framework, which serves as a hybrid of the Elaboration Likelihood Model and Mere Exposure Theory. This framework provides the conceptual basis for analyzing how exposure to specific types of communication materials relates to the subsequent practices of the individuals receiving that information. The study focuses on two primary variables: the independent variable, which is the exposure of students to gender-sensitive educational communication materials, and the dependent variable, which is the practices of students towards gender equality.

To investigate these variables, the researcher employed a quantitative method involving a survey of three hundred ninety-nine students from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Mabini Campus. The methodology aimed to determine the students' perceptions regarding the gender sensitivity of the educational communication materials provided by their teachers. To analyze the data and determine the relationship between the exposure to these materials and the students' actual practices, the study utilized the Pearson’s correlation test. All statistical relationships were tested at a 0.05 level of significance to ensure the reliability of the findings.

The findings of the study reveal a significant relationship between the variables. Specifically, the results indicate that the exposure of students towards gender-biased educational communication materials was negatively correlated with the students’ practice towards gender equality. This negative correlation implies a specific directional relationship: as the exposure to gender-biased educational communication materials increases, the practices of students towards gender equality decrease. This suggests that the content and nature of the communication materials used in the classroom play a role in shaping the gender equality practices of the student body.

The study concludes that the gender sensitivity of educational communication materials is linked to how students manifest gender equality in their own practices. The negative correlation highlights that gender-biased materials may hinder the development or implementation of gender equality practices among students. This underscores the importance of the content used by educators in higher education institutions, as these materials serve as a primary source of information and influence for students. The implications suggest a need for attention toward the development and use of educational communication materials to ensure they are gender-sensitive.

title: Borrowing from Informal Money Lenders: A Case Study on Cognitive Dissonance Theory in Meycauayan City, Bulacan
abstract:
This case study analyzed the persistent demand for informal lenders despite their usurious practices by applying Leon Festinger's Cognitive Dissonance Theory among 31 purposively sampled households who borrowed from informal lenders in Barangay Pantoc, Meycauayan City in the province of Bulacan. The questionnaire was administered to the participants from 17-24 October 2017.

The respondents lacked knowledge on fair and proper lending and borrowing practices. Evidence of contradictory beliefs or cognitive dissonance was found among the respondents  although this may not be apparent to them due to their lack of financial literacy and sophistication. After making the contradictions in their beliefs more apparent by giving them information that informal lenders were disadvantageous to their financial wellbeing, they with with their original action. In the process of forced compliance, they chose to rationalize or justify their irrational behavior by changing their perception of their action and saying that the usurious interest rates were a trade-off to easy access to credit from informal lenders. Enhancing financial literacy and providing information and access to affordable credit through the formal system are recommended.

This study investigates why individuals continue to rely on informal money lenders, such as "5-6" lending, despite being aware of usurious interest rates and predatory practices. Focused on households in Barangay Pantoc, Meycauayan City, Bulacan, the research utilizes Leon Festinger's Cognitive Dissonance Theory to analyze the psychological tension experienced when borrowers' actions conflict with sound financial knowledge. Using a case study method with purposive sampling, the researcher collected data from 31 households via questionnaires to uncover the cognitive processes and justifications used during financial strain.

The findings reveal that a lack of knowledge regarding fair lending practices is a significant factor in the engagement with informal lenders. While evidence of cognitive dissonance was identified, it was not always immediately apparent to respondents due to limited financial literacy. A key finding emerged when respondents were explicitly informed that informal lenders are disadvantageous to their financial well-being; rather than changing their behavior, they engaged in forced compliance. To resolve psychological discomfort, respondents rationalized their behavior by changing their perception of the action, viewing high interest rates as a necessary trade-off for ease of access. The study concludes that reliance on these lenders is driven by a psychological defense mechanism where borrowers rationalize exploitative terms to alleviate dissonance. Consequently, the researcher recommends enhancing financial literacy and improving access to affordable formal credit.

The ease of access outweighs the perceived cost of high interest rates in the minds of borrowers, even when informed of long-term disadvantages. title: Communication and Use of Grindr in HIV Awareness Among College Students in a Private University in Metro Manila
abstract: There were one hundred college students in a private university in Metro Manila surveyed through developed and self-developed research instruments to determine their HIV awareness through Grindr, a gay dating application. Additional self-developed research instrument was used for key informants, which answers supported results on communication and use of Grindr by the respondents. Presumed on the New Media Theory by Vogt (2017), the study determined the correlation between the independent variables (communication and use of Grindr, HIV awareness, Grindr engagements, HIV infection consciousness, expert's view on HIV awareness) and the dependent variable ( contents for the proposed NSTP subject). On the other hand, mediating variables on socio-demographic characteristics of respondents (age, year level, course, sexual role, relationship status, purpose in using Grindr, Grindr activities) also used the theory to test its relevancy. Relationships were tested and were set at 0.05 levels of significance. One way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was used to test the significance of the means and t-test as well as z-test for independent means as intra test. The results generated from the study revealed that college students were not fully aware of the HIV infection until infected with the virus. The study simply interpreted the result that Grindr, as gay dating applications is not focusing on HIV, but heavily on gay dating. Though, HIV awareness is visible in Grindr, the attitudes and values of college students subscribing Grindr implies high risk of getting HIV infection.

The thesis titled Communication and Use of Grindr in HIV Awareness Among College Students in a Private University in Metro Manila was submitted by Walter Huyod Yudelmo in 2018 for a Master of Development Communication degree at the University of the Philippines Open University. The text provides institutional and national context regarding the HIV epidemic in the Philippines, noting that the country has become the country with the fastest growing HIV epidemic in the world. The Philippines is one of eight countries accounting for more than 90% of new HIV infections in Asia and the Pacific. Data from the Department of Health Epidemiology Bureau indicates that two out of three new HIV infections occur among individuals aged 15 to 24.

In response to this epidemic, the Commission on Higher Education issued a memorandum to intensify HIV/AIDS awareness in all higher education institutions. This directive was issued in accordance with the Higher Education Act of 1994 and the Philippine AIDS Prevention and Control Act of 1998. The commission enjoined all higher education institutions to develop mechanisms to ensure increased knowledge regarding HIV transmission and prevention. Additionally, an endorsement was included for a national conference titled Health Communication: Multi-Sectoral Approach on HIV/AIDS and Social Mobilization, held at Trinity University of Asia, intended to involve students, faculty members, and employees to address the epidemic.

This directive was issued in accordance with the Higher Education Act of 1994 and the Philippine AIDS Prevention and Control Act of 1998. The appendices also include an endorsement for a national conference titled Health Communication: Multi-Sectoral Approach on HIV/AIDS and Social Mobilization, held at Trinity University of Asia. This conference was intended to involve students, faculty members, and employees from various higher education institutions to address the epidemic through multi-sectoral approaches.

The author, Walter Huyod Yudelmo, was raised in a farming family in the Municipality of Cabatuan, Province of Iloilo. His academic background includes a Bachelor of Science in Development Communication from West Visayas State University, a Master of Public Administration, a Diploma in Korean Language from the University of Seoul, and studies toward a Doctor of Public Administration at the University of the Philippines Diliman. title: A Perception Study of Behavioral Change Through Communication: The Edukasyon Social Marketing and Mobilization Project
abstract:
Sustainable behavioral change is a by-product of communication through action. This scenario happens when people realize the perceived benefits and values of making a change in one’s behavior, for instance, towards exercising the right of children to education. Given the power of communication as reflected in social marketing and social mobilization programs, this study aimed to analyze the perception of parents towards the potential influence of communication (through the Eduk-Aksyon Program) in insinuating sustained behavioral change. Through focused group discussions, interviews and cross-case analyses of parents who continued to send their children to school even without government reinforcement through the Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT), it was found out that Eduk-Aksyon Program led to a sustained change in behavior of parents. Change was brought about by communication – through – action – via channels including the distribution of school supplies and the realization of perceived benefits of their children’s schooling. The factors intrinsic about the Eduk-Aksyon project that parents mostly value that led them to sustained behavioral change included the distribution of school supplies, the rewards and incentives systems, and the holistic development initiated by the program both mentally and spiritually. These factors were viewed as a means to alleviate the burden from the family by shouldering a portion of the overhead expenses at school. Meanwhile, the parent’s motivations in sending their children to school would be their personal and moral obligation to provide their kids the right to education; and the vision that education is the key to escape the vicious cycle of poverty. As compelling as it sounded, the rationalized benefits from the perceived outcome of completing or graduating from school, contributed to sustained behavioral change of parents. The findings from the content analyses of the transcripts affirm what Bandura suggests – that behavioral change can be determined by an interplay of both personal motivations and external factors. In this case, the respondent’s behavior, together with their responsiveness towards gaining benefit through rewards and incentives that Eduk-Aksyon program provide, led them to have a sustained behavior. Based on these findings, it appeared that the future social marketing and social mobilization programs can
be sealed and ensured if the programs offer both short-term and long-term benefits that could entice parents to be an active influencer for the kids to finish their schooling. For as long as the perceived benefits are rationalized by parents [and the perceived benefits exceeded the costs of education], social marketing and social mobilization programs such as the Eduk-Aksyon could continue to serve as communication platforms that drive behavioral change of the targeted
audience which are the parents.

title: A Narrative of Haribon’s Online Environmental Advocacy
abstract: This qualitative study aims to understand the experience of Haribon Foundation, a non-government environmental organization, in using social media as a communication platform for environmentalism. It describes the mechanisms used by Haribon to make its presence felt online and investigates how environmental communication survived in an online advocacy. This study was written with a problem-solution or issue-realization sequence in six parts based on William Labov and Joshua Waletzky's natural narrative. These are abstract, orientation, complicating action, resolution, evaluation, and coda. The communication officers of Haribon were observed and interviewed for this study. Results revealed the crucial role of the communication officers as vehicles of information between Haribon and its audience. Communication officers are advantaged if they are knowledgeable about the advocacies as well as equipped with the skills in delivering these advocacies to the audience through social media. The strategies in promoting Haribon's advocacy through Facebook (FB), Twitter, and Instagram were the use of informational campaigns through creative posts, sharing trivia about specific topics, riding on popular culture, conversing with the audience, linking and tagging posts to partner international organizations, and using FB boosts and analytics. Through the communication officers' experiences, this study drafted a theoretical framework as a guide in developing a social media strategy or plan for non-government organizations of the same nature.

title: Attributes of the Metro Manila Development Authority’s Facebook Page and Influence on Citizen’s Social Engagement and Participation on Posted Public Issues
abstract:
The Metro Manila Development Authority's (MMDA) Facebook page is among the top 15 government-associated pages in the Philippines. With its goal of widening its reach and promoting active involvement of its followers through their Facebook page, the study examined the attributes of the MMDA Facebook page that influenced active engagement and social participation. This study used the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to investigate and explain the followers' intention and use of the MMDA Facebook page. The data were obtained through an online survey to randomly selected followers, which were analyzed using descriptive statistics through building of regression models. The results demonstrated that performance expectancy, effort expectancy and social influences have a
significant effect on a user's behavioral intention to follow and use the MMDA Facebook Page, while facilitating conditions directly affects their usage behavior or engagement. This means that users believe that the MMDA Facebook page can help improve their performance, easy to use, and are supported by the people in their social circle; which resulted in the increase of their intention to use their page. Moreover, since the resources to use it are available, the more reason that they utilize the page, which improves engagement.

title: Developing and Testing a Predictive Model for Political Communication: The Case of Facebook Analysis of the 2016 Philippine Presidential Election Results
abstract:
The focus of the study is to develop and test a predictive model for political communication through the use of Facebook Analytics and determine how Facebook campaign likes and shares, and the presidential debate likes and shares predict the 2016 Philippine Presidential Election.

The data was gathered from the official Facebook page of the candidates through the use of social net importer. The candidates who reached the highest number of engagement based on likes and shares were identified. Then the model was created and tested in order to identify which model has the best fit. Linear regression was used to analyze the statistical relationship of the independent variables to the dependent variable. The model which best predicts the election result has high-r-square results so it can better explain the linear relationship of the variables. Also, it has low Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) which means that it has the smallest error in the regression line and the P-value should not reach the maximum risk of 0.05 to ensure that it is significant.

After testing the data into the model, the presidential debate was the only significant variable in predicting the election result. Presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte has the highest number of presidential debate post likes that reached up to 1,361,995 and he was declared by COMELEC as the runaway winner who garnered a total of 16,601,997 votes. Hence, this verifies that the model has predicted the 2016 Philippine Presidential Election results.
