Lauron investigates whether Facebook engagement metrics, specifically likes and shares of campaign and presidential debate content, can serve as reliable predictors for the outcome of a presidential election. Focusing on the 2016 Philippine Presidential Election, the research examines the relationship between social media indicators and actual vote counts. Using a social net importer, the researcher extracted data from the official Facebook pages of candidates, focusing on general campaign engagement and engagement specifically related to presidential debate posts.

The methodology involved developing a predictive model for candidates with the highest engagement levels. Statistical analysis was conducted using linear regression, with the model's effectiveness evaluated through r-squared values, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and P-values to ensure statistical significance.

The findings indicate that the presidential debate was the only significant variable in predicting the election result. While various metrics were tested, the likes and shares associated with presidential debates held the most predictive power. For example, Rodrigo Duterte achieved the highest number of likes on debate posts, totaling 1,361,995, which aligned with his eventual victory with 16,601,997 votes. The study concludes that the model successfully predicted the election results, demonstrating that Facebook engagement levels during high-stakes political events like debates serve as a meaningful indicator of electoral success.

The researcher tested various iterations of the model to find the best fit for the data. Statistical analysis was conducted using linear regression to examine the relationship between the independent variables (Facebook engagement metrics) and the dependent variable (election results). This metric aligned with the actual election outcome, as Duterte was declared the winner by the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) with 16,601,997 votes.

title: Nonverbal Communication Between Overseas Filipino Workers and Their Italian Employers in Rome
abstract: The study sought to: (1) examine what types of nonverbal cues do OFWs find difficulty to understand, (2) explore how would understanding nonverbal communication be useful to OFWs' search for gainful employment opportunities, and (3) examine how would nonverbal communication be communicated to OFWs to enhance their employability. To attain the above objectives, 100 OFWs in Rome were recruited and surveyed. To evaluate OFWs' ability in nonverbal communication, personal space was employed as the indicator for proxemics while facial expressions, eye contact, hand gestures, head movement and posture were used as the indicators for kinesics type of nonverbal communication. It was found that although respondents showed a high level of perception of Italian employers' extensive use of nonverbal cues, they lacked the ability in nonverbal communication (total mean score = 50.54). It was also found that the barriers in communicating nonverbal communication both in the Philippines and in Italy were partly responsible of the respondents' difficulties. Respondents considered understanding nonverbal communication useful to their employability (58%), as it helps them predict employers' needs, build a workable environment, improve job performance, etc. A country-specific pre-departure orientation seminar (PDOS) on nonverbal communication is recommended to facilitate OFWs to acquire knowledge and develop the ability to effectively interact with their prospective employers.

Using a quantitative method, the researcher surveyed 100 OFWs, focusing on proxemics (personal space) and kinesics (facial expressions, eye contact, hand gestures, head movements, and posture).

The findings revealed a significant discrepancy between the awareness of nonverbal cues and the ability to interpret them. While respondents were highly aware of the extensive use of nonverbal cues by their Italian employers, they lacked the ability to communicate effectively through these channels, resulting in a total mean score of 50.54. Furthermore, communication barriers were identified in both the Philippines and Italy.

Regarding employability, 58% of respondents believed that understanding nonverbal cues is beneficial. Participants noted that proficiency would help them predict employer needs, foster a better professional environment, and improve job performance. The study concludes that the lack of proficiency in proxemics and kinesics serves as a barrier to effective communication. Consequently, the researcher recommends implementing country-specific pre-departure orientation seminars (PDOS) focused on nonverbal communication to help OFWs interact more effectively with employers and enhance their professional integration.

title: The Identification and Implications of Barriers to Interpretation of Road Signages and Carriageway Markings From A Semiotic Perspective
abstract:
Traffic signs and symbols convey message and meaning to drivers and road users to ensure safety. The ability to comprehend and interpret accurately the intended meaning of road signs and symbols play a significant role in road traffic safety and overall efficiency of the road traffic system.

Despite all efforts and steps taken by the Philippine government to ensure the safety of our roads and traffic system, road traffic incidents and traffic related accidents in Metro Manila are threats faced by both road users and pedestrians, and likewise, takes its toll among the public utility drivers, especially in Metro Manila - which is the focus of this study. Among the highest numbers of driving violations and apprehensions in Metro Manila, the failure to adhere to road signs, symbols and markings was attributed as a major cause among the recorded road traffic apprehensions. These errors in the correct interpretations of traffic signs systems are caused by barriers to semiotic interpretations of road signs and symbols.

This paper studied the barriers to semiotic interpretations of road signs and symbols by public utility drivers in Metro Manila.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
In the study "The Identification and Implications of Barriers to Interpretation of Road Signages and Carriageway Markings From A Semiotic Perspective," Jonnell B. Llanto examines the correlation between frequent road accidents and violations in Metro Manila and the failure of drivers to adhere to road signs and markings. The author argues that these failures are not merely results of driver negligence but are rooted in a breakdown in the communication process between road authorities and drivers.

Focusing on public utility drivers, the research utilizes a semiotic perspective to examine how drivers decode visual signs. The study finds that errors in interpreting traffic signage systems are caused by specific semiotic barriers, where the driver fails to translate a visual sign into the correct cognitive understanding of a required action. This inability to comprehend intended meanings contributes significantly to traffic system inefficiency and accidents, suggesting that current visual communication methods are not functioning optimally for the target audience.

The research implies that improving road safety requires more than increased enforcement; it necessitates improving the clarity and interpretability of signs to ensure they are universally understood and lack ambiguity. The study suggests that traffic authorities should consider semiotic effectiveness and implement better communication strategies and educational programs for public utility drivers. Ultimately, the road "language" must be designed with the end-user's interpretive capacity in mind to ensure messages are acted upon correctly.

title: Efficacy of an Intervention Program Based on the Elaboration Likelihood Model in Changing Parents’ Attitude Towards Reading to Their Child
abstract:
Twenty four B'laan residents of Barangay Kalkam in Tupi, South Cotabato were surveyed to determine how UP Manila Community Health and Development Program (CHDP) attempted to transform them by exploring normative changes.

Anchored on transformational communication framework inspired by Flor and Smith (1997), the study identified the communication approaches employed in transforming B'laan's responses to CHDP using KAP study; and elicit findings on normative changes through videography.

Results showed that health communication interventions are limited to printed media and face-to-face communication; Health Development Education is moderately understandable, readable, and accessible (mean = 2.75); and social mobilization efforts involved little participation (mean = 2.4). It was also revealed that systems approach to communication is open and participatory, but not feedback-driven. Respondents believed that CHDP is not difficult to follow, convincing, ethical and can improve healthy lifestyle (mean = 3.24).

Using videographic codes, normative changes on issues pertaining to malnutrition, dengue campaign and teenage pregnancy were not evident.

Although CHDP is currently not operationalizing the ideal development communication intervention which triggers societal transformation among B'laan entities, the rich use of interpersonal verbal messages, frequent personal interaction and the use of indigenous media can be improved to transform them.

title: The role of social media in the political participation of overseas Filipino workers in Dubai, U.A.E. in the 2016 election
abstract:
Seventy-four active members of the Philippine Institute cf Civil Engineers (PIGE) in Dubai, United Arab Emirates were surveyed to détermine the rôle of social média in their political participation in the 2016 élection.

Based on the Agenda Setting Theory, this study provided a descriptive analysis of how the respondents utilized social média particularly Facebook. Four rôles were identified: (1) Connecter- it connected the OFWs back home, (2) Catalyzer- it served as a channel for the respondents to express and discuss their political views, (3) Mediator- it aiso enabled two-way communication between the OFWs and différent parties, and (4) Information provider- it played a rôle in getting information about the processes and mechanics of Overseas Absentee Voting.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Virgie Leah B. Nemis investigates the role of social media in the political participation of Overseas Filipino Workers located in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, specifically focusing on the context of the 2016 election. The study addresses how migrant workers, who are physically separated from their home country, engage with political processes and utilize digital platforms to maintain their connection to the political landscape of the Philippines. The research utilizes the Agenda Setting Theory to understand how social media influences the importance placed on certain topics and shapes political discourse. To address the research problem, the author employed a descriptive analysis method, utilizing a survey to gather data from seventy-four active members of the Philippine Institute of Civil Engineers (PICE) in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

The findings identify four distinct roles that social media played in the political participation of the surveyed Overseas Filipino Workers. First, social media acted as a connecter, allowing respondents to maintain a link back home to the Philippines. Second, social media functioned as a catalyzer, serving as a vital channel for respondents to express individual political views and engage in discussions. Third, social media acted as a mediator, enabling a two-way communication stream between the workers and different political parties. Finally, social media served as an information provider, helping respondents acquire necessary information regarding the specific processes and mechanics of Overseas Absentee Voting.

title: Environmental Communication on Plastic Use: The Perspectives of the Balaoan Community
abstract: This qualitative study was driven by the need to learn about the viewpoints of the Balaoan community regarding the environmental communication issue on plastic use as this is an interesting and relevant concept under development communication. This study poses the research question: what is the community's view on plastic use? The answer to this question emerged when I explored; (1) what the community knows and believes about plastic use; (2) how the community reacts to plastic use and its regulation (3) and what the community recommends to improve environmental communication to spread awareness on plastic use. The study utilized interviews in gathering data from 10 residents of Balaoan, La Union. The research employed content analysis to make sense of the interviews. The interviews were recorded, translated and transcribed in order to identify codes, themes, and sub-themes that constitute the community's view on plastic use. From the analysis, three major themes were identified: (1) using plastic; (2) regulating plastic use; (3) and communicating proper plastic use. Each major theme has sub-themes which were further discussed in the manuscript. In conclusion, the community's view on plastic use prompts the need to educate the people more about this issue as this may help people understand the components and aspects of plastic and its use that are detrimental to the health and the environment. This calls attention to different stakeholders in communicating proper plastic use and also providing safer and cheaper alternatives of plastic for the community's consumption.

The researcher employed a qualitative methodology, collecting data through interviews with 10 residents of Balaoan, La Union. These interviews were recorded, translated, and transcribed to allow for content analysis. This systematic process enabled the identification of specific codes, themes, and sub-themes that constitute the collective community view.

The findings are organized into three major themes: using plastic, regulating plastic use, and communicating proper plastic use. These themes illustrate a multifaceted relationship with plastic, ranging from daily habits to reactions to regulatory measures. The study concludes that there is a significant need for increased education, as a gap in knowledge exists regarding how plastic use is detrimental to human health and the environment.

The research implies that stakeholders must work toward communicating proper plastic use more effectively. Furthermore, the study suggests that communication alone may be insufficient; the community also requires access to safer and cheaper alternatives to plastic to achieve environmental protection and community well-being.

title: Transforming B’laan Communities Through Communication: The Case of the UP Manila Community Health and Development Program
abstract:
Twenty four B'Iaan residents of Barangay Kalkam in Tupi, South Cotabato were surveyed to détermine how UP Manila Community Heaith and Development Program (CHDP) attempted to transform them by exploring normative changes.

Anchored on transformational communication framework inspired by Flor and Smith (1997), the study identified the communication approaches employed in transforming B'iaan's responses to CHDP using KAP study; and elicit findings on normative changes through videography.

Results showed that heaith communication interventions are limited to printed média and face-to-face communication; Heaith Development Education is moderately understandable, readable, and accessible (mean = 2.75); and social mobilization efforts involved little participation (mean = 2.4). It was aiso revealed that Systems approach to communication is open and participatory, but not feedback-driven. Respondents believed that CHDP is not difficult to follow, convincing, ethical and can improve healthy lifestyle (mean = 3.24).

Using videographic codes, normative changes on issues pertaining to malnutrition, dengue campaign and teenage pregnancy were not évident.

Although CHDP is currently not operationalizing the idéal development communication intervention which triggers societal transformation among B'Iaan entities, the rich use of interpersonal verbal messages, fréquent personal interaction and the use of indigenous média can be improved to transform them.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study investigates the effectiveness of the University of the Philippines Manila Community Health and Development Program (CHDP) in facilitating transformation within the B’laan community of Barangay Kalkam in Tupi, South Cotabato. Using a mixed-methods approach involving a Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices (KAP) study and videography, the research assesses whether communication interventions trigger genuine societal transformation or merely transmit information.

Findings reveal significant limitations in the CHDP's communication strategies. Interventions are primarily restricted to printed media and face-to-face communication. Health Development Education was found to be only moderately understandable, readable, and accessible, while social mobilization efforts were relatively weak, characterized by low levels of participation. Although the program utilizes an open and participatory systems approach, it lacks a feedback-driven mechanism to integrate community responses into program design. While residents viewed the program content favorably—noting it is ethical, convincing, and has the potential to improve healthy lifestyles—videographic analysis showed no evidence of significant normative changes regarding malnutrition, dengue campaigns, or teenage pregnancy.

The study concludes that the CHDP is not currently operationalizing the interventions necessary to trigger societal transformation. While participatory and ethical, the program lacks the depth of engagement required to change social norms due to limited communication channels and a lack of feedback loops. To achieve transformation, the researcher suggests enhancing interpersonal verbal messages, increasing personal interactions, and integrating indigenous media.
one:
This study investigates the effectiveness of the University of the Philippines Manila Community Health and Development Program (CHDP) in facilitating transformation within the B’laan community of Barangay Kalkam in Tupi, South Cotabato. The research explores whether the program's communication interventions have resulted in normative changes among residents, addressing the gap between current communication practices and the ideal development communication interventions required to trigger genuine societal transformation within indigenous communities. The research is anchored on a transformational communication framework to assess whether communication serves to merely transmit information or to actively transform the social reality of the participants.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher employed a Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices (KAP) study and videography to analyze the responses of twenty-four B’laan residents. The findings reveal several limitations in the CHDP's communication strategies. Interventions are primarily restricted to printed media and face-to-face communication. Health Development Education was found to be only moderately understandable, readable, and accessible, yielding a mean score of 2.75. Furthermore, social mobilization efforts were relatively weak, with respondents indicating low levels of participation, evidenced by a mean score of 2.4.

Regarding structural approaches, the study found that while the CHDP utilizes an open and participatory systems approach, it lacks a feedback-driven mechanism. This suggests that while communication flows toward the community, there is insufficient infrastructure to ensure the community's responses and needs are systematically integrated back into the program's design. On a positive note, respondents expressed a favorable view of the program's content, stating it is not difficult to follow, is convincing, is ethical, and has the potential to improve healthy lifestyles, with a mean score of 3.24.

Despite these positive perceptions of the program's intent, videographic analysis found no evidence of significant normative changes. When examining critical health issues such as malnutrition, dengue campaigns, and teenage pregnancy, visual evidence did not show that interventions had successfully altered the community's norms or behaviors. This indicates a disconnect between the delivery of health information and the actual transformation of social practices.

The study concludes that the CHDP is not currently operationalizing the interventions necessary to trigger societal transformation. While the program is participatory and ethical, it falls short of the depth of engagement required to change established social norms due to a lack of feedback loops and limited communication channels. To achieve actual transformation, the researcher suggests moving beyond basic printed and face-to-face methods by enhancing interpersonal verbal messages, increasing the frequency of personal interactions, and integrating indigenous media into the communication strategy.

The study investigates the effectiveness of the University of the Philippines Manila Community Health and Development Program (CHDP) in facilitating transformation within the B’laan community of Barangay Kalkam in Tupi, South Cotabato. The research specifically explores whether the communication interventions implemented by the program have resulted in normative changes among the residents. The core problem addressed is the gap between current communication practices and the ideal development communication interventions required to trigger genuine societal transformation within indigenous communities.

The context of the research is situated within the intersection of development communication and community health. The study focuses on the B’laan people, an indigenous group, and evaluates how external health programs interact with their existing social structures and communication needs. The research is anchored on a transformational communication framework inspired by the work of Flor and Smith (1997), which provides the theoretical basis for assessing whether communication serves merely to transmit information or to actively transform the social reality of the participants.

To address the research problem, the author employed a mixed-methods approach. The study utilized a Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices (KAP) study to identify the specific communication approaches employed by the CHDP and to measure the residents' responses to these interventions. This was supplemented by the use of videography to elicit findings regarding normative changes. By using videographic codes, the researcher was able to observe and analyze behavioral and social shifts—or the lack thereof—concerning specific health issues. The sample consisted of twenty-four B’laan residents from the target barangay.

The findings of the study reveal several limitations in the current communication strategies used by the CHDP. The research found that health communication interventions are primarily restricted to printed media and face-to-face communication. When evaluating the effectiveness of Health Development Education, the results indicated that the information provided was only moderately understandable, readable, and accessible, yielding a mean score of 2.75. Furthermore, social mobilization efforts were found to be relatively weak, with respondents indicating a low level of participation, evidenced by a mean score of 2.4.

Regarding the structural approach to communication, the study revealed that while the CHDP utilizes a systems approach that is characterized as open and participatory, it lacks a feedback-driven mechanism. This suggests that while communication flows toward the community, there is insufficient infrastructure to ensure that the community's responses and needs are systematically integrated back into the program's design. On a positive note, the respondents expressed a favorable view of the program's content, stating that the CHDP is not difficult to follow, is convincing, is ethical, and has the potential to improve healthy lifestyles, with a mean score of 3.24.

Despite these positive perceptions of the program's intent and ethics, the study found no evidence of significant normative changes through videographic analysis. Specifically, when examining critical health issues such as malnutrition, dengue campaigns, and teenage pregnancy, the visual evidence did not show that the communication interventions had successfully altered the community's norms or behaviors. This indicates a disconnect between the delivery of health information and the actual transformation of social practices within the B’laan community.

The study concludes that the CHDP is currently not operationalizing the ideal development communication interventions necessary to trigger societal transformation among B’laan entities. While the program succeeds in being participatory and ethical, it falls short in achieving the depth of engagement required to change established social norms. The lack of feedback loops and the limited variety of communication channels prevent the program from moving beyond simple information dissemination toward true transformative communication.

The implications of these findings suggest a need for a strategic shift in how health programs approach indigenous communities. The researcher suggests that to achieve actual transformation, the program must move beyond basic printed and face-to-face methods. There is a significant opportunity to improve outcomes by enhancing the use of interpersonal verbal messages and increasing the frequency of personal interactions. Additionally, the study highlights the potential of integrating indigenous media into the communication strategy. By leveraging local communication tools and fostering more robust, feedback-driven participatory processes, development programs can better bridge the gap between health education and actual behavioral and societal change in B’laan communities.

title: Social Media as a Tool for Freedom of Expression Among Overseas Filipino Sales Workers in Abu Dhabi, UAE
abstract:
A total of 100 sales workers were surveyed and five were interviewed in-depth as part of this quantitative-qualitative study to identify what social media do Filipino sales workers in Abu Dhabi use as a communication tool to convey complaints and grievances to the Philippine government, determine issues Filipino sales workers in Abu Dhabi face they may want to express through the social media; and find out how the Philippine government can use social media as a communication tool to reach out to Filipino sales workers in Abu Dhabi.

Premised on the Theory of Public Sphere by Jürgen Habermas, the study determined how social media was transformed as the new public sphere. Facebook was identified as the most used social media as a communication tool to express work-related complaints and grievances to the Philippine government. Furthermore, social media as an emerging public sphere in communication through the use of different tools like digital or online platforms can serve as a public sphere among overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) to express their views and opinions about various issues that could affect them and the society as well. Likewise, the exchange of ideas and thoughts between the Philippine government and OFWs could create, amend, and solve issues pertaining to OFW conditions while working outside the country. As the new public sphere, social media can indeed become a potent tool for communication and for exercising freedom of expression.

Four themes were drawn to explain social media use such as facetalkation, facemation, facetagnation, and facewatch.

title: Social Action Through Facebook: The Case of Yellow Boat of Hope Foundation
abstract:
The advancement of social media brought Facebook to billions of people worldwide. It has become a new art of communication and advertisement used by companies and organizations to create brand awareness and to influence its audience to participate from as simple as Liking and Sharing the posts on their Facebook Pages, to mobilize action by donating or volunteering. This study aimed to identify the kind of communication strategies that NGOs can use to create awareness and participation by looking at Yellow Boat of Hope Foundation’s effective use of their Facebook Page as their platforms to do so.

Data collection through observation of posts and emailed questionnaire had served purposes its purpose in achieving the objectives of this study which were to find out the strategies used by Yellow Boat in their Facebook Page usage, and find out if they effectively use the platform in creating awareness through number of people reached or engagement rate in their posts by presenting data of posts per day, number of likes and shares per post, and type of media content posted during a one-month observation period.

Findings revealed that the use of visual media combined with emphatic storytelling or compelling stories can create engagement and participation from followers either by liking and sharing of a post to taking real-life action, volunteering and donating.

title: Influence of Media Richness on Undergraduate Students Learning Through and Acceptance of Social Media
abstract: This study employed quasi-experimental design to examine the influence of media richness on learning through and user acceptance of social media applications as learning tools. The quasi-experiment, which consisted of three stages and took place over an eight-week period, was carried out with 100 undergraduate students who were assigned to two experimental groups (Facebook-based learning condition and Blogger-based learning condition) and a control group (paper-based learning condition). Anchored on Media Richness Theory by Daft and Lengel (1984), the study determined the differences among the three learning conditions in terms of learning performance, perceived learning performance, perceived learning satisfaction, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use. The descriptive statistics results showed that the participants assigned to Blogger-based learning tasks obtained higher pretest and posttest mean scores than Facebook and paper-based group participants. Facebook-based group participants had higher positive ratings of perceived learning performance and perceived learning satisfaction than the two groups. They also reported higher positive ratings of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, making Facebook as a more acceptable learning tool than Blogger-based and paper-based learning platforms.

Ericson H. Peñalba investigates how media richness influences undergraduate learning and the acceptance of social media as educational tools. Grounded in Media Richness Theory, the study examines how the varying capacities of different communication media to transmit information and reduce ambiguity affect student outcomes. The research specifically compares the interactive nature of social media against traditional paper-based or text-heavy blogging methods.

Using a quasi-experimental design, the researcher studied 100 undergraduate students over eight weeks. Participants were divided into three groups: one using Facebook, one using Blogger, and a control group using paper-based methods. Performance was measured through pretest and posttest scores, alongside subjective measures including perceived learning performance, satisfaction, usefulness, and ease of use.

Findings revealed a divergence between academic achievement and student perception. In terms of actual learning performance, students in the Blogger-based group achieved higher mean scores on both pretests and posttests than the Facebook or paper-based groups. However, the Facebook group showed higher levels of student acceptance, reporting higher perceived learning performance, higher satisfaction, and higher ratings for perceived usefulness and ease of use. The study concludes there is a tension between maximizing academic performance and maximizing student satisfaction. While Blogger may be more effective for certain information processing, the social nature of Facebook enhances the perceived value of the learning process.

The study conducted by Ericson H. Peñalba investigates the influence of media richness on how undergraduate students learn through and accept social media applications as educational tools. The research is framed within the context of evolving digital learning environments, specifically examining how different types of media platforms impact student outcomes and their perceptions of these technologies. The core theoretical foundation for this investigation is the Media Richness Theory proposed by Daft and Lengel (1984), which suggests that different communication media possess varying capacities for transmitting information and reducing ambiguity.

The primary problem addressed in this research is determining how the specific characteristics of different media platforms—specifically their "richness"—affect both the actual learning performance of students and their subjective acceptance of these platforms as legitimate learning tools. The study seeks to understand if the interactive and multifaceted nature of social media provides a distinct advantage or disadvantage compared to traditional paper-based methods or more text-heavy blogging platforms.

To address this problem, the researcher employed a quasi-experimental research design. The study was conducted over an eight-week period and involved a sample of 100 undergraduate students. These participants were divided into three distinct groups to facilitate comparison: an experimental group assigned to a Facebook-based learning condition, a second experimental group assigned to a Blogger-based learning condition, and a control group assigned to a paper-based learning condition. The methodology focused on measuring several key variables across these three conditions: actual learning performance (measured via pretest and posttest scores), perceived learning performance, perceived learning satisfaction, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use.

The findings of the study revealed significant differences in outcomes based on the media condition assigned to the students. In terms of actual learning performance, the results indicated that students in the Blogger-based learning condition achieved higher mean scores on both pretests and posttests compared to the participants in both the Facebook-based and the paper-based groups. This suggests that the specific structure of the Blogger platform may have been more effective for the specific learning tasks required during the study period.

However, the findings regarding student perception and acceptance told a different story. While the Blogger group performed better academically, the Facebook-based group reported higher positive ratings in several subjective categories. Specifically, participants in the Facebook-based learning condition reported higher levels of perceived learning performance and higher perceived learning satisfaction than both the Blogger-based and paper-based groups. Furthermore, the Facebook group reported higher positive ratings for perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. These results indicate that, despite the higher academic scores in the Blogger group, students found Facebook to be a more acceptable and user-friendly learning tool.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates a divergence between actual academic achievement and student acceptance of digital learning tools. While the Blogger-based condition yielded superior learning performance in terms of test scores, the Facebook-based condition was more successful in terms of user experience, perceived utility, and ease of use. This suggests that the "richness" and social nature of Facebook may enhance the perceived value and satisfaction of the learning process for students, even if it does not directly translate to higher test scores in this specific experimental context.

The implications of these findings are significant for educators and instructional designers. The results suggest that when selecting digital tools for educational purposes, there is a tension between maximizing academic performance and maximizing student acceptance and satisfaction. While a platform like Blogger might be more effective for certain types of information processing, the higher perceived usefulness and ease of use associated with Facebook suggest that social media platforms can be highly effective for student engagement and acceptance. The study implies that the choice of a learning tool should consider not only the pedagogical effectiveness of the medium but also the psychological and practical factors of user acceptance, as student satisfaction and perceived ease of use are critical components of the modern digital learning experience.

title: Like, Follow, Subscribe: The Influence of Smartphone Usage on Social Behavior Among Millennials
abstract:
The trend of social behavior among millennials has been changing over the course of the years since the introduction of the smartphone. Based on the 2017 survey in the United States, about 3 out of 4 Americans mentioned that they have either an iPhone or an iPad [as smartphones]. The phenomenon has given such an alarm as the iGens (born between 1995 and 2012) have had drastic and unparalleled behavior change – which included rising rates of ‘unhappiness’, depression and worst, suicide rates among the youth have exceeded the homicide rate in 2011.

This study aimed to determine if there is conclusive evidence that the use of smartphones have a significant adverse effect on the youth’s social behavior. This research anchored on the Uses and Gratification Theory and Technological Determinism to investigate and explain the impact of smartphone usage among millennials’ social behavior. Results show that the costs and adverse effects on social behavior [evidenced by the rising cases of exposure to cyberbullying, pornography, sex, behavioral change, rising cases of millennials being ‘anti-social’] can be significantly explained by excessive smartphone usage and costs outweigh the benefits of smartphone usage by a margin of 10%.

Overall, the two ways of smartphone usage which are text messaging and call duration, impact interpersonal communication. The conflicting effects of text messaging and taking calls to the number of bonding hours [reflecting social behavior] can be attributed to the fact that text messaging is more likely possible to be done simultaneously while bonding with one’s family, whereas taking a call takes away time from the family as one concentrates in talking to the caller. Based on the results of this study, institutions, like schools and homes, can implement measures that would regulate the smartphone usage by the millennials and thus, minimized if not totally eliminate the adverse effects of excessive phone usage. Further, as this research is not time-bound and conducted only at the time the survey was handed out, the researcher recommends further study to better quantify the impact of smartphone usage on one’s social behavior and interpersonal communication.

title: Communication and Decision Making: A Symbolic Interaction Study of Choosing Agriculture as an Academic Program
abstract:
The interactions of the youth to their environment have defined their decisions to study agriculture. In this sense, communicative interactions of the youth were studied as the means to understand their decision-making process of selecting agriculture as their course in college.

This qualitative research employed the Symbolic Interactionism methodology of Blumer on six agriculture graduates: four males and two females. For the exploration, individual interview and focus group discussion were utilized. For the inspection, proceedings were transcribed, translated and analyzed by sensitizing of concepts and thematic analysis.

Results showed that the individuals whom interaction have been significant for the youth upon agriculture selection are their families, teachers, agriculture students, friends and workers in agriculture. Selection of agriculture is a family decision as family members encourage the youth to study agriculture and have served as role models. Also, the academe is a catalyst for course selection of agriculture as teachers motivated the youth to study agriculture and offered scholarships in the agriculture course.

Meanwhile, interaction with agriculture students created pessimism on agriculture as it is viewed as the course of hard labor and grime and is for impolite students. Still, studying agriculture is a peer decision as the youth follow peer advices and decision of pursuing agriculture. Conversely, communication to workers in agriculture showed agriculture course as a means for a better life by means of government employment and a way to be rich.

Thus, the role of these communicative interactions of the youth with these people should be recognized as it defined the decision of the youth to study agriculture as their course in college.

Camille Rose Carl T. Rodriguez’s study, "Communication and Decision Making: A Symbolic Interaction Study of Choosing Agriculture as an Academic Program," investigates the communicative processes influencing youth when selecting agriculture as a college major. Using a qualitative design grounded in Blumer’s Symbolic Interactionism, the researcher conducted interviews and focus group discussions with six agriculture graduates to understand how social interactions create meaning during the decision-making process.

The findings reveal that several social groups significantly influence this choice. Families serve as foundational influencers, often making the choice a collective decision where members provide encouragement and act as role models. Within the academe, teachers act as catalysts by providing motivation and practical incentives, such as scholarships. Conversely, interactions with current agriculture students can produce negative social meanings, as peers may view the field through a lens of hard labor or perceive the student body negatively, which can act as a deterrent. Friends also play a role, as the decision can be peer-driven. Finally, communication with agricultural professionals provides an aspirational perspective, framing the degree as a pathway to economic stability or wealth.

The study concludes that choosing agriculture is a product of meanings negotiated through interactions with family, educators, peers, and professionals. Because these interactions provide a complex mix of encouragement, stigma, and aspiration, stakeholders should utilize these insights to develop better recruitment and communication strategies.

By examining these communicative interactions, the study seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms of the decision-making process regarding the pursuit of an agriculture degree.

The context of this research is situated within the academic landscape where students must make critical decisions about their future career paths. The research addresses the need to understand the social and communicative drivers that lead students toward or away from this specific academic program.

To explore this phenomenon, the researcher employed a qualitative research design utilizing the Symbolic Interactionism methodology developed by Blumer. This theoretical framework allows for an investigation into how individuals create meaning through social interaction and how those meanings influence their actions and decisions. The study's participants consisted of six agriculture graduates, comprising four males and two females. Data collection was conducted through two primary methods: individual interviews and focus group discussions. The resulting data were transcribed, translated, and subjected to analysis through the sensitization of concepts and thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and meanings.

The findings of the study reveal that several key social groups provide significant communicative interactions that influence the decision to study agriculture. These influential groups include families, teachers, current agriculture students, friends, and workers within the agricultural sector. Each group contributes a distinct perspective or set of meanings that shape the youth's perception of the course.

Family plays a foundational role in the decision-making process. The research found that selecting agriculture is often a family decision. Family members act as primary influencers by encouraging the youth to pursue the course and by serving as role models for the students. Through these interactions, the family provides the initial motivation and social validation necessary for the student to consider agriculture as a viable academic path.

The academe, specifically teachers, serves as a significant catalyst for course selection. Teachers influence students by providing motivation and offering practical incentives, such as scholarships specifically designated for agriculture courses. This communicative interaction from academic figures helps frame the course as an accessible and supported academic pursuit.

In contrast, interactions with current agriculture students can produce different social meanings. The study found that communication with these peers can create a sense of pessimism regarding the field. Agriculture is sometimes viewed through a lens of hard labor and grime, and there is a perception that the course attracts impolite students. These negative social meanings derived from peer interaction can act as a deterrent or a complicating factor in the decision-making process.

Peer influence also manifests in a different way through friends. The research indicates that studying agriculture can be a peer-driven decision, where youth follow the advice of their friends or mirror the decisions of their peers to pursue the course.

Finally, communication with workers in the agricultural sector provides a more aspirational perspective. Interactions with these professionals frame the study of agriculture as a pathway to a better life. Specifically, the agricultural field is viewed as a means to achieve economic stability through government employment and as a potential route to becoming wealthy.

In conclusion, the study concludes that the communicative interactions of youth with various social actors are instrumental in defining their decision to study agriculture in college. The decision is not made in isolation but is a product of the meanings negotiated through interactions with family, educators, peers, and professionals. These interactions provide a complex mix of encouragement, practical incentives, social stigma, and economic aspiration.

The implications of this research suggest that stakeholders in the agricultural and academic sectors must recognize the power of these communicative interactions. Because social meaning is constructed through interaction, understanding how different groups talk about agriculture is essential for recruitment and program development. Recognizing the role of families, teachers, and professionals can help in crafting better communication strategies to promote agriculture as a viable and desirable career path, potentially mitigating the negative perceptions held by some student groups.

title: Communication and Social Order: A Mother’s Critical Autoethnography of Life with a Child with Down Syndrome
abstract: This study brings the concept of power and authority in the center of my communicative performance as a mother to a child with Down Syndrome (DS). Through a critical autoethnography, I delved into my experience as a mother raising a child with DS as we interact with the family, the medical institution and the educational institution. My narrative, reconstructed from a recollection of past experiences and aided by well-kept documents and records, was used to uncover knowledge about the social order and how this is surfaced in communication. In making sense of my experience through my narrative, the marginalization of the social order against my child with DS emerged. The communication that the medical and educational institutions relegated my child to the margins - in the words that were spoken, in documents, and in practice. The social order was to keep the child with DS in her place in the margins of society. My inquiry revealed that this marginalization shaped my communicative performance as a mother into three constructs: family at the core of the social order, reclaiming power from the medical institution and negotiating with the power of the educational institution.

title: Restoryng as Giving a Voice to Minority Women
abstract: This inquiry covers women belonging to indigenous groups that identified themselves as minorities in their practice of another religion and their geographic  isolation from the political and economic axis of the country. Being women and indigenous, their lack of agency in the public sphere prompted Angeles (1998) to describe them further as a "minority within a minority." This distinction added extra dimensions to their status particularly in their exposure to religious interpretations  and cultural practices that challenge women·s rights. This minority status defines  and influences the way they communicate and tell their stories about gender violence in the context of religious interpretations, legal (state) laws, customs and cultural practices.

title: Understanding Communication Patterns Within the Teen Mom’s Environment
abstract:
Interpersonal communications within the female teens' environment particularly the patterns between them and their parents greatly influence the female teens' behaviors. In this study, communication patterns were reviewed with the aim of explaining the cause of risky behaviors leading to teen pregnancies – the parenting styles, themes, and barriers in communications that drive female teens towards them and the consequent changes after teen pregnancy occurs.

Utilizing a qualitative sampling of female teens and their experiences with teenage pregnancies, the mass of data gathered in the conduct of interviews are transcribed and analyzed using the Miles & Huberman method. The findings were organized around themes that explained the dynamics between the sample teens and their environment before and post-pregnancies. In analyzing this, the effect of communication barriers or noise posited in the Transactional
Communications Model by J. Wood was used.

The study reveals that limitations in communications between parents and female teens start at home, in the limited discussions about sex within Filipino families. This pattern changes after pregnancy, where the barriers identified in the research became relaxed. The study recommends development of intervention programs to minimize teen pregnancies and improve communication patterns particularly between the parents and their female teens.

Alvarado investigates interpersonal communication dynamics between female teenagers and their parents. The research focuses on the connection between communication patterns and the occurrence of risky behaviors leading to teenage pregnancies, specifically examining how parenting styles, communication themes, and barriers contribute to these pregnancies and how these dynamics shift after a pregnancy occurs.

Situated within the social and familial structures of Filipino families, where discussions regarding sex are often limited, the study utilizes J. Wood’s Transactional Communications Model to analyze interactions through the concept of communication "noise." Employing a qualitative research design, the author conducted in-depth interviews with female teenagers who had experienced pregnancies, analyzing the data using the Miles & Huberman method.

The findings reveal that communication limitations frequently originate within the home. A primary driver of risky behaviors is the lack of open discussion regarding sex within the Filipino family structure, which serves as a significant barrier contributing to pregnancy. However, a notable shift occurs post-pregnancy; previously present communication barriers appear to relax once the pregnancy is a reality. The study concludes that the restrictive nature of communication regarding sexual health is a significant factor in teenage pregnancy prevalence. The author recommends targeted intervention programs to improve communication patterns between parents and teenagers to foster open dialogue and mitigate risks.

title: Interrogating the Absence and Exploring the Potential of a Commercial Radio Station in Disaster Risk Education and Preparedness Programming
abstract: Premised on the Anchored Instruction Theory, the study determined how radio could be used to educate people about disaster risk and preparedness. Survey research design was employed with 100 residents along a coastal barangay in Manila and the results emphasized the high level of interest of survey participants to listen to a radio program on disaster risk education and preparedness. Majority of the participants preferred to listen to a radio program with a talk show format during the morning timeslot. Two informants from a commercial radio station were interviewed to find out the reasons for the non-airing of a disaster education program in their entity. Using a problem structure map, it was revealed that a radio station's concerns on its survival and sustainability are the root causes of the absence of a disaster education program. However, the airing of an education program could become plausible should needed mechanisms be effectively implemented and improved by the subject commercial radio station. There is also a necessity to rethink how mainstream media can carry out its noblest role of educating the public.

The study "Interrogating the Absence and Exploring the Potential of a Commercial Radio Station in Disaster Risk Education and Preparedness Programming" investigates the role of commercial radio in disseminating disaster risk and preparedness information. Grounded in Anchored Instruction Theory, the research addresses the gap between the medium's potential to reach wide audiences and the current absence of specialized disaster readiness programming within the commercial sector.

Using a survey research design with 100 residents in a vulnerable coastal barangay in Manila, alongside qualitative interviews with two commercial radio station informants, the researcher explored public interest and the barriers to broadcasting such content. Survey findings indicated a high level of public interest in disaster risk education via radio. Participants expressed a clear desire for this information, specifically preferring a talk show format broadcast during morning timeslots.

Analysis using a problem structure map identified that the primary barriers to implementing these programs are the economic and operational pressures related to the stations' own survival and sustainability. The study concludes that implementing disaster education programs is plausible if stations improve specific mechanisms to facilitate such content. Ultimately, the research suggests that mainstream media must rethink its role in public education, requiring a bridge between the high public interest in disaster preparedness and the necessity of station sustainability.

Grounded in Anchored Instruction Theory, the research explores how radio can serve as an effective tool for educating the public on these critical issues. The central problem addressed is the notable absence of disaster risk education and preparedness programming within commercial radio stations, despite the medium's inherent potential to reach wide audiences. While mainstream media plays a significant role in public education, a gap exists in the implementation of specialized programming focused on disaster readiness within the commercial sector.

To address this problem, the researcher employed a survey research design involving 100 residents living in a coastal barangay in Manila, a demographic chosen due to their vulnerability to disasters. In addition to the quantitative survey, the study utilized qualitative methods by interviewing two informants from a commercial radio station to understand the underlying reasons why such educational programs are not currently aired by these entities.

The findings from the survey of residents indicated a high level of interest among the public regarding radio programs dedicated to disaster risk education and preparedness. Participants expressed a clear desire to consume this type of information through radio. Furthermore, the data revealed specific preferences regarding the delivery of such content; the majority of participants preferred a talk show format and indicated that the morning timeslot would be the most suitable time for broadcasting.

Through the use of a problem structure map, the study identified the root causes for the lack of disaster education programming in commercial radio. The analysis revealed that the primary concerns of radio stations are their own survival and sustainability. These economic and operational pressures act as the fundamental barriers preventing the airing of non-commercial, educational programming.

The study concludes that while there is currently an absence of such programming, the implementation of disaster education programs on commercial radio is plausible. This potential can be realized if commercial radio stations implement and improve specific mechanisms to facilitate the airing of such content. The research suggests that the current state of mainstream media requires a rethinking of its role in fulfilling its "noblest role" of educating the public. The implications suggest that for disaster risk education to be effective through commercial radio, there must be a bridge between the public's high interest and the stations' need for sustainability.

title: Transpinay Online and Offline: Reclaiming Transgender Communication Spaces
abstract: Three full pledged Transgendered Filipina Women (Transpinays) from Metro Manila were interviewed to (1.) define who are the Transgendered Filipina women (Transpinays) (2.) understand who are the Transpinays (3.) explain why and how they became Transpinays, (4.) describe their status as members of the society and (5.) explain how he reclaimed his gender identity offline in the communication spaces engaged in. Inspired by Feminist, Queer, and Elaboration Likelihood theories, a Transpinay's own version of puberty, and four major themes that included self-proclaimed women, identity straggler, discriminated group, and public spaces, were made to answers the aforementioned objectives of the study and were important elements towards human and societal development. Communication spaces were also drawn to explain how the self-proclaimed women were able to reclaim and assert their rights and existence. The study was a contribution to the development of the society and shall serve as a recommendation to the National Government to act on the pending anti-discrimination bills which will protect the rights of the LGBT community, especially of the Transpinays. This study will also help in achieving the 7th Sustainable Development Goal agreed by 193 countries members of the United Nations that covers gender identity and equality in the country and empower the Transpinays.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Dennise Allan F. Castro’s study, "Transpinay Online and Offline: Reclaiming Transgender Communication Spaces," investigates the lived experiences and communication practices of transgender Filipina women, or Transpinays, in Metro Manila. The research aims to define the Transpinay identity, understand the processes and reasons behind their transition, describe their current societal status, and explain how they reclaim their gender identity within various communication spaces. The study utilizes Feminist, Queer, and Elaboration Likelihood theories to explore identity construction in both digital and physical environments.

Using a qualitative methodology involving in-depth interviews with three Transpinay women, the analysis employs a framework consisting of a Transpinay's own version of puberty and four major themes: self-proclaimed women, identity straggler, discriminated group, and public spaces. Findings reveal that Transpinays assert their womanhood as "self-proclaimed women." The "identity straggler" theme addresses the complexities of the transition process, while the "discriminated group" theme highlights the prejudices and marginalization they face. The "public spaces" theme examines how they utilize online and offline environments to reclaim their rights and assert their existence.

The study concludes that Transpinays use communication spaces to navigate identities and combat discrimination. Nationally, the research recommends that the Philippine government act on anti-discrimination bills to protect the LGBT community. Globally, it contributes to the United Nations' 7th Sustainable Development Goal regarding gender identity and equality.

The theme of "discriminated group" highlights the societal challenges, prejudices, and marginalization faced by Transpinays in their daily lives. Finally, the theme of "public spaces" examines the environments—both online and offline—where these women engage with society. The study specifically looks at how communication spaces are utilized as tools for Transpinays to reclaim their rights and assert their existence in a world that often denies them recognition.

In conclusion, the research demonstrates that Transpinays actively use communication spaces to navigate their identities and combat discrimination. By reclaiming these spaces, they are able to assert their presence and demand recognition of their gender identity. The study underscores the importance of communication in the process of identity reclamation and the assertion of human rights for transgender individuals.

The implications of this study are both local and global. On a national level, the research serves as a recommendation to the Philippine government to take action on pending anti-discrimination bills. Such legislation is presented as a necessary step to protect the rights of the LGBT community, with a specific focus on the protections required by Transpinays. On a global scale, the study contributes to the achievement of the United Nations' 7th Sustainable Development Goal, which focuses on gender identity and equality. By documenting the experiences of Transpinays, the research aims to contribute to the broader movement of empowering transgender women and ensuring their inclusion in societal development.

title: A Policy Study on Disaster Risk Reduction and Management in Guagua, Pampanga and the Inclusion of Persons with Disability (PWDS) in Their Disaster Plans
abstract:
The study describes the current practice of risk communication, warning and response in the Municipality of Guagua, determines if its disaster risk reduction and management plan is consistent with the National Council’s standards, and identifies the gaps in knowledge, capacities, and resources that address the needs of Persons with Disability (PWDs) during disasters.

The researcher used a descriptive survey research method where participants were interviewed using survey questionnaires. The main research instrument was adopted from the UNISDR 2013 Survey on Living with Disabilities and Disasters. The questions in the questionnaire were patterned after the objectives of the study.

The study population consisted 244 Persons with Disability age 18 and up in Guagua, Pampanga who were randomly selected from the total list. The sample size of 244 was computed using Raosoft sample size calculator. The random numbers were generated using the random number generator in the site “randomizer.org.”
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:

Mercado’s study investigates risk communication, warning, and response practices in the Municipality of Guagua, Pampanga, specifically focusing on the needs of Persons with Disability (PWDs). The research evaluates the alignment of local disaster risk reduction and management plans with national standards and identifies gaps in knowledge, capacities, and resources regarding inclusive disaster management.

Using a descriptive survey method, the researcher collected data from 244 randomly selected PWDs, Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction Officers, PWD Focal Persons, and 31 barangay leaders. The findings reveal significant challenges regarding the inclusion and protection of PWDs. While many respondents rely on television for updates, they reported a lack of awareness regarding the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Council. A critical finding is the absence of current protocols, specific guidelines, and specialized warning signals designed specifically for PWDs. During disasters, respondents identified recurring issues such as a lack of information, insufficient space within evacuation centers, and failure to receive relief goods. Beyond food, respondents expressed a need for medical and financial assistance. Furthermore, both barangay officials and the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office were found to lack sufficient knowledge, resources, and capacities to effectively handle PWDs.

The study concludes there is a disconnect between general disaster management and the specific requirements of the PWD community. The lack of specialized protocols suggests current strategies are not sufficiently inclusive. The study implies a pressing need for policy reform and capacity building, including tailored warning signals and better training for officials.

The research specifically focuses on determining whether the local disaster risk reduction and management plan aligns with the standards set by the National Council. A primary objective of the work is to identify existing gaps in knowledge, capacities, and resources regarding how the needs of Persons with Disability (PWDs) are addressed during disaster events.

The research was conducted within the context of disaster management for vulnerable populations. The study seeks to understand the intersection between local government disaster policies and the lived experiences of PWDs to determine if current protocols are sufficient for inclusive disaster risk reduction and management.

To achieve these objectives, the researcher employed a descriptive survey research method. To provide a comprehensive perspective, the researcher also interviewed Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction Officers, Persons with Disabilities Focal Persons, and 31 barangay leaders, ensuring representation from every barangay in Guagua to facilitate unbiased interpretations.

A significant portion of the PWD population experienced movement disabilities that prevented them from being able to care for themselves. These individuals reported having experienced various types of disasters, including storms, floods, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions. In terms of information gathering, respondents often rely on television for disaster updates, though they noted that barangay officials occasionally visit their homes to provide information.

A critical finding is the absence of current protocols, specific guidelines, and specialized warning signals designed specifically for PWDs. Furthermore, the respondents identified several recurring issues during disaster events, most notably a lack of information, insufficient space for them within evacuation centers, and a failure to receive relief goods. Beyond immediate disaster-related needs, these individuals also expressed a need for financial and medical assistance in addition to food.

On the institutional side, the study found that both the barangay officials and the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office lack sufficient knowledge, resources, and capacities to effectively handle Persons with Disability during a disaster.

The conclusions drawn from the study highlight a disconnect between general disaster management practices and the specific requirements of the PWD community in Guagua. The lack of specialized protocols and warning systems suggests that current disaster management strategies are not sufficiently inclusive. The findings indicate that while some information reaches the PWD population, the systemic response—specifically regarding evacuation space, relief distribution, and specialized communication—is inadequate to meet their unique needs.

The implications of this study suggest a pressing need for policy reform and capacity building within the Municipality of Guagua. There is a clear requirement for the development of specific protocols, guidelines, and warning signals tailored to the needs of PWDs to ensure they are not left behind during emergencies. Furthermore, the study implies that local government units must increase their capacity by providing better training and resources to both barangay leaders and Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officers. Addressing the gaps in information dissemination, evacuation center accessibility, and the provision of medical and financial assistance is essential for creating a truly inclusive disaster risk reduction and management framework.

title: Examining Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Through the Lens of Local Knowledge and Collective Behavior: The Case of Community-Based Flood Early Warning System (CBFEWS)
abstract:
After Typhoon Sendong devastated Cagayan de Oro City in 2011, the city's City Disaster Risk Reduction Management Office (CDRRMO) took a proactive approach to mitigate the effects of flood brought by typhoons by operationalizing the Community-Based Flood Early Warning System (CBFEWS) in the local barangays.

In Barangay Consolacion, the CBFEWS is a component of the Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committee (BDRRMC). In its initial implementation, the system is composed of three methods: the recorrida, text brigade, and interpersonal communication from the barangay officials.

This study sought how the residents described their experience with Sendong and in the initial implementation of the CBFEWS. Furthermore, it looked into how the residents' experience with Sendong affected their response to the warning message from the CBFEWS.

This qualitative study used transcendental phenomenology as methodology to answer the research objectives. Eight participants from the seven districts of the barangay were interviewed. From the transcription of the interviews, narratives were done to present the participants' stories. Significant statements from these narratives were then highlighted to develop themes that would describe the participants' experiences.

Based on the themes that emerged from the narratives of the participants, there was a strong emphasis on communal coping in the neighborhood when Typhoon Sendong struck the community. This experience with the disaster has established their social relationship, which put the CBFEWS in their barangay in the outside. In addition, their local knowledge of the river, based on their experience with Sendong, has also played a significant part of their decision on whether to evacuate or not during impending floods. Because of these, it recommends that the barangay consider incorporating these two - collective action of the residents and their local knowledge - into the design of the CBFEWS to make it more effective in prompting the residents to act thoroughly during impending floods.

title: Information and Communication Technology from the Point of View of a Person Afflicted Cerebral Palsy
abstract:
Access to information and communication technologies like mobile phones, the Internet, and computers is essential to develop not only the economy of the country but also its people. With the growth of such technologies and the increased number of people using ICTs, the United Nations (UN) will no doubt fulfill one of its development goals - that is, to make the benefits of new technologies available to all, particularly to developing countries. The word "all" in that premise includes persons with disabilities. This study then delves into the use of information and communication technologies by persons with disability and answers how and why they use such technologies.

The data generated from the interviews with the subject, a person afflicted cerebral palsy, a sample of a person with disability, and the observations prove that although he is aware of ICTs and use it personally, there are still barriers to their access to such technologies (e.g., lack of awareness, affordability, type of disability). It was also interesting to learn the reasons for significance of using ICT from the perspective of a person who has cerebral palsy. The reasons why and how he utilize ICTs may be simple and different from another person of disability, but they are essential in understanding the needs of persons with disability in general in order to address the issues of accessibility to ICTs and digital divide.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study explores the intersection of information and communication technology (ICT) and disability, focusing on the lived experiences of individuals with cerebral palsy. Positioned within the framework of development communication, the research argues that technological advancement is not truly universal unless it is inclusive of those with physical or cognitive impairments. As digital tools become essential to modern life, there is a risk that persons with disabilities will be left behind if accessibility is not prioritized.

Using a qualitative case study methodology, the research gathered data through interviews and direct observations of a single subject with cerebral palsy. The findings reveal a complex relationship between the subject and ICTs. While the subject utilizes technology for personal purposes, significant barriers prevent full and effective access. These obstacles include a lack of awareness regarding available tools, issues of affordability, and the specific physical requirements of the disability, which may necessitate specialized hardware or software. The study emphasizes that accessibility is not a one-size-fits-all concept, as the needs of a person with cerebral palsy may differ from other disabilities.

The study concludes that awareness and usage do not automatically equate to seamless accessibility. To fulfill global development goals, policymakers and developers must address specific barriers like cost and physical requirements. Inclusive design is essential to prevent marginalization and promote true digital inclusion.

The study explores the intersection of information and communication technology (ICT) and disability, specifically focusing on the lived experiences of individuals with cerebral palsy. The central problem addressed is the accessibility of ICTs, such as mobile phones, the Internet, and computers, for persons with disabilities. While the growth of these technologies is intended to foster economic and human development, the author notes that the United Nations' goal of making technological benefits available to "all" must explicitly include persons with disabilities. The research seeks to understand how and why individuals with disabilities utilize these technologies, aiming to bridge the gap in understanding their specific needs to address the digital divide.

The context of the research is rooted in global development goals and the increasing ubiquity of digital tools. As ICTs become essential for modern life, there is a risk that persons with disabilities may be left behind if accessibility is not prioritized. The study positions itself within the framework of development communication, suggesting that the benefits of technological advancement are not truly universal unless they are inclusive of those with physical or cognitive impairments. By focusing on the specific perspective of a person with cerebral palsy, the research attempts to provide a nuanced view that moves beyond generalities to understand the practical application and barriers faced by individuals with specific physical conditions.

The methodology employed in this study is qualitative, utilizing a case study approach. The researcher gathered data through interviews with a single subject—a person afflicted with cerebral palsy—and supplemented these interviews with direct observations. This method allowed the researcher to capture the personal significance of ICT use and the specific ways in which the subject interacts with technology. By focusing on a single subject, the study provides a deep, qualitative look at the individual's relationship with digital tools, which serves as a representative sample for understanding the broader challenges faced by persons with disabilities.

The findings of the study reveal a complex relationship between the subject and ICTs. The subject is aware of various information and communication technologies and utilizes them for personal purposes. However, the research identifies significant barriers that prevent full and effective access to these technologies. These barriers include a lack of awareness regarding available tools, issues of affordability, and the specific nature of the disability itself, which may require specialized hardware or software that is not readily available or accessible. The study highlights that the ways in which a person with cerebral palsy utilizes ICTs may be distinct from other types of disabilities, emphasizing that "accessibility" is not a one-size-fits-all concept.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that while ICTs offer immense potential for empowerment, there are persistent obstacles that prevent persons with disabilities from fully participating in the digital world. The subject's experience confirms that awareness and usage do not automatically equate to seamless accessibility. The research concludes that understanding the specific, individual reasons why and how persons with disabilities use technology is vital. Without this granular understanding, efforts to close the digital divide may fail to address the actual needs of the community.

The implications of this research are significant for policymakers, technology developers, and development practitioners. To fulfill global development goals, there must be a concerted effort to address the specific barriers identified, such as cost and the physical requirements of different disabilities. The study implies that technological design and distribution must be inclusive from the outset to prevent the further marginalization of persons with disabilities. By understanding the unique perspectives of individuals with cerebral palsy, stakeholders can better design interventions and technologies that promote true digital inclusion and support the broader goal of making technological benefits available to all members of society.
