title: Content framing of the Tulong Na Tabang Na Tayo Na Project of ABS-CBN’s Lingkod Kapamilya Foundation., Inc. and influence on viewer’s response
abstract:
Guided by Goffinan's (1974) Framing Theory and Gerbner and Gross'es Cultivation Theory ( I 976), this descriptive study explored how the framing of Tulong Na Tabang Na Tayo Na project of ABS-CBN Lingkod Kapamilya Foundation Inc. had influenced the responses of I 14 students from three higher education institutions in the Philippines towards it. The project was a call to help the victims ofTyphoon Yolanda in Tacloban, Leyte. Through a survey, data were obtained and analyzed using frequency counts and percentages. Of the 114 (76%) student­respondents, 89 (78%) are female and 25 (22%) male. Most student-respondents (67 or 58.7%) belonged to the 14-18 years old bracket. The study recorded 78 or 68% of student-respondents were actively watching television and assumed to be capable of deciding whether to support or ignore the project's framed content. Twenty percent of student-respondents shared that the framed content by using emotional appeal (i.e. crying people asking for help) accompanied by emphatic messages (i.e. Kapamilya, magkapit-bisig po tayo sa panahon ng sakuna, bukas po ang aming tanggapan para sa inyong mga donasyon (Members of the ramify in this time of disaster, let us hold hands, our office is open for your donations) had influenced them to support the project because of their experience. While personal experience did not form part of the communication frame as forwarded by Lakoff (2004 ), it surfaced that audiences' decision to support a project is motivated by it. Most student-respondents have experienced floods and strong typhoons, making the situation familiar. Thus, empathizing with the victims would be easy to establish. Moreover, long exposure to television and continuous watching of the project led them, as espoused by the cultivation theory, to support the project. Suffice to say that in developing a communication material, inclusion of a related experience of intended audiences 
may be considered.

title: Dual-Lens Sensemaking in Higher Education Leadership Transition: Integrating Weick’s Theory and the Cynefin Framework
abstract:
This convergent parallel mixed-methods study used dual-lens framework aimed at determining sensemaking engagement, examining contextual sensemaking triggers, exploring the interpretation of leadership transition, and identifying emerging constructs expanding the sensemaking framework. Quantitative surveys and qualitative narratives were collected from 26 middle managers from a Philippine state university.

Quantitative results showed strong sensemaking engagement through retrospection, ongoing process, and plausibility that showed respondents’ preference for coherence, dialogue, and trust. Narrative analysis, referenced with the Cynefin framework, revealed shifting domains from Clear or Chaotic toward Complex domain where negation and collaboration were necessary to maintain institutional alignment. Further, using Weick’s sensemaking properties, seven themes were generated by Reflexive Thematic Analysis - Identity as an Adaptive Self, Retrospection as Negotiated Reality, Situated Intentional Action, Collaboration through Dialogue as Core the Core of Sensemaking, Sensemaking as an Ongoing Engagement, Cues as Cornerstone of Meaning Construction, and Plausibility as Pragmatic Truth.

The integration of contextual and interpretive dimensional frameworks refined sensemaking scholarship by advancing the idea of adaptative sensemaking and collaborative actions as theoretical enhancements in dealing with uncertainty during leadership transition in an academic context.

two:
The study addresses the problem of navigating uncertainty during leadership transitions within higher education institutions. Specifically, it investigates how leaders engage in sensemaking processes to interpret and manage the shifts in organizational structure and culture that occur when leadership changes. The research seeks to determine the level of sensemaking engagement among managers, examine the contextual triggers that initiate sensemaking, explore how leadership transitions are interpreted, and identify emerging constructs that can expand existing sensemaking frameworks.

The context of this research is a Philippine state university, focusing on the experiences of 26 middle managers. These individuals occupy a critical position in the organizational hierarchy, acting as a bridge between upper administration and faculty during periods of institutional change. The study utilizes a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, which allows for the simultaneous collection and analysis of both quantitative and qualitative data to provide a comprehensive view of the phenomenon.

The methodology employed a dual-lens framework to analyze the data. Quantitatively, the researcher used surveys to measure sensemaking engagement. Qualitatively, the researcher collected narratives from the participants, which were then analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. To interpret the qualitative findings, the study integrated Weick’s theory of sensemaking with the Cynefin framework, a decision-making tool used to categorize environments based on their level of complexity and predictability.

The quantitative findings indicated strong levels of sensemaking engagement among the middle managers. This engagement was characterized by three specific properties: retrospection, an ongoing process, and plausibility. The data showed that the respondents demonstrated a clear preference for coherence, dialogue, and trust when navigating organizational shifts. This suggests that for these managers, making sense of a transition is not a one-time event but a continuous effort to create a shared, believable reality through communication and interpersonal trust.

The qualitative narrative analysis, interpreted through the Cynefin framework, revealed a significant shift in the organizational environment during the transition. The findings showed that the institutional context moved from domains characterized as Clear or Chaotic toward the Complex domain. This shift implies that leadership transitions introduce levels of unpredictability and non-linear cause-and-effect relationships that cannot be managed with simple, standardized procedures. In this complex domain, the study found that negation and collaboration became essential tools for maintaining institutional alignment.

Through the application of Reflexive Thematic Analysis and Weick’s sensemaking properties, the study generated seven distinct themes that characterize the sensemaking process in this context. The first theme, Identity as an Adaptive Self, suggests that managers must adjust their professional identities to meet new organizational demands. The second theme, Retrospection as Negotiated Reality, highlights how looking back at past events helps managers construct a shared understanding of the current situation. The third theme, Situated Intentional Action, emphasizes that sensemaking is tied to specific, localized actions taken within a particular context.

The fourth theme, Collaboration through Dialogue as the Core of Sensemaking, underscores the necessity of communication in building a collective understanding. The fifth theme, Sensemaking as an Ongoing Engagement, reinforces the idea that sensemaking is a continuous, rather than a discrete, activity. The sixth theme, Cues as Cornerstone of Meaning Construction, identifies how managers use specific environmental signals or "cues" to interpret the direction of the institution. Finally, the seventh theme, Plausibility as Pragmatic Truth, suggests that in times of uncertainty, managers prioritize ideas that are "good enough" to act upon, focusing on what is functional and believable rather than what is objectively certain.

The study concludes that the integration of contextual and interpretive dimensional frameworks provides a more nuanced understanding of organizational change. By combining Weick’s properties with the Cynefin framework, the research demonstrates that sensemaking is not just a cognitive process but a social and adaptive one that is deeply influenced by the complexity of the environment. The findings suggest that during leadership transitions, the ability to navigate the "Complex" domain through collaborative dialogue is vital for institutional stability.

The implications of this research are significant for both sensemaking scholarship and higher education leadership. Theoretically, the study advances the field by introducing the concepts of adaptive sensemaking and collaborative actions as theoretical enhancements for understanding how individuals deal with uncertainty. Practically, the findings suggest that university administrators should prioritize fostering environments of dialogue and trust to support middle managers. By recognizing that leadership transitions move institutions into complex domains, higher education leaders can better prepare their management teams to use collaboration and negation as tools for maintaining institutional alignment and navigating the ambiguity of change.

title: Centrality of Online Advocates in the Structure of Critical Communication Movement: Case of Stop a Dam Network in the Philippines
abstract:
This study investigates how centrality in social networks, specifically of Facebook accounts advocating for the Stop Kaliwa Dam campaign, shape communication structures and communication flows. Guided by the Cybernetics Tradition of Communication theories, particularly General Systems Theory and Network Theory, the research examined how the format, categories, and engagement patterns of the uploaded posts as well as the ensuing centrality shaped advocacy effectiveness. Data were collected from purposely sampled Facebook accounts active between February 1 to May 1, 2023, covering the event of “Alay-Lakad Laban sa Kaliwa Dam”, held on February 15-23, 2023. The centrality measures of the network based on likes and comments were degree, betweenness, and closeness.

Visual content, particularly images, infographics, and videos, and advocacy-themed posts generated the highest levels of engagement, underscoring the role of visual storytelling in mobilization. Likes primarily signaled visibility and affective approval, aligning with degree centrality, while comments facilitated dialogue and bridging functions, corresponding to betweenness and closeness centrality. Frequent posting or more follower counts did not consistently translate to higher centrality; rather, strategic positioning across clusters proved more decisive. Based on the findings, a framework is proposed to enhance centrality: optimizing inputs through visual and narrative formats, balancing throughputs by cultivating both likes and comments; and monitoring outputs through centrality measures. This study contributes to Development Communication by demonstrating how network positioning (like centraility), beyond message sharing (uploading), empowers marginalized advocacy groups to amplify their voices and sustain influence in digital environments.

This study investigates the structural dynamics of digital advocacy by examining how Facebook accounts involved in the "Stop Kaliwa Dam" movement in the Philippines utilize the platform to shape communication flows and mobilize support. The research focuses on how the centrality of various actors within the social network influences the reach and resonance of environmental messages regarding the Kaliwa Dam Project. Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher combined content analysis with Social Network Analysis (SNA) to analyze 310 posts from 25 Facebook accounts active between February and May 2023.

Content analysis revealed that visual storytelling is a primary driver of engagement, with images, infographics, and videos—particularly those categorized under "People" and "Activism Advocacy"—generating the highest levels of interaction. While "likes" served as a measure of visibility and affective approval, "comments" facilitated deeper dialogue and bridging functions. A significant finding was that high follower counts or frequent posting did not consistently guarantee high network centrality; instead, an account's ability to act as a bridge between different clusters of users was a more decisive factor in its influence. The study concludes that network positioning is as critical as message content. Effective digital strategy requires optimizing content for visual impact and strategically positioning accounts to serve as information brokers that connect fragmented groups.

This study investigates the structural dynamics of digital advocacy by examining how Facebook accounts involved in the "Stop Kaliwa Dam" movement in the Philippines utilize the platform to shape communication flows and mobilize support. The research focuses on how the positioning of various actors within the social network—their centrality—influences the reach and resonance of environmental messages.

**Problem and Context**
The Kaliwa Dam Project is a government-led infrastructure initiative intended to meet the water demands of Metro Manila. However, it has faced significant opposition due to its potential environmental impact on the Sierra Madre mountain range and the social implications for Indigenous Peoples (IPs), specifically the Dumagat-Remontado communities. While social media is a known tool for mobilization, a research gap exists regarding how inter-organizational communication dynamics function within such movements. Specifically, it is unclear how different types of content and engagement patterns contribute to the network centrality of advocates, which determines their ability to amplify messages and sustain influence in a digital environment.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a mixed-methods approach, combining content analysis with Social Network Analysis (SNA). The study focused on 25 Facebook accounts (15 personal profiles and 10 organizational pages) that were active between February 1 and May 1, 2023. This period was selected to capture the "Alay-Lakad Laban sa Kaliwa Dam" march. A total of 310 posts were analyzed. Content analysis was used to categorize the posts by format (text, image, video, reels, external links, and art cards) and theme (such as people, solutions, impacts, and activism). SNA was then applied to measure network centrality—specifically degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality—based on audience engagement metrics, namely "likes" (reactions) and comments. The study was grounded in the Cybernetics Tradition of Communication, utilizing General Systems Theory and Network Theory to view the advocacy movement as an interdependent system of information exchange and feedback.

**Findings**
The content analysis revealed that visual storytelling is a primary driver of engagement. Posts utilizing images, infographics, and videos—particularly those categorized under "People" (focusing on community-centered narratives) and "Activism Advocacy"—generated the highest levels of interaction. Specifically, visual formats like art cards and videos were more effective at capturing attention than plain text.

Regarding engagement, the study found that "likes" primarily served as a measure of visibility and affective approval, correlating with degree centrality. In contrast, "comments" facilitated deeper dialogue and bridging functions, which were more closely linked to betweenness and closeness centrality. A significant finding was that high follower counts or frequent posting did not consistently guarantee high network centrality. Instead, an account's strategic positioning within the network—its ability to act as a bridge between different clusters of users—was a more decisive factor in its influence.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that in digital advocacy, network positioning is as critical as message content. Centrality determines how information circulates and whose voice is amplified within the movement. The research demonstrates that while some accounts act as "hubs" for visibility, others serve as vital "information brokers" or "social mediators" that connect fragmented groups, thereby sustaining the movement's momentum.

The implications of this research are significant for Development Communication and environmental advocacy. For organizations and activists, the study suggests that effective digital strategy requires more than just high-volume posting; it requires optimizing content for visual and narrative impact to trigger engagement and strategically positioning accounts to bridge different social clusters. The researcher proposes a framework for enhancing centrality: optimizing inputs through visual/narrative formats, balancing throughputs by cultivating both likes (for reach) and comments (for dialogue), and monitoring outputs through centrality measures to ensure sustained influence. Ultimately, the study shows how digital networks empower marginalized groups to amplify their voices and challenge systemic environmental injustices.

title: From Facebook to Local Bestsellers: An Autoethnographic Study of the Shift from Textseryes to Novel-Type Books
abstract:
This dissertation investigated the transmedia storytelling evolution of "textseryes" and their transformation into commercially successful novels. The study scrutinized three seminal textserye works—"Dear Diary: My BFF's BF," "Dear Diary: Dear Doctor Joey," and "Behind the Clouds"—addressing the core research question: What are the influential factors shaping the transmedia storytelling process of textseryes when transitioning to a commercially viable novel?

The researcher, drawing upon her diverse background as a writer, government servant, teacher, and cultural participant, provided a unique autoethnographic perspective to the study. Grounded theory and thematic analysis were employed to reach theoretical saturation, indicating a thorough understanding of the narrative transition process. 

The Textserye to Novel Narrative Evolution Framework was introduced, serving as a conceptual guide for the systematic transition of narratives. This framework outlined critical adaptation components such as Scene Alterations, Emotional Scene Integration, and Dialogue Adaptation, which were central to the successful adaptation of textserye narratives.

The study also identified the importance of a collaborative ecosystem involving authors, editors, publishers, and a management team to navigate the complexities of transmedia storytelling and ensure consistent engagement across media platforms.

By integrating Henry Jenkins' participatory culture theory, the research emphasized the evolution from passive audience consumption to active engagement, while also examining how consumer preferences and political economy influenced media dynamics.

The culmination of this research was the Economic-Engagement Nexus Theory of Transmedia Storytelling, which advocated for a balanced approach that considered both economic viability and audience engagement. The theory provided a strategic framework comprising Economic Dynamism, Audience Co-Creation, Narrative Flexibility, Experiential Monetization, and Storyworld Sustainability for crafting resonant transmedia narratives.

In conclusion, the dissertation advanced practical applications of the Economic-Engagement Nexus Theory, offering strategies for creators and industry professionals to effectively navigate the transmedia adaptation process. This dissertation, titled "From Facebook to Local Bestsellers: An Autoethnographic Study of the Shift from Textseryes to Novel-Type Books" by Ayris A. Alcachupas, investigates the transmedia storytelling evolution of "textseryes"—serialized narratives delivered via text messages or social media posts—as they transition into commercially successful physical novels.

**Problem**
The research addresses a gap in transmedia studies regarding the specific narrative evolution that occurs when stories move from the informal, digital format of "textseryes" on platforms like Facebook to the structured, traditional format of printed novels. While transmedia storytelling is a growing phenomenon, the complex transformation involving changes in plot, character development, and thematic depth during this specific migration remains largely under-researched. The study seeks to identify the influential factors and necessary adaptations required to make these digital-first narratives commercially viable in the print market.

**Context**
The study is situated within the contemporary Philippine literary landscape, where digital platforms like Facebook and Wattpad have democratized storytelling. The researcher utilizes an autoethnographic approach, leveraging her personal experience as a writer of three specific works: *Dear Diary: My BFF's BF*, *Dear Diary: Dear Doctor Joey*, and *Behind the Clouds*. These works serve as case studies to examine how discursive practices on social media are altered when rewritten for print. The context is further shaped by the rise of participatory culture, where audiences move from passive consumption to active engagement, and the economic realities of the publishing industry.

**Method**
The researcher employed an autoethnography, a method that combines autobiographical elements with ethnographic inquiry to analyze personal experience within a broader cultural context. To ensure a rigorous analysis of the narrative transition, the study utilized a grounded theory approach and thematic analysis to reach theoretical saturation. The researcher analyzed the subject books by examining narrative changes across various dimensions, including plot development, characterization, and themes. The methodology also involved an assessment of the collaborative ecosystem, including the roles of agents, editors, and publishers in the adaptation process.

**Findings**
The study identifies several critical components necessary for a successful transition from textserye to novel. A primary finding is the necessity of significant narrative alterations, specifically in scene alterations, emotional scene integration, and dialogue adaptation. The research highlights that textseryes rely heavily on casual, conversational text-based communication, which must be expanded into descriptive prose to provide the depth required for a novel. Key findings include:

*   **Narrative Evolution:** The transition requires shifting from plot-driven, fragmented text messages to a more cohesive structure involving enhanced setting, atmosphere, and dramatic intensification.
*   **Emotional Depth:** Successful adaptation requires integrating emotional scenes and character backstories that may have been only hinted at in the original digital snippets.
*   **Collaborative Ecosystem:** The process is not solitary; it involves a complex interplay between the author, editors, and publishers to ensure the story meets market demands while maintaining its original essence.
*   **The Framework:** The researcher developed the "Textserye to Novel Narrative Evolution Framework," which serves as a guide for systematic adaptation through scene alterations, emotional integration, and dialogue adaptation.

**Conclusions**
The dissertation concludes that the transition from digital textseryes to printed novels is a complex transmedia process that requires more than simple transcription; it requires a fundamental reimagining of the narrative structure. The researcher introduces the "Economic-Engagement Nexus Theory of Transmedia Storytelling," which posits that successful transmedia narratives must balance economic viability with high levels of audience engagement. This theory is built upon five strategic pillars: Economic Dynamism, Audience Co-Creation, Narrative Flexibility, Experiential Monetization, and Storyworld Sustainability. The study confirms that the shift from passive consumption to active, participatory engagement is a hallmark of modern transmedia storytelling.

**Implications**
The research offers several implications for various stakeholders. For content creators and writers, it provides a strategic framework and an assessment guide to navigate the complexities of adapting digital content for traditional media. For publishers and the industry, it highlights the importance of understanding consumer preferences and the economic potential of digital-first narratives. Academically, the study contributes to the fields of media studies, literary studies, and digital communication by providing a structured way to analyze the evolution of new narrative forms. Finally, it suggests that educational curricula could benefit from incorporating transmedia and textseryes to prepare future creators for a changing media landscape.

title: Establishment of a Competitive Intelligence (CI) Function to Institutionalize Macroanalysis in the Metals Industry Research and Development Center
abstract:
The Metals Industry Research and Development Center (MIRDC) is a Research and Development Organization (RDO) under the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) mandated to serve the local metals, engineering and allied industries. Following the agency’s rationalization in 2010, the Planning and Management Division (PMD) was tasked with conducting macroanalysis of the metals and engineering industries. However, this function has not been formally institutionalized, creating a critical gap in strategic planning. This study addresses this challenge by proposing the formal establishment of Competitive Intelligence (CI) processes and structures to institutionalize its macroanalysis function. CI is defined as the process and forward-looking practices used in producing knowledge about the competitive environment to improve organizational performance.

Employing a case study design with MIRDC as the unit of analysis, the study utilized document analysis, observations, and consultations with key personnel to examine current MIRDC practices and identify intelligence gaps. Findings revealed that MIRDC already incorporates CI elements across multiple processes and practices. However, such efforts operated more in silos without formal coordination or systematic integration. Analysis using Pellissier and Nenzhelele’s unified CI process model identified critical gaps across four influential factors: Process and Structure, Decision-makers, Organizational Awareness, and Culture and Feedback mechanisms. Using the McKinsey 7S Framework, the study examined the organizational and management implications that MIRDC must address to successfully establish its CI capabilities. Establishment of a Competitive Intelligence (CI) Function to Institutionalize Macroanalysis in the Metals Industry Research and Development Center

The study proposes an organizational framework designating PMD as the central coordinating unit for the CI function in MIRDC. Intelligence needs are organized into three broad categories: Context of the Organization, Stakeholder Needs and Wants, and Competitor Analysis. Four distinct roles shall be assigned to concerned MIRDC personnel: Scout / Collector, Subject Matter Expert, Analyst / Integrated and Manager. A four-year implementation plan is recommended to institutionalize CI in MIRDC and address strategic planning gaps and provide systematic intelligence to support decision-making.

Following a rationalization process in 2010, the agency’s Planning and Management Division (PMD) was assigned the responsibility of conducting macroanalysis for these specific industries. Despite this mandate, the study identifies a significant problem: the macroanalysis function has not been formally institutionalized within the organization. This lack of formal structure creates a critical gap in the agency's strategic planning capabilities, as there is no systematic way to gather and utilize environmental intelligence to guide organizational direction.

To address this gap, the research proposes the formal establishment of Competitive Intelligence (CI) processes and structures. In this context, CI is defined as the set of forward-looking practices and processes used to produce knowledge regarding the competitive environment, with the ultimate goal of improving organizational performance. The study seeks to move the agency from ad hoc information gathering toward a structured intelligence capability that can support long-term strategic goals.

The researcher employed a case study design, utilizing the MIRDC as the primary unit of analysis. The methodology involved a multi-faceted approach consisting of document analysis, direct observations, and consultations with key personnel. These methods were used to examine current organizational practices and identify specific intelligence gaps that prevent effective macroanalysis. To evaluate these gaps, the study utilized Pellissier and Nenzhelele’s unified CI process model, which focuses on four influential factors: Process and Structure, Decision-makers, Organizational Awareness, and Culture and Feedback mechanisms. Additionally, the McKinsey 7S Framework was applied to examine the organizational and management implications necessary for the successful establishment of CI capabilities.

The findings of the study indicate that MIRDC does not lack intelligence-gathering activities entirely; rather, it lacks integration. The research revealed that the organization already incorporates various elements of Competitive Intelligence across multiple existing processes and practices. However, these efforts currently operate in silos. There is no formal coordination or systematic integration between the different departments or individuals performing these tasks, which prevents the organization from having a cohesive understanding of the competitive landscape.

Through the application of the Pellissier and Nenzhelele model, the study identified critical gaps across all four influential factors. This suggests that the current approach to macroanalysis is hindered by fragmented processes, a lack of clear roles for decision-makers, insufficient organizational awareness regarding the importance of intelligence, and a lack of established culture and feedback mechanisms to refine intelligence outputs.

In response to these findings, the study proposes a specific organizational framework designed to institutionalize the CI function. The proposed structure designates the Planning and Management Division (PMD) as the central coordinating unit for all CI activities within MIRDC. To ensure the intelligence produced is relevant and actionable, the study categorizes intelligence needs into three broad areas: the Context of the Organization, Stakeholder Needs and Wants, and Competitor Analysis.

To operationalize this framework, the study assigns four distinct roles to concerned MIRDC personnel to ensure a systematic flow of information. These roles include the Scout/Collector, who gathers raw data; the Subject Matter Expert, who provides specialized knowledge; the Analyst/Integrated, who processes and synthesizes information; and the Manager, who oversees the intelligence cycle. This division of labor is intended to move the organization away from siloed activities and toward a coordinated intelligence lifecycle.

The study concludes that the formalization of a CI function is essential for MIRDC to fulfill its mandate effectively. By transitioning from informal, fragmented practices to a structured CI framework, the agency can bridge the current gaps in its strategic planning. To achieve this, the researcher recommends a four-year implementation plan. This long-term approach is intended to allow the organization to gradually build its capabilities, address existing strategic planning gaps, and ultimately provide systematic, high-quality intelligence to support informed decision-making within the metals and engineering sectors. title: Exploring the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) Skills of Japanese Lifelong Learners: a Multi-method Case Study
abstract:
In our interconnected world, continuous foreign language learning is indispensable for personal, professional, and social growth, transcending age barriers, especially for the elderly. However, language acquisition for older individuals presents unique challenges, such as brain maturation, native language interference, and social changes. These challenges necessitate tailored learning methods distinct from those used for younger learners. This research delves into the English language proficiency of Japanese lifelong learners engaged in EFL (English as a Foreign Language) learning at community centers in Machida and Yokohama, Japan. Utilizing a multi-method approach with 33 participants, the study illuminates learners' strategies in narrowing the gap between their language skills and identifies means to enhance their productive language capabilities. The findings reveal a "fair" level of competence in listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills, with slightly more proficient reading skills. Learners actively engage in language activities, benefiting from voluntary activities and local community group studies, fostering valuable connections and potential benefits for the "aging workforce" in countries like Japan. Embracing digital technology, learners exhibit a greater inclination towards open communication.

These findings bear implications for future works, emphasizing the multifaceted nature of language education and the significance of lifelong language learning in our globalized society. To enrich the language skills of lifelong learners, language teachers and tutors are recommended to incorporate relevant activities.

title: The Relationship of Informal Digital Learning of English With the Vocabulary and Writing Development of Filipino Senior High School Students
abstract: Informal Digital Learning of English (IDLE) refers to the informal, self-directed English learning using different digital devices (e.g., smartphones, laptops) and resources (e.g., apps, social media) independent of formal contexts. This study examined what IDLE activities Filipino senior high school students are engaged in and investigated whether the time spent on these activities had any correlation with their (a) vocabulary performance and (b) writing performance. It also looked into how IDLE activities affect the students’ vocabulary knowledge and writing skills. This research used quantitative methods including a survey and vocabulary and writing tests among 99 SHS students from Bacolod City, and qualitative methods, namely interviews among selected participants from the sample and their family members. This study demonstrates that the participants engage in a variety of IDLE activities, with the presence of multitasking and parental influence. However, the time they spend on these had no significant correlation with their vocabulary and writing performance. Even with a lack of correlation among the variables, the interview participants cited the different ways how IDLE activities had contributed to their vocabulary knowledge, which may be attributed to their engagement in form- and meaning-focused language learning. Moreover, the results indicate the possibility that the participants’ writing errors were caused by the informal English, slang, and errors in English that they were exposed to online. However, the interview participants still identified the positive influence of IDLE on their writing, such as providing models of good writing. Educators and parents may consider integrating IDLE in their children’s learning of English.

Adizon investigated the relationship between Informal Digital Learning of English (IDLE) and the development of vocabulary and writing skills among 99 senior high school students in Bacolod City. IDLE refers to the self-directed use of digital devices and resources, such as smartphones and social media, to learn English outside formal educational settings. Using a mixed-methods approach involving surveys, tests, and interviews, the study aimed to identify specific activities and determine if time spent on these activities correlates with language performance.

The findings indicate that students engage in a diverse range of IDLE activities, often characterized by multitasking, and that parental influence affects how these activities are conducted. Quantitatively, the study found that the amount of time spent on IDLE had no significant correlation with performance on vocabulary and writing tests. However, qualitative data provided more nuanced insights, as interview participants described various ways IDLE activities contributed to their vocabulary knowledge through both form-focused and meaning-focused language learning.

The relationship between IDLE and writing development is complex. Exposure to informal English, slang, and linguistic errors online may contribute to certain writing errors, yet digital platforms also provide models of good writing. The study concludes that while time spent does not statistically predict performance, the activities themselves play a role in language acquisition. Educators and parents should consider integrating IDLE into English learning processes.

Despite the prevalence of these activities, the quantitative results showed that the amount of time students spent on IDLE had no significant correlation with their performance on the vocabulary and writing tests.

However, the qualitative data provided more nuanced insights into the impact of IDLE. Even though a statistical correlation was not found between time spent and test performance, interview participants described various ways in which IDLE activities contributed to their vocabulary knowledge. The researcher suggests that these contributions may be attributed to the students' engagement in both form-focused and meaning-focused language learning through their digital interactions.

Regarding writing development, the results suggest a complex relationship. The study indicates that the informal English, slang, and linguistic errors encountered online may be responsible for certain writing errors made by the students. Conversely, the interview participants also identified positive influences of IDLE on their writing skills, noting that digital platforms can provide them with models of good writing.

In conclusion, while the time spent on informal digital learning does not statistically predict vocabulary or writing performance in this sample, the activities themselves play a role in language acquisition. The students experience both the benefits of exposure to diverse writing models and the drawbacks of exposure to non-standard English and slang. Based on these findings, the study suggests that educators and parents should consider the possibility of integrating IDLE into the English learning processes of children.

title: Practices and Perceptions of English Language Teachers on the Use of Multimedia Materials for a Communication Course in Higher Education
abstract: There is a growing need to understand the practices and perceptions on the use of multimedia materials in higher education language classrooms, especially considering the pedagogical adjustments needed to address the changing needs of 21st century learners and to deal with disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic. As a potential contribution to addressing this need, this study focused on looking into the experiences and perspectives of language teachers tasked to teach a core course in Communication in selected state universities in the Philippines. Through hermeneutical phenomenology, the study examined the practices of using multimedia materials to deliver lessons in Purposive Communication. Data revealed that all teacher participants still predominantly use teacher-centered strategies, specifically lectures, although multimedia resources and interactive activities were incorporated. Most of the multimedia used by the teacher participants are standalone types and specifically fall under narrative media, the kind that supports learning through acquisition. Moreover, the TPACK and RAT frameworks were adopted to examine how multimedia are integrated. While findings from the data suggest an interest in using various multimedia, there were noted challenges to integrating such materials seamlessly. The most common challenge reflected troubleshooting problems, specifically navigating equipment and devices. The typical approach adopted to deal with the challenges in multimedia use was to consider their previous experiences and to rely on assistance from others. Based on these findings, policy recommendations and a training program on multimedia use for language teachers were suggested.

title: Teachers' Language Ideologies and Early Reading Instruction Practices in Philippine Multilingual Classrooms
abstract:
Philippine linguistic diversity is recognized in the Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) policy. MTB-MLE is one of the salient features of the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013. The mother tongue is the primary mode of instruction (MOI) from kindergarten to the third grade of elementary education. From first to third grade, Mother Tongue, Filipino (the national language), and English are taught as separate subjects. Filipino and English, the country’s official languages, are gradually introduced as MOI from fourth to sixth grade. Beginning reading is first taught in the mother tongue. Through a solid foundation in the mother tongue, stronger literacy abilities are developed, which are expected to transfer across languages. However, recent studies have shown that only one-third of schools are implementing MTB-MLE, due to factors like resistance in using the mother tongue for academic purposes and opposition thrown against it because of misconceptions favoring the dominant official languages. Against this backdrop, the present study aimed to answer the following questions: (1) What are the teachers’ language ideologies on the use of the local language alongside Filipino and English as the language of instruction in early reading classes?; (2) What are the teachers’ early reading instruction practices in the local language, Filipino, and English?; and (3) Are the teachers’ language ideologies reflected in their use of language/s in early reading instruction?

This qualitative study involved 13 public school early grades teachers in a linguistically diverse province in Northern Philippines where the local languages Bolinao, Iloko, and Pangasinan are used in MTB-MLE. Semi-structured interviews were first conducted, recorded, and transcribed. The transcriptions were manually coded first, then uploaded to Atlas.ti, a qualitative data analysis software, to further review and finalize the codes. The research themes were extracted from these codes. Data triangulation was conducted through classroom observations of early reading classes, review of relevant documents, and focus group discussions.

The study by Jackson G. Orlanda investigates the relationship between teachers' language ideologies and their early reading instruction practices within the context of the Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) policy in the Philippines. Under the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013, the mother tongue is designated as the primary mode of instruction from kindergarten to the third grade. The pedagogical theory suggests that establishing a solid literacy foundation in the mother tongue facilitates the transfer of literacy skills to other languages. However, implementation of this policy faces significant hurdles, as only one-third of schools currently utilize MTB-MLE. This discrepancy is attributed to resistance regarding the use of local languages for academic purposes and misconceptions that favor the dominant official languages, Filipino and English.

The research specifically sought to identify teachers' language ideologies regarding the use of local languages alongside Filipino and English, to describe their early reading instruction practices across these languages, and to determine if their ideologies are reflected in their actual classroom language use. The study was conducted in a linguistically diverse province in Northern Philippines, where Bolinao, Iloko, and Pangasinan are the local languages used in the MTB-MLE framework.

This qualitative study utilized a sample of 13 public school early grades teachers. The methodology involved semi-structured interviews, which were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using manual coding followed by Atlas.ti software to extract research themes. To ensure data triangulation, the researcher employed classroom observations of early reading classes, reviews of relevant documents, and focus group discussions.

The findings revealed several hegemonic language ideologies held by the teachers. First, English was viewed as a highly valued language, and Filipino was identified as a preferred language. These preferences were driven by the perceived social, academic, and economic benefits of these official languages. Second, teachers reported significant challenges in implementing MTB-MLE, often perceiving the linguistic diversity and variations of local languages as confusing and complex due to an adherence to the concept of standardized languages. Third, teachers expressed resistance toward MTB-MLE, believing that the inclusion of the mother tongue in early reading instruction might hinder the acquisition of official languages. This created a language hierarchy that marginalized local languages. Fourth, while teachers used translations as a component of translanguaging to bridge different languages, this practice primarily benefited the dominant languages. Conversely, the study identified a counter-hegemonic ideology among teachers, which focused on language preservation and the fostering of identity. Some teachers believed that using the mother tongue was essential to safeguarding community history and language.

Regarding early reading instruction practices, five themes emerged. Teachers utilized the "big six" of reading, with a specific emphasis on phonics instruction as the starting point for beginning reading. They also integrated learners' personal experiences into instruction to promote engagement and comprehension. The study found that teachers strategically and purposefully used different language patterns involving the three languages used in early reading instruction. Translanguaging was employed as a tool to teach learners how to read in multiple languages. Finally, the learning environment and resources were shaped by the availability or unavailability of technology and print-rich classroom materials.

The study concluded that teachers' language ideologies are clearly manifested in their actual use of language during early reading instruction. The ideologies held by the educators directly influence how they navigate the multilingual classroom.

The implications of this research suggest that for MTB-MLE to be successfully implemented and to overcome questions regarding its legitimacy, the language ideologies that shape early reading instruction must be revisited and thoroughly examined. The author warns that if local languages continue to be marginalized in the classroom, it will negatively affect the development of learners' reading skills in other languages. Furthermore, failing to address these ideologies may lead to the persistence of language discrimination, rather than achieving the policy's goal of fostering cultural identity and heritage among learners.

title: Evaluation of an Early Childhood Language and Literacy Program
abstract: This study evaluated the early childhood language and literacy program of Dubai Flower Preschool, a group of nurseries and early learning centers with 26 locations in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The study sought to identify the preschool’s challenges and problems in the implementation of the early years education program; focusing on language and literacy instruction, strategies, and evidence-based practices. It also examined the quality of learning in the preschool, with particular focus on instructional materials, level of content knowledge of the educators, and instructional strategies used in teaching language and literacy, particularly in the UAE setting. It looked at the relationship between the educators’ level of content knowledge and their teaching strategies, relationship between the educators’ level of professional development and level of content knowledge, and how instructional materials enhance student engagement and student learning. The study utilized the descriptive survey method with the application of both quantitative and qualitative analyses of data. Participants of the study were the Senior Educators (Lead Teachers) of Dubai Flower Preschool. Six teachers were observed through purposive sampling to examine and evaluate their instructional strategies, and to determine how the instructional materials enhanced language and literacy learning in their classrooms. Evidence and data on teachers’ level of content knowledge in language and literacy instruction, perceived frequency of effective implementation and program characteristics of Dubai Flower Preschool were gathered to investigate teachers’ concerns, needs, and challenges regarding curriculum, planning, and instructional practices.

Using a descriptive survey method with quantitative and qualitative analyses, the researcher observed six Senior Educators to examine the relationships between educators' content knowledge, teaching strategies, professional development, and the use of instructional materials.

The findings indicate that the curriculum integrates various approaches within the British Early Years Foundation Stage framework, balancing play, music, brain development, and emotional well-being. Despite these needs, student engagement remained high due to innovative, child-centered approaches. The study concludes that professional development, effective strategies, and appropriate materials are imperative for enhancing language and literacy.

The study conducted by Anna Lissa S. Villar evaluates the early childhood language and literacy program implemented by Dubai Flower Preschool, an organization consisting of 26 nurseries and early learning centers located in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The research was prompted by the need to identify specific challenges and problems encountered during the implementation of the early years education program, with a particular emphasis on language and literacy instruction, teaching strategies, and the application of evidence-based practices. Furthermore, the study aimed to examine the quality of learning within the preschool setting by focusing on instructional materials, the level of content knowledge possessed by educators, and the specific instructional strategies employed to teach language and literacy within the unique context of the UAE.

The research objectives included examining the relationship between educators' levels of content knowledge and their chosen teaching strategies, as well as the relationship between educators' levels of professional development and their content knowledge. Additionally, the study sought to investigate how instructional materials contribute to enhancing student engagement and student learning. To achieve these objectives, the researcher utilized a descriptive survey method, employing both quantitative and qualitative data analyses. The participants consisted of Senior Educators, also known as Lead Teachers, from Dubai Flower Preschool. Through purposive sampling, six teachers were observed to evaluate their instructional strategies and to determine the effectiveness of instructional materials in enhancing language and literacy learning within their classrooms. Data regarding teachers' content knowledge in language and literacy instruction, as well as the perceived frequency of effective implementation and program characteristics, were gathered to investigate teacher concerns, needs, and challenges related to curriculum, planning, and instructional practices.

The findings indicate that Dubai Flower Preschool promotes language and literacy education through robust program characteristics that integrate and balance various curriculum approaches within the British Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) curriculum framework. The curriculum is designed to integrate play and music, brain development, and emotional well-being into the teaching of language and literacy. Educators utilized a diverse range of instructional materials, including Information and Communication Technology (ICT) materials and online resources, to support instruction. It was observed that many teachers successfully integrated language and literacy into both academic and non-academic activities, such as mathematics, music, and playtime.

Regarding the factors influencing teaching effectiveness, the study found that an educator's preschool teaching experience was not perceived as a major contributing factor specifically for effective language and literacy teaching practices, although it was viewed as a major factor for overall effective teaching practices. While teaching experience and educational background were positively associated with teacher confidence and preparedness, the results indicated that these factors do not necessarily ensure effective instructional practices. Instead, the most influential factors were identified as the teachers' attitudes, their daily work, the experiences gained through ongoing instructional practices, their personal backgrounds, and the knowledge of theories acquired during teacher training. Consequently, the study found that for these educators, teaching effectiveness increases alongside experience and an openness to further learning and professional development.

The study also identified specific needs among the teaching staff, which were expressed through interviews. Teachers indicated a need for further training in the fundamentals of instructional design, specific teaching strategies for reading, and assessment methods within the realm of language and literacy. Despite these identified needs, the study observed a high level of student engagement, which was attributed to the educators' use of innovative and child-centered teaching approaches and strategies.

In conclusion, the research demonstrates that strong professional development, effective instructional strategies, and the use of appropriate instructional materials are imperative components of the teaching-learning process to enhance language and literacy learning in the early years. The findings suggest that while teachers possess various strengths, there is a clear demand for specialized training in instructional design and assessment. The implications of this study suggest that the results can be used to assist in structuring early years programs and developing continuing professional development initiatives designed to further improve teaching practices in early childhood education settings.

title: Linguistic and Non-linguistic Factors that Explain Discrepancies  Between Competence and Performance of  Online English Teacher
abstract: The purpose of the study was to understand how linguistic and non-linguistic factors explain and predict the discrepancy between language competence and language performance, as defined by Noam Chomsky. This research used a mixed-methods approach, gathering quantitative and qualitative data on the factors affecting the second language acquisition of the participants, which include lnterlanguage, L2 input, Language Aptitude, Age, Motivation, Attitude, Leaming Strategies, and Education Culture. The study involved 31 Filipino online English teachers with discrepancies in their competence and performance results using standard language assessment tools. It revealed that L 1 interference, poor L2 input in their households, low language aptitude, lack of practice during the Critical Period of Language Acquisition, being instrumentally motivated, use of indirect learning strategies, and limited experience with the Communicative Language Teaching approach all contribute to this gap between competence and performance. Motivation and Leaming Strategies were also proven to be predictors of the discrepancy. This has provided us with an approximate learning profile of second language learners who are likely to manifest competence and performance discrepancies, making early intervention possible to rectify this gap.

Rolando C. Delos Reyes III investigates the discrepancy between language competence and language performance among 31 Filipino online English teachers. Using Noam Chomsky’s theoretical framework, the study explores why underlying linguistic knowledge does not always manifest in actual language use. The research aims to identify the drivers of this gap to create a learning profile that helps educators and institutions identify at-risk learners for early intervention.

The researcher employed a mixed-methods approach, examining linguistic variables—including interlanguage, L2 input, language aptitude, and age—and non-linguistic factors, such as motivation, attitude, learning strategies, and education culture. Findings reveal a complex interplay of these factors. Significant linguistic contributors include L1 interference, poor L2 input within the participants' households, low language aptitude, and a lack of practice during the Critical Period of Language Acquisition.

Regarding non-linguistic factors, instrumental motivation, the use of indirect learning strategies, and limited experience with the Communicative Language Teaching approach contribute to the discrepancy. Notably, motivation and learning strategies were identified as significant predictors of the gap. The study concludes that the discrepancy results from a combination of these elements, identifying a specific profile of learners characterized by low aptitude, specific motivational types, and certain learning strategies. These findings allow institutions to implement targeted strategies, such as increasing exposure to communicative approaches, to improve instruction and help teachers reach their full linguistic potential.

The study successfully identifies a specific profile of second language learners—characterized by factors such as low aptitude, specific motivational types, and certain learning strategies—who are most likely to manifest these discrepancies.

title: Teaching in Large Classes: An Evaluative Case Study on a Speech Communication Course
abstract: The case study evaluated the changes brought about by the implementation of the large lecture­small recitation class mode in the delivery of an introductory speech communication course in terms of 1) syllabus; 2) teaching strategies; 3) teacher-student interaction; 4) the effectiveness of current teaching strategies in achieving said course objectives and; 5) teacher concerns regarding the mode. Six Speech Communication l (SPCM 1) large lecture class teachers of the University of the Philippines Los Banos (UPLB) and 716 students were surveyed and/or interviewed during the 2nd Semester 2014-2015. Results showed that the syllabus content remained unchanged. Large class teachers cited dissatisfaction with the synchronized, time-bound schedule and large student number that constricted use of different teaching strategies and minimized teacher­student interaction. They used a wide variety of group dynamics and interactive teaching strategies in the generally expository nature of their lecture classes. Students' perceptions of their lecture teachers as influential and friendly leaders were found higher compared to their teachers self. Student responses towards the large class mode were generally positive with only few students calling for policy recall. Nonetheless, the SPCM 1 teachers remained concerned about the effectiveness of the large class mode in achieving the course objectives. The study concluded that the SPCM 1 large class mode has been received positively by the students and has worked because of the concerned teachers' personal efforts despite persistent beliefs that small classes are the best approach to delivering a communication course. The study recommended significant institutional measures, incentives and continuous professional faculty and staff development and mentoring programs on large class teaching and other educational changes.

This study examines the differences in interpersonal dynamics and communication between small classes of 20–30 students and large lecture classes of 100 or more students within a speech communication course. The research focuses on the experiences of teachers who have instructed the SPCM 1 course in both settings.

Findings reveal a significant disparity in teacher-student interaction based on class size. In small classes, teachers reported closer interpersonal relationships, often becoming friends with students due to coursework involving rehearsals and group work. These settings allow instructors to cater to individual needs through one-on-one discussions, which encourages students to express themselves more freely.

In contrast, teachers perceived that large classes result in significantly less interaction. The scale makes it difficult to establish personal connections, shifting the instructor's role primarily to lecturing due to insufficient time for physical and personal engagement. A major challenge identified is the inability to memorize a large number of student names, which can lead to a perception that the teacher is less caring.

Furthermore, large class sizes impact student performance and engagement. Teachers observed that students in large classes often experience communication apprehension or a lack of self-confidence, preventing them from answering in front of a large audience. This creates a feedback loop where teachers are unsure if students have understood the material due to a lack of visible reactions. Ultimately, large class sizes shift the dynamic from a personal, interactive environment to one characterized by diminished interpersonal connection.

Teachers also noted difficulty maintaining close relationships when students do not react to their teaching.

Several specific challenges were identified regarding large class instruction. A major issue is the inability to memorize student names; while managing 20–30 names is feasible, memorizing 100 or more is described as impossible. This lack of name recognition can lead to a perception that the teacher is less caring, though teachers clarified this is a result of time constraints rather than a lack of genuine concern for student welfare.

Furthermore, large class sizes impact student performance and engagement. Teachers observed that students in large classes often experience communication apprehension or a lack of self-confidence, which prevents them from answering the teacher in front of a large audience. This creates a feedback loop where teachers are unsure if students have understood the material because the students do not provide visible reactions or engagement.

The findings suggest that large class sizes fundamentally alter the pedagogical relationship between instructor and student. The transition from a small class to a large lecture format shifts the classroom dynamic from a personal, interactive environment to one characterized by lecturing and diminished interpersonal connection. Ultimately, large class sizes may hinder the ability of instructors to provide individualized attention and may exacerbate student anxiety and communication apprehension, affecting the communicative quality of the course.

title: Implementing Mother Tongue Based-Multilingual Education in an Area of Armed Conflict in Southern Philippines: A Case Study
abstract:
The use of the mother tongue in the classroom to learn concepts has been practiced by many of the countries that garnered the highest points in international assessments as shown in the 20 I 5 report of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Several studies have also shown the benefits of using the mother tongue in learning and this has been recognized by the Philippines through Republic Act I 0533, "An Act Enhancing the Philippine Basic Education Sy.stem by Strengthening its Curriculum and Increasing the Number of Years for Basic Education." 

With Philippine schools adopting the use of mother tongue as the medium of instruction from Kindergarten to Grade 3, this study looked into how Mother Tongue Based-Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) was implemented in an area of armed conflict. 

The current study specifically answered the following questions: I) How is MTB­MLE implemented in an area of armed conflict in terms of the use of mother tongue as subject, medium of instruction, and auxiliary language; 2) How is the mother tongue integrated in peace education in an area of anned conflict particularly in the curriculum, instructional materials, and strategies.

title: Effects of Metacognitive Strategy Instruction on the Metacognitive Awareness and Reading Comprehension Performance of BEED Students
abstract:
Reading is a complex activity, and its most obvious goal is comprehension. As students progress through school, they are asked to read increasingly complex graphical and informational texts in their courses (Think Literacy, 2007). The reading process for managing
these information-getting tasks is typically highly complex and requires both cognitive and metacognitive processing (Magliano & Trabasso, 1999; Wade & Reynolds, 1989 as cited in Hong-Nam & Leavell, 2011). Ideally, students that reach university level would be aware of
using effective reading strategies, but it is observed that many students do not read analytically and cannot adjust their reading to the different materials they encounter (Gaerlan, 2012). Nevertheless, students can overcome their difficulties when they receive appropriate training on reading strategies and introduced to the concept of metacognition.

The present study aimed at examining the effects of metacognitive strategy instruction on the metacognitive awareness and reading comprehension performance of BEEd students and if there was a relationship between metacognitive awareness and reading comprehension. Metacognitive reading strategies (planning, monitoring, and evaluating) were taught to 45 students for five weeks using the Gradual Release of Responsibility model of instruction. Data were gathered through the use of the Gray Silent Reading Tests (GSRT), the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MA), and students’ reading logs. Pre-test and post-test scores were compared using T-test for paired samples, and the relationship between the two variables was tested using Spearman’s rho. A frequency test was also done to find out which metacognitive reading strategies were learned more after the intervention.

Reading is a complex process centered on comprehension, requiring both cognitive and metacognitive processing. As students encounter increasingly difficult academic texts, many struggle to read analytically or adjust their approaches. This research investigated whether metacognitive strategy instruction could address these challenges by examining its effects on the metacognitive awareness and reading comprehension performance of Bachelor of Elementary Education students.

The study utilized the Gradual Release of Responsibility model to teach specific strategies, including planning, monitoring, and evaluating, over five weeks. Data were collected through the Gray Silent Reading Tests, the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory, and student reading logs. Analysis involved a T-test for paired samples, Spearman’s rho, and a frequency test.

The findings revealed that explicit instruction of metacognitive reading strategies improved both reading comprehension performance and metacognitive awareness. A moderate positive relationship was identified between metacognitive awareness and reading comprehension, suggesting that awareness of cognitive processes enhances text comprehension. Frequency tests and qualitative data from reading logs confirmed that students learned a variety of strategies.

The study concludes that metacognition is a skill that can be effectively taught at the tertiary level. Structured, scaffolded instruction helps students navigate complex texts. Consequently, tertiary curricula should incorporate explicit metacognitive instruction, and teacher education should train future educators in these techniques. Future research should explore the long-term effects of such instruction on literacy and comprehension.

title: The Effect of Comparison and Contrast and KWL Chart on Reading Comprehension of Unfamiliar Texts
abstract:
Comprehension is the basis of reading and reading without comprehension is not considered as reading. Very often students can become easily frustrated when they do not understand what they are reading in unfamiliar texts. As a result, they become demotivated. A
teacher needs to find out what are the causes and design and tech strategies in order to help students close the gaps in their understanding of the unfamiliar texts. This study investigated the effect of comparison and contrast and KWL chart as pre-reading activities on reading comprehension of unfamiliar texts.

Specifically, the study answered the following questions: (1) is there a significant difference between the students’ reading comprehension scores on familiar texts and their scores on unfamiliar texts? And (2) Is there a significant increase in reading comprehension
scores as a result of using KWL chart for activating prior knowledge and using comparison and contrast for unlocking vocabulary of unfamiliar texts?

Data were elicited from thirty-six 1st year Chinese Malaysian students consisting of 18 males and 18 females who were randomly selected from a secondary school.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Ong Kian Teong investigates the challenges students face when encountering unfamiliar texts, noting that reading without comprehension does not constitute true reading. Because students often experience frustration and demotivation when they cannot understand unfamiliar content, this research focuses on the effectiveness of two pre-reading activities: the KWL chart, used to activate prior knowledge, and the comparison and contrast strategy, used to unlock vocabulary.

The study employed a descriptive and quasi-experimental method using a one-group pretest-posttest design with thirty-six 1st-year Chinese Malaysian students. Participants read three familiar and three unfamiliar texts, followed by comprehension tests. For the unfamiliar texts, initial tests served as pre-tests, followed by interventions using the KWL chart and comparison and contrast strategies before a post-test.

Findings revealed significant differences regarding topic familiarity and intervention effectiveness. A t-test analysis showed that subjects achieved significantly higher scores on familiar texts, indicating that topic familiarity facilitates reading comprehension. Furthermore, a t-test of pre-test and post-test scores revealed that subjects achieved significantly higher scores after the interventions were applied. This demonstrates that using the KWL chart and comparison and contrast strategies has a positive effect on comprehension performance when dealing with unfamiliar texts. The study concludes that explicit pre-reading strategies are effective tools for improving comprehension, suggesting that educators and textbook writers should incorporate these strategies into reading tasks.

Riñon’s study, "Teachers' Readiness For and Their Attitude Toward New Literacy," examines the role of educators in helping students navigate the digital landscape through new literacy—the skills and strategies required to use the Internet and Information and Communication Technologies. The research investigated teachers' readiness regarding knowledge, competence, and training, their attitudes toward applying new literacy, and whether differences exist based on gender and department.

Using a descriptive survey method with 43 purposively sampled teachers at Bicol University Polangi Campus, the study utilized both quantitative and qualitative data. Findings revealed significant gaps in preparedness: while teachers possessed some knowledge, they demonstrated only little competence and had only some training related to new literacy instruction. Psychologically, teachers held a negative attitude toward new literacy, characterized by anxiety, fear, and a lack of confidence in using these tools for instruction.

Statistical analysis showed a weak relationship between teachers' readiness and their attitude. Furthermore, t-test results indicated significant differences in knowledge, competence, training, and attitude when categorized by gender and department. The study concludes that a lack of competence combined with anxiety and fear may hinder the effective development of new literacy skills in students. New literacy is defined as the skills, strategies, and dispositions necessary to use the Internet and Information and Communication Technologies to meet global societal demands. Because online information is diverse and can be difficult to navigate, teachers are responsible for developing these skills in their learners.

The research aimed to determine how prepared teachers are to fulfill this instructional role by addressing four primary questions: the extent of teachers' readiness regarding knowledge, competence, and training; their attitudes toward applying new literacy; the relationship between readiness and attitude; and whether differences in these variables exist based on gender and department.

Using a descriptive survey method with both quantitative and qualitative data, the researcher studied 43 teachers at the Bicol University Polangi Campus in Polangi, Albay, selected through purposive sampling. Readiness was assessed through instruments measuring knowledge and competence, while teacher profiles were used to assess training. Data analysis involved both descriptive and inferential statistics.

The findings revealed significant gaps in teacher preparedness. While teachers possessed some knowledge of new literacy, they demonstrated only little competence. Furthermore, teachers had only some training related to new literacy instruction. Regarding psychological disposition, the study found that teachers held a negative attitude toward new literacy, characterized by a lack of confidence and expressions of fear and anxiety regarding its use in instructional practices.

Statistical testing provided further insights into the variables. Using the Pearson r at a 0.05 level of significance, the study found a weak relationship between teachers' readiness for new literacy and their attitude toward it. Additionally, t-test results indicated significant differences in knowledge, competence, training, and attitude toward new literacy when categorized by department and gender.

The study concludes that the lack of competence and the presence of anxiety and fear among teachers may hinder the effective development of new literacy skills in students. Based on these findings, the researcher provided recommendations for administrators, teachers, and future researchers to address these identified gaps and conduct further studies in this area.

title: Development of a Thematic and Integrated Learning Unit for English IV
abstract:
The core of reading and language teaching is the learning and assessment activities. Without a carefully planned lesson, language teaching will not be successful.

This project aimed to contribute to holistic and integrated reading instruction through the preparation of prototype instructional and assessment materials in reading and language teaching for fourth-year high school. The literacy learning package developed in this project
uses a thematic approach and intends to supplement the reading and language textbooks currently used in Bayugan National Comprehensive High School (BNCHS).

The validation of the literacy package was aimed at answering the following questions: 1) are the reading selections in the literacy package appropriate for fourth-year high school students, in terms of readability level, intersterility, relevance, and value? 2) Are the learning and assessment activities in the learning package effective, as perceived by teachers’ evaluators? Specifically: Do they clearly support the unit theme, goals, and objectives? Do they develop the strategic and metacognitive reading skills of students? Do they provide for diverse learning styles?

To address this, the project sought to contribute to holistic and integrated reading instruction by developing prototype instructional and assessment materials for fourth-year high school students at Bayugan National Comprehensive High School (BNCHS). This literacy learning package was intended to serve as a supplement to existing reading and language textbooks.

The research aimed to create a thematic and integrated learning unit for English IV to provide engaging and effective instructional tools. The study focused on validating the literacy package by determining if the reading selections were appropriate regarding readability, interest, relevance, and value, and whether the activities were effective in supporting unit themes, developing strategic and metacognitive reading skills, and accommodating diverse learning styles.

The findings indicate that the nine reading selections are appropriate for fourth-year high school students. Readability and interest level measurements showed that the selections are challenging yet remain within the students' readability levels. Cloze test results revealed that the selections are generally moderate in readability. Expert observers concluded that the selections are appealing and meet standard qualifications. Additionally, teachers and student-observers found the learning and assessment activities to be effective in supporting unit themes, fostering reading skills, and catering to diverse learning styles. The study concludes that integrating relevant reading selections with interactive materials increases student involvement and can develop students into critical, creative, and productive learners.
