title: Exploring the Effect of Audiobook Sequence om EFL University Students' Learning
abstract:
This exploratory small case study investigates the effects of two audiobook sequencing methods—Reading Before Listening (RBL) and Listening Before Reading (LBR)—on Korean university EFL students’ reading comprehension, spelling accuracy, and motivation to read. The study aimed to determine whether one sequencing approach offered stronger outcomes and whether alternating the two could enhance learning. Three students participated in switching sequencing methods midway through the study. Data were collected through formative assessments, pre- and post-surveys, reading logs, group discussions, and guided interviews.

Findings indicate that RBL sequencing supported stronger spelling accuracy and comprehension, while LBR sequencing helped students grasp broader meaning and develop listening strategies. Students who began with RBL and switched to LBR showed noticeable gains in comprehension, while those who switched from LBR to RBL demonstrated improved spelling accuracy. Despite the small sample size and an early participant dropout, consistent engagement and learner strategy development were observed across cases.

These results support theories of Cognitive Load, Dual Coding, and Transfer Stage theory, highlighting the cognitive benefits of multimodal input and strategic sequencing. The study offers practical implications for educators aiming to integrate audiobooks into reading programs, suggesting that flexible sequencing—tailored to learner needs—can enhance both comprehension and spelling outcomes. Future research should involve larger samples, varied text types, and classroom-based implementations to build on these initial insights.

title: Students' Perceptions of Dimensions of Peer Teaching in the University's Communication Courses
abstract: This study sought to determine to what extent peer teaching is employed at the university’s communication courses and the different peer teaching activities utilized. Also, it sought to know the students' perceptions of the dimensions that characterize the peer teaching activities and its benefits. title: Unlocking the Power of Teaching Controversial Issues: Unveiling Teacher Efficacy Through a Mixed Methods Study
abstract:
Understanding controversial issues is a crucial aspect of democratic citizenship. By appreciating controversial issues, students learn how to partake in significant socio-political issues and be exposed to diverse perspectives as an essential aspect of democratic living. It is
assumed that the teacher's efficacy in teaching controversial issues as part of Social Studies Education is crucial to the impact on student learning. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study aimed to determine the level of teachers' efficacy in teaching controversial
issues. It also sought to determine the correlation between their work-related characteristics and their level of teachers' efficacy. Furthermore, this study intended to ascertain how the level of teachers' self-efficacy correlates with their teaching outcomes, i.e., teaching behavior, motivation, engagement, effectiveness, and overall satisfaction in teaching the subject. Quantitative data were collected through a survey using a self-administered structure questionnaire, while qualitative data were collected through interviews using an interview guide. Random sampling was used to identify 86 survey respondents. Cluster-purposive sampling was used to select six informants, i.e., two key teachers or master teachers per zone, which were identified as part of the qualitative study. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, whereas qualitative data was processed using thematic analysis. The significant findings that were generated from the quantitative aspects of the study were validated, and the qualitative findings helped explain the quantitative results to provide depth to the findings of the study.

title: Digital Storytelling as a Teaching-Learning Tool: Experiences of the Humanities and Social Sciences Students of Auton Academy
abstract: This action research explored the experiences of the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) Students of Auton Academy in understanding disciplines and ideas in the Social Sciences with digital storytelling as a teaching-learning tool. Digital storytelling focuses on a specific theme or topic incorporating a distinct perspective that combines the art of telling stories and the use of a mixture of digital media. Digital stories are typically between two and ten minutes in length and saved in a digital format (Robin, 2016). To explore the possibility of using digital storytelling as a teaching-learning tool in senior high school Social Science subjects, a qualitative research design and an exploratory action research approach using three data collection techniques: survey questionnaire, reflective questions based on the 5R Framework Model, and observation were employed. A class under the Humanities and Social Sciences Strand taking the Disciplines and Ideas in the Social Sciences (DISS) subject was purposively selected. Findings were categorized into themes based on the generated codes to make sense of the participants’ collective meanings and experiences shared. The findings of this action research suggested that digital storytelling is an entrancing instructional tool that provides senior high school students with meaningful learning experiences beyond their usual classroom curriculum. By incorporating the 5R Framework Model, digital storytelling becomes a valuable tool for Social Studies teachers to identify challenges and assess learning through reflections. The outcome of this project can influence educators to consider the integration of digital storytelling to transform classrooms, engaging students emotionally and intellectually. Additional factors within this context can be explored in future studies.

title: Content Analysis of  the K to 12 Kasaysayan ng Daigdig Modyul para sa Mag-aaral ng  Gabay sa Pagtuturo
abstract:
his study sought to analyze the content of the Kasaysayan ng Daigdig Modyul para sa Mag-aaral and Gabay sa Pagtuturo under the K to 12 Social Studies curriculum of the Department of Education. This study aims to I) analyze how consistent the content of the learning modules and teaching guides is with the learning standards the DepEd has set, in tenns of a) historical content - content standards; b) learning activities -performance standards; and c) assessment/evaluation tools - learning competencies; 2) determine and analyze the evidences of contextualization in the teaching guides; 3) determine the approach/es evident in the teaching guides; 4) determine the historical thinking skill/s aimed to be developed in the learning modules and teaching guides; and 5) analyze how sufficient the historical content, learning activities, and assessment tools of the learning modules, and provisions of contextualization and approaches in the teaching guides are in the development of historical thinking skills. 

A content analysis that employed both quantitative and qualitative approaches was used in this study. The findings of the study revealed that only the first three learning modules are consistent with the content standards of DepEd. Also, half of the learning activities are not consistent with the perf onnance standards while the assessment/evaluation tools are not consistent with more than half of the learning competencies set by the Department of Education. Moreover, there is a low provision for contextualization in the teaching guides. Nevertheless, the evidences of contextualization range from general to specific examples that are localized to the Philippine setting. In addition, the teaching approaches evident in the teaching guides, i.e. from the most often used to least used, are the following: inquiry approach, conceptual approach, integrative approach, interdisciplinary approach, chronological .. thematic approach, and multidisciplinary approach, respectively. The teaching guides, however, put more emphasis on the inquiry approach to teaching. Thus, the teaching guides show an unequal balance in the use of teaching approaches, outlined in the Social Studies curriculum. The historical thinking skills that are found in the learning modules and teaching guides, in no particular order, include Analyzing Historical Sources and Evidence: "Primary Sources" and "Secondary Sources"; Making Historical Connections: "Comparison'' and "Contextualization"; Chronological Reasoning: "Causation," "Patterns of Continuity and Change over Time," and "Periodization"; and '"Creating and Supporting a Historical Argument-Argumentation." Furthermore, the study found out that the learning modules and teaching guides do not provide equal opportunities for the development of various historical thinking skills as "Analyzing Historical Sources and Evidence-Secondary Sources" has greater sufficiency than the rest, while the learning modules and teaching guides do not help develop the skill, "Making Historical Connections-Synthesis."

Arnie Garcia Dizon’s study, "Content Analysis of the K to 12 Kasaysayan ng Daigdig Modyul para sa Mag-aaral and Gabay sa Pagtuturo," examines the alignment and quality of instructional materials for the Philippine K to 12 World History curriculum. Using a content analysis method, the research scrutinized the relationship between learning competencies, student activities, and assessment items to determine if they effectively support intended learning outcomes and adhere to multidisciplinary Social Studies requirements.

The findings reveal significant discrepancies within the materials. Regarding assessment, the study identified invalid test items that failed to align with the themes of intended learning competencies. For example, an item on Italian geography focused on Geography and Economics rather than History, failing to establish necessary disciplinary connections. Additionally, ten specific learning competencies—covering topics such as Mercantilism, National Monarchy, the contributions of the Bourgeoisie and the Catholic Church, and phases of imperialism and colonization—were omitted from pre-test items.

Student activities also showed gaps, as several activities, including a crossword puzzle and various map-based tasks, were not based on any module themes. While some activities aligned with historical context and causality, many failed to connect to intended themes. The study concludes that these misalignments result in a fragmented instructional experience rather than a multidisciplinary approach, suggesting a need for more rigorous quality assurance to ensure all assessments and activities are directly derived from specified competencies.

Furthermore, ten specific learning competencies—including topics such as Mercantilism, National Monarchy, the contributions of the Bourgeoisie and the Catholic Church, and the phases of imperialism and colonization—were not included in the pre-test items.

The findings highlight a failure to implement a truly multidisciplinary approach, leading instead to a fragmented instructional experience. Consequently, the study suggests a need for more rigorous quality assurance and content validation during development. title: Transitioning to a Bichronous (Synchronous+Asynchronous) ODL Set-up in High School Education: An Autoethnographic Study
abstract: Within the framework of Autoethnography, this study answered the research question: How did a high school teacher transition from a full face-to-face instruction to a Bichronous (Synchronous +Asynchronous) Online Distance Learning (ODL) Set-up in High School Education during the Covid 19 Pandemic? The autoethnographic genre of qualitative research enabled the researcher to craft a narrative and arrive with a deeper analysis of this narrative. After analyzing different data set and examination of artifacts such as email, curricular documents, discussion posts, video recordings, a workplace calendar, a personal journal, professional development logs, and personal experience; the study revealed, as reflected byseveral periods in the findings, that the author’s transition includes: (a) structuring the course (designing pedagogy in ODL) – designing the Leanring Contiuity Plan, In- service Training for Teachers, and Designing the Theresian Learner’s Study Guide (TLSG); (b) effectively using the ODL technologies to implement a Bichronous ODL set-up – structuring the course in the Learning Management System for the asynchronous mode and conducting real-time teaching using video conferencing tools for the synchronous mode; (c) establishing teacher presence in the asynchronous and synchronous modes; and (d) providing student-support mechanism - cognitive, affective, and systemic. The importance of designing a school’s ODL set-up for future remote teaching and learning scenario should be looked into and teachers should receive proper training on ODL Pedagogy and Technologies.

title: Structural Model of Grit, Expectancy-Value and 21st Century Skills on the Physics Achievement of College Freshmen Students in HyFlex Universities and Its Implications on Tertiary STEM Education
abstract:
This study aimed to develop a structural model of the physics achievement of college STEM freshmen students and its interaction with grit, expectancy-value, and 21st century skills.
A total of 1,176 freshmen students enrolled in STEM-based college courses participated in the study. Forty-five percent (45%) of the participants had a STEM background in senior high school, while the remaining 55% did not have a STEM background, but were enrolled in STEMbased college courses. Results showed that more than 90% of the participants, regardless of having a STEM background in senior high school, had very low physics achievement. In contrast, the participants demonstrated high level of grit, moderate level of 21st century skills, and high expectancy-value. In terms of the interaction among college STEM freshmen students’ physics achievement, grit, expectancy-value, and 21st century skills, the study established that grit did not have a significant effect on physics achievement. On the other hand, expectancy value (e.g. students’ enjoyment and perceived usefulness of a task) mediated the influence of 21st century skills (e.g. effective communication and leadership) on physics achievement. Implications on tertiary STEM education and basic education are discussed, particularly on the aspects of Physics content, assessment, pedagogy, and learning resources; the use of technology, guidance and counseling; and teacher professional development.

The study conducted by Alwielland Q. Bello investigates the complex relationship between grit, expectancy-value, and 21st century skills in relation to the physics achievement of college freshmen students within HyFlex universities. The research seeks to develop a structural model that explains how these specific psychological and skill-based factors interact to influence the academic performance of students enrolled in STEM-based college courses. This inquiry is situated within the broader context of tertiary STEM education, aiming to understand the underlying drivers of success or struggle in foundational science subjects during the transition to higher education.

The problem addressed by this research centers on the achievement levels of college freshmen in physics. Despite the importance of physics in the STEM curriculum, there appears to be a significant gap in student performance. The study focuses on students in HyFlex universities, which utilize flexible learning modalities, to determine how non-cognitive factors and modern skill sets contribute to academic outcomes in this specific educational environment. By examining grit, expectancy-value, and 21st century skills, the researcher attempts to identify which elements are most predictive of physics achievement and how they function together.

To investigate these relationships, the study utilized a sample of 1,176 freshmen students enrolled in STEM-based college courses. The participant demographic was divided between those who possessed a STEM background in senior high school and those who did not. Specifically, 45% of the participants had a STEM background in senior high school, while the remaining 55% did not have a STEM background but were nonetheless enrolled in STEM-based college courses. This composition allowed for an analysis of how prior academic preparation interacts with the variables under study.

The findings of the research reveal a concerning trend regarding academic performance. Regardless of whether the students had a STEM background in senior high school, more than 90% of the participants demonstrated very low physics achievement. This suggests that prior specialized training in high school may not be sufficient to ensure success in college-level physics within the HyFlex university model. However, the study also found that the students possessed other positive attributes. The participants demonstrated a high level of grit and a high expectancy-value. Additionally, the students showed a moderate level of 21st century skills.

When analyzing the interaction among these variables, the structural model provided specific insights into the mechanisms of physics achievement. The results established that grit did not have a significant effect on physics achievement. While the students demonstrated high levels of grit, this perseverance did not translate into higher physics scores in this specific context. Conversely, the study found a significant relationship involving expectancy-value. Specifically, expectancy-value, which includes factors such as students' enjoyment and the perceived usefulness of a task, was found to mediate the influence of 21st century skills on physics achievement. This means that the impact of 21st century skills, such as effective communication and leadership, on physics achievement is channeled through the students' expectancy-value.

The conclusions drawn from this study highlight the importance of understanding the motivational and skill-based components of learning. The fact that expectancy-value serves as a mediator suggests that simply possessing 21st century skills may not lead to academic success in physics unless students also find the tasks enjoyable or perceive them as useful. The lack of a significant effect from grit on physics achievement suggests that persistence alone may be insufficient to overcome the challenges presented by the physics curriculum in the HyFlex setting.

The implications of these findings are significant for both tertiary STEM education and basic education. The study suggests that educators and policymakers should focus on several key areas to improve student outcomes. Regarding physics content, assessment, pedagogy, and learning resources, there is a need to address the low achievement levels observed. The findings point toward the importance of the use of technology, guidance and counseling, and teacher professional development. By focusing on how students perceive the value and utility of their studies, and by integrating 21st century skills through meaningful, high-value tasks, educators may be able to better support STEM students in achieving success in physics.

title: Determinants of Student Learning Satisfaction and Academic Performance in High School Chemistry: a Prediction Model Building Study for Online Learning
abstract:
Learning satisfaction is a key indicator to enriching student learning whether it is face-to-face or online mode of delivery. Learning has shifted more to remote online learning due to the Covid-19 pandemic. This study aimed to identify the determinants of Student Learning Satisfaction (SLS) in online learning and develop a model that represents the relationship of the determinants to SLS. The study explored both internal and external determinants hypothesized to influence SLS among 169 students in grades 9-12 taking Chemistry at the Philippine Science High School Cordillera Administrative Region Campus (PSHS CARC). The internal factors included gender, academic self-concept (ASC), academic motivation (AM), interest to learn (IL), and mental well-being (MW), while the external factors comprised of teacher-related indicators (Teacher), assessment-related indicators (Assessment), learning guide-related indicators (LG) and Knowledge Hub-related indicators (KHub).

The study utilized Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with SmartPLS software to develop the SLS model and Academic Performance (AP) model. Both online learning platforms used by PSHS CARC, the LG, and KHub, were found to influence student learning satisfaction.

This dissertation by Melba C. Patacsil investigates the factors influencing Student Learning Satisfaction (SLS) and Academic Performance (AP) among high school Chemistry students at the Philippine Science High School Cordillera Administrative Region Campus (PSHS CARC) during the online learning transition necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

**Problem and Context**
The study was prompted by the abrupt global shift from traditional face-to-face instruction to remote online learning. While online education offers benefits like accessibility and personalized pacing, it presents significant challenges regarding student engagement, mental well-being, and the maintenance of educational quality. The researcher identified a need to understand how specific determinants—both internal to the student and external to the learning environment—impact how satisfied students are with their online Chemistry courses and how these factors ultimately influence their academic success. The study specifically addresses the unique context of PSHS students, who are high-achieving learners, to determine if existing educational models are applicable to this specific demographic.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a quantitative research design, utilizing Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with SmartPLS software to build predictive models for SLS and AP. The study involved 169 students from grades 9 to 12 enrolled in Chemistry during the 2021-2022 school year. Data were collected through several validated survey instruments designed to measure external determinants (Teacher, Assessment, Learning Guides [LG], and Knowledge Hub [KHub]) and internal determinants (Gender, Academic Self-Concept [ASC], Academic Motivation [AM], Interest to Learn [IL], and Mental Well-Being [MW]). The researcher used path analysis to examine the direct and indirect causal relationships between these variables.

**Findings**
The study revealed a distinct divergence in the drivers of satisfaction versus academic success. The findings indicated that external determinants—specifically Learning Guides (LG), the Knowledge Hub (KHub), Teacher-related factors, and Assessment-related factors—dominated the Student Learning Satisfaction models. Conversely, the Academic Performance models were primarily driven by internal determinants, such as Academic Self-Concept, Academic Motivation, Interest to Learn, and Mental Well-Being.

Regarding specific external factors, both the LG and KHub were found to be crucial in ensuring student satisfaction. Qualitative data indicated that students valued clarity, completeness, and modularity in Learning Guides, though they often struggled with the time required to complete them. For the KHub, ease of use and navigation were praised, while slow response times and notification issues were noted as sources of dissatisfaction. Teacher-related factors, such as subject mastery and clear communication, were vital, with students expressing a strong preference for teachers who are considerate regarding deadlines. Assessment satisfaction was influenced by reasonable time allotments and clear instructions, though students reported stress when assessments were overly difficult or too numerous.

In terms of internal factors, the study found that gender, LG, and Academic Self-Concept (ASC) directly influenced Academic Performance. The results validated that while external tools and instructional methods are essential for keeping students satisfied with the learning process, the students' internal psychological and motivational states are the primary drivers of their actual academic achievement in Chemistry.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that Student Learning Satisfaction and Academic Performance are governed by different sets of primary determinants in an online Chemistry learning environment. Satisfaction is largely a product of the quality of the instructional delivery and the digital tools provided by the institution, whereas academic success is more heavily dependent on the student's internal psychological state and motivation.

The implications of these findings are significant for educators and administrators. For teachers, the study suggests that to improve student satisfaction, they should focus on the clarity and modularity of learning materials, timely feedback, and being flexible with deadlines. To improve academic performance, teachers should focus on fostering students' academic motivation and self-concept. For school administrators, the results highlight the importance of investing in robust digital infrastructure (like the KHub) and ensuring that online learning guides are designed to be manageable in terms of time and workload. Ultimately, the study provides a framework for PSHS and similar institutions to design more effective online curricula that address both the emotional satisfaction of the learner and the cognitive requirements for academic excellence.

title: Engagement and its Dimensions as Student Factors of Academic Performance and Attitude Towards Biology in a Garden-Based Learning Environment
abstract:

A descriptive-correlational research design was employed to provide a relevant interpretation of the relationship between variables such as respondents’ demographic profile, dimensions of engagement in garden-based learning, academic achievement of students and their attitude towards Biology.

The study consisted of seventy (70) Grade -11 students enrolled in a public senior high school of City Schools Division of Tanauan taking up the core subject Earth and Life Science during the first semester of School Year 2020-2021. Over the course of eight weeks, garden-based learning approach was used to teach plant-related topics and students were given the task to complete fourteen (14) garden-based learning activities. Data were collected using expert-validated researcher-made instruments tested for reliability such as the Learning Engagement Survey Questionnaire (LESQ) and Life Science Achievement Test (LSAT) and Students’ Perception toward Garden-Based Learning (GBL), in addition to the researcher-developed Garden-based Learning Manual and the adopted instrument on Attitude Towards Biology Survey (ATBS). These three self-report survey questionnaires and the achievement test were all administered at the end of eight weeks of exposing the students to garden-based learning activities. Data obtained were analyzed using both descriptive and correlational tests. The descriptive statistics computed were measures of central tendency, frequency, and percentages. The scores on Life Science Achievement Test obtained by the student were used in analyzing their level of academic achievement by comparing it to the DepEd standards. On the other hand, Kendall’s Tau Rank Correlation and Cramer’s V was employed to determine the association between the extent of engagement, profile variables, academic performance, and attitude towards Biology. In addition, qualitative analysis was conducted through focus group interviews, attitude questionnaires, activity reports, reflection journals, and in-depth probing interviews to better understand students' perceptions of garden-based learning.

To conduct this investigation, the researcher employed a descriptive-correlational research design. This design allowed for a relevant interpretation of the relationships between the respondents' demographic profiles, the dimensions of engagement in the garden-based environment, the students' academic achievement, and their attitudes toward Biology. Data collection involved several instruments, including the researcher-developed Garden-based Learning Manual and expert-validated, reliability-tested tools: the Learning Engagement Survey Questionnaire (LESQ), the Life Science Achievement Test (LSAT), and the Students’ Perception toward Garden-Based Learning (GBL) instrument. Additionally, an adopted instrument, the Attitude Towards Biology Survey (ATBS), was used. These tools were administered to the students at the conclusion of the eight-week exposure to the GBL activities.

The analysis of the data utilized both descriptive and correlational statistical methods. Descriptive statistics, including measures of central tendency, frequency, and percentages, were used to summarize the data. The students' academic achievement was analyzed by comparing their scores on the Life Science Achievement Test against established DepEd standards. To determine the associations between the extent of engagement, profile variables, academic performance, and attitude toward Biology, the researcher employed Kendall’s Tau Rank Correlation and Cramer’s V. Furthermore, the study incorporated qualitative analysis to gain a deeper understanding of student perceptions. This qualitative component included focus group interviews, attitude questionnaires, activity reports, reflection journals, and in-depth probing interviews.

The findings of the study indicated that garden-based learning, when used as a teaching strategy, is effective in promoting learning engagement and fostering positive attitudes toward Biology among students, regardless of their age or sex. However, the correlation between academic performance and the extent of learning engagement in the garden-based setting was found to be low. Regarding student attitudes, the study revealed that cognitive, behavioral, and emotional engagement all have a weak positive association with the students' attitude towards Biology.

Based on these results, the study concludes that garden-based learning provides demonstrated benefits for student engagement and attitude. Consequently, the researcher suggests that policy makers, curriculum designers, and developers should consider incorporating garden-based learning methods into the broader Biology curriculum. Furthermore, the study implies that future curriculum design should allow for the personalization of learning experiences to better cater to the individual strengths and specific requirements of students.

title: Assessing Dyscalculic Tendencies Among Children Through a Mobile Application Screening Tool
abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate the psychometric properties of the first Philippine mobile application screening tool for dyscalculic tendencies and establish norms and cut-off scores for Grade 3 pupils. Additionally, it investigated the weaknesses of at-risk pupils and compared them to the different core deficit hypotheses of dyscalculia. Also, the study assessed the experience of children in using the mobile application. The screening tool consisted of 11 tasks divided into arithmetic calculation, basic number skills, and other cognitive tasks. The norming group is comprised of 248 Grade 3 pupils. The findings revealed that the screening tool has an excellent level of face and content validity and an acceptable to excellent level of internal consistency and test-retest reliability. This suggests that the screening tool is a valid and reliable instrument to identify children with dyscalculic tendencies. The study provided stanine norms and cut-off scores that can be easily utilized by teachers, parents, and other researchers. In terms of the analysis of weaknesses, children with dyscalculic tendencies obtained relatively lower scores in arithmetic calculation, number line estimation, and verbal Arabic matching tasks. These weaknesses favored the approximate number system (ANS) deficit and access deficit hypotheses of dyscalculia which supported the assumption of multiple deficit hypothesis. To add support, using the K-means clustering approach, five distinct profile clusters of children with dyscalculic tendencies were identified. Finally, in terms of children's experience in the use of the mobile application, the children had high level of engagement and overall satisfaction as indicated by their enjoyment and interest in completing all the tasks. Likewise, the app quality in terms of functionality and aesthetics were evaluated to be very good. Hence, resulting in an overall positive experience. The use of the mobile application screening tool is highly recommended to mathematics teachers and parents for the initial identification of dyscalculic tendencies among children. To strengthen the psychometric properties and the quality of the instrument, measures of concurrent and predictive validity, sensitivity, specificity, and continuous norming and testing in a larger population could be explored.

title: Teacher Mathematical Pedagogical Content Knowledge, Student Learning Style, Instructional Plan, and Classroom Interactions in Mathematics: A Multi Case Study
abstract:
This multiple case study examined the interaction patterns in selected Grade 8 mathematics classrooms in a science high school through a systematic observation approach of the most prévalent classroom interactions of the students and teachers. It aiso determined how these interactions differed by student leaming style and by teacher mathematical pedagogical content Knowledge (MPCK).

Three Grade 8 classes and their teachers participated in the study. Data were collected using the interaction patterns instrument, classroom observation snapshot, questionnaires, interview guides, tests, and the instructional plan rubric. Content analysis was performed on classroom interaction patterns, classroom observation snapshots, instructional plans, and interview transcripts. A thematic analysis was aIso performed to examine interaction patterns.

Results show that the most prévalent classroom interactions were scaffolding student learning (teacher-initiated) and initiating unnecessary remarks/behaviors (student-initiated). It was aIso observed that mathematics classes were still teacher-centered and students were predominantly auditory and kinesthetic. Furthermore. The three teachers had almost the same level of MPCK and the same most prévalent classroom interaction pattern—scaffolding student leaming. Teacher MPCK aIso influenced instructional planning of teachers. The study further found that experienced teachers considered the student learning style in instructional planning and novice one considered it even while in the process of implementing the instructional plan.

The study conducted by Flordelina Jr. C. Orteza examines the complex dynamics within Grade 8 mathematics classrooms at a science high school. The research focuses on the relationship between teacher mathematical pedagogical content knowledge (MPCK), student learning styles, instructional planning, and the resulting classroom interactions. By investigating these variables, the study seeks to understand how teacher expertise and student characteristics influence the pedagogical environment and the nature of communication between instructors and learners during mathematics instruction.

The context of this research is situated within a science high school setting, specifically focusing on three Grade 8 mathematics classes and their respective teachers. The problem addressed by the study is the need to understand the interaction patterns that emerge in a mathematics classroom and how these patterns are shaped by the teacher's subject-specific pedagogical knowledge and the diverse learning styles of the students. The researcher aimed to determine if there were significant differences in classroom interactions based on these two factors and how they relate to the instructional plans developed by the teachers.

To address these research questions, the author employed a multi-case study design utilizing a systematic observation approach. Data collection was comprehensive, involving several instruments: an interaction patterns instrument, classroom observation snapshots, questionnaires, interview guides, tests, and an instructional plan rubric. The methodology integrated multiple qualitative and quantitative approaches, including content analysis of classroom interaction patterns, observation snapshots, instructional plans, and interview transcripts, as well as thematic analysis to examine the identified interaction patterns.

The findings of the study reveal several key characteristics of the mathematics classroom environment. Regarding classroom interactions, the most prevalent patterns identified were teacher-initiated scaffolding of student learning and student-initiated unnecessary remarks or behaviors. Despite the focus on student learning, the observations indicated that mathematics classes remained predominantly teacher-centered. In terms of student characteristics, the majority of the students were identified as having auditory and kinesthetic learning styles.

The study also examined the level of teacher mathematical pedagogical content knowledge (MPCK) and its relationship to classroom dynamics. The results showed that the three participating teachers possessed nearly identical levels of MPCK. Consequently, they also exhibited the same most prevalent classroom interaction pattern, which was scaffolding student learning. The research further established that a teacher's MPCK plays a significant role in influencing their instructional planning.

A notable finding emerged regarding how teachers of different experience levels incorporate student learning styles into their teaching practices. The study found that experienced teachers proactively considered student learning styles during the instructional planning phase. In contrast, novice teachers tended to consider student learning styles only while they were in the process of implementing the instructional plan.

The conclusions drawn from this multi-case study highlight the significant role of teacher MPCK in both the planning and execution of mathematics instruction. The research confirms that teacher expertise is a driving force behind the scaffolding of student learning, which was the most common positive interaction pattern observed. However, the persistence of teacher-centered instruction and the occurrence of student-initiated unnecessary remarks suggest areas where classroom management and student engagement strategies could be refined.

The implications of these findings are significant for mathematics education. The study suggests that professional development should focus not only on content knowledge but also on enhancing pedagogical content knowledge to help teachers move away from teacher-centered models toward more student-centered approaches. Furthermore, the distinction between how experienced and novice teachers approach instructional planning suggests that novice teachers may require more targeted mentorship or training in the pre-planning stage to effectively integrate student learning styles into their lesson designs. By addressing these areas, educators can foster more interactive and responsive mathematics learning environments that cater to the auditory and kinesthetic needs of their students.

Lilibeth Pinpin’s study, "Persistence of Filipino-American Students in Undergraduate Biology Major: A Phenomenographic Study," investigates how Filipino-American students experience the factors influencing their ability to persist in an undergraduate biology major. Using a phenomenographic research design and semi-structured individual interviews, the study explores the qualitative meanings students attach to persistence within their specific cultural and social contexts.

The findings refine existing persistence theories by highlighting the complex interrelationships between the individual, family, ethnic community, and educational institutions. A major finding is that familial influence is not a unidirectional force; instead, it is a multidirectional and iterative process involving continuous negotiation between the student and the family unit. Additionally, the research identifies a dual role played by these students. Rather than being merely recipients of support, Filipino-American biology students act as both recipients and as agents of change. Occupying both roles enhances their self-efficacy, which increases their opportunities to persist in their studies.

The study also notes the role of gender, finding that while male and female students share common experiences, female students' lived experiences may be uniquely shaped by cultural factors and institutional biases that have historically acted as barriers to women in scientific disciplines. These findings suggest that educational institutions can enhance recruitment and retention by tailoring support systems to account for multidirectional familial influence, student agency, and gendered institutional biases.

one:
This study investigated the effects of the team-based flipped classroom (TBFC) model on student attitude, motivation, engagement, and achievement in mathematics. The research compared the outcomes of the TBFC approach against a conventional classroom (CC) setting and analyzed how the model affects students with different achievement levels. Additionally, the study sought to determine which variables—attitude, motivation, or engagement—serve as significant predictors of mathematics achievement.

The research employed a combination of quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative component utilized a Matching-Only Pretest-Posttest Control Group Design. Achievement was measured through a researcher-made achievement test consisting of 100 items. Readiness was assessed using a series of ten 10-item readiness tests. Student attitudes were measured using the modified attitude towards mathematics inventory by Tapia and Marsh (2000), motivation was assessed via the mathematics motivation scale by Liu and Lin (2010), and student engagement was measured using the student engagement instrument by Fredricks et al. (2016).

The findings revealed that students exposed to the TBFC model demonstrated significantly higher positive attitudes towards mathematics compared to students in the conventional classroom group. Students in the TBFC group also exhibited higher levels of engagement and achieved higher scores on the achievement test than their counterparts in the conventional classroom. Within the TBFC group, students showed higher levels of self-confidence, value, and emotional engagement. Among students in the TBFC group, those categorized as outstanding students demonstrated higher levels of cognitive engagement.

The research explored the relationships between variables through a path diagram, indicating that attitude, motivation, and engagement are interrelated. However, the analysis revealed that only engagement significantly predicted achievement. Qualitative themes suggested that advanced assignments help boost self-confidence and that the collaborative nature of the model meant team sharing equated to team enjoyment. The TBFC environment fostered a "we can do it!" drive. Students reported that reviewing online materials helped them prepare significantly, and sharing information within the team was synonymous with being engaged.

The study offers several implications and recommendations for mathematics education. There is a recommendation to launch an educational platform specifically for mathematics education to facilitate the delivery of advanced assignments. To support educators, the study suggests offering capacity-building sessions for mathematics educators to train them on the implementation of the team-based flipped classroom model. Finally, the researcher suggests that future studies should explore the effectiveness of the team-based flipped classroom model within a full virtual set-up.

title: Effect of Flipped Classroom with Peer Instruction (FCPI) on the Chemistry Achievement and Classroom Environment of Grade 7 JHS Students
abstract:
determine the effect of flipped classroom with peer instruction (FCPI) on the chemistry achievement and classroom environment of Grade 7 junior high school students. In this specific setting, students were introduced to lesson content through these digital resources prior to class. During actual classroom hours, the teacher focused the discussion on concept questions, which students answered through peer instruction. This was compared against a control group utilizing a Traditional Classroom with Peer Instruction (TCPI) setup. The TCPI setup functioned as a variation of the traditional lecture method, where students were required to answer formative assessments with their peers.

The study utilized a multi-method approach to measure effectiveness, incorporating a researcher-developed chemistry achievement test as a primary quantitative tool. This was supplemented by qualitative and observational data collected through classroom observations, journal entries, a perception survey, and focus group discussions.

The findings of the study indicate that both instructional groups experienced a significant increase in chemistry achievement following the implementation of their respective strategies. However, the FCPI setup proved more effective than the TCPI setup in terms of academic gains. Specifically, students in the FCPI group demonstrated an estimated increase in chemistry achievement of 4.99%, whereas students in the TCPI group showed an increase of only 3.67%.

Beyond academic achievement, the study found significant differences in classroom participation and environment. Students in the FCPI setup demonstrated superior classroom participation compared to those in the TCPI setup. The FCPI design encouraged students to complete assigned tasks on time, exhibit a cooperative and supportive attitude during discussions and activities, share ideas in class, and show respect for the opinions of others. Conversely, students in the TCPI setup performed poorly in these specific areas of participation.

Regarding the classroom environment, the FCPI setup outperformed the TCPI setup across several observed dimensions. These dimensions included positive climate, teacher sensitivity, regard for student perspective, behavior management, productivity, quality of feedback, language modeling, instructional learning format, and concept development. Statistical analysis confirmed that the classroom environment on specific observation days—namely days 8, 9, 10, 13, and 14—was significantly different between the two groups, with the FCPI setup consistently providing a better classroom environment.

The conclusions drawn from this research suggest that the integration of flipped classroom elements with peer instruction provides a more robust framework for science education than traditional lecture-based methods combined with peer instruction. The FCPI model not only facilitates higher academic achievement in chemistry but also fosters a more productive, respectful, and engaging classroom atmosphere. By shifting the initial content delivery to digital media, the classroom time is optimized for active learning and peer interaction, which appears to enhance both student engagement and the quality of the instructional environment.

The implications of these findings suggest that educators may benefit from adopting flipped classroom models to improve student outcomes in science subjects. The study highlights that the way instructional time is structured—moving from passive listening to active, peer-supported problem-solving—can lead to measurable improvements in student performance and classroom dynamics. The results support the use of technology-based courseware to prepare students for meaningful in-class discussions and collaborative learning.

title: Statistical Approach in Tertiary Physics Laboratory: Effects on Student Achievement, Attitude, and Psychomotor Skills
abstract:
This study is on the effects of statistical supplementary materials for the General Laboratory information (GLI) of a physics first-year laboratory course offered at a leading university in the Philippines, to: (a) students’ attitudes toward rules on decimal place and significant digits calculations, accuracy and precision, and probability interval estimation; (b) students self-perception of mathematics-/statistics-related attitudes and anxiety; (c)students’ self-perception of the relevance of mathematics and statistics; (d) laboratory physics achievement; (e) knowledge of relevant statistical concepts; (f) students’ self-perception of their psychomotor domain skills; (g) associations between one-semester changes in students’ self-perception of attitudes and anxiety toward mathematics and statistics, on the other hand, and students’ start-of-semester self-perception of their psychomotor domain skills, on the other hand; and, (h) correlations between laboratory physics achievement, on the other hand, and the attitudes and self-perceptions considered in (a), (b), and ( c), on the other hand.

The holistic evaluation of the new materials, modifies based on authoritative guidelines and directed at developing statistical thinking, involved all 48 enrolled students and the two instructors of the course, and included the students’: attitude changes, sources of anxiety, and self-perceptions of these based on Osborne’s (1976) semantic differential scales and the Mathematics and Statistics Perception Scale (Cherney & Cooney, 2005); actual physical performance in certain assigned laboratory experiments; and, final course grades and
responses in the start- and end-of-semester assessments on basic statistical knowledge.

half:
Justine Leon A. Uro conducted a study at a leading university in the Philippines to investigate the impact of integrating statistical supplementary materials into the General Laboratory Information of a first-year physics laboratory course. The research focused on freshman physics majors to determine how materials modified to promote statistical thinking influenced student performance, perception, and attitudes toward statistical rules such as decimal places, significant digits, accuracy, precision, and probability interval estimation. The study also evaluated mathematics and statistics-related anxiety, perceived relevance, laboratory physics achievement, knowledge of statistical concepts, and psychomotor domain skills.

The methodology involved a holistic evaluation of 48 students and two instructors using semantic differential scales, perception scales, physical performance assessments, final course grades, and pre- and post-semester assessments. Findings revealed that the materials did not significantly increase positive self-perceptions regarding statistical rules, nor did they significantly increase physics laboratory achievement or gains in basic statistical knowledge. However, the materials appeared to mitigate decreases in positive self-perceptions and anxiety regarding mathematics and statistics. Students using the materials demonstrated better psychomotor performance, though the researcher noted the potential for a Hawthorne effect. Correlation analysis showed no significant link between changes in attitudes and initial psychomotor skills, nor a positive correlation between achievement and mathematics or statistics self-perception. The study concludes that while the materials may not boost broad achievement, they are beneficial for teaching concepts like central location and dispersion, helping students understand the statistical justifications behind laboratory rules.
one:
Justine Leon A. Uro conducted a study at a leading university in the Philippines to investigate the impact of integrating statistical supplementary materials into the General Laboratory Information (GLI) of a first-year physics laboratory course. The research focused on freshman physics majors and aimed to determine how these specialized materials, modified to promote statistical thinking, influenced student performance and perception. Specifically, the study measured attitudes toward statistical rules—including decimal places, significant digits, accuracy, precision, and probability interval estimation—as well as self-perceptions regarding mathematics and statistics-related anxiety and relevance. The research also evaluated laboratory physics achievement, knowledge of statistical concepts, and self-perceptions of psychomotor domain skills.

The methodology involved a holistic evaluation of 48 students and two instructors. Attitudes and anxiety were assessed using Osborne’s semantic differential scales and the Mathematics and Statistics Perception Scale. Psychomotor skills were evaluated through physical performance during assigned experiments, while academic outcomes were measured via final course grades and pre- and post-semester assessments of basic statistical knowledge.

The findings revealed complex results regarding the efficacy of the materials. The introduction of the materials did not significantly increase positive self-perceptions regarding rules on decimal places, significant digits, accuracy, precision, and probability interval estimation, though some exceptions were noted regarding accuracy and precision related to laboratory difficulty. While differences between conventional and experimental groups were often not significant, the materials appeared to help mitigate decreases in positive self-perceptions and anxiety regarding mathematics and statistics, as well as their perceived relevance. However, the materials did not significantly increase physics laboratory achievement or gains in basic statistical knowledge.

Regarding psychomotor skills, students taught with the supplementary materials demonstrated better performance than those who were not, though the researcher noted the potential for a Hawthorne effect and acknowledged that results might depend on specific laboratory activities. Correlation analysis showed no significant link between one-semester changes in mathematics or statistics-related attitudes and anxiety and the students' initial self-perceptions of psychomotor domain skills. Furthermore, the materials did not result in a positive correlation between physics laboratory achievement and any self-perception of mathematics or statistics. A negative correlation was found between final course grades and self-perceptions of attitudes highly related to task difficulty, but no correlation was found with attitudes related to task enjoyability or significance.

The study concludes that while the materials may not significantly boost broad achievement or knowledge, they serve a specific pedagogical purpose. For instructors teaching concepts like central location, central dispersion, and least squares, these materials can be beneficial. When used with discretion, they can help students know, understand, and appreciate the statistical justifications behind rules regarding significant digits, accuracy, precision, and the best fit line.

The research was situated within a leading university in the Philippines and focused on freshman physics majors. The primary objective was to determine how these specialized materials, which were modified based on authoritative guidelines to promote statistical thinking, influenced various dimensions of student performance and perception. Specifically, the study sought to measure effects on students' attitudes toward specific statistical rules—such as decimal places, significant digits, accuracy, precision, and probability interval estimation—as well as their self-perceptions regarding mathematics and statistics-related anxiety and relevance. Furthermore, the research aimed to evaluate laboratory physics achievement, knowledge of statistical concepts, and self-perceptions of psychomotor domain skills. The study also explored associations between changes in attitudes and anxiety over a semester and initial psychomotor skill perceptions, alongside correlations between physics achievement and various student attitudes and self-perceptions.

The methodology employed a holistic evaluation involving all 48 enrolled students and two instructors. To assess attitudes and anxiety, the researcher utilized Osborne’s (1976) semantic differential scales and the Mathematics and Statistics Perception Scale (Cherney & Cooney, 2005). Psychomotor skills were evaluated through actual physical performance during specific assigned laboratory experiments. To measure academic outcomes, the study analyzed final course grades and responses from assessments administered at the beginning and end of the semester regarding basic statistical knowledge.

The findings of the study revealed complex results regarding the efficacy of the statistical supplementary materials. In terms of student attitudes, the introduction of the materials did not significantly increase positive self-perceptions regarding rules on decimal places, significant digits, accuracy, precision, and probability interval estimation, though there was a possible exception regarding certain aspects of accuracy and precision related to laboratory difficulty. While differences between conventional and experimental groups were not significant in many respects, there was an indication that the supplementary materials might help mitigate the decrease in positive self-perceptions and anxiety regarding mathematics and statistics, as well as their perceived relevance. However, the materials did not significantly increase physics laboratory achievement or gains in basic statistical knowledge.

Regarding psychomotor skills, the study found that students taught with the statistical supplementary materials demonstrated better performance than those who were not, though the researcher noted the possibility of a Hawthorne effect and acknowledged that results might depend on the specific laboratory activity. In terms of associations, the study found no significant link between one-semester changes in mathematics or statistics-related attitudes and anxiety and the students' start-of-semester self-perceptions of their psychomotor domain skills. Correlation analysis showed that the new GLI materials resulted in a negative correlation between final course grades and self-perceptions of attitudes highly related to the difficulty of tasks, but no correlation was found with attitudes related to the enjoyability or significance of tasks. Additionally, the use of the supplementary materials did not result in a positive correlation between physics laboratory achievement and any self-perception of mathematics or statistics.

The study concludes that while the statistical supplementary materials may not significantly boost achievement or knowledge in a broad sense, they serve a specific pedagogical purpose. For instructors teaching concepts such as central location, central dispersion, and least squares to freshman physics majors, the use of these materials can be beneficial. When used with discretion, these materials can lead students to partly know, understand, and appreciate the statistical justifications behind rules regarding significant digits, accuracy, precision, and the best fit line.

title: Students’ Mathematics Problem Solving Difficulties and Coping and Strategies: A Model Building Study
abstract:
Problems. difficulties and pressures abound everywhere. In Mathematics, much has been sard and heard of students struggling with problem solving. This study therefore p·imarily aimed to develop models that could address the problem solving diff;culties of students through their coping strategies. Specifically, it aimed to determine the students' strategies in coping with their difficulties along the four phases of problem solving namely: understanding the problem (UP), devising a plan (DP), ca:-rying out the plan (CP) and looking back (LB) according to a) sex and b) academic programs namely: 

The study employed case-study-design approach. The respondents of the study involved thirteen classes with 425 college freshmen who were enrolled during the firs! seri,ester of SY 2018-2019. Two hundred ninety-seven of them composed the model development group while 128 respondents composed the validation group.

Results of the problem solving test revealed the following difficulties of the respondents: a) inability to distinguish the known from the unknown information and inability to identify the type of problem and recall basic concepts in the UP phase, b) inc.1bility to transform a problem into a mathematical equation and inability to draw tables/charts out of the information and organize information and connect to a concept in the DP phase, c) inability to completely perform the working procedure systematically and accurately and inability to start with the computational process in the CP Phase, and d) inability to complete the checking procedure and inability to start the evaluation of the correctness of the obtained solution in the LB phase. 

Moreover, the study revealed that the looking back (LB) phase has the most encountered difficulty, followed by the carrying out the plan (CP) phase. There were more females who encountered the above mentioned difficulties in all phases of problem solving than males. The respondents were likewise grouped into two: STEM­related acacemic programs and the non-STEM-related academic programs. The study found out that the majority of the male respondents from the STEM-related academic programs encountered the observed difficulties in all phases of problem solving.

Dinah C. Vidad’s dissertation, "Students’ Mathematics Problem Solving Difficulties and Coping Strategies: A Model Building Study," investigates the cognitive and behavioral responses students exhibit when facing complex mathematical tasks. Using Polya’s four-phase framework—understanding the problem, devising a plan, carrying out the plan, and looking back—the study identifies specific difficulties encountered during these stages and the methods students employ to overcome them. The research specifically examines how these challenges manifest across different demographics, focusing on sex and academic course.

The study utilizes a model-building design to develop representations that assist in overcoming these obstacles. Data was collected through a problem-solving test centered on linear equations in one variable and a questionnaire regarding coping strategies. The findings categorize difficulties and coping mechanisms across the four problem-solving phases, segmented by sex and course. This analysis pinpoints whether struggles occur during initial comprehension, strategic planning, the execution of operations, or the final verification of results.

The research concludes with the development of models representing the relationship between problem-solving difficulties and coping strategies. These models provide a structured understanding of the student experience by analyzing the intersection of sex, course, and the four problem-solving phases. These findings offer a framework for educators to develop targeted interventions and personalized instructional approaches, helping students move from struggle to effective strategic management of mathematical tasks.

title: Multiple-Representation Physics Lesson Study, Pre-Service Teacher Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Critical Thinking and Student Achievement
abstract:
The study probed the effects of the Multiple-Representation Lesson Study (MRLS) on pre-service Physics teachers’ technological-pedagogical-content knowledge, critical thinking, and student achievement inPhysics. The study also identified the challenges and the coping
mechanisms in conducting the MRLS.

The two-phase study employed a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with the participation of 18 pre-service Physics teachers and 12 intact Grade 8 classes of a public high school. The comparison group was exposed to Traditional Instructional Planning Approach
(TIPA) while the experimental group was exposed to MRLS. 

Phase 1 of the study was conducted in Summer 2016 while Phase 2 was conducted during the practice teaching stage in the first semester of SY 2016-2017. Data from multiple sources were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test, ANOVA, t-test, and constant
comparative qualitative method. Results revealed significantly higher media scores of the MRLS group than the TIPA in the overcall TPCK and critical thinking, as well as in the various components of the two constructs both in Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the study. Moreover, results suggest encouraging effects of the MRLS on student achievement.

Meanwhile, seven dominant challenges and six coping mechanisms were revealed in the conduct of MRLS. Finding indicate a positive influence of the MRLS on pre-service teachers’ TPCK, critical thinking, and on the academic achievement of students; hence, the integration of the MRLS in the pre-service teacher education curriculum is recommended. Likewise, the extensive use of technology-generated and conventional multiple representations in Physics instruction is proposed to reinforce higher order thinking and student motivation.

The study conducted by Billy A. Danday investigates the effects of the Multiple-Representation Lesson Study (MRLS) on several educational outcomes. The research probes how this approach influences the technological-pedagogical-content knowledge (TPCK) and critical thinking skills of pre-service Physics teachers. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of the MRLS on student achievement within the context of Physics instruction. Beyond measuring these specific variables, the research seeks to identify the various challenges encountered during the implementation of the MRLS and the specific coping mechanisms utilized to address those difficulties.

The research is situated within teacher education and secondary school instruction and was carried out in two distinct phases. Phase 1 took place during the Summer of 2016, while Phase 2 was conducted during the practice teaching stage in the first semester of SY 2016-2017. The participants included 18 pre-service Physics teachers and 12 intact Grade 8 classes from a public high school. To determine the effectiveness of the MRLS, the researcher employed a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design. This design allowed for a comparison between an experimental group, which was exposed to the Multiple-Representation Lesson Study, and a comparison group, which was exposed to the Traditional Instructional Planning Approach (TIPA).

To analyze the data collected from multiple sources, the researcher utilized several statistical and qualitative methods. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test, ANOVA, and t-test. For the qualitative aspects of the study, the constant comparative qualitative method was applied. This multi-method approach allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the quantitative shifts in TPCK, critical thinking, and student achievement, while also providing a detailed understanding of the qualitative experiences regarding challenges and coping strategies.

The findings indicate that the Multiple-Representation Lesson Study has a significant positive impact on pre-service teachers. Results revealed that the MRLS group achieved significantly higher media scores than the TIPA group in overall TPCK and critical thinking. This superiority was observed across the various components of both constructs during both Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the study. In addition to the benefits seen in the pre-service teachers, the results suggest that the MRLS also has encouraging effects on student achievement in Physics.

The research revealed seven dominant challenges encountered during the conduct of the Multiple-Representation Lesson Study. To manage these obstacles, the study identified six coping mechanisms that were employed. Based on these findings, the researcher recommends the integration of the MRLS into the pre-service teacher education curriculum and proposes the extensive use of both technology-generated and conventional multiple representations in Physics instruction to reinforce higher order thinking and increase student motivation.

Based on these findings, the study reaches several important conclusions and offers specific recommendations for the field of education. The results indicate a positive influence of the MRLS on the TPCK and critical thinking of pre-service teachers, as well as on the academic achievement of students. Consequently, the researcher recommends the integration of the MRLS into the pre-service teacher education curriculum to better prepare future educators. Furthermore, the study proposes the extensive use of both technology-generated and conventional multiple representations in Physics instruction. Such an approach is suggested as a means to reinforce higher order thinking and to increase student motivation in the subject matter.

title: Collaborative Teaching: Effects on Science Teachers’ Pedagogical Content Knowledge and Students’ Understanding of Particulate Nature of Matter
abstract: This study is about an alternative school-based model of professional development for Science teachers and sought to help address the research gap about improving the Science teachers' pedagogical content knowledge to improve science teaching and student learning. It is a qualitative case study that analyzed the changes in the pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of Particulate Nature of Matter (PNM) of teachers who underwent Collaborative Teaching (CT), and how these changes affected the conceptual understanding of PNM of their students. The study involved six Grade 8 Science teachers, the Collaborative Teaching group who underwent CT for almost eight weeks and six other Science teachers who were assigned to the Conventional Teaching group. The changes in the PCK of PNM of the teachers and their students' conceptual understanding of PNM were monitored using multiple sources of data: classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, lesson plans, pre-lesson reflection guides, and questionnaires. Analysis of data from these various sources using the constant comparative method shows that the PCK of the six teachers from the Collaborative Teaching group improved. Their knowledge of science content (KSC) about PNM improved as demonstrated by their corrected misconceptions about PNM and ability to explain phase changes using macroscopic, sub-microscopic and symbolic representations. Their knowledge of students' understanding (KSU) improved as they reflected awareness of students' misconceptions and learning difficulties in their lesson plans and adjusted teaching strategies to address these misconceptions and learning difficulties. Their knowledge of teaching strategies (KTS) also improved as they shifted from more lecture-based teaching to using interactive strategies, models and higher order thinking skills (HOTS) questioning. These PCK improvements were supported by data from the PCK-PNM Observation Rubric which showed that the PCK of teachers from the Collaborative Teaching group improved from "Emergent" to "Proficient" whereas that of the Conventional Teaching group remained as "Emergent".

This dissertation by Reynaldo R. Ibasco investigates the impact of Collaborative Teaching (CT) as a school-based professional development model on science teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) and their students' conceptual understanding of the Particulate Nature of Matter (PNM). The research addresses a critical gap in improving science education in the Philippines, where national achievement scores have shown a downward trend and students often struggle with scientific literacy and specific misconceptions regarding the microscopic nature of matter.

The study focuses on the specific domain of PNM, a fundamental chemistry concept that is frequently misunderstood by students. The researcher identifies that effective teaching requires more than just subject matter expertise; it requires PCK, which is the ability to represent content in ways that make it comprehensible to learners. The study specifically examines three components of PCK: Knowledge of Science Content (KSC), Knowledge of Students' Understanding (KSU), and Knowledge of Teaching Strategies (KTS).

The research employed a qualitative case study design involving twelve Grade 8 science teachers. These participants were divided into two groups: a Collaborative Teaching group, which underwent an eight-week intervention consisting of six cycles of collaborative planning, implementation, evaluation, and revision, and a Conventional Teaching group. Data were collected through multiple sources, including classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, lesson plans, pre-lesson reflection guides, and questionnaires. The researcher used the constant comparative method to analyze the data.

The findings indicate that the Collaborative Teaching intervention significantly improved the PCK of the participating teachers. In terms of KSC, teachers corrected their own misconceptions regarding PNM and demonstrated an improved ability to explain phase changes using macroscopic, sub-microscopic, and symbolic representations. Regarding KSU, teachers showed an increased awareness of student misconceptions and learning difficulties, which they used to adjust their teaching strategies. In terms of KTS, teachers shifted from traditional lecture-based methods to more interactive strategies, including the use of models and higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) questioning. Quantitative data supported these qualitative findings, showing a 40% increase in the PCK scores of the Collaborative Teaching group from pretest to posttest, whereas the Conventional Teaching group saw only a 26% increase.

The study also found that improvements in teacher PCK directly facilitated better conceptual understanding among students. Students in the Collaborative Teaching group showed a 95 percent increase in their Particulate Nature of Matter Assessment (ParNoMA) mean scores, compared to a 50.7 percent increase in the Conventional Teaching group. Specifically, the intervention helped students correct misconceptions regarding particle size during phase changes, shift from a continuous view of matter to a particle view, and develop the ability to visualize and represent particles during various phase changes. Statistical testing confirmed that the gain scores of the Collaborative Teaching group were significantly higher than those of the Conventional Teaching group.

The researcher concludes that Collaborative Teaching is an effective, accessible, and affordable mode of professional development. It empowers teachers to act as "donor-and-acceptor" of knowledge, fostering a professional learning community within the school. The study demonstrates that when teachers collaborate to study content and pedagogy together, they are better equipped to address the unique learning needs and misconceptions of their students.

The implications of this research are significant for science education reform. The study recommends that Collaborative Teaching be utilized as a framework for designing professional development programs, with an intentional focus on the different components of PCK. For school administrators and the Department of Education, the study suggests that school-based, teacher-directed models are more sustainable and effective than top-down, one-size-fits-all seminars. Furthermore, the assessment tools developed in this study, such as the PCK-PNM Questionnaire and the ParNoMA, are suggested as useful instruments for monitoring teacher development and student mastery of essential science concepts.

title: Metacognitive-Creative Problem Solving Method: Effects on Students’ Metacognition, Creativity, Conceptual Understanding and Performance in Physics
abstract:
The purpose of this study was to determine the effects of the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method (MCPSM) on metacognition, creative thinking skills, conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance in Physics of Grade 9 students using a
quasi-experimental and pretest-posttest two group research design. Metacognition was measured using a modified Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (Schraw & Denisson, 1994) while researcher-made scoring rubrics rated creative thinking skills and problem-solving
performance of students. A researcher-made multiple-choice test assessed conceptual understanding.

The significant difference in the composite mean ratings in metacognition and creative thinking of the metacognitive-creative problem-solving group and the conventional group was determined using one-way MANOVA. The same procedure was used in determining significant difference in the composite mean ratings in conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance of the two groups of students. Multiple regression analysis determined significant predictors of conceptual understanding from among the dimensions of metacognition and creative thinking. The same analysis was performed to determine significant predictors of problem-solving performance from among the dimensions of metacognition, creative thinking and conceptual understanding.

Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method (MCPSM) was effective in improving metacognition and creative thinking of students. It was also effective in improving joint conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance in Physics.

This study investigated the effects of the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method (MCPSM) on Grade 9 Physics students, focusing on metacognition, creative thinking, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving performance. Using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design, the researcher compared an MCPSM group with a conventional group using a modified Metacognitive Awareness Inventory, scoring rubrics, and a multiple-choice test. Statistical analyses included a one-way MANOVA and multiple regression analysis.

The findings indicated that the MCPSM effectively improved metacognition, creative thinking, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving performance. Regression analysis revealed specific predictors for academic outcomes: declarative knowledge predicted engaging in the problem and executing mathematical operations, while planning was associated with executing mathematical operations. Elaboration and fluency were related to applying concepts, planning solutions, and formulating equations. Additionally, checking solutions was influenced by elaboration and flexibility, while originality influenced concept application and solution planning. The avoidance of misconception was positively related to applying concepts, planning solutions, formulating equations, and executing mathematical operations, and flexibility was a significant predictor of avoiding misconceptions. Notably, metacognitive knowledge and cognitive control showed no significant relationship with conceptual understanding.

The study concludes that the MCPSM is an effective instructional strategy for enhancing cognitive and academic skills in Physics. The researcher recommends implementing this method in classrooms and teacher training programs, suggesting future research investigate the method's specific strengths, weaknesses, and target student populations.
