Furthermore, the avoidance of misconception had a positive relationship with applying concepts, planning solutions, formulating equations, and executing mathematical operations. Finally, analyzing concepts was found to influence the planning of solutions.

The purpose of this study was to determine the effects of the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method (MCPSM) on several key educational outcomes for Grade 9 students studying Physics. Specifically, the research aimed to measure how this method influences metacognition, creative thinking skills, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving performance. The study sought to establish whether the implementation of the MCPSM provided significant advantages over conventional teaching methods in the context of Physics education.

The research was conducted within the context of Physics instruction for Grade 9 students. To investigate the effectiveness of the MCPSM, the researcher employed a quasi-experimental research design utilizing a pretest-posttest approach with two distinct groups. The study utilized several specialized instruments to gather data: a modified Metacognitive Awareness Inventory was used to measure metacognition, while researcher-made scoring rubrics were developed to rate both creative thinking skills and problem-solving performance. Additionally, a researcher-made multiple-choice test was utilized to assess the students' level of conceptual understanding.

The methodology involved complex statistical analyses to compare the two groups. A one-way MANOVA was used to determine significant differences in the composite mean ratings for metacognition and creative thinking between the MCPSM group and the conventional group. The same statistical procedure was applied to compare the composite mean ratings for conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance. Furthermore, multiple regression analysis was employed to identify significant predictors of conceptual understanding based on the dimensions of metacognition and creative thinking. A similar regression analysis was conducted to identify significant predictors of problem-solving performance based on the dimensions of metacognition, creative thinking, and conceptual understanding.

The findings indicated that the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method was effective in improving students' metacognition and creative thinking. The method was also found to be effective in improving both conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance in Physics. The study revealed several specific relationships between cognitive dimensions and academic outcomes. For instance, flexibility was identified as a significant predictor of the dimension of avoidance of misconception. Interestingly, the study found that metacognitive knowledge and cognitive control had no significant relationship with conceptual understanding, suggesting that students tended to be selective in their learning, focusing only on the concepts required to solve specific problems.

The regression analysis provided detailed insights into the predictors of performance. Declarative knowledge was found to be a significant predictor of engaging in the problem and executing mathematical operations. Additionally, planning as a dimension of cognitive control was associated with the execution of mathematical operations. The study found that both elaboration and fluency were related to applying concepts, planning solutions, and formulating equations. Furthermore, the dimension of checking solutions was influenced by both elaboration and flexibility, while originality influenced the application of concepts and the planning of solutions. The avoidance of misconception was found to have a positive relationship with applying concepts, planning solutions, formulating equations, and executing mathematical operations. Finally, the analysis showed that analyzing concepts also influenced the planning of solutions.

Based on these results, the study concludes that the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method is an effective instructional strategy for improving various cognitive and academic skills in Physics. The method's ability to enhance metacognition, creativity, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving performance suggests it is a valuable tool for addressing the complexities of the subject matter.

The implications of this research suggest that the Metacognitive-Creative Problem-Solving Method should be recommended for classroom instruction to facilitate the learning of problem-solving skills, particularly when dealing with multi-step problems. The researcher also recommends that this method be included in the preparation of future teachers and incorporated into in-service training programs. For future research, the study suggests investigating the specific strengths and weaknesses of the metacognitive-creative problem-solving approach in Physics, as well as identifying the specific types of students and other learning areas where this teaching and learning strategy is most effective.

title: Influence of Lesson Study on Elementary School Science Teachers’ Pedagogical Content Knowledge on the Nature of Science
abstract: This qualitative study, which employed the design research approach, explored the influence of Lesson Study on elementary school science teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) on the Nature of Science (NOS) relevant to the new science curriculum. PCK on NOS prior to and throughout the Lesson Study Engagement was established from questionnaires, interviews, research lesson, classroom observations and field notes. Before Lesson Study, the teachers possessed acceptable and unacceptable conceptions about the properties of matter, exhibited difficulties in differentiating between observation and inference, and were unfamiliar with NOS. these limited knowledge bases led to inadequate lesson planning and classroom practices. During the Lesson Study engagement, improvements in PCK on NOS were evident based on the research lesson. The teachers demonstrated more acceptable notions on properties of matter and the process skills of observing and inferring. Accordingly, they translated these understandings into an inquiry activity appropriate for the learners. Lesson Study appears to have positive influences the teachers’ PCK on NOS because they implemented its designed features authentically. It is argued that if any of these features were omitted or altered, the observed improvements could have not been as remarkable. These findings imply that PCK on NOS can be acquired in the teachers’ own classrooms through carefully planned and meticulously implemented on-site interventions, like Lesson Study. Means to address teachers’ inadequacies on the knowledge domains pertinent to PCK o NOS were suggested. Recommendations were forwarded about how properly design Lesson Study will contribute to instructional improvement and enhance student engagement and learning

title: Development and Effectiveness of Facilitated Learning Modules in Introductory Analytical Chemistry
abstract:
This study involved development and assessment of facilitated learning modules that emphasized mathematical and statistical tools in introductory analytical chemistry. These facilitated learning modules were deemed to address the need of medical technology students for supplementary learning materials that address students' difficulty in solving quantitative problems involved in introductory analytical chemistry. 

The first phase of the study covered the development of seven facilitated learning modules on selected topics in introductory analytical chemistry which require mathematical and statistical tools. These topics were considered necessary because they involve mathematical and statistical treatments which students find difficult because of their insufficiency in mathematical and statistical background. The development of facilitated learning modules employed both qualitative and quantitative analyses. The qualitative aspect involved evaluation of the facilitated learning modules face content and form by chemistry education experts. Relevant comments and suggestions incorporated into the modules' final forms characterized the essential features of the  facilitated leaming modules. The quantitative aspect focused on lhe evaluation of analytical chemistry instructors on the facilitated learning modules' objectives in terms of attainability, clarity, and relevance. It also included their evaluation of the modules' content in terms of appropriateness, appeal, innovativeness, and conformity to standards using a questionnaire developed by Lumaque (2011 ). The instructors found the objectives of the learning modules to be highly attainable, very clear, and very relevant. They rated the modules' content to be very appropriate, very innovative, very appealing, and strongly conforming to standards. Part of the quantitative aspect was the determination of the facilitated learning modules' student's involvement index, grade level, and communication index. Using Romey's procedure (1965), students involvement index of the modules was 1.34, which indicated that the modules could keep the interest of users while reading the modules. Fry's Readability Graph ( 1968) indicated Grade 11 as the grade level of the modules, which matched that of the intended users. Further, Talisayon's procedure (1983) indicated that communication index of the learning modules was acceptable at 0.009.

title: Consensus-Based Instruction: Effects on Students’ Attitude Towards Biology and Achievement in Bioenergetics
abstract:
In this study, the effects of consensus-based instruction (CBI) on attitude towards biology and achievement in biocnergctics of college students in a biological science class were investigated. The aim was to compare the CBI class with the class taught using the conventional instruction approach (CIA) in terms of their component and overall posttest mean scores in the Attitude Towards Biology Scale (ATBS) and their post1est mean scores in the Bioenergetics Achievement Test (BAT). The moderating effects of sex and learning styles as well as the relationship between students' attitude and their achievement were also examined. 

Two intact classes were compared using the non-equivalent pretcst-posttest control group quasi-experimental design. One group used CIA while the other employed the CBI approach. In CBI, students were given the chance to raise an issue in the learning plan, negotiate, propose an alternative, participate in a 'grand conversation', decide using consensus, and adhere to the agreed implementation process. They were also tasked to arrive at a consensus answer on a focus question related to the day's lesson. Aside from the standardized Canfield Learning Style Inventory, data were collected using expert-validated researcher-made instruments tested for reliability such as the Learning Needs Analysis Protocol, Questionnaire on the Importance of Democratic Practices in Classroom, A TBS and BAT. Videos, journal and informal interviews were used as additional data sources.

title: Eco-Inquiry Modules: Effects on Students’ Achievement and Understanding of Environmental Concepts and the Nature of Science
abstract:
The study developed a set of Eco-inquiry modules (also known as Eco-inquiry) and determined its effects on students’ achievement, understanding of environmental concepts and the nature of science among undergraduate tourism major students. Eco-inquiry was evaluated in terms of subject matter and pedagogical experts’ assessment and readability. Using quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design for quantitative and qualitative data analyses, the following problems were addressed: (1) correlation between the pre and post-test scores in the achievement test and students’ grades in their prerequisite subjects, (2) difference in the scores for the achievement test, understanding of environmental concepts and the natures of science among and between students exposed to inquiry-based learning and those exposed to conventional approach, (3) correlation between the experimental students’ inquiry-based learning posttest scores in the achievement test and conceptual understanding of environmental concepts and (4) students’ assessment of inquiry-based learning through Eco-inquiry. Tourism major students from a College in Manila, the Philippines who were enrolled in Ecotourism (ECOTOUR) class for the 3rd Term of Academic Year 2014-2015 were the subjects of the study. The assignment of two sections to either experimental (use of inquiry-based learning) or the control (use of conventional approach) group was randomly done through a drawing of lots. All parametric and nonparametric statistical tests were processed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS Version 21) software for MS Windows. 

Results in all criteria for evaluation of Eco-inquiry which include attainment of objectives, characteristics as inquiry-based learning, integration of the nature of science, content accuracy, modules originality, modules clarity and evaluation indicators by the subject matter and
pedagogical experts showed that it is nearly outstanding. Subsequently, the readability index of Eco-inquiry is found to be appropriate for college level.

Benigno Glenn R. Ricaforte investigated the development and effectiveness of Eco-inquiry modules for undergraduate tourism students to determine how inquiry-based learning affects student achievement, environmental concept understanding, and understanding of the nature of science (NOS) compared to conventional methods. Conducted during the 2014-2015 academic year in Manila, Philippines, the study utilized a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design. Data were collected through achievement tests, the Student Understanding of Science and Scientific Inquiry (SUSSI) scale, concept mapping, and faculty observations.

The findings revealed that experts rated the modules as nearly outstanding. Students in the experimental group performed significantly better on achievement tests than those in the control group, though no correlation was found between prerequisite grades and achievement scores. Through concept mapping, the experimental group demonstrated a significantly better understanding of environmental concepts, showing increased propositional complexity and a shift toward network-type maps. Furthermore, the experimental group showed a significantly better understanding of the nature of science, specifically regarding creativity, imagination, and social and cultural embeddedness.

Faculty observations rated the implementation of inquiry-based learning as outstanding, noting that students were encouraged to ask questions and produce creative works. The study concludes that inquiry-based learning effectively enhances achievement, conceptual understanding, and understanding of the nature of science. The researcher recommends integrating inquiry-based learning with conventional approaches and suggests that administrators provide training in these strategies.

The study conducted by Benigno Glenn R. Ricaforte investigated the development and effectiveness of Eco-inquiry modules designed for undergraduate tourism major students. The primary objective was to determine how these modules, which utilize inquiry-based learning, affect student achievement, the understanding of environmental concepts, and the understanding of the nature of science (NOS) compared to conventional teaching methods. The research sought to address specific correlations between prerequisite grades and achievement, differences in performance between experimental and control groups, and the relationship between achievement scores and conceptual understanding. Additionally, the study examined student assessments of the inquiry-based learning approach.

The research was situated within the context of tourism education, specifically for students enrolled in an Ecotourism (ECOTOUR) class at a college in Manila, Philippines, during the 2014-2015 academic year. The study employed a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design. To ensure scientific rigor, two sections were randomly assigned via a drawing of lots to either the experimental group, which utilized inquiry-based learning through the Eco-inquiry modules, or the control group, which was taught using a conventional approach. Data collection involved quantitative measures, such as achievement tests and the Student Understanding of Science and Scientific Inquiry (SUSSI) scale, as well as qualitative measures, including concept mapping and faculty observations.

The methodology involved a rigorous evaluation of the Eco-inquiry modules themselves before implementation. Experts in subject matter and pedagogy assessed the modules based on several criteria, including the attainment of objectives, characteristics of inquiry-based learning, integration of the nature of science, content accuracy, originality, and clarity. The modules were also tested for readability to ensure they were appropriate for the college level. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS Version 21, utilizing both parametric and nonparametric tests to analyze the data collected from the experimental and control groups.

The findings revealed that the Eco-inquiry modules were rated as nearly outstanding by subject matter and pedagogical experts across all evaluation criteria. The readability index confirmed the modules were appropriate for the target college-level audience. Regarding student performance, the study found no positive correlation between students' pretest and posttest achievement scores and their grades in prerequisite subjects. However, students in the experimental group, exposed to inquiry-based learning, performed significantly better on the achievement test than those in the control group.

In terms of conceptual understanding, students in the inquiry-based learning group demonstrated significantly better understanding of environmental concepts through concept mapping than the control group. Analysis of these concept maps through propositional complexity showed that the experimental group had a higher pretest-posttest percent difference. Furthermore, an examination of graphical sophistication indicated a notable shift from simple to network-type concept maps among students in the experimental group. Interestingly, the study found no correlation between the experimental group's posttest achievement scores and their conceptual understanding of environmental concepts via concept maps.

The study also found that the experimental group showed a significantly better understanding of the nature of science through the SUSSI scale compared to the control group. Specifically, there was a significant difference in the experimental group's pretest and posttest mean scores regarding the social and cultural embeddedness and the creativity and imagination aspects of the nature of science. Student evaluations of the Eco-inquiry modules as learner-centered materials showed that students learned topics related to environmental issues, protection, and tourism impact in the cognitive domain, while professionalism received the highest mark in the affective domain. Qualitative observations by faculty members rated the implementation of the inquiry-based learning—specifically planning, preparation, classroom management, instruction, and professionalism—as outstanding. Faculty noted that students were encouraged to produce creative works and were prompted to ask questions and provide feedback during presentations. Finally, the experimental group's mean scores for the college's learner-centered practices were equal to or higher than those of the control group.

The conclusions of the study suggest that inquiry-based learning is an effective pedagogical tool for enhancing student achievement, conceptual understanding, and understanding of the nature of science. The results indicate that the Eco-inquiry modules serve as effective learner-centered instructional materials. Based on these findings, the researcher recommends that inquiry-based learning be integrated with conventional teaching and menu-type guided approaches in scientific investigations to better reflect how professional scientists generate and validate knowledge.

The implications for educators and administrators are significant. Because tourism education is multidisciplinary, the study suggests that teachers should design scientific investigations that incorporate aspects of the nature of science and environmental concepts. For administrators, the study recommends organizing training, seminars, and workshops focused on inquiry-based strategies integrated with the nature of science. Finally, the researcher suggests that because the outcomes of inquiry-based learning are multifaceted, future research should expand to include variables such as literacy skills, scientific skills, attitudes toward specific disciplines, inquiry skills, and higher-order thinking skills.

title: Institutional Characteristics, Mathematics Teacher Educator Qualities and Extent of Curriculum Adaptation
abstract:
The study aimed to explore institutional characteristics. qualities of mathematics teacher educators (MTEs), and extent of cuniculum adaptation by institutions and by MTEs as to adoption time, compliance le,·cl. and degree of innovation in adapting the revised Bachelor of Secondary Education-Mathematics (BS Ed-Math) cun-iculum; as well as the effects of institutional characteristics and MTE qualities on extent of curriculum adaptation at the institutional and classroom levels. At the classroom level, cuniculum adaptation by the MTEs focused on the use of inquiry mathematics teaching and technology integration in their BSEd-Math classes. 

Combining qualitative and quantitative approaches, the mixed-methods research was conducted in 10 state teacher education institutions (TEis) in Central Luzon offering the BS ED-Math curriculum. Initially, survey data were collected from 10 administrators and 37 MTEs from the 10 state TEis. For the follow-up inquiry, one low-performing, one middle-performing, and two high-performing institutions were selected based on the numbers of their BSED-Math graduates and percentages of passers in the Licensure Examination for Teachers in the last five years prior to the survey. Data were gathered through interviews with MTEs and BSEd-Math students, classroom observations, and related documents. The content validated survey instruments were tried out in two satellite campuses of a state university in the Region, yielding acceptable Cronbach alpha coefficients (0. 77 to 0.85). Triangulation was used to establish credibility and authenticity of information. Qualitative data were content analyzed and coded using appropriate rubrics for quantitative treatment. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, linear regression, and correlation. Critical comparative analysis was also used to explore the underlying factors of curriculum adaptation at the institutional and classroom levels

title: Small-Group Case-Based Teaching: Effects on Student Achievement, Critical Thinking, And Attitude Toward Chemistry
abstract:
The effects of Small-Group Case-Based Teaching (SGCBT) on college chemistry students’ achievement, critical thinking, and attitude toward chemistry including the relationships between each of these variables were determined.

A quasi-experimental counterbalanced design with pre-post control group was used to determine the effects of SGCBT on Engineering students of four intact classes (two treatment groups and two control groups) in one of the State Universities in Mindanao. The independent variables are the type of teaching approach (SGCBT versus pure lecture-discussion teaching or PLDT) while the dependent variables are chemistry achievement (exam scores) and scores in critical thinking and chemistry attitude.

Both Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) and t-tests (within and between groups and gain scores) were used to compare the effects of SGCBT versus PLDT on students’ chemistry achievement, critical thinking, and attitude toward chemistry, while Pearson product-moment
correlation coefficients were calculated to determine the relationships between each of the variables.

Results show that the use of SGCBT fosters positive attitude toward chemistry and provides some indications as well on improved chemistry achievement of students compared with PLDT. Meanwhile, the effects of PLDT and SGCBT on critical thinking are comparable.
Furthermore, correlational analysis and focus group interviews indicate that the use of SGCBT not only supports the development of positive attitude towards chemistry but also improves chemistry achievement of students.

Implications are provided in view of the recent findings on SGCBT and topics for further research are presented as well.

Reynante E. Autida investigated the effects of Small-Group Case-Based Teaching (SGCBT) on educational outcomes for college chemistry students. The study focused on determining how this approach influences student achievement, critical thinking skills, and attitudes toward chemistry, while exploring the potential relationships between these three variables. This research addressed the need to evaluate whether moving from traditional methods toward a collaborative, case-based approach can yield better results in science education.

The study was situated within a State University in Mindanao, focusing on Engineering students. The researcher utilized a quasi-experimental counterbalanced design involving a pre-post control group setup. Four intact classes were divided into two treatment groups and two control groups. The independent variable was the type of teaching approach, comparing SGCBT against the traditional pure lecture-discussion teaching (PLDT) method. The dependent variables included chemistry achievement, quantified through exam scores, as well as scores related to critical thinking and attitudes toward chemistry.

The findings indicate that SGCBT has a notable impact on student perceptions and performance. The results show that SGCBT fosters a positive attitude toward chemistry among students. Regarding academic performance, the data provides indications of improved chemistry achievement for students taught via SGCBT compared to those taught through PLDT. However, when examining critical thinking skills, the study found that the effects of PLDT and SGCBT were comparable.

Focus group interviews provided deeper insight into the student experience. Both the correlational analysis and qualitative feedback indicate that SGCBT does more than support a positive attitude; it also serves to improve chemistry achievement. This suggests a synergistic relationship where the engagement provided by case-based learning may contribute to better academic outcomes. The research demonstrates that SGCBT is an effective pedagogical tool for enhancing student attitudes and achievement in college-level chemistry.

title: Lesson Study, Impact on Teachers’ Practices, Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK), and On Students’ Cognitive Skills and Attitude Toward Biology
abstract:
Grounded on the research-established advantages of Lesson Study (LS) on the professional development of teachers in other countries as well as in the basic education in the Philippines, a study aimed at establishing the impact of Lesson Study on the practices,
pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPCK) of two College Biology teachers was conducted. Following the design-based research, the effect of the artifact developed by the LS- participating teachers constitutes LS- generated teaching materials which included one Lesson Guide for each lesson on the attitude and cognitive skills of 57 college Biology students was also determined. Findings show that LS improved the practices and self-evaluated PCK and TPCK, and student-rated subject matter knowledge and TPCK of teachers whereas LS-generated teaching materials significantly increase the cognitive skills and improve the attitudes of students toward Biology. In conclusion, participating in three cycles of LS contributed to better preparation of teachers for their classes, their PCK and TPCK and these were translated to enhanced cognitive skills and attitude of students. A professional development model that is able to address the challenges of adopting LS in the College is also proposed.

Using a design-based research methodology, the study involved two college biology teachers participating in three cycles of LS. The primary artifacts produced during this process were a set of LS-generated teaching materials, including one Lesson Guide for each lesson.

The findings indicate that the Lesson Study process positively impacted the participating teachers, leading to improvements in their professional practices and self-evaluated levels of PCK and TPCK. Student ratings further reflected improvements in the teachers' subject matter knowledge and TPCK. Beyond teacher development, the teaching materials generated through the LS process significantly increased the cognitive skills of the 57 college biology students involved. Additionally, the students demonstrated improved attitudes toward Biology as a result of the intervention.

The study concludes that the three cycles of Lesson Study contributed to better class preparation for teachers, which translated into enhanced cognitive skills and improved attitudes among students. The research demonstrates that the collaborative and iterative nature of Lesson Study is an effective mechanism for enhancing both teaching quality and student learning outcomes in a college biology setting. Consequently, the study proposes a professional development model designed to address the specific challenges of implementing Lesson Study within a higher education setting.

The findings revealed significant differences in mathematics anxiety among the groups. title: Integrated Metacognitive Instruction: Effects on Students Learning Strategies, Volition, and Achievement in Biology
abstract: The study investigated the effects of integrated metacognitive instruction (IMI) to student leaming strategies, volition, and achievement in Biology. Using a quasi-experimental design, it utilized both quantitative and qualitative methods of data analysis to (1) determine the change in the leaming strategies of students in the control and experimental groups; (2) analyze IMI effect on students' volition; (3) identify the improvement in students' achievement using IMI compared to the conventional approach; (4) correlate students' achievement with their leaming stratégies and volition in IMI; and (5) identify the IMI strategies that students prefer after its implementation. The sample consisted of two intact classes each with 36 freshmen Bachelor of Science in Biology students enrolled at a state university in central Philippines taking up five-unit General Biology I in the first semester of the Academic Year 2013-2014. The control group was taught using the usual chalk-and-board method and provîded with varied visual teaching aids through power point présentations, video clips, and charts. On the other hand, aside from this usual method, the experimental group was exposed to reflective questions, collaborative group discussions, writing journals, and concept mapping. Semi-structured interviews on students' learning perceptions through open-ended questions, student's written reflections, questionnaires, journal notes, and interviews with key informants, and the teacher's observation of action in the natural setting were analyzed qualitatively. Statistical tools used in the study employed both descriptive and inferential statistics. Based on frequency and percent age, there is a difference between the most and least preferred leaming strategies between the experimental and control groups. The experimental group ranked high the rehearsal, critical thinking, and peer learning while they ranked low the organization, and time and study environment management after exposing them to IMI. IMl approach has signifîcantly changed students' volition after its implementation as indicated in Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test (Z=2.134, p=0.033). However, the Mann-Whitney U test for independent samples shows no significant difference in the volition mean scores between the control and IM groups after the intervention (p > 0.05). Both groups performed well in the achievement tests, however, the IMI group performed signifîcantly better than the control group after the intervention (p < 0.05). A significant correlation between critical thinking leaming strategy in the experimental group and emotional control in the volition strategy of the control group and students' academic achievement in Biology were observed using Spearman correlation coefficient (p < 0.05). Based on the content analysis of students' responses on interview and excerpts from their journal notes, the students in the experimental group liked some of the IMI components such as student collaboration, conceptual learning, and active student involvement while some students indicated some issues with IMI implementation such as the lack of time, lack of cooperation, and lack of self-confîdence. Though IMI has potentially improved students' achievement, its implementation should consider these issues. If mitigated, students may respond differently, and would find learning more fun and easy.

title: Gender Difference in Mathematics Achievement in Korea Singapore: Influence of Sociocultural Factors and Student Attitude Towards Mathematics
abstract:
This study examined, for Korean and Singaporean eight-grade students, if there were significant sociocultural differences that influenced different gender performance levels in mathematics achievement in the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study
(TIMSS) in 2011. From TIMSS 1995 to TIMSS 2011, Korean girls have been consistently underperforming compared with boys, and Singaporean girls have been consistently outperforming the boys in mathematics achievement. Compared to Singapore, Korea maintains
a relatively lower gender equity level. This developed a conceptual model to analyze the influence of sociocultural factors and student attitude towards mathematics-on-mathematics achievement for Korean and Singaporean students.

The TIMSS 2011 mathematics achievement scores and student questionnaire responses form 5,165 Korean and 5, 923 Singaporean eight-grade students were analyzed for the study. Inferential statistics such as correlation analysis, factor analysis, multiple regression analysis,
and path analysis were conducted for the study. Interviews were conducted individually with 13 Korean students and 2 teachers to substantiate the quantitative analysis of the study.

half:
This study investigates gender differences in mathematics achievement between eighth-grade students in Korea and Singapore, focusing on the influence of sociocultural factors and student attitudes. Analysis of TIMSS data from 1995 to 2011 reveals a distinct divergence: Korean girls consistently underperform compared to boys, whereas Singaporean girls consistently outperform boys. Furthermore, Korea maintains a lower level of gender equity than Singapore.

Using a mixed-methods approach involving TIMSS 2011 data and qualitative interviews, the researcher found significant differences in parental involvement. In Korea, girls receive less parental involvement than boys, which negatively impacts their confidence and mathematics achievement. Qualitative data confirmed that Korean girls experience lower confidence, lower levels of liking mathematics, and lower levels of valuing mathematics compared to Korean boys. Conversely, Singaporean students showed no significant gender differences in parental involvement, liking, or valuing mathematics. Teacher influence was found to be relatively equitable in both nations.

Regarding achievement predictors, being confident with mathematics was the most significant predictor in both countries. For Korean students, both valuing and feeling confident with mathematics significantly affected achievement, though liking the subject had no significant effect. For Singaporean students, valuing mathematics had no significant effect on achievement. title: Development and Validation of Small-Scale Chemistry Experiments Using Local Materials
abstract:
Small-scale chemistry experiments were developed and validated in response to a perceived need to carry out laboratory chemistry activities individually among freshmen in tertiary institutions and to disseminate widely a laboratory capability for chemistry activities
among secondary schools. For this purpose, the researcher developed and validated a General Chemistry Laboratory Module of Small-Scale Experiments on the following topics: Element, Compound and Mixture; Physical and Chemical Changes; Ionic and Covalent Bonding; Types of Chemical Reactions; and Acids and Bases. Accordingly, the study investigated the effects of the small-scale chemistry experiments on achievement, concept understanding, level of participation, and attitude of students.

The study is quasi-experimental and followed a non-equivalent pretest-posttest control design. Forty-four freshman B.S Medical Technology students enrolled in Chemistry 101 served as participants. The experimental and control groups consisted of five groups each composed of 22 students. They were drawn through random selection from the ten peer-defined groups formed in the laboratory class at the start of the semester. The experimental group used the develop small-scale chemistry experiments while the control group used the traditional macroscale laboratory experiments.

Validated multiple-choice test with a KR-20 of 0.66 over the five percent topics, measured the achievement of the students while concept mapping assessed their conceptual understanding the concept maps were scored by the researcher and validated by another
expert. Interrater reliability averaged 0.81 and 0.85 for pretest and posttest results respectively. Results show, in general, again in achievement and concept understanding between pretest and posttest for each group, with the experimental group exhibiting a higher overall mean of percent gain both achievement and conceptual understanding. The two groups, however, do not significantly differ in achievement and conceptual understanding in each test period. The multiple-choice test and concept map scored of the experimental group show remarkable associations in the five experiments in both pretest and posttest.

title: Students' Academic Performance and Conceptual Knowledge in Microbiology and Parasitology taught with Problem Based Learning Approach
abstract:
Problem-based learning (PBL) is a student-centered educational approach in which complex problems serve as the context and stimulus for learning. It was developed in medical education where traditional forms of instruction left students with plenty of knowledge but lack skills in using that knowledge in solving patients’ problematic health cases. The lecture method in health science education by rote memorization promotes difficulty in achieving deep content learning with influences the learner’s ability to apply knowledge to novel problems. It is in this context that this study aimed to investigate the effect of the PBL-based approach on students’ academic performance and conceptual knowledge in the Microbiology and Parasitology course.

The study used a quasi-experimental research design and involved 62 second-year nursing students who were enrolled in a Microbiology and Parasitology course during the second semester of the academic year 2010-2011. These students were grouped into the
control and treatment groups based on the teaching strategy employed. The control group received the conventional lecture approach while the treatment group received the PBL-based approach. The students’ academic performance and conceptual knowledge were measured through the use of pre-posttests and final examination. The group did not differ in their pretest scores but showed significant differences in the posttest results (posttest I t = .000; p>0.05, posttest II t = .000; p<.0.05) in favor of the PBL group. Final Examination of the PBL group is significantly higher than the lecture group (t = .000; p<0.05). While Wilcoxon signed-rank, the test revealed no significant difference between the pre and post-test (I and II) of the lecture group (p = 0.116 and p = 0.092, respectively; p>.05). The results indicated significantly higher academic achievement and better conceptual knowledge in the PBL mode. No statistically significant differences were found between male and female students in terms of their learning in Microbiology and Parasitology concepts thru PBL-based approach.

title: Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge in Proportional Reasoning of Undergraduate Students
abstract:
This study investigated the causal relationships between conceptual and procedural knowledge in mathematics using an East Asian perspective. In particular, it studied if supplemental self-paced instruction that focuses on the mastery of either concepts or procedures through repetition with variation helps young adults improve their performance in tasks designed to assess their proportional reasoning understanding and skills. It also studied if a task’s type of physical principle of type of mathematical principle influences the effects of a
type of instruction.

This experimental research used a pretest-posttest control group design with participants randomly assigned to three groups (conceptual, procedural, and control). The participants were 46 undergraduates (mostly freshman) from three sections of a college algebra course in a private, Catholic, coeducational university in the Bicol Region. The pretest/posttest consisted of 69 multiple-choice questions that varied in physical and mathematical principles. Each participant in the two treatment groups was to answer one worksheet per day for eleven consecutive days. The worksheets for the conceptual group involved non-numeric tasks and those for the procedural group involved numeric tasks. Because of the small sample size, a non-parametric two-tailed test of hypothesis (Kruskal-Wallis one-way analyses of variance by ranks) was used.

There was evidence that supplemental procedural instruction significantly differed from supplemental conceptual instruction and from the absence of supplemental instruction in affecting the degree of procedural knowledge.

There was no evidence that the type of supplemental instruction affected the degree of conceptual knowledge, or that the type of physical principle or the type of mathematical principle affected how a type of supplemental instruction affected the degree of conceptual knowledge.

Future studies using larger sample size and a longer treatment period could provide additional evidence for this study’s findings.

title: Realistic Mathematics Approach, Mathematical Communication and Problem-Solving Skills of High-Functioning Autistic Children: A Case Study
abstract:

title: Effects of Language and Other Correlates in Learning College Organic Chemistry
abstract:
English is used as a Second Language across the Philippine curriculum including the tertiary level but literature still lacks evidence concerning the effectiveness of the use of the second language in science teaching. Science teachers are faced with a challenge because
students who are English learners have at least two major tasks to accomplish: 1) they must learn English, and 2) they must learn new knowledge contained in that language. In the light of the ongoing advocacy for bilingual instruction, the main objective of the study was to create a language model in one of the major universities in Baguio City that supports instruction in two or more languages in the tertiary level that could complement the linguistic and cultural heterogeneity of the City. Using a non-equivalent quasi-experimental design, the study compared the academic achievements of the two intact organic chemistry classes for one semester in the first semester of the school year 2011-2012 where one was taught using monolingual English instruction (control group), while the other was taught using bilingual instruction (experimental group). The two groups were comparable except on their knowledge of general and inorganic chemistry concepts prior to the treatment. The latter obtained a significantly higher mean rating than the former. Moreover, both groups were comparable in their high level of English and Filipino proficiencies and good science attitude before and after the treatment. Majority of both groups preferred bilingual mode in learning organic chemistry. In terms of language preference in teaching, majority of the experimental group preferred bilingual while majority of the other group preferred English. In the scientific idea test, the mean score of the experimental group was higher than the mean score of the control group but the difference was not statistically significant. After seven quizzes and three examinations, the mean gain scores of the two groups were significantly different, with the experimental group achieving a high gain. In the experimental group, there were significant positive correlations between academic performance and English language proficiency, Filipino language proficiency and Chemistry Diagnostic Test result while in the control group there were significant positive correlations between academic performance and English language proficiency, attitude toward science and Chemistry Diagnostic Test result. Multiple regression analysis revealed that Filipino language proficiency was a significant predictor of academic performance in the experimental group while Chemistry Diagnostic test result, attitude towards science, mothers’ years of schooling and Ilokano home language was a significant predictor of academic performance in the control group. The results of the study show that students in the experimental group were not disadvantaged by bilingual teaching instead it resulted in several benefits on the part of the
Filipino learner. Quantitative and qualitative analyses revealed that majority of the students had shown support to bilingual instruction indicating that it is possible for tertiary schools in Baguio City to develop bilingual policy that supports the use of Filipino and English languages in teaching science subjects. The results, in general, suggest that academic achievement and scientific ideas learned in organic chemistry are influenced by the language used in class taking into consideration student characteristics which include English and Filipino language proficiencies, scientific attitude, language preference and general chemistry background. However, context variables involving ethnicity, parents’ educational attainment and language spoken at home do not pose significant effects on science academic achievement.

title: Experiential-Learning Approach and Scientific Literacy Dimensions of Objectivism, Personal and Social Constructivism
abstract:
This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the Experiential-learning Approach in enhancing the development of scientific literacy of students in Biological Science (NSCS002).

A total of 62 students participated in the study. They were divided into two sections and each section was randomly assigned to either the Traditional Lecture method (TLM) or the Experiential Learning Approach (ELA) group. The researcher employed the Experiential-learning Approach (ELA) in teaching the topics in Biology to the students in the ELA group while the Traditional Lecture Method (TLM) of teaching that involved lecture was used in the TLM group.

The improvement in the three dimensions of scientific literacy and skills of the students in both groups was determined through the use of the pre-post Scientific Literacy Test. The t-test was conducted to determine any significant difference in the performance of the students in both groups. The results, however, were triangulated with Jourdan writing and interview. 

The study found out that the posttest score of the ELA group was computed to be 32.7% higher than the mean score of the TLM and is significant at p = 0.05. In terms of the level of scientific literacy, 61% of the population in ELA group achieved personal constructivism after the intervention while there was none in the TLM group. It was also the ELA group that showed more progress in the achievement of different skills. These results may imply a greater improvement in the retention and understanding of biological concepts among the students in the former than in the latter group. The results underscore the fact the ELA has an edge over TLM.

title: Multimodal-Representation Approach: Effects on Students Conceptual Understanding, Science Process Skills, and Attitude in Genetics
abstract:
This study investigated the effects of the multimodal-representation approach in teaching college biology on students’ conceptual understanding, science process skills, and science attitude.

An instructional material based on a standard tertiary level General Biology course employing multimodal- representation (descriptive, mathematical, analogical, and experimental of scientific concepts and processes was designed and compared against the traditional
approach to teaching. The topic content focused on genetics, which comprised a unit in a three-unit General Biology (Natural Science 2). The instruments developed and used were the Genetics Conceptual Understanding Test, Science Process Skills Rubrics, Science Literacy
Test, Science Attitude Scale and Focus Group Discussion Guide. 

This research employed a quasi-experimental design where data was gathered from two intact classes of college non-science freshman from a local university in the province of Laguna. The researcher handled the experimental and control groups for the duration of one semester with actual intervention of five weeks equivalent to 25 hours.

The study utilized a quasi-experimental design involving two intact classes of non-science freshman students at a university in Laguna. The experimental group received instruction using descriptive, mathematical, analogical, and experimental representations over five weeks, while the control group was taught using traditional methods.

The findings revealed that students in the experimental group achieved significantly higher scores in both the Genetics Conceptual Understanding Test and the Science Process Skills rubrics compared to the control group. While quantitative results showed no reliable statistical evidence of improved science attitudes, qualitative data from focus group discussions indicated an improved appreciation and attitude towards science.

Correlational analyses showed that prior science knowledge positively correlated with conceptual understanding. Regarding demographics, male students performed better in science process skills, and students from high-income families showed an advantage in both conceptual understanding and science process skills. Among the modalities, descriptive representation was most preferred, while mathematical representation was least preferred. The study concluded that the multimodal-representation approach is effective for enhancing conceptual understanding and science process skills, particularly when representations are repeated, helping students master complex biological topics.

title: Context Based Mathematics Problem Solving Cognitive and Affective Effects on BIT and BS Voc-Tech Students
abstract:
This study compared the cognitive and affective effects of the Context-Based and Traditional approach on voc-tech students taking the ladderized Bachelor of Industrial Technology major in Electricity/Electronics (BIT) and the fourth-year Bachelor of Science in Electricity/Electronics (BS Voc-tech) degree program. The study was conducted for twelve weeks and included units of instruction in fractions, decimals, percent, ratio and proportion, measurement and linear equations. Four intact classes of 27 students each at a state college in Western Visayas participated in the study.

Quantitative data were collected using a Pretest and Posttest examination in mathematics problem solving to assess the levels of students’ problem-solving performance and an attitude, beliefs and confidence (A-B-C) questionnaire to assess the voc-tech students,
attitude, belief and confidence. For qualitative analysis, the students’ journals, interview responses, and the teacher observers’ and raters’ notes and comments were analyzed.

Based on the pretest of the mathematics problem-solving test and the A-B-C questionnaire, the results showed that the students have a very low analytic level and limited content knowledge in mathematics prior the intervention. However, the context-based approach,
anchored on a constructivist belief, enhanced the students’ problem-solving skills as exhibited by the numerically higher scores and improvement in the quality of the experimental class’ solutions and responses to the problem-solving posttest. Also, the students had a neutral attitude towards problem-solving, a constructivist-traditional belief, and an average confidence level at the onset of the study.

title: The Actuarial Science Program in the Philippines: A Historical and Curricular Development Perspective
abstract:
The primary objective of this research was to trace the history and the development of the Actuarial Science Program curriculum in the Philippines through the use of the historical method which is a qualitative research method.

The study also sought the congruence of the goals and constructs of the Actuarial Science Program with the needs of the learners, the society, and the fund of knowledge. It analyzed how the learning objectives, curriculum content, and learning resources have  contributed towards the accomplishment of the Program goals. It assessed the impact of major economic, political, and social developments and trends on the Actuarial Society of the  Philippines (ASP), and foreign universities. The study likewise assessed the sustainability of the
present set-up and its implications with regard to the maintenance of the professional status of Actuarial Science.

Data and information were gathered from three universities in Metro Manila through the use of document analysis, questionnaires, and interviews with students, graduates and their employers, faculty members, and chairpersons of the Actuarial Science Program.

half:
Sabina Rachel B. Arada’s research investigates the historical and curricular evolution of the Actuarial Science Program in the Philippines. Using a qualitative approach and the historical method, the study examined three universities in Metro Manila through document analysis, questionnaires, and interviews with students, graduates, employers, faculty, and program chairpersons. The research aimed to trace curriculum development and evaluate its congruence with the needs of learners, society, and the existing fund of knowledge.

The findings reveal that the program was established to satisfy the growing domestic demand for actuaries and the requirements of the Actuarial Society of the Philippines (ASP). A significant finding is that the program's goals, curriculum content, syllabi, learning materials, and teaching processes were largely influenced by the ASP examination syllabus. Although curriculum revisions occurred as actuaries entered non-traditional areas, these changes were slower than the social, political, and economic developments affecting the field. The research noted that curricula were not updated to include subjects related to these non-traditional areas, and there were no changes in faculty characteristics or teaching processes despite a continuous need for more actuaries.

The study concludes that the curriculum must remain consistent with university goals, the actuarial profession, society, and student growth to maintain the field's professional status. Recommendations include conducting data-driven curriculum reviews every three to five years and establishing stronger linkages with corporate agencies, the ASP, and foreign universities.

title: Sustained Community-Based In-Service Training and the Teaching Competency of Secondary School Chemistry Teachers
abstract:
This study attempted to determine the impact of a sustained community-based in-service training (SCBINSET) on the teaching competency of secondary school chemistry teachers. The in-service training was done by conducting seminar workshops for four Saturdays, followed by collaboration among the trained teachers and researchers to sustain the application of new learning to their classrooms. The topics covered were Chemical Change and Energy, Solutions, Solutions at Work, and Carbon Compounds.

The impact of the in-service training in improving the teachers’ competency in knowledge content was determined by comparing the pretest and posttest scores of 21 chemistry teacher-participants and by analysis of mastery of the subject matter through classroom
observations of six case teachers. The influence of the teachers’ characteristics on their content knowledge was analyzed by comparing the gain scores and classroom performances of teachers grouped according to characteristics. The influence of the training in improving the teachers’ competency in employing teaching strategies, asking different types of questions, constructing evaluation items, and giving of assignments was analyzed by observing six case teachers in the classroom, interview, and documentary analysis of lesson plans and quarterly examinations.

The instruments used were the chemistry test, survey questionnaire on teacher’s profile, questionnaire on chemistry teaching efficacy belief, questionnaire on attitudes toward teaching chemistry and in-service training, classroom observation form, and post-training interview form. The pretest and posttest results in the chemistry test were compared by t-test for dependent samples. Comparison in gain scores of teachers grouped according to characteristics was analyzed by using Wilcoxon Mann-Whitney test for two groups and Kruskal Wallis for three groups.

The research addressed the need to improve teacher performance through a training model that extends beyond traditional one-time seminars by incorporating ongoing collaboration between trained teachers and researchers to ensure the application of new learning within the classroom setting.

The context of the research involved a group of 21 chemistry teacher-participants. The training program consisted of seminar-workshops conducted over four Saturdays, focusing on specific chemistry topics: Chemical Change and Energy, Solutions, Solutions at Work, and Carbon Compounds. To ensure the training was sustained, the researchers engaged in collaborative efforts with the teachers following the workshops to support the implementation of new pedagogical approaches and content knowledge in their respective classrooms.

The researcher employed a multi-faceted methodology to assess the impact of the SCBINSET. However, the content knowledge gained was influenced by the number of years of teaching chemistry and the teachers' attitudes toward in-service training.

The training also improved the quality of classroom interaction through the types of questions asked by teachers. Furthermore, the teachers showed increased competency in constructing evaluation items, specifically through an increased number of items covering the topics addressed in the training and a shift toward higher levels of learning outcomes.

These collaborative efforts enabled teachers to explain unexpected results from class experiments, facilitated the use of improvised apparatus, provided instructional ideas for specific lessons, and helped correct teacher misconceptions and errors.

The conclusions drawn from the study indicate that the knowledge and teaching strategies acquired through the SCBINSET were durable, as teachers continued to apply them in the school year following the program. title: The Quality of the Student's Mathematical Proofs as a Function of Classroom Assessment A Qualitative-Quantitative Analysis
abstract:
In this quasi-experimental study mathematical proof writing is views as a problem-solving activity success at which requires adequate knowledge of relevant mathematical content and logical rules of inference, familiarity with heuristic proof-writing techniques, metacognitive skills, and positive effects towards self and mathematics. The extent to which two types of classroom assessment – traditional (TA) and learner-centered (LCA) – provided these cognitive and affective requisites is described on the basis of a quantitative and qualitative analysis of their effects on the quality of students’ mathematical proofs and selected affective variables such as attitudes towards mathematics, motivation, self-confidence, mathematics anxiety, and test anxiety.

Two intact undergraduate classes of fifty-one (51) students in Linear Algebra at the University of the Philippines Visayas Main Campus in Miag-ao, Iloilo during the Second Semester, 2002-2003, constituted the sample for the study. The traditional and learner-centered
classroom assessments were randomly assigned to the control and experimental groups, respectively.

Each member of the experimental (LCA) and control (TA) groups wrote proofs for seven propositions which were scored blind by two raters using 4-point criteria (key mathematical understanding, logical validity, mathematical communication, and clarity and simplicity) specified in a researcher-constructed anaholistic proof-writing rubric. The proofs were also qualitatively assessed to determine the nature and extent of the subjects’ understanding of the key mathematical content and identify logical fallacies committed as well as instances of inappropriate use of language, mathematical terminology and notation. The long-term effects of classroom assessment on proof quality were determined through a comparison of the mean index values obtained by the two groups in all criteria indicators, including the frequencies of manifestations of validity, soundness, consistency, and fallacious reasoning in these profs.

The researcher defines proof writing as a complex activity requiring mathematical content knowledge, logical inference, heuristic techniques, metacognitive skills, and positive affective states. The research aims to determine whether traditional assessment (TA) or learner-centered assessment (LCA) better provides the cognitive and affective requisites for successful proof writing.

Using a quasi-experimental design with two intact Linear Algebra classes at the University of the Philippines Visayas Main Campus, the study employed a mixed-methods approach. Proof quality was assessed through seven propositions scored via an anaholistic rubric, while affective variables were measured using a 38-item Affective Inventory and qualitative interviews.

Findings indicate no significant differences in proof quality between the TA and LCA groups for the first five propositions. However, for the more difficult Propositions 6 and 7, the LCA group obtained consistently higher ratings, with a statistically significant difference for Proposition 7. This suggests LCA improves proof quality as task difficulty increases. Regarding affective outcomes, the LCA group reported more positive attitudes toward mathematics and felt more challenged by difficult problems. Conversely, the TA group exhibited increased test anxiety and discomfort with mathematical symbols. The results suggest that learner-centered assessments may be more effective than traditional assessments in fostering long-term improvements in proof writing and positively impacting students' affective relationship with mathematics.

This is further supported by mean index values, which showed a greater cumulative improvement in proof-writing skills for the LCA group over time.

Significant differences were also found in affective outcomes. Students in the LCA group reported more positive attitudes toward mathematics, noting they liked the subject more, viewed it as their favorite, and felt more challenged by difficult problems. They also felt a stronger influence from the teacher and were less motivated by material incentives. In contrast, the TA group showed a significant reduction in frustration regarding previous learning and a greater interest in knowing more about the subject, but they also exhibited increased test anxiety and discomfort with numbers and mathematical symbols. The results suggest that learner-centered assessments may be more effective than traditional assessments in fostering long-term improvements in mathematical proof-writing, particularly as tasks increase in difficulty, and have a profound impact on students' affective relationship with mathematics.

The study investigates the relationship between different types of classroom assessment and the quality of mathematical proof writing among undergraduate students. The researcher views mathematical proof writing as a complex problem-solving activity that requires a combination of mathematical content knowledge, logical rules of inference, familiarity with heuristic techniques, metacognitive skills, and positive affective states toward mathematics and the self. The core problem addressed is determining the extent to which traditional assessment (TA) and learner-centered assessment (LCA) provide the necessary cognitive and affective requisites for successful proof writing.

The research was conducted during the second semester of the 2002-2003 academic year at the University of the Philippines Visayas Main Campus in Miag-ao, Iloilo. The sample consisted of two intact undergraduate Linear Algebra classes, each containing 51 students. The study employed a quasi-experimental design where the traditional assessment group served as the control group and the learner-centered assessment group served as the experimental group.

The methodology utilized a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative analyses. To assess the quality of mathematical proofs, students from both groups wrote proofs for seven different propositions. These proofs were scored blindly by two raters using a researcher-constructed anaholistic rubric featuring a 4-point scale based on four criteria: key mathematical understanding, logical validity, mathematical communication, and clarity and simplicity. Qualitatively, the proofs were analyzed to determine the depth of understanding of mathematical content and to identify logical fallacies, as well as the inappropriate use of language, terminology, and notation.

To measure the long-term effects of the assessments on proof quality, the researcher compared mean index values across all criteria indicators and analyzed the frequencies of validity, soundness, consistency, and fallacious reasoning. To assess affective variables, the study used a 38-item Affective Inventory administered as pre- and post-tests. This quantitative data was supplemented by qualitative interview data regarding the students' perceptions and impressions of their learning experiences in the course. Additionally, the researcher identified four specific categories of learning difficulties encountered by both groups: difficulties with the form and substance of a proof, difficulties understanding proofs for theorems and theoretical exercises, difficulties understanding key content and their relationships, and confusion regarding mathematical terminology and notation.

The findings indicate that there were no significant differences in the quality of proofs produced by the TA and LCA groups for Propositions 1 through 5. However, a divergence appeared with the more difficult Propositions 6 and 7. For these more challenging propositions, the LCA group obtained consistently higher ratings than the TA group, a difference that was found to be statistically significant for Proposition 7. This suggests a consistent and significant improvement in the quality of proofs produced by the LCA group during the final three weeks of the teaching experiment. This conclusion is reinforced by the mean index values and the frequencies of logical manifestations; the cumulative change in mean index values for the LCA group in Proofs 5 through 7 was greater than that of the TA group, indicating a greater cumulative improvement in proof-writing skills over time.

The study also revealed significant differences in the affective outcomes between the two groups. Students in the LCA group reported more positive attitudes toward mathematics, noting that they liked the subject more, regarded it as their favorite subject, and felt more challenged by difficult problems. They also showed a stronger agreement regarding the influence of the teacher on their performance and felt less motivated by material incentives like money. Conversely, the TA group experienced a significant reduction in frustration regarding their previous learning of mathematics, showed a greater interest in knowing more about the subject, and expressed a preference for discussing and learning mathematics with others. However, the TA group also exhibited increased levels of test anxiety and discomfort when dealing with numbers and mathematical symbols. Interestingly, the TA group reported a better understanding of geometry and trigonometry than algebra.

The implications of these findings suggest that learner-centered classroom assessments may be more effective than traditional assessments in fostering long-term improvements in mathematical proof-writing skills, particularly when students encounter increasingly difficult mathematical tasks. The results also suggest that the type of assessment used has a profound impact on students' affective relationship with mathematics, with learner-centered approaches appearing to foster more positive attitudes and a greater sense of challenge, while traditional approaches may impact anxiety levels and specific subject interests.

Juanita M. Costillas investigated the effectiveness of the situated-cognition teaching model in enhancing the mathematical problem-solving skills of first-year engineering students at SLSU and the extent to which these skills transfer to other academic domains. Using a Non-Equivalent Control Group Design during the 2007-2008 academic year, the study compared an experimental group receiving 42 hours of "Enrichment Math" via the situated-cognition model against a control group taught through a conventional model. Data were collected through pretests, posttests, formative tests, interviews, teaching plans, student journals, and domain-specific problem-solving tests.

The findings indicated that the situated-cognition model resulted in significantly better mathematical problem-solving skills than the conventional model. Regarding skill transfer, the situated-cognition model showed a significantly better extent of transfer to General Chemistry, while the conventional model showed a significantly better extent of transfer to Solid Mensuration. No significant difference was found regarding transfer to Analytic Geometry. English proficiency was found to moderate mathematical problem-solving skills and significantly moderated the transfer of skills to Solid Mensuration and General Chemistry, though no interaction effect was found between English proficiency and the teaching model. Qualitative data suggested the situated-cognition model fostered cooperation, common sense, and an eagerness to learn. The researcher recommends implementing the situated-cognition model to complement conventional teaching and suggests conducting parallel studies across different subjects.

Costillas investigated the effectiveness of the situated-cognition teaching model in enhancing the mathematical problem-solving skills of first-year engineering students at SLSU and determining the extent to which these skills could be transferred to other academic domains. The study specifically examined whether students exposed to the situated-cognition model demonstrated superior problem-solving abilities and a greater ability to apply those skills in Analytic Geometry, Solid Mensuration, and General Chemistry compared to students taught through a conventional model. Additionally, the researcher investigated whether English proficiency acted as a moderator in the development and transfer of these skills.

The control group consisted of BSCE students taught through a conventional model. Data were collected using various instruments, including pretests, posttests, formative tests, an interview schedule, situated teaching plans, student journals, and problem-solving tests in target domains.

The findings indicated that the situated-cognition teaching model resulted in significantly better mathematical problem-solving skills (p-value=0.023) than the conventional model. Regarding skill transfer, the situated-cognition model showed a significantly better extent of transfer to General Chemistry (p-value=0.000), where 58% of the experimental group successfully completed the "Looking Back" phase of Polya’s framework compared to 23% of the control group. Conversely, the conventional model showed a significantly better extent of transfer to Solid Mensuration (p-value=0.033), while no significant difference was found regarding transfer to Analytic Geometry.

English proficiency was found to moderate mathematical problem-solving skills, with higher proficiency correlating to better abilities. English proficiency also significantly moderated the transfer of skills to Solid Mensuration (p<-0.05) and General Chemistry (p<0.01), though no interaction effect was found between English proficiency and the specific teaching model used. Qualitative data suggested the situated-cognition model fostered values such as cooperation, common sense, and an eagerness to learn, while improving interactions between teachers and students.

The study concluded that the situated-cognition model can improve mathematical problem-solving skills and their transfer, particularly to General Chemistry, especially for students with higher English proficiency. The study conducted by Juanita M. Costillas investigated the effectiveness of the situated-cognition teaching model in enhancing the mathematical problem-solving skills of students and determining the extent to which these skills could be transferred to other academic domains. The research specifically focused on whether students exposed to the situated-cognition model demonstrated better problem-solving abilities and a greater ability to apply those skills in Analytic Geometry, Solid Mensuration, and General Chemistry compared to students taught through a conventional teaching model. Additionally, the researcher sought to determine if English proficiency acted as a moderator in the development of these problem-solving skills and the subsequent transfer of those skills to other subjects.

The research was conducted during the 2007-2008 academic year with first-year engineering students at SLSU. The study utilized a Non-Equivalent Control Group Design involving two intact classes. One group, consisting of BSME and BSEE students, served as the experimental group exposed to the situated-cognition model, while the BSCE group served as the control group. The intervention consisted of 42 hours of "Enrichment Math" instruction covering Arithmetic, Advanced Algebra, and Trigonometry. The instruction was delivered by the researcher during regular scheduled time slots in the same room for both groups.

To gather data, the researcher employed several instruments, including a Semantic Differential Scale for the content validation of pretests and posttests, formative tests, an interview schedule, 28 situated teaching plans for the experimental group, student journals, and problem-solving tests administered in the other target domains.

The findings indicated that the situated-cognition teaching model resulted in significantly better mathematical problem-solving skills (p-value=0.023) than the conventional teaching model. Regarding the transfer of these skills to other domains, the situated-cognition model showed a significantly better extent of transfer to General Chemistry (p-value=0.000). In this domain, 58% of students in the experimental group were able to successfully navigate through the fourth phase of Polya’s framework, "Looking Back," whereas only 23% of the control group achieved this. Interestingly, the conventional teaching model showed a significantly better extent of transfer of problem-solving skills to Solid Mensuration (p-value=0.033), while no significant difference was found regarding the transfer of skills to Analytic Geometry.

The study also explored the moderating effect of English proficiency. The results showed that English proficiency did moderate mathematical problem-solving skills, with students possessing higher English proficiency tending to demonstrate better problem-solving abilities. English proficiency also significantly moderated the extent of transfer of these skills to Solid Mensuration (p<-0.05) and General Chemistry (p<0.01). However, the study found no interaction effect between English proficiency and the specific teaching model used.

Qualitative data gathered during the study provided further insight into the impact of the situated-cognition model. The results suggested that this model helped develop specific values in students, such as cooperation during group tasks, the use of common sense to obtain more accurate data, and an eagerness to learn new things. Students also realized the importance of mathematical problem-solving skills in both the classroom and everyday life. Furthermore, the model appeared to foster better interactions between teachers and students, as well as among the students themselves.

In conclusion, the study revealed that the situated-cognition teaching model can improve mathematical problem-solving skills and the transfer of those skills to selected domains, particularly General Chemistry, especially for students with higher English proficiency. These findings support the theory of Choi and Hanaffin (1995), which emphasizes the importance of providing realistic ways for students to conceptualize situations to become better problem solvers.

Based on these conclusions, the researcher recommends that the situated-cognition model be implemented as a teaching model to enhance student problem-solving skills or used to complement the conventional model. The study suggests this can be achieved through training for proper dissemination, modeling, and mentoring. Finally, the researcher recommends that parallel studies be conducted using the situated-cognition model across different school subjects, contents, and courses to further confirm these results.
