title: Learning Strategies of High School Biology Students and Improvement of Biology Instruction
abstract:
The study aimed to look into students’ (1) learning aids and strategies as affected by personal factors, and (2) learning environment and their influence on how they learn biology, for the purpose of culling from them some cues that may be useful in improving instruction in high school biology and in motivating students to study harder and to participate actively in the biology class. With the view of eliciting students’ ways of learning biology, journal notes, questionnaire-checklist on personal learning aids/strategies, instructional aids checklist, learning resources rating scale, and class activities rating scale questionnaire were administered to 30 second year students in one of the public high schools in the Visayas.

The respondents represented high, middle and low performers; they were observed in class and interviewed in-depth in separate venues. Class observation report was focused on teaching aids, teaching-learning activities and assessment. To verify and validate the finding in the qualitative data, triangulation was employed.

In quantitative analysis, the statistical tools used were mean, frequencies and percentages. Krushkall Wallis and Mann-Whitney U test were used to determine if there is a significant difference among the respondents in the learning aids/strategies commonly used in
reading, in reviewing for an exam, and in taking down lecture notes when they are grouped according to learning performance, learning style and gender.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Lucy G. Diaz investigated the learning aids, strategies, personal factors, and environmental influences affecting biology instruction among 30 second-year students at a public high school in the Visayas. Utilizing qualitative and quantitative methods, including observations and interviews, the study analyzed high, middle, and low academic performers.

The findings indicate that students differ significantly in their learning strategies and capabilities. A primary finding is that students generally possess inadequate learning skills, specifically lacking proficiency in elaboration, integration, metacognition, organization, recall, study reading, and test-taking. While the textbook is the most dominant instructional tool, students lack the basic skills required to understand it effectively. Furthermore, a lack of science equipment and unavailable materials prevents students from performing necessary experiments.

Environmental factors, such as teaching strategies and classroom setup, significantly impact learning. Students expressed a strong preference for active, hands-on, and collaborative activities, such as laboratory and field work. Conversely, they reported the least interest in lectures, tests, and copying notes from the blackboard, often describing class discussions as teacher-dominated talk.

The study concludes that both personal strategic deficiencies and environmental factors heavily influence biology learning. To improve instruction, educators should address students' needs in metacognition and organization, shift from teacher-dominated lectures toward active and collaborative experiences, and improve the availability of science equipment and learning resources.

The research aimed to identify cues to improve instruction and increase student motivation and participation. The study was conducted at a public high school in the Visayas with 30 second-year students representing high, middle, and low academic performers. Data were collected through journal notes, questionnaires, checklists, and rating scales, utilizing class observations and in-depth interviews. Quantitative analysis included mean, frequencies, percentages, and the Krushkall Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests to determine significant differences based on performance, learning style, and gender.

The findings reveal that learners differ significantly in their strategies, approaches, and capabilities for learning biology. Through learning and social acculturation, students develop individual preferences for reading, reviewing, and note-taking. A significant finding is that respondents generally possess inadequate learning skills and strategies. Specifically, they lack proficiency in elaboration, integration, metacognition, organization, recall, study reading, and test-taking strategies, all of which influence their ability to learn biology.

Regarding instructional aids, the textbook is the most commonly used tool and dominates the curriculum, yet students lack the basic skills necessary to understand it effectively. Furthermore, the unavailability of certain materials and limited science equipment prevent students from performing various experiments or exercises.

Environmental factors, including teaching strategies, physical classroom setup, class activities, and teacher behavior, significantly affect students. Respondents indicated they most enjoy hands-on activities, such as laboratory and field work, as well as collaborative group work. Students prefer activities that are active, enjoyable, exciting, goal-oriented, challenging, and relevant to real life. Conversely, they reported enjoying class discussions less, describing them as teacher-dominated talk. They showed less interest in lectures, tests, and expensive model making, while the most disliked activities were long lectures and copying notes from the blackboard.

The study concludes that learning environmental factors and personal learning strategies greatly influence biology learning. To improve instruction, educators must address students' inadequate learning skills, particularly in metacognition and organization. There is a need to move away from teacher-dominated lectures toward active, collaborative, and hands-on experiences. Additionally, improving the availability of science equipment and learning resources is essential for effective science education. The study conducted by Lucy G. Diaz aims to investigate the learning aids and strategies used by high school biology students and how these are affected by personal factors. Additionally, the research examines the learning environment and its influence on how students learn biology. The ultimate goal of the research is to identify cues that can be used to improve biology instruction in high school settings and to find ways to motivate students to study more diligently and participate more actively in biology classes.

The research was conducted in one of the public high schools in the Visayas, involving 30 second-year students. These respondents represented a range of academic levels, including high, middle, and low performers. To gather data, the researcher utilized several instruments, including journal notes, a questionnaire-checklist regarding personal learning aids and strategies, an instructional aids checklist, a learning resources rating scale, and a class activities rating scale questionnaire. The methodology involved observing students in class and conducting in-depth interviews in separate venues. Class observations specifically focused on teaching aids, teaching-learning activities, and assessment methods. To ensure the validity of the qualitative data, triangulation was employed. Quantitative analysis was performed using mean, frequencies, and percentages. Furthermore, the Krushkall Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests were utilized to determine if significant differences existed among respondents regarding their commonly used learning aids and strategies for reading, reviewing for exams, and taking lecture notes when grouped by learning performance, learning style, and gender.

The findings of the study reveal that learners differ significantly in their strategies, approaches, and capabilities for learning biology. Through processes of learning and social acculturation, students acquire individual preferences for specific strategies used when reading assigned topics, reviewing for exams, taking lecture notes, and performing other learning tasks. A significant finding is that, generally, the respondents possess inadequate learning skills and strategies. Specifically, they lack proficiency in elaboration, integration, metacognition, organization, recall, study reading, and test-taking strategies, all of which greatly influence their ability to learn biology.

Regarding instructional aids, the textbook is the most commonly used tool by the teacher and dominates the classroom curriculum. However, the study found that students lack the basic skills and strategies necessary to effectively understand the biology textbook. Furthermore, the availability of materials is an issue; the unavailability of certain materials and a limited number of science equipment prevent students from performing various experiments or exercises.

The study also found that students are significantly affected by environmental factors, including teaching strategies, the physical setup of the classroom, class activities, and teacher behavior. When evaluating class activities, the respondents indicated that they most enjoy hands-on activities, such as laboratory and field work, as well as group work. Students expressed a preference for activities that allow for active participation and are collaborative, enjoyable, exciting, goal-oriented, challenging, and relevant to real life. Conversely, students reported enjoying class discussions less, describing them as teacher-dominated talk. They also showed less interest in lectures, tests, and expensive model making. The activities most disliked by the students were long lectures and the practice of copying notes from the blackboard.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that learning environmental factors—such as teaching strategies, learning resources, the physical setup of the classroom, teacher behavior, and classroom activities—alongside the personal learning strategies of students, greatly influence the learning of biology in the classroom. The students themselves identified specific instructional changes through their assessment of class activities that they believe would encourage them to study harder and participate more actively in class.

The implications of this research suggest that to improve biology instruction, educators must address the inadequacy of students' learning skills, particularly in areas like metacognition and organization. There is a clear need to move away from teacher-dominated lectures and note-copying toward more active, collaborative, and hands-on learning experiences, such as laboratory and field work. Additionally, the findings imply that improving the availability of science equipment and learning resources is essential for effective science education. By addressing both the personal strategic deficiencies of students and the environmental factors of the classroom, instruction can be improved to better support student engagement and academic success in biology.

title: Integration of Values and English in Mathematics Teaching: Effects of Understanding, Confidence and Problem Solving
abstract:
This study determined the effects of integrated mathematics curriculum to high school geometry students. It sought to determine the effects of integrating Values and English in Mathematics on problem-solving skills among the respondents, their mathematics confidence,
their level of critical and creative thinking, and their conceptual understanding. The values referred to in the integrated Mathematics-Values-English curriculum are critical and creative thinking. Moreover, this study determined if there is a significant effect of integrative instruction and mental ability on the problem-solving skills, conceptual understanding and mathematics self-confidence of students.

The quantitative and qualitative methods of descriptive and experimental research were used to gather data from the two third-year classes of one of the schools in the Division of Tarlac Province in SY 2007-2008. For the quantitative experimental research, one group was
exposed to integrative instruction while the other one was exposed to traditional instruction. For the analysis and interpretation of the data gathered, the Pearson-Product Moment Correlation Method, the Chronbach’s alpha, the t-test for independent sample, the Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MONOVA) and the Friedman Two-Way Analysis of Variance were used. Classroom observation, interview, analysis and review of the written documents, such as test papers and journal of the students were the data gathering techniques for the qualitative data and needed in the second part.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Edgard C. Domingo investigated the effects of an integrated Mathematics-Values-English (MVE) curriculum on high school geometry students. The study examined whether integrating Values and English into Mathematics instruction impacts problem-solving skills, mathematics self-confidence, critical and creative thinking, and conceptual understanding. Conducted during the 2007-2008 school year in the Division of Tarlac Province, the research employed descriptive and experimental designs, comparing an MVE group receiving integrative instruction with a traditional instruction (TM) group. Data were gathered through classroom observations, interviews, student journals, and test papers, using various statistical analyses including t-tests and Multivariate Analysis of Variance.

The findings revealed that students in the MVE group demonstrated better problem-solving performance than the TM group. MVE respondents exhibited higher levels of mathematics self-confidence, critical thinking skills, analytical thinking skills, and a superior ability to solve problems involving quantitative reasoning. However, both groups were comparable regarding creative skills in problem-solving, and there was no significant difference in confidence levels across groups during the pretest and posttest phases.

The study concluded that integrative instruction is more effective than traditional methods for teaching geometry, particularly for low-ability students. Results suggest that higher achievement scores are driven more by the integrative teaching method than by the mental ability of the students. Recommendations include encouraging teachers to use integrative instruction and designing materials that integrate English and values.

The study conducted by Edgard C. Domingo investigates the effects of an integrated mathematics curriculum on high school geometry students. The primary problem addressed is whether integrating Values and English into Mathematics instruction impacts students' problem-solving skills, mathematics self-confidence, levels of critical and creative thinking, and conceptual understanding. In this context, the "values" integrated into the Mathematics-Values-English (MVE) curriculum are defined as critical and creative thinking.

The findings of the study revealed several significant differences between the MVE and TM groups. Students in the MVE group demonstrated better performance in problem-solving than those in the TM group, as evidenced by significant differences in pretest-posttest results. The data showed significant differences in pretest and posttest scores based on the teaching method used, as well as the interaction between the teaching method and mental ability. Furthermore, the MVE respondents exhibited higher levels of mathematics self-confidence and critical thinking skills compared to the TM respondents. The MVE group also demonstrated higher analytical thinking skills and a superior ability to solve problems involving quantitative reasoning. However, the study found that respondents in both groups were comparable regarding their creative skills in problem-solving. title: Cooperative Learning: Its Influence on Academic Achievement, Social Interaction and Self Concepts of College Biology Students
abstract:
This quantitative-qualitative research on cooperative learning used as an intervention in teaching college biology, identified and analyzed the influence of cooperative learning on academic achievement, social interaction, and self-concept among college biology students.
Three cooperative learning strategies were utilized- Group Investigation (GI). Team Assisted Individualization (TAI) and Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC). Three cooperative learning groups were used- Personal Selection (PS), Random Selection (RS) and Equal Distribution (ED). Academic achievement was measured by using Biology Achievement Test (BAT) cumulative Academic Scores obtained from nine activities performed during the period intervention... Three biology topics were covered including Development Biology, Ecology and Genetics in the implementation of the cooperative learning intervention during the final term of school year 2000-2001.

Treatment of data, generated from various instruments namely Cumulative Academic Scores, Biology Achievement Test (BAT), Thirty Statement Test (TST), Rubric on cooperation and Collaboration (RCC) and Self Attention Scale (SAS), utilized Analysis of Variance (ANOVA),
t-test and the Pearson’s correlation while descriptive analysis dealt with the different social interactions exhibited by the students during cooperative learning.

half:
This study investigated how cooperative learning interventions influence the academic achievement, social interaction, and self-concept of college biology students studying Developmental Biology, Ecology, and Genetics. The research examined three cooperative learning strategies—Group Investigation (GI), Team Assisted Individualization (TAI), and Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC)—alongside three group formation methods: Personal Selection (PS), Random Selection (RS), and Equal Distribution (ED). Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher utilized quantitative tools such as the Biology Achievement Test (BAT) and the Thirty Statement Test (TST), alongside qualitative descriptive analysis of student behaviors.

Findings indicated that group formation significantly influenced academic achievement and social interaction, but not self-concept. The Personal Selection group achieved the highest BAT scores and greatest social interaction enhancement, while Equal Distribution most influenced cumulative academic scores but had the least influence on social interaction. Regarding strategies, GI yielded the highest BAT scores and was most effective for social interaction, whereas TAI was most effective for enhancing self-concept. Compared to traditional environments, cooperative learning groups demonstrated better mean scores in academic achievement, though no significant differences were found in self-attention or self-concept. Correlation analysis showed a high correlation between BAT scores and self-concept, but a moderately negative correlation between social interaction and self-concept. Qualitative observations noted that verbal and non-verbal interactions fostered social interdependence. The study concludes that cooperative learning effectively enhances achievement and social interaction.

This study investigated how cooperative learning interventions influence the academic achievement, social interaction, and self-concept of college biology students. Conducted during the final term of the 2000-2001 school year, the research focused on three biology topics: Developmental Biology, Ecology, and Genetics. The study examined the effects of three cooperative learning strategies—Group Investigation (GI), Team Assisted Individualization (TAI), and Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC)—alongside three group formation methods: Personal Selection (PS), Random Selection (RS), and Equal Distribution (ED).

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher collected quantitative data through cumulative academic scores, a Biology Achievement Test (BAT), a Rubric on Cooperation and Collaboration (RCC), a Thirty Statement Test (TST), and a Self Attention Scale (SAS). Qualitative data was gathered through descriptive analysis of student behaviors.

The findings regarding group formation indicated that the method of grouping significantly influenced academic achievement and social interaction, but not self-concept. The Personal Selection (PS) group achieved the highest mean scores on the BAT and showed the greatest enhancement in social interaction. Conversely, the Equal Distribution (ED) group most influenced cumulative academic scores but had the least influence on social interaction.

The effectiveness of cooperative learning strategies varied by the parameter measured. For academic achievement, Group Investigation (GI) yielded the highest mean score on the BAT, though no significant difference was found in cumulative scores. Regarding social interaction, GI was the most effective strategy. For self-concept, however, Team Assisted Individualization (TAI) was the most effective. When compared to traditional learning environments, students in the cooperative learning group demonstrated better mean scores in academic achievement, though no significant differences were found regarding self-attention or self-concept.

Correlation analysis revealed a significant but weak correlation between self-attention and both academic achievement and social interaction. A very weak correlation existed between self-attention and self-concept. While academic scores and social interaction showed a weak correlation, a high correlation was found between BAT scores and self-concept. Notably, a moderately negative correlation was identified between social interaction and self-concept.

Qualitative observations showed that social interactions in cooperative learning occurred through verbal and non-verbal means, such as haptics, kinesics, and facial expressions, which helped foster social interdependence and interpersonal skills.

The study concludes that cooperative learning is an effective intervention for enhancing academic achievement and social interaction in biology students. The results suggest that Group Investigation is particularly effective for achievement and social interaction, while Team Assisted Individualization is most effective for enhancing self-concept. The findings imply that selecting the appropriate strategy and grouping method is critical for successful intervention in a biology classroom.
two:
The study investigated the influence of cooperative learning as a teaching intervention on the academic achievement, social interaction, and self-concept of college biology students. The research was conducted during the final term of the 2000-2001 school year, focusing on three specific biology topics: Developmental Biology, Ecology, and Genetics. The study aimed to identify how different cooperative learning strategies and different methods of group formation affect these three specific student outcomes.

The research employed a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both quantitative and qualitative data. To implement the intervention, the researcher utilized three specific cooperative learning strategies: Group Investigation (GI), Team Assisted Individualization (TAI), and Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC). To examine the influence of group formation, three different grouping methods were used: Personal Selection (PS), Random Selection (RS), and Equal Distribution (ED).

Data collection involved several instruments to measure the variables of interest. Academic achievement was assessed through cumulative academic scores from nine activities and a Biology Achievement Test (BAT). Social interaction was evaluated using a Rubric on Cooperation and Collaboration (RCC) and descriptive analysis of student behaviors. Self-concept was measured using a Thirty Statement Test (TST), and self-attention was measured using a Self Attention Scale (SAS). Statistical analysis included Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), t-tests, and Pearson’s correlation to determine significant differences and relationships between variables.

The findings regarding the influence of group formation revealed significant differences. Using ANOVA at a .05 level of significance, the study found that the type of group formation significantly influenced academic achievement and social interaction, but not self-concept. Specifically, the Personal Selection (PS) group showed the highest mean scores on the Biology Achievement Test (BAT), while the Equal Distribution (ED) group most influenced cumulative academic scores. Regarding social interaction, the Personal Selection (PS) group showed the greatest enhancement, followed by Random Selection (RS), while Equal Distribution (ED) had the least influence.

The findings regarding the cooperative learning strategies showed varying effects depending on the parameter being measured. In terms of academic achievement, Group Investigation (GI) yielded the highest mean score on the Biology Achievement Test (BAT) compared to CIRC and TAI, though there was no significant difference in cumulative academic scores. This suggests that cooperative strategies have a bivalent effect on achievement depending on the measurement parameter. Regarding social interaction, Group Investigation (GI) was found to be the most appropriate strategy, yielding the highest mean score. However, for self-concept, Team Assisted Individualization (TAI) was the most effective strategy, yielding the highest mean score.

When comparing students exposed to cooperative learning against those in traditional learning environments, the results showed that academic achievement varied significantly, with students in the cooperative learning group demonstrating better mean scores. However, there were no significant differences between the two groups regarding self-attention or self-concept.

The study also identified several correlations between the variables. Pearson’s correlation indicated a significant but weak correlation between self-attention and academic achievement, as well as a significant but weak correlation between self-attention and social interaction. There was a very weak correlation between self-attention and self-concept. A weak correlation was found between academic scores and social interaction in reference to the BAT. Furthermore, a weak correlation existed between academic achievement (in reference to academic scores) and self-concept, though a high correlation was found between academic achievement (in reference to the BAT) and self-concept. Notably, the study found a moderately negative correlation between social interaction and self-concept.

Qualitatively, the study observed that social interactions in cooperative learning manifested through both verbal and non-verbal means. Non-verbal interactions included haptics, kinesics, and facial expressions, while verbal interactions helped promote interpersonal skills. These interactions were deemed essential for fostering social interdependence, ensuring that students remained individually active and responsible.

The study concludes that cooperative learning can be an effective intervention for enhancing academic achievement and social interaction in college biology students, though its impact on self-concept is more specific to the strategy used. The results suggest that Group Investigation is particularly effective for academic achievement and social interaction, while Team Assisted Individualization is most effective for enhancing self-concept. The findings imply that the choice of cooperative strategy and the method of group formation are critical factors in determining the success of the intervention in a biology classroom. By utilizing these strategies, educators can promote meaningful learning tasks through cooperation and collaboration, fostering both academic success and the development of interpersonal skills.

title: Enhanced-Group Moore Method: Effects on Van Hiele Levels of Geometric Understanding, Proof-Construction Performance and Beliefs
abstract:
This study aimed to improve the van Hiele levels of geometric understanding, enhance proof-construction performance and determines the beliefs about proofs of the prospective mathematics teachers using the Traditional Method (Instructor Based) and the Enhanced-Group Moore Method. The impact of the two teaching methods was analyzed to find out which would yield better results in terms of raising van Hiele levels and enhancing beliefs about proofs and proof-construction performance.

The study used the quasi-experimental method of research and employed qualitative and quantitative analysis. The Bachelor of Secondary Education (BSEd) major in Mathematics  students (20) officially enrolled in Math 233 (Plane and Solid Geometry) at a State University in the Eastern Visayas were the subject of this study. These future teachers were alternately distributed into two groups (control and experimental) based on their ranked mean grade on their prerequisite subjects (Basic Mathematics and College Algebra). The two groups were
comparable in terms of their mathematical ability. 

The study used three instruments, the van Hiel Geometry Test, the Proof-Construction Test and the Proof Beliefs Questionnaire.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Douglas A. Salazar conducted a quasi-experimental study to compare the effectiveness of the Enhanced-Group Moore Method against the Traditional Method in teaching Plane and Solid Geometry to prospective mathematics teachers. The study involved twenty Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Mathematics students, divided into control and experimental groups based on prior mathematical ability. Using the van Hiele Geometry Test, the Proof-Construction Test, and the Proof Beliefs Questionnaire, the researcher employed both qualitative and quantitative analyses.

The findings indicated that the Enhanced-Group Moore Method was more effective in improving geometric understanding, raising students from van Hiele level 1 to level 3, while the Traditional Method only reached level 2. In proof-construction, the experimental group improved from a "clueless" status to an "intermediate" level, outperforming the control group, who reached a "novice" level. A significant relationship was found between proof-construction performance and van Hiele levels within the experimental group. However, the study found no noteworthy changes in students' beliefs regarding the nature of mathematical proofs.

Qualitative results showed that the Enhanced-Group Moore Method fostered self-confidence, communication, and collaborative values. While both groups struggled with proving theorems due to poor prerequisite skills and preferred two-column proof formats, the Enhanced-Group Moore Method proved superior for developing geometric understanding and proof-construction skills through its collaborative environment, though it did not significantly alter students' deeply held beliefs about proofs.
one:
Douglas A. Salazar conducted a study to investigate the effectiveness of the Enhanced-Group Moore Method compared to the Traditional Method (Instructor Based) in teaching Plane and Solid Geometry to prospective mathematics teachers. The research aimed to determine which instructional approach better improves van Hiele levels of geometric understanding, enhances proof-construction performance, and impacts students' beliefs regarding mathematical proofs.

The study utilized a quasi-experimental research design involving twenty Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Mathematics students at a State University in the Eastern Visayas. Participants were divided into a control group and an experimental group based on ranked mean grades from prerequisite subjects, Basic Mathematics and College Algebra, to ensure comparable initial mathematical ability. The researcher employed a combination of qualitative and quantitative analysis using three instruments: the van Hiele Geometry Test, the Proof-Construction Test, and the Proof Beliefs Questionnaire.

The findings revealed significant differences between the two methods. Regarding geometric understanding, the Enhanced-Group Moore Method was more effective, raising students' van Hiele levels from level 1 to level 3, whereas the Traditional Method only raised levels from level 1 to level 2. In proof-construction performance, the experimental group improved from a "clueless" status to an "intermediate" level, outperforming the control group, who moved from "clueless" to "novice." Quantitative results confirmed significant differences in both van Hiele levels and proof-construction performance for students before and after the study, with the Enhanced-Group Moore Method yielding better results. Additionally, a significant relationship was identified between proof-construction performance and van Hiele levels within the experimental group.

However, the study found no noteworthy changes in the students' beliefs about proofs. Students maintained that a theorem has no exception, that the dual role of proof is to convince and explain, and that proof validity depends on internal logic.

Qualitative assessments indicated that the Enhanced-Group Moore Method created a "damay effect," fostering self-confidence, effective communication, the exchange of ideas, and values such as sharing and helping others. Both groups reported difficulties in proving theorems, which they attributed to poor prerequisite skills. Regarding proof formats, students preferred the two-column form used in direct proof over the paragraph form used in proof by contradiction. Both groups expressed favor toward the lesson presentation sequence and the incentives provided.

The research suggests that the Enhanced-Group Moore Method is a superior pedagogical approach for developing geometric understanding and proof-construction skills. While it significantly impacts skill and understanding through a collaborative environment, it is less influential in altering deeply held beliefs about the nature of mathematical proofs.
two:
The study conducted by Douglas A. Salazar investigated the effectiveness of the Enhanced-Group Moore Method compared to the Traditional Method (Instructor Based) in teaching Plane and Solid Geometry to prospective mathematics teachers. The primary problem addressed was how to improve the van Hiele levels of geometric understanding, enhance proof-construction performance, and determine the impact of different teaching methodologies on students' beliefs regarding mathematical proofs. The research sought to identify which instructional approach would yield superior results in these three specific areas of mathematical competence and perception.

The context of the research was a State University in the Eastern Visayas, involving twenty Bachelor of Secondary Education (BSEd) major in Mathematics students enrolled in a Plane and Solid Geometry course. To ensure a controlled environment, the researcher utilized a quasi-experimental research design. The participants were divided into two groups: a control group and an experimental group. These groups were assigned based on the ranked mean grades from their prerequisite subjects, Basic Mathematics and College Algebra, ensuring that both groups were comparable in terms of their initial mathematical ability.

The methodology employed a combination of qualitative and quantitative analysis. To measure the variables, the researcher utilized three specific instruments: the van Hiele Geometry Test, the Proof-Construction Test, and the Proof Beliefs Questionnaire. These tools allowed for a comprehensive assessment of the students' geometric understanding, their ability to construct proofs, and their underlying beliefs regarding the nature and purpose of mathematical proofs.

The findings of the study revealed significant differences between the two instructional methods. Regarding geometric understanding, the Enhanced-Group Moore Method was more effective, raising the van Hiele levels of the future teachers from level 1 to level 3. In contrast, the Traditional Method only raised the levels from level 1 to level 2. In terms of proof-construction performance, the experimental group improved from a "clueless" status to an "intermediate" level, which outperformed the control group, who moved from "clueless" to "novice."

Quantitative results confirmed significant differences in both van Hiele levels and proof-construction performance for the students before and after the study. Specifically, the students exposed to the Enhanced-Group Moore Method yielded better results in both categories compared to those taught via the Traditional Method. Furthermore, the study identified a significant relationship between proof-construction performance and van Hiele levels within the experimental group. However, the study found that no noteworthy changes occurred in the future teachers' beliefs about proofs. Despite the instructional shifts, the students maintained specific beliefs: they believed that a theorem has no exception, that the dual role of proof is to convince and to explain, and that the validity of a proof depends on its internal logic.

Qualitative assessments provided deeper insight into the student experience. The Enhanced-Group Moore Method was found to create a "damay effect," which contributed to the development of self-confidence, effective communication, and the exchange of ideas among the students. This method also fostered values such as sharing and helping others. Interestingly, both groups reported difficulties in proving theorems, which they attributed to poor prerequisite skills. Regarding the format of proofs, students expressed a preference for the two-column form associated with direct proof over the paragraph form, which they associated with proof by contradiction. Finally, students in both groups expressed favor toward the sequence of lesson presentations and were agreeable to the incentives provided during the study.

The implications of this research suggest that the Enhanced-Group Moore Method is a superior pedagogical approach for developing geometric understanding and proof-construction skills in prospective mathematics teachers. By fostering a collaborative environment that encourages communication and the exchange of ideas, this method helps move students through higher levels of geometric reasoning more effectively than traditional instructor-based methods. While the method significantly impacts skill and understanding, it appears less influential in altering deeply held beliefs about the nature of mathematical proofs. The findings highlight the importance of addressing prerequisite skill deficiencies to assist students in mastering theorem proving and suggest that collaborative, group-based learning can enhance both academic performance and interpersonal values in mathematics education.

title: Effects of Contrastive and Generative Teaching Strategy in Chemistry
abstract:
This study evaluated the effectiveness of contrastive and generative teaching strategy in teaching the concepts of the mole, stoichiometry, and molarity among third year high school students. Contrastive and generative teaching strategy refers to those instances in which an unfamiliar domain is made understandable through a more familiar domain during class discussion. This study specifically investigated the change in students’ conceptual understanding, problem-solving abilities, and attitude towards chemistry using paper and pencil
tests and interview.

This study made use of quasi-experimental research design involving intact classes, with a total of 98 students, assigned as control group (n = 49) and experimental group (n = 49). The control group underwent traditional lecture method while contrastive and generative teaching strategy was used for the experimental group.

Lawson’s Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning was used to identify the cognitive level of students selected for case studies in determining attitude change towards chemistry, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving skills. The same test was used to determine to
equivalence of the two groups of students in terms of ability to learn the mole concept, stoichiometry, and molarity.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Esteban A. Malindog Jr. investigated the effectiveness of the contrastive and generative teaching strategy compared to traditional lecture methods in teaching three fundamental chemistry concepts: the mole, stoichiometry, and molarity. This strategy aims to make abstract domains understandable by relating them to familiar domains, bridging the gap between existing knowledge and new, complex scientific information. The research evaluated how this approach influences conceptual understanding, problem-solving abilities, and attitudes toward chemistry.

The study employed a quasi-experimental design involving 98 third-year high school students, divided into a control group taught via traditional lecture and an experimental group taught using the contrastive and generative strategy. Assessment tools included Lawson’s Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning, pre-tests and post-tests featuring various multiple-choice and open-ended problems, an attitude questionnaire, and qualitative interviews.

Findings indicate that the contrastive and generative strategy has a positive impact on student performance. The strategy improved the quality of conceptual understanding and led to greater completeness in solutions to numerical open-ended problems compared to the traditional method. However, there was no significant difference in attitudes toward chemistry between the groups. Qualitative data revealed that students in the experimental group preferred the strategy, noting it helped them visualize abstract concepts. Additionally, the research identified a specific misconception regarding stoichiometry not previously cited in literature. The study concludes the strategy is an effective tool for enhancing cognitive learning and problem-solving rigor.

Specifically, the strategy improved the quality of students' conceptual understanding compared to the traditional method. However, the study found no significant difference in attitudes toward chemistry between the control and experimental groups.

The research also identified a specific misconception regarding stoichiometry that had not been previously cited in existing literature.

The study concludes that while the strategy may not significantly alter general attitudes toward chemistry, it is an effective tool for enhancing cognitive learning. Using analogies to connect new information to familiar domains appears particularly beneficial for mastering the abstract and mathematical nature of the mole, stoichiometry, and molarity. two:
The study conducted by Esteban A. Malindog Jr. investigates the effectiveness of the contrastive and generative teaching strategy compared to traditional lecture methods in the context of teaching chemistry. The research specifically focuses on three fundamental chemical concepts: the mole, stoichiometry, and molarity. The core premise of the contrastive and generative teaching strategy is to make unfamiliar or abstract domains understandable by relating them to more familiar domains during classroom discussions. This approach seeks to bridge the gap between a student's existing knowledge and new, complex scientific information.

The research problem centers on evaluating how this specific instructional strategy influences three key areas of student performance: conceptual understanding, problem-solving abilities, and attitudes toward chemistry. By comparing this method to the traditional lecture method, the study aims to determine if making connections between known and unknown concepts provides a pedagogical advantage in the teaching of quantitative and abstract chemistry topics.

To address this problem, the researcher employed a quasi-experimental research design involving two intact classes of third-year high school students. The total sample consisted of 98 students, divided equally into a control group of 49 students and an experimental group of 49 students. The control group was taught using the traditional lecture method, while the experimental group was taught using the contrastive and generative teaching strategy. To ensure the validity of the comparison and to avoid bias, the researcher developed five parallel lesson plans. The first three lesson plans were dedicated to the concept of the mole, while the final two lesson plans focused on stoichiometry and molarity.

The methodology utilized several assessment tools to measure the variables of interest. To determine the equivalence of the two groups regarding their ability to learn the specific chemistry topics, Lawson’s Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning was employed. This same test was also used to identify the cognitive levels of students selected for subsequent case studies. To assess conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance, students were given assessment tests both before and after the lessons. These tests were comprehensive, featuring four distinct question types: fixed response multiple-choice, modified multiple-choice, fixed multiple-choice problems, and open-ended problems. Additionally, students' attitudes toward chemistry were measured using a dedicated attitude questionnaire, and qualitative data regarding student experiences was gathered through interviews.

The findings of the study indicate that the contrastive and generative teaching strategy, which utilizes analogies, has a positive impact on student performance in specific areas. Specifically, the results showed that this strategy improved the quality of students' conceptual understanding compared to the traditional method. Furthermore, students in the experimental group demonstrated greater completeness in their solutions to numerical open-ended problems. However, the study did not find a significant difference in the attitudes toward chemistry between the control group and the experimental group.

Qualitative data from interview transcripts provided deeper insight into the student experience. Students in the experimental group reported a preference for the contrastive and generative teaching strategy, noting that it assisted them in understanding and visualizing abstract chemistry concepts and ideas. Additionally, the research identified a specific misconception regarding stoichiometry that had not been previously cited in the existing research literature.

The conclusions drawn from this research suggest that while the strategy may not significantly alter a student's general attitude toward the subject of chemistry, it is an effective tool for enhancing the cognitive aspects of learning. The use of analogies and the connection of new information to familiar domains appear to be particularly beneficial for mastering the abstract and mathematical nature of the mole, stoichiometry, and molarity.

The implications of these findings suggest that chemistry educators might benefit from incorporating contrastive and generative strategies into their pedagogy to improve the depth of conceptual understanding and the rigor of problem-solving skills. By helping students visualize abstract ideas through familiar comparisons, teachers may be able to mitigate misconceptions and improve the completeness of students' scientific reasoning and mathematical applications in chemistry.

title: Teaching-Learning Processes in the Preservice Education of General Science Teachers
abstract:
This study analyzed the preservice general science curricula of selected Teacher Education Institutions (TEIs) in Region I in terms of their provision for the development of chemistry teaching competencies and examined the different teaching-learning process and
strategies employed in their preservice science teacher education programs. Specifically, it looked into: a) the chemistry teaching competencies expected of prospective general science teachers bases on the Department of Education (DepED) general science curriculum and those that are developed by the TEIs; 2) the qualification of teacher educators and cooperating teachers to train prospective science teachers; 3) the confidence and competency levels of prospective a novice teachers to teach chemistry topics included in the DepED science
curriculum; and 4) the relationship between their actual teaching competence and perceived level of confidence in teaching these.

Involved in the study were six TEIs which graduate at least five science majors annually, 61 prospective teachers, 28 teacher educators, 61 novice teachers, and 38 cooperating teachers. Quantitative and qualitative data were gathered through document analyses, survey
questionnaires, classroom observations and unstructured interviews.

Results of the study revealed that the DepEd General Science syllabus prescribes a minimum of 25 chemistry learning competencies that need to be acquired by prospective general science teachers, most of which are of the domain-specific category and fall under
declarative knowledge classification. 

The TEIs’ curricular offerings meet CHED’s prescribed number of units for a science major/concentration, but many of the chemistry competencies prescribed by DepEd are not provided for in their courses’ syllabi.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Emilia M. Racela investigated teaching-learning processes in the preservice education of general science teachers, focusing on chemistry teaching competencies in Region I. The study analyzed the curricula of selected Teacher Education Institutions to determine how well they develop competencies expected by the Department of Education. The research employed a mixed-methods approach involving document analyses, survey questionnaires, classroom observations, and unstructured interviews with various participants, including prospective teachers, teacher educators, novice teachers, and cooperating teachers.

Findings revealed that the Department of Education General Science syllabus prescribes a minimum of 25 chemistry learning competencies, most of which are domain-specific declarative knowledge. While institutions meet the Commission on Higher Education prescribed number of units for a science major, many prescribed chemistry competencies are not provided for in course syllabi. Regarding educator qualifications, teacher educators satisfy the basic requirement of holding baccalaureate degrees in science, but a considerable number do not meet the minimum degree requirement of a master’s degree. Some cooperating teachers are not science specialists, and many have not attended training regarding their role as critic teachers.

Teacher educators and cooperating teachers self-rate highly regarding chemistry teaching competencies, but both encounter problems concretizing abstract concepts. Classroom observations of cooperating teachers revealed weaknesses such as misconceptions, evaluation tools that fail to measure objective attainment, a tendency to prioritize conceptual knowledge over procedural knowledge, and limited attempts to develop higher-order thinking skills. While prospective and novice teachers reported high confidence in teaching chemistry, observations showed that the competencies they claimed to have acquired were not demonstrated.

Emilia M. Racela investigated teaching-learning processes in the preservice education of general science teachers, focusing on chemistry teaching competencies. The research was situated in Region I and analyzed the curricula of selected Teacher Education Institutions to determine how well they develop these competencies. The investigation examined chemistry teaching competencies expected of prospective general science teachers based on the Department of Education general science curriculum compared to those developed by the institutions. The study also looked into the qualifications of teacher educators and cooperating teachers, the confidence and competency levels of prospective novice teachers in teaching chemistry topics, and the relationship between actual teaching competence and perceived confidence levels.

The researcher employed a mixed-methods approach involving quantitative and qualitative data through document analyses, survey questionnaires, classroom observations, and unstructured interviews. Participants included six institutions, 61 prospective teachers, 28 teacher educators, 61 novice teachers, and 38 cooperating teachers.

Findings revealed that the Department of Education General Science syllabus prescribes a minimum of 25 chemistry learning competencies that prospective teachers must acquire, most of which are domain-specific and classified as declarative knowledge. While institutions meet the Commission on Higher Education prescribed number of units for a science major, many chemistry competencies prescribed by the Department of Education are not provided for in the syllabi of their courses. Regarding educator qualifications, teacher educators satisfy the basic requirement of holding baccalaureate degrees in science, but a considerable number do not meet the minimum degree requirement of a master’s degree. Some cooperating teachers are not science specialists, and many have not attended training or seminars regarding their role as critic teachers. While teacher educators possess civil service eligibilities and science teaching experience, some cooperating teachers are non-eligible. Most respondents have attended science-related seminars, though some reported not attending any in the last five years. Furthermore, while respondents are engaged in administrative and curricular activities, they are least involved in research.

Teacher educators and cooperating teachers self-rate highly regarding the extent to which they demonstrate chemistry teaching competencies, but both groups encounter the problem of concretizing abstract concepts or relating chemistry concepts to everyday life. Classroom observations of cooperating teachers revealed weaknesses including misconceptions or errors in lessons, the use of evaluation tools that fail to measure objective attainment, a tendency to prioritize conceptual knowledge over procedural knowledge, and limited attempts to develop higher-order thinking skills. While prospective and novice teachers reported high levels of confidence in teaching chemistry topics, classroom observations showed that the competencies they claimed to have acquired were not demonstrated, and the strategies they identified as most important were not the ones they actually employed.

Racela investigates the teaching-learning processes within the preservice education of general science teachers, specifically focusing on the development of chemistry teaching competencies. The research was situated in Region I and aimed to analyze the curricula of selected Teacher Education Institutions (TEIs) to determine how well they provide for the development of these competencies. The investigation specifically examined the chemistry teaching competencies expected of prospective general science teachers based on the Department of Education (DepED) general science curriculum compared to those developed by the TEIs. Additionally, the study looked into the qualifications of teacher educators and cooperating teachers, the confidence and competency levels of prospective novice teachers in teaching chemistry topics from the DepED science curriculum, and the relationship between actual teaching competence and perceived confidence levels.

To achieve these objectives, the researcher employed a mixed-methods approach involving both quantitative and qualitative data. Data collection methods included document analyses, survey questionnaires, classroom observations, and unstructured interviews. The participants involved in the study consisted of six TEIs that graduate at least five science majors annually, 61 prospective teachers, 28 teacher educators, 61 novice teachers, and 38 cooperating teachers.

The findings revealed that the DepEd General Science syllabus prescribes a minimum of 25 chemistry learning competencies that prospective general science teachers must acquire, most of which are domain-specific and classified as declarative knowledge. While the TEIs meet the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) prescribed number of units for a science major or concentration, many of the chemistry competencies prescribed by DepED are not provided for in the syllabi of their courses. Regarding the qualifications of educators, teacher educators satisfy the basic requirement of holding baccalaureate degrees in science, but a considerable number do not meet the CHED minimum degree requirement of a master’s degree. Some cooperating teachers are not science specialists, and many have not attended training or seminars regarding their role as critic teachers. While teacher educators possess civil service eligibilities and science teaching experience, some cooperating teachers are non-eligible. Most respondents have attended science-related seminars, though some reported not attending any in the last five years. Furthermore, while respondents are engaged in administrative and curricular activities, they are least involved in research.

The study also found that teacher educators and cooperating teachers self-rate highly regarding the extent to which they demonstrate chemistry teaching competencies. However, both groups encounter the common problem of concretizing abstract concepts or relating chemistry concepts to everyday life. Classroom observations of cooperating teachers revealed several weaknesses, including misconceptions or errors in lessons, the use of evaluation tools that fail to measure objective attainment, a tendency to prioritize conceptual knowledge over procedural knowledge, and limited attempts to develop higher-order thinking skills. While prospective and novice teachers reported high levels of confidence in teaching chemistry topics included in the DepED curriculum, classroom observations showed that the competencies they claimed to have acquired were not demonstrated, and the strategies they identified as most important were not the ones they actually employed.

Based on these findings, several implications and recommendations are offered for various educational stakeholders. For TEIs, it is recommended that they articulate their curricula with the DepED to increase effectiveness and relevance, consider offering more educational science and strategy courses, conduct periodic assessments of preservice programs, and establish networking relationships among TEIs to share human and material resources and research activities. TEIs should also provide prospective teachers with a pool of competent teacher educators and cooperating teachers by promoting professional updating in content, pedagogy, and communication skills, supported by administrative assistance for facilities and supplies. For the DepED, the study suggests closer coordination with TEIs to support new programs, exploring the practicability of articulating learning competencies into domain-general objectives, and delineating the most important chemistry concepts for students. For CHED, the recommendations include closer monitoring of TEIs, imposing measures to hold TEIs accountable for graduate performance, and intensifying scholarship and research programs for faculty members. Finally, the study suggests that further research is needed to analyze weaknesses, effectiveness, and relevance in preservice education, as well as how to encourage teachers to adapt activity-oriented approaches and the influence of Centers of Excellence in Education on improving teaching-learning processes.

title: Pedagogical Content Knowledge, Instructional Design and Teaching Practice of High School Biology Teachers
abstract:
The pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of six high school biology teachers was investigated using an interview, a questionnaire and class observations. The interview investigated the teacher’ content knowledge by proving their view of the organization of biology
and the levels of importance that they associate with the topics included within the scope of the subject matter. The data from the interview was used in the construction of a diagram of the teachers’ subject matter structures (SMS), while the levels of importance identified was used as a basis for class observation. A questionnaire was used to determine teacher knowledgeability in the various biological topics and to produce a background profile of each of the teachers.

Class observations were conducted to determine if differences exist in the way teachers teach topics associated with their levels of importance and those in which their knowledgeability varies.

Not all of the teachers had a well-developed PCK. The data show that the teachers with a more developed PCK tend to vary their teaching methodologies slightly, from teacher-dominated to student-centered strategies when teaching topics that they perceive as

half:
This study investigated the pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of six high school biology teachers to understand how subject matter structures, perceived topic importance, and knowledgeability relate to instructional designs and classroom practices. Using a multi-method approach of interviews, questionnaires, and class observations, the researcher examined the intersection of content knowledge and pedagogical skill.

The findings revealed significant differences in PCK among the participants. Teachers with well-developed PCK demonstrated specific patterns: they varied their teaching methodologies, shifting from teacher-dominated to student-centered strategies when addressing topics they perceived as essential. For these educators, the major ideas in their subject matter structures coincided with topics they identified as most important and areas of high knowledgeability. Furthermore, there was a close correspondence between their instructional designs and actual teaching practices.

In contrast, teachers with less developed PCK did not vary their teaching methodologies. Their subject matter structures reflected textbook sequences or standard logic rather than personal perceptions of topic relationships. For these teachers, instructional designs were generally behaviorist and followed traditional methodologies. The study concluded that strong content knowledge is the factor with the greatest influence on PCK development. This depth of knowledge is facilitated by continuing education, as teachers with master's degrees and those who attended more in-service training demonstrated better-developed PCKs and a deeper understanding of complex biological relationships.

The research focused on understanding how these teachers' subject matter structures, their perceived importance of specific biological topics, and their overall knowledgeability in various biological areas relate to their actual instructional designs and classroom teaching practices.

The context of the research involves the professional development and instructional efficacy of high school biology educators. The study sought to identify the relationship between a teacher's internal organization of biological concepts and the way they translate that knowledge into classroom instruction. By examining the intersection of content knowledge and pedagogical skill, the research aimed to determine what factors contribute to a well-developed PCK.

The researcher employed a qualitative and quantitative multi-method approach to gather data. The methodology included three primary instruments: an interview, a questionnaire, and class observations. The interview was designed to probe the teachers' content knowledge by exploring their views on the organization of biology and the levels of importance they assign to specific topics within the subject matter. The information gathered from these interviews was used to construct a diagram of each teacher's subject matter structure (SMS). The levels of importance identified during the interviews served as a basis for the subsequent class observations. The questionnaire was utilized to determine the teachers' knowledgeability across various biological topics and to establish a background profile for each participant. Finally, class observations were conducted to see if teaching methodologies changed when teachers addressed topics they deemed important versus topics where their knowledgeability varied.

The findings revealed significant differences in the PCK of the participating teachers. It was determined that not all teachers possessed a well-developed PCK. Teachers who demonstrated a more developed PCK exhibited specific patterns in their teaching. These teachers tended to vary their teaching methodologies, shifting from teacher-dominated strategies to student-centered strategies when teaching topics they perceived as essential for student learning. Furthermore, the major ideas of biology expressed in their SMSs were the same topics they identified as most important for students to learn. These topics also coincided with areas where the teachers demonstrated high knowledgeability.

In contrast, teachers with a less developed PCK did not vary their teaching methodologies. Their subject matter structures appeared to reflect the sequences found in textbooks or a standard logic of presentation rather than a personal perception of the relationships between biological topics. For these teachers, instructional designs were generally behaviorist and followed traditional teaching methodologies. The study found a very close correspondence between the instructional designs and the actual teaching practices of teachers who possessed more developed PCKs.

The study concluded that a strong knowledge of content is the factor that appears to have the greatest influence on the development of PCK. This depth of content knowledge is facilitated by continuing education. Specifically, teachers who held master's degrees and those who had attended more in-service training were found to have better-developed PCKs. These educators demonstrated a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between various topics within the field of biology.

title: Constructivist Approach: Its Impact on Prospective Maguidanaoan Teachers' Conceptions of Selected Topics in Environmental Chemistry
abstract:
This study attempted to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of constructivist teaching guides in teaching the concepts of soil and water chemistry in the environment and investigate the change in the conception of prospective Maguindanaon teachers. It also looked into the influence of traditional practices and beliefs of the students on the change of their conceptions from everyday views to scientific views.

The study made use of quasi-experimental research design and involved the third year Bachelor of Science in Islamic Studies students at the University of Southern Mindano, Kabacan, Cotabato enrolled in Environmental Issues were used and randomly assigned as the
control and experimental groups. The control group underwent traditional lecture method (TLM) while the developed teaching guides based on constructivist teaching approaches (CTA) were used in the experimental group.

Seven teaching guides base on constructivist teaching approaches (CTA) developed in soil and water, namely: (1) Use of Water; (2) The Water Cycle; (3) Water, A Unique Substance; (4) Water Pollution; (5) Water Treatment; (6) Soils; and (7) Issues and Concerns About Soil.
Each lesson consisted of the following: (a) background information, which provides the teacher on overview of the lesson and the traditional practices and beliefs of the students that may influence their understanding of the lesson; (b) objectives, which include the process skills and values to be developed; and (c) teaching sequence, which was patterned after Trowbirdge and Bybee (1996) and consisted of five phases, namely: engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration and evaluation. The traditional practices and beliefs of the students related to the lesson were brought up in the engagement phase in the elaboration phase of the teaching guide.

Evelyn T. Cabading investigated the effectiveness of constructivist teaching guides in facilitating conceptual change among prospective Maguindanaon teachers at the University of Southern Mindanao. Focusing on environmental chemistry topics like soil and water chemistry, the study examined whether a constructivist approach could help students transition from everyday views, often shaped by local beliefs, to scientific views.

The research utilized a quasi-experimental design involving third-year Bachelor of Science in Islamic Studies students. Participants were divided into a control group taught via the traditional lecture method and an experimental group taught using seven constructivist teaching guides. These guides followed a five-phase sequence: engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration, and evaluation, specifically integrating students' traditional practices.

Findings showed that while most students initially held concepts rooted in traditional beliefs, the constructivist guides effectively facilitated conceptual change. The experimental group achieved significantly higher posttest mean scores than the control group. Success was particularly noted in topics regarding the water cycle, the unique properties of water, water treatment, and soil issues.

The study revealed that traditional beliefs can act as both facilitators and hindrances; some correlate positively with scientific understanding, while others act as distractors. Ultimately, the research concludes that constructivist approaches are superior to traditional methods for promoting scientific understanding. Educators in culturally diverse settings should develop instructional materials that acknowledge and incorporate students' existing cultural frameworks to guide them toward scientific literacy.

Evelyn T. Cabading investigated the effectiveness of constructivist teaching guides in facilitating conceptual change among prospective Maguindanaon teachers at the University of Southern Mindanao. The study focused on environmental chemistry topics, specifically soil and water chemistry, to determine if a constructivist approach could help students transition from everyday views—often shaped by traditional practices and local beliefs—to scientific views.

The research employed a quasi-experimental design with third-year Bachelor of Science in Islamic Studies students. Participants were randomly assigned to either a control group, taught via the traditional lecture method (TLM), or an experimental group, taught using seven constructivist teaching guides (CTA). These guides covered topics including the water cycle, water as a unique substance, water pollution, water treatment, soils, and soil-related issues. Each guide included background information, objectives, and a five-phase teaching sequence: engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration, and evaluation. A key feature was the integration of students' traditional practices during the engagement and elaboration phases.

Findings indicated that prior to intervention, most students in both groups held everyday concepts rooted in traditional beliefs and personal observations. However, the constructivist teaching guides were effective in facilitating conceptual change, as evidenced by significantly higher posttest mean scores in the experimental group compared to the control group. The effectiveness varied by topic; the guides were specifically successful for concepts regarding the uses and importance of water, the water cycle, the unique properties of water, water treatment, and soil issues.

The study also revealed that traditional beliefs played a dual role. Some beliefs acted as facilitators, positively correlating with scientific answers and helping the transition to scientific understanding. Others acted as hindrances, negatively correlating with gain scores when they functioned as distractors.

The study concludes that constructivist teaching approaches are superior to traditional lecture methods for promoting scientific understanding in environmental chemistry. While traditional beliefs can act as obstacles, they can also be leveraged to facilitate learning if they align with scientific concepts. The research suggests that educators in culturally diverse settings should move away from purely traditional methods and instead develop instructional materials that acknowledge and incorporate students' existing cultural frameworks. By identifying which traditional beliefs facilitate or hinder learning, teachers can better design curriculum phases to guide students toward scientific literacy, allowing for a more inclusive pedagogical transition from everyday observations to formal scientific knowledge.
two:
The study conducted by Evelyn T. Cabading investigates the effectiveness of constructivist teaching guides in facilitating conceptual change among prospective Maguindanaon teachers. The research specifically focuses on teaching selected topics in environmental chemistry, namely soil and water chemistry. A central concern of the study is how these students transition from everyday views—often shaped by traditional practices and local beliefs—to scientific views. The researcher seeks to determine if a constructivist approach can bridge this gap and how the students' existing cultural beliefs influence this transition.

The context of the research is situated within the University of Southern Mindanao in Kabacan, Cotabato. The participants were third-year Bachelor of Science in Islamic Studies students. This specific demographic is significant as the study explores the intersection of traditional Maguindanaon practices and scientific education. The research addresses the need for effective instructional materials that can accommodate the unique cultural backgrounds of students while meeting scientific educational standards.

To address the research problem, the study employed a quasi-experimental research design. The participants were randomly assigned into two distinct groups: a control group and an experimental group. The control group was taught using the traditional lecture method (TLM), while the experimental group utilized teaching guides developed based on constructivist teaching approaches (CTA). The researcher developed seven specific teaching guides covering the following topics: the use of water, the water cycle, water as a unique substance, water pollution, water treatment, soils, and issues and concerns regarding soil.

Each constructivist teaching guide was structured with three specific components: background information, objectives, and a teaching sequence. The background information provided teachers with an overview of the lesson and identified the traditional practices and beliefs of the students that might influence their understanding. The objectives focused on developing both process skills and values. The teaching sequence followed the five-phase model proposed by Trowbridge and Bybee (1996), which includes engagement, exploration, explanation, elaboration, and evaluation. A key feature of this method was the integration of students' traditional practices and beliefs during the engagement and elaboration phases. To measure conceptual change, students provided explanations for their answers to multiple-choice questions. Additionally, a scale measuring soil and water practices and beliefs was used to correlate these beliefs with the students' gain scores.

The findings of the study indicate that prior to any intervention, the majority of students in both the experimental and control groups exhibited everyday concepts. These concepts were rooted in traditional beliefs, previous personal experiences, and direct observations of their surroundings. The results demonstrated that the constructivist teaching guides were effective in facilitating conceptual change from everyday views to scientific views, as evidenced by significantly higher posttest mean scores in the experimental group compared to the control group.

However, the effectiveness of the teaching guides was not uniform across all topics. Further analysis revealed that the guides were specifically effective for concepts related to the uses and importance of water, the water cycle, the unique properties of water, water treatment, and issues and concerns regarding soil. The study also found that traditional beliefs played a dual role in the learning process. Some beliefs acted as facilitators or hindrances to conceptual change. Specifically, beliefs that were negatively correlated with gain scores hindered conceptual change when they functioned as distractors in questions. Conversely, traditional beliefs that were positively correlated with scientific answers helped facilitate the transition to scientific understanding.

The study concludes that constructivist teaching approaches, when structured through specialized guides, are superior to traditional lecture methods in promoting scientific understanding in environmental chemistry. The research highlights that while traditional beliefs can sometimes act as obstacles to scientific learning, they can also be leveraged to facilitate it if they align with scientific concepts. The integration of student background and local practices into the curriculum is a vital component of the constructivist method.

The implications of this research suggest that educators teaching in culturally diverse settings should move away from purely traditional lecture methods. Instead, they should develop instructional materials that explicitly acknowledge and incorporate the students' existing cultural frameworks. By identifying which traditional beliefs facilitate or hinder scientific learning, teachers can better design engagement and elaboration phases to guide students toward scientific literacy. This approach is particularly relevant for science education in regions where traditional practices are deeply ingrained, as it allows for a more inclusive and effective pedagogical transition from everyday observations to formal scientific knowledge.
