title: Conceptual Ecology of High School Biology Students in a Multicultural Classroom
abstract:
This research is a qualitative multicultural classroom study in its natural setting aimed to describe the students’ conceptual ecology, explore the action of this ecology in the process of conceptual change, examine the influence of indigenous knowledge and identify what
conceptual change model can best describe the students’ conceptual restructuring related to the topic on Human Reproduction.

It involved three high school biology classes who worked in 25 small collaborative groups which are formed based on ethnolinguistic affiliation – the Chavacano, Bisaya, Tausug and Yakan, in Zamboanga City. Two students (dyad) from each of the selected fifteen groups
were used as targets or cases. Students’ knowledge was assessed before and after instruction through the use of student-generated concept maps, written or oral interview transcripts, observation notes and classroom artifacts.

A students’ conceptual ecology was found to include student-generated metaphors, epistemological beliefs, science knowledge, worldview as expressed through student’s religious orientation, prior knowledge and indigenous knowledge consisting of traditional beliefs and cultural practices. Three map patterns were identified – spoke (observed) only during map training), chain (2 groups each of Chavacano, Bisya and Yakan and all four Tausug groups) and the net patterns (2 Chavacano, 2 Bisaya and 1 Yakan). There are four patterns of conceptual change demonstrated by the dyad: 1) retention of naïve or incorrect knowledge, 2) framework reorganization/adjustment, 3) contextual switching and 4) radical restructuring.

Milagros M. Cosadio-Tan investigates the relationship between a student's existing mental frameworks and the acquisition of new scientific concepts. Focusing on the "conceptual ecology" of high school biology students in a multicultural classroom in Zamboanga City, the qualitative study examines how this ecology functions during conceptual change, the influence of indigenous knowledge, and which models best describe the restructuring of knowledge regarding human reproduction. The study involved three multicultural classes, utilizing concept maps, interviews, observations, and classroom artifacts to map knowledge structures.

The findings reveal that conceptual ecology is a multifaceted construct composed of metaphors, epistemological beliefs, science knowledge, religious orientation, prior knowledge, and indigenous knowledge, including traditional beliefs and cultural practices. Analysis of concept maps identified spoke, chain, and net patterns. Regarding conceptual change, the study identified four patterns: the retention of naïve or incorrect knowledge, framework reorganization or adjustment, contextual switching, and radical restructuring. 

The research concludes that conceptual ecology is a complex, diverse construct that serves as an essential prerequisite for meaningful learning. It influences conceptual change by affecting the persistence of prior knowledge and helping new conceptions appear intelligible and plausible. While the patterns of retention and radical restructuring align with the Posner et al. model, framework reorganization aligns with the accretion and tuning or framework adjustment models, and contextual switching conforms to the Kinchin model.

Milagros M. Cosadio-Tan investigates the relationship between a student's existing mental frameworks and the acquisition of new scientific concepts. The study focuses on the "conceptual ecology" of high school biology students in a multicultural classroom in Zamboanga City. Specifically, the research seeks to describe how this ecology functions during conceptual change, how indigenous knowledge influences this process, and which existing conceptual change models best describe the restructuring of student knowledge regarding human reproduction.

The qualitative study involved three high school biology classes with a multicultural student population, including Chavacano, Bisaya, Tausug, and Yakan ethnolinguistic groups. The researcher utilized 25 small collaborative groups, selecting two students from fifteen of these groups as target dyads for intensive study. Data collection methods included student-generated concept maps, written or oral interview transcripts, observation notes, and various classroom artifacts to map existing knowledge structures and observe shifts during instruction.

The findings reveal that a student's conceptual ecology is a multifaceted construct composed of interconnected elements: student-generated metaphors, epistemological beliefs, science knowledge, religious orientation, prior knowledge, and indigenous knowledge, which includes traditional beliefs and cultural practices. Analysis of student-generated concept maps identified three distinct patterns: spoke patterns (observed only during map training), chain patterns (found in two Chavacano, two Bisaya, and all four Tausug groups), and net patterns (found in two Chavacano, two Bisaya, and one Yakan groups).

Regarding the process of conceptual change, the study identified four patterns demonstrated by student dyads: the retention of naïve or incorrect knowledge, framework reorganization or adjustment, contextual switching, and radical restructuring. The research concludes that the conceptual ecology is a complex, diverse construct where various components interact. This ecology serves as an essential prerequisite for understanding new concepts and achieving meaningful learning. Furthermore, the ecology influences conceptual change in three ways: it affects the persistence of prior knowledge, helps render new conceptions intelligible, and helps make new conceptions appear plausible to the learner.

The study also examined how these restructuring patterns align with established scientific models. The patterns of "retention of naïve or prior knowledge" and "radical restructuring" conform to the conceptual change model proposed by Posner et al. (1982, 1992). However, "framework reorganization/adjustment" and "contextual switching" do not fit the Posner model. Instead, framework reorganization aligns with the "accretion and tuning" model of Pearsall et al. (1997) or the "framework adjustment" model of Luffiego et al. (1995), while contextual switching conforms to the "contextual switching" model proposed by Kinchin (2000).

The research conducted by Milagros M. Cosadio-Tan addresses the complex relationship between a student's existing mental frameworks and the process of learning new scientific concepts. The study focuses on the "conceptual ecology" of high school biology students within a multicultural classroom setting. The primary problem addressed is the need to describe how this ecology functions during the process of conceptual change, how indigenous knowledge influences this process, and which existing conceptual change models best describe the restructuring of student knowledge regarding the topic of human reproduction.

The context of the study is a natural classroom setting in Zamboanga City, involving three high school biology classes. The researcher focused on the multicultural nature of the student population, specifically looking at groups formed based on ethnolinguistic affiliations, including Chavacano, Bisaya, Tausug, and Yakan. To conduct the qualitative study, the researcher utilized 25 small collaborative groups. From these fifteen selected groups, two students from each group were chosen as target cases or dyads for intensive study.

The methodology employed was qualitative, utilizing various tools to assess student knowledge both before and after instruction. Data collection methods included the use of student-generated concept maps, written or oral interview transcripts, observation notes, and various classroom artifacts. By analyzing these tools, the researcher was able to map out the students' existing knowledge structures and observe how they shifted during the instructional period.

The findings reveal that a student's conceptual ecology is a multifaceted construct. It is composed of several interconnected elements: student-generated metaphors, epistemological beliefs, science knowledge, and the student's worldview as expressed through religious orientation. Furthermore, the ecology includes prior knowledge and indigenous knowledge, which encompasses traditional beliefs and cultural practices. When analyzing the structure of student-generated concept maps, the researcher identified three distinct patterns: spoke patterns (which were only observed during map training), chain patterns (found in two groups each of Chavacano, Bisaya, and Yakan, and all four Tausug groups), and net patterns (found in two Chavacano, two Bisaya, and one Yakan groups).

Regarding the process of conceptual change, the study identified four specific patterns demonstrated by the student dyads: the retention of naïve or incorrect knowledge, framework reorganization or adjustment, contextual switching, and radical restructuring. The research concludes that a student's conceptual ecology is complex and diverse, with its various components interacting with one another. This ecology serves as an essential prerequisite for understanding new concepts and achieving meaningful learning.

The study further concludes that the conceptual ecology influences the process of conceptual change in three specific ways. First, it affects the persistence of prior knowledge. Second, it helps in rendering new conceptions intelligible to the student. Third, it plays a role in making new conceptions appear plausible to the learner.

In terms of theoretical implications, the study examined how these observed patterns of restructuring align with established scientific models. The findings showed that the patterns of "retention of naïve or prior knowledge" and "radical restructuring" conform to the conceptual change model proposed by Posner et al. (1982, 1992). However, the patterns of "framework reorganization/adjustment" and "contextual switching" do not fit the Posner model. Instead, the pattern of framework reorganization aligns with the "accretion and tuning" model of Pearsall et al. (1997) or the "framework adjustment" model of Luffiego et al. (1995). The pattern of contextual switching conforms to the "contextual switching" model proposed by Kinchin (2000).

title: STSE Approach in Environmental Science for Nonscience Students in a Local Culture: Academic and Sociocultural Analysis
abstract:
The aim of the study is to use the STSE approach in teaching an environmental science course. STSE is an approach using the interactions of four important factors namely, science, technology, society and environment. Using activities derived from the local environment, a
learning climate unique to the STSE approach was developed and used to determine its influence on academic achievement and environmental science self-efficacy of students as well as the sociocultural perspectives of the students. The study further aimed to determine what sociocultural perspectives of nonscience students will surface when exposes to the STSE approach.

Quantitative and qualitative designs were used in the study. An experimental design using Solomon’s Four Group Design was used for the quantitative part, while observation interview of students was used in the qualitative part.

The STSE approach was used in an Environmental Science course for the first year nonscience students. Effect on academic achievement was determined using two-way ANOVA on the posttest scores of four groups, while the effects on efficacy and sociocultural perspective
were determined through the t-test of weighted means derived from the answers to the questionnaire. Observation and focused group interview were used for qualitative analysis of lessons especially for efficacy and sociocultural perspectives
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Bernadette I. Del Rosario investigated the application of the Science, Technology, Society, and Environment (STSE) approach within an Environmental Science course for first-year nonscience students. The study explored how this pedagogical method, which emphasizes the interactions between science, technology, society, and the environment, influences academic achievement, environmental science self-efficacy, and sociocultural perspectives. The researcher utilized a mixed-methods design, employing a Solomon’s Four Group Design for quantitative assessment and observation and focused group interviews for qualitative insights.

The findings indicate that the STSE approach is highly effective in improving the academic performance of nonscience students, with statistical analysis revealing a significant difference in posttest scores compared to a control group. Additionally, the approach led to a significant increase in environmental science self-efficacy. Regarding sociocultural analysis, the most dominant perspective identified was political, centered on the belief that the government is primarily responsible for environmental protection and sustainable development. Moral values regarding environmental and population issues also frequently emerged, though religious values did not surface significantly. 

The study concluded that while the STSE approach successfully enhances academic achievement and self-efficacy by connecting scientific concepts to local contexts, it does not significantly alter underlying sociocultural perspectives. The results suggest that while the method is a viable tool for increasing engagement with societal issues, it may not be sufficient for fundamental cultural transformation.

Del Rosario investigated the application of the Science, Technology, Society, and Environment (STSE) approach within an Environmental Science course designed for first-year nonscience students. The study addressed how this pedagogical approach, which emphasizes the interactions between science, technology, society, and the environment, influences academic achievement, environmental science self-efficacy, and sociocultural perspectives. The quantitative component utilized an experimental design using Solomon’s Four Group Design to assess the impact on academic performance and self-efficacy. Academic achievement was measured using a two-way ANOVA based on posttest scores, while environmental science self-efficacy and sociocultural perspectives were assessed via a questionnaire analyzed through t-tests of weighted means. The qualitative component involved observation and focused group interviews to gain deeper insights into student efficacy and sociocultural perspectives during lessons.

The findings indicate that the STSE approach is highly effective in improving the academic performance of nonscience students. Statistical analysis revealed a significant difference in posttest scores between the sections that utilized the STSE approach and those that did not. Furthermore, the STSE approach was responsible for a significant increase in environmental science self-efficacy compared to the control group.

Regarding sociocultural analysis, the study identified several distinct perspectives. The most dominant was the political perspective, characterized by the belief that the government holds primary responsibility for environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development. Moral values regarding what is considered "right" in relation to environmental and population issues also frequently emerged. However, religious values did not surface significantly in the discussions. When comparing sociocultural questionnaire results between groups, the study found no significant difference, suggesting that school group culture is strong and individual culture is difficult to change through this instructional method.

The study concludes that the STSE approach is an effective strategy for improving academic achievement and self-efficacy in nonscience students. While it successfully engages students in discussions regarding political and moral responsibilities, it does not significantly alter underlying sociocultural perspectives. The implications suggest that the STSE approach is a viable tool for enhancing academic competence and engagement with societal issues by connecting scientific concepts to local contexts, though it may not be sufficient for fundamental cultural transformation.

The study conducted by Bernadette I. Del Rosario investigates the application of the Science, Technology, Society, and Environment (STSE) approach within an Environmental Science course specifically designed for first-year nonscience students. The core problem addressed is how this specific pedagogical approach, which emphasizes the interactions between science, technology, society, and the environment, influences the academic achievement, environmental science self-efficacy, and sociocultural perspectives of students who are not pursuing science majors. The researcher sought to determine if integrating activities derived from the local environment could create a unique learning climate that impacts these specific student outcomes.

The context of the research is centered on the education of nonscience students, a group that may interact with environmental science differently than science majors. By utilizing activities rooted in the local environment, the study attempts to bridge the gap between theoretical scientific concepts and the lived experiences of the students. The research aims to identify what specific sociocultural perspectives emerge when these students are exposed to the STSE framework, particularly regarding how they view environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development.

To address these objectives, the researcher employed a mixed-methods research design, utilizing both quantitative and qualitative methodologies. For the quantitative component, an experimental design using Solomon’s Four Group Design was implemented. This design allowed for a rigorous assessment of the STSE approach's impact on academic performance and self-efficacy. The effects on academic achievement were measured using a two-way ANOVA based on posttest scores from four distinct groups. To assess environmental science self-efficacy and sociocultural perspectives, the researcher utilized a questionnaire, with the results analyzed through t-tests of weighted means.

The qualitative component of the study involved observation and focused group interviews with the students. These methods were specifically used to gain deeper insights into the students' efficacy and their sociocultural perspectives during lessons. This dual approach allowed the researcher to supplement statistical data with descriptive insights into the nature of the students' discussions and values.

The findings of the study indicate that the STSE approach is highly effective in improving the academic performance of nonscience students. Statistical analysis via two-way ANOVA revealed a significant difference in posttest scores between the two sections that utilized the STSE approach and the two sections that did not. Furthermore, the STSE approach was found to be responsible for a significant increase in the environmental science self-efficacy of the students compared to those in the control group, as measured by the t-test.

In terms of sociocultural analysis, the study identified several distinct perspectives. The most dominant perspective that surfaced among the students was the political perspective, characterized by the belief that the government holds the primary responsibility for environmental protection, conservation, and sustainable development. Additionally, moral values—specifically regarding what is considered "right" in relation to environmental concerns and population issues—frequently emerged during discussions. Interestingly, religious values, even when linked to cultural practices such as farming, population control, and environmental conservation, did not surface significantly in the discussions. When comparing the sociocultural questionnaire results between the groups, the study found no significant difference, suggesting that group culture within the school is strong and that individual culture is difficult to change through this instructional method.

The conclusions drawn from the research affirm that the STSE approach is an effective teaching strategy for improving both the academic achievement and the self-efficacy of nonscience students in an Environmental Science course. While the approach successfully engages students in discussions regarding political and moral responsibilities toward the environment, it does not significantly alter their underlying sociocultural perspectives, as students in both the experimental and control groups exhibited common ideas and values.

The implications of this study suggest that the STSE approach is a viable and beneficial pedagogical tool for educators teaching environmental science to nonscience majors. By connecting scientific concepts to local environmental contexts and societal issues, instructors can enhance student performance and their confidence in their own scientific efficacy. However, the findings also imply that educators should be aware that while such approaches can stimulate discussion on political and moral grounds, they may not be sufficient to shift deeply ingrained sociocultural or religious perspectives. Therefore, the STSE approach serves best as a method to enhance academic competence and engagement with societal issues rather than as a tool for fundamental cultural transformation.

title: Knowledge Restructuring in Selected Topics in Chemistry Using the Process Workshop Approach
abstract:
This study explored the changes in knowledge level and in structural complexity of knowledge held by students about chemical equilibrium, oxidation-reaction and electrochemistry by using the process workshop approach. The study also attempted to determine if changes in knowledge restricting is affected by learning mode employed by students.

The study was quasi-experimental in research design, involving twenty freshman B.S. Environmental Science students enrolled in Chemistry 18/L during the Second Semester of AY 2002-2003 at the College of Science, Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City.
The Inventory of Learning Process, pre- and post-intervention cognitive test, pre- and post-intervention concepts maps, and interviews served as the instruments for gathering data.

Two meaning learners (MLs) and two rote learners (RLs) were selected for the qualitative aspect of the study.

The teaching method used in the study was the process workshop approach. There were seven process workshop activities, two in chemical equilibrium, three in oxidation-reduction and two in electrochemistry.

This study investigated changes in knowledge levels and structural complexity regarding three chemistry topics: chemical equilibrium, oxidation-reduction, and electrochemistry. The research aimed to determine if the effectiveness of knowledge restructuring is influenced by a student's learning mode. Conducted at Palawan State University during the 2002-2003 academic year, the quasi-experimental study involved twenty freshman B.S. Environmental Science students. Data were collected via an Inventory of Learning Process, cognitive tests, concept maps, and interviews. The intervention utilized a process workshop approach consisting of seven specific activities.

Before the intervention, meaning learners (MLs) possessed higher knowledge levels than rote learners (RLs), though both groups had comparable pre-intervention knowledge structures. Following the workshop, both groups showed improvements in knowledge levels and structures. However, the improvement in knowledge level was significantly better in MLs than in RLs, and MLs achieved a more complex knowledge structure.

The study identified two types of structural change: turning, where the knowledge framework is completely revamped through the addition of a new concept, and restricting, where the framework is modified or rearranged through the addition or deletion of a concept within the first two hierarchies. The results suggest that while the process workshop facilitates improvement for both groups, meaning learners achieve higher knowledge levels and more complex structural organization than rote learners.

A primary objective was to determine if the effectiveness of knowledge restructuring is influenced by the student's learning mode.

The research was conducted at Palawan State University during the second semester of the 2002-2003 academic year. Using a quasi-experimental design, the study involved twenty freshman B.S. Environmental Science students. Data were collected through an Inventory of Learning Process, pre- and post-intervention cognitive tests, pre- and post-intervention concept maps, and interviews. For qualitative analysis, two meaning learners (MLs) and two rote learners (RLs) were selected to provide metacognitive reflections. The intervention utilized a process workshop approach consisting of seven specific activities.

Prior to the intervention, MLs possessed a higher knowledge level than RLs, as evidenced by pre-intervention cognitive test scores. However, when assessing overall pre-intervention knowledge structures through concept map scores, the MLs and RLs had comparable structures.

Following the implementation of the process workshop activities, both MLs and RLs showed improvements in their knowledge levels. However, the improvement in knowledge level was significantly better in the meaning learners than in the rote learners. Similarly, while both groups showed improvement in their knowledge structures, the meaning learners achieved a more complex knowledge structure than the rote learners.

The study identified two predominant types of structural change in both groups: turning and restricting. In turning, the students' earlier knowledge framework was completely revamped or changed through the addition of an introduced concept, resulting in an entirely new knowledge framework. In restricting, the earlier knowledge framework was simply modified and rearranged due to the addition or deletion of a concept within the first one or two hierarchies of the concept map.

The results suggest that while the process workshop approach facilitates knowledge improvement for both types of learners, meaning learners are able to achieve higher levels of knowledge and more complex structural organization than rote learners. The study highlights that the nature of structural change—whether it involves a complete revamp of the knowledge framework or a simple modification and rearrangement—is a key component of how students restructure their understanding of complex chemistry topics.

title: Metacognitive Learning Cycle Model: Effects on Conceptual Understanding and Problem-Solving Skills in Genetics
abstract:
This study compared the effects of the combined strategies following the Metacognitive Learning Cycle (MLC) Model and the Traditional Model on the conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills of first year college students in Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics. The MLC strategies include the discussion of discrepant events, use of a research-made learning manual during group work activities done under a cooperative learning atmosphere, class problem solving that employed think-aloud and modeling strategies, and metacognitive reflections by the students after each phase of the lesson. The traditional model includes lectures, discussions and problem-solving with teacher modeling the solution followed by individual seatwork activities.

Four intact classes, two from the high-ability and two from the low-ability groups, consisting of 185 first year college students enrolled at a teacher education institution in Tacloban City, Leyte were randomly assigned to the experimental and control groups.

The students in the sample were pretested simultaneously on the researcher made tests (e.g., Conceptual Understanding Test and Problem-solving Skills Test with reliability coefficient values of 0.64 and 0.80, respectively) as well as the four moderator variables (mental ability,
prior knowledge, disembedding ability test and cognitive level).
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Rosalina Hidalgo-Coral investigated whether the Metacognitive Learning Cycle (MLC) model is more effective than traditional teaching methods in helping first-year college students master complex Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics. The study involved 185 students at a teacher education institution in Tacloban City, Leyte, during the 2003-2004 school year. Using a quasi-experimental design, the researcher compared an experimental group using the MLC model—which integrated discrepant events, a researcher-made manual, cooperative group work, think-aloud strategies, and metacognitive reflections—against a control group taught through lectures, discussions, and individual seatwork.

Results indicated that while both groups improved, the MLC group achieved significantly higher posttest mean scores in both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. Conceptual trace analysis showed that both high- and low-ability groups in the experimental condition outperformed the control groups. While no moderating effect was found between moderator variables and the treatment regarding conceptual understanding, a moderating effect was observed in problem-solving. Specifically, prior knowledge and cognitive level moderated learning in problem-solving, with the MLC model proving more effective for students with low prior knowledge and those at the concrete level of cognition. Qualitative analysis suggested that stimulation activities helped concretize abstract concepts, while the learning manual and written reflections enhanced learning and scientific conceptions. The study concludes the MLC model is an effective approach for genetics education.

The research investigated whether the Metacognitive Learning Cycle (MLC) model is more effective than a traditional teaching model in helping students achieve both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills.

The study involved 185 first-year students at a teacher education institution in Tacloban City, Leyte, during the 2003-2004 school year. The sample included four intact classes categorized into high-ability and low-ability groups. Using a quasi-experimental design over eight weeks, the researcher assessed students through pretests and posttests focused on conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. The study also examined moderator variables including mental ability, prior knowledge, disembedding ability, and cognitive level. Student profiles indicated that most participants had average mental ability, low prior knowledge, were at the concrete level of cognition, and were field-independent. Pretest results showed very low initial levels of both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills.

The findings revealed that while both groups showed significant improvements, the MLC model group achieved significantly higher posttest mean scores in both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills compared to the control group. Conceptual trace analysis showed that both high- and low-ability groups in the experimental condition outperformed the control groups. Correlation analyses showed high correlations between pre- and posttest scores, and all four moderator variables were highly correlated to the mean scores. While no moderating effect was found between the moderator variables and the treatment regarding conceptual understanding, a moderating effect was observed in problem-solving. Specifically, prior knowledge and cognitive level moderated learning in problem-solving, with the MLC model being more effective for students with low prior knowledge and those at the concrete level of cognition.

Qualitative analysis of metacognitive reflections indicated that stimulation activities helped concretize abstract concepts, while heuristics and modeled exercises assisted in problem-solving. The study conducted by Rosalina Hidalgo-Coral addresses the challenge of teaching complex biological concepts, specifically Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics, to first-year college students. The research focuses on the effectiveness of the Metacognitive Learning Cycle (MLC) model compared to a traditional teaching model. The problem addressed is the difficulty students face in achieving both conceptual understanding and the necessary problem-solving skills required for genetics.

The context of the research involves 185 first-year college students enrolled at a teacher education institution in Tacloban City, Leyte, during the second semester of the 2003-2004 school year. The sample consisted of four intact classes, divided into two high-ability groups and two low-ability groups. The researcher served as the instructor for both the experimental and control groups. The experimental group was taught using the MLC model, which integrates several strategies: the discussion of discrepant events, the use of a researcher-made learning manual during cooperative group work, class problem-solving utilizing think-aloud and modeling strategies, and student metacognitive reflections after each lesson phase. In contrast, the control group was taught via a traditional model consisting of lectures, discussions, and teacher-modeled problem-solving followed by individual seatwork.

The methodology employed a quasi-experimental design lasting eight weeks, totaling 24 contact hours. Before the intervention, students were pretested using researcher-made Conceptual Understanding and Problem-solving Skills tests. The study also assessed four moderator variables: mental ability, prior knowledge, disembedding ability, and cognitive level. Data collection included quantitative analysis of pre- and post-test scores and qualitative analysis of conceptual trace analysis, posttest answers, and students' written metacognitive reflections.

The findings regarding student profiles showed that the majority of students possessed average mental ability (44%), low levels of prior knowledge (55%), and were at the concrete level of cognition (83%). Most students were field-independent (64%). Pretest results indicated that students initially possessed very low levels of both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in genetics.

Following the intervention, both the experimental and control groups showed significant increases in scores for both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. However, students in the MLC model group achieved significantly higher posttest mean scores in both categories compared to those in the traditional model group. Conceptual trace analysis showed that the experimental high- and low-ability groups outperformed the control groups across three categories of conceptual change: no change, change for the better, and change for the worse.

Correlation analyses revealed a high correlation between pre- and posttest scores for both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. Furthermore, all four moderator variables were highly correlated to the pre- and post-test mean scores in both tests. While no moderating effect was observed between the moderator variables and the treatment conditions regarding conceptual understanding, a moderating effect was found regarding problem-solving. Specifically, prior knowledge and cognitive level were found to moderate learning in problem-solving. The MLC model was found to be more effective for students with low prior knowledge and those at the concrete level of cognition in achieving higher performance in problem-solving compared to the traditional model.

Qualitative analysis of metacognitive reflections provided insight into why the MLC model was effective. Students reported that stimulation activities helped concretize abstract genetic concepts. They noted that the enrichment parts of simulation activities, heuristics for solving problems, and modeled exercises assisted in solving genetic problems. The reflections also indicated that the written component helped students realize that personal effort and involvement enhanced the intelligibility, plausibility, and fruitfulness of their learning. Additionally, the researcher-made learning manual was identified by students as a key tool in developing scientific conceptions and improving problem-solving skills for both high- and low-ability students.

The study concludes that the Metacognitive Learning Cycle model is an effective instructional approach for enhancing students' conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics. The research demonstrates that the integration of simulation activities and problem-solving exercises within a structured metacognitive framework facilitates student progress. The primary contributions of this work to biology education are the validation of the MLC model and the identification of the researcher-made learning manual as a beneficial tool for facilitating learning in genetics.

title: Developing Problem-Posing Abilities Among Preservice Mathematics Teachers
abstract:
This study was conducted to develop and enhance prospective mathematics teachers’ skills in formulating problems. This was done by providing them direct instruction on problem posing with utilizes constructivist-inspired teaching strategies, such as reflective writing,
small-group discussions, peer critiquing, and self-assessment. The study looked into the changes in the subjects’ skills in problem-solving, problem posing, and conceptual understanding after their exposure to the formal instruction on problem posing. It also investigated the relationships among students’ ability in solving problems, formulating problems, and understanding some mathematical concepts.

The study involved 17 third-year pre-service education students who have mathematics as their area of concentration and who were enrolled in the course, “Strategies in Teaching Mathematics,” during the second semester of AY 2001-2002 in the University of San
Jose-Recoletos, Cebu City. 

Since the study involved only one group, high and low-achieving students in the group were identified based on their scores in the problem-solving test administered before the intervention. Data from the two sets of students were analyzed qualitatively to establish a
detailed comparison of the perceivable changes in their problem-posing performance, problem-solving skills, and conceptions of some mathematical concepts.

Belen C. Lariego investigated the development of problem-posing abilities among preservice mathematics teachers, distinguishing this skill from problem-solving. The study aimed to determine how direct instruction using constructivist-inspired teaching strategies influences problem-solving, problem-posing, and conceptual understanding. Additionally, the researcher examined the relationships between a student's ability to solve problems, their ability to formulate problems, and their mathematical conceptual understanding.

The research was conducted during the 2001-2002 academic year at the University of San Jose-Recoletos with 17 third-year mathematics majors. Using a qualitative approach, the researcher employed constructivist-inspired strategies such as reflective writing, small-group discussions, peer critiquing, and self-assessment. Data collection included test score analysis, journal entries, oral interviews, and researcher observations.

Findings indicated that formal instruction on problem posing led to significant improvements. Following the intervention, students formulated and solved problems more effectively, generating better-constructed problems and demonstrating increased accuracy. Regarding conceptual understanding, initial misconceptions regarding common and decimal fractions, measurement, and linear equations in one unknown were corrected. Quantitative results showed positive linear relationships among problem-posing, problem-solving, and conceptual understanding. The study concludes that constructivist-inspired teaching strategies effectively promote problem-solving and problem-posing skills while enhancing comprehension of mathematical concepts. The research suggests the development of instructional materials, such as session guides containing problem-posing activities, to help teachers integrate these tasks into mathematics classes.

title: Nontraditional Problem Solving for Developing and Assessing Critical Thinking, Affective and other Cognitive Skills of Students
abstract:
This study compared the effects of the nontraditional problem solving or problem-based approach and the traditional or algorithmic approach on students’ critical thinking skills, conceptual knowledge in mathematics, competence in problem-solving, attitude and confidence towards mathematics and problem solving, and their learning patterns and behavior. Both approaches included the use of non-routine mathematic problems, small-group discussions, journal writing, and a free choice of appropriate problem-solving techniques in solving given problems. While the nontraditional problem-solving approach introduced concepts by using problem situations, the traditional approach introduced concepts by using problem situations, the traditional approach introduced the same concepts mainly through lecture discussions. Research-designed lessons were used to implement and assess the treatments involved.

The study used the quasi-experimental method of research and employed both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Two intact classes consisting of a total of 100 students enrolled in College Algebra I during the second semester of AY 2001-2002 in the University of
San Carlos, Cebu City, were the subjects of the study. These students were classified as high ability and low ability on the basis of their IQ scores.

The students in both the experimental and control classes showed initial comparability on all the factors being compared. The performance scores improve after the students were exposed to their respective treatments.

The study conducted by Corazon C. Raffinan investigates the comparative effectiveness of two distinct instructional methodologies in a mathematics classroom setting: the nontraditional problem-solving approach (also referred to as the problem-based approach) and the traditional or algorithmic approach. The research sought to determine how these different methods influence several key student outcomes, including critical thinking skills, conceptual knowledge in mathematics, competence in problem-solving, attitudes and confidence toward mathematics and problem-solving, and general learning patterns and behaviors.

The context for this research was established during the second semester of the 2001-2002 academic year at the University of San Carlos in Cebu City. The subjects were two intact classes of College Algebra I students, totaling 100 individuals. To ensure a comprehensive analysis, the researcher classified these students into high-ability and low-ability groups based on their IQ scores. Both the experimental and control groups were found to be comparable across all measured factors prior to the implementation of the treatments. The nontraditional approach was characterized by introducing concepts through problem situations and allowing students to use a free choice of appropriate problem-solving techniques, small-group discussions, and journal writing. In contrast, while the traditional approach also utilized problem situations, it primarily introduced concepts through lecture discussions.

To implement and assess these treatments, the researcher utilized research-designed lessons and employed a quasi-experimental research method. The study integrated both qualitative and quantitative analyses to provide a holistic view of the students' performance and psychological responses to the different teaching styles.

The findings of the study revealed varying degrees of success for each approach depending on the specific metric being measured. In terms of conceptual knowledge, the results were significant in favor of the control class, particularly because the pretest-to-posttest measures contained more algorithmic items. However, when measuring problem-solving abilities, the results favored the experimental class at a significance level of p = .10. While the quantitative data did not show a significant difference between the experimental and control groups regarding critical thinking skills or confidence and attitude toward mathematics, the qualitative results indicated a trend in favor of the experimental group.

Qualitative assessments of representative students showed that the experimental group generally outperformed the control group. This was evidenced by numerically higher scores and higher-quality solutions and responses that demonstrated superior critical thinking skills, conceptual knowledge, and problem-solving abilities. Furthermore, journal entries, interview protocols, and observation notes suggested that students in the experimental class exhibited higher levels of motivation and enthusiasm for solving mathematics problems compared to the control class, despite the experimental group facing a disadvantage regarding their class schedule.

The study also examined how the treatments affected different demographics. Regarding problem-solving abilities, a significant difference (p = .10) was found in favor of the males in the experimental class compared to the males in the control class. Among high-ability groups, the difference was very significant in favor of the experimental group. However, no significant differences were found between the low-ability groups of the two classes, nor were there significant differences between the female groups of the two classes.

In conclusion, the overall assessment of the data indicated that the nontraditional problem-solving approach provided several benefits to students. These included an increased frequency of critical thinking skill indicators in overall performance, better understanding and retention of course concepts, improved problem-solving abilities and the quality of solutions presented, a more positive attitude and confidence toward mathematics and problem-solving, and positive changes in learning patterns and behavior. The research concluded that the nontraditional approach increased students' confidence in their ability to solve problems, which subsequently improved their overall performance in the course.

The implications of this study extend to both students and educators. For students, the nontraditional approach offers a pathway to increased confidence and improved problem-solving competence. For teachers, the study provides insights into the efficacy of allowing students to use their own chosen techniques and peer assistance to improve their capabilities. Additionally, the research suggests that this approach allows teachers to become more aware of the students' thinking processes, enabling them to use the students' own points of view as a starting point to help improve the understanding of mathematical concepts.

title: Determinants of student Performance in the Science Component of the National Secondary Assessment
abstract:
Determinants of student performance in the National Secondary Achievement Test (NSAT) were investigated in this study. It aimed to identify the factors that affect student performance in the science component of the NSAT. It was conducted to assess the interplay of
curriculum context and instructional processes and practices as factors that affect the students’ performance in the test.

Quantitative analysis included the comparison of school profiles as associated with the student NSAT performance in the science are while qualitative analysis included the classroom discourses that depict what a science teacher is in terms of instructional process followed by them.

The sample consisted of 638 Palawan State University freshman students who came from the 78 secondary schools within the school divisions of Palawan during the Academic Year 2001-2002.

Data were gathered through questionnaire, checklist, interview guide, class observations, IQ test and scores in the NSAT.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
This study investigated the determinants of student performance in the science component of the National Secondary Achievement Test (NSAT) within Palawan school divisions during the 2001-2002 Academic Year. Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher analyzed 638 Palawan State University freshmen from 78 secondary schools to assess the interplay between curriculum context and classroom instructional processes.

The findings regarding student profiles indicated that the sample contained more females than males, most were average learners, and most expressed a neutral attitude toward science. In terms of learning styles, the majority were concrete learners preferring visual and tactile modes, intermediate information processors, and superficial learners motivated by external stimuli. Personality traits showed students were moderately self-confident and preferred working independently. Regarding parental characteristics, most mothers were college graduates who were not working, while most fathers were high school graduates.

The study identified that General Weighted Average (GWA), IQ, attitude, and age significantly related to science NSAT performance. Higher IQ, GWA, and positive attitudes were associated with better performance, while age showed a weak negative correlation. Notably, no significant relationships were found between school characteristics and NSAT performance. Furthermore, no strong positive or significant relationship existed between teacher characteristics and their instructional processes. The study concluded that individual student factors—specifically cognitive ability, academic history, attitude, and age—are significant predictors of performance, suggesting interventions should focus on the individual learner's cognitive and attitudinal profiles.

two:
The study investigated the determinants of student performance in the science component of the National Secondary Achievement Test (NSAT). The primary objective was to identify the specific factors that influence how students perform in this assessment. Specifically, the research sought to assess the interplay between the curriculum context and the instructional processes and practices used in the classroom to determine how these elements affect student outcomes.

The research was conducted within the context of the school divisions of Palawan during the 2001-2002 Academic Year. The study utilized a sample of 638 Palawan State University freshman students who had graduated from 78 different secondary schools. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of the problem, the researcher employed a mixed-methods approach. Quantitative analysis was used to compare school profiles in relation to NSAT performance, while qualitative analysis was used to examine classroom discourses to understand the instructional processes followed by science teachers. Data collection methods included questionnaires, checklists, interview guides, classroom observations, IQ tests, and the students' actual NSAT scores.

The findings regarding the student profiles revealed that the sample contained more females than males and that most students were classified as average learners. In terms of their current college enrollment at Palawan State University, 23% were in the College of Science, 22% in the College of Humanities, 20% in the College of Education, 18% in the College of Business and Accountancy, and 17% in the College of Engineering and Technology. Notably, the students who obtained the highest mean NSAT scores were enrolled in the College of Business and Accountancy. While most respondents expressed an interest in science, their general attitude toward the subject was largely neutral, falling neither into a distinctly positive nor a distinctly negative category.

The study further identified specific learning styles among the respondents. In terms of perceptual processing, the majority were concrete learners who preferred visual and tactile modes. Regarding information processing, they were intermediate between being passive and active processors. In terms of motivation, they were characterized as superficial learners who preferred external stimuli that were familiar, appealing, and less complex. Regarding personality, they were described as moderately self-confident learners who preferred working independently, were considered clever, and were not afraid to leave tasks unfinished. Regarding parental characteristics, the findings showed that most mothers were college graduates, though most were not working, while the majority of fathers were high school graduates.

A significant portion of the findings focused on the correlation between various factors and NSAT performance. The study found that students' General Weighted Average (GWA), IQ, attitude, and age significantly related to their NSAT performance. Specifically, higher IQ and GWA scores were associated with better science NSAT performance. Similarly, a more positive attitude toward science correlated with better NSAT performance. However, age showed a weak negative correlation, meaning that as students got older, their NSAT performance tended to be poorer. Interestingly, the study found no significant relationships between school characteristics and NSAT performance in the science component.

The study also examined teacher characteristics and instructional practices. Most teacher-respondents held a Bachelor of Secondary Education degree, were female-dominated, and were primarily aged 41-45. Many teachers had been teaching for 32 years, though a significant number had been teaching science for five years or less. Most teachers were based in public schools in rural areas and attended local seminars. The research found no strong positive or significant relationship between the personal characteristics of the teachers and their instructional processes or practices.

The observed instructional processes of the teachers included the use of lectures, classroom discussions, and problem-solving as instructional strategies. The process skills taught included observation, communication, classification, number recognition, and problem-solving. In terms of the types and levels of questions asked, teachers focused on cognitive memory, comprehension, and analysis. For evaluation, teachers primarily used completion and selection type tests. Additionally, the study noted that teachers used highly varied instructional materials.

The conclusions drawn from the study highlight that individual student factors, such as cognitive ability (IQ), academic history (GWA), attitude toward the subject, and age, are significant predictors of performance on the science component of the NSAT. While teacher characteristics and school profiles did not show significant relationships with performance in this specific sample, the instructional methods were identified as being centered on traditional strategies like lectures and discussions. The implications suggest that interventions aimed at improving science performance should focus on the individual learner's cognitive and attitudinal profiles, as these were the most significant determinants of success in the assessment.

title: Effects of Integrating History of Mathematics on High School Students Cognitive and Affective Learnings
abstract:
The study looked into the relative effects of integrating History of Mathematics in the teaching of Algebra and Trigonometry on the cognitive and affective learnings of fourth year high school students. Furthermore, it tried to find out the relative contribution of ability level and gender on their mathematics achievement, attitude towards mathematics, perception of the usefulness of mathematics, confidence in learning mathematics, mathematics anxiety and beliefs about mathematics.

Some 118 fourth year high school students enrolled in the Secondary Education Development Program of a public high school located in Iligan City were the subjects of this study. These students composed the four sections of Mathematics IV (Algebra and
Trigonometry) which were taught by one teacher. Two groups composed of one high ability section and one low ability section, randomly chosen as the experimental group, were taught Algebra and Trigonometry with the integration of History of Mathematics while other two groups were taught Algebra and Trigonometry the traditional way. Fifteen lessons for each group were prepared by the researcher.

At the beginning of the second semester, the learners have given the Otis Lennon School Ability Test the scores of which matched the learners between the experimental and control groups. At the same time, the Mathematics Achievement test, Attitude towards
Mathematics Inventory, Perception of the Usefulness of Mathematics Scale, Confidence in learning Mathematics Inventory, Mathematics Anxiety Scale and Inventory on Beliefs about Mathematics were also administered. These instruments were also used as posttests.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
Myrna E. Lahoylahoy investigated the effects of integrating the history of mathematics into Algebra and Trigonometry instruction, focusing on the cognitive and affective learning of fourth-year high school students. Using a quasi-experimental design with 118 students in Iligan City, the study compared an experimental group receiving history-integrated lessons against a control group taught via traditional methods. The researcher employed a triangulation method, combining quantitative data from tests and inventories with qualitative data.

Quantitative findings revealed no significant difference in mathematics achievement between the groups, regardless of gender or ability level. However, high-ability learners in the experimental group perceived mathematics to be more useful than those in the control group. While quantitative data showed no significant differences in attitude, confidence, anxiety, or beliefs across demographics, an interrelation was found between achievement and affective learning; high-achieving students tended to have more positive attitudes, lower anxiety, and higher confidence.

Qualitative results suggested that historical integration improved learners' attitudes, perceptions of usefulness, beliefs, confidence, and anxiety levels. High-ability students in the experimental group showed increased motivation, enthusiasm, and active participation. Although the researcher noted a gap between teaching methods and assessment, the qualitative results were positive regarding historical integration's effectiveness in enhancing learning. Recommendations include modifying achievement tests to include open-ended questions and adopting strategies to measure affective behaviors.

The research utilized a quasi-experimental design involving 118 students at a public high school in Iligan City. To ensure comparability, the Otis Lennon School Ability Test was used to match learners between groups. The researcher employed a triangulation method, combining quantitative data from various inventories and tests with qualitative data.

Regarding affective variables—including attitude, confidence, anxiety, and beliefs—the quantitative data showed no significant differences across gender or ability levels. The study did find an interrelation between achievement and affective learning, noting that students with high achievement tended to possess more positive attitudes, lower anxiety, higher confidence, and a greater perception of the subject's real-life utility.

Qualitative results provided a different perspective, suggesting that the integration of history improved learners' attitudes, views, perceptions of usefulness, beliefs, confidence, and anxiety levels. High-ability students in the experimental group demonstrated increased motivation, enthusiasm, active participation, and a tendency to volunteer for problem-solving. While teacher-student interaction was described as active and lively, it was noted to be teacher-dominated. Overall, students showed positive acceptance toward the integration of history.

In conclusion, the quantitative data did not support the initial hypotheses, as historical topics did not improve mathematical achievement scores. However, qualitative results were positive regarding the effectiveness of historical integration in enhancing cognitive and affective learning. The researcher suggested a gap exists between teaching methods and assessment, as students felt their affective views improved despite stagnant achievement scores.

Recommendations include modifying achievement tests to include open-ended questions that measure concept formation and authentic problem-solving. two:
The study conducted by Myrna E. Lahoylahoy investigated the relative effects of integrating the history of mathematics into the teaching of Algebra and Trigonometry. The research specifically focused on the cognitive and affective learnings of fourth-year high school students. Beyond examining the impact of historical integration, the study sought to determine the relative contributions of gender and ability level on several key variables: mathematics achievement, attitude towards mathematics, perception of the usefulness of mathematics, confidence in learning mathematics, mathematics anxiety, and beliefs about mathematics.

The research was conducted at a public high school in Iligan City, involving 118 fourth-year high school students enrolled in the Secondary Education Development Program. These students were divided into four sections of Mathematics IV (Algebra and Trigonometry) taught by a single teacher. The researcher utilized a quasi-experimental design where two groups—one high-ability section and one low-ability section—were randomly selected to serve as the experimental group. These students were taught Algebra and Trigonometry with the integration of the history of mathematics. The remaining two sections served as the control group and were taught using traditional methods. The researcher prepared fifteen lessons for each group.

To ensure the groups were comparable, the Otis Lennon School Ability Test was administered at the beginning of the second semester, and scores were used to match learners between the experimental and control groups. The study employed a triangulation method, combining quantitative and qualitative research approaches. Quantitative data were collected using several instruments: a Mathematics Achievement test, an Attitude towards Mathematics Inventory, a Perception of the Usefulness of Mathematics Scale, a Confidence in Learning Mathematics Inventory, a Mathematics Anxiety Scale, and an Inventory on Beliefs about Mathematics. These instruments were administered both at the beginning of the study and again as posttests.

The quantitative findings indicated that there was no significant difference in the mathematics achievement of learners taught with the integration of history of mathematics compared to those taught through traditional methods, regardless of ability level or gender. However, a specific difference was noted among high-ability learners; those exposed to the integration of history perceived mathematics to be more useful than those in the control group. Regarding affective variables—specifically attitude towards mathematics, confidence in learning mathematics, mathematics anxiety, and beliefs towards mathematics—the quantitative data showed no significant differences across different ability levels or gender before or after the experiment. Notably, the integration of history appeared to be more beneficial to high-ability students. The study also found an interrelation between achievement and affective learnings, suggesting that learners with high mathematics achievement tend to possess a positive attitude, lower anxiety, a perception of mathematics as useful in real-life situations, improved beliefs about mathematics, and higher confidence in learning the subject.

The qualitative results provided a different perspective, yielding positive outcomes regarding the integration of history. The qualitative data suggested that the integration of history improved learners' attitudes and views about mathematics, fostered a positive perception of its usefulness and beliefs, increased confidence, and lessened anxiety. High-ability students in the experimental group demonstrated increased motivation, enthusiasm in answering the teacher, active participation in class discussions, confidence in answering, and a tendency to volunteer to solve problems on the board. While the teacher-student interaction was described as active and lively, it was noted to be teacher-dominated. Overall, the students showed positive acceptance toward the integration of the history of mathematics in their Algebra and Trigonometry lessons.

In conclusion, the study found that the quantitative data did not support the initial hypotheses and theories drawn from the study's conceptualization. Specifically, the historical topics did not improve students' mathematical achievement. However, the qualitative results were positive regarding the effectiveness of historical integration in enhancing both cognitive and affective learning. The researcher noted a potential gap between what is taught and what is assessed, as the students felt the learning process improved their affective views and attitudes despite the lack of significant change in achievement scores.

Based on these findings, several implications and recommendations were proposed. To address the discrepancy between teaching methods and assessment results, it is recommended that the achievement tests be modified or improved to include open-ended questions that measure concept formation and authentic problem-solving abilities. Regarding affective learning, the study suggests that a deliberate strategy for measuring affective behaviors should be adopted. Finally, the researcher recommends follow-up studies using interpretive methods, such as participant observational fieldwork, to identify specific causal linkages that experimental methods might miss and to develop new theories regarding the influences on the patterns identified in the survey data.

title: Analysis of Task Sequence and Critical Behaviors of Engineering Students and their Understanding of Conic Sections
abstract:
This study investigated the quantitative and qualitative aspects of the sequence of steps taken in a solution path for solving conic sections (parabola, ellipse and hyperbola) problems. It identified critical behaviors or incidents, habits or mannerisms of students during
problem-solving to determine the relation of these to the understanding of the concept of conics. The think-aloud interview technique was used in conjunction with an interpretive method of case study observation.

The data came from sixteen (16) case studies of first-year students in the Bachelor of Science in Agricultural/Civil Engineering programs, also referred as General Engineering. The result of the Prior Knowledge Test on Conics was the basis in selecting the subjects. Starting
with the highest score, the 8 top-scoring students were classified as the Top-8 Group, and the 8 lowest scoring students were classified as the Bottom-8 Group. The subjects were asked to solve six problems in conic sections, two problems each (one routine and the other an
application problem) on parabola, ellipse and hyperbola. Their verbalizations were tape-recorded, and their behavioral characteristics were observed as they individually solved the problems.
faculty: Faculty of Education
half:
This study investigated the quantitative and qualitative aspects of problem-solving sequences used by sixteen first-year General Engineering students when solving problems involving parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas. Participants were divided into a Top-8 Group and a Bottom-8 Group based on a Prior Knowledge Test on Conics. Using think-aloud interviews and interpretive case study observations, the researcher monitored students as they solved six routine and application problems for each conic type.

The findings revealed significant differences between the two groups. Unsuccessful problem solvers faced obstacles such as insufficient recall of standard equations, incomplete use of graphing properties, poor understanding of asymptotes, and lack of mastery in algebraic manipulation. These students also struggled with inaccurate operations, confusion regarding point coordinates, poor English comprehension, failure to create illustrations, inability to explore real-world applications, incorrect variable representation, and a failure to develop algorithmic procedures.

Successful problem solvers generated solutions with an appropriate number of steps and possessed organized, integrated knowledge. They utilized powerful heuristics, such as the development of algorithmic procedures, and exhibited higher levels of confidence. In contrast, unsuccessful students often attempted rapid solutions in only one or two steps but ultimately took many steps due to repetitive actions. Their task sequences were neither well-ordered nor accurately organized, frequently relying on trial-and-error, guessing, or hit-and-miss techniques. Behaviorally, they displayed unusual mannerisms, high self-consciousness, confusion, anxiety, and a lack of interest in generating correct solutions.

The research aimed to identify critical behaviors, habits, or mannerisms that relate to a student's conceptual understanding of these mathematical concepts.

These students also demonstrated a lack of mastery in algebraic manipulation, inaccurate operations, and confusion regarding point coordinates. Additional difficulties included poor English language comprehension, failure to create illustrations, inability to explore real-world applications, incorrect variable representation, and a failure to develop algorithmic procedures.

Through an analysis of computation worksheets, verbalizations, and observation protocols, the researcher identified 25 behavioral tendencies that distinguished the two groups. Successful problem solvers generated solutions with an appropriate number of steps and possessed organized, integrated knowledge. They utilized powerful heuristics, such as the development of algorithmic procedures, and exhibited higher levels of confidence with minimal body gestures.

In contrast, unsuccessful students often attempted to find rapid solutions in only one or two steps but ultimately took many steps due to repetitive actions. Their task sequences were neither well-ordered nor accurately organized. These students struggled to remember and apply concepts in appropriate sequential steps, frequently relying on trial-and-error, guessing, or hit-and-miss techniques. Behaviorally, they displayed unusual mannerisms, high self-consciousness, confusion, anxiety, and a lack of interest in generating correct solutions.

The study concludes that there is a clear distinction in the cognitive and behavioral approaches used by students based on their level of understanding. The findings suggest a significant need for instructional programs for teachers that focus on developing intervention strategies to address the specific difficulties students encounter when solving problems related to conic sections.

This study investigated the quantitative and qualitative aspects of the sequence of steps taken in a solution path for solving conic sections problems, specifically focusing on the parabola, ellipse, and hyperbola. The research aimed to identify critical behaviors, habits, or mannerisms exhibited by students during the problem-solving process to determine how these behaviors relate to their conceptual understanding of conics.

The context of the research involved first-year students enrolled in Bachelor of Science in Agricultural/Civil Engineering programs, referred to as General Engineering. To select the participants, the researcher utilized a Prior Knowledge Test on Conics. Based on the results of this test, sixteen students were selected and divided into two distinct groups: the Top-8 Group, consisting of the eight highest-scoring students, and the Bottom-8 Group, consisting of the eight lowest-scoring students.

The methodology employed a combination of the think-aloud interview technique and an interpretive method of case study observation. The subjects were tasked with solving six specific problems related to conic sections, with two problems assigned to each type of conic: one routine problem and one application problem for the parabola, the ellipse, and the hyperbola. During the problem-solving process, the students' verbalizations were tape-recorded, and their behavioral characteristics were observed by the researcher.

The findings revealed significant differences between the two groups. The unsuccessful problem solvers encountered difficulties due to several specific factors. These included insufficient knowledge and recall of standard equations for conics under specific conditions, the incomplete use or total non-use of properties for graphing curves, and a poor understanding of the concept of asymptotes. Additionally, these students demonstrated a lack of mastery in algebraic manipulation skills, failed to carry out operations accurately, and experienced confusion when using coordinates of points. Other contributing factors included a poor understanding of the English language, a failure to create illustrations based on task information, an inability to explore real-world application problems, incorrect representation of variables, and a failure to develop algorithmic procedures.

Through an in-depth analysis of computation worksheets, think-aloud utterances, and observation protocols, the researcher identified 25 behavioral tendencies that distinguished successful problem solvers from unsuccessful ones. Successful problem solvers were characterized by generating solutions that required neither too few nor too many steps. They possessed more organized and integrated knowledge and utilized powerful heuristics or strategies, such as the development of algorithmic procedures. Furthermore, these students exhibited higher levels of confidence and manifested minimal body gestures.

In contrast, unsuccessful subjects attempted to find rapid solutions in only one or two steps, but often ended up taking many steps due to repetitive actions that indicated a lack of mastery over concepts and procedures. Their sequences of tasks were neither accurately organized nor well-ordered. These students showed an inability to correctly remember and identify concepts and to apply them in appropriate sequential steps. They frequently relied on trial-and-error, hit-and-miss techniques, or guessing. Behaviorally, they demonstrated obvious and unusual mannerisms, high self-consciousness, confusion, and anxiety, as well as a facial and verbal lack of interest in generating correct solutions.

The study concludes that there is a clear distinction in the cognitive and behavioral approaches used by students depending on their level of understanding of conic sections. The findings suggest a significant need for the development of instructional programs for teachers. Such programs should focus on creating intervention strategies designed to ease the specific difficulties students face when solving problems related to conic sections.

title: Enhancing Laboratory Performance and Scientific Attitudes of General Botany Students Through Inquiry-Oriented Laboratory Activities
abstract:
The study determined the General Botany students’ laboratory performance using inquiry-oriented laboratory activities and traditional laboratory activities in terms of acquired laboratory skills and scientific attitudes. It also determined the student factors (specifically
gender, high school science rating, and laboratory-related personal traits) related to laboratory performance and selected scientific attitudes.

The study sample consisted of 36 General Botany students of the University of Nueva Caceres, divided into 18 students for the experimental group and 18 students for the control group. A pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design was employed to determine the laboratory performance of the experimental and control groups. A laboratory manual on inquiry-oriented laboratory activities developed and used by the experimental group while the control group used the traditional laboratory activities. A 150 points practical test was administered before and after the treatment to assess 12 laboratory skills. A scientific attitudes inventory was constructed and administered to the two groups and before and after the treatment. A laboratory-related personal traits inventory was also constructed and administered to the two groups only before the treatment. Gender and high school science ratings of the respondents were also investigated if related to the laboratory performance and scientific attitudes of the respondents.

Alba conducted a study at the University of Nueva Caceres to investigate the effectiveness of inquiry-oriented laboratory activities compared to traditional laboratory activities in enhancing the laboratory performance and scientific attitudes of General Botany students. Using a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design, the study involved 36 students divided into an experimental group using an inquiry-oriented manual and a control group using traditional activities. Performance was measured via a 150-point practical test, and scientific attitudes were assessed using a constructed inventory.

The findings revealed that gender, high school science ratings, and various laboratory-related personal traits—such as being an organizer, orderly, patient, persistent, creative, and curious—had no significant relationship to either laboratory performance or scientific attitudes.

Regarding laboratory performance, both groups showed improvement from pretest to posttest, but the experimental group achieved much higher scores. The experimental group's posttest scores and gain scores were significantly higher than those of the control group, indicating that inquiry-oriented activities are more effective. Similarly, for scientific attitudes, the experimental group showed significant improvement from pretest to posttest, while the control group did not. The experimental group's posttest and gain scores were significantly higher, implying that inquiry-oriented activities are more successful in fostering scientific attitudes. The study concludes that inquiry-oriented activities can be successfully implemented even in poorly equipped environments to help students acquire skills and manage cognitive demands.
