title: Post Disaster Analysis: Assessment on Vegetation Damage by Typhoon “Odette” in Surigao City, Surigao Del Norte, Philippines
abstract:
With the country being known to experience several typhoons, post disasterrehabilitation programs formulated by local government primarily focus on resolving displacement situations with which over time is assumed to end once affected residents return and rebuild their homes. Struggles in the livelihood resources as a result of the typhoon comes in secondary which eventually contributes to the socio-economic crisis that most displaced households encounter, especially in upland communities who rely on forest-based resources such as coconut, banana and other fruit trees. This study therefore attempts to identify and delineate the effect of Typhoon Rai, locally known as “Odette”, to the agricultural and forest vegetation of selected
areas in Surigao City, Surigao del Norte using remote sensing method and GIS software. In order to understand the changes in vegetation, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Difference in NDVI were computed using free QGIS software which was correlated with elevation, slope and land surface temperature. Results of the study show significant changes in vegetation after landfall of Typhoon Odette specifically for Barangay San Roque and Togbongon with 24.7% and 10.8% loss in vegetation area respectively. Relating vegetation damage to geomorphological properties, correlation graphs displayed greater impact of slope, wind speed and wind direction and finally elevation to the degree of vegetation damage. The study shall serve as baseline data in improving forest management strategies and post-disaster agricultural and forest restoration programs of local government especially in severely damaged areas in Surigao City, Surigao del Norte.

The research specifically quantifies the environmental and economic impacts of Typhoon Rai (Odette) on agricultural and forest vegetation in selected areas of Surigao City, Surigao del Norte.

Using remote sensing and Geographic Information System (GIS) software, the researcher employed the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Difference in NDVI to compare vegetation health and density before and after the typhoon. These metrics were correlated with environmental variables, including elevation, slope, and land surface temperature, to identify drivers of vegetation change.

The findings reveal significant vegetation loss following the typhoon. Barangay San Roque recorded a 24.7% loss in vegetation area, while Barangay Togbongon experienced a 10.8% loss. Correlation analysis determined that slope, wind speed, and wind direction had the greatest impact on the degree of vegetation damage, while elevation had a comparatively lesser impact. These results underscore the vulnerability of local ecosystems and the livelihoods tied to them. The study provides baseline data to assist in improving forest management strategies and refining post-disaster agricultural and forest restoration programs to ensure more resilient recovery.

title: Financial Inclusion in the Digital Era: Communicative Practices in Organizing Facebook Live Transactions
abstract:
This study investigates the communicative practices that characterize Facebook Live selling and buying transactions—commonly referred to as Facebook Live selling—and examines their role in advancing digital financial inclusion. Grounded in ethnomethodology and conversation analysis, the research explores how sellers and buyers engage in patterned, real-time interactions—such as item claiming, product descriptions, transaction confirmations, and payment verification—to facilitate online commercial exchanges. By attending to the sequential organization of talk and turn-taking, the study demonstrates how social actions in live selling are organized, interpreted, and made intelligible to participants. These communicative practices not only enable smooth transaction processes but also serve as mechanisms for fostering trust, enhancing accessibility, and promoting financial participation in digitally mediated settings. The findings suggest that financial inclusion is not merely the outcome of technological access but
is actively achieved through structured communicative routines that orient users to informal financial engagement. In doing so, the study offers a communication-centered understanding of how digital financial inclusion is constructed in everyday interactions within emerging online marketplaces. This aligns closely with the goals of development communication, which emphasizes the strategic use of communication processes and media to promote social and economic development. By highlighting how communication itself serves as infrastructure for participation, trust, and digital
engagement, the study affirms that development efforts must go beyond technological solutions to consider how people use talk and interaction to navigate and reshape financial realities in marginalized or informal contexts.

title: Vulnerability to Fake News: The Case of the Overseas Filipino Workers in  Taiwan
abstract:
This study examines the vulnerability of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Taiwan to fake news circulating on social media. Using a qualitative, thematic analysis grounded in the Uses and Gratifications framework and elements of Grounded Theory, the research explores OFWs’ information‐seeking behavior, levels of awareness and understanding of fake news, social media habits, and cues that shape truth judgments. Data were gathered through semi‐structured interviews and analyzed via iterative coding, theme development, and constant comparison. Findings point to the roles of habitual social media use, heuristic processing, media trust, and confirmation bias in misperception. The study proposes a communication model and programmatic
recommendations for MECO and partner agencies that emphasize digital/media literacy, lateral reading, fact‐checking routines, and transparent communication. Implications for policy and practice are discussed.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Francis Albert D. Eugenio’s thesis, "Vulnerability to Fake News: The Case of the Overseas Filipino Workers in Taiwan," investigates why Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Taiwan are susceptible to social media misinformation. Because OFWs rely heavily on platforms like Facebook, TikTok, and Messenger for news and connection to the Philippines, they are uniquely exposed to false narratives that can impact their safety, finances, and well-being. Using a qualitative research design anchored in Grounded Theory, the study employed thematic analysis to examine the lived experiences of nine OFWs in Taiwan through in-depth, semi-structured interviews. The research utilized a dual-theory framework involving Uses and Gratifications Theory and Grounded Theory to identify a "relational credibility loop," where information is judged by the identity of the sender rather than content accuracy.

The findings revealed four dominant themes: social media acts as an unfiltered "digital plaza"; verification is primarily peer-based and relational, with OFWs trusting "kabayan," family, or church members over official sources; emotional and situational triggers accelerate information sharing by bypassing critical reasoning; and a significant gap exists between general awareness of fake news and actual media literacy skills. The study concludes that vulnerability stems from cognitive heuristics, emotional contagion, and social validation. To address this, the author proposes the "MECO-Led Communication Model for Digital Awareness and Fake News Resilience," which positions the Manila Economic and Cultural Office as a trusted hub to promote digital literacy and community-driven verification.

Francis Albert D. Eugenio’s thesis, "Vulnerability to Fake News: The Case of the Overseas Filipino Workers in Taiwan," investigates why Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Taiwan are susceptible to social media misinformation. Because OFWs rely heavily on platforms like Facebook, TikTok, and Messenger for news, emotional support, and connection to the Philippines, they are uniquely exposed to false narratives that can impact their safety, finances, and well-being. The research explores the psychological and social mechanisms behind this vulnerability, specifically looking at information-seeking behaviors, awareness levels, and social media habits.

Using a qualitative research design anchored in Grounded Theory, the study employed thematic analysis to examine the lived experiences of nine OFWs in Taiwan working in sectors such as factory work, caregiving, engineering, and household service. Data were collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews. The researcher utilized a dual-theory framework: Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) to explain motivations for media use, and Grounded Theory (GT) to uncover the social processes and "rules of trust" governing information interaction. This framework helped identify a "relational credibility loop," where information is judged by the identity of the sender rather than the accuracy of the content.

The findings revealed four dominant themes. First, social media acts as an indispensable, yet often unfiltered, "digital plaza" for OFWs. Second, verification is primarily peer-based and relational; OFWs tend to trust information from "kabayan" (fellow Filipinos), family, or church members over official institutional sources. Third, emotional and situational triggers, such as fear regarding health, disasters, or politics, accelerate the sharing of information by bypassing critical reasoning. Finally, while there is a high general awareness that fake news exists, there is a significant gap in actual media literacy skills, as participants often lack the technical ability to verify sources.

The study concludes that OFWs are active media users whose vulnerability stems from cognitive heuristics, emotional contagion, and a reliance on social validation. Awareness of fake news does not automatically ensure resilience; without practical verification skills, the tendency to share information "just in case" remains high.

To address this, the author proposes the "MECO-Led Communication Model for Digital Awareness and Fake News Resilience." two:
This thesis, titled "Vulnerability to Fake News: The Case of the Overseas Filipino Workers in Taiwan" by Francis Albert D. Eugenio, investigates the susceptibility of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Taiwan to misinformation circulating on social media. The study addresses the growing problem of digital disinformation, which exploits the high connectivity and social media dependency of the Filipino diaspora. Because OFWs rely heavily on platforms like Facebook, TikTok, and Messenger for news, connection to the Philippines, and emotional support, they are uniquely exposed to false narratives that can impact their safety, finances, and social well-being.

The research problem centers on the psychological and social mechanisms that make OFWs vulnerable. The study notes that while fake news is not a new phenomenon, the speed and reach of social media have amplified its impact. The researcher sought to understand the information-seeking behaviors, levels of awareness, and social media habits of OFWs, as well as the specific factors—such as emotional triggers and peer influence—that lead them to believe or share false information.

To address these questions, the study employed a qualitative research design using thematic analysis anchored in Grounded Theory. This approach allowed the researcher to move beyond existing frameworks and let themes emerge inductively from the participants' lived experiences. The participants consisted of nine OFWs in Taiwan, representing diverse sectors including factory work, caregiving, engineering, and household service. Data were collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews conducted in person, which were then transcribed verbatim and analyzed through iterative coding and constant comparison.

The study utilized a dual-theory framework to interpret the data. Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) was used to explain the motivations behind media use, such as the need for social connection, convenience, and identity affirmation. Grounded Theory (GT) was used to uncover the specific social processes and "rules of trust" that govern how OFWs interact with information. Together, these theories helped explain how the functional need for social media creates a "relational credibility loop," where information is judged based on the identity of the sender rather than the accuracy of the content.

The findings revealed four dominant themes. First, social media serves as the default information ecosystem for OFWs, providing a "digital plaza" that is indispensable for daily life but often unfiltered. Second, verification is primarily peer-based and relational; OFWs tend to trust information shared by "kabayan" (fellow Filipinos), church members, or family, rather than official institutional sources. Third, emotional and situational triggers—such as fear regarding disasters, health rumors, or political instability—act as accelerators for sharing, often bypassing critical reasoning. Finally, while there is a high general awareness that fake news exists, there is a significant gap in actual media literacy skills; participants often lack the technical ability to verify sources, relying instead on visual cues or the popularity of a post.

The study concludes that OFWs are not passive victims but active media users whose vulnerability is a product of their specific digital habits and social structures. Their susceptibility is driven by a combination of cognitive heuristics (mental shortcuts), emotional contagion, and a reliance on social validation. The research highlights that awareness of fake news does not automatically equate to resilience against it; without practical verification skills, the tendency to share information "just in case" remains high.

Based on these findings, the author proposes a "MECO-Led Communication Model for Digital Awareness and Fake News Resilience." This model positions the Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO) as a central, trusted information hub. The model's core components include promoting digital literacy and critical thinking through short, accessible modules; conducting regular information sessions on media verification; and fostering multi-sector collaborations with government agencies (like the DFA-OVS), NGOs, and technology platforms. A key feature of the model is the promotion of "community-driven verification," which encourages the use of peer networks and "lateral reading" to transform the OFW community from passive consumers into active participants in truth promotion.

The implications of this research are both practical and policy-oriented. For government agencies and overseas offices, the study suggests that anti-misinformation campaigns must move beyond official advisories and instead engage with the existing trust networks of the diaspora. By embedding media literacy into the social and digital spaces where OFWs already congregate—such as Facebook groups and community chats—institutions can build a more resilient and digitally literate migrant community.

title: WIP: A Video Game About the Challenges in Doing Something for the First Time
abstract:
Video games are a form of multimedia that is typically considered for entertainment. However, apart from being a form of leisure, it can also be an
opportunity to connect with other people through various meaningful narratives that allows us to explore and understand experiences and situations that acknowledges us or recognizes the circumstances that we have never been in. This Capsule Project aims to illustrate the challenges we face whenever we want to do something for the first time through a functional video game — but without explicit narration. Instead of employing texts to tell the tale, the player will shape their own journey and get a semblance of the experience through the game’s mechanics and systems that mimics what it is like to finally work on something for the first time. In this way, the player can give it their own interpretation, and perhaps it can even be a chance for reflection. Applications and softwares utilized for this project were mainly IbisPaint for the Art and Ren’Py as the game engine. However, other softwares such as image processors, word processors, and online tools like Canva and Milanote were used as needed either to enhance, support, or ease up the game making process. I was able to create a functional video game that relies solely on game mechanics which allowed the testers to play the game based on their own liking. However, the struggle of doing something for the first time was not clearly understood since all the testers were left confused while playing. It is important that I set clear expectations and define how I want them to be achieved. In this way, I can decide if suggestions such as adding more clues and dialogues is something that I should consider or perhaps if I should approach the story in an entirely different way.

Kayce Racelle G. Tampinco’s capstone project, "WIP: A Video Game About the Challenges in Doing Something for the First Time," explores the psychological and practical hurdles involved in initiating new endeavors. The research addresses universal struggles such as procrastination, fear of failure, and perfectionism, which create a gap between intention and action. Motivated by personal experiences of being held back by perceived technical deficiencies, the author aimed to create a functional video game that communicates these themes through gameplay mechanics rather than explicit narration, utilizing a "show, don't tell" approach.

The development followed a standard lifecycle using Ren’Py and IbisPaint to create a desktop-themed interface. In this setting, players attempt to complete a main puzzle game representing a project while being tempted by a distraction mini-game featuring social media-style icons.

Findings from testing revealed a tension between artistic intent and player comprehension. While the mechanics successfully simulated the feeling of distraction, the lack of explicit narration caused significant confusion; many testers did not grasp the game's objectives or the significance of the timer. Additionally, the high difficulty of the initial level raised questions regarding player fulfillment. The author concludes that while the game effectively simulated deadline pressure, storytelling through mechanics alone is exceptionally difficult. Future iterations should balance immersion with clarity by using subtle clues to ensure the narrative purpose is understandable.

Tampinco explores the psychological and practical hurdles involved in initiating new endeavors. The work addresses universal struggles such as procrastination, fear of failure, and the tendency to overanalyze risks, which often prevent individuals from taking the first step toward a goal. This research was motivated by the author's personal experience of being held back from game development by perceived deficiencies in technical skills like programming and art.

The central problem identified is the difficulty of transitioning from intention to action. The author notes that humans often fall into traps of perfectionism, waiting for a perfect moment, or becoming paralyzed by the fear of being perceived as irresponsible or foolish. These internal barriers, combined with external pressures like time and mental exhaustion, create a significant gap between wanting to do something and actually doing it. To address this, the author aimed to create a functional video game that communicates these themes through gameplay mechanics rather than explicit narration, using a "show, don't tell" approach to allow players to experience the tension and resilience required to complete a task.

The methodology followed a standard game development lifecycle consisting of pre-production, production, and post-production. The author used Milanote for organization, Ren’Py as the game engine, and IbisPaint for pixel art assets. The production phase involved creating a desktop-themed interface where players must complete a main puzzle game representing a project while being tempted by a distraction mini-game involving social media-style icons.

Findings from the development and testing phases revealed a tension between artistic intent and player comprehension. While the mechanics successfully simulated the feeling of being distracted, the lack of explicit narration led to significant confusion among testers. Many participants did not immediately grasp the game's objective or the significance of the timer. Additionally, the high difficulty of the first level raised questions regarding whether the game should be more forgiving to ensure player fulfillment.

In conclusion, the project successfully produced a functional game that uses mechanics as a metaphor for human struggle, but the author concludes that storytelling through mechanics alone is exceptionally difficult. The results suggest that while the game effectively simulated the pressure of a deadline, it failed to clearly communicate its narrative purpose to players lacking prior context. The capstone project titled "WIP: A Video Game About the Challenges in Doing Something for the First Time" by Kayce Racelle G. Tampinco explores the psychological and practical hurdles associated with initiating new endeavors. The author addresses the universal struggle of overcoming procrastination, fear of failure, and the tendency to overanalyze risks, which often prevents individuals from taking the first step toward a goal. The project is motivated by the author's personal experience of wanting to create a game for years but being held back by perceived lacks in technical skills such as programming and art.

The central problem identified is the difficulty of "transitioning" from intention to action. The author notes that humans often fall into traps of perfectionism, waiting for the "perfect moment," or being paralyzed by the fear of being perceived as irresponsible or foolish. These internal barriers, combined with external pressures like time and mental exhaustion, create a significant gap between wanting to do something and actually doing it.

To address this, the author aims to create a functional video game that communicates these themes through gameplay mechanics rather than explicit narration. The objective is to use "show, don't tell" storytelling to allow players to experience the tension, distraction, and eventual resilience required to complete a task. The project seeks to emphasize that challenges are an inherent part of any process and that persistence is key.

The methodology follows a standard game development lifecycle consisting of pre-production, production, and post-production. During pre-production, the author utilized Milanote for organization and created wireframes to visualize the desktop-themed interface. The choice of Ren’Py as the game engine was made due to its accessibility for visual novel-style development, while IbisPaint was used for creating pixel art assets. The production phase involved creating art assets—including wallpapers, icons, and cards—and coding the main game and mini-games. Post-production focused on personal testing and beta-testing to evaluate if the intended message was communicated effectively.

The findings from the development and testing phases reveal a tension between artistic intent and player comprehension. The game's design features a desktop environment where the player must complete a "main" puzzle game (representing the project) within a limited time, while being tempted by a "distraction" mini-game (a memory card game involving social media-style icons and thought cards). The author discovered that while the mechanics successfully simulated the feeling of being busy or distracted, the lack of explicit narration led to significant confusion among testers. Many testers did not immediately grasp the game's objective or the significance of the timer. Furthermore, the difficulty of the first level was so high that even the author struggled to complete it within the time limit, leading to questions about whether the game should be more forgiving to ensure a sense of fulfillment.

In conclusion, the project successfully produced a functional game that utilizes mechanics as a metaphor for human struggle. However, the author concludes that storytelling through mechanics alone is exceptionally difficult because the creator's vision must meet the player's assumptions halfway. The results suggest that while the game effectively simulated the "pressure" of a deadline, it failed to clearly communicate its narrative purpose to players who lacked prior context.

The implications of this work highlight the importance of balancing immersion with clarity in game design. The author suggests that for games relying on non-verbal storytelling, developers must carefully calibrate the amount of "context" provided. Too little context leads to confusion and aimless wandering, while too much may strip the player of their ability to personally interpret the experience. The project recommends that future iterations include subtle clues, such as monologues or environmental hints, and improved user accessibility to ensure the player's journey is both meaningful and understandable.

title: Work Environment, Burnout, and Job Satisfaction Among Nurses in Al Ain, Abu Dhabi, UAE
abstract:
This study examined the nursing work environment, burnout, and job satisfaction among staff nurses in a selected hospital in Al Ain, Abu Dhabi, UAE.
Utilizing a descriptive-correlational research design, the study surveyed a final analytic sample of 143 full-time clinical staff nurses, yielding an effective response rate of 71.5%. Data were collected using the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI), the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), and the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire-Short Form (MSQ-SF). Analysis was performed using STATA MP-Parallel Edition (Version 18), employing descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation. The findings revealed a moderately favorable work environment, with
"Collegial Nurse-Physician Relations" emerging as the strongest domain, while "Staffing and Resource Adequacy" was identified as the most significant area for improvement. The burnout assessment indicated moderate levels of personal and work-related exhaustion, contrasted with low levels of client-related burnout, suggesting that nurse fatigue in this context was predominantly organizational rather than clinical in origin. Job satisfaction was moderate overall, characterized by high intrinsic fulfillment derived from patient care but constrained by lower extrinsic satisfaction related to pay and workload. Correlation analysis demonstrated that a favorable work environment is significantly associated with lower burnout and higher job satisfaction, while burnout serves as a critical pathway through which structural deficits erode professional fulfillment. The study concludes that the current workforce is professionally engaged but structurally strained, and that it relies heavily on nurses' intrinsic motivation as a finite buffer against systemic pressures. Recommendations include establishing a Nursing Workforce Task Force, implementing shared governance structures, and
reviewing staffing standards and weekly working hours to ensure the long-term sustainability of high-quality care.

The study conducted by Junah Balungcas Corona investigates the complex relationship between the nursing work environment, burnout levels, and job satisfaction among full-time clinical staff nurses working in a selected hospital located in Al Ain, Abu Dhabi, UAE. The research addresses a critical intersection in healthcare management: how the structural and interpersonal conditions of a clinical setting influence the psychological well-being and professional contentment of the nursing workforce.

The context of this research is situated within the specific healthcare landscape of the United Arab Emirates, where maintaining high standards of patient care requires a stable and satisfied nursing workforce. The researcher identifies a potential tension between the professional dedication of nurses and the systemic pressures inherent in hospital environments. By focusing on Al Ain, the study provides localized insights into how organizational structures impact frontline clinicians.

To investigate these variables, the researcher employed a descriptive-correlational research design. The study utilized a final analytic sample of 143 full-time clinical staff nurses, achieving an effective response rate of 71.5%. Data collection was facilitated through three validated psychometric instruments: the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI) to assess the work environment, the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI) to measure burnout, and the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire-Short Form (MSQ-SF) to evaluate job satisfaction. The quantitative data were analyzed using STATA MP-Parallel Edition (Version 18), utilizing descriptive statistics to profile the sample and Spearman’s rho correlation to determine the relationships between the three primary variables.

The findings of the study provide a detailed profile of the nursing experience in the studied facility. Regarding the work environment, the results indicated a moderately favorable setting. Within this environment, "Collegial Nurse-Physician Relations" was identified as the strongest domain, suggesting a positive level of professional collaboration between different healthcare roles. However, the study also identified "Staffing and Resource Adequacy" as the most significant area requiring improvement, highlighting a deficit in the physical and human resources available to the staff.

The assessment of burnout revealed a nuanced pattern. Nurses reported moderate levels of both personal exhaustion and work-related exhaustion. Notably, the levels of client-related burnout were found to be low. This distinction is significant as it suggests that the fatigue experienced by these nurses is predominantly organizational in origin rather than being driven by the clinical demands of patient interaction. This indicates that the strain is linked more to the structure of the work than to the nature of patient care itself.

Job satisfaction among the participants was found to be moderate overall. The data revealed a dichotomy in what drives satisfaction: nurses reported high levels of intrinsic fulfillment, largely derived from the act of providing patient care. Conversely, they reported lower levels of extrinsic satisfaction, specifically regarding their pay and their workload. This suggests that while the nurses find meaning in their professional roles, the external conditions of their employment are a source of dissatisfaction.

The correlation analysis provided critical insights into how these three factors interact. The study found that a favorable work environment is significantly associated with lower levels of burnout and higher levels of job satisfaction. Furthermore, the research identified burnout as a critical pathway through which structural deficits in the workplace erode professional fulfillment. This implies that when the work environment is lacking, it triggers burnout, which in turn diminishes the nurse's satisfaction with their job.

In conclusion, the study finds that the nursing workforce in the studied hospital is professionally engaged but structurally strained. The findings suggest that the current stability of the nursing staff relies heavily on the nurses' own intrinsic motivation, which acts as a finite buffer against systemic and organizational pressures. While the nurses' passion for patient care keeps them engaged, the structural deficits in staffing and resources pose a risk to their long-term well-being and professional longevity.

The implications of these findings suggest a need for targeted organizational interventions to ensure the sustainability of high-quality care. The researcher recommends the establishment of a Nursing Workforce Task Force to address these systemic issues. Additionally, the study suggests the implementation of shared governance structures to improve the work environment and empower staff. Finally, the researcher recommends a formal review of staffing standards and weekly working hours to mitigate the organizational exhaustion identified in the study and to support the long-term professional health of the nursing staff.

title: An Autoethnographic Analysis of Social Enterprise's Advocacy Communication
abstract:
This comprehensive study on Autoethnographic Analysis of Social Enterprise’s Advocacy Communication explored my journey as a social entrepreneur and a communication scholar, showcasing the evolving motivations, transformative shifts in purpose, challenges, through my life’s experiences and exposures. In this research, I utilized vignettes, immersion, and reflection guided by theories and principles of ontology, epistemology, teleology, and praxeological positions. These key findings and contributions created knowledge that challenges some traditional research standards unmuting my voice to integrate personal narratives and empower the study through personal experiences as primary values of autoethnography to contribute to
the field of social entrepreneurship and its context of advocacy communication. Valuable insights in the research denotes silent empowerment as a
fundamental factor in advocacy communication, as it centers its role on credibility, lasting impact, and authenticity especially in the digital landscape. Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) in this said context uncovers positive workplace behavior as a crucial aspect in the success of an advocacy and of an any organization. Moreover, this study also concluded that digital platforms are fundamental for advocacy communication. It recognizes the paramount significance of technology in identifying markets, reaching broader audience, and effectively communicating an advocacy of a social enterprise. Storytelling and leadership are also remarkable results that this research was able to unveil. The importance of both signified a positive reception of advocacy from the audiences and considered key tools that affect insights, behavior, and culture of a market or an organization especially in the field of social entrepreneurship Through my social interactions and reflections in social entrepreneurship and past journeys leading to it—in this comprehensive delved of knowledge and experiences, I was able to gain insightful and remarkable definition of what social entrepreneurship specifically is: Social entrepreneurship refers to pursuing purposeful and socially driven business process with equal prioritization to its profitability. It surpasses traditional corporate social responsibility approaches, as it is not merely an auxiliary business afterthought but centers its conception and existence on its social causes. This research concludes a reflection on personal growth and overcoming doubts and overall challenges in business, furthering the role of being an advocating and integrating it with entrepreneurship. This autoethnographic study enriches knowledge of the intricate relationship between social entrepreneurship and advocacy communication. title: Teleacting an Authority in A Communicative Practice: Compliance Certificate as a Non-human Agent in Solid Waste Management
abstract:
This study is anchored on the Non-Human Agency Framework advanced by Francois Cooren (2006), which attempts to explain ‘how one can act from a distance’ or ‘teleact’ or the act of making present or presentifying something or someone in communicative practices. Teleaction can happen in a manner that non-humans represent other entities. By examining a compliance certificate used by a government regulatory body in solid waste management, the study sought to answer the research questions: 1) what figures appeared in the solid waste management compliance certificate that ventriloquized its authority; 2) what does the compliance certificate perform in solid waste management? Using Cooren’s (2010) Ventriloquial Analysis
Approach, this study analyzed the Municipal Solid Waste Management Compliance Certificate (MSWMCC), a document issued by the Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Office (MENRO), a local government regulatory body in solid waste management in a municipality in the Province of (Name of the Province). From the analysis, it was revealed that there is a total of ten (10) figures explicitly invoked in the certificate – 1) official logo, 2) letterhead, 3) certificate number, 4) RA 9003, 5) declaration of compliance, 6) date of issuance, 7) place of issuance, 8) date of inspection, 9) signatory, and 10) QR code. These explicit figures that appeared in the compliance certificate implicitly convey significant messages relative to environmental
protection and sustainability. Also found in the analysis are six (6) acts that the compliance certificate performs in accomplishing solid waste management – 1) representing the government, 2) regulating business operations in accordance with solid waste management practices, 3) affirming business entity’s compliance, 4) informing the general public of the business entity’s participation in solid waste management, 5) authorizing business operations in consideration with solid waste management, and 6) documenting business entity’s participation in solid waste management. From the findings of this study, the researcher advances the Ventriloquized- Animated Authority Theory. Non-human agents, like the compliance certificate, possess ventriloquized and animated authority. Ventriloquized-Animated Authority is that kind of authority that the non-human agents derive from their being ventriloquized (given voices to speak) and animated (acted upon to act) by some higher unseen principals. The voices given to non-human agents by more powerful unseen principals grant them the strength and the power to speak about influential messages that move human agents to act. Likewise, the force of persuasion exerted on the non-human agents by a more powerful unseen principal also pushes the human actors to perform
something geared toward the accomplishment of organizational goals. Thus, as a textual agent, the compliance certificate possesses this authority that compels business entities to participate in solid waste management, contributing to the accomplishment of organizational goals and the national vision. With this, this study contributes this concept that non-human agents, like the compliance certificate which is a textual agent, really exert influences on and contribute to organizational dynamics and accomplishment as they participate in various communicative practices that shape
and define organizations, as emphasized by the concept of CCO (Communication as Constitutive of Organization) under the Montreal School of Organizational Communication.

title: Lingkod Bayang Makakalikasan:  Examining the Determinants of Employees' Intention to Engage in Green Behavior in a Public Organization
abstract: How do employees in a public organization intend to practice the principle of Lingkod Bayang Makakalikasan? Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior developed by Icek Ajzen, this study examines the determinants of employees’ intention to engage in Employee Green Behavior (EGB) in a public organization in the Philippines. It explores how attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence intention, and how socio-demographic characteristics and environmental knowledge shape these constructs. EGB includes workplace practices such as energy conservation, waste reduction, and participation in sustainability initiatives. Using a quantitative survey design, data were collected from 285 employee-respondents and analyzed using statistical techniques. Results show that attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly influence intentions to engage in green behavior. Environmental knowledge indirectly strengthens intention by influencing attitudes and perceived control, while socio-demographic factors show limited direct effects. The findings highlight the importance of fostering supportive norms, positive attitudes, and a strong sense of behavioral control to institutionalize sustainable practices in the public sector.

half:
This research addresses the need for climate action by examining the determinants of employee green behavior within a public organization in the Philippines. Because the subject organization lacks a structured sustainability policy, most environmental efforts are driven by the voluntary actions of employees. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, the study utilizes a descriptive-correlational research design to examine how socio-demographic characteristics, environmental knowledge, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence intentions to engage in green behavior. Data was collected via an online survey from 285 employees of a government-owned and controlled corporation.

The findings show the respondent group is predominantly female (68.8%) and belongs to the Millennial generation (55.4%). Most are frontline employees in Member Services (34.4%) with between 1 and 10 years of government service (50.5%). Respondents perceived their environmental knowledge to a large extent (mean = 3.77). Attitudes toward green behavior were high (mean = 4.26), and subjective norms showed an overall mean of 3.76. Perceived behavioral control was also high, with respondents feeling capable of protecting the environment.

Results demonstrate that attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly influence intentions to engage in green behavior. Environmental knowledge indirectly strengthens intention by influencing attitudes and perceived control. Socio-demographic factors showed limited direct effects. The study concludes that while employees are knowledgeable and willing, the lack of formal policy means behaviors remain voluntary. Organizations can institutionalize these practices through leadership-driven initiatives and peer recognition programs.

This research addresses the urgent need for climate action and the role of organizations in mitigating environmental degradation. While much research on employee green behavior has focused on the private sector, a significant gap exists regarding the public sector, particularly in the Philippines. In the subject public organization, there is currently no structured sustainability policy or program in place, meaning most green efforts are driven by the voluntary or personal actions of employees. This study seeks to understand the determinants of employees' intention to engage in employee green behavior by examining how socio-demographic characteristics, environmental knowledge, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence these intentions.

The study is grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, which posits that an individual's intention to perform a behavior is shaped by their attitude toward that behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. The researcher employed a descriptive-correlational research design, collecting data through an online survey questionnaire administered to 285 employees of a selected government-owned and controlled corporation in the Philippines, specifically those assigned to NCR branches of the Operations. Participants were selected using a simple random sampling technique.

The findings reveal that the respondent group is predominantly female (68.8%) and belongs to the Millennial generation (55.4%). Most respondents are frontline employees in Member Services (34.4%) and have between 1 and 10 years of government service (50.5%). Regarding environmental knowledge, respondents perceived themselves as possessing knowledge to a large extent (mean = 3.77). Attitudes toward employee green behavior were also high, with an overall mean of 4.26, indicating strong agreement that promoting green living and raising environmental awareness are essential. Subjective norms showed an overall mean of 3.76, suggesting that respondents generally agree that their social circles expect them to perform employee green behavior, though they reported a neutral stance on feeling direct social pressure. Perceived behavioral control was also high, with respondents feeling capable and confident in their ability to protect the environment.

The results demonstrate that attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly influence intentions to engage in green behavior. Environmental knowledge was found to indirectly strengthen intention by influencing attitudes and perceived control. In contrast, socio-demographic factors showed limited direct effects on the constructs. The study concludes that employees in the public organization possess a strong positive attitude toward environmental protection and feel capable of performing green behaviors. The findings suggest that while employees are knowledgeable and willing, the lack of formal organizational policy means these behaviors remain largely voluntary. Organizations can institutionalize sustainable practices by fostering supportive norms and positive attitudes through leadership-driven green initiatives and peer recognition programs.

Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, such as mean scores and frequency distributions, as well as inferential statistics, including Pearson or Spearman Correlation coefficients and Multiple Regression Analysis.

The findings reveal that the respondent group is predominantly female (68.8%) and belongs to the Millennial generation (55.4%). Most respondents are frontline employees in Member Services (34.4%) and have between 1 and 10 years of government service (50.5%). Environmental knowledge was found to indirectly strengthen intention by influencing attitudes and perceived control. In contrast, socio-demographic factors showed limited direct effects on the constructs.

The study concludes that employees in the public organization possess a strong positive attitude toward environmental protection and feel capable of performing green behaviors. title: Perceived Professional Practice Environment, Organizational Commitment, and Turnover Intention Among Nurses in a Tertiary Government Hospital in Metropolitan Manila, Philippines
abstract:
Following the pandemic, many nurses continue to choose to work abroad and leave their local healthcare organizations, including the selected tertiary hospital. This can be attributed to their professional practice environment and organizational commitment. This study aims to correlate variables related to the demographic profile, perception of the professional practice environment, organizational commitment, and turnover intention among staff nurses in a selected tertiary hospital in Metro Manila. This study employed a descriptive, correlational, cross-sectional design. The participants (n = 355) were recruited through convenience sampling via an online poll. The tools used were a self-constructed demographic profile questionnaire, the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index (PES-NWI), the Organizational Commitment Scale, and the Turnover Intention Scale (TIS-6). STATA 13.1 was used to analyze the data. Overall, perceptions in the professional practice environment and organizational commitment are inversely related to turnover intention (p < 0.0001), such that poor perceptions in the professional practice environment and deficient organizational commitment are associated with higher turnover intention among nurses, and vice versa. Furthermore, the demographic profile has influenced the professional practice environment and organizational commitment. The results suggest that if the professional practice environment and organizational commitment
are not nurtured during the nurses' worthwhile stay in their healthcare organization, they may leave; however, if they are nurtured, they may stay longer.

This research addresses the issue of nurses choosing to work abroad or leaving local healthcare organizations following the pandemic, specifically within a selected tertiary government hospital in Metro Manila, Philippines. The study investigates how the professional practice environment and organizational commitment influence the intention of staff nurses to leave their current positions. Using a descriptive, correlational, cross-sectional design, the researcher examined the relationships between the demographic profile of the nurses, their perceptions of the professional practice environment, their organizational commitment, and their turnover intention.

Data was collected from 355 participants through convenience sampling via an online poll. The methodology utilized a self-constructed demographic profile questionnaire, the Practice Environment Scale of the Nursing Work Index, the Organizational Commitment Scale, and the Turnover Intention Scale. Statistical analysis was performed using STATA 13.1 to determine correlations between the variables.

The findings reveal significant relationships, showing an inverse relationship between perceptions of the professional practice environment and organizational commitment relative to turnover intention, with a p-value of less than 0.0001. Poor perceptions of the work environment and deficient organizational commitment are associated with higher turnover intention, while better perceptions and higher commitment are associated with lower turnover intention. Additionally, the demographic profile of the nurses influences both the perceived professional practice environment and organizational commitment. The study concludes that improving the professional practice environment and strengthening organizational commitment are critical for mitigating turnover intentions and retaining nursing staff.

title: Mapping the Underwater Forest: A Deep Learning Approach to Seagrass Mapping Distribution in Calatagan, Batangas, Philippines, Using Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery
abstract:
Around 71 percent of the earth’s surface is covered by water primarily saltwater found in the oceans which are essential to the survival of a variety of marine ecosystems. Particularly considering the environmental issues facing the Philippines this study highlights the significance of seagrass beds essential but usually disregarded ecosystems that support the maintenance of water quality and carbon sequestration. To produce an accurate map of the distribution of seagrass in Calatagan, Batangas, high-resolution sentinel-2 imagery is analyzed using deep learning and advanced remote sensing
techniques. The approach which includes spectral band selection, data collection and model training produces a deep learning model with an F1 score of 85 percent, precision of 86 percent and overall accuracy of 97.31 percent. The efficiency of remote sensing in monitoring vital coastal habitats in the face of increasing human threats is demonstrated by this study. Through the combination of deep learning algorithms and remote sensing technology
this work offers a novel approach to improve ecological analysis in coastal management. This study provides an important step in maintaining and preserving biodiversity by integrating scientific findings into practical conservation plans and strategies.
faculty: Faculty of Management and Development Studies
half:
In the research titled "Mapping the underwater forest: A Deep Learning Approach to Seagrass Mapping Distribution in Calatagan, Batangas, Philippines, Using Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery," Dexter K. Dag-uman addresses the need for efficient monitoring of seagrass ecosystems, which provide essential services like carbon sequestration and coastal protection. Traditional monitoring methods, such as field surveys, are often limited by high costs and environmental constraints like water turbidity.

The study utilized high-resolution multispectral imagery from the Sentinel-2 satellite and implemented a deep learning workflow in ArcGIS Pro. The methodology involved training a model using the ResNet-34 backbone architecture with a U-Net model type for pixel classification. The findings demonstrate the high efficacy of this approach, with the trained model achieving an overall accuracy of 97.31%, a precision of 86%, and an F1 score of 85%. Notably, the model achieved a 100% producer’s accuracy for the seagrass class. While highly reliable for detecting seagrass presence, the study noted that multi-class detection and spectral confusion compared to NAMRIA’s baseline data remain areas for improvement.

The research concludes that integrating deep learning with Sentinel-2 data is a viable, scalable, and cost-effective method for mapping seagrass meadows. The author recommends deploying this method across the Philippines to create a national baseline dataset and suggests integrating these maps into the management plans of the DENR, BFAR, and LGUs.
one:
In the research titled "Mapping the underwater forest: A Deep Learning Approach to Seagrass Mapping Distribution in Calatagan, Batangas, Philippines, Using Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery," Dexter K. Dag-uman addresses the need for efficient monitoring of seagrass ecosystems. These habitats provide essential services like carbon sequestration, coastal protection, and nursery grounds for marine life, yet they face threats from pollution, climate change, and coastal development. Traditional mapping methods, such as field surveys and aerial photography, are often limited by high costs, labor intensity, and environmental constraints like water turbidity.

The study focuses on Calatagan, Batangas, located within the biodiverse Verde Island Passage. To overcome the limitations of manual monitoring, the researcher employed a methodology combining remote sensing and deep learning. Using high-resolution multispectral imagery from the Sentinel-2 satellite, the study utilized ArcGIS Pro to implement a deep learning workflow. This involved pre-processing imagery, generating training datasets through digitized seagrass polygons, and training a model using the ResNet-34 backbone architecture with a U-Net model type for pixel classification.

The findings demonstrate the high efficacy of this approach. The trained model achieved an overall accuracy of 97.31%, a precision of 86%, and an F1 score of 85%. Notably, the model achieved a 100% producer’s accuracy for the seagrass class, indicating an exceptional ability to correctly identify seagrass areas. While highly reliable for detecting seagrass presence, the study noted that multi-class detection—distinguishing seagrass from other benthic features like sand or coral—could be improved. Additionally, a 326-hectare difference was noted compared to NAMRIA’s baseline data, attributed to spectral confusion and acceptable variability in satellite-based classifications.

The research concludes that integrating deep learning with Sentinel-2 data is a viable, scalable, and cost-effective method for mapping seagrass meadows. This approach provides actionable data that bridges the gap between scientific research and practical environmental management. The author recommends deploying this method across the Philippines to create a national baseline dataset for marine spatial planning. 

Technical recommendations include using cloud computing and GPU-accelerated virtual machines to manage high computational requirements. For governance, the study suggests integrating these high-resolution maps into the management plans of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), and Local Government Units (LGUs). Ultimately, this methodology is highly transferable and can be adapted to monitor other critical habitats, such as mangroves, coral reefs, and tidal flats, providing a versatile framework for long-term coastal ecosystem management.

The research titled "Mapping the underwater forest: A Deep Learning Approach to Seagrass Mapping Distribution in Calatagan, Batangas, Philippines, Using Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery" by Dexter K. Dag-uman addresses the critical need for efficient and accurate monitoring of seagrass ecosystems. Seagrasses are vital marine habitats that provide essential ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration (often referred to as "blue carbon"), coastal protection from erosion and storm surges, and nursery grounds for diverse marine life. Despite their importance, these ecosystems face increasing threats from human activities such as coastal development, pollution, overfishing, and climate change.

The study identifies a significant problem in traditional seagrass mapping methodologies. Conventional methods, such as field surveys (snorkeling or SCUBA diving) and aerial photography, are often costly, labor-intensive, and limited in spatial and temporal scale. Fieldwork is frequently restricted by environmental factors like water turbidity, tides, and weather, and it often produces only localized data. While aerial photography offers broader coverage, it remains dependent on specialized equipment and clear weather conditions. Consequently, there is a pressing need for scalable, cost-effective, and high-resolution monitoring tools that can provide continuous data for effective coastal management.

The research is situated in the municipality of Calatagan, Batangas, Philippines. This area is part of the Verde Island Passage, a region recognized for its immense marine biodiversity. Calatagan’s coastal environment is characterized by diverse seagrass species, such as *Enhalus acoroides* and *Thalassia hemprichii*, which support local fisheries and eco-tourism. However, the area faces environmental pressures from land reclamation, sedimentation from inland runoff, and unregulated boating, all of which threaten the stability of these "underwater forests."

To address these challenges, the author employed a methodology combining remote sensing and deep learning. The study utilized high-resolution multispectral imagery from the Sentinel-2 satellite mission, specifically leveraging the Multispectral Instrument (MSI) which provides 13 spectral bands. The research utilized ArcGIS Pro and its Image Analyst Extension to implement a deep learning workflow. The process involved several key stages: pre-processing the Sentinel-2 imagery (layer stacking, clipping, and enhancement), generating training datasets by digitizing seagrass polygons, and exporting these as image chips. The core of the methodology involved training a deep learning model using the ResNet-34 backbone architecture with a U-Net model type for pixel classification. The model was trained for 30 epochs with a batch size of 16 and a validation set of 20%. The accuracy of the model was assessed by comparing its predictions against reference data obtained through conventional validation methods, including high-resolution imagery from Google Earth.

The findings demonstrate the high efficacy of the deep learning approach. The trained model achieved an overall accuracy of 97.31%, a precision of 86%, and an F1 score of 85%. Specifically, the model showed a perfect producer’s accuracy of 100% for the seagrass class, indicating an exceptional ability to correctly identify seagrass areas. While the model was highly reliable in detecting the presence of seagrass, the results indicated that its capacity for multi-class detection—distinguishing seagrass from other benthic features like coral or sand—could be further improved. The study also noted a 326-hectare difference compared to NAMRIA’s baseline data, which the author attributes to acceptable variability in satellite-based classifications and spectral confusion.

The study concludes that the integration of deep learning with Sentinel-2 satellite data is a viable, effective, and scalable method for mapping seagrass meadows. The high accuracy and ability to extrapolate coverage over large areas make this approach a powerful tool for coastal resource estimation. The research proves that advanced artificial intelligence can bridge the gap between scientific research and practical environmental management, providing actionable data that is more efficient and less costly than traditional manual methods.

The implications of this research are significant for conservation and policy. The author recommends deploying this deep learning-based approach across various coastal areas in the Philippines to create a national baseline dataset for seagrass distribution. This data is crucial for marine spatial planning and fulfilling international biodiversity commitments. Furthermore, the study suggests that the model should be enhanced to distinguish between various benthic habitats (such as coral reefs and algae) to provide a more comprehensive ecological picture. 

From a technical and management perspective, the study recommends utilizing cloud computing and GPU-accelerated virtual machines to overcome the high computational requirements of deep learning. For local governance, the author emphasizes the importance of integrating these high-resolution maps into the management plans of Local Government Units (LGUs), the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR). Finally, the research suggests that this methodology is highly transferable and can be adapted to monitor other critical habitats, such as mangroves, coral reefs, and tidal flats, thereby providing a versatile framework for long-term, data-driven coastal ecosystem management.

title: Assessing Strategies for Retaining Internationally Trained Personnel at a Public Rice Research Center
abstract:
Despite the high rate of returning international scholars at the National Grain Innovation Center (NGIC), a critical need remains to strengthen institutional retention strategies. Current frameworks exhibit significant gaps in design, execution and system necessitating a stronger approach to employee integration. Employing a qualitative (thematic analysis) and quantitative (descriptive analysis) methods, this study identified the reasons, challenges, and trends associated with scholar retention. Data were gathered through open-ended question interviews with 11 NGIC employees who completed international Master’s or Doctoral programs. Applying Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, the analysis revealed that while basic job stability prevented immediate dissatisfaction, it failed to generate active motivation. Fifty percent (50%) of respondents reported high satisfaction, citing strong motivators like professional recognition. However, 30% of participants demonstrated lower commitment, identifying a lack of career pathways as a primary turnover driver, while 20% cited failures in hygiene factors. In conclusion, high retention is concentrated among PhD-level employees with
high intrinsic motivation and a sense of public duty. In contrast, Master’s-level graduates display conditional loyalty and remain vulnerable to external attrition. These findings indicate that NGIC’s current strategy succeeds only where individual mission-alignment already exists, highlighting a need for structural job enrichment to retain the broader scholar population.

title: Problem-Based Learning with GenAI: Effects on Students' Statistical Thinking
abstract:
The purpose of this study was to determine the effects of a problem-based learning (PBL) environment, with and without the support of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), on senior high school students’ statistical thinking. An embedded mixed-methods quasi-experimental design was employed involving three intact Grade 11 STEAM classes randomly assigned to GenAI-PBL, PBL, and conventional groups. Over 12 weeks, students studied four statistics lessons through either a PBL cycle or lecture-discussion format. Data sources included the Statistical Thinking Test (TST), end-of-lesson evaluations, daily journals, the Course Experience Questionnaire (CEQ), focus group discussions, and ChatGPT conversation logs. Results showed no significant differences in overall TST scores among groups, although patterns emerged in specific subtasks. The GenAI-PBL group performed relatively better in designing sampling plans, the PBL group excelled in justifying statistical tests, and the conventional group demonstrated steady
procedural improvement over time. Subtask E, explaining the purpose of hypothesis testing, consistently received the lowest scores across groups. Students positively perceived PBL components such as authentic problems, collaboration, and teacher facilitation, though some reported difficulty with limited lectures, autonomy, and workload. CEQ results revealed no significant differences in good teaching, generic skills, and student support, but the GenAI-PBL group reported heavier workloads and lower overall satisfaction compared with the conventional group. Thematic analysis confirmed the value of collaboration, facilitation, and real-world problems, while highlighting challenges in pacing, role specialization, and overreliance on ChatGPT. The study concludes that PBL, with or without GenAI, can foster engagement and reasoning but does not significantly improve statistical thinking scores compared to conventional teaching. Recommendations include embedding mini-activities to strengthen sampling, test justification, and EDA; adopting a blended model that combines GenAI support, PBL collaboration, and conventional structure; refining the TST for validity; extending statistical investigations to broader topics; and exploring structured and ethical GenAI use in future studies.

title: Communicating and Building Trust in the Profession: A Critical-Semiotic Inquiry of a Legal Aid Clinic
abstract:
This study investigated how communication practices, space, and visual cues mediate or discourage the indigent clients’ trust in the Legal Aid Clinic. It draws upon Critical Tradition which theorizes communication according to Craig (1999) as a
“reflective challenge of unjust discourse” and Semiotic Tradition which theorizes communication as meaningful signs and symbols that can be interpreted in various ways (Craig, 1999). This study used multimodal analysis. Reflective essays of the student law practitioners were subjected to thematic analysis, while the Legal Aid Clinic to socio-spatial analysis, and the observations during the legal consultations to critical semiotic analysis.

The communication practices that emerged which may engender or discourage trust were affiliative humor, persuasive communication, mitigative communication, plain language communication, affective communication, adaptive dual-channel communication. Furthermore, the semiotic resources of legal aid clinic spatial (architectural design and layout), visual, (organizational shirt, posted materials), gestural (non-verbal cues such as side eying, and eye contact).

This study also found out that legal trust is multilayered and multidimensional. It is relational, procedural, and symbolic. Moreover, types of legal trust surfaced: unequivocal trust, provisional trust, involuntary trust, and pseudo or fake trust.

Additionally, semiotic resources including spatial resources like architectural design, visual resources like organizational shirts and posted materials, and gestural resources like eye contact influence client perception.

title: Project Aspen: A Single-Source-of-Truth Approach to Digital Transformation in Higher Education
abstract: Effective data management is critical for evidence-based decision-making to achieve equitable quality education. Centralizing data from various sources enhances accuracy and institutional responsiveness, while learning analytics plays a vital role in monitoring student progress. Project Aspen, implemented at the University of the Philippines Open University’s Faculty of Information and Communication Studies, exemplifies an approach to academic digital transformation by centralizing academic and institutional data into a single-source-of-truth system. This is achieved by federating employee and student information databases into a unified repository, leveraging flexible, low-cost, no-code tools like Airtable. Real-time reporting, automated analytics, and dynamic portfolio generation enable streamlined processes, improved accountability, and flexible reporting. This paper highlights Aspen’s ability to integrate data efficiently to address fragmented reporting and redundant data entry, describing implementation challenges and key successes to suggest actionable insights for smaller institutions seeking to modernize their data infrastructures for digital transformation.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Project Aspen addresses the significant burden placed on faculty members regarding data entry requirements within higher education settings. At the University of the Philippines Open University Faculty of Information and Communication Studies, faculty must navigate ten or more distinct reporting requirements for various internal and external stakeholders. This fragmentation leads to redundant labor, as the same information must be entered multiple times into different systems. The central objective of the project is to determine how to reduce this faculty data entry burden while simultaneously ensuring that the data collected remains complete and accurate.

The research serves as a prototype-stage proof of concept designed to test a single-source-of-truth approach to digital transformation. This approach is built upon the principle of entering data once, storing it centrally, and using it everywhere. title: GIS-Based Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Land Cover Changes in Barangay Monte Calvario within the Buhi-Barit Watershed, Buhi, Camarines Sur (2015-2024)
abstract:
This study titled “GIS-Based Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Land Cover Changes in Barangay Monte Calvario within the Buhi-Barit Watershed, Buhi, Camarines Sur (2015– 2024)” examined the spatial and temporal patterns of land cover transformation and their implications for watershed health and sustainability. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Sentinel-2 satellite data, and National Power Corporation (NAPOCOR) land cover maps, the research analyzed environmental dynamics over a nine-year period. The findings revealed a dominant tree cover that expanded from 83% in 2017 to nearly 90% in 2024, reflecting ecological regeneration and reforestation efforts. However, concurrent increases in built-up areas and transitions in cropland and rangeland underscore continuing anthropogenic pressures from
agriculture and settlement expansion.

The integration of ground truthing proved vital to the accuracy of this study, as field validation uncovered misclassified features such as informal housing, mixed cropping systems, and degraded lands inaccurately represented in satellite imagery. These findings highlighted the limitations of remote sensing alone in heterogeneous rural landscapes and reinforced the need for a hybrid approach that combines geospatial analysis with on-site verification. Recommendations emphasize adopting a hybrid monitoring framework that institutionalizes regular ground truthing alongside satellite- based classification to improve land use mapping, policy planning, and
watershed governance. Such integration ensures data accuracy, supports participatory management, and strengthens adaptive, community-based environmental strategies.

Ultimately, the study contributes to developing sustainable and climate-resilient land use policies that balance ecological preservation and local development within the Buhi-Barit Watershed system.

The research addresses how shifting land use patterns, driven by natural and anthropogenic factors, impact the stability and resilience of watersheds that support hydropower, irrigation, and domestic water supplies. The methodology utilized a hybrid approach combining geospatial analysis of Esri Sentinel-2 and NAPOCOR maps with field validation via GPS-enabled devices to address remote sensing limitations.

Findings reveal significant transformations between 2015 and 2024. While tree cover remains dominant, it shows annual fluctuations from intermittent deforestation and regrowth. Net increases from reforestation efforts were countered by expanding built-up areas and the transition of cultivated lands into grasslands. Ground truthing revealed that Sentinel maps often overestimated forested zones and failed to detect small-scale residential structures, informal housing, mixed-use cropping, and small-scale livestock operations. Drivers of change include rural development, informal settlement expansion, shifts in agricultural practices, and unregulated tourism-related construction, alongside natural factors like steep topography and rainfall variability.

The study concludes that encroachment of built-up areas and shifting agricultural patterns pose risks to biodiversity and watershed integrity. Recommendations include integrating high-resolution remote sensing with community-based ground truthing, harmonizing GIS standards between agencies, and updating local zoning ordinances and Comprehensive Land Use Plans.

two:
The study titled "GIS-Based Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Land Cover Changes in Barangay Monte Calvario within the Buhi-Barit Watershed, Buhi, Camarines Sur (2015-2024)" investigates the transformation of land cover in a critical ecological zone in the Philippines. The research addresses the problem of how shifting land use patterns—driven by both natural and anthropogenic factors—impact the health, stability, and resilience of watersheds. Specifically, the study focuses on the need to understand the extent and trends of these changes to inform sustainable land use planning and watershed management in a region facing pressures from urbanization, agricultural expansion, and climate change.

The context of the research is situated within the Buhi-Barit Watershed, a vital sub-watershed of the Rinconada Watershed that supports hydropower, irrigation, and domestic water supplies. Barangay Monte Calvario, located on the slopes of Mount Malinao, is an ecologically significant area characterized by diverse topography ranging from steep uplands to lowland plains. This area is subject to a Type II climate with high annual rainfall and frequent typhoons, making its land cover stability essential for preventing soil erosion, managing runoff, and ensuring water security for downstream communities.

The methodology employed a hybrid approach combining geospatial analysis with field validation. The researcher utilized secondary data from two primary sources: the Esri Sentinel-2 Land Cover Explorer, which provided annual time-series data from 2017 to 2024, and the National Power Corporation (NAPOCOR) land cover maps from 2020. These datasets were analyzed using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to map and quantify land cover transitions. To address the inherent limitations of remote sensing, the researcher conducted ground truthing using GPS-enabled devices to verify classifications and identify features missed by satellite imagery.

The findings reveal significant spatio-temporal land cover transformations between 2015 and 2024. Tree cover remained the dominant land cover category but exhibited annual fluctuations, suggesting a cycle of intermittent deforestation and regrowth. While there was a net increase in tree cover in some periods, reflecting reforestation efforts like the Buhi-Barit Tree Planting project, this was countered by the steady expansion of built-up areas and the transition of cultivated lands into grasslands or rangelands. Ground truthing was critical in this phase, as it revealed that satellite data often misclassified or overlooked essential local features, such as informal housing (shanties), mixed-use cropping systems, upland water tanks, and small-scale livestock operations. The study found that Sentinel maps often overestimated forested zones by including semi-open spaces or agroforestry crops in the "trees" category, while failing to detect small-scale residential structures in upland zones.

The drivers of these changes were identified as a combination of natural and anthropogenic factors. Anthropogenic drivers included rural development, the expansion of informal settlements, shifts in agricultural practices (such as moving toward low-water rice varieties, abaca, and banana farming), and unregulated tourism-related construction. Natural drivers included the area's steep topography, soil types, and rainfall variability. Furthermore, climate variability and land tenure uncertainty were noted as factors influencing land abandonment or the adoption of climate-resilient crops.

The study concludes that while there are signs of ecological regeneration, the encroachment of built-up areas and the shifting of agricultural patterns pose substantial risks to biodiversity, food security, and watershed integrity. The research emphasizes that neither satellite imagery nor single-year agency maps are sufficient on their own for accurate monitoring. Instead, a multi-layered approach that integrates high-resolution remote sensing with regular, community-based ground truthing is necessary to capture the complex, heterogeneous reality of rural landscapes.

The implications of this research are significant for policy and local governance. The author recommends the harmonization of GIS classification standards between agencies like NAPOCOR and the DENR to prevent conflicting interpretations of land use. There is a call for the institutionalization of a "local land cover observatory" within the Municipal Planning and Development Office to conduct annual reviews of satellite data validated by local communities. Furthermore, the study suggests that local zoning ordinances and Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs) must be updated to reflect actual land use, particularly in ecologically vulnerable or hazard-prone zones. The researcher advocates for participatory land management that involves local farmers and residents, supporting practices like agroforestry and Sloping Agricultural Land Technology (SALT) to enhance watershed resilience and ensure that environmental protection aligns with local socioeconomic needs.
