Using a multi-method approach including autoethnography, focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and user acceptability tests, the study collected data from one hundred farmers and ten key informants in the Philippines and Indonesia. The findings indicate that the success of digital crop advisories depends on understanding specific farmer motivations and needs. The research proposes the Planning-Communication-Evaluation (PCE) model, anchored in complexity theory, which accounts for the interactions of adaptive agents such as content developers and various farmer personas.

The study concludes that e-farming is a fluid, non-linear process. Successful knowledge transfer requires moving beyond simple information dissemination to a model that accounts for the adaptive nature of all participants. Pragmatically, the research provides a framework for developers and policymakers to design more effective advisories. Pedagogically, it offers insights into how knowledge is adapted within digital environments, supporting the creation of tools that are both technologically advanced and socially responsive to marginalized farmers.

Complexity theory in communication provides a framework for pedagogy and practice in e-farming knowledge transfer, particularly for smallholder and marginalized farmers. While the theory has been applied in fields such as management, social science, digital social advocacy, and neo-diffusionism communication, this study seeks to apply it specifically to digital knowledge transfers in agriculture. The primary goal is to understand how to drive social impact through the effective utilization of crop advisories delivered via digital media, mobile applications, and the Internet of Things (IoT).

To investigate these dynamics, the study employed a multi-method qualitative and quantitative approach. The researcher utilized autoethnography, Focus Group Discussions (FGD), Key Informant Interviews (KII), and User Acceptability Tests (UAT) as qualitative methods, supplemented by desktop quantitative research. The study's scope included data collection from one hundred farmer respondents and ten key informants located in the Philippines and Indonesia. This comparative geographical approach allowed for a broader understanding of the e-farming landscape in Southeast Asia.

The findings of the study indicate that the success of digital crop advisories is heavily dependent on understanding farmer motivations and specific needs. A central outcome of the research is the proposal of the Planning-Communication-Evaluation (PCE) model, which is anchored in complexity theory. This model is designed to account for the various interactions of adaptive agents within the social system. These agents include content developers, various farmer personas, and other stakeholders within the e-farming ecosystem. The research highlights that the social and digital adaptiveness of these agents, as well as the "muted voices" of different farmer personas, are critical elements that must be addressed to ensure the success of e-farming initiatives.

The study concludes that e-farming is not a linear process but a fluid one, characterized by non-linear patterns of interaction among agents. The research suggests that digital e-farming communication, particularly when integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), offers a way to engage with the sociality and reproduction of society through these interacting agents. By viewing the e-farming system as a complex social system, the research demonstrates that successful knowledge transfer requires moving beyond simple information dissemination to a model that accounts for the adaptive nature of all participants.

The implications of this research are both pragmatic and pedagogical. Pragmatically, the study provides a framework for developers and policymakers to design more effective digital farming advisories by considering the adaptive roles of different nodes or agents in the system. Pedagogically, the research offers insights into how knowledge is transferred and adapted within digital agricultural environments. By leveraging complexity theory, the study provides a foundation for creating digital tools that are not only technologically advanced but also socially responsive to the diverse needs of smallholder and marginalized farmers.

title: Evaluation of an RDO's Automated Fare Collection System (AFCS) for Compliance with the Interoperable Automated Fare Collection System (IAFCS) Philippine National Standard (PNS)
abstract:
This study explored how an RDO, through its subsidiary, can strategically expand and promote technology acceptance and utilization of the Automated Fare Collection System (AFCS), in the Philippine public transportation sector. Specifically, this study aims to assess the RDO’s capabilities against the requirements needed to fulfill the business and operational rules in operating a local AFCS infrastructure.

In line with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap (DPTR) is the government’s initiative to implement an Interoperable Automated Fare Collection System (IAFCS). The IAFCS applies to all public transportation modes for the improvement of the public transport environment, passenger convenience, and the implementation of the transfer system among all public transportation modes.

In 2024, the RDO and its subsidiary along with other partner organizations, had successfully launched a proof of concept in implementing an interoperable automated fare collection system among identified buses within Metro Manila. Following this success, the RDO’s subsidiary agreed to conduct research that focuses on evaluating the conformance of an RDO’s AFCS solution that is aligned with the objectives of the Philippine National Standard.

The research is rooted in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap, which seeks to implement an Interoperable Automated Fare Collection System (IAFCS) across all public transportation modes to enhance passenger convenience and facilitate seamless transfers. Following a successful 2024 proof of concept involving buses in Metro Manila, this study evaluates whether the AFCS solution conforms to the objectives set forth in the Philippine National Standard (PNS).

The findings center on the evaluation of the AFCS solution's alignment with the PNS and its ability to meet the requirements for local infrastructure. The study concludes that adhering to the Philippine National Standard is essential to achieve true interoperability. While the Metro Manila proof of concept provides a foundation, full-scale implementation requires strict conformance to the IAFCS. Compliance allows the RDO to integrate into the national digital payment ecosystem, supporting a modernized, digitally integrated transportation network.

title: Communication Leadership in a Community from the Perspective of a Development Worker: A Rhetorical Study
abstract: This study is situated under the Rhetorical Tradition of Communication Theory and the research paradigm is Qualitative Communication Research and is supportive of the Philosophy of Development Communication, Participatory Communication Theory, and Theory of Communicative Actions. It attempts to answer two research questions; a) What are the rhetorical practices in communication leadership in a community?, and b) What do the rhetorical practices in communication leadership in a community intend to accomplish? Using autoethnography and rhetorical study, the ten songs I wrote about my work were analyzed to come up with answers to the research questions. The results show that my work as a development worker is to establish community communication and facilitate the community development process within a defined timeframe, in which process local leaders develop communication and leadership skills through experience, which enable them to perform communication leadership. The results reveal a rhetorical model of communication leadership, where communication leadership is central to the participatory communication system. The rhetorical practices in communication leadership of building relations, understanding community problems, conceptualizing solutions, empowering leaders, mobilization/action planning, mobilizing, evaluating, synthesizing learning, and transitioning roles are approaches in communication leadership that intend to accomplish good communicative relations, collective understanding of problems, collective concept of solutions, empowered leaders, action plan, realized solution/s, understanding of strengths and weaknesses and recommendations, collective knowledge, and sustained communication leadership.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Valentin E. Gando’s study, "Communication Leadership in a Community from the Perspective of a Development Worker: A Rhetorical Study," investigates the nature of communication leadership within community settings. Grounded in the Rhetorical Tradition of Communication Theory and supported by participatory and communicative action theories, the research utilizes a qualitative paradigm. The author employs a methodology combining autoethnography and rhetorical study, using ten original songs written about his professional experiences as a development worker as the primary data source to extract insights regarding the lived experience of facilitating community development.

The findings indicate that a development worker’s role is to establish community communication and facilitate development within a specific timeframe. Through this process, local leaders engage in experiential learning, developing the skills necessary to eventually perform communication leadership within their own communities. The study identifies several rhetorical practices linked to specific intended accomplishments: building relations to achieve good communicative relations; understanding community problems to foster collective understanding; conceptualizing solutions to create a collective concept of solutions; and empowering leaders to produce empowered leaders. Additionally, mobilization and action planning aim to result in an action plan, while mobilization aims at realizing solutions. Finally, evaluating and synthesizing learning helps the community understand its strengths and weaknesses, leading to collective knowledge and sustained communication leadership.

title: Digital Communication, the K-pop Army, and the Filipino Collective Psyche
abstract: The arrival of the Hallyu Wave made a big impression globally and was warmly received by Filipinos. South Korean pop culture introduced K-pop, a music genre famously known for its impressive lyricism and deliberate production which captured the interest of listernes. As literature suggests, music is a powerful driving force that has the ability to enable a group or community to move or think as one unit, such as how jazz musicians harnessed the power of music to communicate their social struggles. Deriving from this premise, the question this study aimed to answer was “How does digital communication shape the K-Pop Army that translates to the Filipino Collective Psyche?” I explored my lived experience as a member of the K-pop army by employing an autoethnographic study. I used vignettes to synthesize what it meant to be a member of the K-pop army, acclimatized its culture, and made sense of my K-pop journey. Each experience discussed in vignettes showed a clear picture of the journey that thickened the discussion throughout the research. The vignettes served as an example of how the Filipino Collective Psyche was shaped. More than the provision of world-class entertainment and global popularity, the K-pop Army follows their K-pop idols because of their altruism and actions to address social issues which have always been evident in digital communication platforms. With the proliferation of social media and the K-pop Army’s exposure to these communication platforms especially during the time where being “connected online” was the norm, it was evident that the fandom moved as if with one mind, reflecting the very essence of the Filipino Collective Psyche.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study investigates the relationship between digital communication, the K-pop fandom known as the K-pop Army, and the Filipino Collective Psyche within the global Hallyu Wave. The research explores how digital platforms facilitate unity within the fandom and how this collective movement reflects broader psychological and social patterns within the Filipino population. Using an autoethnographic method, the researcher utilized personal lived experiences and vignettes to illustrate the process of acclimatizing to the fandom's culture and how digital interactions shape the Filipino Collective Psyche.

The findings reveal that the K-pop Army is driven by more than entertainment consumption; a significant driver is the altruism of K-pop idols and their proactive engagement with social issues. As being connected online became a social norm, the proliferation of social media allowed the fandom to utilize these platforms to organize and act. The study concludes that the K-pop Army exhibits a tendency to move "as if with one mind," a unified movement that reflects the essence of the Filipino Collective Psyche. This ability to coalesce around shared values and social causes through digital means serves as a manifestation of how collective identity is formed in a digital age. Ultimately, the study suggests that digital platforms are vital spaces where collective identities are forged and social movements are coordinated, highlighting the influence of K-pop and digital media on the social and psychological fabric of Filipino society.

title: Agile Communication in an International Educational Organization: A Phenomenological Study
abstract: Using phenomenology, the researcher explored staff members' experiences in an international educational organization and made sense of the dynamic nature of their communicative practices in an ever-changing work environment. Based on the Husserl and Habermas frameworks, the study provided a comprehensive understanding of communication practices and organizational dynamics in the context of agile communication and the staff’s lifeworld. Through in-depth interviews and employing the Discourse of Understanding grounded on the Phenomenological Tradition of Communication, the researcher made sense of the experiences of selected staff members, resulting in an emergent communication-centric concept of Agile Communication. The inquiry revealed that Agile Communication is flexible, adaptive, and stakeholder-centered, enabling quick response to changing circumstances and delivering value to stakeholders. It is a collaborative, innovative, and iterative process that promotes efficient work environments by working hand-in-hand with the iteration process. Agile communication is direct and transparent, promoting simple, face-to-face interaction that leads to consistent feedback loops. It is embedded in organizational culture and process, allowing for pivot strategies, structures, and processes. Finally, it maintains the quality of work outputs, enabling stakeholders to respond to changes without compromising quality and ensuring the timely delivery of projects. Hence, Agile Communication is a flexible, user-centric, collaborative, and transparent approach that prioritizes organizational quality. It lies in the social interaction and communicative activities of people within the organization, which allow the utilization of appropriate strategies, processes, and tools in managing and responding to change. More importantly, the study revealed that agile communication had become a concept that limits the systems to colonize the staff members' lifeworld.

The findings reveal the emergence of Agile Communication, defined as a flexible, adaptive, and stakeholder-centered approach. Rather than a static process, Agile Communication is collaborative, innovative, and iterative, working alongside iterative work processes to promote efficient environments. It is characterized by directness and transparency, utilizing simple, face-to-face interactions to facilitate consistent feedback loops. This communicative style is deeply embedded within the organizational culture and existing processes, allowing for the implementation of pivot strategies and structures when necessary.

Agile Communication helps maintain the quality of work outputs, enabling stakeholders to respond to changes effectively without compromising project delivery. Ultimately, it is a user-centric approach residing within the social interactions and communicative activities of the people within the organization. The study concludes that Agile Communication serves as a concept that limits the ability of organizational systems to colonize the staff members' lifeworld. By recognizing communication as a social process rather than just technical tools, organizations can better support staff navigating change.

The study explores the communicative practices of staff members within an international educational organization, specifically focusing on how they navigate an ever-changing work environment. The central problem addressed is the need to understand the dynamic nature of communication in such a setting and how staff members experience these shifts. The researcher seeks to make sense of how communication functions within the context of agile communication and the staff’s lifeworld, aiming to uncover the essence of these communicative experiences.

The context of the research is an international educational organization characterized by constant change. To investigate this, the researcher employs a phenomenological approach, utilizing the frameworks of Husserl and Habermas. The methodology involves conducting in-depth interviews with selected staff members. The researcher applies the Discourse of Understanding, which is grounded in the Phenomenological Tradition of Communication, to analyze the data and make sense of the participants' lived experiences.

The findings of the study lead to the emergence of a communication-centric concept termed Agile Communication. This concept is characterized by several key dimensions. First, Agile Communication is described as flexible, adaptive, and stakeholder-centered. This allows the organization to respond quickly to changing circumstances and ensures that value is delivered to stakeholders. It is not a static process but rather a collaborative, innovative, and iterative one that works in tandem with iterative work processes to promote efficient environments.

Furthermore, the study found that Agile Communication is characterized by directness and transparency. It promotes simple, face-to-face interactions, which facilitate consistent feedback loops. This communicative style is not an external addition to the organization but is deeply embedded within the organizational culture and its existing processes. This embedding allows for the implementation of pivot strategies, structures, and processes when necessary.

Another significant finding is that Agile Communication helps maintain the quality of work outputs. It enables stakeholders to respond to changes effectively without compromising the quality of their work, thereby ensuring the timely delivery of projects. Ultimately, the study defines Agile Communication as a flexible, user-centric, collaborative, and transparent approach that prioritizes organizational quality. It is found to reside within the social interactions and communicative activities of the people within the organization, which allows for the use of appropriate strategies, processes, and tools to manage and respond to change.

The conclusions drawn from the research emphasize that Agile Communication is fundamentally rooted in the social interactions of the staff. It is the communicative activities of individuals that allow the organization to utilize the necessary tools and processes to navigate change. A significant and profound conclusion of the study is that agile communication serves as a concept that limits the ability of organizational systems to colonize the staff members' lifeworld.

The implications of this study suggest that understanding communication through a phenomenological lens provides a deeper insight into organizational dynamics than traditional methods. By recognizing Agile Communication as a social and interactive process rather than just a set of technical tools, organizations can better support their staff in navigating change. The findings imply that for communication to be truly agile, it must be integrated into the culture and the lived experiences of the employees, ensuring that the drive for efficiency and responsiveness does not come at the expense of the staff's lifeworld.

title: The Agency of Film in History Education: A Ventriloquial Analysis of ZOOM Teaching Interactions
abstract: The study examined the film performance in the context of history education; the agentive role of film in history-making; and the film as a mediated communication in history education through the use of a ventriloquial analysis with agency framework as a lens. This study was essentially constructed from the video lectures (recorded teaching materials via Zoom meeting) of the history teacher in three of his class sessions. The teacher-participant’s conversation and interactions in the Zoom video lecture were transcribed to analyze and to determine the performative role of film in the context of history education, and were used to know how the historical film acted as an agent that participated in history-making. Also, this study examined the agency of interactions to determine what way the film mediated in teaching history and what knowledge in the interaction had been produced. The researcher divided those film performances according to their discussed themes, so as to identify the film agentive roles that emerged repeatedly using thematic clustering and assigning of activity. Thus, this study established some theoretical propositions that may contribute to understanding what the film performed; its agentive role; the way the film mediated; and what knowledge generated in the context of history education through the voice of the teacher-participant.

The dissertation "The Agency of Film in History Education: A Ventriloquial Analysis of ZOOM Teaching Interactions" by Benigno B. Agapito, Jr. investigates the role of historical films within the digital classroom. Moving away from the traditional view of film as a passive instructional tool, the study explores how film functions as an active agent that participates in the construction of historical knowledge and the process of history-making during online teaching interactions.

The research problem centers on the need to understand the performative capacity of digital media. While film is often treated as a mere visual aid, Agapito, Jr. argues that it possesses a form of agency that influences the thoughts, characters, and behaviors of both teachers and students. The study seeks to address three primary research questions: what film performs in the context of history education through the teacher's voice; how historical film acts as an agent in history-making; and how film mediates teaching and the production of knowledge during interactions.

The study is situated in the context of modern digital pedagogy, specifically focusing on the shift toward online learning via platforms like Zoom. The theoretical foundation is the Agency Framework, which posits that non-human elements—such as films—can act as agents that "voice" or represent the standpoints of others. This is linked to the concept of ventriloquism, where the teacher acts as the "dummy" or ventriloquist, animating the historical narrative provided by the film to facilitate academic discussion.

The methodology employs a ventriloquial analysis, a qualitative approach used to examine how different components of an interaction contribute to the realization of a communicative goal. The researcher utilized abductive reasoning to analyze data collected from three recorded Zoom video lectures of a single history teacher-participant. These lectures covered topics such as the controversies surrounding the first Philippine presidency, the importance of historical sources, and the authenticity of historical evidence. The analysis involved transcribing these interactions and identifying "figures"—both explicit (direct references to the film) and implicit (indirect connotations)—to determine how the film's presence shaped the educational discourse.

The findings are categorized into three main areas: film performance, the agentive role of film, and film as mediated communication. In terms of performance, the study identified both explicit and implicit figures. Explicit performances occurred when the teacher directly used the film to illustrate, describe, or resolve historical controversies. Implicit performances were embedded within the dialogue, where the film's themes influenced the teacher's reasoning. Regarding its agentive role, the film was found to participate in "history-making" by providing a platform for constructing and deconstructing historical narratives. The film acted as an agent that mobilized the teacher to engage in critical discussions, such as debating the validity of primary versus secondary sources. Finally, as a form of mediated communication, the film served as a bridge between the filmmaker's creative vision and the teacher's pedagogical goals, translating historical facts into a visual language that facilitates student engagement.

The study concludes that historical film is not a static tool but a dynamic agent in the classroom. It performs a vital role in the "forever quest for truth" by providing a visual and auditory framework that stimulates historical responsiveness. The research demonstrates that through the teacher's mediation, the film helps students navigate the complexities of historiography, such as distinguishing between eyewitness accounts and secondary interpretations.

The implications of this research are significant for both film and history educators. For history teachers, the study suggests that film should be utilized not just for entertainment, but as a sophisticated medium for developing critical thinking and analytical skills. For film educators and scholars, the study proposes a new way of analyzing cinematic narratives—not just as artistic works, but as active participants in social and academic knowledge construction. The author suggests that this ventriloquial approach can lead to a new "film language" for the audio-visual retelling of history, encouraging a more profound appreciation of how media shapes our understanding of the past.

title: Kdrama and Filipino TV Series Demystified: A Comparative Close Reading Analysis of its Technical and Narrative Elements
abstract: Anchored on John Fiske’s Codes of TV Production, Stuart Hall’s Encoding and Decoding Mode, and Jacques Lacan’s Psychoanalytic Theory, the study compared and analyzed two high rated shows on Netflix, Extraordinary Attorney Woo, a Korean drama text and House Arrest of Us, a Filipino TV series based on technical and narrative elements as well as meanings and contexts through close reading. A highly budgeted Extraordinary Attorney Woo had a strong synergy of cinematography, directing, editing, production, lighting, graphics, and audio design that led to a superior output. As a textual medium, it served as a vehicle for knowledge sharing, inclusion of popular culture, presenting multi-faceted characters, and boasting of a strong plot. On the other hand, while House Arrest of Us shared several similarities, variations in the manner of execution, creative choices, and cultural differences differed. In terms of the narrative elements, House Arrest of Us also integrated popular culture, transformed the text using literary devices, information education, and Koreanization of the text. The difference lay in the integration of Filipino songs and dances, the exploration of various comedic styles, and the tackling of current local issues. The House Arrest of Us showed improvement in their craft even if they were greatly challenged in terms of budget, staffing, and production culture. Hence, there is a need to sharpen the skills of the production crew, lobby for government support to fuel the creative economy, introduce a change in the industry of drama production, and forge a strong public and private partnerships.

half:
In the dissertation "Kdrama and Filipino TV Series Demystified: A Comparative Close Reading Analysis of its Technical and Narrative Elements," Rhoda G. Campillan investigates the production and structural differences between South Korean and Filipino television dramas. Using a qualitative design and close reading analysis, the study compares the South Korean drama *Extraordinary Attorney Woo* with the Filipino series *House Arrest of Us*. The research is anchored in theories including John Fiske’s Codes of TV Production, Stuart Hall’s Encoding and Decoding model, and Jacques Lacan’s Psychoanalytic Theory, while utilizing the Political Economy of Communication for socio-economic context.

The findings reveal significant disparities in technical execution. *Extraordinary Attorney Woo* demonstrates high synergy across cinematography, directing, editing, production design, lighting, graphics, and audio design, facilitated by a high production budget. In contrast, *House Arrest of Us* exhibited technical flaws in lighting, directing, and continuity, which the researcher attributes to systemic challenges in the Philippine production culture, such as insufficient budgets and "hand-to-mouth" shooting practices. Narratively, the Korean drama utilized multi-faceted characters and cohesive plots, while the Filipino series relied on local songs, dances, and comedic styles. The study concludes that Korean success stems from a supportive political economy with government support and robust funding, whereas the Philippine industry follows a profit-oriented model. To compete globally, the researcher suggests improving technical expertise, stabilizing working conditions, and providing better financial and institutional infrastructure.

In the dissertation "Kdrama and Filipino TV Series Demystified: A Comparative Close Reading Analysis of its Technical and Narrative Elements," Rhoda G. Campillan investigates the production and structural differences between South Korean and Filipino television dramas. The study is motivated by the massive popularity of transnational content on streaming platforms like Netflix and the growing trend of Filipino audiences comparing the quality of local "teleseryes" to high-budget Korean productions. The researcher aims to benchmark the technical and narrative executions of Korean dramas to provide a basis for improving the development of Filipino television series.

The research problem centers on the perceived gap in viewing quality between the two industries. While Korean dramas have achieved global dominance, Filipino dramas often face criticism regarding their production value. The study seeks to answer how these two types of dramas are constructed in terms of technical and narrative elements and to identify the specific similarities and differences between them through a comparative close reading analysis.

The study utilizes a qualitative research design, specifically employing close reading analysis to examine two high-rated Netflix productions: the South Korean drama *Extraordinary Attorney Woo* and the Filipino series *House Arrest of Us*. The analysis is anchored in three theoretical frameworks: John Fiske’s Codes of TV Production, Stuart Hall’s Encoding and Decoding model, and Jacques Lacan’s Psychoanalytic Theory. Additionally, the researcher uses the Political Economy of Communication—specifically Mosco’s tenets of history and social change, social totality, moral philosophy, and praxis—to contextualize the findings within the socio-economic landscapes of both South Korea and the Philippines.

The findings reveal a significant disparity in technical execution. *Extraordinary Attorney Woo* is characterized by a high level of synergy across cinematography, directing, editing, production design, lighting, graphics, and audio design. The study notes that the high production budget (approximately 20 billion Won) allowed for world-class technical outputs, including sophisticated visual storytelling and meaningful mise-en-scene. In contrast, *House Arrest of Us* exhibited various technical flaws and mishaps, such as issues with lighting, directing, and continuity. The researcher attributes these shortcomings to systemic challenges in the Philippine production culture, including insufficient budgets and the "hand-to-mouth shoot" practice, where episodes are filmed and edited under extreme time constraints.

Narratively, both shows successfully integrated popular culture and used literary devices to engage audiences. However, their executions differed. The Korean drama utilized multi-faceted characters and a strong, cohesive plot that served as a vehicle for knowledge sharing. The Filipino series, while sharing some narrative similarities, relied more on the integration of local songs and dances, specific comedic styles, and the exploration of local issues. The study notes that while the Filipino production showed improvement, it was heavily influenced by the "aesthetics of poverty" and a production culture that prioritizes mass-market appeal to satisfy advertisers.

The conclusions of the study highlight that the success of Korean dramas is not merely a result of storytelling but is deeply rooted in a supportive political economy. In South Korea, government support, the rise of independent production houses, and a robust system of funding (including product placement and municipal sponsorships) have created a high-standard production culture. Conversely, the Philippine industry is characterized by a profit-oriented commercial model where networks hold significant power, and production workers often face grueling schedules and inadequate support. The study concludes that while Filipino creators are competent, they are often victims of a systemic lack of institutional support and financial resources.

The implications of this research are directed toward several stakeholders in the creative economy. For scriptwriters and directors, the study provides a framework for combining coherence and sequence to meet audience expectations. For TV producers and policymakers, the research emphasizes the need to challenge the status quo by lobbying for government support, such as budget allocations and policy reforms similar to those in South Korea. The researcher recommends that the Philippine government and private sectors forge stronger partnerships to institutionalize artists' welfare and provide capability-building programs. Ultimately, the study suggests that for the Filipino creative industry to achieve a paradigm shift and compete globally, there must be a concerted effort to improve technical expertise, stabilize working conditions, and provide the necessary financial and institutional infrastructure to support high-quality content creation.

title: Social Media Culture Among Automobile Training Industry Associates and Trainees and Their Performance in the Workplace
abstract:
202 Saudi national trainees and 32 multinational associates at an automobile training industry were participants to examine the association between their social media culture (SMC) and performance. Cochran’s formula with a 95% confidence level and 5 confidence interval was utilized. Generally, all variables were analyzed with chi square and phi coefficient for the frequency distribution and cross tabulation used. Data were gathered through a one-shot survey research design; wherein qualitative methods were employed for triangulation.

In a multicultural organization, it could be inferred that SMC was typically propagated by a combination of factors. It emerged organically among members while organizational policies, leadership support, and communication channels could have shaped and influenced it. The study found out that their participation in SMC translated into tangible actions. In addition, it not only disclosed that the emerging SMC was often created to foster stakeholders’ connectivity, knowledge exchange, and engagement, but it also confirmed its added value to organizational communication.

Ultimately anchored with computer-mediated communication (CMC) (Walther, 2011), it revealed a slightly moderate direct positive association between SMC shareholders and their workplace performance. This implies that engagement with SMC can have some beneficial effects in a professional setting.

title: Authority of Non-Human Agents: Speech Act Analysis of Peace Process Documents
abstract: The study answered the questions “what is the authority of peace agreements” and “how do the peace agreements perform/invoke its power.” Exploring Francois Cooren’s seminal concepts on nonhuman agency and Searle’s Speech Act Theory, the study analyzed the two milestone peace agreements in the Philippines’ Mindanao peace process, namely (1) 1996 Final Peace Agreement and Implementation of 1976 Tripoli Agreement, and (2) 2014 Comprehensive Agreement of Bangsamoro (CAB). The authority of the peace agreement lies, first, on its assertives – its power to affirm and assure the implementation of those written provisions. Second is in directives, third is in commissives and last are expressives and declarations. The peace agreement has the authority to force two settling parties to enter into an agreement. Moreover, the agreements performed the following roles; under the assertives, the peace agreements in Mindanao assert to: (1) recognize the Bangsamoro identity for the realization of the lasting peace, (2) affirm the autonomy of the Bangsamoro, (3) highlight the need of transition, and (4) upholds the significance of socio-economic, cultural and educational development; and under the directives, the agreements command or order to (a) implement significant monitoring and transition mechanisms, (b) draft and pass the basic law, (c) devise a normalization program, and, (d) mandate equal representation.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Norman Ralph B. Isla’s dissertation, "Authority of Non-Human Agents: Speech Act Analysis of the Peace Process Documents," investigates the communicative power of written agreements within the Mindanao peace process. Focusing on the 1996 Final Peace Agreement and the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB), the study utilizes Francois Cooren’s theory of non-human agency and John Searle’s Speech Act Theory to argue that documents are active agents capable of influencing social organization rather than mere containers of information.

The research employs a qualitative speech act analysis to categorize the communicative actions performed by these texts. Findings reveal that the agreements exercise authority through several functions. As assertives, they affirm Bangsamoro identity, autonomy, and the necessity of transition. As directives, they function as commands that mandate the implementation of monitoring mechanisms, the drafting of basic laws, and the creation of normalization programs. Additionally, the documents serve as commissives by representing the commitments made by involved parties.

The study concludes that these documents possess "textual agency," allowing for "action at a distance" by acting on behalf of the institutions that created them. They do not merely describe a peace process but actively shape the political landscape by creating the structures and mandates required to implement it. Ultimately, the research suggests that peacebuilding should focus on the communicative power and structural agency of the resulting documents.

The research is grounded in the socio-cultural tradition of communication and utilizes Francois Cooren’s theory of non-human agency to argue that documents are active agents capable of influencing social organization rather than being mere containers of information. This is complemented by John Searle’s Speech Act Theory to categorize the communicative actions performed by the texts. Using a qualitative speech act analysis, the author examines how the documents function through various illocutionary points.

The findings reveal that the authority of these agreements is exercised through several distinct functions. As assertives, the documents affirm and assure by recognizing Bangsamoro identity and autonomy, highlighting the necessity of transition, and upholding the importance of socio-economic, cultural, and educational development. As directives, the documents function as commands or orders, mandating the implementation of monitoring and transition mechanisms, the drafting of basic laws, the creation of normalization programs, and the requirement for equal representation. Additionally, the study identifies the role of commissives, which represent the commitments made by the involved parties.

The results demonstrate that these documents possess a unique "textual agency," allowing for "action at a distance" by acting on behalf of the institutions that created them. For instance, the documents establish the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and various committees that continue to direct political processes long after the initial signing. The study shows that the documents do not just describe a peace process; they actively shape the political landscape by creating the structures and mandates required to implement it.

In conclusion, the study finds that peace agreements are powerful non-human agents. Their authority is derived from their ability to assert identities, command political actions, and commit parties to long-term processes. They act as "mediating objects" that facilitate the transition from conflict to structured, autonomous governance. The research suggests that peacebuilding should focus not only on human actors but also on the communicative power and structural agency of the resulting documents. The author recommends that policymakers recognize the agency inherent in the legal and symbolic codes created to resolve conflicts.

title: Online Communication and Social Construction of Reality on Disaster
abstract:
Human interaction produces a shared reality that is “subjectively meaningful and objectively factual.” This dissertation investigated the online communication and construction of social reality on disaster through the lens of Socio-Cultural Tradition which claims that communication is viewed as the creation and enactment of social reality. That is, as people talk, they collectively “co-construct their own social worlds.” Specifically, the study looked into the local government unit’s (LGU) online communication practices, the online discourse that arise from the LGU’s disaster communication, what the online communication reveals about disaster, and the social construction of reality on disaster.

Through the LGU’s official social media platform, which is publicly accessible and the primary online resource in information dissemination during the first six months of COVID-19 in the Philippines, the posts and comments used in the discourse were carefully examined. A qualitative approach particularly content analysis and thematic analysis was utilized to explore the meanings embedded in the online posts and texts.

Top-down online communication expressed the planning, monitoring, implementation and collaborative efforts of the local government while the online discourse related to disaster communication revealed expression of gratitude, acknowledged the efforts of stakeholders and examined the strategic plan of the local government among others. Online communication revealed that disaster is a construct that converges stakeholders, connects people together and strengthens community resilience. The permanence of language and its detachability from the “here and now” permeates the reconstruction of subjectivity that influences conversations and narratives in online communication.

This dissertation, titled "Online Communication and Social Construction of Reality on Disaster" by Joseleanor Melliza Magno-Mendoza, investigates how social reality is shaped through digital interaction during a crisis. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as a primary case study, the research explores the relationship between local government communication and the resulting public discourse on social media.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, which the author frames as a global disaster that disrupted social functions and necessitated a shift from traditional to digital communication. While disaster communication is essential for public safety and preparedness, the rise of social media has fundamentally changed the communication ecology. Unlike traditional media, social media allows for real-time, two-way interaction, creating a "network society" where the public is no longer a passive recipient of information but an active participant. The researcher identifies a need to understand how this participatory environment affects the way a disaster is perceived and understood by the community.

**Methodology**
The study employs a qualitative research approach, specifically utilizing qualitative content analysis and thematic analysis. The primary data source was the official Facebook pages of a Local Government Unit (LGU) in Cebu, Philippines—specifically the Public Information Office (PIO) and the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (LDRRMO)—along with the public comments and engagements on those posts. The research focused on the first six months of the COVID-19 outbreak in the Philippines. The study is grounded in the Socio-Cultural Tradition of communication, which posits that communication is the process through which individuals collectively co-construct their social worlds.

**Findings**
The findings are categorized into three main areas: the nature of LGU communication, the nature of public discourse, and the resulting social construction of reality.

Regarding LGU communication, the study found a "top-down" approach characterized by the planning, monitoring, and implementation of pandemic protocols. The LGU used its platforms to disseminate official updates, health guidelines, and collaborative efforts to manage the crisis.

The public's online discourse revealed several distinct themes. The research identified expressions of gratitude toward leaders and frontliners, acknowledgments of stakeholders, and expressions of faith and hope. However, the discourse was not solely positive; it also included inquiries for information, recommendations for local authorities, and critiques regarding relief distribution, information dissemination, and the enforcement of health guidelines.

The study concludes that online communication reveals disaster to be a construct that converges stakeholders, connects people, and strengthens community resilience. The findings suggest that the "reality" of the pandemic was not just a biological event but a social one, shaped by the continuous interaction between official government mandates and the public's lived experiences and responses.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The researcher concludes that social reality is socially constructed in online communication through the interplay of language and interaction. The permanence and detachability of digital text allow for a reconstruction of subjectivity that influences ongoing narratives. Through social media, the pandemic became a shared social experience that was constantly being revised through comments, shares, and debates.

The implications of this study are threefold:
Theoretically, it contributes to the field of communication by applying the social construction of reality lens to the digital landscape, demonstrating how online discourse creates a shared meaning of a disaster.
Methodologically, it highlights the utility of qualitative content analysis in studying dynamic, time-sensitive digital phenomena.
Practically, the study offers insights for LGUs and disaster management agencies. It suggests that effective disaster communication requires more than just disseminating information; it requires managing the interactive, participatory nature of social media to foster trust, address public critiques, and mitigate the "infodemic" of misinformation.

title: The Reproduction of the Rule Regime in Licensure Examination Through the Communicative Practices of Personnel of a Regulatory Body: An Ethnomethodological Study
abstract:
This study explored the communicative practices of personnel assigned in licensure examinations and how their communicative practices reproduce rule regime in licensure examination administration. The research framework used in this Study is the Socio-Cultural Tradition of Communication Theory, which theorizes communication as the (re)production of social order (Craig, 1999). Using this framework, this Study assumed that rule regime is reproduced by the communicative practices established from the participants. The use of Ethnomethodology as a qualitative research method in this Study explored the participants’ acts of communication in licensure examinations towards surfacing themes that described their communicative practices. Eight (8) participants were identified in this Study, each with rich experiences in their specific roles in the licensure examination administration. The participants’ narratives were subjected to Grounded Theory Method (GTM) and Thematic Analysis for data interpretation. 

Fifteen (15) communicative practices of assigned personnel in licensure examinations emerged in the analysis: (1) roaming around; (2) resolving issues; (3) retaining professional composure; (4) reviewing exam statistics; (5) re-checking documents; (6) securing retrieval procedures; (7) reprimanding; (8) reporting incidents and violations; (9) reporting issues; (10) reminding procedures to prevent cheating; (11) removing prohibited materials or items in the examination room; (12) rendering support to ensure consistency; (13) the wearing of respective badges; (14) referring issues to higher authority; and (15) ensuring the record of accountable persons. 

These communicative practices reproduced five dimensions of the rule regime in the licensure examination: (1) rule alignment; (2) rule implementation; (3) rule compliance; (4) rule preservation; and (5) rule authority. 

Roaming around, resolving issues, and retaining professional composure align knowledge and actions with the rules. Reviewing exam statistics, re-checking documents, and securing retrieval procedures of examination paraphernalia are performed to ensure that rules are implemented. Reprimanding, reporting of violations, and reporting of issues are done when rules are not complied. Reminding procedures to prevent cheating, removing prohibited materials or items in the examination room, and rendering support to ensure consistency are meant to preserve the integrity of the examination process. Finally, by putting in place respective badges, referring issues to higher authority, and recording of accountable persons, the established authority is recognized.

The dissertation titled "The Reproduction of the Rule Regime in Licensure Examination Through the Communicative Practices of Personnel of a Regulatory Body: An Ethnomethodological Study" by Yourgin O. Montejo explores how the social order and institutional rules of licensure examinations are maintained and reproduced through the daily communicative actions of the personnel involved in their administration.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the context of government regulatory bodies tasked with administering licensure examinations to ensure professional competency and protect public interest. While these institutions are governed by formal rules and policies, the author notes that the mere existence of rules does not guarantee a smooth or orderly examination process. The researcher identifies a gap in communication research: most existing literature focuses on the pedagogical relationship between teachers and students in academic settings, leaving the communicative dynamics of professional licensure administration—specifically the "muted voices" of the administrative personnel—largely unexplored. The problem addressed is how the "rule regime" (the complex of rules and social relations) is actually manifested and sustained through the practical, communicative interactions of the staff responsible for implementing these rules.

**Methodology**
The study utilizes the Socio-Cultural Tradition of Communication Theory, which views communication as a symbolic process that produces and maintains social order. To explore this, the researcher employed an ethnomethodological qualitative research design. This approach allowed for the exploration of the participants' communicative acts to surface themes describing their practical realities. The study involved eight participants selected for their rich, specific experiences in various roles within licensure examination administration. Data were collected through Key Informant Interviews (KII) and subjected to analysis using the Grounded Theory Method (GTM) and Thematic Analysis to interpret the narratives.

**Findings**
The analysis revealed fifteen distinct communicative practices performed by examination personnel, including roaming around, resolving issues, retaining professional composure, reviewing exam statistics, re-checking documents, securing retrieval procedures, reprimanding, reporting incidents and violations, reporting issues, reminding procedures to prevent cheating, removing prohibited materials, rendering support to ensure consistency, wearing respective badges, referring issues to higher authority, and ensuring the record of accountable persons.

These communicative practices were found to reproduce five specific dimensions of the rule regime:
1. Rule Alignment: Achieved through roaming around, resolving issues, and maintaining professional composure to align knowledge and actions with established rules.
2. Rule Implementation: Facilitated by reviewing statistics, re-checking documents, and securing the retrieval of examination paraphernalia.
3. Rule Compliance: Enforced through reprimanding, reporting violations, and reporting issues when rules are not followed.
4. Rule Preservation: Maintained by reminding examinees of procedures to prevent cheating, removing prohibited items, and rendering support to ensure consistency, all aimed at protecting exam integrity.
5. Rule Authority: Recognized through the use of official badges, the process of referring issues to higher authorities, and the meticulous recording of accountable persons.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that the rule regime in licensure examinations is not merely a static set of written policies but is a dynamic social reality continuously reproduced through the communicative practices of personnel. These interactions create an "institutional paradigm" that allows for the coordination of diverse roles—such as room watchers, supervisors, and coordinators—to achieve the collective goal of a credible examination.

The implications of the study are categorized into three areas:
Theoretical implications suggest that future research could apply different communication traditions (such as Phenomenological, Semiotic, or Critical) to different aspects of the examination process, such as the lived experiences of volunteers or the role of digital communication in computer-based testing. Methodological implications suggest that feminist perspectives could be used to study the gendered nature of the volunteer pool, and ethnography could be used to study the everyday culture of examination staff. Practical implications suggest that regulatory bodies should provide better orientation, briefing sessions, and manuals to ensure personnel are well-equipped to act as effective rule implementers. By understanding these communicative patterns, agencies can develop enhanced guidelines that foster cooperation and safeguard the integrity and inviolability of the licensure process.

title: Communicating Identity through eBook Reading Habit: A Study Among Digital Natives
abstract:
Reading is currently in the most significant decline among young adult readers in human history. The general problem is that reading is viewed through a narrow lens that does not consider how young adult readers interact with eBooks and digital text. The problem is that for reading advocates to bolster readership among young adult readers, research must consider the relationship between eBook reading and reader identity in this age group. The study aims to explore how digital natives reading identity and investigate the phenomenon of their eBook reading behavior. By examining the eBook reading habits and behaviors of the digital natives, the study provided insights on developing more effective communication strategies for promoting eBooks and digital reading. 

The quantitative research design selected for this study was a survey research approach. Several key findings have emerged in this comprehensive study of eBook reading behavior among digital natives. The acquisition of eBooks was examined and showed that eBook readers primarily purchased their eBooks while borrowing and renting was not a familiar process for the participants. There was a positive correlation between Readers' identity and eBook Reading Behavior. Adolescent Development, a readers’ identity factor, predicts eBook reading behavior significantly. Increased reading hours and a positive eBook reading experience positively influenced eBook purchases. 

Research recommendations include longitudinal studies to track changes in eBook reading behavior, cross-cultural research to explore differences among digital natives, experimental designs to test eBook design elements, in-depth interviews for deeper insights, and interventions to enhance reader identities.

Napalan’s dissertation, "Communicating Identity through eBook Reading Habit: A Study Among Digital Natives," investigates the relationship between digital reading technologies and the formation of reader identity among young adults. The study addresses the decline in annual book reading among young adults and challenges the perception that eBook reading is a distracting or soulless experience. It seeks to understand how the transition to digital formats influences how digital natives perceive themselves as readers, specifically looking at the connection between reader identity and eBook reading behaviors.

Using a quantitative survey research approach, the study measured eBook Reading Behavior—including hours spent reading, acquisition methods, satisfaction, ease of use, and reading while traveling—and Reader Identity, measured through dimensions such as autonomy, decision making, and adolescent development. Data from American young adult digital natives were analyzed using Pearson Correlation Analysis and Multiple Linear Regression Analysis.

The findings revealed that eBook readers primarily purchase their books, while borrowing and renting are uncommon. A significant positive correlation exists between a reader's identity and their eBook reading behavior, with "Adolescent Development" identified as a significant predictor. Additionally, increased reading hours and a positive eBook reading experience positively influence eBook purchases. The study concludes that reading identity is vital for motivating lifelong readers and suggests that publishers, educators, and marketers should adapt to the preferences and identities of digital natives.

The study addresses a significant decline in reading among young adult readers, noting that longitudinal data shows a steady decrease in the number of books read annually. The author argues that the current discourse surrounding this decline is often viewed through a narrow lens that fails to account for how digital natives interact with eBooks and electronic text. There is a prevailing perception that eBook reading is a "soulless" or "distracting" experience compared to print. The study focuses on "digital natives"—individuals raised in an environment characterized by ubiquitous digital technology. The author explores the tension between traditional print culture and the emerging digital landscape, noting that while eBooks offer convenience, portability, and interactivity, they also face criticism regarding screen time, lack of tactile experience, and potential for distraction.

A significant finding was the existence of a positive correlation between a reader's identity and their eBook reading behavior. Specifically, the factor of "Adolescent Development" was found to be a significant predictor of eBook reading behavior. Furthermore, the study determined that increased reading hours and a positive overall eBook reading experience had a positive influence on eBook purchases.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that reading identity is a vital component in motivating lifelong readers and that digital reading is an integral part of the daily lives of digital natives. The research suggests that the way individuals perceive themselves as readers directly impacts their engagement with digital formats.

The implications of this research are multifaceted. For publishers and content creators, the findings suggest a need to enhance eBook design, interactivity, and engagement features to better align with the preferences of digital natives. For educators and reading advocates, the study highlights the importance of understanding reader identity to develop more effective communication strategies that promote digital reading. The results also suggest that marketing and pricing strategies should be tailored to the specific behaviors of digital natives, such as their preference for purchasing over renting. Finally, the study calls for further research, including longitudinal studies to track changes in behavior over time, cross-cultural studies to explore global differences, and experimental designs to test specific eBook design elements.

title: Spiritual Communication for Social Transformation: Prayer Warriors’ Intercession as Communicative Acts in Building the Parachurch Culture and Identity for National Development
abstract: Cooperation for the shared goal of social transformation is highly aspired yet greatly challenging among Evangelical churches and partner institutions. Though parachurches function to assist churches, organizational structures and traditions threaten church-parachurch dynamics. The Davao City House of Prayer (HOP) parachurch bridges this divide by establishing its unique niche of intercessory prayers for good governance and nation-building. The study used ethnographic field work to observe HOP members conduct the Prayer Watch, a 3-hour continuous prayer or "soaking" in God's presence. The Prayer Watch is the encompassing communicative performance where members' shared values, symbols, and meaning-making activities through intercessory prayers blend together to (co)create the parachurch culture and identity for social transformation. Communicative acts bring to life this particular culture and identity as unifying yet separating and innovative but not competitive toward the church. The Prayer Watch demonstrates communication as the means of achieving interdependence or balance between autonomy and dependency where organizational strengths of the church and parachurch are maximized and limitations are complemented by each other.

The dissertation "Spiritual Communication for Social Transformation: Prayer Warriors’ Intercession as Communicative Acts in Building the Parachurch Culture and Identity for National Development" by Mayme F. Olegario explores the intersection of organizational communication, spirituality, and social change. The study focuses on the Davao City House of Prayer (HOP), a parachurch organization dedicated to 24/7 intercessory prayer for the Philippines.

**Problem and Context**
The research is situated within the tension between traditional Evangelical churches and parachurches. While parachurches are designed to assist churches by providing specialized ministries, they often face challenges regarding organizational structure, cultural differences, and perceived competition. These tensions can lead to strained relationships, ministry rivalries, and a lack of cooperation. The study specifically addresses the lack of research regarding intercessory prayer as a communicative act within an Evangelical/prophetic parachurch context. The central problem is understanding how the shared values, symbols, and communicative performances of intercessory prayer help establish a unique parachurch culture and identity that complements, rather than competes with, the local church to facilitate national development and good governance.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed an ethnographic field work design to study the Davao City HOP. The primary method of data collection involved observing the "Prayer Watch," a three-hour continuous prayer session (or "soaking") where members engage in collective intercession. Data were gathered through participant observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions. The study utilized Organizational Cultural Theory, specifically the framework provided by Pacanowsky and O'Donnell-Trujillo, which views culture as being constituted through communication. This allowed the researcher to analyze "cultural performances"—ritual, passion, courtesy, politics, and enculturation—to understand how meaning is made within the group.

**Findings**
The findings are categorized into several key areas:

*Shared Values and Mission:* The parachurch culture is built upon shared values of Bible supremacy and reverence for God. Their mission is to serve the Body of Christ by providing a specific niche of intercessory prayer that focuses on national needs and good governance. The study found that the parachurch plays a complementary role to the church, though tensions can arise if roles are not clearly defined.

*Shared Symbols:* Several symbols facilitate meaning-making among members. The "House of Prayer" itself serves as a symbol of the group's purpose. "Intercessory prayer" is viewed as a symbol of spiritual warfare at both micro and macro levels. Additionally, the "Prayer Leader" acts as a symbolic figurehead for the organization's direction.

*Communicative Performances:* The Prayer Watch serves as a site for various cultural performances. These include rituals (such as the "Soaring with the Scepter of Strength" national online event), passions (the use of metaphors like "mountain" or "spring of living water" to describe spiritual warfare), courtesies (social acts that build rapport), politics (the recruitment of allies and the affirmation of members), and enculturation (the process of teaching newcomers the significance of specific spiritual metaphors and roles).

*Transforming Effects and Identity:* Intercessory prayer has transformative effects on both the nation and the individual. On a national level, it is viewed as a tool for social transformation and good governance. On an individual level, it transforms the intercessor's identity, creating a sense of self-identity, work identity, and organizational identity. This transformation is characterized by a deep sense of being "called" to a specific spiritual assignment.

*Church-Parachurch Dynamics:* The study identifies a process of "complementation" where the church and parachurch can work together. To maintain this balance, members use specific strategies, such as prioritizing church responsibilities, respecting ministry limits, and ensuring that parachurch activities do not substitute for local church membership.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that spiritual communication through intercessory prayer is a powerful communicative act that builds a distinct parachurch culture and identity. This culture is not a replacement for the local church but a specialized extension of the church's mission. Through shared symbols, values, and ritualized communicative performances, the HOP creates a sense of community and purpose that drives members toward the goal of national transformation.

The implications of this research are threefold. For parachurch administrators, the study suggests the importance of establishing clear boundaries and communication protocols with local churches to avoid conflict and foster cooperation. For communication scholars, the work expands the field of organizational communication by applying sociocultural and cultural performance theories to the realm of spiritual and religious communication. Finally, for further research, the study suggests exploring how these spiritual communicative acts impact specific social and political outcomes in different cultural contexts.

title: Kinasiasino Ti Bigueño: A Grounded Theory of Vigan Cultural Heritage Communication
abstract: Establishing an identity is anchored on how one’s culture is appreciated, understood, and preserved the cultural heritage through communication. Cultural heritage is part of what people are. It is a testament to the past human existence that defines the present and the future. Guided by the concepts of cultural heritage and communication, 17 participants involved in communicating cultural heritage and residents of Vigan City, a renowned UNESCO World Heritage Site participated in in- depth interviews to document their narratives on their becoming a Bigueňo. Findings led towards the development of a theory on cultural heritage communication (CHC) through the rigors of Kathy Charmaz’ constructivist grounded theory. The theorizing revealed that Kinasiasino ti Bigueňo or the becoming of a Bigueňo identity, is the core of cultural heritage communication. The CHC explains that cultural heritage symbolizes the becoming of individual identities. Thus, cultural heritage is not only regarded as inherited old structures (tangible) and practices (intangible) but the development of one’s persona. Findings also revealed that through panangiburay (knowledge sharing), tungtongan (dialogue), panangital-o (promotion), panagsukisok (research), panangiyallatiw (education), artistiko a panangiyebkas (artistic expression), and pannakisarsarita (continual communicative experience), cultural heritage communication allows individuals and communities to shape their image and how this is exude in public. Hence, as originally defined in this study, the Cultural Heritage Communication Theory is the process of completely and accurately exchanging information and knowledge through multi-approaches using various channels for different stakeholders to understand, appreciate, and preserve cultural heritage that is significant in inculcating one’s identity relevant to the development of a nation

The findings resulted in the development of a new theory termed Cultural Heritage Communication (CHC). At the core of this theory is the concept of Kinasiasino ti Bigueño, which refers to the "becoming" of a Bigueño identity.

The study identifies several specific communicative processes: panangiburay (knowledge sharing), tungtongan (dialogue), panangital-o (promotion), panagsukisok (research), panangiyallatiw (education), artistiko a panangiyebkas (artistic expression), and pannakisarsarita (continual communicative experience). These approaches enable individuals and communities to shape and exude their public image. Ultimately, the study defines Cultural Heritage Communication as the process of exchanging information and knowledge through multi-approaches to ensure stakeholders can understand, appreciate, and preserve cultural heritage.

title: Transcendence of Theater as Communication: Lived Experiences of Practitioners in e-Theater during the Pandemic
abstract:
With the sudden shift of theater to digital, there were minimum studies conducted on this in the Philippine setting. Thus, this study focused on unraveling the lived experiences of theater practitioners during the pandemic to answer how theater as communication is accomplished in its new seeing place in the virtual space. The study explored how theater practitioners experience theater as communication in e-theater, basically on their adaption, the challenges encountered, and the unique strategies utilized under the communicative ecology. 

The research utilized the transcendental phenomenology research method to explore the lived experiences of the participants. In-depth interview was used as the primary data-gathering tool together with the analysis of qualitative digital materials.

The results revealed ten overarching themes: Views on the Performance Space, Theatrical Perspectives, Theater Resurgence, Anticipations for the Theater, Theater Metamorphism, Communication in the e-theater, Pandemic-responsive Theater, e-theater Productions of Stage@Home and Phillippine High School for the Arts, Observed Elements of Theater in the New Seeing Place, and Realizations on e-theater.

This metamorphosis offers a glimpse into the essence of the e theater experience, where the participants' lived encounters underscore how theater's evolution transcends its traditional theatrical confines, embracing the expansive landscapes of the digital world.

title: Regional News Writing in the Digital Age: A Narrative Inquiry into the Practices of Filipino Journalists in Western Visayas
abstract: The world of journalism is constantly evolving alongside social reality to where it belongs. Thus, it is vital to understand the experiences of journalists in news writing and narrate their practices as they catch up with the increasing demands of the public. Through this study, media practitioners and educators can understand the current practices of Filipino journalists and the influences in news writing in Western Visayas. Nine local journalists participated in an online in-depth interview resulting to the discussion of (1) journalistic practices in the new media, (2) practices that implicate objectivity in news writing, (3) assessment of the hierarchy of influence model in the news writing process, and (4) news writing framework. Results showed that the news writing process has evolved because of the emergence of new media. Technology and mobile devices revolutionized the news writing process, which involves gathering, writing, and selecting news content. Moreover, this study concludes that the emergence of new media considerably impacted objectivity in news writing and has a significant influence in the practices of multimedia journalists.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
This study explores how new media has shaped news writing practices among Filipino journalists in the Western Visayas region. The research addresses a changing landscape where traditional gatekeeping faces challenges from user-generated content and the rapid spread of misinformation. A central problem is the difficulty of maintaining accuracy and objectivity in an era where digital platforms allow for the viral spread of fake news and the mobilization of troll armies. Using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, the research examined the lived experiences of nine journalists with years of service ranging from 10 to 39 years.

Findings reveal that the news writing process has evolved due to technological advancements. Because digital consumers often have short attention spans, journalists have adapted by packaging news in a quick, direct, and fast-paced manner. Digital news gathering has been revolutionized by mobile devices, allowing journalists to monitor competitors and conduct research from anywhere. The use of smartphones has turned journalists into multimedia practitioners capable of capturing high-quality audio and video on the go.

Journalists in Western Visayas continue to prioritize human interest stories that emphasize local context. While they strive for accountability by correcting errors immediately, they face threats such as cybercrime and cyber libel. News content is impacted by individual values, professional ethics, organizational pressures, and external influences, including the issue of envelopemental journalism. The study concludes that while technology makes news gathering more accessible, it introduces pressures related to speed and disinformation.

A central problem is the difficulty of maintaining accuracy and objectivity in an era where digital platforms allow for the viral spread of fake news and the mobilization of troll armies. The study seeks to understand how journalists in this region navigate these challenges and what hierarchy of influences shapes their news production.

The research utilized a qualitative narrative inquiry design to understand the lived experiences of nine Filipino journalists in Western Visayas, including six females and three males. These participants had years of service ranging from 10 to 39 years and represented various fields such as investigative, watchdog, broadcast, online, opinion, and political journalism. Data were gathered through online in-depth interviews via Zoom and analyzed using thematic coding.

Findings reveal that the news writing process has evolved due to technological advancements. One major theme is the emergence of a short attention span audience. Because digital consumers are often multitasking, journalists have adapted by packaging news in a quick, direct, and fast-paced manner, often using fewer words to compete with other digital content. Digital news gathering has been revolutionized by technology and mobile devices, allowing journalists to monitor competitors, contact sources efficiently, and conduct research from anywhere. The use of smartphones has turned journalists into multimedia practitioners capable of capturing high-quality audio and video on the go.

Journalists in Western Visayas continue to prioritize human interest stories that impact the daily lives of the local community, emphasizing local context and flavor. Regarding accountability, findings highlight the importance of correcting errors immediately to maintain transparency, though journalists face threats such as cybercrime and cyber libel. The research found that news content is impacted by individual values, professional ethics, organizational pressures, and external influences. Participants noted a disparity in salaries between local and national journalists and discussed the issue of envelopemental journalism, where receiving money from sources or political figures threatens objectivity.
