The study explores how the emergence of new media has shaped the news writing practices of Filipino journalists specifically within the Western Visayas region. The research addresses the evolving landscape of journalism where traditional gatekeeping is being challenged by user-generated content and the rapid spread of misinformation. A central problem identified is the difficulty of maintaining accuracy and objectivity in an era where digital platforms allow for the viral spread of fake news and the mobilization of troll armies. The study seeks to understand how journalists in this specific region navigate these challenges, how their practices impact objectivity, and what hierarchy of influences shapes their news production.

The research was conducted using a qualitative narrative inquiry design, which focuses on understanding the lived experiences and personal accounts of individuals. The participants consisted of nine Filipino journalists working in Western Visayas, including six females and three males. These participants possessed extensive experience in the industry, with years of service ranging from 10 to 39 years. They represented various fields such as investigative, watchdog, broadcast, online, opinion, and political journalism, and had experience in both traditional and digital newsrooms. Data were gathered through online in-depth interviews conducted via Zoom, and the resulting transcripts were analyzed using thematic coding.

The findings reveal that the news writing process has undergone a significant evolution due to technological advancements. One major theme is the emergence of a "short attention span" (SAS) audience. Because digital consumers are often preoccupied and multitasking, journalists have had to adapt by packaging news in a quick, direct, and fast-paced manner, often using fewer words and focusing on essential details to compete with other digital content. Digital news gathering has also been revolutionized; technology and mobile devices allow journalists to monitor competitors, contact sources more efficiently and cheaply, and conduct research from anywhere. The use of smartphones has turned journalists into multimedia practitioners capable of capturing high-quality audio and video on the go.

The study also identified specific practices regarding news selection and accountability. Journalists in Western Visayas continue to prioritize human interest stories, focusing on news that impacts the daily lives and routines of the local community. There is a strong emphasis on providing local context and "local flavor" to stories, which distinguishes regional reporting from national news agencies. Regarding accountability, the findings highlight the importance of correcting errors immediately through explanation stories or updates to maintain transparency. However, the study also notes challenges such as the threat of cybercrime and cyber libel, which requires journalists to be cautious about legal implications in the digital space.

The research assessed the hierarchy of influences and found that various levels impact news content. While individual values and professional ethics remain core, journalists are subject to organizational pressures, such as editorial decisions on which stories to publish, and external influences, such as agencies asking for favors. A significant finding involves the economic and social realities of regional journalism. Participants noted a disparity in salaries between local and national journalists and discussed the persistent issue of "envelopemental journalism," where receiving money from sources or political figures threatens journalistic objectivity and credibility.

In conclusion, the study concludes that the emergence of new media has considerably impacted objectivity and the practical routines of multimedia journalists. While technology has made news gathering more manageable and accessible, it has also introduced new pressures related to speed, audience attention spans, and the fight against disinformation. The study suggests that journalists must continuously reinvent themselves by learning new technological skills, such as photojournalism and graphics, to remain relevant.

The implications of this research are significant for media organizations and journalism educators. For media organizations, the findings suggest a need to review news production practices to better serve the digital audience while maintaining strict policies against corruption and errors. For educators, the study highlights the necessity of incorporating real-life digital challenges and technological proficiency into journalism curricula. Ultimately, the study emphasizes that for regional journalism to remain a vital "gatekeeper of truth and democracy," practitioners must balance the speed of the digital age with the fundamental responsibility of providing accurate, contextualized, and ethical information to the public.

title: COVID-19 Infodemic in the Twitterverse: Characterization of Misinformation Spread and Twitter Bot Activity by Critical Mass, Energy Decay, Entanglements, and Node Synchronization Using Multilayer and Spectral Graph Visualizations, Kuramoto Modeling, Sonification, and Wavefunction Simulation
abstract: No communication framework for “infodemiology” or investigate techniques within the discipline of communication have covered measurement of Twitter bots’ “virality and (massive) “misinformation spread” by energy and mass equivalence because these belong to quantum mechanics. To posit infodemical measurements, this study of “COVID-19 infodemic” on Twitter characterized misinformation spread and Twitter bot activity by critical mass, energy decay, entanglements, and node synchronization using multilayer and spectral graph visualizations, Kuramoto modeling, sonification, and wavefunction simulation. The Python-based analytics pipeline was developed based on fundamental conceptualizations of 7 communication theories and quantum mechanics. Simulation and (stochastic) modeling were implemented to investigate the intra- and interlayer relationships between bots, humans, and tweets. This study endeavored on (1) theorizing “virality” and bot activity (2) data mining using Hoaxy® and bot detection set at ≥.43 using Botometer®, and (3) comprehensive data analysis using state-of-the-art techniques and statistics. Misinformation spreads more frequently with user replies than with retweets and faster through interlayer edges. Super spreaders were detected using centrality- based metrics. Bots that had high betweenness and eigenvector centralities, random walk score, and PageRank score were false human accounts. Bot cliques emerged inconsistently by edge entanglement with humans. False human accounts were central spreaders and were detectable by an increase in percolation centrality, random walk and PageRank scores. Spammers were peripheral spreaders with scores decreased or unchanged whenever connected indirectly to human hubs. False human accounts connect by power-law distribution. Many cross-links were shown between bots and humans. Overall, bots (re)produced the intrinsic “virality” of tweets with human users. Bots synchronized (partially) around 400 seconds (6.67 minutes) at peak before reaching 200 seconds (3.33 minutes). Time to critical mass can be anticipated at .00025 seconds when bots have synchronized. Based on wavefunction simulation, a 13.55% tweet increase can generate a 29.45% network energy inflation at .70 (70%) bot “virality” within 9 months (peaked at 7th month). Energy from critical mass due to bots can equal to 9.61 x 10^6 J, which can start to decay at .0015 seconds. Bots oscillated from <25 dB to 94.12 dB at 2090.91 Hz with 2 plateaus throughout the cycle. Bots maybe disbanded within .26 seconds at 50 J counter energy. On the other hand, a bot mass of 9.51 x 10^-30 can equal to 1.58 x 10^-13 J of kinetic energy per 2.14 x 10^-18 J energy increment in the network or as much as .02 micro-Sievert/hour of ionizing radiation produced by a plain chest-x ray. A full-length Twitter data sonification is required to validate these findings while all logical and seed values have to be standardized. Model validation must be conducted in the future.

title: Who is speaking? Who is listening? A Network Approach in Analyzing Communication Structures and Social Construction of Knowledge in Online Asynchronous Discussion Forums
abstract: Network plays a central role in the knowledge construction formed from the interactions and collaboration of online learners in asynchronous discussion forums. The very nature of networks to form connections, relationships, and links uncovers unique and wider opportunities for online learners to create higher levels of knowledge the more they interact and collaborate with each other. The opportunities to construct knowledge among online learners elevate as the connections and links formed from interacting with each other widen and enlarge reach. This study employed multi-analysis methodologies, with Social Network Analysis as the primary research approach, in combination with Interaction Analysis Model (IAM) and Cluster Analysis to uncover and understand connections, links, patterns, and structures formed from online interactions (speaking and listening) that may influence the social construction of knowledge that occurred in the online discussion forums. This paper suggests that the network structures of online interactions (speaking and listening), both in terms of posts contributed and posts viewed, have potential influence on the knowledge construction of online learners based on the results of the study.

title: Conservation Communication and Local Governance of Xenconservation: A Peatland in Jimenez, Misamis Occidental, Philippines
abstract: This study focuses on XenConservation's revelatory conservation communication in local governance, a small matrix of lowland freshwater mangrove wetland situated in Jimenez, Misamis Occidental, southern island of Mindanao, Philippines. A qualitative exploratory single case study in criterion-i purposeful sampling was employed to examine the nature of the conservation communication of the locale. The study revealed a transformative conservation communication in local governance continuum of care in private type governance alongside protected areas (PAs): convergent care, ancillary care, and diversified care, in a gradation of polarities within conservation communication in its conservation actions. In conclusion, the study theorizes in a constructivist and transformative worldview as a hobbyist in the in- situ conservation of threatened species. Tacit minority practice of affordances in a conservation communication's ancillary view of convergent-ancillary-diversified continuum of care encompasses a criterion-i conservation communication. Hence, a better protection policy and improved governance management for seasonal wetland and peatland of local conservation sites' agro-biodiversity and tree count status need to be strengthened.

This dissertation explores the intersection of conservation communication and local governance through a case study of XenConservation, a small, privately-owned habitat matrix located in Jimenez, Misamis Occidental, Philippines. The study focuses on a 2,880-square-meter site that contains a seasonal wetland and peatland, serving as a refuge for threatened species such as the *Carallia brachiata* (Bakauan-Gubat), a freshwater mangrove tree.

The research problem centers on the role of communication in the protection of small, non-government-managed areas. While large Protected Areas (PAs) are well-documented, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding how communication functions within "Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures" (OECMs), particularly in private, small-scale settings. The author notes that local stakeholders, such as lumber yard owners, often misidentify threatened species like the Bakauan-Gubat as low-value timber, highlighting a critical need for effective conservation communication to bridge the gap between ecological necessity and local perception.

The context of the study is situated within the broader global and national discourse on biodiversity conservation. Globally, the UN Convention on Biological Diversity and the IUCN have emphasized OECMs as a way to complement PAs. Nationally, the study is framed by the Philippine National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act and the need for urban development to incorporate buffer zones and ecological corridors. XenConservation serves as a unique "normative minority" case—a hobbyist-led, in-situ conservation effort on private land that operates alongside larger protected landscapes like the Mount Malindang Range.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative exploratory single case study design using criterion-i purposeful sampling. Data was gathered through a review of existing literature and interviews with key stakeholders, including representatives from the Municipal Planning and Development Office, the Municipal Environmental and Natural Resources Office, and the academe. The study utilized a theoretical framework that integrates governance characteristics—specifically governance authority (diversity), governance quality (voice/care), and governance vitality (management)—with the concept of "affordances" in communication.

The findings reveal that conservation communication in XenConservation operates through a "continuum of care" within a private governance model. This continuum is characterized by three distinct modes: convergent care, ancillary care, and diversified care. The study identifies a "transformative conservation communication" that emerges when private governance works in tandem with local governance. The research highlights that even small, private habitats can provide significant "ancillary care" by acting as seasonal wetlands and peatlands that support biodiversity and ecological connectivity. The results suggest that communication in this context is not merely about information dissemination but is a "revelatory" process that validates the role of private citizens in the broader conservation landscape.

In conclusion, the study theorizes a "constructivist and transformative worldview" for hobbyist-led conservation. It posits that the "tacit minority practice" of using communication affordances allows small habitat matrices to function as effective OECMs. The research concludes that XenConservation’s model of private, local-level governance provides a vital, albeit small-scale, contribution to the protection of threatened species and the maintenance of ancient ecosystems like peatlands and freshwater mangroves.

The implications of this research are both practical and theoretical. Practically, the study calls for strengthened protection policies and improved governance management for seasonal wetlands and peatlands in local conservation sites to safeguard agro-biodiversity. It suggests that local government units (LGUs) should better integrate these small, private conservation efforts into municipal urban development and zoning frameworks. Theoretically, the study contributes to the field of communication science by proposing an "ancillary view" of conservation communication, demonstrating how small-scale, private initiatives can fill critical gaps in national and global biodiversity targets. It encourages future research to explore how such "small habitat matrices" can be scaled or better supported to enhance ecological connectivity and climate resilience.

title: Prison Inmates' Experiences in the Gorgona Penal Colony, Italy: Towards a Theory of Communicative Support
abstract:
The study explored how inmates in the Gorgona penal colony engaged in communication for social support from their perspective and context. The Gorgona Agricultural Penal Colony is a men-only detention center with rehabilitative philosophies and strategies in helping prepare prisoners to successfully re-enter society. Guided by Charmaz’s Constructivist Grounded Theory, the study employed a qualitative methodology, using non-participant observations and in-depth semi-structured interviews among 20 inmates from September to November in 2021. 

The inmates’ interactions revealed four concepts of communicative support, namely: 1) communicating accountability and protection; 2) validating feelings, thoughts, or actions; 3) providing social companionship; and 4) expressing emotions. A theory of communicative support applicable outside the prison system is proposed with these concepts: 1) accountability; 2) validation; 3) social integration; and 4) self-expression.

half:
Catalina Doran conducted a phenomenological study in 2022 to explore the lived communication experiences of special education teachers at Miller County Schools. The research aimed to understand how these educators navigate communicative interactions within their professional environment, specifically focusing on processes occurring in self-contained and inclusive classes, individual education program meetings, and parent conferences. Using a qualitative approach, the researcher employed unstructured interviews with five respondents. The interview prompts were informed by direct observations of the teachers during classroom instruction and formal meetings with parents.

The findings reveal that cognizant-sensitive communication is a central element in the lived experiences of these teachers. This concept serves as an essential basis for all teaching, learning, and communication processes. When implemented, cognizant-sensitive communication allows for improved student achievement. The study indicates that these strategies facilitate appropriate approaches and place a high value on equality, which are necessary conditions for creating a full-fledged process of communication, teaching, and learning for students with special needs.

Regarding teacher-parent interactions, the study identified specific communicative dynamics that highlighted a significant need for understanding, the building of relationships, and the provision of truthful feedback. Beyond the classroom, the research identified several communication challenges categorized into five distinct themes: misunderstanding, behavioral issues, a lack of response, an unclear understanding of the special needs of the children, and a struggle to adapt to changes. In response to these challenges, the research outlines recommendations focusing on the necessity of awareness and sensitivity and the importance of prioritizing the interests of the students to mitigate difficulties in the educational environment.

The study culminates in the theorization of cognizant-sensitive communication. This theory describes a process in which the messenger delves deeply into the abilities, thoughts, interests, and limitations of the receiver. This deep engagement allows the messenger to better formulate, select, structure, and relay the message. The phenomenon of cognizant-sensitive communication was found to be common among the lived communication experiences of the special education teachers studied. Through this theoretical framework, the research emphasizes that effective communication in special education requires a profound awareness of the receiver's unique characteristics to ensure successful teaching and learning.

The inquiry suggests that cognizant-sensitive communication serves as an essential basis for all teaching, learning, and communication processes. When implemented, this type of communication allows for improved student achievement. The study indicates that cognizant-sensitive communication strategies facilitate appropriate approaches and place a high value on equality, which are necessary conditions for creating a full-fledged process of communication, teaching, and learning for students with special needs.

The study further identifies specific communicative dynamics regarding teacher-parent interactions. These interactions highlighted a significant need for understanding, the building of relationships, and the provision of truthful feedback. Beyond the classroom, the research identified several communication challenges that teachers face. These challenges are categorized into five distinct themes: misunderstanding, behavioral issues, a lack of response, an unclear understanding of the special needs of the children, and a struggle to adapt to changes.

In response to these identified challenges, the research outlines recommendations and solutions. These solutions focus on two primary themes: the necessity of awareness and sensitivity, and the importance of prioritizing the interests of the students. These elements are presented as ways to mitigate the difficulties encountered in the educational environment.

The study culminates in the theorization of cognizant-sensitive communication. This theory describes a process in which the messenger delves deeply into the abilities, thoughts, interests, and limitations of the receiver. This deep engagement allows the messenger to better formulate, select, structure, and relay the message. The phenomenon of cognizant-sensitive communication was found to be common among the lived communication experiences of the special education teachers studied. Through this theoretical framework, the research emphasizes that effective communication in special education requires a profound awareness of the receiver's unique characteristics to ensure successful teaching and learning.

title: Music As Communication: An Autoethnography On Rhetoric In Musical Composition And Performance
abstract:
I analyzed rhetoric through the confluence of performer-music-audience (ethos-logos-pathos) using performances comprising works of other artists and my original compositions viewed through autoethnographic lens. Data came from recollection and reflection on past musical performances alongside interviews with mentors, co-artists, and the audience. 

Results indicated that rhetoric patterns of meanings as energy forms are created and shared by an individual through entrainment, association, identity formation, feminism, silence, and spirituality in various connections formed consciously or unconsciously in communication practice as espoused in the proposed Constellation Rhetorical Theory. 

The concepts identified extend the persuasive character of classical rhetoric of Aristotle comprising ethos, logos, and pathos. In performer-music-audience analysis, individuals value meanings in communication as energy forms circulating in the environment that when absorbed, patterns develop and meanings seek new levels. When not absorbed, meanings remain suspended until they find themselves in consciousness and feelings of individuals. 

Because of the infinite power of music in communicating my emotions and thoughts through sound utterance or in music’s infinite power to elucidate musical nuances, these energy forms are everlasting themes guiding through my performance in unique ways. Indeed, musical performance is a perfect language in communicating profundities, in exhuming deep layers of meanings, in affecting others with clusters of understanding meanings or even beyond.

Using an autoethnographic approach grounded in his experiences as a pianist, composer, and teacher, Olobia argues that instrumental music conveys complex messages, emotions, and social identities without the need for lyrics.

The research provides a historical analysis of rhetoric in music, noting how Baroque music functions as dialogue through polyphony, Classical music utilizes tonality for emotional states, Romanticism focuses on individual expression, and 20th-century music employs experimentation and dissonance. The theory suggests musical meanings act as "energy forms" that circulate in the environment and develop into patterns of understanding when absorbed by the audience. The study concludes that music is a sophisticated communicative practice and a "perfect language" for communicating profundities, serving as a powerful tool for building both individual and collective consciousness.

In the dissertation *Music As Communication: An Autoethnography On Rhetoric In Musical Composition And Performance*, Leoncio Peralta Olobia explores the intersection of music and communication through the lens of classical rhetorical theory. The study seeks to understand how musical performance functions as a persuasive communicative phenomenon by analyzing the interrelationship between the performer, the music, and the audience.

**Problem and Context**
The research addresses a perceived gap in existing literature regarding the exhaustive analysis of the relationship between the performer, the musical structure, and the audience within a single framework. While music is often viewed as a mathematical or theoretical discipline, Olobia argues that it is a vital form of communication capable of imitating emotions and persuading listeners. The study specifically focuses on instrumental music—sound without lyrics—to examine how musical "grammar" and structure can convey complex messages, emotions, and social identities without the aid of spoken or sung words.

**Methodology**
Olobia employs an autoethnographic research approach, utilizing his own lived experiences as an international pianist, composer, and teacher to generate data. The methodology is deeply personal and interpretive, relying on the researcher's own voice to connect individual experience to broader cultural contexts. Data collection methods included personal narratives, recollections of past performances, interactive interviews with mentors, co-artists, and audience members, as well as the analysis of music sheets, photographs, videos, and journals. The study is limited by its subjective nature, as the findings are grounded in the author's personal insights rather than being intended for broad generalizability.

**Findings**
The findings are organized into three primary parts: the historical rhetoric of Western music, the rhetorical elements of performance, and the resulting communication theory.

In the historical analysis, Olobia examines how different eras utilized rhetoric. Baroque music is characterized as a musical dialogue through polyphony, where independent voices interact. Classical rhetoric is linked to tonality, where specific keys and chord patterns are used to evoke specific emotional states. Romantic rhetoric shifted toward subjectivity and individual expression, where music became a tool for personal transcendence. Finally, 20th-century rhetoric is characterized by democratization and experimentation, including the use of dissonance and the exploration of silence.

Regarding the elements of performance, the study applies Aristotle’s rhetorical triad:
*   **Ethos (The Performer):** The author explores how a performer’s credibility and character are manifested through physical gestures, facial expressions, and the technical mastery required to interpret a score.
*   **Logos (The Music):** The study identifies "logos" within the musical structure itself. Elements such as melody, harmony, rhythm, dynamics, texture, and form serve as the "logic" or "grammar" of the musical discourse.
*   **Pathos (The Audience):** The study examines how music elicits emotional responses and engagement from the audience, transforming them through the absorption of musical "energy."

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes with the proposal of the "Constellation Rhetorical Theory." This theory posits that musical communication occurs through the confluence of the performer, the music, and the audience. Olobia suggests that meanings in music function as "energy forms" that circulate in the environment. When these forms are absorbed by the audience, they develop into patterns of understanding; when they are not absorbed, they remain suspended until they enter an individual's consciousness.

The research highlights that musical performance is a "perfect language" for communicating profundities and exhuming deep layers of meaning. The implications of this study suggest that musical performance is not merely an aesthetic act but a sophisticated communicative practice. By understanding music through rhetoric, performers can become more sensitive to audience reactions, and composers can more intentionally use musical structures to achieve persuasive effects, whether through emotional connection, cultural preservation, or social protest. The study ultimately asserts that music is a powerful tool for building both individual and collective consciousness.

title: Discursive and Pedagogical (Counter)Imperatives in Textbook Tasks: A Critical Politico-Communicative Inquiry
abstract:
By employing the discourse of suspicion and critical discourse analysis, textbook tasks were systematically subjected to a process of examination that problematized the text (micro), the discursive practice (meso), and the broader social context (macro). Critical discourse analysis bears significant relevance when adopted as a theoretical and methodological bases in qualitative research considering its “multiplicity of analysis”, “plurality of approach”, and “multiplicity of conceptions” (Al Maghlouth 2017: 56, 57 & 69). 

Consistent with the value-commitment and transformative orientation of the critical tradition and drawing from (1) Mihailidis’ civic intentionality, (2) Langran and DeWitt’s critical place-based inquiry, and (3) McLaren, Crawford and Freire’s critical praxis, this study identified and mapped the discursive and pedagogical counter-imperatives that are embodied and interwoven in the media education textbook tasks. This communication inquiry also went on to analyze these counter-discourses and counter- pedagogies’ mutually reinforcing contribution in actualizing the potential of media and information literacy as a socially situated practice of engaged scholarship, communication activism, and social justice education. 

Through the discursive and pedagogical examination of the corpus of collated instructional materials, the researcher also sought to generate new and alternative perspectives in reimagining and redesigning media education textbook tasks that will deviate from the orthodox paradigms, processes, and practices.

The core objective is to identify how these tasks can be redesigned to serve media and information literacy as a transformative practice.

The study views media and information literacy as a socially situated practice linked to engaged scholarship, communication activism, and social justice education. The theoretical framework is grounded in Mihailidis’ concept of civic intentionality, Langran and DeWitt’s critical place-based inquiry, and the critical praxis advocated by McLaren, Crawford, and Freire. Methodologically, the author employs a multiplicity of analysis using critical discourse analysis and a "discourse of suspicion" to examine instructional materials across micro, meso, and macro levels.

Findings reveal that discursive and pedagogical counter-imperatives work in a mutually reinforcing manner, supporting the potential of media and information literacy to function as a vehicle for social justice and communication activism. The study concludes that textbook tasks are embedded in discursive struggles. By integrating alternative perspectives, educators can deviate from orthodox paradigms to foster socially responsible communicators, ensuring media education empowers students to engage in transformative social and communicative practices.

title: Weaving Rhizomes: An Onto Epistemological Approach in Communication Research Creation
abstract:
Anchored on Deleuze's Ontology of Immanence in Transcendental Empiricism, this postqualitative inquiry puts philosophical concepts to work in the doing of inquiry to produce knowledge differently. It adheres to ontoepistemology where the act of knowing is through performativity. Guided by Deleuze and Guattari's Rhizome concept, the dissertation is a living Rhizome: a thought in motion.

Letting thought guide the work, I experimented with how materialities in photography are constituted in photographing Cambodia's Angkor temples. Together with my co-photographers, I attuned to the molecular becomings of visuals while being entangled in the knowledge-creation process: its deterritorializations/reterritorializations from virtual to actual.

The inquiry was able to surface Photography as a surface event of becomings where subjectivity only emerges from the intra-action of humans and non-humans. Such surface event is a communication phenomenon when virtual meets the actual, a rhizomatic becoming. Responding to the Ontological turn, the inquiry generated a possible discourse on the Posthuman concept of communication as a force of relation that recognizes the dynamics of humans and matters that are always imbricated in a genesis of infinite becomings.

The experimental inquiry yielded an ontoepistemological research-creation approach in studying communication phenomena as becomings. Called Weaving Rhizomes, this research-creation approach disrupts the colonial and stabilizing methods in research, by acknowledging the dynamic relations of humans and non-humans as always imbricated in the doing-making of research. As an approach to speculative inquiry, Weaving Rhizomes does not prescribe any method rather, allows experimentation.

This dissertation contributed widely to debates on photography and communication as becomings in the Ontological turn. It also added to the growing field of visual research methods foregrounding visuals as active agencies in research-creation, an entangled performativity. The inquiry experimented with mobile camera as prosthetics of the body and was able to develop Luminous entanglement, a way of sensing visual data as rhizome that disrupts anthropocentric gaze in analyzing data. Remaining consistent with the Ontology of Immanence, this dissertation was written as a rhizome, data are woven as rhizomes and maps a probable future approach in research-creation.

title: Pandemic Narrative: Foucauldian Discourse Analysis of Messages Communication the Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions as COVID-19 Mitigation Strategies
abstract: Built on the Foucauldian Discourse Analysis' (FDA) theoretical-methodological assumptions, and Jager & Maier's methodological toolbox on discourse, the study systematically illustrates and accounts the discursive formations, socio-historical events and socio-cultural practices that constitutes Non pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) communicated on social media from March 25 to June 25 2020 which covers the implementation of Republic Act No. 11469 also known as "Bayanihan to Heal as One Act [Bayanihan refers to a spirit of civic unity and cooperation among Filipinos] in the country. The collective and individual narratives on Non-pharmaceutical interventions [NPIs] (Stay-a-home, handwashing, social distancing and wearing of masks) found in the Department of Health Facebook page on social media to mitigate the risks of infection and transmission of COVID-19 raise the prevailing discourse and assertions that non-pharmaceutical interventions are sets of health protective behaviors and public health standards for prevention, detection, and treatment of COVID-19. Individual willingness to comply, support and cooperate largely driven by concern, empathy, frustration, worries, hopelessness, disappointment, and anger are constructed which are provoked by uncertainties, ongoing social, political, historical, and cultural realities and social conditions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic health crisis.

title: Communicative Construction of Teacher Identity: A Phenomenological Study of Being a Non-Native English-Speaking Teacher in the United States
abstract:
Addressing the need of non-native English-speaking teachers (NNESTs) to construct an identity as legitimate professionals in the English language teaching arena, this study focuses on the importance of dialogues in creating a more empowering conceptualizations of self. Teacher identity construction has been studied under the various traditions of communication theory; however, this study explored identity construction by situating this to Phenomenological Tradition wherein the concept of "otherness" or discourses between self and others is applied.

This is a qualitative study that used the methodologies of autoethnography and narrative inquiry. In this study, the researcher used dialogic reflection as a NNEST teaching native English-speaking students in the United States. The autoethnographic data were collected and analyzed to answer the research questions: (1) What is my view of English language teaching as a non-native English-speaking teacher teaching native English-speaking students? and (2) How does my view of English language teaching, through my discourses and interactions with my native English-speaking students, parents, and colleagues, shape my professional identity as an English teacher?

Dialogues were used to generate rich, detailed views of language teaching. Data analysis from narrative dialogues illuminated five global themes: language teaching (1) requires extra effort; (2) needs accountability; (3) entails engagement and practicality; (4) based on teachers' personal qualities; and (5) requires knowledge, skills, and professionalism. These views shape the researcher's identity as a (1) supporter; (2) facilitator; and (3) motivator. The findings of the study suggest that dialogues are a strong motivational factor for the construction of teacher identity, and that they can be used to explore personal experiences and be connected to wider cultural and social understandings of identity formation.

title: Research and Development Scientists’ Construction of Working Online: A Phenomenological Study of Virtual Communication During the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: Applying transcendental phenomenology, I explored my experience working in a Research and Development organization and made sense of how scientists could carry out a laboratory-based job yet working from home. Through zoom interviews, the lived experience of Research and Development scientists was reconstructed to discover how working from home is reflected in communication. Making sense of the lived experience of R&D scientists, the concept of communication resiliency emerged. My inquiry revealed that communication resiliency in R&D organizations showed the inclination to adopt new methods of communicating. Resilient communication strategy during the pandemic allows to perceive threats, maintain an acceptable level of operation and to arrive at decisions needed by the R&D scientists through digital technology that enabled the teams to achieve their goals. R&D scientists showcased the boldness and courage to work through obstacles, explore, and learn by imbibing the reality of the new approach to move forward and reach expected outcomes through virtual communication. R&D scientists needed to adapt according to the changing environment regardless of the limitations to ensure that research and development continuously serve its functions. Hence, communication resiliency refers to the collective and assertive efforts to continuously fulfil task, ability to stay connected to other people delivering a common goal and create new opportunities for flexibility and productivity despite the challenges of communicating online.

title: Big Data as Climate Change, Intervention: A Policy Delphi study on data analytics maturity within the climate action system
abstract:
The effects of climate change are being felt now and continues to be one of the most urgent issues facing the world particularly for developing nations such as the Philippines. Despite the significant measures being taken to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, some degree of climate change will remain and cause considerable economic, social, and environmental impacts. Individuals, communities, and organizations need to take action to prepare for and adjust to the current effects cf climate change as well as the predicted impacts in the future. Climate change adaptation is an emerging area of study. Adaptation is essential to alleviate the inevitable damages brought about by climate change. Data analytics can provide organizations the ability to anticipate a range of potential climate conditions, enabling them to take action before the worst impacts happen. 

This research aimed to contribute to the development of an analytics maturity framework relevant to development programs and institutions focused on climate change. This demands an understanding of the epistemological challenges presented by big data and the existing knowledge in the area of data and analytics. A Policy Delphi was organized involving experts from the academe, data analytics and climate sectors comprising three Delphi rounds. The Delphi method was used to construct consensus views and forecasts from the panel of experts in an iterative manner which enabled the identification of important dimensions of a data-driven climate action ecosystem. This research adopted the cybernetics stance that conceptualizes big data as a complex system where the interacting elements, whether living or nonliving, macro or micro, influence one another and are able to function, and why they often malfunction. The analytics maturity framework discussed in this dissertation could potentially help uncover important variables, patterns, challenges, and opportunities in the data and analytics processes of climate communities which could create and promote an ecosystem that enables insight and action.

The dissertation "Big Data as Climate Change Intervention: A Policy Delphi Study on Data Analytics Maturity Within the Climate Action Ecosystem" by Anna Liza Calleja Po explores the intersection of big data analytics and climate change adaptation. The study addresses the urgent need for development programs and institutions to move beyond traditional data collection methods, such as household surveys and census data, which may be too slow to address the rapid environmental changes caused by climate change.

**Problem and Context**
The research is situated in the context of the escalating climate crisis, specifically focusing on the vulnerability of developing nations like the Philippines. While global efforts like the Paris Agreement aim to mitigate emissions, the inevitable impacts of climate change—such as rising sea levels and extreme weather events—require robust adaptation strategies. The author identifies a significant knowledge gap: while big data offers the potential to provide real-time insights and predictive modeling to protect vulnerable populations, many organizations struggle to define the scope of their analytics programs or create roadmaps to increase the value derived from their datasets. There is a critical need to understand the "maturity" of data analytics within the climate action ecosystem to ensure that data can be effectively transformed into actionable insights.

**Methodology**
The study employs a Policy Delphi method to construct consensus views and forecasts regarding data analytics maturity. This iterative process involved three rounds of engagement with a panel of experts drawn from three specific sectors: the academe, data analytics specialists, and climate scientists/professionals. The research adopts a cybernetics stance, viewing big data as a complex system where interacting elements—whether living or nonliving, macro or micro—influence one another. This systems perspective allows the researcher to analyze how various components of the climate action ecosystem function or malfunction. The methodology aimed to identify the dimensions and sub-dimensions of an analytics maturity framework specifically tailored to the unique requirements of climate change programs.

**Findings**
The findings are organized by the perspectives of the different expert sectors involved in the Delphi process. The research identifies the current state of data and analytics within the climate community along an analytics maturity continuum. Through the iterative rounds, the study identified key dimensions and sub-dimensions necessary for a robust analytics ecosystem. The experts highlighted various challenges and obstacles that currently hamper progression along the maturity continuum. These challenges include the difficulty of defining the scope of analytics programs and the technical and organizational hurdles in managing the volume, variety, velocity, veracity, and value of big data. The results suggest that as an organization's analytics program matures, its architecture must evolve to include more sophisticated tools, specialized skills, and integrated processes to support data-driven decision-making.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The dissertation concludes with the development of a conceptual framework designed to help development institutions elevate their level of data and analytics maturity. This framework is intended to help uncover important variables, patterns, and opportunities within the data processes of climate communities. By moving toward an optimized analytics ecosystem, organizations can better anticipate potential climate conditions and take preemptive action before the most severe impacts occur.

The implications of this research are significant for both policy and practice. For climate action organizations, the study provides a roadmap for transitioning from traditional, reactive data methods to proactive, predictive analytics. By understanding their position on the maturity continuum, institutions can better allocate resources toward the necessary people, processes, and technologies. Ultimately, the research contributes to the broader body of knowledge by bridging the gap between big data solutions and climate change intervention, promoting an ecosystem that enables insight and impactful action for environmental and socioeconomic sustainability.

title: Persuasive Communication in the Digital Milieu: A Rhetorical Anaylsis of Vlogging Entries of a Vegan Advocate
abstract:
The study assumes vlogging as a rhetorical act to contribute to the understanding of the nature of persuasive communication in the digital milieu.

The study is framed within the Rhetorical Tradition of Communication Theory that theorizes communication as a practical art of discourse and problematizes it as a social exigency requiring collective deliberation and judgment (Craig, 1999). With modern technology and mobility, we communicate in a dynamic and intricate system of personal and professional relationships, and each of us is linked to all others by fewer degrees of separation than ever before. These technological advancements have revolutionized how persuasion is performed and accomplished. The evolution of media to social media become the fulcrum that links and influences the modern world (Baym, 2015). Do the techniques and functions of persuasion change as technology changes?

By employing rhetorical analysis of vlogging entries of a vegan advocate, the study attempted to answer the following research questions: (1) What rhetorical strategies are used by a YouTube vlogger in communicating veganism as an advocacy? And (2) how do these rhetorical strategies accomplish the goal of advocating veganism through YouTube? Using netnography, a digital ethnographic research method, online data collection, observation, and immersion were employed to analyze the social interactional dynamics of a vlogosphere.

With veganism having a limited place for discussion anywhere except in social media platforms, the study particularly examined the vegan advocate Ed Winters’ YouTube channel. From the selected YouTube vlog, three vlogging rhetorical acts emerged which can be applied to all forms of advocacy in the digital sphere. The vlogger made use of: 1) misconception about the advocacy and/or its opposition; 2) morality about the advocacy and/or its opposition, and 3) move to action.

The rhetorical acts accomplish the goal of communicating an advocacy which is the required collective deliberation and judgment through YouTube by first addressing a misconception about the advocacy and/ or its opposition. The rhetor or the vlogger introduced and explained it as one of the common reasons people fail to move to action or commit to advocacy. The rhetorical act of morality about the advocacy and/or its opposition allows the viewers to be informed of the moral issues and to question the status quo. Lastly, the rhetorical act of moving to action attempts to influence the viewers to commit to the advocacy presented by the vlogger that represents the collective deliberation and judgment.

These three rhetorical acts serve as a powerful instrument for the advancement of any advocacy as they illustrate how an advocate constructs the discourse to understand and explain that the situation or issue is important enough to speak rhetorically about it through a YouTube vlog to accomplish collective deliberation in any persuasive situation in the digital age.

The research theorizes that advocacy vlogging is a new genre that creates a shared culture and community, participating in a sensemaking process that restructures the identities and perspectives of both the creator and the audience.

Buera investigates how persuasion functions within the digital landscape, specifically through the medium of YouTube vlogging. The study seeks to understand the rhetorical strategies employed by digital advocates and how these strategies facilitate the achievement of their communicative goals.

The research problem is centered on the evolving nature of persuasion in the digital age. As technology advances, the traditional boundaries of communication are shifting, and social media platforms like YouTube have become significant agents of persuasion rather than mere channels for message delivery. The author notes that while classical rhetoric provides a foundation for understanding discourse, there is a need to explore how these principles manifest in the "viogosphere"—the digital community of vloggers and viewers. Specifically, the study addresses the challenge of communicating veganism, an advocacy that often faces social constraints and requires collective deliberation to drive social change.

The context of the study is the digital milieu, characterized by high connectivity and the rise of social media as a fulcrum for global influence. The researcher focuses on the YouTube channel of Earthling Ed, a prominent vegan advocate, as the primary subject. The study is framed within the Rhetorical Tradition of Communication Theory, which views communication as a practical art of discourse and a social exigency requiring collective deliberation and judgment. The researcher posits that vlogging serves as a unique rhetorical act that allows individuals to address social problems and propose changes in the material and social environment.

To address the research questions, the author employs a qualitative methodology combining netnography and rhetorical analysis. Netnography, a digital ethnographic method, was used to observe and immerse the researcher in the social interactional dynamics of the YouTube community. This allowed for an understanding of the "viogosphere" from an emic perspective. The rhetorical analysis focused on the structural and discursive elements of the selected vlogs, utilizing an expanded rhetorical situation framework that considers the rhetor, the medium, the audience, the rhetoric, and the exigence.

First, the viogger addresses misconceptions regarding the advocacy or its opposition, which serves to remove barriers that prevent people from committing to the cause. Second, the viogger employs morality, presenting the moral implications of the issue to inform viewers and encourage them to question the status quo. Third, the viogger utilizes a "move to action," which attempts to influence viewers to commit to the advocacy, thereby facilitating the collective deliberation and judgment necessary for social change. These acts demonstrate how a vlogger constructs discourse to establish the importance of an issue and move an audience from mere understanding to active participation.

The study concludes that vlogging is a powerful and complex rhetorical act that functions as a persuasive agent in the digital age. It is characterized as being complex, continuous, and contextual. The research theorizes that advocacy vlogging is a new genre that allows for the creation of a shared culture and a sense of community that transcends geographic boundaries. The findings suggest that vlogging does not just transmit information but actively participates in the sensemaking process, helping to restructure the identities and perspectives of both the creator and the audience.

title: Communication and Education: Reflexive Dialogue Through Experiencing Theater as Play
abstract:
With communication and education being interwoven, this study sought to generate an abstract theoretical understanding of the communication processes emerging from an educational experience. Specifically, this constructivist grounded theory was guided by the question "How do participants experience the Bahay-bahayan theater as play?" in the context of the immersive play "Pailah: Ugat ng Lipi." Immersing in the performance space together with the research participants, and doing successive levels of comparative analysis, the following social processes emerged pagpapasigla (activating), pagtatauli (reacting), pagmamasid (observing), paggaya (imitating), pagsubok (testing), paglubog (immersing), pagtugon (responding), pagsasakatawan (embodying), pag-angkin (owning), and pagpapadayon (lingering). These processes are mutually supportive and constitutive. It was revealed that meaning-making is very much influenced by, and in turn, influences cultural contexts and behaviours, as the participants go back and forth these processes.

The Wari at Yari: Proseso ng Pakikipag-dayalogo (Discern and Design: Process of Reflexive Dialogue) is therefore forwarded as a middle range theory describing creative processes of making sense of communication contexts and transforming these through playing, replaying, and re-playing possibilities, actions, and reflections. Permeating the entire play experience are pakikiramdam (sensing) and pagbabanyuhay (transforming). How each process is placed in the infinity model represents the processual and intuitive nature of theater as play. 

The model has important implications for the design of learning experiences anchored not only on outcomes, but also on playful dialogic interactions. Further research may look into the experiences of the audience-players since this study privileged the voices of the actor-players.

title: The Liberating Potential of Social Media in the Philippine Context
abstract: This qualitative study on the liberating potential of social media in the Philippines used the Grounded Theory design which utilized information from the ground to come up with a developing theory that describes an evolving phenomenon involving the Filipino's way of navigating the sphere of virtual communication. The findings in this study were anchored on a well represented cross section of the population in terms of generation, gender, social status and experiences. It utilized the linear snowball sampling which resulted in 10 participants who contributed in the making of meaning. The research questions revolved around social media and the shape of this phenomenon in the Philippine context and whether it indeed enable individuals and communities to overcome their sense of powerlessness and lack of influence, take advantage of the blurring of borders and thus achieve personal and social liberation. The resulting theory is the Theory of Virtual Deliverance which posits that social media has become a contemporary liberating tool that is potentially effective in addressing social ills in acceptable ways that somehow manage to circumvent existing structures, specifically in a community like the Philippines where they tend to be perceived as unequal, discriminatory and oppressive. Participant accounts support that the Filipino's notion of liberation is the very definition of deliverance mentioned as 'kaluwasan,' which is the action of being rescued and set free in a way that involves faith and an effort to overcome fate. The virtual space that social media offers has somehow provided a redefined leverage not only to those with means but especially to those who have very little leverage in their actual physical space.

Calderon-Dionzon’s dissertation, "The Liberating Potential of Social Media in the Philippine Context," investigates whether digital communication serves as a tool for emancipation within the Philippines. The study explores the tension between social media's capacity for empowerment and its potential for manipulation, such as reinforcing consumerism and social conformity. Using a qualitative design grounded in Strausslan Grounded Theory, the researcher conducted remote "Active Interviews" with ten participants representing diverse demographics during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The findings are categorized into five core hypotheses. Social media acts as a voice for the voiceless, allowing marginalized sectors to amplify concerns. It serves as an enabler for pursuing passions, social struggles, and community engagement. It functions as a new human media for education, organization, and identity expression. It offers economic liberty through digital entrepreneurship. Finally, the study identifies social media as a double-edged tool susceptible to misinformation, political manipulation, and the creation of false needs.

The researcher proposes the "Theory of Virtual Deliverance," suggesting social media can address social ills by bypassing oppressive structures, providing leverage to those with little influence in physical reality. The study concludes that liberating potential depends on usage. To achieve true liberation, users must transition from "thoughtlessness" to "mindfulness," distinguishing authentic needs from neoliberal consumerism and adopting a "new sensibility" that prioritizes authentic expression and collective responsibility.
one:
Jade Snow C. Calderon-Dionzon’s dissertation, "The Liberating Potential of Social Media in the Philippine Context," investigates whether digital communication serves as a tool for emancipation within the specific socio-cultural landscape of the Philippines. Given the country's high social media usage, the study explores the tension between the technology's capacity for empowerment and its potential for manipulation, specifically the risk of reinforcing consumerism and social conformity. The research seeks to determine if social media functions as a techno-social system capable of circumventing oppressive physical structures to provide a platform for human agency and social reform.

The study utilized a qualitative research design grounded in Strausslan Grounded Theory, allowing themes to emerge from participants' lived experiences. Data was collected via remote "Active Interviews" during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using linear snowball sampling, the researcher interviewed ten participants representing various genders, generations, and social statuses. Data analysis involved constant comparative analysis through open, axial, and selective coding until theoretical saturation was reached.

The findings are categorized into five core hypotheses. First, social media acts as a voice for the voiceless, allowing marginalized sectors to amplify concerns and expose truths suppressed by traditional media. Second, it serves as an effective enabler for pursuing passions, social struggles, and community engagement. Third, it functions as a new human media that facilitates education, organization, and the expression of identity beyond physical limitations. Fourth, it offers economic liberty through digital entrepreneurship and new livelihood avenues. Finally, the study identifies social media as a double-edged tool, noting its susceptibility to misinformation, political manipulation, and the creation of false needs.

The researcher proposes the "Theory of Virtual Deliverance" to synthesize these findings. This theory suggests that social media is a contemporary tool that can address social ills by bypassing oppressive structures. In the Philippine context, this is linked to the concept of *walay kasalatan*, or deliverance, providing leverage to those with little influence in physical reality.

The study concludes that the liberating potential of social media is not inherent to the technology but depends on how it is used. The dissertation "The Liberating Potential of Social Media in the Philippine Context" by Jade Snow C. Calderon-Dionzon explores the transformative power of digital communication within the specific socio-cultural landscape of the Philippines. The study investigates whether social media serves as a tool for emancipation, allowing individuals and communities to overcome powerlessness and achieve personal and social liberation.

**Problem and Context**
The research is situated in a context where the Philippines is recognized as a global leader in social media usage, with citizens spending significant daily time on platforms like Facebook. While social media offers unprecedented connectivity, the author notes a tension between its potential for empowerment and its capacity for manipulation. Drawing on critical theories from Marx, Marcuse, and Fuchs, the study addresses the risk of "one-dimensional" existence, where digital spaces might merely reinforce consumerism, false needs, and social conformity. The central problem is determining if social media in the Philippines functions as a "techno-social system" that can circumvent oppressive or unequal physical structures to provide a platform for genuine human agency and social reform.

**Methodology**
The study employs a qualitative research design using Strausslan Grounded Theory. This approach was chosen to allow themes and theories to emerge directly from the participants' lived experiences rather than being forced into preconceived categories. Data collection was conducted through online research interviews using an "Active Interview" approach, which treats participants as active collaborators in the meaning-making process. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, these interviews were conducted remotely. The researcher utilized linear snowball sampling to select ten participants representing a cross-section of the population in terms of gender, generation, and social status. Data analysis followed a rigorous process of constant comparative analysis, moving through open, axial, and selective coding to reach theoretical saturation.

**Findings**
The findings are organized into five core hypotheses that describe the multifaceted nature of social media in the Philippines:

First, social media acts as a **Voice for the Voiceless**. It provides a platform for open discourse and real-time information, allowing marginalized sectors to scale borders, amplify their concerns, and expose truths that might otherwise be suppressed in traditional media.

Second, it serves as an **Effective Enabler**. The digital space facilitates the pursuit of passions, social struggles, and community engagement. It acts as a tool for outreach, agitation, and defense, empowering individuals toward personal enlightenment and social emancipation.

Third, the study identifies social media as a **New Human Media**. It functions as a tool for education, organization, and the promotion of alternative worldviews. It creates a sense of international fellowship and provides a medium for expressing identity and finding community beyond physical limitations.

Fourth, social media offers **Economic Liberty**. It provides new avenues for livelihood, such as digital entrepreneurship, vlogging, and virtual transactions. This facilitates personal freedom by offering more options for income, mobility, and time management.

Finally, the study concludes that social media is a **Double-Edged Tool**. While it has liberating potential, it is equally susceptible to being used for the colonization of culture, misinformation, political manipulation, and the creation of "false needs" that perpetuate social inequality.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The researcher proposes the "Theory of Virtual Deliverance" (or Virtual Liberation) to synthesize these findings. This theory posits that social media is a contemporary liberating tool that can effectively address social ills by circumventing existing, often oppressive, social structures. In the Philippine context, this liberation is described through the concept of *walay kasalatan* (deliverance)—a process of being rescued or set free through effort and faith. The virtual space provides a redefined leverage for those who possess little influence in their physical reality.

The implications of this study suggest that the liberating potential of social media is not inherent to the technology itself but depends on how it is wielded. To achieve true liberation, users must move from "thoughtlessness" to "mindfulness," critically distinguishing between true needs and the false needs imposed by neoliberal consumerism. The study implies that for social media to fulfill its role as a tool for social reform and personal freedom, there must be a shift toward a "new sensibility" that prioritizes authentic expression and collective responsibility over mere digital conformity and superficial engagement.

title: Social Inclusion and the Use of Inset Sign Language During the 2019 Philippine State of the Nation Address
abstract: Guided by Radcliffe-Brown's (1881-1955) Structural Functionalism Theory, this phenomenological study explored how inset sign language was used for social inclusion during the delivery of the 2019 Philippine State of the Nation Address (SONA) on GMA Network, Inc. Through in-depth interviews with eight participants, (four deaf and four sign language interpreters (S-L-Is)), their lived experience was analyzed. Four major themes emerged: exposure and familiarization to the deaf community culture which is the Filipino Sign Language (F-S-L); adjustment of the TV inset size for deaf visual signs recognition and understanding; validation of TV insets interpreting with a deaf consultant; accessibility to communication through clear policy and guidelines of TV inset interpreting. The study concludes that while sign language interpreters used F-S-L, social inclusion could only be invoked by adjusting the size of the TV inset, as for the inset sign language system, the visuals signs of the S-L-Is which includes the hand gestures and facial expressions matters. S-L-Is also need to be exposed and familiar with the deaf community culture to increase their knowledge on the signs that considers the schooled and non-schooled deaf. As policy and guidelines, TV networks should consider adjusting the size of the TV inset, involve the deaf as a consultant to validate the signing and assuring the access to communication of the deaf to make them socially included. Structurally, inset sign language implementation must have a model to follow to make it functional.

title: Schematizing and Theorizing the Click Between Institution and Communication
abstract: This study examined how instruction (teaching-learning) and communication are linked using Reflective Research Methodology that involved schematizing, theorizing, validating schemas, or mental models guided by a Dual Ladder of Inference Framework. This study elucidated instruction (teaching-learning process), identified communication and learning theories, and highlighted the key indicators that link instruction and communication in an intertwined fashion. As gleaned from the Literature review, the types of Instructional Communication studies have remained the same for decades. There is a need for a unified view of Instructional Communication and the need to advance its theory and model. There is a prevailing view of communication as a vital part of instruction, but some scholarly works view instruction as communication. Instruction and communication are two different terms. However, under rigorous scrutiny, instruction visibly occurs as communication that results in learning. This study involved schematizing, theorizing, validating schemas or mental models guided by a Dual Ladder of Inference Framework within its Reflective Research Methodology. This study presents a methodological approach to theory and model building that hinges on the Ladder of Inference, a Systems Thinking approach that requires iterative research validation of Mental Models or schemas, beliefs, and assumptions. This study has ontological and epistemological values to the field of Instructional Communication. As part of its major outcomes, this study suggests that Instructional Communication must be viewed from its planning phase (design) to its implementation phase, assessments, and evaluation phase. The alignment of all instructional elements is key in evaluating the impacts and effectiveness of instructional communication. This study offers insights valuable to face-to-face (on-site) and online (synchronous or asynchronous) instruction. Sparked by the schema, Instruction Communication, this study offers an enhanced general model of Instructional Communication, Instruction = Communication → Learning. In addition, an enhanced theory, definition, and a holistic Instructional Communication Model are proposed.

Myrene Agustin Magabo’s dissertation, "Schematizing and Theorizing the Link Between Instruction and Communication," explores the fundamental relationship between instruction and communication, proposing that instruction is a specialized, highly purposeful form of communication. The research seeks to bridge the gap between instructional design and communication theory by developing a conceptual framework that illustrates how instructional processes function through communicative dynamics to achieve learning outcomes.

Adopting a multidisciplinary perspective rooted in communication and education, the study utilizes a theoretical and conceptual development approach. By synthesizing existing theories such as Berlo’s communication theory, Argyris’ Ladder of Inference, and Bloom’s Taxonomy, the author employs a systems approach to construct new models.

The findings are presented through interconnected schemas, most notably the conceptualization of "Instruction = Communication + Learning." The research introduces an "Instructional Communication Model: A Systems Approach," a "dual ladder of inference," and a "wheel of theory alignment model." The study demonstrates that instruction occurs within communicative dynamics and identifies a "point of convergence" where instruction and communication meet to facilitate learning. Key findings suggest that learning occurs at various levels of communication, the instructional design process is cyclical, and instruction is a non-linear process linking communication styles to instructional styles. Ultimately, the study concludes that instruction and communication are inextricably linked, suggesting that effective instructional design requires a deep understanding of communicative competence.

title: Exploring Education Communicationally: A Symbolic Interaction Study of Indigenous People Learners
abstract:
The main objective of this study was to explore the meanings of education from how it was communicated by the indigenous people through the lens of symbolic interactionism.

Mead explained that “our thoughts, self-concept, and the wider community we live in are created through communication—symbolic interaction” (Griffin, 2012). Herbert Blumer, the student of Mead, adapted this concept. For Blumer: Meaning arises out of the social interaction that people have with each other. In other words, meaning is not inherent in objects; it’s not pre-existent in a state of nature. Meaning is negotiated through the use of language —hence the term symbolic interactionism (Griffin, 2012). More than just knowing the views of the IPs about education, the study also explored possible refinement on the existing policies that involve the IPs.

As a qualitative type of research, the study utilized narrative approach or pakikipagkuwentuhan (exchanging stories) for the data gathering. Guide questions were used to organize easily the data gathered. The narratives of the IPs were audio recorded and transcribed, and emerging themes were derived. Four female indigenous people served as the research participants. Three were already married and one was still single when the study was conducted. They were selected because they were among the IPs in their community who have resumed their studies after more than ten years of hiatus. They were enrolled in a home-based education program which provided them with the chance to be part of a formal schooling again. Three of the IPs identified themselves as Dumagats and one as a Remontado which implicates that one’s identity is determined by personal choice. Prior to being part of the home- based program, all of them had only reached first year high school due to reasons like lack of financial support, distance of school from their home, and discrimination.

Based on the results of the study, the following communication patterns were observed:

First, when the indigenous people learners communicate education as a sense of self- fulfillment, they are attributing it to value of education, development of personality, improvement of individual capabilities, good traits and qualities, and obtained academic support. It is interpreted as their cherished desire to finish their studies in order for them to reach their personal goals in life and to develop their self-confidence, which can be considered as an off shoot of the discrimination they experienced when they were still part of the formal school system.

Second, the IPs also communicate education as a way to give family support, and they are attributing it to strong family ties, passive interactions, motivation, socio-economic conditions, and discipline. It is interpreted as their uplifted hope to improve the living condition of their family and to give in return to their parents.

Finally, when they are communicating education to become relevant to their community, they are attributing it to being involve in the community and to aspire for the development of their community. It is interpreted that for the IPs, education can be their way to support the needs of their community.

The study further explained that symbolic interactionism as theoretical framework can be used to locate how communication between individuals and their significant others can be interpreted.

Nataño investigates how indigenous people (IP) learners construct the meaning of education through social interaction. The research context is rooted in the systemic barriers faced by indigenous communities in the Philippines, specifically in Tanay, Rizal. The author notes that while education is a fundamental right, IPs often lack equal access due to the remoteness of ancestral domains, poverty, the high cost of schooling, and social discrimination. The data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed to derive emerging themes regarding their communication patterns and views on education.

The findings reveal three primary themes regarding how IP learners communicate the meaning of education through their symbolic interactions:

First, education is communicated as a sense of self-fulfillment. Through interactions with others, learners attribute education to the development of personality, the improvement of individual capabilities, and the acquisition of academic support. This serves as a way for them to build self-confidence and achieve personal goals, acting as a psychological response to the discrimination they previously experienced within the formal school system.

Second, education is communicated as a way to provide family support. The narratives highlight that learners view education through the lens of strong family ties and socio-economic necessity. Third, education is communicated as a means of becoming relevant to the community. The participants expressed that education is a tool to become active members of their society and to contribute to the overall development of their indigenous communities.

For community project implementers, the findings provide guidance on how to design programs that align with the actual motivations and social realities of IP learners. For policymakers, the study suggests the need for refinements in existing policies to ensure that educational provisions are culturally and linguistically appropriate, thereby supporting the empowerment of indigenous groups. title: A Physician’s Auto-Hermeneutics of Medical Praxis: Curating Meanings and Voice Themes Using Dialogical Prism
abstract: This study is an auto hermeneutic phenomenological inquiry on the lived experience of medical praxis of 40 years of a family medicine specialist. It utilized the\ dialogical lens to extricate the essential meanings she finds most defined in the three main dialogical landscapes of clinical, educational, and societal (administrative/advocative) she has traversed. The dialogical vertical (spiritual) and horizontal (self, others both, in actual and virtual platforms) scaffoldings were elucidated through a structured methodology of collecting self narratives, integrating, and interpreting. The resulting prism, which may be universally applied to any professional praxis, consists of curated meaning typologies of trust-building, nurturing, redeeming, stewarding, and inspiring. These typologies are illustrated by conversational snippets and were juxtaposed with pre-existing theories and models including most upheld Filipino cultural values. The congruence of her analyzed vertical and horizontal scaffoldings along these typologies was also a major explication of this work Implications to professional praxis, life-long learning, and qualitative research were drawn. A reflection on the process of doing (auto) hermeneutic phenomenology as either/both personal and scholarly undertaking informs (and hopefully inspires) readers to do the same.
