The thesis titled "Nurse-Patient Interaction and Rehospitalization Among Older Persons with Heart Failure in a Skilled Nursing Facility in New York, USA" by Amil Kusain Tan Jr. investigates the impact of a Nurse-led Interdisciplinary Heart Failure Team Program (NLI-HFTP) on two specific outcomes: the quality of nurse-patient interaction (NPI) and the 30-day rehospitalization rate among older adults living in a skilled nursing facility (SNF).

**Problem and Context**
The study addresses a significant gap in healthcare literature regarding the prevalence and management of heart failure (HF) specifically within skilled nursing facilities. While heart failure is a leading cause of hospital readmission, the researcher notes that most interdisciplinary care studies focus on acute care settings rather than long-term care environments. Furthermore, the researcher identified a specific clinical problem at an affiliated SNF in New York, where the annual average 30-day rehospitalization rate was 26%, with some months reaching as high as 38%—significantly exceeding the national average of 18%. The study seeks to determine if a nurse-led, interdisciplinary approach can improve patient-centered interactions and reduce these avoidable hospitalizations.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a post-test one-group, descriptive, and correlational research design. The study was conducted at a 520-bed SNF in Manhattan, New York. The sample consisted of 46 participants who met specific inclusion criteria: they were aged 65 or older, cognitively intact (scoring between 13 and 15 on the Brief Interview for Mental Status), had a diagnosis of heart failure, were able to provide informed consent, and were proficient in English.

The independent variable was the NLI-HFTP, an intervention where a registered nurse (RN) and an advanced practice nurse (APN) lead a team—including dietitians, social workers, and cardiologists—to conduct weekly visits. These visits focused on clinical assessments, patient education, and goal setting. The dependent variables were measured using the Nurse-Patient Interaction Scale (NPIS), a 14-item Likert-scale tool, and the 30-day rehospitalization rate, a standardized metric used by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). Data were analyzed using non-parametric statistical techniques to account for the small sample size.

**Findings**
The demographic and clinical profile of the participants revealed a group primarily composed of "young-old" adults (ages 65–74) who were African American, non-Hispanic women. Clinically, the majority had a primary diagnosis of heart failure that was not unspecified (70%), most were in NYHA Class I (61%), and 46% had heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Common comorbidities included hypertension (89%), coronary heart disease (72%), and arrhythmia (46%).

Regarding the primary outcomes, the study found a high level of nurse-patient interaction, with a median score of 8.4 on a 10-point scale. Participants reported that interactions with nurses made them feel good, and they specifically valued when nurses asked how they were doing. In terms of clinical outcomes, the study found a significant decrease in the 30-day rehospitalization rate following the implementation of the NLI-HFTP. However, correlational analysis showed no significant association between the level of nurse-patient interaction and the 30-day rehospitalization rate. A significant and very strong association was found between the NYHA functional classification and the 30-day rehospitalization rate.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The researcher concludes that the findings align with Duffy and Hoskins' Quality Caring Model, which posits that caring relationships are linked to positive health outcomes through professional encounters. The study demonstrates that the NLI-HFTP is a feasible and effective intervention for SNFs to reduce 30-day rehospitalization rates and manage heart failure exacerbations. The high level of NPI reported suggests that the nurse-led model successfully fosters a caring environment.

The implications of this study are multifaceted. For nursing practice, it provides evidence that nurse-led programs can improve patient satisfaction and reduce readmissions through daily interactions, such as weight monitoring and medication education. For nursing administration, it suggests that a nurse-caring model can serve as an effective organizational framework for interdisciplinary care. For nursing education, the study highlights the vital role of nurses in providing specialized patient education for chronic conditions. Finally, for nursing research, the study contributes to the empirical evaluation of middle-range nursing theories in a long-term care setting.

title: Health Literacy and Health Promoting Behaviors Among Adults at Risk for Diabetes in A Rural Setting
abstract: Due to the lack of baseline data assessing the health literacy and health behaviors of adults in a remotely located upland barangay, which employs vigorous statistical sampling, that could support the existing relationship between health literacy and health promoting behaviors among adults at risk for diabetes, this study came into fruition. This descriptive correlational research design study generally aimed to determine the existing correlation between the health literacy and health promoting behaviors of adults at high risk for diabetes. A total of 400 adults in Barangay Vizcaya, President Roxas, Capiz, aged 18-59 years old, were included in the final sample after they were were randomly selected utilizing a proportionate stratified sampling technique by age and sex. Data were collected through face-to-face interview using the Health Literacy and Health Promoting Behavior Questionnaires. Both adults at high and low risk for diabetes were found out to have limited health literacy and negative health promoting behaviors, with disease prevention and physical activity as having the worst health literacy and health behavior subscale scores, respectively. A statistically and practically significant difference exists between the health literacy of adults with high and low risk for diabetes, but no significant difference exists between their health promoting behaviors. Furthermore, there is a moderately positive correlation between the health literacy and health promoting behaviors of adults at high risk for diabetes. Thus, healthcare workers need to focus on increasing the health literacy of adults, especially those who are at high risk for diabetes, to facilitate development of health promoting behaviors. An all population-based inclusion should still be implemented when conducting health information campaigns, so as to reach the greater percentage of the adults who have lower levels of health literacy.

This thesis, titled "Health Literacy and Health Promoting Behaviors Among Adults at Risk for Diabetes in a Rural Setting," investigates the relationship between health literacy and health-promoting behaviors among adults at risk for diabetes in Barangay Vizcaya, a medically underserved, upland community in the Philippines. Using a descriptive correlational research design with a cross-sectional approach, the study sampled 400 adults aged 18–59 years. Participants were categorized as high-risk or low-risk for diabetes using the Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) tool. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using the Health Literacy Survey Short Form 12 and the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II.

The findings revealed that both high-risk and low-risk adults exhibited limited health literacy and negative health-promoting behaviors. The lowest scores were recorded for disease prevention within health literacy and physical activity within health-promoting behaviors. While a significant difference in health literacy levels existed between the high-risk and low-risk groups, no significant difference was observed between the groups regarding health-promoting behaviors. Notably, a moderately positive correlation was identified between health literacy and health-promoting behaviors among high-risk adults. This thesis, titled "Health Literacy and Health Promoting Behaviors Among Adults at Risk for Diabetes in a Rural Setting," investigates the relationship between health literacy and health-promoting behaviors among adults at risk for diabetes in a medically underserved, upland barangay in the Philippines.

**Problem and Context**
The study is set in Barangay Vizcaya, President Roxas, Capiz, a remote agricultural community characterized by a diet rich in sugar and starch. While the prevalence of diabetes is rising in the municipality, there is a significant lack of baseline data regarding the health literacy and health behaviors of adults in such marginalized, rural areas. The researcher notes that while many studies examine health literacy and behaviors in urban populations or among those already diagnosed with diabetes, there is a dearth of literature focusing on individuals categorized by their risk level for developing the disease, particularly in underserved settings. The study seeks to determine if a correlation exists between health literacy and health-promoting behaviors among those at high risk for diabetes, which could inform targeted nursing interventions.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a descriptive correlational research design with a cross-sectional approach. The study utilized Pender’s Health Promotion Model and the HLS-EU Conceptual Model of Health Literacy as theoretical frameworks. The sample consisted of 400 adults aged 18–59 years residing in Barangay Vizcaya, selected through a proportionate stratified random sampling technique based on age and sex. Participants were categorized into "high risk" or "low risk" for diabetes using the simplified Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) tool.

Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using two primary instruments: the Health Literacy Survey Short Form 12 (HL-SF12) and the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP II). To ensure data quality, the researcher conducted training and orientation for ten Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) who assisted in the data collection. The study addressed various validity issues through statistical controls, such as blocking for confounding variables (age, sex, income, etc.), and ensured reliability through Guttman’s Lambda-2 coefficients.

**Findings**
The study revealed that both adults at high and low risk for diabetes exhibited limited health literacy and negative health-promoting behaviors. Specifically, the subscale scores for "disease prevention" (within health literacy) and "physical activity" (within health-promoting behaviors) were the lowest among the participants.

Regarding differences between groups, the results showed a statistically and practically significant difference in the level of health literacy between adults at high risk and low risk for diabetes. However, no significant difference was found between the two groups regarding their health-promoting behaviors. Crucially, the study found a moderately positive correlation between health literacy and health-promoting behaviors among adults at high risk for diabetes.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The researcher concludes that health literacy is a significant factor associated with health-promoting behaviors in high-risk populations. Because a correlation exists, increasing health literacy is a viable pathway to improving health behaviors in this demographic.

The implications of these findings are multifaceted. For healthcare workers, the study suggests that interventions should focus on increasing health literacy, particularly for those identified as being at high risk for diabetes, to facilitate the development of better health behaviors. For public health administrators and legislators, the findings provide evidence to support the importance of health literacy campaigns and the implementation of diabetes risk assessments as strategic tools for early detection and prevention. Finally, the study emphasizes the need for all-population-based inclusion in health information campaigns to ensure that those with lower literacy levels are not left behind, particularly in medically underserved and remote rural areas.

title: Analyzing the Creative Freedom in the Age of AI and 3D Animation: A Qualitative Study of Animators in the Animation Industry
abstract:
This study examines how AI-assisted tools and 3D technologies influence animators’ creative freedom. Specifically, this study focuses on the shift to 3D workflows and the integration of AI, and how these influence animators’ creative decision-making. For this study, animators working locally in the Philippines were interviewed to provide their thoughts and overall experience to both AI and 3D animation. In addition, these animators were asked how the studio they work for has adapted in response to these changes and how they see the future of animation now that these changes are in effect.

The results of the study show that while AI tools improve efficiency, they also limit aspects of creative control. Meanwhile, the 3D animation workflow process reshapes the artistic decision-making. Despite these changes to the creation of animated media, animators continue to adapt their methods in order to maintain the creative expression. The study in this paper highlights the evolving balance between technological advancement and artistic freedom in contemporary animation practice

This qualitative study by Joel Ramon L. Lopez investigates how the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and 3D animation workflows influences the creative freedom of professional animators. Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with eight professional animators at Top Peg Animation and Creative Studio Inc. in the Philippines. The research explores whether these technological shifts limit or expand creativity, reshape decision-making, and affect how animators maintain control over their work.

The findings indicate that while awareness of AI and 3D animation is high, practical integration remains limited. Most professionals view AI as a supplementary tool for minor, repetitive, or entry-level tasks, such as cleaning or generating references, rather than a transformative force. AI is perceived as unable to replicate unique artistic styles, fine details, or human emotion, necessitating human intervention to ensure quality. Consequently, AI is viewed as a tool for efficiency rather than a replacement for the animator. Regarding 3D animation, the shift in workflows requires animators to adapt technical skills to manage digital models and rigging to maintain artistic direction.

While software is becoming more available, the cost of advanced AI-capable tools remains a barrier. Creative decisions are primarily driven by client instructions rather than direct audience feedback. Ultimately, AI and 3D workflows influence creative freedom by reshaping how it is expressed rather than eliminating it. Human judgment remains central to the process.

This qualitative study, conducted by Joel Ramon L. Lopez, investigates how the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and 3D animation workflows influences the creative freedom of professional animators. The research addresses a gap in existing literature, which often focuses on the technological risks or economic impacts of these trends without accounting for the lived experiences and perspectives of the artists themselves. The study seeks to understand the extent to which these industry shifts limit or expand creativity, how they reshape artistic decision-making, and how animators maintain control over their work in an increasingly automated environment.

The research was conducted using a qualitative descriptive approach, employing semi-structured interviews with eight professional animators working at Top Peg Animation and Creative Studio Inc. in the Philippines. The participants were selected through purposive sampling, ensuring they had direct experience with 3D workflows and exposure to AI-assisted tools. The study's conceptual framework posits that AI-assisted tools and 3D workflows act as independent variables that influence creative freedom (the dependent variable), with the creative decision-making process serving as a mediator.

The findings reveal that while there is high awareness of AI and 3D animation among professionals, their practical integration into the workflow is currently limited. Most respondents view AI as a supplementary tool rather than a transformative one, using it primarily for minor, repetitive, or entry-level tasks such as cleaning, generating references, or providing suggestions. A significant finding is that AI is often perceived as lacking the ability to replicate unique artistic styles, fine details, or human emotion, which necessitates human intervention to ensure quality and consistency. Consequently, AI is seen as a tool for efficiency rather than a replacement for the animator's creative role.

Regarding 3D animation, the study found that the shift to 3D workflows changes the production process by requiring animators to manage digital models, rigging, and the blending of different styles (such as 2D and 3D). While this changes how visual elements are integrated, it does not necessarily reduce artistic control; instead, it requires animators to adapt their technical skills to maintain the intended artistic direction. The study also noted that while new software is more available and increasingly affordable, cost remains a barrier to accessing the most advanced AI-capable tools.

The research further explored the influence of audience reception and client demands. The findings suggest that creative decisions are primarily driven by client instructions rather than direct audience feedback. However, animators remain aware of audience trends, noting that clients often seek to replicate the success of popular works. Despite the rise of automation, the respondents expressed a generally optimistic view of the future of animation. They noted a strong public preference for "genuine" or "authentic" animation and a growing opportunity for indie animators due to the accessibility of digital tools and social media.

In conclusion, the study finds that AI and 3D animation workflows influence creative freedom in a limited and evolving manner. These technologies do not eliminate creative freedom but rather reshape how it is expressed. While they offer significant improvements in efficiency and production capabilities, they also introduce constraints related to software limitations and structured production lines. Ultimately, the study concludes that human judgment and artistic decision-making remain central to the animation process, as technology serves to support rather than replace the animator's essential role.

Based on these findings, several implications and recommendations are offered. For animators and studios, the study recommends a balanced approach that utilizes AI to enhance efficiency while prioritizing human artistic input and decision-making. Studios are encouraged to design flexible workflows that preserve creative control within technical environments. For educational institutions, the researcher suggests updating curricula to include the ethical and practical use of AI and 3D technologies, while maintaining a strong emphasis on foundational skills like anatomy, movement, and creative storytelling. For future researchers, the study suggests expanding the scope to include more diverse geographic regions and a broader range of studios to provide a more comprehensive global perspective on how these technological trends continue to evolve.

title: Communication for Sustained Volunteerism: The Case of Pawikan Conservation
abstract:
This study examined how volunteerism is sustained in a pawikan conservation initiative, with emphasis on the role of communication strategies and support systems. Guided by symbolic interactionism and development/environmental
communication, it employed an embedded mixed-methods single-case design. Quantitative data were drawn from a short anonymous survey completed by all currently active volunteers in the organization (N = 30), while qualitative data came from one focus group discussion with six volunteers. The study investigated the communication strategies and support systems associated with sustained volunteerism, how volunteers interpret these practices and relate them to
commitment and continued participation, how organizational values shape the framing and enactment of sustaining practices, and what challenges and opportunities affect continued involvement. Results show very high levels of sustained volunteerism and perceived communication support within the case organization. What mattered most was not the mere number of support practices volunteers experienced, but the perceived quality of support. Feedback and learning, recognition, mentoring, and coordination emerged as the strongest correlates of commitment, continuance, and role identity. Storytelling and values-in-action were also highly endorsed and helped anchor ecological purpose, pride, and a family-like sense of belonging, although storytelling did not significantly differentiate sustained volunteerism because it appeared to function as a shared baseline across respondents. The focus group further revealed that volunteerism is relationally produced through intergenerational recruitment, everyday mentoring, recognition rituals, and practical coordination, while its most persistent constraints are time, physical demands and safety concerns, and costs or
logistics. The study concludes that communication sustains volunteerism when it helps volunteers feel guided, recognized, heard, and connected to impact, but communication alone is insufficient without realistic material support. It recommends strengthening structured mentoring, regular two-way feedback, fair and visible recognition, streamlined coordination, and volunteer welfare mechanisms, while deepening participatory voice in organizational communication.

Communication and coordination issues were rated as the least significant barriers. For engagement to be sustainable, communicative efforts must be coupled with practical support addressing real-world constraints.

This thesis, titled "Communication for Sustained Volunteerism: The Case of Pawikan Conservation," investigates the communicative mechanisms that maintain long-term volunteer engagement within a community-based sea turtle conservation initiative. The research addresses a critical gap in environmental and development communication: while much scholarship focuses on how to recruit volunteers or report ecological successes, less is understood about the specific communication strategies and support systems that prevent volunteer fatigue and foster long-term commitment.

The study is situated within the context of pawikan (sea turtle) conservation in the Philippines, where community-based efforts are vital for protecting endangered species from poaching and habitat loss. The researcher posits that volunteerism is not merely a series of tasks but a social practice sustained through interaction, shared values, and meaning-making. The primary problem addressed is how volunteerism is sustained in these initiatives and the specific role that communication strategies and support systems play in ensuring continued participation over time.

To investigate this, the author employed an embedded mixed-methods single-case design, utilizing a post-positivist philosophical orientation. The methodology combined quantitative data from an anonymous survey of 30 active volunteers with qualitative insights from a focus group discussion (FGD) involving six volunteers. The study was theoretically grounded in symbolic interactionism, which views identity and commitment as products of social interaction and shared symbols, and development communication, which emphasizes participatory and culturally situated engagement.

The findings reveal very high levels of both sustained volunteerism and perceived communication support within the organization. A key finding is that the quality of communication support is a much stronger predictor of sustained volunteerism than the sheer quantity of support practices experienced. Specifically, the study found that feedback and learning, recognition, mentoring, and coordination have the strongest correlations with volunteer commitment, continuance, and role identity. While storytelling and values-based messaging were highly endorsed by participants, they functioned as a shared baseline for all members rather than a differentiating factor for those who stayed longer.

Qualitative data from the focus group provided deeper context, revealing that volunteerism in this initiative is often relationally produced. Recruitment is frequently intergenerational or invitation-based, where the role of a "steward" is modeled by elders and passed down through social ties. The sense of "family-like" belonging was a central theme, suggesting that volunteers stay because the organization provides a sense of dignity, community, and shared purpose. Furthermore, the study found that organizational values like stewardship and empathy are not just abstract concepts but are "values-in-action," enacted through daily routines and interpersonal interactions.

However, the research also identified significant barriers to sustained involvement. The primary challenges are not communicative or ideological but are rooted in material and practical realities. Volunteers cited time constraints (due to work, school, or family), physical demands, safety concerns, and the costs associated with participation (such as transportation and food) as the most significant obstacles. Interestingly, communication and coordination issues were rated as the least significant barriers, suggesting that the organization’s current communication infrastructure is relatively effective at managing logistics.

The study concludes that communication is essential for sustaining volunteerism, but it is not a panacea. Communication effectively fosters commitment and identity when it helps volunteers feel guided, recognized, and connected to a larger ecological impact. However, communication alone cannot overcome the material burdens of volunteering. For engagement to be truly sustainable, communicative efforts must be coupled with practical, material support that addresses the real-world constraints faced by volunteers.

Based on these findings, the researcher offers several implications and recommendations for community-based conservation organizations. First, organizations should systematize and prioritize mentoring, regular two-way feedback, and visible recognition, as these are the most effective tools for building volunteer identity and commitment. Second, there is a need to strengthen "volunteer voice" by creating more structured, institutionalized spaces for participatory decision-making and feedback, moving beyond informal, problem-centered conversations. Third, communication strategies should be integrated with resource mobilization efforts. Since time, cost, and safety are the primary barriers, communication should be used to advocate for and facilitate welfare mechanisms, such as equipment support, transportation assistance, or healthcare provisions. Finally, the study suggests that while storytelling is vital for anchoring shared meaning, organizations must ensure that the "story" of the mission is backed by the "reality" of practical support to prevent burnout and ensure long-term community resilience.

title: Cultural and Anti-Stigma Analysis of Public Messaging Towards Reframing HIV Communication
abstract: The research investigated the concept of public messaging pertaining to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Philippines with emphasis on the approach used in adopting stigma and culture. It followed a qualitative approach, particularly textual analysis, to analyze HIV materials that are publicly accessible within the past three years. Results indicated positive changes in the direction of supportive and empowerment-focused and neutral messages, such as localized Bisaya and service-oriented content. Nevertheless, there was an implicit stigma that was perpetuated in risk framing and moral undertones; cultural adaptation is disproportionate, and priority groups were being underrepresented or tokenized. Obstruction of access was caused by over-medicalized language and inconsistent application of the plain-language requirements. The research suggests that stigma- free communication guidelines be institutionalized, representation of key population groups be made authentic, local language and cultural adaptation be reinforced, and health workers', non-governmental organizations', and media practitioners’ capacity- building be implemented.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies

Vanessa N. Pamisaran’s thesis, "Cultural and Anti-Stigma Analysis of Public Messaging Towards Reframing HIV Communication," investigates the effectiveness of HIV-related public messaging in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Philippines. The study examines how language, imagery, and cultural alignment in communication materials impact social perceptions and the mitigation or perpetuation of stigma. Despite legal frameworks like Republic Act No. 11166, misinformation and social stigmas continue to hinder prevention and care.

Using a qualitative design and textual analysis, the research evaluated posters, social media posts, and brochures produced by government institutions and NGOs over the last three years. These materials were assessed based on language tone, cultural sensitivity, Gender and Development alignment, stigma reinforcement, visual inclusivity, and communication standards.

Findings indicate that while most materials utilize positive or neutral language focused on empowerment rather than fear, significant gaps remain. Some campaigns successfully used the local Bisaya dialect and community-centric imagery, providing practical, destigmatizing information. However, implicit stigma persists through subtle messaging that links HIV to "bad life choices" or portrays people living with HIV (PLHIV) as threats. Representation of key populations like the LGBTQ+ community and youth is often tokenistic, and over-medicalized jargon can obstruct access for those with lower health literacy.

The researcher recommends that agencies adopt person-centered, empowering communication and ensure authentic representation of marginalized groups. The study also suggests institutionalizing culturally responsive frameworks and conducting future research incorporating the direct perspectives of PLHIV and healthcare providers.

The thesis titled "Cultural and Anti-Stigma Analysis of Public Messaging Towards Reframing HIV Communication" by Vanessa N. Pamisaran investigates the effectiveness of HIV-related public messaging in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Philippines. The research focuses on how language, imagery, and cultural alignment in communication materials impact the social perception of HIV and its potential to either mitigate or perpetuate stigma.

The problem addressed is that despite legal frameworks like Republic Act No. 11166 and increasing HIV cases in Northern Mindanao, communication barriers remain a significant obstacle. The study identifies that misinformation, cultural misunderstandings, and existing social stigmas hinder effective HIV prevention, treatment, and care. The researcher notes that while government and NGO materials exist, it is unclear how effectively these messages confront local cultural norms and the stigma associated with the virus.

The study was conducted within the context of a growing HIV epidemic in the Philippines, where regional data shows a rising number of new cases. The researcher highlights a gap in patient-provider communication and the need for health communication that is not just informative, but also culturally responsive and gender-sensitive.

To address these issues, the researcher employed a qualitative research design using textual analysis. This method was chosen to examine how communication texts—such as posters, social media posts, and brochures—construct meanings regarding HIV, stigma, and gender sensitivity. The study utilized purposive sampling to collect publicly available HIV-related materials from government institutions, NGOs, and social media platforms in Malaybalay City produced within the last three years. The analysis was guided by a measurement matrix that evaluated materials based on language tone, cultural sensitivity, Gender and Development (GAD) alignment, stigma reinforcement, visual inclusivity, and adherence to communication standards.

The findings reveal a complex landscape in HIV messaging. On a positive note, the majority of the analyzed materials utilized positive or neutral language, focusing on empowerment, resilience, and prevention rather than fear. Some materials demonstrated high cultural sensitivity by using the local Bisaya dialect and community-centric imagery, such as the concept of "bayanihan" (community solidarity). Some campaigns were also successful in providing practical, destigmatizing information, such as guides on HIV disclosure etiquette and materials clarifying that HIV has no specific physical appearance.

However, several significant gaps were identified. The research found that implicit stigma remains a persistent issue; while explicit moral judgments were rare, subtle messaging often linked HIV to "bad life choices" or portrayed people living with HIV (PLHIV) as potential threats. Furthermore, representation was found to be disproportionate or tokenistic. Key population groups, including the LGBTQ+ community, sex workers, and youth, were often represented only symbolically (e.g., through rainbow symbols) without authentic storytelling or depth. Additionally, there was an uneven application of communication standards, with some materials relying on over-medicalized jargon that could obstruct access for those with lower health literacy.

The researcher concludes that while HIV communication in Malaybalay City has made gradual progress toward more supportive and empowering tones, it remains uneven. The effectiveness of these messages is limited by the presence of implicit stigma, a lack of authentic representation for marginalized groups, and inconsistent cultural and linguistic adaptation. The study confirms that while overt stigma is decreasing, the subtle, implicit forms of stigma and the failure to fully include diverse populations continue to pose challenges to effective public health communication.

Based on these conclusions, the study offers several implications and recommendations. For public health agencies, the researcher recommends moving away from fear-based or moralizing messages in favor of person-centered, empowering communication. There is a call for the authentic and meaningful representation of PLHIV, LGBTQ+ individuals, and rural communities in all visual and textual content. For policymakers, the study suggests institutionalizing culturally responsive and stigma-free communication frameworks that align with national GAD policies and local community needs. Finally, the researcher recommends capacity-building initiatives for healthcare workers and media practitioners to ensure they are equipped to use anti-stigma language. For future research, the study suggests incorporating the direct perspectives of PLHIV and healthcare providers to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how these messages are received and interpreted in real-world settings.

title: Sponsor Management and Letter of Guarantee (LoG) Coverage Integration System for International School Manila (ISM)
abstract:
International School Manila has four separate systems for handling sponsorship billing and Letter of Guarantee (LoG) coverage: PowerSchool (SIS), the Student Charging Portal (SCP), NetSuite (ERP), and the Online Billing System (OBS).
Prior to the development of this project, coverage decisions were manually interpreted at charge entry and this could lead to inconsistent assignments to Bill-To, causes for delay in the correction process, lack of audit trails and further reconciliation efforts. The project created and implemented a pilot Sponsor Management and LoG Coverage Integration System that combines all the master data of sponsors, tracks LoG records, handles workflows based on the roles and assesses coverage using the deterministic business rules.

The deployed pilot web application was done with ASP.NET Core including REST API endpoints, role-based authentication for Administrator, Admissions and Cashier users, local credentials for authentication for ISM staff accounts, and Azure deployment for production-style validation. The system enables the management of sponsor profiles, prevention of sponsor duplication, creation and activation of LoG, sponsor change requests, sponsor views, coverage preview, creation of audit trail and reporting support. The web interface has been responsive and is PWA-ready, but has not been fully developed as a Progressive Web App as the PWA installable features, service worker caching, offline behavior and the web app manifest were not in the scope of the pilot. A total of 110 test cases were found in total, of which 95 passed, 12 noted and 3 known non-critical items were noted; none of them were critical or blocking. 60 user acceptance testing (UAT) workflow scenarios were verified; 54 were successful and 6 were non-blocking issues for refinement. The proven workflows covered sponsor search, sponsor maintenance, creation and viewing of the LoG, coverage check, restricted access, report generation, and sponsor self-service actions. There are minor usability and validation issues such as the delayed LoG reassignment display after sponsor merge, the lack of visibility for attachments in one change-request flow, unclear confirmation messages, incomplete report header metadata, and improved sponsor access-error messages. The pilot proved to show that existing manual interpretation can be minimised, governance is enhanced, audit preparedness is improved and a practical roadmap towards production integration with current ISM systems is achieved with a centralized Sponsor Master and deterministic coverage engine. The pilot web application deployed is a working example that shows that there is no need to replace ISM’s existing core platforms, and that consistent and explainable decisions on coverage of sponsors can be made. International School Manila (ISM) faces significant operational challenges regarding sponsorship billing and the management of Letters of Guarantee (LoG). Currently, the institution relies on four separate systems: PowerSchool (SIS), the Student Charging Portal (SCP), NetSuite (ERP), and the Online Billing System (OBS). Because these systems were implemented at different times for various needs, they lack a unified approach to sponsorship coverage. This fragmentation requires staff to manually interpret LoG provisions during charge entry, which leads to inconsistent assignments of Bill-To designations, delays in correction processes, a lack of audit trails, and difficult reconciliation efforts. These manual processes, often involving spreadsheets and CSV files, increase the risk of inaccurate postings and regulatory exposure, particularly concerning the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) policy on Ease of Paying Taxes (EoPT), which demands clear and well-documented billing.

To address these issues, the researcher developed and implemented a pilot Sponsor Management and LoG Coverage Integration System. The primary objective was to create an integrated system that automates the process of covering Student Charging Portal LoG entries within the PowerSchool system. The project aimed to synchronize PowerSchool, NetSuite, the Student Charging Portal, and the Online Billing System using common identifiers and a centralized Sponsor Master. A key goal was to implement a deterministic rules engine to provide real-time, explainable coverage determinations at the point of charge entry, thereby ensuring that Bill-To decisions and sponsor-parent allocations are accurate and consistent across all platforms.

The methodology followed a DevOps approach, utilizing a structured lifecycle of planning, design, continuous integration, testing, release, deployment, operation, and feedback. The system was designed as a role-based web application hosted on Microsoft Azure. The technical stack included an ASP.NET Core backend with REST API endpoints, an ASP.NET Core MVC front-end, and an Azure SQL (MSSQL) database layer. The system architecture was designed to act as a centralized Sponsor Management layer that sits between the existing core platforms, providing a common reference point for sponsor profiles, LoG rules, and coverage evaluations. This design allows the institution to achieve integration without the massive cost and risk of replacing its existing enterprise resource planning or student information systems.

The pilot implementation included several core functional services: Sponsor Master Data Management, LoG Rule Authoring, Coverage Evaluation, Decision Auditing, and Identifier Synchronization. The coverage evaluation component uses deterministic rules to classify charge line items as Covered, Split, or Not Covered, providing a specific reason code and rule version for every decision. This ensures that the decision made at the point of entry is the final determination that propagates to the finance system and the final statements presented to parents and sponsors.

The project was assessed through various testing methodologies, including functional testing, user acceptance testing (UAT), security testing, performance testing, and deployment readiness testing. Functional testing confirmed that all workflows for various roles—Administrator, Admissions, Cashier, and Sponsor—were operational. In the UAT phase, 11 testers participated in 165 executed role-based test cases, achieving an overall pass rate of 96.4%. Security testing focused on OWASP areas, and the results showed that all high and medium-risk issues were resolved. Performance testing using Postman demonstrated that the system could handle significant loads, with 10,000 virtual users resulting in a 0.00% error rate.

The findings from the pilot demonstrate that the proposed system successfully minimizes manual interpretation and enhances governance. The pilot proved that a centralized Sponsor Master and a deterministic coverage engine can provide consistent and explainable decisions on coverage without requiring the replacement of ISM’s existing core platforms. The implementation of the API and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation layer provides a solid foundation for future system-to-system exchange. While the pilot was successful, some minor usability and validation issues were identified, such as delayed LoG reassignment displays after a sponsor merge and the need for improved error messages for sponsor access.

The study concludes that the integration-first approach is a practical, lower-risk, and institution-specific solution for managing sponsorship billing. By moving the decision locus to the point of charge entry, the system ensures that the Bill-To and allocation data are accurate before they reach the financial ledger and billing statements. This provides a comprehensive, line-level audit chain that meets regulatory requirements and improves the reliability of the student ledger.

The implications of this work suggest a clear roadmap for transitioning the pilot into a full production environment. Future work should focus on increasing the reliability and resilience of the system, specifically regarding Azure coverage preview endpoints and error handling for failed or partial transactions. Expanding functional and integration coverage to include more complex scenarios, such as sponsor merges and automated Sponsor ID assignment, is recommended. Additionally, the researcher suggests hardening the deployment through stricter authentication, rate limiting, and comprehensive training and operational runbooks to ensure long-term operational sustainability and readiness for full institutional use.

title: Filipino Virtual Assistants as Global Communications Practitioners: A Phenomenological Study
abstract: The study explored how Filipino Virtual Assistants (VAs) view themselves as global communication practitioners in the digital world. Anchored in Heideggerian phenomenology, the lived experiences of 10 VAs working in fully remote, transnational environments were analyzed from December 2023 to April 2024. Becoming a VA is often shaped by life transitions, economic necessity, and the pursuit of flexibility; sustained participation in virtual work then transforms how participants perceive professionalism, identity, and communication. They described their work as deeply communicative, relational, and emotionally labor-intensive, extending beyond task execution to include trust-building, cultural adaptation, and identity negotiation. Filipino Virtual Assistants occupy a distinct and critical position within the global digital economy as fully remote communication workers whose labor is fundamentally relational, interpretive, and identity-forming. They do not simply adapt to global communication norms; rather, they actively negotiate professional identity through culturally informed communication practices characterized by adaptability, emotional intelligence, relational sensitivity, and a strong sense of responsibility toward clients. These traits rooted in Filipino sociocultural values become strategic assets in transnational virtual environments. At the same time, the study reveals a paradox at the core of virtual work. While remote work offers autonomy, flexibility, and economic mobility, it also exposes Filipino VAs to structural vulnerabilities, including job insecurity, blurred work-life boundaries, limited legal protection, and emotional fatigue Filipino Virtual Assistants as Global Communications Practitioners xv arising from continuous digital presence. These conditions shape how participants experience selfhood, productivity, and belonging. Viewed through a phenomenological lens, the experiences of Filipino VAs illustrate that virtual work is not a neutral technological arrangement but a lived, embodied condition that reshapes identity, communication, and meaning making. Filipino Virtual Assistants emerge not as invisible background workers, but as global communication practitioners whose voices and experiences deserve scholarly and institutional recognition.

two:
The dissertation titled "Filipino Virtual Assistants as Global Communications Practitioners: A Phenomenological Study" by Marianne Remo Cabral explores the lived experiences and professional identities of Filipino Virtual Assistants (VAs) operating in the global digital economy.

**Problem and Context**
The study is situated within the context of the rapid digitalization of the global workforce, a trend significantly accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. As remote work transitioned from a niche arrangement to a sustained feature of modern employment, the Philippines emerged as a dominant global hub for virtual labor. Despite the massive scale of this industry—with the Philippines ranking as a top outsourcing destination due to English proficiency and cost-effectiveness—the researcher identifies a significant gap in academic literature. Existing studies primarily focus on the technological, economic, or platform-based aspects of remote work, such as job satisfaction or work-life balance. There is a notable lack of empirical research regarding how Filipino VAs experience their work as communicative labor and how they construct their professional identities while navigating transnational, digitally mediated environments.

**Methodology**
The researcher employed a qualitative approach using Heideggerian hermeneutic phenomenology to capture the "lived experiences" of the participants. The study focused on 10 Filipino Virtual Assistants working in fully remote, transnational environments. Data collection took place between December 2023 and April 2024. The primary data collection tool was semi-structured interviews conducted via video conferencing platforms (Zoom or Google Meet), supplemented by demographic data gathered through Google Forms. The researcher utilized NVivo software for data analysis, applying a Heideggerian phenomenological interpretation to move from individual descriptions to deeper thematic understandings of the participants' "becoming" as virtual workers.

**Findings**
The findings reveal that the transition into virtual assistance is often driven by life transitions, economic necessity, and a desire for flexibility. Once established, the work is experienced as a deeply communicative and relational endeavor rather than mere task execution. The study identifies several key themes:

First, the research characterizes the work as "re(entering) the (un)familiar world," where participants must navigate the complexities of a digitally constructed workspace. Second, the study identifies the "come-on and stay-on" factors, noting that while economic benefits draw workers in, the relational and professional aspects sustain them. Third, the findings reposition Filipino VAs as "Global Communications Practitioners." Rather than being invisible background workers, they are active agents who use culturally informed communication—leveraging traits like adaptability, emotional intelligence, and relational sensitivity—to negotiate professional identities.

The study also highlights a "paradox of virtual work." While the role offers unprecedented autonomy, flexibility, and economic mobility, it simultaneously exposes workers to structural vulnerabilities. These include job insecurity, the blurring of work-life boundaries, limited legal protections, and emotional fatigue caused by the requirement of a continuous digital presence.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The study concludes that virtual work is not a neutral technological arrangement but a lived, embodied condition that reshapes identity and meaning-making. Filipino VAs are not merely remote laborers; they are skilled communicators who perform essential relational and interpretive labor that facilitates global business operations. Their ability to navigate cross-cultural nuances through digital mediation is a strategic asset in the global market.

The implications of this research are multi-faceted. For virtual managers, the study suggests a need for more human-centered and culturally informed management strategies that account for the unique communication dynamics of remote teams. For the online working community, it provides a realistic view of the profession's complexities. For transglobal companies, the findings offer insights into how to enhance organizational identity and performance through inclusive virtual workforce policies. Finally, for the academic community, the study contributes original constructs regarding how "being-in-the-world" is re-articulated in an "always-on" digital environment, calling for greater scholarly recognition of digital labor as a legitimate field of communication study.

title: Banning Single-Use Plastics and Compliance Intentions in a Public Market in Davao City
abstract:
This study examined the factors influencing public market vendors' compliance intentions toward the proposed Single-Use Plastics (SUP) ban in Davao City using Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior. A quantitative correlational design
was employed involving 276 vendors selected through simple random sampling. A researcher-made questionnaire was used, and data were analyzed using mode and Pearson's correlation coefficient. The findings showed that attitude, subjective
norms, and perceived behavioral control were all positively associated with compliance intention, with perceived behavioral control emerging as the strongest predictor. The findings highlight the importance of understanding compliance within
the unique socio-cultural context of Davao City. The results suggest that vendors’ intention to comply is not solely driven by environmental awareness or social pressure, but also by a long-standing culture of discipline, civic responsibility, and
respect for local ordinances.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
The global increase in single-use plastic production has caused environmental challenges like landfill accumulation and harm to marine life. In the Philippines, the volume of plastic waste is driven by the convenience of small sachets and bags. To address this, Davao City approved City Ordinance No. 0500-21, known as the No to Single-Use Plastics Ordinance, in May 2021. This ordinance aims to ban and regulate items such as cups, straws, and cutlery, though implementation has faced delays due to pending implementing rules and regulations. This study examines how attitudes, social pressures, and perceived abilities influence the intention to follow the ban among vendors at the Bankerohan Public Market.

Using a quantitative correlational research design, the study employed simple random sampling to select 276 vendors. Data were collected via a survey questionnaire measuring demographic profiles and the constructs of the Theory of Planned Behavior: attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. Findings revealed that all three factors have significant positive relationships with the intention to comply. Perceived behavioral control emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by attitude, while subjective norms showed the lowest correlation. Vendors are more likely to comply when they perceive the ban as beneficial to the environment and market hygiene.

The study concludes that compliance is driven by individual business capabilities and personal values rather than social pressure. Vendors are more likely to support the ordinance when they believe they possess the necessary knowledge and resources to transition to alternative packaging. Compliance in Davao City is also rooted in a culture of discipline and civic responsibility referred to as being "DCplinado." Effective communication is essential to shape positive attitudes and increase perceived behavioral control. Strategies should focus on providing practical information, such as demonstrating how to comply and promoting the availability of eco-friendly alternatives, to transform legal requirements into a shared social practice.

The researcher employed simple random sampling to select 276 vendors from the Bankerohan Public Market to ensure representation across various stall types, including food and dry goods. The questionnaire utilized a five-point Likert scale to measure these variables, alongside a five-item scale for compliance intention. Statistical analysis was conducted using mode to determine predominant perceptions, Pearson’s r to examine relationships between variables, and Cronbach’s Alpha to ensure the reliability of the research instrument.

Among these three factors, perceived behavioral control emerged as the strongest predictor of compliance intention, followed by attitude, while subjective norms showed the lowest correlation. The results suggest that vendors base their decisions more on their individual business capabilities and personal values rather than social pressure from peers or customers.

The study concludes that the intention of market vendors to comply with the single-use plastic ban is significantly influenced by their attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. The dominance of perceived behavioral control as a predictor suggests that vendors are more likely to support the ordinance when they believe they possess the necessary knowledge, resources, and capability to transition to alternative packaging. Furthermore, the findings highlight that compliance in Davao City is deeply rooted in a unique socio-cultural context characterized by a strong culture of discipline and civic responsibility, often referred to as being "DCplinado." Strengthening the perceived capability of vendors through continuous engagement and support can bridge the gap between policy intention and actual behavioral change.

title: Verifiable Academic Records for ISM (VERACISM) : A Permanent, Decentralized,  Blockchain-Backed Storage for Immutable Reports
abstract:
International School Manila (ISM) has extensive collection of Academic and Administrative Reports that are crucial for accreditation, audits and external verification, and the authenticity and integrity of these reports is critical. Currently, no cryptographic bindings exist between the reports and their metadata in centralized storage systems, which can be modified without being detected, and which have no IT-independent audit trails or slow verification. This project suggests a hybrid platform called VERACISM (Verifiable Academic Records for ISM) that will allow to attach finalized reports to decentralized content-addressed storage while maintaining identity, access control, and operational monitoring within the
governance of ISM. Reports are created with the existing ISM applications are uploaded via api integreation. In VERACISM,scanned files were validated using ClamAV and YARA, and by MIME type and file size, then hashed with SHA-256, and written to IPFS with Filecoin-backed deals, using Lighthouse. The file is given a unique Content Identifier (CID) and is stored with report metadata and immutable audit events in MSSQL under strict RBAC/ABAC rules. Both a web-based console and a public verification portal enable tenant and integrator administration and provide both internal and external parties with the ability to verify report integrity via CIDs or QR codes, with an optional option of cross-checking storage evidence in public explorers. The project is implemented using a DevSecOps lifecycle approach which includes secure design, automated checks of security and scheduled VAPT, following the OWASP Top 10 risks. Planned evaluation integrates task-based user testing for administrator, tenant offices, integrators and verifiers, structured security testing and defined acceptance criteria. VERACISM will help enhance the record governance of ISM, lower verification overhead, and offer a pattern for storing academic records in a tamper-proof fashion.

The methodology employed a DevSecOps lifecycle, integrating security into every phase from planning to deployment. title: Subtrack: A Subscription Management and Analytics System for International School Manila
abstract:
This capstone project presents the design and development of SubTrack: A Subscription Management and Analytics System for International School Manila (ISM). The system addresses inefficiencies in managing over one hundred educational and operational applications used by more than 2,000 students and 600 faculty and staff. Existing subscription management processes at ISM involve multiple offices, including the EdTech Coordinators, IT Office, Purchasing Office, and, when required, the Legal Office, all operating through independent and largely manual workflows. This fragmented approach results in redundant requests, delayed renewals, limited visibility, and increased financial and compliance risks.

SubTrack was developed to centralize and automate the subscription management lifecycle. The system features a consolidated database, multi-office workflow automation, and analytics capabilities for budget forecasting and utilization tracking. It also includes a conditional legal review module to support contract validation and data privacy compliance for high-value or sensitive subscriptions. The platform was built using ASP.NET Core Web API for the backend, Razor Pages with Bootstrap for the frontend, and Microsoft SQL Server as the primary database, with deployment on Azure App Services to ensure scalability and reliability. The system was evaluated through technical testing, simulated workflows, and automated security assessment to verify functionality, workflow correctness, and system integrity. These validation approaches confirmed that SubTrack effectively supports end-to-end subscription management processes within a controlled and non-human testing environment.

Through SubTrack, ISM is provided with a unified platform for monitoring, approving, and analyzing subscription usage and expenditures. The system enhances operational efficiency, improves transparency across departments, and supports data- driven decision-making, contributing to the institution’s broader digital transformation initiatives in educational technology management.

title: CADENCE: An AI-Powered Operations Platform for Greenrock Agrifarms SG Trading Inc.
abstract: GreenRock Agrifarms SG Trading Inc. currently operates on a file based system to track sales and inventory. Staff spend hours manually preparing reports that may lead to operational incidents due to the risk of human errors during data processing. This project aims to design, develop, and build CADENCE, an AI-powered operations platform that will provide insights on poultry operations like inventory and sales. The solution will run on AWS, will be integrated with Claude AI for operational insights, display dashboard KPIs, improve data entry & processing accuracy, and allow immediate reports generation. Ultimately, allowing GreenRock executives and shareholders to make data driven tactical and strategic plans.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
GreenRock Agrifarms SG Trading Inc. currently faces operational challenges due to its reliance on a file-based system to track sales and inventory. This manual approach requires staff to spend hours preparing reports, a process that introduces significant risks. The manual nature of data processing increases the likelihood of human errors, which can lead to various operational incidents. Because the current system lacks automation and real-time data integration, the company struggles with the inefficiencies inherent in manual data entry and the time-consuming nature of report preparation.

To address these issues, the project aims to design, develop, and build CADENCE, an AI-powered operations platform specifically tailored for the company. The primary objective is to provide meaningful insights into poultry operations, specifically focusing on inventory and sales management. The methodology involves the development of a solution hosted on AWS that integrates Claude AI to provide advanced operational insights. The technical approach focuses on creating a system that can display dashboard KPIs, improve the accuracy of data entry and processing, and facilitate the immediate generation of reports.

The findings center on the improvement of operational efficiency and data integrity. By utilizing AI and cloud infrastructure, the platform is expected to reduce the time staff spend on manual reporting and minimize errors. The integration of Claude AI allows for the extraction of insights that were previously difficult to obtain. The ability to generate reports immediately and view key performance indicators provides a level of visibility that the current system cannot offer.

The conclusions suggest that implementing CADENCE will modernize the operations of GreenRock Agrifarms SG Trading Inc. By automating the tracking of sales and inventory and reducing the reliance on manual data entry, the company can stabilize its operational processes. This shift allows the organization to move toward a more sophisticated management model where strategic decisions are supported by reliable and immediate operational intelligence.

title: Community Nutrition Information System of Barangay San Andres, Cainta, Rizal
abstract:
Barangay San Andres operates various health center satellites in Cainta, Rizal, which use a manual system for child nutrition record management across the satellite centers. The
manual process causes data inconsistencies, leading to redundant record encoding and other errors, such as duplicate, incomplete, and outdated entries. The manual approach is also inefficient for searching and retrieving information, especially when individuals move between satellite centers or when records are lost due to damage or destruction of physical
documentation. From this analysis of existing issues, a Community Nutrition Information System (CNIS), a progress web application, was created to aid in the efficient management of nutritional status monitoring. The CNIS was developed using PHP and a MySQL database and included functions such as nutritional profiling, record management, and food and supplement recommendations. Evaluations were carried out using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, in which participants, including barangay health workers, parents, and IT/IS professionals, completed Likert-scale questionnaires to evaluate the software. Results indicated that the indicators considered “strongly agree” were followed by general favorable ratings of “agree.” Performance, load, and security testing further demonstrated efficient resource utilization, stable operation with up to 50 concurrent users, and protection against common
web vulnerabilities. Overall, the CNIS is efficient, reliable, and suitable for deployment to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and security of community nutrition records in the said barangay.
faculty: Faculty of Information and Communication Studies
half:
Developed by Roel Pillas Malubay, the Community Nutrition Information System (CNIS) is a progressive web application (PWA) designed to modernize child nutritional record management in Barangay San Andres, Cainta, Rizal. The project addresses inefficiencies inherent in manual, pen-and-paper systems used across six health center satellites, which historically caused data inconsistencies, redundant encoding, and errors that could exclude children from vital nutrition initiatives.

Utilizing the V-Model development life cycle and anchored in the Health Belief Model, the system was built using PHP and a MySQL database. Its PWA architecture allows for offline functionality via service workers. The CNIS features a recommendation engine that uses anthropometric measurements—height, weight, and mid-upper arm circumference—cross-referenced with age, sex, medical history, and dietary restrictions to provide personalized recommendations based on DOST-FNRI guidelines.

Evaluated via the ISO/IEC 25010 model, the system received high satisfaction ratings across all user groups. Technical testing showed an accessibility score of 95%, meeting WCAG 2.2 Level AA standards. Security testing resolved all identified medium and low-risk vulnerabilities, while performance testing resulted in an "A" grade with a 99% performance score. Load testing confirmed stability for up to 50 concurrent users. The CNIS streamlines data entry for healthcare workers, provides growth transparency for parents, and offers data analytics for officials to support evidence-based policymaking.

The project addresses inefficiencies in a manual, pen-and-paper system used across six health center satellites. This manual approach has historically caused data inconsistencies, redundant encoding, and errors such as duplicate or outdated entries. Such inefficiencies make retrieving information difficult and can lead to the exclusion of children from vital nutrition initiatives like feeding programs.

The researcher utilized the V-Model system development life cycle, emphasizing rigorous verification and validation. The system's theoretical framework is anchored in the Health Belief Model (HBM). Built using PHP and a MySQL database, the CNIS features a PWA architecture to allow for offline functionality via service workers, ensuring usability in areas with unstable internet. The system includes a rule-based and knowledge-based recommendation engine that uses anthropometric measurements—height, weight, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)—to assess nutritional status. These assessments are cross-referenced with age, sex, medical history, and dietary restrictions to provide personalized recommendations based on DOST-FNRI guidelines.

The system was evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, including alpha and beta testing, accessibility testing via WCAG 2.2, security testing via OWASP ZAP, and performance testing via Grafana k6. Findings indicated high satisfaction across all user groups. The system received "Strongly Agree" ratings for functional appropriateness and recognizability. Barangay health workers reported high satisfaction regarding functionality, availability, and time behavior, while IT professionals confirmed it met technical standards for testability, risk management, and accountability. Technical testing showed an accessibility score of 95%, meeting WCAG 2.2 Level AA standards. Security testing resolved all identified medium and low-risk vulnerabilities, and performance testing resulted in an "A" grade with a 99% performance score. Load testing confirmed the system can stably accommodate up to 50 concurrent users.

The Community Nutrition Information System (CNIS) of Barangay San Andres, Cainta, Rizal, developed by Roel Pillas Malubay, is a progressive web application (PWA) designed to modernize the management of child nutritional records. The project addresses critical inefficiencies in the local healthcare delivery system to promote preventive care and better health outcomes for children.

**Problem and Context**
Barangay San Andres is a large community with over 120,000 residents, approximately 28% of whom are under the age of 15. The barangay operates six health center satellites that rely on a manual, pen-and-paper system for managing child nutrition records. This manual approach has led to significant operational challenges, including data inconsistencies, redundant record encoding, and errors such as duplicate, incomplete, or outdated entries. Furthermore, the lack of a centralized system makes searching and retrieving information difficult, especially when residents move between satellite centers. These inefficiencies result in unsynchronized data, which can lead to the exclusion of children in need from vital nutrition initiatives like feeding programs or vitamin distributions. The study is situated within the broader context of malnutrition in the Philippines, where conditions such as stunting and undernourishment remain prevalent due to socioeconomic factors and low medical check-up rates.

**Method**
The researcher utilized the V-Model system development life cycle, which emphasizes rigorous verification and validation through corresponding testing stages for every development phase. The theoretical framework for the system is anchored in the Health Belief Model (HBM), which posits that individuals are more likely to take health-related actions if they perceive susceptibility to a condition, understand its severity, and believe the benefits of an intervention outweigh the barriers.

The CNIS was developed as a progressive web application (PWA) using PHP and a MySQL database, with a front-end built on HTML5, CSS3, Bootstrap 5, and Vanilla JavaScript. The PWA architecture was specifically chosen to allow for offline functionality via service workers, ensuring the system remains usable in areas with unstable internet connectivity. The system features a rule-based and knowledge-based recommendation engine that utilizes anthropometric measurements—height, weight, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)—to assess nutritional status. These assessments are cross-referenced with age, sex, medical history, and dietary restrictions to provide personalized food and supplement recommendations based on guidelines from the Department of Science and Technology – Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI).

The system underwent comprehensive evaluation using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model. Testing included alpha testing for internal functionality, beta testing with target users (barangay health workers and parents) and IT professionals, accessibility testing via Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, security testing using OWASP ZAP, and performance/load testing using Grafana k6.

**Findings**
The evaluation results indicated high levels of satisfaction across all target user groups. According to the ISO 25010 criteria, the system received "Strongly Agree" ratings for functional appropriateness and recognizability. Barangay health workers reported high satisfaction regarding the system's functionality, availability, and time behavior. IT professionals confirmed that the software met critical technical standards, particularly in testability, risk management, user safety, recoverability, and accountability.

Technical testing confirmed the system's robustness. Accessibility testing yielded a score of 95%, meeting the WCAG 2.2 Level AA standards. Security testing via OWASP ZAP showed that all identified medium and low-risk vulnerabilities were successfully resolved. Performance testing via GTmetrix resulted in an "A" grade, with a 99% performance score. Load testing demonstrated that the system could stably accommodate up to 50 concurrent users with zero HTTP request failures and efficient response times, which meets the expected workload of the barangay's healthcare staff.

**Conclusions**
The study concludes that the CNIS is a viable and effective digital solution for community nutrition monitoring. By transitioning from a reactive, paper-dependent process to a proactive, digitally organized system, the CNIS enables more accurate nutritional assessments and tailored dietary recommendations. The integration of rule-based algorithms ensures that recommendations are medically appropriate and localized to the Filipino context. The system successfully bridges the gap between data collection and actionable health interventions, providing a reliable tool for both healthcare workers and parents to monitor the nutritional health of children.

**Implications**
The implementation of the CNIS has significant implications for community health management. For healthcare workers, it streamlines data entry and retrieval, reducing errors and administrative burdens. For parents, it provides transparency and actionable information regarding their children's growth and dietary needs. For barangay officials, the system's data analytics and reporting capabilities offer insights for evidence-based policymaking and targeted health programs.

The researcher suggests several avenues for future work, including expanding the demographic scope to include adolescents, pregnant women, and the elderly. Future iterations could incorporate advanced technologies such as machine learning for predictive analytics (e.g., predicting stunting risks), biometric authentication for enhanced security, and cloud integration for real-time synchronization. Additionally, integrating the system with broader electronic medical record (EMR) systems could provide a more holistic view of a child's health, combining nutritional status with other medical conditions. Finally, the system offers a scalable model that could be adapted for other municipalities or public school health programs.

title: Assessment of Monitoring Compliance to Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) Conditions: Two Cases in Metro Dumaguete, Negros Oriental, Philippines
abstract:
Project proponents are mandated by the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement (PEIS) System through the issuance of the Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) to prepare Environmental Management Plans (EMPs) and
Environmental Monitoring Plans (EMoPs). But studies have indicated that organizations would go through the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process in order to obtain an ECC with none to limited follow-through in terms of implementing the EMPs and EMoPs. The focus of this study is to examine the actual environmental compliance monitoring conducted by Orient Foods Industries Corporation (OFIC), a food processing facility that is not strictly covered or does not need to undergo the process of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and get an ECC; Dumaguete Business Park Incorporated (DBPI), that owns and manages a property intended for mixed-use development, thus required to have an ECC; and the Provincial Environmental Management Unit (PEMU) of the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) that monitors projects in Negros Oriental and Siquijor. The research design adopts a qualitative case study that looks into pertinent documents, conducts interviews of key personnel, and observes the site of OFIC, DBPI, and the EMB PEMU. The collected data are subjected to thematic and cross- case comparison analysis in order to characterize the policies or practices in monitoring environmental compliance as well as assessing its extent and frequency, and identifying implementation gaps and constraints. The result of the investigation shows contrasting environmental compliance monitoring practices. OFIC is not strictly covered, but it has an in-house Pollution Control Officer (PCO) that manages and monitors the facility’s environmentalrequirements by undergoing regular testing of air and water quality and wastewater treatment, submission of self-monitoring reports, and coordination with the EMB for the issuance of its permits and other regulatory requirements. DBPI, on the other hand, is covered by the PEIS system documentary requirements and was issued an ECC. But it has not fully implemented the conditions that were laid down in the ECC, such as organizing a Multi-Partite Monitoring Team, and does not have an accredited PCO or similar technical personnel appointed to manage environmental compliance. The main problem lies in the fact that when the ECC was granted to DBPI, there was no proper turnover of the documents to the new management during organizational transition. The EMB PEMU has a very lean staff, comprising only of two (2) personnels that include the unit head. With the vast workload of monitoring the entire Negros Oriental province and Siquijor, it became a challenge for this local regulatory agency to do field inspections, reports, and providing guidance and follow-up to project proponents. The findings indicate that the success of the PEIS system is not only about a project having an ECC and its accompanying strict monitoring requirement, but it also depends on how fully committed and capable the project proponents are as well as the effectiveness of the EMB PEMU to monitor, guide, and ensure that conditions are followed. The study concludes that the monitoring phase is where the PEIS system is
put to the test. In projects granted with an ECC, inadequate staffing, poor communication channels and internal systems can pose as a significant challenge to compliance. Consequently, the study recommends that the EMB PEMU should augment its workforce, enhance its presence in the field, and implement systems to help proponents get oriented and be reminded about the roles of the Multi-PartiteMonitoring Teams and the PCO. Furthermore, the study suggests having clear guidelines on delineating the responsibilities of personnel involved in ECC-related tasks when management changes. Finally, the study recommends conducting further in-depth research on how to monitor compliance in other areas and places.
