The study titled "Assessment of Monitoring Compliance to Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) Conditions: Two Cases in Metro Dumaguete, Negros Oriental, Philippines" investigates the effectiveness of environmental compliance monitoring under the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement (PEIS) System. The research focuses on the gap between the issuance of an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) and the actual implementation of Environmental Management Plans (EMPs) and Environmental Monitoring Plans (EMoPs) during the post-ECC phase.

The problem addressed is that while the PEIS system is designed to ensure environmental protection from project inception through operation, studies suggest that organizations often view the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process merely as a procedural hurdle to secure an ECC, with little follow-through on actual environmental commitments. The researcher identifies a potential disconnect between legal requirements and ground-level enforcement, particularly at the local level.

The study is situated in Metro Dumaguete, Negros Oriental, and examines three specific entities to provide a comparative perspective: Orient Foods Industries Corporation (OFIC), a food processing facility not strictly covered by the PEIS system; Dumaguete Business Park Incorporated (DBPI), a mixed-use development project that is required to have an ECC; and the Provincial Environmental Management Unit (PEMU) of the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB), which serves as the local regulatory agency.

The researcher employed a qualitative case study research design. Data were collected through a triangulation of methods: document reviews of ECCs, EMPs, EMoPs, Self-Monitoring Reports (SMRs), and permits; semi-structured interviews with key informants, including Pollution Control Officers (PCOs), project managers, and EMB officials; and site observations of the facilities and the EMB office. The collected data were analyzed using thematic and cross-case comparison analysis to characterize monitoring practices, identify implementation gaps, and assess the effectiveness of current systems.

The findings reveal contrasting environmental compliance monitoring practices among the three cases. OFIC, despite not being formally required to undergo the EIA process due to its age and production scale, demonstrates proactive compliance. The company employs an accredited in-house PCO, conducts regular air and water quality testing, submits quarterly SMRs, and maintains regular coordination with the EMB. In contrast, DBPI, which is covered by the PEIS system and holds an ECC, shows weak compliance. The study found that DBPI has not fully implemented its ECC conditions, specifically failing to organize a Multi-partite Monitoring Team (MMT) or appoint an accredited PCO. A significant cause for this failure was identified as a lack of proper document turnover during a management transition in 2007, leaving current management unaware of their specific environmental obligations. Finally, the EMB PEMU faces significant institutional constraints. The unit is severely understaffed, consisting of only two personnel responsible for monitoring projects across the entire province of Negros Oriental and the island of Siquijor. This lack of manpower limits the agency's ability to conduct regular field inspections, provide guidance to proponents, and thoroughly verify submitted reports.

The study concludes that the monitoring phase is the true test of the PEIS system. The mere issuance of an ECC does not guarantee environmental protection; rather, success depends on the commitment of project proponents and the capacity of regulatory agencies. Inadequate staffing at the regulatory level, poor internal communication within companies, and failures in information transfer during management changes are significant barriers to compliance. The research highlights that compliance monitoring is not just a technical requirement but an organizational and institutional challenge.

Based on these findings, the researcher offers several implications and recommendations. For regulatory agencies like the EMB PEMU, the study recommends augmenting the workforce to increase field presence and implementing systems to better orient and remind proponents of their responsibilities, particularly regarding the roles of PCOs and MMTs. For project proponents, the study suggests establishing clear guidelines for the turnover of ECC-related responsibilities during organizational transitions to ensure continuity of environmental management. Finally, the researcher recommends further in-depth research into monitoring compliance across different geographical areas to broaden the understanding of these local dynamics.

title: Public Involvement in Media Accountability in the Philippines: Examining Citizen Participation in the Iloilo Media-Citizen Council
abstract:
This study examined citizen participation in the Iloilo Media-Citizen Council (IMCC), one of several recently established by the Philippine Press Institute. While citizen or non-media members are integral to press councils globally, little research
has explored their actual roles in media self- or co-regulation bodies. Anchored in the Social Responsibility Theory (Hutchins Commission, 1947; McQuail, 2010; Bertrand, 2000), the study utilized the Civic Voluntarism Model or CVM (Verba et al., 1995), Role Theory (Katz & Kahn, 1978; Biddle, 1979), and the Ladder of Citizen Participation (Arnstein, 1969) to examine why and how citizens participate in the council’s processes. Using a qualitative case study approach, data were collected through interviews, document reviews, and observations of council activities and events. Findings identified five key roles – public representation, ethical oversight, capacity-building, providing expertise, and public engagement – through which citizen members were regarded as partners in promoting ethical journalism. Drivers of participation reflected the three CVM dimensions: recruitment through professional and personal networks; resources such as skills, expertise, and institutional support; and psychological engagement grounded in personal values and a sense of civic duty. Participation among core non-media members demonstrated genuine engagement, particularly through leadership roles and contributions to internal decision-making. However, interaction with the broader public, especially those outside formally represented sectors, remains limited and underdeveloped.

Using a qualitative case study methodology involving semi-structured interviews, document reviews, and direct observations, the researcher analyzed the council's internal dynamics.

The findings identify five distinct roles fulfilled by citizen members: public representation, ethical oversight, capacity-building, the provision of expertise, and public engagement. Through these functions, citizens act as partners in promoting ethical journalism. Applying the CVM, the study found that recruitment is facilitated through professional and personal networks, participants contribute specialized expertise and institutional support, and participation is driven by psychological engagement rooted in personal values and civic duty.

The study concludes that while the IMCC serves as a functional model for media-citizen partnership, its reach into the wider community is underdeveloped. To be truly effective, the council must move beyond a small group of represented stakeholders to foster deeper interaction with the general public.

title: Voices from the Field: Exploring the Perceived Impact of the Riceboost Initiative Package of Technology on the Livelihood and Farming Practices of Rice Farmers
abstract: The RiceBoost Initiative is a field-based technology demonstration platform that promotes improved rice production through certified inbred seeds, recommended crop management practices, mechanization, and other science-based technologies. This study assessed the perceived impact of the RiceBoost Initiative Package of Technology on rice farmers, focusing on technology acceptance, livelihood effects, and factors influencing adoption. A qualitative exploratory design was used involving farmer-cooperators and RiceBoost personnel from eight branch stations. Data were gathered through focus group discussions, key informant interviews, semi-structured interviews, and field observations and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed improved access to quality seeds and technologies, experiential learning, increased openness to innovation, strengthened stakeholder collaboration, and perceived improvements in productivity and income. However, delayed inputs and financial support, transportation and manpower limitations, environmental conditions, and coordination challenges constrained implementation. Overall, the initiative was perceived as a platform for technology dissemination, farmer capability development, experiential learning, and stakeholder collaboration. The study recommends timely resource provision, stronger coordination, adaptive approaches, continued field-based learning, and regular monitoring of technology adoption and livelihood outcomes.

Data were collected via focus group discussions, key informant interviews, semi-structured interviews, and field observations, then analyzed using thematic analysis.

Findings indicate several positive impacts, including improved access to quality seeds and modern technologies. The program functioned as a platform for experiential learning, which increased farmers' openness to innovation and strengthened stakeholder collaboration. Economically, participants reported perceived improvements in both productivity and income. However, implementation was hindered by constraints such as delayed provision of inputs and financial support, logistical challenges regarding transportation and manpower, environmental conditions, and coordination issues.

The study concludes that while the initiative is a vital platform for technology dissemination and farmer capability development, its potential is limited by logistical, financial, and coordination-related barriers. To improve the initiative, the researcher recommends the timely provision of resources to prevent delays, stronger stakeholder coordination, and more adaptive approaches to environmental variables. Finally, the study emphasizes the need for regular monitoring of technology adoption rates and long-term livelihood outcomes.

title: Digital Farmers' Produce System: A Cloud-based Platform for Optimizing Crop Management and Market Linkages
abstract: Farming is the main livelihoods in Municipality of sinacaban, Misamis Occidental. Most farmers are crop producers as indicated by interview surveys with farmers and verified by the Municipal Agriculture Office. Common issues mentioned by farmers include lack of access to real time pricing information, connections to potential buyers, timing of buying transactions, and awareness of produce currently available at the barangay level. These result in smaller than desired profit margins for farmers and occasionally lost crops. This project aims to develop and deploy the Digital Farmers’ Produce System, a cloud- a cloud-based platform that allows farmers to post their available crops by season, request aid from their municipal agriculture office, and connect with buyers interested in their crops. The system allows farmers to post details of their produce availability and schedules, buyers can search for and view crop postings by region and crop category, and DA/MAO officers can view crops stock and request statuses per barangay. The system was built using PHP 8 and the Flight microframework, HTML, CSS, Javascript, Bootstrap, and MySQL it is using RAD development framework. Security and reliability measures included role-based permissions, HTTPS encryption, input validation, prepared queries, password hashing, and a backup strategy. User acceptance was gathered via survey from 12 participants, consisting of 5 farmers, 4 buyers, and 3 DA/MAO officers. With a positive user acceptance was observed, with mean ratings of 4.60 from farmers, 4.83 from buyers, and 4.69 from DA/ORO officers. While the results of this study are limited by the scope and available resources, they show promise that a localized, farmer-driven agricultural system can help improve market visibility as well as coordination between farmers and government agricultural institutions. More work would have to be done to ensure appropriate training is provided, all stakeholders can consistently connect to the system, and all security risks are mitigated before rollout.

The Digital Farmers’ Produce System is a cloud-based web application designed to optimize crop management and market linkages in the Municipality of Sinacaban, Misamis Occidental. The project addresses critical challenges faced by local smallholder farmers, including a lack of access to real-time pricing information, limited connections to potential buyers, delays in transactions, and poor awareness of available produce at the barangay level. These issues contribute to information asymmetry, reduced profit margins, and significant post-harvest losses. While national programs like e-Kadiwa exist, they often fail to reach rural areas due to poor internet connectivity, low digital literacy, and a lack of localization.

The system serves four primary user roles: farmers, buyers, agricultural officers, and administrators. Farmers can post produce details (price, quantity, harvest dates, and location), submit requests for agricultural resources, and communicate with buyers. Buyers can search, filter, and view available crops by region or category and contact farmers directly. Department of Agriculture/Municipal Agriculture Office (DA/MAO) officers can monitor crop stocks, review resource requests, and issue announcements or SMS alerts. Administrators manage user accounts and system parameters. To accommodate users with varying digital literacy and intermittent connectivity, the system includes a Bisaya language toggle and SMS notification capabilities.

The researcher employed the Rapid Application Development (RAD) methodology, which emphasizes rapid prototyping and continuous user feedback. The development process followed four phases: Requirements Planning, where interviews and surveys were conducted; User Design, involving the creation of wireframes and user flows; Construction, where the PHP 8 and MySQL-based system was built using the Flight microframework and Bootstrap; and Cutover, which included deployment, testing, and documentation. The technical infrastructure utilizes a cloud-hosted environment accessible via desktop and mobile web browsers.

The project was evaluated through functional, non-functional, and user acceptance testing. Functional testing confirmed that all core features—such as registration, produce listing, messaging, and resource request management—operated as intended. Non-functional testing, including performance and security audits, showed that the system was stable and responsive. Performance simulations using ApacheBench demonstrated that the server could handle up to 100 concurrent users without failure. Security testing via OWASP ZAP identified no high-risk vulnerabilities, and the developer implemented mitigations for medium and low-risk alerts, such as configuring Content Security Policy (CSP) headers and implementing input validation to prevent SQL injection and XSS attacks.

User acceptance was measured using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) through a survey of 12 participants (5 farmers, 4 buyers, and 3 DA/MAO officers). All participants were first-time users, many of whom were in the 46-and-above age group, indicating the system's accessibility for older users with limited digital experience. The results showed strong positive acceptance across all roles, with mean ratings for perceived usefulness, ease of use, attitude toward using, and behavioral intention to use all falling within the "Strongly Agree" range. Buyers reported the highest overall satisfaction, while farmers reported highly positive attitudes toward the initiative.

The study concludes that the Digital Farmers’ Produce System successfully achieves its objectives of improving produce visibility, facilitating market linkages, and enhancing coordination between farmers and local government institutions. The system provides a viable, low-cost, and adaptable solution for municipal-level agricultural coordination. The findings suggest that localized, user-centered digital platforms can bridge the gap between smallholder farmers and the broader market, provided they are designed with simplicity and mobile responsiveness in mind.

The implications of this work suggest that digital agricultural coordination is most effective when it incorporates institutional engagement. By providing DA/MAO staff with organized data, the system aids in better resource allocation and monitoring. However, the researcher notes that the system's long-term success depends on sustained user engagement, particularly from buyers, and the provision of ongoing training and technical support to farmers.

Future work for this project includes expanding the system's capabilities to include online payment processing, order management, and delivery scheduling. To address the challenges of intermittent connectivity in rural areas, future iterations may incorporate offline capabilities, such as USSD or SMS-based workflows and data-efficient web pages. Additionally, the researcher suggests integrating the system with existing provincial or national agricultural databases and conducting longitudinal studies to measure the actual economic impact on farmer income and post-harvest loss reduction.

title: Status Review of Guinayangan Quezon Mangrove Forest: An Assessment of Species Diversity and Habitat Analysis
abstract:
This study was conducted to determine the status of the Mangrove Walk located in Brgy. Calimpak, Guinayangan, Quezon. Three main procedures were undertaken: species identification; habitat analysis using percent crown cover, regeneration per m², and average height; and the computation of diversity indicators such as species richness, relative abundance, Shannon–Wiener diversity index, and species evenness using PAST software. A total of 183 mangrove trees were recorded across three transect lines and two quadrats. Seven (7) out of the 23 mangrove species listed by the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) for the Municipality of Guinayangan, Quezon were identified at the study site, representing three families: Acanthaceae, Lythraceae, and Rhizophoraceae. In the habitat analysis using the parameters by Deguit et al. (2004), the results showed that the average percent crown cover of 5.63 falls under the poor condition category, as it lies within the 0–25% crown cover range. The average tree height of 9.04 meters is classified as excellent, as it exceeds the 5-meter threshold. For regeneration density, the computed value of 0.83 individuals per m² is considered good, as it falls within the range of 0.7 to less than 1 individual per m². In terms of diversity indices, relative abundance across all sampling stations showed that the dominant species were Sonneratia alba (39%), Avicennia marina (16.5%), and Rhizophora mucronata together with Sonneratia apetala (11.0%). Sonneratia alba was observed to dominate all three transects and two quadrats. In contrast, species with lower relative abundance included Bruguiera cylindrica (9.9%), Bruguiera parviflora (9.9%), and Rhizophora apiculata (2.7%). In terms of species richness, Transect Lines 1 and 3 recorded the highest values with seven species each, followed by Transect Line 2 with six species. Quadrats 1 and 2 recorded the lowest species richness, each with five species. For the Shannon–Wiener diversity index, Transect Line 3 obtained the highest value (1.83), followed by Transect Line 2 (1.71), Transect Line 1 (1.64), Quadrat 1 (1.43), and Quadrat 2 (1.42). Based on the
interpretation scale, all transects, and quadrats exhibited a poor Shannon–Wiener diversity status. However, species evenness across all sampling units was balanced. In terms of species richness, all sampling units recorded values above five, indicating an integrated mangrove community structure.

Using a quantitative descriptive research design, the study utilized field observations across three 75-meter transect lines and two 15 × 15-meter quadrats to record biometric data for 183 individual trees.

The study identified seven mangrove species from the Acanthaceae, Lythraceae, and Rhizophoraceae families: *Avicennia marina*, *Sonneratia alba*, *Rhizophora mucronata*, *Sonneratia apetala*, *Bruguiera cylindrica*, *Bruguiera parviflora*, and *Rhizophora apiculata*. All species are classified as "Least Concern" by the IUCN Red List. The species exhibit natural zonation, with *Avicennia* and *Sonneratia* in the fringing zone and *Rhizophora* and *Bruguiera* in the inland zones. *Sonneratia alba* was the most dominant species with a 39% relative abundance.

Habitat analysis revealed an average tree height of 9.04 meters ("excellent") and a regeneration density of 0.83 individuals per m² ("good"), but a percent crown cover of only 5.63% ("poor"). While species richness was high and evenness was balanced, Shannon–Wiener diversity index values were interpreted as "poor." The researcher recommends using drones for future documentation and incorporating water and soil quality analysis. Findings should assist MENRO and the Tourism Office in developing sustainable ecotourism and rehabilitation plans.

The study titled "Status Review of Guinayangan Quezon Mangrove Forest: An Assessment of Species Diversity and Habitat Analysis" by Charisse Angelique M. Escobal investigates the ecological condition of the Mangrove Walk in Brgy. Calimpak, Guinayangan, Quezon. The research addresses the critical issue of mangrove degradation in the Philippines, where significant forest loss has been driven by anthropogenic activities, most notably the conversion of coastal areas into aquaculture fishponds. Despite existing conservation policies, the continued pressure on these ecosystems necessitates ongoing monitoring and assessment to support effective management and protection strategies.

The primary objectives of the study were to identify the mangrove species present at the Mangrove Walk, assess the current habitat condition using specific structural parameters, and calculate diversity indices including species richness, relative abundance, Shannon–Wiener diversity index, and species evenness. The researcher focused specifically on the Mangrove Walk, a site used for ecotourism and nature observation, which is part of a broader coastal resilience initiative but had not previously undergone this specific assessment.

The study employed a quantitative descriptive research design. Data collection involved field observations and measurements across three 75-meter transect lines and two 15 × 15-meter quadrats. The researcher identified species in situ using the Field Guide Manual to Philippine Mangroves. Biometric data, including trunk diameter, tree height, crown diameter, and crown height, were recorded for 183 individual trees. Habitat analysis was conducted based on three parameters: percent crown cover, regeneration density per square meter, and average tree height. Diversity indices were calculated using the Paleontological Statistical Software Package (PAST) and interpreted using established scales.

The findings revealed that seven mangrove species were present at the study site, representing three families: Acanthaceae, Lythraceae, and Rhizophoraceae. All identified species—*Avicennia marina*, *Sonneratia alba*, *Rhizophora mucronata*, *Sonneratia apetala*, *Bruguiera cylindrica*, *Bruguiera parviflora*, and *Rhizophora apiculata*—are classified as "Least Concern" by the IUCN Red List. The species distribution followed a typical natural zonation pattern, with *Avicennia* and *Sonneratia* species occupying the fringing zone and *Rhizophora* and *Bruguiera* species located in the inland zones. *Sonneratia alba* was identified as the most dominant species, accounting for 39% relative abundance.

Habitat analysis yielded contrasting results across the three measured parameters. The average percent crown cover was 5.63%, which falls into the "poor" condition category. However, the average tree height was 9.04 meters, which is classified as "excellent." The regeneration density was calculated at 0.83 individuals per m², which is considered "good." Regarding biodiversity, the Shannon–Wiener diversity index values across all sampling units were interpreted as "poor." Despite this, the study found that species evenness was balanced and species richness was high, with all sampling units recording values above five, indicating an integrated mangrove community structure.

The study concludes that while the Mangrove Walk maintains an integrated community structure with excellent tree height and good regeneration, it faces challenges indicated by poor crown cover and low Shannon–Wiener diversity. The dominance of certain species like *Sonneratia alba* and the overall low diversity index suggest areas where the ecosystem's complexity may be limited.

Based on these findings, the researcher offers several recommendations for management and future research. To improve the accuracy of future assessments, it is suggested that researchers increase the number of transects and quadrats and utilize advanced technologies like drones and high-resolution cameras for better spatial and structural documentation. For local management, the findings should serve as a baseline for rehabilitation programs and help the Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Office (MENRO) and the Tourism Office develop sustainable ecotourism plans, potentially including a minimal entrance fee for site maintenance. Finally, the researcher suggests that future studies should incorporate water and soil quality analysis, as well as hazard assessments, to provide a more holistic understanding of the mangrove ecosystem's health.

title: Celebrity Endorsements of Online Gambling in the Philippines:  A Discursive Study
abstract:
This study examined how Reddit users constructed meanings around celebrity endorsements of online gambling in the Philippines. Using a social constructionist discourse-analytic approach, it analyzed 407 comments from one selected Reddit
thread as a discursive episode in which users debated celebrity influence, gambling-related harm, personal choice, commercial work, and institutional responsibility. The analysis focused on discursive strategies, broader Discourses,
subject positions, micro-outcomes, discursive constellations, and the episode-level outcome produced through their interaction. The findings show that celebrity-endorsed online gambling was constructed as a contested object of public meaning-making. Commenters used seven discursive strategy groups to assign, resist, soften, or redirect responsibility. These strategies drew on broader Discourses of Public Moral Responsibility, Social Protection, Self-Governance, Market Rationality, Institutionalized Gambling, and Institutional Responsibility. The Discourses aligned into two competing constellations. The Civic Responsibility Constellation connected celebrity influence with ethical obligation, public welfare, and protection from harm, while the Neoliberal Constellation made endorsement and gambling understandable through paid work, personal choice, legal market participation, and regulatory recognition. Although civic criticism kept harm, vulnerability, celebrity influence, and public responsibility visible, it did not displace the stronger Neoliberal Constellation, whose assumptions were supported by existing legal, commercial, and government-recognized institutional practices. The episode-level outcome was therefore the continued normalization of celebrity-endorsed online gambling despite sustained civic criticism. From a Development Communication perspective, the findings show that communicative resistance may remain limited without institutional support capable of sustaining alternative Discourses.

This study investigates the discursive construction of meaning among Reddit users regarding celebrity endorsements of online gambling in the Philippines. The research addresses the tension between commercial activities and the potential for social harm, specifically focusing on how public discourse navigates the intersection of celebrity influence, individual agency, and institutional oversight. The problem centers on the social implications of gambling advertisements featuring high-profile figures and how these endorsements are interpreted within a digital public sphere.

The context of the research is rooted in the Philippine digital landscape, specifically within the community of Reddit, which serves as a site for public debate and meaning-making. The study treats a single Reddit thread containing 407 comments as a discrete discursive episode. This episode serves as a microcosm for broader societal debates concerning the ethics of celebrity influence, the nature of personal choice in gambling, the legitimacy of commercial work, and the extent of institutional responsibility in regulating harmful activities.

To analyze this phenomenon, the researcher employed a social constructionist discourse-analytic approach. This method focuses on how language and communication are used to construct social realities and power dynamics. The analysis was structured around several key dimensions: discursive strategies, broader Discourses, subject positions, micro-outcomes, discursive constellations, and the episode-level outcome resulting from the interaction of these elements. By using this framework, the study moves beyond simple content analysis to understand the underlying ideological structures that shape how users perceive and argue about online gambling.

The findings reveal that celebrity-endorsed online gambling is a highly contested object of public meaning-making. Users did not reach a consensus; instead, they engaged in a complex negotiation of meaning. The analysis identified seven distinct groups of discursive strategies used by commenters to assign, resist, soften, or redirect responsibility. These strategies were not isolated but were embedded within six broader Discourses: Public Moral Responsibility, Social Protection, Self-Governance, Market Rationality, Institutionalized Gambling, and Institutional Responsibility.

These Discourses organized themselves into two competing constellations. The first, the Civic Responsibility Constellation, linked celebrity influence to ethical obligations and the necessity of protecting public welfare and vulnerable populations from harm. This perspective emphasizes the social impact of celebrity actions and the duty of influential figures to act in the interest of the common good. The second, the Neoliberal Constellation, framed celebrity endorsements through the lenses of paid professional work, individual personal choice, participation in legal markets, and the legitimacy provided by regulatory recognition. This constellation views gambling as a legitimate commercial activity and places the burden of decision-making on the individual consumer.

The study found that while the Civic Responsibility Constellation succeeded in keeping issues such as vulnerability, celebrity influence, and public responsibility at the forefront of the debate, it failed to displace the Neoliberal Constellation. The Neoliberal perspective proved more resilient because its core assumptions—such as the legality of gambling and the primacy of individual choice—are reinforced by existing legal frameworks, commercial structures, and government-recognized institutional practices.

The episode-level outcome of this discursive interaction was the continued normalization of celebrity-endorsed online gambling. Despite the presence of sustained civic criticism and arguments regarding social harm, the dominant discursive framework remained one that accommodates and legitimizes these endorsements within the current socio-economic and legal order. The debate, while active, ultimately did not shift the prevailing social acceptance of these advertisements.

The implications of this study are significant from a Development Communication perspective. The findings suggest that communicative resistance—the act of debating and criticizing harmful social trends in digital spaces—may have limited efficacy if it is not supported by institutional changes. The study concludes that for alternative Discourses, such as those emphasizing social protection and public welfare, to gain traction and effect change, there must be institutional support capable of sustaining them. Without structural, legal, or regulatory shifts that align with civic concerns, digital discourse alone may struggle to challenge the normalization of practices supported by dominant market and legal systems.

title: Blue Carbon Potential of the old Caaluan Mangrove Conservation Area, Tinambac: Biomass and Carbon Stock Assessment
abstract: Mangrove forests are recognized as important blue carbon ecosystems because of their capacity to sequester and store substantial amounts of atmospheric carbon. This study assessed the biomass and carbon stock potential of the Old Caaluan Mangrove Conservation Area in Tinambac, Camarines Sur, Philippines. Specifically, biomass and carbon stocks were estimated in three Rhizophora stylosa plantation stands aged 7, 10, and 15 years using stratified quadrat sampling and standardized allometric equations. Measurements of diameter at breast height, tree height, and stand density were used to determine aboveground biomass and corresponding carbon stocks. Results revealed that the 15-year-old plantation stand exhibited the highest biomass (54.50 t ha−1) and carbon stock (24.53 t C ha−1), associated with larger mean diameter at breast height (8.32 cm) and tree heights ranging from 12 to 13 m. The 7-year-old stand recorded higher biomass and carbon stock values than the 10-year-old stand despite its younger age, primarily because of its greater stem density. These findings indicate that plantation age, stand density, and stand structure are important determinants of carbon accumulation and storage in mangrove ecosystems. The results demonstrate the substantial blue carbon potential of the Old Caaluan Mangrove Conservation Area and underscore its ecological importance for climate change mitigation, coastal protection, biodiversity conservation, and community resilience. The study provides baseline information that can support local carbon accounting, mangrove management, and conservation planning. Furthermore, the findings establish a foundation for long-term monitoring and future assessments that incorporate belowground biomass, soil carbon, and sediment carbon pools to improve estimates of total ecosystem carbon storage.

Mangrove forests are vital blue carbon ecosystems due to their capacity to sequester and store significant amounts of atmospheric carbon, playing a critical role in regulating greenhouse gas emissions and mitigating climate change. In the Philippines, mangroves serve as essential coastal defenses against storm surges and saltwater intrusion while supporting biodiversity and local livelihoods. Despite their importance, many mangrove areas remain vulnerable to degradation. The Old Caaluan Mangrove Conservation Area in Tinambac, Camarines Sur, is a 72-hectare site managed by the Provincial Government through EDMERO and the Bantay Bakawan program. While the area is recognized for its ecological and socio-economic contributions, there has been limited empirical data regarding its specific biomass and carbon sequestration potential. This study sought to address this gap by quantifying the biomass and carbon stock of selected mangrove stands to establish a scientific baseline for local climate action and forest management.

The research focused on Rhizophora stylosa plantation stands of varying ages, specifically 7, 10, and 15 years. A stratified quadrat sampling approach was utilized, with each plot measuring 10 m × 10 m. To determine the age of the stands, the researcher triangulated data from community interviews, historical records, DENR permit records, and LGU environmental program archives. Diameter at breast height (DBH) was measured at 1.3 meters above ground level for all trees with a diameter of at least 2.5 cm. Biomass estimation was conducted using non-destructive allometric equations adapted from Komiyama et al. (2005), covering aboveground biomass (stem, branches, and leaves) and root biomass (stilt roots and pneumatophores). Biomass values were converted to carbon stock using the IPCC default conversion factor of 0.47. The study also integrated community participation by involving Bantay Bakawan personnel and EDMERO staff in the field sampling process to ensure local relevance and continuity of monitoring.

The findings revealed that the 15-year-old plantation stand exhibited the highest biomass at 54.50 t ha⁻¹ and carbon stock at 24.53 t C ha⁻¹, which was associated with the largest mean DBH of 8.32 cm and tree heights ranging from 12 to 13 m. Interestingly, the 7-year-old stand recorded higher biomass (28.59 t ha⁻¹) and carbon stock (12.86 t C ha⁻¹) than the 10-year-old stand (24.28 t ha⁻¹ and 10.93 t C ha⁻¹), despite being younger. This was attributed to the 7-year-old stand having a much higher stem density, ranging from 82 to 98 stems per plot, compared to 36 to 58 stems per plot in the 10-year-old stand. The study confirmed that plantation age, stand density, and stand structure are critical determinants of carbon accumulation. When compared to the Banacon Island in Bohol case study, the biomass and carbon stocks in Old Caaluan were lower, which was attributed to the smaller scope of the study site and the younger age of the stands in Old Caaluan.

The results demonstrate the substantial blue carbon potential of the Old Caaluan Mangrove Conservation Area and underscore its ecological importance for climate change mitigation and coastal protection. The study concludes that the 15-year-old plantation is particularly effective at carbon sequestration. Furthermore, qualitative data from interviews with local residents and Bantay Bakawan members confirmed that the mangrove plantations have provided significant socio-economic benefits, including increased fish and crab catches, honey production from mangrove pollen, and protection from storm surges. The El Verde program, which facilitates these plantations, has helped improve the livelihoods of community members, assisting with expenses such as education.

Based on these findings, the study recommends several actions to strengthen mangrove management. To improve scientific accuracy, future research should incorporate GIS mapping for better stand age verification and include soil and sediment carbon sampling to capture the full extent of the ecosystem's carbon pools. Additionally, expanding the species scope beyond Rhizophora stylosa would provide a more comprehensive view of the ecosystem's dynamics. For policy and management, the study suggests integrating carbon stock data into local climate action plans and disaster risk reduction strategies. A proposed management framework was developed, suggesting a zonation approach: a Strict Protection Zone for biodiversity and carbon storage, a Sustainable Use Zone for regulated extractive activities like shellfish collection, and a Restoration Zone for reforestation efforts. This framework aims to balance environmental conservation with sustainable livelihood opportunities through incentive mechanisms such as performance-based cash incentives for stewards and stewardship contracts for community members.

title: A Spatial and Metric Analysis of Urban Green Spaces of Bonifacio Global City, Taguig City, Philippines
abstract: Rapid urbanization affects both ecological sustainability and urban livability, if managed unwisely as exemplified by a number of urban open green spaces within Metro Manila. This poses various concerns in physical and emotional health, community wellness, as well as the overall quality of life. This study focused on the urban metrics of Bonifacio Global City (BGC), Taguig, to investigate the tree canopy cover, urban open green spaces, heat effects, impervious spaces, and accessibility to urban green spaces. It addresses the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goal Number 11 on inclusive, safe and sustainable cities using spatial analysis. The research measured the distribution of land cover and assessed the city's performance in relation to global urban sustainability recommendations from United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), United Nations-Habitat (UN-Habitat), and World Health Organization (WHO). The results showed that the tree canopy was lower at BGC by 16.22% compared with the recommended values of 30% based on UNECE. On the other hand, 6.55% of the total area are urban open green spaces, while the remaining 93.45% are impervious surfaces which are below international recommendation of UN-Habitat. The study showed a ratio of for every 1 sqm of tree canopy, there is approximately 5.76 sqm of impervious space, which suggests little or natural shade that results in little natural cooling or shade, that contributes to increase in local temperatures. To improve environmental resilience, walkability, and fair access to green spaces in the urban center at BGC, the study recommends integrated green infrastructure, nature-based solutions, and inclusive landscape planning.

title: Are Networks (Becoming) Conscious? Primary Materials from the 2016 CogNovo ColLaboratoire Workshop on Internet Consciousness and Embodied & Distributed Cognition
abstract:
These are primary materials produced during the week-long ColLaboratoire workshop in August 2016, at the University of Plymouth - Cognition Institute, as part of the CogNovo doctoral training program. Some materials were originally published on a public workshop website, now offline; others survive as original workshop files, presentations, photographic records, and later institutional press documentation. The present bundle is an archival reconstruction compiled from the original files, notes, and presentations. The original intellectual work dates to 2016; this compilation and its metadata are dated 2026

The workshop asked whether highly-connected networks—such as the Internet—could be said to be conscious, or could become conscious. It approached this question through the lenses of embodied, situated, enactive, extended, and distributed cognition. The intent of the workshop was to explore the suggestion that highly connected networks such as the Internet could be considered conscious and whether such a network might be more likely to be conscious if it had a body. It frames these questions through theories of extended, situated, enactive, and embodied cognition. The background sets out two contrasting positions. Some theories suggest that consciousness might emerge from sufficiently complex or highly networked systems. The proposal, however, notes that connectedness alone may be insufficient: a conscious agent may need to be situated within an environment, while embodied approaches to cognition emphasize the importance of a physical body. In particular, the proposal highlights the sensorimotor dimensions of embodiment and suggests that the nervous system may have evolved in relation to the need to navigate and interact safely with the physical world.

The proposal organizes its questions into three broad areas: the body, the group mind, and the environment. Under the question of the body, it considers whether the Internet of Things, together with sensors, actuators, and human users, could constitute something analogous to the Internet’s hands, arms, legs, feet, ears, eyes, skin, noses, and tongues. It also raises the possibility of modeling such distributed organization on systems such as slime mold. Under the question of the group mind, it asks whether increasingly sophisticated social networks might themselves constitute conscious group minds, or alternatively function as extensions of human minds. Under the question of the environment, it asks what environment such an intelligence would inhabit and how it might interact with physical space.

The proposal identifies the intended output as a research proposal built around focused research questions, a cross-disciplinary literature review, and innovative methodologies. Suggested methods include digital ethnography, big-data analytics, network analysis, visual analytics, data mining, social-media sentiment analysis, sculpture, computational modeling, and performance. Possible proofs of concept include visualizations, maps, diagrams, performances, and interactive installations. The document includes references to a broad set of readings comprising popular articles, books, scholarly articles, and online resources.

The 2016 CogNovo ColLaboratoire workshop, titled "Are Networks (Becoming) Conscious?", addressed the speculative and theoretical question of whether highly-connected networks, specifically the Internet, could be considered conscious or could evolve toward consciousness. Held at Plymouth University, the workshop brought together a multidisciplinary group of postgraduate students from fields including neuroscience, philosophy, computer science, and the arts to explore this problem through the lenses of embodied, situated, enactive, and distributed cognition.

The central problem identified by the organizers was the tension between theories suggesting consciousness emerges from complex networked systems and the critique that connectedness alone is insufficient. Critics argue that a conscious agent requires a physical body and a relationship with an environment to facilitate sensorimotor interaction. The workshop sought to bridge this gap by investigating whether the "Internet of Things" (IoT)—comprising sensors, actuators, and human users—could function as a distributed sensorimotor system, effectively serving as the "body" of the network.

The research was organized into three primary investigative areas: the body, the group mind, and the environment. Regarding the body, the participants explored whether the Internet could be modeled after biological systems like slime mold, which exhibit intelligent behavior despite simple structures. Regarding the group mind, the workshop questioned whether sophisticated social networks constitute emergent "group minds" or merely serve as extensions of individual human minds. Regarding the environment, the researchers investigated what kind of space an internet-based intelligence would inhabit and how it might interact with physical reality.

The methodology for this inquiry was intentionally diverse and cross-disciplinary, reflecting the complexity of the subject matter. Proposed and utilized methods included digital ethnography, big data analytics, network analysis, visual analytics, data mining, and social-media sentiment analysis. The workshop also embraced artistic and speculative methodologies, such as sculpture, performance, and computational modeling. A specific speculative software prototype called "SemantiCreeper" was developed; it was a Markov-chain-based tool designed to act as a "probe" to identify early indicators of intelligence or emergent organization within networked information, much like searching for amino acids in an extraterrestrial environment.

The findings of the workshop were expressed through the development of a theoretical model rather than a definitive empirical proof of consciousness. The participants produced a "distributed, situated, enactive, embodied model of human-machine cognition." This model posits that the Internet can be viewed simultaneously as an agent, a collection of agents, and an environment. The model suggests a symbiotic, co-evolutionary relationship between humans and machines, where information is not just transferred but transformed as it moves through the network. The researchers noted that the Internet is "information rich but meaning poor," and they explored the idea of "tremes"—machines or programs that, while initially modeled on human cognition, might eventually become autonomous.

In their conclusions, the workshop participants avoided claiming they had discovered a model of consciousness. They cited the "harder problem" of consciousness: the phenomenological reality that consciousness can only be asserted from a first-person perspective. Because they could not access a first-person perspective for a network, they could only offer a model of distributed cognition. They concluded that while the Internet may not be conscious in human terms currently, it may serve as a unique environment for emerging digital life or a host for different levels of consciousness.

The implications of this work are both scientific and philosophical. Scientifically, the workshop suggests that the study of consciousness must expand to include non-biological, distributed systems and that traditional markers of consciousness (such as self-awareness, agency, and sensorimotor loops) might need to be redefined for digital entities. Philosophically, the work challenges the boundaries between the self and the environment, suggesting that the "extended mind" hypothesis may be a necessary framework for understanding modern technological existence. The workshop ultimately served as a provocation to hasten the development of methods to detect or even foster artificial consciousness within the digital architectures humans have built.

title: Respondr: Barangay Reporting and Disaster Response System with Geo-Tagging
abstract: Barangay San Antonio 1, Noveleta, Cavite, still relies on manual and fragmented channels for incident reporting, emergency communication and response coordination. Such practices may hinder information flow, make it harder to check reports and limit the capability of barangay officials to see affected areas in emergency situations. This project developed Respondr, a geo-tagged barangay reporting and disaster response system to provide a localized web and mobile platform for residents, barangay officials, and administrators. Respondr lets residents send incident reports with description, photos and saved coordinates; track report status; view alerts and announcements; and view community locations on a map. Barangay officials can view incoming reports, update the lifecycle of the incident, add entries for response, manage alerts and announcements, monitor SMS logs, view analytics and manage vital mapped locations such as evacuation centers and community landmarks. Role-based access controls allow administrators to manage users and monitor system activity. The system was evaluated in terms of automated backend API tests, a full-stack manual regression matrix, production smoke and performance checks, a backend security review and a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) user evaluation. Manual regression matrix completion had 100 passed cases out of 100 and automated backend API integration suite had 31 passed tests out of 31. Fifteen (15) participants took part in the TAM evaluation, 10 residents and 5 barangay officials. The results indicated high acceptance with a mean overall TAM of 4.81. These results show that Respondr met the functional requirements tested and the system was found useful and easy to use by users in enhancing the reporting of incidents, communication during disasters, and coordination of responses at the barangay level.

The research addresses the limitations inherent in the current incident reporting and emergency coordination processes within Barangay San Antonio 1, located in Noveleta, Cavite. At present, the barangay relies on manual and fragmented communication channels to manage incident reporting, emergency communications, and response coordination. These traditional methods present several challenges, including the potential for hindered information flow, difficulties in verifying reports, and limitations in the ability of barangay officials to visualize affected areas during emergency situations. These systemic inefficiencies can impact the speed and effectiveness of local disaster response and community management.

To address these issues, the study developed Respondr, a localized web and mobile platform designed to streamline reporting and disaster response through geo-tagging technology. The system is designed to serve three primary user groups: residents, barangay officials, and administrators. For residents, the platform provides the ability to submit incident reports that include detailed descriptions, photographs, and saved geographic coordinates. Residents can also use the system to track the status of their submitted reports, view community-wide alerts and announcements, and view various community locations on an interactive map.

Barangay officials are provided with a suite of tools to manage incoming reports and coordinate responses. They can view new reports, update the lifecycle of an incident as it progresses, and add specific entries regarding the response actions taken. Additionally, officials can manage community alerts and announcements, monitor SMS logs, and view analytics. The system also allows officials to manage vital mapped locations, such as community landmarks and evacuation centers. To ensure security and organized management, the system incorporates role-based access controls, which allow administrators to manage users and monitor overall system activity.

The methodology employed for this project involved a multi-faceted evaluation process to ensure the system's functionality, stability, and usability. The technical integrity of the system was assessed through automated backend API tests, a full-stack manual regression matrix, production smoke and performance checks, and a backend security review. To evaluate the human element and user experience, the researcher utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The TAM evaluation involved fifteen participants, consisting of ten residents and five barangay officials.

The findings from the technical testing phase demonstrated high reliability and functional accuracy. The manual regression matrix achieved a perfect success rate, with 100 passed cases out of 100. Similarly, the automated backend API integration suite showed complete success, with all 31 tests passing. These results indicate that the system's core functionalities operate as intended according to the testing parameters.

The results from the TAM evaluation indicated high levels of user acceptance. The participants provided a mean overall TAM score of 4.81, suggesting that the platform is perceived very positively by those intended to use it. This high score reflects the users' perception of the system's utility and ease of use.

In conclusion, the study demonstrates that Respondr successfully met all tested functional requirements. The system was found to be both useful and easy to use by the target users. By transitioning from manual, fragmented channels to a centralized, geo-tagged digital platform, the system provides a more robust framework for managing community incidents and disasters.

The implications of this research suggest that implementing such a system can significantly enhance the reporting of incidents, communication during disaster scenarios, and the overall coordination of responses at the barangay level. By providing real-time data, visual mapping of affected areas, and streamlined communication tools, Respondr offers a technological solution to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of local government unit operations in emergency management.

title: Toward a Future-Oriented Physics Instructional Design (FOP-ID) for Senior High School: Integrating Best Practices, ICT, Opportunities, and Challenges
abstract:
This study employed a convergent mixed-methods approach to develop a Future-Oriented Physics Instructional Design (FOP-ID) for Senior High School (SHS) by integrating best practices, ICT, and opportunities and challenges in physics
education. Quantitative data were gathered through a survey with 50 SHS physics teachers, while qualitative data were collected through key informant and in-depth interviews with selected SHS teachers, higher education professors, and industry employers.

Quantitative findings revealed that lecture-based, collaborative, and inquiry- based strategies remain the most commonly used instructional approaches, with ICT tools such as videos, simulations, and learning management systems frequently employed to enhance engagement and conceptual understanding. Thematic analysis of qualitative data further demonstrated that effective practices are characterized by experiential learning, conceptual scaffolding, and real-world relevance, although the adoption of progressive approaches such as project-based and flipped learning remains limited due to time, resource, and training constraints. Qualitative findings also showed both systemic and pedagogical opportunities, including interdisciplinary learning, technology-enhanced instruction, and personalized learning pathways. These are paired with persistent challenges such as rigid curricula, insufficient professional development, inconsistent digital access, and gaps in learners’ foundational skills. Stakeholders across all groups emphasized core future-oriented skills such as critical thinking, inquiry, adaptability, resilience, digital fluency, and problem-solving. They also identified emerging skills, including research competence, futures literacy, interdisciplinary thinking, systems thinking, and regulatory awareness, which are not yet explicitly reflected in current national or international skills frameworks.

In response to these findings, the FOP-ID was developed as a learner-centered, inquiry-driven, technology-enabled, and industry-informed instructional  framework anchored on TPACK, constructivism, inclusive education, and future- oriented instruction. Expert validation affirmed the design’s pedagogical coherence, contextual flexibility, and relevance for preparing future-ready SHS learners.

The study addresses the need to develop a Future-Oriented Physics Instructional Design (FOP-ID) for Senior High School (SHS) students. The research focuses on integrating best practices, Information and Communication Technology (ICT), and the various opportunities and challenges present in modern physics education to better prepare students for future demands.

The context of the research is situated within the current landscape of Senior High School physics instruction, where there is a recognized need to move toward more progressive pedagogical models. The study seeks to bridge the gap between traditional teaching methods and the emerging skills required in a rapidly changing world. By examining the perspectives of various stakeholders, including SHS teachers, higher education professors, and industry employers, the research aims to create a framework that is both pedagogically sound and relevant to the needs of future learners and industries.

To achieve this, the researcher employed a convergent mixed-methods approach. Quantitative data were collected through a survey administered to 50 SHS physics teachers to identify current instructional trends and technology usage. Qualitative data were gathered through key informant and in-depth interviews with selected SHS teachers, higher education professors, and industry employers to gain deeper insights into effective practices, systemic opportunities, and persistent challenges.

The findings from the quantitative data revealed that lecture-based, collaborative, and inquiry-based strategies are still the most frequently utilized instructional approaches among teachers. In terms of technology, ICT tools such as videos, simulations, and learning management systems are commonly used to improve student engagement and conceptual understanding.

The qualitative thematic analysis provided a more nuanced view of instructional practices. Effective teaching was characterized by experiential learning, conceptual scaffolding, and the use of real-world relevance. However, the study found that the adoption of more progressive methods, specifically project-based learning and flipped learning, remains limited. These limitations are attributed to constraints regarding time, available resources, and teacher training.

The research also identified several systemic and pedagogical opportunities. These include the potential for interdisciplinary learning, technology-enhanced instruction, and the creation of personalized learning pathways. Conversely, several persistent challenges were identified, such as rigid curricula, insufficient professional development for educators, inconsistent access to digital tools, and gaps in the foundational skills of learners.

A significant finding of the study concerns the specific skills required for the future. Stakeholders across all surveyed groups emphasized the importance of core skills, including critical thinking, inquiry, adaptability, resilience, digital fluency, and problem-solving. Furthermore, the study identified a set of emerging skills that are not yet explicitly reflected in current national or international skills frameworks. These emerging skills include research competence, futures literacy, interdisciplinary thinking, systems thinking, and regulatory awareness.

In response to these comprehensive findings, the researcher developed the Future-Oriented Physics Instructional Design (FOP-ID). This instructional framework is designed to be learner-centered, inquiry-driven, technology-enabled, and industry-informed. The FOP-ID is theoretically anchored in several key educational frameworks: Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), constructivism, inclusive education, and future-oriented instruction.

The study concludes that the developed FOP-ID is a viable model for modernizing physics education. Expert validation of the design confirmed its pedagogical coherence, its contextual flexibility, and its overall relevance in preparing Senior High School learners to be future-ready. The implications of this research suggest that for physics education to remain relevant, instructional designs must evolve to incorporate emerging skills like systems thinking and futures literacy while overcoming the practical barriers of resource scarcity and rigid curricular structures.

title: Digital Engagement: Use of Mobile Smart Phones and Social Engagement Among Low-Income Rural Families in a barangay in Ramon, Isabela, Philippines
abstract: The study examined the relationship between digital access and social engagement among low-income rural community household heads in a barangay in Ramon, Isabela. Underpinned by the Digital Divide theory, the study used a survey design with 184 low-income rural family heads triangulated by Key Informant Interviews of two participants and Focus Group Discussions among 16 participants. The quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation. The survey respondents were predominantly middle-aged, male, high school graduates, and earning below ₱10,000 monthly from farming or informal labor. A rather counterintuitive finding is that despite belonging to low-income households, the participants demonstrated regular engagement with digital technologies. This is because they used free data services to obtain access to information online. Such a strategy highlights how economically disadvantaged individuals actively seek alternative means of maintaining digital connectivity. The KII and FGD showed that they frequently utilized digital resources for online communication, information retrieval, and access to online educational resources and livelihood opportunities. Further, digital access enhanced their social engagement at the personal, family, institution, and community levels. However, with the growing challenges of misinformation and cybersecurity risks, sustained efforts are needed to enhance digital literacy and cybersecurity awareness. Recommendations include a multi-sectoral approach to community-based digital literacy programs to ensure digital inclusion for personal and community development.

title: Unfolding Development Communication Values for Agricultural Development in Western Visayas, Philippines
abstract:
Narrative inquiry enables the gathering of in-depth, detailed stories that capture the authentic experiences of individuals and communities. This study is anchored using a qualitative research method using narrative inquiry in understanding the
stories, experiences, and journey of agri-information officers and extension workers. Development Communication’s pivotal role in its academic and professional landscape, with numerous institutions dedicated to its study and graduates contributing to various developmental sectors. While some perspectives, such as 'archaic' and 'cute', might suggest obsolescence or outdatedness, this view is strongly contradicted by a significant body of research and the continued impact observed by practitioners who recognize the practice as an indispensable force for transformative social change. The purpose of this study is to identify the emerging Devcom values of agri-information officers and extension workers in Western Visayas: 1) Narrate their individual stories; 2) Analyze their individual stories; and 3) Identify the emerging Devcom Values. There were three (3) participants who served as the sources of the data using local research methodology: pakikipagkwentuhan (storytelling), pagtatanong (asking questions), pagpapakuwento (narrative interviewing). The experiences of Syd, Heart, and August result to the emerging Devcom values: resilient, dynamic, and people-oriented. Syd's proactive and determined acquisition of new skillsets, driven by a commitment to social change within the agricultural sector, exemplifies resilience as a form of adaptive capacity. This transcends mere persistence, highlighting a purposeful engagement with challenges aimed at enhancing their abilities through communication for development.

The thesis titled "Unfolding Development Communication Values for Agricultural Development in Western Visayas, Philippines" by Bengie A. Panes explores the evolving professional identity and core values of development communication (DevCom) practitioners working within the agricultural sector.

The problem addressed by the study is the perceived obsolescence of development communication. The author notes that despite the discipline's historical importance in agricultural information and extension, some perspectives—including comments made during a 2020 Senate budget hearing—suggest that the field may be "archaic" or "cute." This study seeks to counter such views by identifying and mapping the actual, emerging DevCom values utilized by agri-information officers and extension workers in the Western Visayas region, thereby providing a practical, value-driven framework for the profession.

The context of the research is rooted in the history of DevCom in the Philippines, which began in the 1950s at the University of the Philippines Los Baños under Dr. Nora C. Quebral. The study focuses on the Western Visayas region, specifically looking at the roles of information officers and extension workers within the Department of Agriculture (DA). These professionals serve as vital intermediaries, bridging the gap between research and farmers to facilitate social change and economic growth. The research is anchored in Social Constructionism Theory, which posits that human reality is shaped by social and interpersonal influences.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative research method using narrative inquiry. The study utilized local research methodologies from *Sikolohiyang Pilipino* (Filipino Psychology), specifically *pakikipagkwentuhan* (informal storytelling), *pagtatanong* (unstructured questioning), and *pagpapakuwento* (narrative interviewing). The participants consisted of three individuals—Syd, Heart, and August—who are graduates of West Visayas State University (WVSU) and currently serve as agri-information officers or extension workers within the Department of Agriculture in Western Visayas. Data was analyzed using a five-phase framework involving transcription, axial coding, narrative construction, critical analysis, and participant validation.

The findings are presented through the individual narratives of the three participants. Syd’s story highlights a transition from journalism to agricultural communication, where she had to teach herself new skills like graphic design and participatory rural appraisal (PRA) to meet community needs. Her journey emphasizes the importance of empathy and proactive service. Heart’s narrative reveals a lifelong connection to community development through her upbringing in NGOs, which eventually led her to DevCom. Her work focuses on using success stories to provide evidence of the impact of agricultural programs. August’s story details his journey from a student journalist to a marketing specialist for the Young Farmers Challenge, where he had to adapt to diverse roles and even master business math to better support farmers.

From these narratives, the study identifies three emerging DevCom values: resilient, dynamic, and people-oriented. Resilience is exemplified by Syd’s adaptive capacity to acquire new skillsets to serve her community. Dynamism is seen in Heart’s ability to continuously refine communication strategies to match the practical realities of the field. A people-oriented approach is demonstrated by August’s commitment to empowering youth and farmers through diverse communication and marketing efforts. The study concludes that these values are not separate but are mutually reinforcing constructs that define an effective DevCom practitioner.

The conclusions of the study suggest that the formative experiences and academic training of these practitioners provide a vital foundation, but the real-world challenges of the agricultural sector require more than just theoretical knowledge. The transition from classroom theory to professional practice is a transformative process that necessitates resilience, flexibility, and a deep commitment to community engagement. Ultimately, DevCom is not merely about disseminating information but about using communication as a tool for empowerment and social change.

The implications of this research are significant for the field of development communication and agricultural extension. The study suggests that recognizing these emerging values can help modernize the perception of the discipline. The researcher recommends that the insights gained from this localized approach be used to inform more effective communication strategies for agricultural stakeholders in Western Visayas. Furthermore, the study serves as a foundation for future research into DevCom in various agricultural contexts across the Philippines, advocating for a greater appreciation of the crucial role communication plays in facilitating regional development.

title: Communication Strategies and Adoption of Urban Gardening Among Tricycle Drivers
abstract: This study, titled “Communication Strategies and the Adoption of Urban Gardening Among Tricycle Drivers,” explores how communication influences the awareness, adoption, and continued practice of urban farming among tricycle drivers in Manggahan, Pasig City during the COVID-19 pandemic. Conducted as a qualitative case study, the research gathered insights through in-depth interviews with tricycle drivers who sustained urban gardening practices amid mobility restrictions and economic challenges brought by the health crisis. Using the Social Cultural Tradition theory as a guiding lens, the study examines how everyday communication—rooted in family interactions, peer networks, social media and community exchanges—shaped the respondents’ understanding, motivation, and persistence in urban farming. While the theory is not tested, it offers a framework to understand how meanings and behaviors are shaped within social and cultural contexts. Findings reveal that communication played a critical role not only in the initial adoption of urban gardening but also in its continuity during the pandemic, as respondents relied on conversations with family, spouses, and social networks for encouragement, knowledge sharing, and emotional support. The practice of urban gardening became both a coping mechanism and a sustainable response to food insecurity. The study suggests that community-centered communication strategies grounded in shared traditions and everyday relationships can support long-term engagement in grassroots environmental initiatives, particularly in times of crisis.

Faced with income loss and food insecurity due to lockdowns, these informal workers adopted urban gardening as a survival strategy. title: Communicative Practices of an Educator in Integrating Broadcasting Experience in Teaching Documentary Filmmaking to Amplify Marginalized Voices
abstract:
Despite the growing recognition of documentary filmmaking as a pedagogical tool for amplifying marginalized voices, the communicative practices through which practitioner-educators translate professional media experience into documentary instruction remain underexamined in the literature. This study investigates how my professional broadcasting experience, accumulated through more than a decade of work in radio, news writing, and digital production, is enacted as a structured set of communicative practices within documentary filmmaking pedagogy in a Bachelor of Arts in Communication program at Ramon Magsaysay Memorial Colleges in General Santos City, Philippines.

Using auto-ethnomethodology, I analyzed instructional artifacts from my own courses, including course syllabi, documentary proposal guidelines, and consultation and feedback texts. The analysis revealed six broadcast-informed communicative practices: structuring, institutionalizing, and monitoring an accountable documentary production workflow; critiquing, mentoring, and refining through dialogic and iterative processes; constructing, structuring, and diagnosing audience-centered narrative coherence; designing and making visual meaning in documentary storytelling; representing and probing context-sensitive and inclusive documentary subjects; and applying and enforcing professional broadcasting standards in documentary outputs. Each practice is underpinned by a corresponding development communication perspective, positioning documentary pedagogy as participatory, ethically grounded, and socially responsive.

The findings demonstrate that the amplification of marginalized voices is not a single act but a cumulative communicative outcome built progressively across all six practices, each functioning as a distinct mechanism through which marginalized communities are represented deliberately, refined iteratively, and carried into public discourse with credibility.

This study contributes to film education and development communication scholarship by demonstrating how broadcasting-derived communicative practices constitute a coherent pedagogical infrastructure for amplifying marginalized voices, with particular relevance for practitioner-educators and regional higher education institutions in the Global South.
